meta.what: English for each entry of Radak's Sefer HaShorashim the site shows. 'sense' is the line that stands in the root's row, so a reader scanning the list sees what the root means before opening anything. 'more' is what the open panel adds above his Hebrew: a few short labelled parts, each one thing his entry holds. Both are the guide's summary of his entry, not his words and not a translation, and the page says so.
rules: Report only what the entry holds. Where he names a view and its holder, name both. Where he disputes one, say so and say whom. Nothing from outside the entry.
Every Hebrew phrase quoted gets its English, or a reader without Hebrew gets nothing from the part that carries the point.
Lead with what the word means. Grammar is named only where he rests something on it, and then by what it does, since binyan names are not English.
Do not narrate the entry. 'He brings X for reading Y' is about the page; what X reads, and why, is about the word.
A part earns its place by being worth knowing. Where his entry is one line, the gloss is one line.
meta.keyed_by: Radak's headword as references/shorashim.json stores it, so an entry serving two roots (גרז for both גרז and גרזן) is glossed once.
meta.same letters, other word: A root's letters sometimes carry a word he treats and a word our entry means, and his dictionary has only the first. The throat entry names ג-ר-ן, and his only entry under those letters is the threshing floor; he has no headword for גרון at all. The gloss says plainly what his entry is about, which is what tells a reader the two are different words. Checking for this mechanically was tried and abandoned: asking whether his entry cites any of the entry's own words flags 123 roots, and nearly all of them are ours naming a later form (גניזה, דירה, הרהור) of the very root he does treat.
meta.a corrupt entry: Sefaria's entry under נצח is broken at the source, not in our copy: it opens with מנצחים להעביד את העם and a reference with no book, then runs straight into material about reaching and overtaking that belongs to another root and never returns. Re-fetching gives the same 367 characters. Its gloss says the text breaks off, and the root wants a human eye and a better text before it can be glossed properly. Looking for others of its kind mechanically was tried and failed: testing whether an entry's text carries its own headword's letters flags 18 roots, all but none of them hollow roots like גוח against גחי, and it does not flag נצח at all, since מנצחים carries the letters perfectly well. Reading is what catches this.

אבד.sense: To be lost or to perish, a sense he calls known; where the verb takes an object, to destroy; and the nouns, a lost thing and destruction.

more.t: אֲבֵדָה (Vayikra 5:22), a lost thing; with a nun added, אֲבַדּוֹן (Iyov 28:22), destruction, which also comes without the nun, וַאֲבַדֹּה (Mishlei 27:20), and destruction; and אַבְדָן (Esther 9:5), destruction, which may instead be an infinitive with a nun added.

In the light form the verb stands alone, taking no object, for אֲרַמִּי אֹבֵד אָבִי (Devarim 26:5) means that Yaakov my father was lost: my father was a lost Arami. He is called an Arami because he lived in Aram, and there he was lost, for he was twenty years there in great distress, as he complained to Lavan, by day the heat consumed me, and the frost by night (Bereishis 31:40). In the heavy forms it takes an object, as וְהֶֽאֱבִיד שָׂרִיד מֵעִֽיר (Bamidbar 24:19), and he will destroy the survivor from the city.

צון.sense: The small livestock, the sheep and the goats.

more.t: Sometimes it takes in both together (Vayikra 3:6); sometimes one of them alone, as at Shmuel I 25:2, where it is the sheep, the goats being counted beside them; sometimes only the females (Bereishis 30:39), and likewise at Bereishis 31:10, of the he-goats that mount the flock; and sometimes the small livestock and the cattle together, as at Shmuel I 8:17, where the parsha names no cattle.

It is a name for all of them together and is not found in the plural: וּשְׁתֵּי־ צֹֽאן (Yeshayahu 7:21), and two of the flock, וְאַרְבַּע ־צֹאן (Shemos 21:37), and four of the flock, and וּמֵאָה צֹאן (Melachim I 5:3), and a hundred of the flock.

The word is written with an alef and read as a vav: צֹאן אֹֽבְדוֹת הָיֻה [הָיוּ] עַמִּי (Yirmiyahu 50:6), my people have been lost sheep. It appears without the alef, and with a heh added, in צֹנֶה וַֽאֲלָפִים כֻּלָּם (Tehillim 8:8), sheep and oxen, all of them; and that heh turned into an alef is seen in וּגְדֵרֹת לְצֹנַֽאֲכֶם (Bamidbar 32:24), and pens for your sheep.

רמס.sense: To tread with force and with destruction; and written with a sin, a word close to it in sense, of treading and going.

more.t: מִרְמָס, a thing trampled underfoot.

more.h: The word spelled with a sin
more.t: Written with a sin, the word is close to it in sense: כָּל־ רֹמֵשׂ בָּֽאֲדָמָה (Devarim 4:18), anything that goes on the ground, and הָֽרֹמֶשֶׂת עַל־הָאָֽרֶץ (Bereishis 1:28), that goes upon the earth, with the noun רֶמֶשׂ. The sense is treading and going.

גרז.sense: To be cut off; and from it the axe, הגרזן, is named, since it cuts the trees.

more.t: נִגְרַזְתִּי מִנֶּגֶד עֵינֶיךָ (Tehillim 31:23), I am cut off from before Your eyes, which he explains as נכרתי, I am cut off.

אחה.sense: אָח, a brother, and אָחוֹת, a sister, with the noun אַחֲוָה, brotherhood. In a second sense of the root, אָחוּ, a plant that cattle graze on.

more.t: The forms of אָח: אֲחִי, brother of, in the construct, where the yud stands in place of the heh that is the root's third letter; אָחוֹת, a sister, where that missing heh has turned into a vav and the tav marks the feminine; the plurals אַחִים, brothers, and אַחְיוֹת, sisters; and which vowel the alef takes under each ending.
The noun from the first sense is לְהָפֵר אֶת־הָאַחֲוָה (Zecharyah 11:14), to break the brotherhood.
In a second sense of the root, יִשְׂגֶּה אָחוּ בְלִי מָיִם (Iyov 8:11), can the grazing plant grow without water; here the vav, the root's third letter, stands in place of the heh.

It is a plant that cattle graze on, the one Chazal call אספסתא (Bava Basra 28b). The plural is כִּי הוּא בֵּן אַחִים יַפְרִיא (Hoshea 13:15), for he will be fruitful among the plants, though by rule the form should be אַחֲוִים; some explain that word from אָח, among brothers, and Radak calls that correct by the way of grammar. In וַתִּרְעֶינָה בָּאָחוּ (Bereishis 41:18), and they grazed on the plant, the bais is an added letter, as in לַֽחֲמוּ בְֽלַֽחֲמִי (Mishlei 9:5), eat my bread; or else the ground the plant grows on is called by the plant's name, and the bais does its ordinary work.

ענה.sense: To answer; close to it, to testify and to raise the voice in song. To afflict and submit; עָנִי, poor; near it, עֲנָוָה, lowliness of spirit. Apart, עִנְיָן, business.

more.t: Mostly it is the returning of speech, a reply, but sometimes it opens the speech, as the first וַיַּעַן אִיּוֹב (Iyov 3:2), and Iyov answered, at the start of his words. In the passive, נַעֲנֶה and נַעֲנֵיתִי mean to be entreated, and he says he will return to that under the root עתר.

The noun is the answer given: כִּי אֵין מַעֲנֵה אֱלֹהִים (Michah 3:7), there being no answer from Hashem, אֲשֶׁר לֹא מָצְאוּ מַעֲנֶה (Iyov 32:3), who found no answer, and מַעֲנֵה לָשׁוֹן (Mishlei 16:1), the answer of the tongue. In וְרוּחַ מִבִּינָתִי יַעֲנֵנִי (Iyov 20:3) the spirit of his understanding compels him to answer.
לֹא תַעֲנֶה בְרֵעֲךָ עֵד שָׁקֶר (Shemos 20:13), do not testify against your fellow as a false witness.

In song, וַתַּעַן לָהֶם מִרְיָם (Shemos 15:21), Miriam sang out to them; the sense of all of them is the raising of the voice in song. Some of it is in mourning, and so in the words of Chazal (Moed Katan 3:8), who explain the ענוי of mourning as all of them answering at once.

From this sense is אֵין קוֹל עֲנוֹת גְּבוּרָה וְאֵין קוֹל עֲנוֹת חֲלוּשָׁה (Shemos 32:18), which he explains as neither the shout of those who win the battle nor the shout of those who are beaten. It can also be read of this sense that אֶל עָנְיֵךְ (Bereishis 16:11) is to your cry and not your affliction, since out of her affliction she surely cried out to Hashem; and this is the view of Onkelos, who renders צְלוֹתִיךְ, your prayer. Had affliction been meant, Radak says, the pasuk would have said רָאָה, saw, and not שָׁמַע, heard.

וַיְעַנְּךָ וַיַּרְעִבֶךָ (Devarim 8:3), He afflicted you and let you hunger. To this belong עָנִי, the poor man, and לֶחֶם עֹנִי (Devarim 16:3), the bread of affliction, called so because they were afflicted in Mitzrayim. Close to this sense are עָנָו and עֲנָוָה, whose sense is lowliness of spirit, and from it is עָנִי וְרֹכֵב עַל חֲמוֹר (Zecharyah 9:9), humble and riding on a donkey, as Yonasan renders it, עִנְוְתָן, humble.

Beside afflicting stands submitting: נִגַּשׂ וְהוּא נַעֲנֶה (Yeshayahu 53:7), he was pressed and he was brought low, and לֵעָנֹת מִפָּנָי (Shemos 10:3), to humble yourself before Me, whose proper form is לְהֵעָנוֹת. So too טֶרֶם אֶעֱנֶה אֲנִי שֹׁגֵג (Tehillim 119:67), which he explains: before I submitted, when I sinned, I sinned in error, for I did not turn to Your word or lay it to heart and remember it; and now that I have seen that I sinned by turning my heart from Your word, I have submitted and gone back to keeping it and remembering it always, so as not to err in any of Your mitzvos.

more.h: A matter one is busy with
more.t: עִנְיָן in Koheles is an affair one is busied with: הוּא עִנְיַן רָע (Koheles 1:13), it is a bad business to be busied with, and וָכַעַס עִנְיָנוֹ (Koheles 2:23), and vexation is his business; and כִּי בָּא הַחֲלוֹם בְּרֹב עִנְיָן (Koheles 5:2), for the dream comes through much business, in affairs and in many guises. Radak's father brings לֵב צַדִּיק יֶהְגֶּה לַעֲנוֹת (Mishlei 15:28) here, and Radak reads it against וּטְהֹרִים אִמְרֵי־נֹעַם (Mishlei 15:26) above it, and pleasant words are pure: the heart of the tzaddik meditates on a matter and thinks to bring out a matter, and does not speak without one. Rabbi Yonah brings לַמַּעֲנֵהוּ (Mishlei 16:4) to this sense, that is, for the matter He desires, and Radak allows that it may be read בעבורו, for His sake. Rabbi Yonah also explains עִנְיַן and לַעֲנוֹת in Koheles 1:13, מַעֲנֶה in Koheles 5:19 and וְעַנְוָתְךָ in Tehillim 18:36 as the sense of השגחה, watching over; Radak allows that מַעֲנֶה בְּשִׂמְחַת לִבּוֹ may be of the sense of עֵדוּת, testimony. The Gaon Rabbi Yitzchak ibn Giat takes עִנְיָן and לַעֲנוֹת בּוֹ as the intent in a desire and a man's being busied with it, so that וְעַנְוָתְךָ תַרְבֵּנִי means Your help and Your will make me great, and לַמַּעֲנֵהוּ is for the sake of His desire and will, which is the cause, the reason and the desire. Rabbi Yonah brings אֶעֱנֶה אֶת־הַשָּׁמָיִם וְהֵם יַעֲנוּ אֶת־הָאָרֶץ (Hoshea 2:23), I will answer the heavens and they will answer the earth, to the sense of intent. In Radak's own view they are of the first sense, the returning of speech: from the long withholding of rain it is as though the heavens asked Him for rain and He rains upon them, and they answer the earth as though the earth asked them for it. So too וְהַכֶּסֶף יַעֲנֶה אֶת־הַכֹּל (Koheles 10:19), and silver answers everything, as though all a man's needs asked it of the silver and the silver fills them all; and from this sense he reads כִּי הָאֱלֹהִים מַעֲנֶה בְּשִׂמְחַת לִבּוֹ (Koheles 5:19), for Elokim answers him in the joy of his heart: He desires his joy and provides it for him.

מַעֲנָה, as כְּבַחֲצִי מַעֲנָה (Shmuel I 14:14), in about half a furrow, and in another form לְמַעֲנִיתָם (Tehillim 129:3), their furrows: the line the plowman plows with his oxen as far as he wishes, before he turns back and makes another like it, and so on until he has plowed the whole field.

Last, and likewise in another sense, he brings בְּאָסְרָם לִשְׁתֵּי (Hoshea 10:10), when they are bound to their two, the word at issue being the one that closes the pasuk. He does not say what it means; he says only that its singular is עוֹנָה and that the two hint at the two kingdoms, Ephraim and Yehudah.

כבשֹ.sense: The lamb, כֶּבֶשׂ, so called within its first year, since one older is called אַיִל, a ram; the female is כַּבְשָׂה or כִּבְשָׂה, a ewe lamb.

more.h: The lamb and the ewe lamb
more.t: כֶּֽבֶשׂ־אֶחָד בֶּן־שְׁנָתוֹ (Bamidbar 7:15), one lamb in its first year, and כְּבָשִׂים בְּנֵֽי־שָׁנָה (Bamidbar 7:17), lambs in their first year. The female is וְכַבְשָׂה אַחַת בַּת־שְׁנָתָהּ (Bamidbar 6:14), and one ewe lamb in its first year, with patach under the kaf, and כִּי אִם־כִּבְשָׂה אַחַת קְטַנָּה (Shmuel II 12:3), but one little ewe lamb, with chirik; its plural is שֶׁבַע כִּבְשׂת הַצֹּאן לְבַדְּהֶֽן (Bereishis 21:28), seven ewe lambs of the flock by themselves.
It is called a כבש while it is within its first year, because one older than a year is called אַיִל, a ram.

כבשׁ.sense: To subdue and to seize by force. In another sense כֶּבֶשׁ, a single sloping step, a ramp; and in another, כִּבְשָׁן, a kiln for lime or for earthenware.

more.t: וְכָֽבְשׁוּ אַבְנֵי־קֶלַע (Zecharyah 9:15), and they shall subdue the slingstones: Rabbi Yonah reads it as their subduing their enemies with slingstones. Or it may mean that they subdue the men of the slingstones, that is, the slingers will be captured, so that they do not save them.

In another sense, וְכֶבֶשׁ בַּזָּהָב לַכִּסֵּא מָֽאֳחָזִים (Divrei HaYamim II 9:18), and a כֶּבֶשׁ of gold for the throne, fastened: כֶּבֶשׁ is a step, as in the Mishnah (Zevachim 5:2), עלה בכבש, he went up on the kevesh. It is not made of steps of stone or wood one above another, but is a single sloping rise going up from the ground to the place one climbs to. That is why the mizbe'ach was given a kevesh, steps being forbidden to it, as it says וְלֹא־תַֽעֲלֶה בְמַֽעֲלֹת (Shemos 20:23), do not go up by steps. The throne's kevesh stood before its steps, near the ground, and from it one went up to the steps; מָֽאֳחָזִים goes back to the steps, which were fastened to the throne.

In another sense, פִּיחַ כִּבְשָׁן (Shemos 9:8), soot of the kiln, and כְּעֶשֶׁן הַכִּבְשָׁן (Shemos 19:18), like the smoke of the kiln. The כִּבְשָׁן is where stones are burnt for lime; or, what earthenware is fired in is called כִּבְשָׁן, and what bread is baked in by sticking it on is called תנור, an oven.

חרשֹ.sense: חֶרֶשׂ, earthenware and a potsherd; and in חַדּוּדֵי חָרֶשׂ, pearls shining like the sun.

more.t: כְּלִי חֶרֶשׂ (Vayikra 6:21), an earthen vessel, and יָבֵשׁ כַּחֶרֶשׂ כֹּחִי (Tehillim 22:16), my strength is dried up like a potsherd. In תַּחְתָּיו חַדּוּדֵי חָרֶשׂ (Iyov 41:22), beneath him, the last two words are pearls shining like the sun, the word from הָאֹמֵר לַחֶרֶס וְלֹא יִזְרָח (Iyov 9:7), who says to the sun and it does not shine.

וַיִּקַּח לוֹ חֶרֶשׂ לְהִתְגָּרֵד בּוֹ (Iyov 2:8), and he took himself a sherd to scratch himself with, he reads plainly: the Satan had struck him with a dry boil, so he needed a potsherd to scratch himself with. Some read חֶרֶשׂ there as the illness of dry scab, as in וּבַגָּרָב וּבֶחָרֶס (Devarim 28:27), with the scab and with the חֶרֶס: Iyov chose this illness called חֶרֶשׂ for himself out of all illnesses, because scratching gives some relief in it, the Satan having told him beforehand that he might choose whichever illness of suffering he wished. Radak calls that reading far-fetched. The illness may be called so, he says, because it is dry like a sherd, or because one needs a sherd to scratch with.

חרשׁ.sense: To be silent, which is making oneself deaf, and חֵרֵשׁ, a deaf man. In other senses: to plow; חָרָשׁ, a craftsman; thought; and חֹרֶשׁ, a bough.

more.t: The words for keeping silent are all from the sense of חֶרֶשׁ, deafness, since one who keeps silent is as though he does not hear what others say, and makes himself like a deaf man.

more.h: Silent in love, and the east wind
more.t: יַחֲֽרִישׁ בְּאַהֲבָתוֹ (Tzefaniah 3:17), He will be silent in His love: He will keep silent over the transgressions you have already done, in His love for you. רוּחַ קָדִים חֲרִישִׁית (Yonah 4:8), an east wind, חרישית, may be read from this sense: a wind so strong that people became as though deaf while it blew; and so Targum Yonasan renders it, שְׁתִיקָא, silent.

A second sense: עַל־גַּבִּי חָרְשׁוּ חֹרְשִׁים (Tehillim 129:3), plowmen plowed upon my back; לֹא־תַֽחֲרֹשׁ בְּשׁוֹר־וּבַֽחֲמֹר יַחְדָּֽו, you shall not plow with an ox and a donkey together; לוּלֵא חֲרַשְׁתֶּם בְּעֶגְלָתִי (Shoftim 14:18), had you not plowed with my heifer; and אִם־יַֽחֲרוֹשׁ בַּבְּקָרִים (Amos 6:12), does one plow with oxen. The words על דרך משל, by way of a figure, stand between these last two and may belong to either. The noun is בֶּֽחָרִישׁ וּבַקָּצִיר (Shemos 34:21), in plowing and in harvest; the tool one plows with is מַֽחֲרַשְׁתּוֹ (Shmuel I 13:20), his plowing tool; and the passive is צִיּוֹן שָׂדֶה תֵֽחָרֵשׁ (Yirmiyahu 26:18), Tzion shall be plowed as a field.
Rabbi Yonah explained רוּחַ קָדִים חֲרִישִׁית (Yonah 4:8), an east wind, חרישית, from this sense, plowing: that is, the wind of the plowing season, which is cold and dry.
חֲרוּשָׁה עַל־לוּחַ לִבָּם (Yirmiyahu 17:1), חרושה on the tablet of their heart, is חרותה, engraved.

A third sense is the craftsman: וְאָבִיו אִֽישׁ־צֹרִי חֹרֵשׁ נְחֹשֶׁת (Melachim I 7:14), and his father was a man of Tzor, a worker in copper; וְחָרָשׁ לֹא יִמָּצֵא בְּכֹל אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל (Shmuel I 13:19), and no craftsman was to be found in all Eretz Yisrael; הַפֶּסֶל נָסַךְ חָרָשׁ (Yeshayahu 40:19), a craftsman cast the image; and חָֽרָשֵׁי מַשְׁחִֽית (Yechezkel 21:36), craftsmen of destruction. In construct it is חָרַשׁ, with patach under the resh: חָרַשׁ בַּרְזֶל מַֽעֲצָד (Yeshayahu 44:12), the ironworker with the axe; חָרַשׁ עֵצִים נָטָה קָו (Yeshayahu 44:13), the woodworker stretched a line; and מַֽעֲשֵׂה חָרַשׁ אֶבֶן (Shemos 28:11), the work of a stoneworker. In לֹטֵשׁ כָּל־חֹרֵשׁ נְחשֶׁת וּבַרְזֶל (Bereishis 4:22) the word may be a noun: sharpening every tool of the crafts of copper and iron.

A fourth sense is thought: אַל־תַּֽחֲרֹשׁ עַל־רֵֽעֲךָ (Mishlei 3:29), do not think against your fellow; חֹרְשֵׁי אָוֶן (Iyov 4:8), those who think out iniquity; and וְיוֹעֵץ וַֽחֲכַם חֲרָשִׁים (Yeshayahu 3:3), the counsellor and the one wise in thoughts. The sense of all of them is thought. From this sense too, in the heavy form, עָלָיו שָׁאוּל מַֽחֲרִישׁ הָֽרָעָה (Shmuel I 23:9), that Shaul was thinking out the evil against him.

more.h: Who the חרש and the מסגר are
more.t: וְהֶֽחָרָשׁ וְהַמַּסְגֵּר (Melachim II 24:16) may be from this sense: the wise men of standing, masters of wisdom and counsel. Or it may be from the first sense: the great ones before whom the people kept silent and made themselves as deaf when they spoke. Targum Yonasan renders it אוּמָנַיָא וְתַרְעַיָא, craftsmen and gatekeepers.

A last sense: וְחֹרֶשׁ מֵצַל (Yechezkel 31:3), whose sense is a bough, called מֵצַל, shading, because its shade is broad. So too כַּֽעֲזוּבַת הַחֹרֶשׁ וְהָאָמִיר (Yeshayahu 17:9), like the forsaken bough and treetop; וְהוּא יוֹשֵׁב בַּֽחֲרֹשֶׁת הַגּוֹיִֽם (Shoftim 4:2), and he dwelt among the boughs of the nations; וַיֵּשֶׁב דָּוִד בַּחֹרְשָׁה (Shmuel I 23:18), and David stayed among the boughs; and וּבֶֽחֳרָשִׁים בָּנָה בִּֽירָנִיּוֹת וּמִגְדָּלִֽים (Divrei HaYamim II 27:4), and among the boughs he built fortresses and towers. The Targum renders בַיַּעַר (Devarim 19:5), in the forest, as בְּחֻרְשָׁא.

נטה.sense: To turn aside; to turn a thing aside and bring it to something; and, near to that, to spread and stretch, from which come מִטָּה, a bed, and מַטֶּה, a staff and a tribe.

more.t: כִּי יוֹאָב נָטָה אַחֲרֵי אֲדֹנִיָּה וְאַֽחֲרֵי אַבְשָׁלוֹם לֹא נָטָה (Melachim I 2:25 in his edition), Yoav had leaned after Adoniyah and after Avshalom he had not leaned. Both of them rebelled, he says, and the pasuk tells us that Yoav was not party to Avshalom's rebellion but was party to Adoniyah's, leaning after him to hold the kingdom in his hand, since David was old and Yoav did not fear him. Rabbi Yonah read the אַבְשָׁלוֹם of that pasuk as standing for Shlomo; Radak answers that no such exchange is found, one man named in place of another, and likewise in זֶרַע יַעֲקוֹב וְדָוִד (Yirmiyahu 33:26), the seed of Yaakov and David, Yaakov is not Aharon but Yaakov himself. Ibn Ezra explains that pasuk: how should I reject one who is of Yaakov's seed? For the Torah said no king should rule Yisrael but from Yaakov, and this one is of David's family besides, so that there are two distinctions in him.
Two words are written up under the root מטט as well: מִטָּה, a bed, and מַטָּה, which Radak says may also be of this root; he gives it no meaning here.

These and their like, he says, are intransitive verbs: וּכְאֹרֵחַ נָטָה לָלוּן (Yirmiyahu 14:8), like a traveller who turns aside to lodge; נְטֵה לְךָ עַל־יְמִינְךָ (Shmuel II 2:21), turn aside to your right; נְטוֹת הַיּוֹם (Shoftim 19:8), the turning of the day; אִם תִּטֶּה אַשֻּׁרִי מִנִי הַדָּרֶךְ (Iyov 31:7), if my step has turned from the way; וַיִּטּוּ אַחֲרֵי הַבָּצַע (Shmuel I 8:3), they turned after gain; and אַל־תֵּט יָמִין וּשְׂמֹאול (Mishlei 4:27), turn neither right nor left.

Those he calls transitive: וַיֵּט שָׁמַיִם וַיֵּרַד (Tehillim 18:10), He bent the heavens and came down; וַיֵּט מֹשֶׁה אֶת־יָדוֹ (Shemos 10:22), Moshe stretched out his hand; וַיֵּט אָהֳלֹה בֵּית־אֵל (Bereishis 12:8), he pitched his tent by Beis El; וּבִזְרוֹעַ נְטוּיָה (Devarim 4:34), with an outstretched arm; כְּקִיר נָטוּי (Tehillim 62:4), a leaning wall; יָמַי כְּצֵל נָטוּי (Tehillim 102:12), my days like a lengthening shadow; and נָטִיתִי לִבִּי לַעֲשׂוֹת חֻקֶּיךָ (Tehillim 119:112), I have turned my heart to perform Your statutes.

Of the heavy form he says ענינם ענין ההסיה וההגעה אל הדבר, that its sense is turning a thing aside and bringing it to something: לֹא־תַטֶּה מִשְׁפָּט (Devarim 16:19), do not turn judgment aside, with וְהָעִיר מָלְאָה מֻטֶּה (Yechezkel 9:9), and the city is full of מֻטֶּה, which he explains as turned judgment; הַטֵּה אֱלֹהַי אָזְנְךָ (Daniel 9:18), turn Your ear, my God; וַיַּט אֶת־לְבַב כָּל־אִישׁ־יְהוּדָה (Shmuel II 19:15), he turned the heart of every man of Yehudah; and וְעָלַי הִטָּה־חֶסֶד (Ezra 7:28), and He turned kindness to me. Of this root and this sense is וְאַט אֵלָיו אוֹכִיל (Hoshea 11:4), which he explains ואטה אליו מאכל, and I held food out to him. Likewise סוּרוּ מִנֵּי־דֶרֶךְ הַטּוּ מִנֵּי־אֹרַח (Yeshayahu 30:11), turn from the way, turn us aside from the path: though the second verb looks intransitive like סוּרוּ, it is transitive, turn us aside from Hashem's way to another, as the pasuk says after it השביתו מפנינו את קדוש ישראל, put the Holy One of Yisrael away from before us.

A sense near to this is ענין פשיטה ומתיחה, spreading and stretching: נוֹטֶה שָׁמַיִם (Tehillim 104:2), spreading out the heavens; כִּנְחָלִים נִטָּיוּ (Bamidbar 24:6), spread out like streams; and וְקָו יִנָּטֶה (Zechariah 1:16), and a line shall be stretched out.

Rabbi Yonah puts וְעַל־בְּגָדִים חֲבֻלִים יַטּוּ אֵצֶל כָּל־מִזְבֵּחַ (Amos 2:8), and on garments taken in pledge they stretch out beside every altar, in that sense of spreading, which Radak spells out as their stretching themselves and leaning beside every altar. Or it is of the first sense, and that, Radak says, is the correct one. צָץ הַמַּטֶּה (Yechezkel 7:10), the מַטֶּה has sprouted, Rabbi Yonah explains of the first sense, and Radak says he explained it well, since the pasuk says with it פָּרַח הַזָּדוֹן, insolence has blossomed.

more.h: The bed, the staff and the tribe
more.t: From this sense the bed is called מִטָּה, as הַשֹּׁכְבִים עַל־מִטּוֹת שֵׁן (Amos 6:4), those who lie on beds of ivory; it is called so because a man lies on it, stretches himself out and leans on it, and its proper form, he says, would be מִנְטָה. From this too is said מַטֶּה, a staff, אֶת־מַטֵּה הָאֱלֹהִים בְּיָדוֹ (Shemos 4:20), the staff of Hashem in his hand, called so because a man leans on it. The tribe is called מַטֶּה as well, אֶלֶף לַמַּטֶּה (Bamidbar 31:5), a thousand to a tribe, since שבט and מטה are one in sense, all of them the sense of support. So too בְּשִׁבְרִי לָכֶם מַטֵּה־לֶחֶם (Vayikra 26:26), when I break for you the staff of bread, that is, its support and strength.

מטט.sense: מִטָּה, a bed. נָמוֹטּוּ, slipped, belongs here only in the sefarim that give it a dagesh; מַטָּה, below, may belong here too, or to נָטָה.

more.h: Which root the word belongs to
more.t: בַּל נָמוֹטּוּ פְעָמָי (Tehillim 17:5), my steps have not slipped: some sefarim give it a dagesh, and if so it is from this root; if it has none, it is from the root מוט, where he has written it already.

From this root, וַיֵּשֶׁב עַל הַמִּטָּה (Bereishis 48:2), and he sat on the bed, מִטָּתוֹ שֶׁלִּשְׁלֹמֹה (Shir HaShirim 3:7), Shlomo's bed, and מִטּוֹת זָהָב וָכֶסֶף (Esther 1:6), beds of gold and silver. They are written under נָטָה as well.

מַטָּה may be of this root too: וְיִהְיוּ תֹאֲמִם מִלְּמַטָּה (Shemos 26:24), and they shall be doubled from below. The heh is an addition, since the word is stressed on the syllable before it, and even so it is never found without the heh; whereas מַעֲלָה is said without the heh, as אַל יִדְרְשֵׁהוּ אֱלוֹהַּ מִמָּעַל (Iyov 3:4), let God above not seek it. And מַטָּה may be of the root נָטָה, and it is written there.

שֹבע.sense: To eat one's fill and be sated, of food and of other things; to give another his fill; and the nouns שָׂבְעָה and שֹׂבַע, fullness and plenty.

more.t: לֹא תִשְׂבַּע עַיִן לִרְאוֹת (Koheles 1:8), the eye is never filled with seeing; שָׂבְעָה בְרָעוֹת נַפְשִׁי (Tehillim 88:4), my soul has had its fill of troubles; כִּי רַב שָׂבַעְנוּ בוּז (Tehillim 123:3), we have had our fill of contempt; and דָּוִיד זָקֵן וְשָׂבַע יָמִים (Divrei HaYamim I 23:1), David old and full of days.

שָׂבְעָה, as לֹא יָדְעוּ שָׂבְעָה (Yeshayahu 56:11), they know no fullness, and שֹׂבַע, as וַאֲכַלְתֶּם לָשֹׂבַע (Vayikra 25:19), and you shall eat to the full; and another form, וְנִשְׁכַּח כָּל הַשָּׂבָע (Bereishis 41:30), and all the plenty will be forgotten.

Of food and drink: וְאָכַל וְשָׂבַע וְדָשֵׁן (Devarim 31:20), he will eat and be satisfied and grow fat; וְאָכַלְתָּ וְשָׂבָעְתָּ (Devarim 6:11), you will eat and be satisfied; אַתָּה תֹאכַל וְלֹא תִשְׂבָּע (Michah 6:14), you will eat and not be satisfied; וּבַבֹּקֶר תִּשְׂבְּעוּ־לָחֶם (Shemos 16:12), in the morning you will have your fill of bread; and לִשְׁתּוֹת מַיִם וְלֹא יִשְׂבָּעוּ (Amos 4:8), to drink water and not be satisfied.

Where the thing one is filled with stands as the object, he reads it as though it said of it: פֶּן־תִּשְׂבָּעֶנּוּ וַהֲקֵאתוֹ (Mishlei 25:16), lest you be filled with it and vomit it, he glosses פן תשבע ממנו, lest you have your fill of it; and likewise וּשְׂבַעְתֶּם אֹתוֹ (Yoel 2:19), which he glosses ושבעתם ממנו, you will have your fill of it.

The adjective is a man full of something: וְשָׂבֵעַ יָלִין בַּל־יִפָּקֶד רָע (Mishlei 19:23), he rests satisfied and is not visited by evil; וּשְׂבַע יָמִים (Iyov 42:17), full of days; שְׂבַע קָלוֹן (Iyov 10:15), full of disgrace; וּשְׂבַע־רֹגֶז (Iyov 14:1), full of turmoil; and שְׂבֵעִים בַּלֶּחֶם נִשְׂכָּרוּ (Shmuel I 2:5), those full of bread hired themselves out. שִׂבְעַת־לֶחֶם וְשַׁלְוַת הַשְׁקֵט (Yechezkel 16:49), fullness of bread and quiet ease, is another form of the noun.

The heavy forms give another his fill: וָאַשְׂבִּעַ אוֹתָם וַיִּנְאָפוּ (Yirmiyahu 5:7), I gave them their fill and they went whoring; וּמַשְׂבִּיעַ לְכָל־חַי רָצוֹן (Tehillim 145:16), satisfying every living thing with favour; וְנֶפֶשׁ נַעֲנָה תַּשְׂבִּיעַ (Yeshayahu 58:10), you satisfy the afflicted soul; נַפְשָׁם לֹא יְשַׂבֵּעוּ (Yechezkel 7:19), they will not satisfy their appetite; and שַׂבְּעֵנוּ בַבֹּקֶר חַסְדֶּךָ (Tehillim 90:14), satisfy us in the morning with Your kindness. Of all of them he says their sense is known.

שׁבע.sense: Seven and the seventh; seven used for many rather than the exact count; and the week. In another sense, to swear, and to put another under oath.

more.t: בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי (Shoftim 14:15), at Shimshon's feast, he holds is the Shabbos, and the fourth of the days of the feast rather than the seventh of them; Rabbi Yonah read שביעי there as standing for רביעי, and Radak rejects it: שביעי never means רביעי, since such an exchange is not found and could not be. He brings the other reading as well, that it is the seventh day of the feast, the Pelishtim having pressed her only after three days of failing at the riddle, and that she had already wept the whole seven.

דָּוִיד הַשְּׁבִעִי (Divrei HaYamim I 2:15) he holds against Rabbi Yonah likewise: the seventh is not the eighth. Shmuel I 16:10, which counts seven sons passing before Shmuel besides David, he settles by saying Yishai may have had a son from another wife, the brothers from David's own mother being seven with him.

וְנִמְצָא יְשַׁלֵּם שִׁבְעָתָיִם (Mishlei 6:31), and being found he pays שבעתים, which he glosses כפלים, manifold, as the law lays on him: if he stole an ox and a sheep, he pays seven besides the principal.

more.h: Seven for a number simply large
more.t: לָכֵן כָּל־הֹרֵג קַיִן שִׁבְעָתַיִם יֻקָּם (Bereishis 4:15) he reads as many vengeances taken from whoever kills him, not seven exactly, since שֶׁבַע and שִׁבְעָה come for a reckoning that is not their own number but more: עַל־אֶבֶן אַחַת שִׁבְעָה עֵינָיִם (Zecharyah 3:9) is many watchings, and שֶׁבַע כְּחַטֹּאתֵיכֶם (Vayikra 26:21) and שֶׁבַע יִפּוֹל צַדִּיק (Mishlei 24:16) are many times.

They come by this reckoning, he says, because all the days of the world are weeks: וַחֲצִי הַשָּׁבוּעַ (Daniel 9:27), half the week, מַלֵּא שְׁבֻעַ זֹאת (Bereishis 29:27), fill out this one's week, said of Leah, and שָׁבֻעִים שִׁבְעִים (Daniel 9:24), seventy weeks. In the feminine שִׁבְעָה שָׁבֻעֹת (Devarim 16:9), seven weeks. On שְׁבֻעֹת חֻקּוֹת קָצִיר (Yirmiyahu 5:24), the weeks, the set laws of harvest, his father read that in those weeks of harvest Hashem keeps for him the harvest's set laws, since rain did not fall in Eretz Yisrael in the days of harvest, which is why Shmuel said he would call and Hashem would give thunder.

וַאֲשֶׁר נִשְׁבַּע לִי (Bereishis 24:7), and who swore to me, וַיִּשָּׁבַע לוֹ (Bereishis 24:9), and he swore to him, וּבִשְׁמוֹ תִּשָּׁבֵעַ (Devarim 6:13), by His name you shall swear, and וְהִשָּׁבֵעַ לַשֶּׁקֶר (Yirmiyahu 7:9), swearing falsely. The noun is כִּי הַשְּׁבוּעָה הַגְּדוֹלָה (Shoftim 21:5), the great oath. שְׁבֻעוֹת מַטּוֹת אֹמֶר סֶלָה (Chavakuk 3:9) he takes as the oath sworn to the tribes; others read it of the lightnings, which are like arrows and staves, as though they had sworn to keep His word.

Where the verb takes an object it is laying the oath on someone: וְהִשְׁבִּיעַ הַכֹּהֵן (Bamidbar 5:21), the kohen puts her under oath, and וַיַּשְׁבִּעֵנִי אֲדֹנִי (Bereishis 24:37), my master put me under oath. On וּבְשֵׁם אֱלֹהֵיהֶם לֹא־תַזְכִּירוּ וְלֹא תַשְׁבִּיעוּ (Yehoshua 23:7) he glosses that a man may not put his fellow under oath by them, or even a gentile, as Chazal explain it (Sanhedrin 63b), ולא ישמע על פיך, nor let it be heard through you.

ספר.sense: To count, and to tell. A סֵפֶר is a book and a סֹפֵר a scribe, writing being close to telling. In another sense, סַפִּיר, a stone the authorities identify differently.

more.t: סָפַר אֶת הָעָם (Shmuel II 24:10), he counted the people, and וְסָפַרְתָּ לְךָ (Vayikra 25:8), you shall count for yourself. The nouns are מִסְפַּר, a number, and הַסְּפָר, the count itself.

In the sense of telling and relating, ספור and הגדה, the verb always takes the heavy form: סַפְּרוּ נָא לִי (Bereishis 40:8), tell it to me. That form can still mean counting, as אֲסַפֵּר כָּל עַצְמוֹתָי (Tehillim 22:18), I count all my bones, from how lean I have grown. The difference between telling and relating he sets out under נָגַד.

The sense of all of these, he says, is writing: סֵפֶר, a book or a written document, and סֹפֵר, a scribe, as בָּרוּךְ בֶּן נֵרִיָּהוּ הַסֹּפֵר (Yirmiyahu 36:32), Baruch son of Neriyahu the scribe. לֹא יָדַעְתִּי סֵפֶר (Yeshayahu 29:12) he glosses: I do not know how to read it. The two senses lie close, he says, because writing a book is itself the telling of the matter.

מִי יְסַפֵּר שְׁחָקִים בְּחָכְמָה (Iyov 38:37), who in wisdom יְסַפֵּר the skies, is read three ways, and he does not choose. Some take it from the sense he has just named, telling. Rabbi Yonah takes it from writing. Radak's father takes it from סַפִּיר, that He made them like sapphire, as in וְתַחַת רַגְלָיו כְּמַעֲשֵׂה לִבְנַת הַסַּפִּיר (Shemos 24:10), and under His feet like the work of a sapphire brick.

Which stone it is he leaves open. Some say the precious stone called zafir in the vernacular, and if so, he notes, the comparison in סַפִּיר גִּזְרָתָם (Eichah 4:7), their form was sapphire, is one of worth and greatness and not of appearance, since a man is praised for his appearance only by redness or whiteness. Ibn Ezra says it is a precious red stone. The Gaon says it is white, the one called crystal. And the Midrash in Eichah Rabbah tells of a man who went to sell a sapphire in Rome: the buyer set it on an anvil and struck it with a hammer, and the anvil split and the hammer broke while the stone stood where it was. By that midrash, he says, it is the diamond, white and clear.

חלל.sense: חָלָל, one slain, and to slay; to begin; to profane, with חֹל, the common; חָלִיל, a hollow instrument of music, and מָחוֹל, the dance; hollows, and חַלּוֹן, a window.

more.t: וַיִּפְּלוּ חֲלָלִים (Shmuel I 31:1), they fell slain, and חַלְלֵי חֶרֶב מֵחַלְלֵי רָעָב (Eichah 4:9), better the slain of the sword than the slain of hunger. In the intensive the verb is to kill, and he glosses מְחֻלְלֵי חֶרֶב (Yechezkel 32:26) as those killed by the sword.

וַיָּחֶל נֹחַ (Bereishis 9:20), Noach began, and הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה אָחֵל תֵּת פַּחְדְּךָ (Devarim 2:25), this day I begin to put your dread. The noun is תְּחִלָּה, as תְּחִלַּת חָכְמָה יִרְאַת י"י (Mishlei 9:10), the beginning of wisdom is the fear of Hashem.

כִּי חִלֵּל יְהוּדָה (Malachi 2:11), for Yehudah has profaned. אֲשֶׁר נָטַע כֶּרֶם וְלֹא חִלְּלוֹ (Devarim 20:6) he explains as one who planted a vineyard and has not made it chullin, since it is holy until he redeems it. לֹא יַחֵל דְּבָרוֹ (Bamidbar 30:3) is of this sense too: he shall not make his word chullin, but his word shall stand, as if he had declared it holy. The noun is חֹל, as וּלְהַבְדִּיל בֵּין הַקֹּדֶשׁ וּבֵין הַחֹל (Vayikra 10:10), to distinguish between the holy and the common. חָלִילָה, far be it, is of the sense of profaning too, he says, which stands in place of holiness.

מְחַלְּלִים בַּחֲלִלִים (Melachim I 1:40), piping upon flutes. The instrument is the חָלִיל, one of the instruments of music, and he says it is named for being hollow; Rabbeinu Shlomo says it is what they call קלמי"ל [ קרמל"ש ] in the vernacular, and Yonasan renders it צֶלְצְלִין, cymbals. From this too מָחוֹל, the dance, is named, because they make merry within it with flutes.
וּבִמְחִלּוֹת עָפָר (Yeshayahu 2:19), hollows dug under the earth after the manner of caves; and חַלּוֹן, a window, as חַלּוֹן הַתֵּבָה (Bereishis 8:6), the window of the ark.

The entry opens with וְלִבִּי חָלַל בְּקִרְבִּי (Tehillim 109:22), my heart has been slain within me, which he reads as a past verb, as though it said נחלל, it has been slain. On וָאֹמַר חַלּוֹתִי הִיא (Tehillim 77:11), and I said, it is my being slain, he has the navi speaking out of galus: my being slain is my death and my being killed in the length of this galus, but I shall remember the years of the right hand of the Most High, the years when the Most High roused His right hand and brought us out of the galus of Mitzrayim, and so He will rouse it again to bring us out of the galus we are in.

אָז הוּחַל לִקְרֹא בְּשֵׁם (Bereishis 4:26): he explains that in the days of Enosh men strayed after avodah zarah, and then the calling by the Name of Hashem was profaned. Some explain the word from beginning instead, that men then began to call the names of idols and images by the Name of Hashem.

אִשָּׁה זֹנָה וַחֲלָלָה (Vayikra 21:7), a woman who is a zonah or profaned, is the adjective from this sense. וְאַתָּה חָלָל רָשָׁע (Yechezkel 21:30) may belong here, he says, or with the first sense, the slain; Targum Yonasan renders it as one liable to death, wicked one.

וְהוּא דֶּרֶךְ חֹל (Shmuel I 21:6), and it is a common way: he explains that though we went out on a common errand and did not suppose we would need holy bread, the young men's vessels were holy, for we purified ourselves on setting out. וַיִּתֶּן לוֹ הַכֹּהֵן קֹדֶשׁ (Shmuel I 21:7), and the kohen gave him holy bread, is the todah loaves, which a Yisrael may eat in purity, the only other bread there being the lechem hapanim, which is forbidden to those outside the kehunah. His father explains the pasuk the same way.

His father puts רוּחַ צָפוֹן תְּחוֹלֵל גָּשֶׁם (Mishlei 25:23) under this sense: the north wind holds back the rain, תְּחוֹלֵל being תמניע, from the sense of חָלִילָה, which is a sense of holding back. Radak notes that he has already written on it at the root חול.

דבר.sense: To speak, like saying in sense but not in usage; a דָּבָר is a word or matter. Also דֶּבֶר, plague; מִדְבָּר, wilderness or pasture; a bee; and the inner house.

more.t: In sense it is like saying; the difference is in usage. Saying, אמירה, is never without someone spoken to, even where the pasuk does not say who: אִמְרִי נָא אֲחֹתִי אָתְּ (Bereishis 12:13), say that you are my sister, means say it to those who ask you. Speaking, דבור, stands without anyone spoken to, since it points at speech itself, the thing that belongs to man, which is why one says a man is living and speaking and not living and saying. Speaking is never said of what cannot speak, even in a figure, as saying, telling and relating are: וְיֹאמְרוּ לְךָ הִנֵּנוּ (Iyov 38:35), and they say to you, here we are; וְעוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם וְיַגֶּד לָךְ (Iyov 12:7), and the bird of the heavens will relate it to you; וִיסַפְּרוּ לְךָ דְּגֵי הַיָּם (Iyov 12:8), and the fish of the sea will tell you. The two take different words after them as well: saying takes אֶל and the lamed alone, while speaking takes בְּ and אֶת besides. Either can mean to think: דִּבַּרְתִּי אֲנִי עִם לִבִּי (Koheles 1:16), I spoke with my heart, means I thought, and so does אָמַרְתִּי אֲנִי בְּלִבִּי (Koheles 2:1), I said in my heart.

more.h: A matter, or anything at all
more.t: עַל דְּבַר הַכֶּסֶף (Bereishis 43:18), on the matter of the money, and אֵין מַחְסוֹר כָּל דָּבָר (Shoftim 19:19), no lack of anything, of any kind a man needs.
דֶּבֶר כָּבֵד מְאֹד (Shemos 9:3), a very heavy pestilence, whose sense, he says, is death; and from it אֱהִי דְבָרֶיךָ מָוֶת (Hoshea 13:14), I will be your plagues, O death.

כְּעֵדֶר בְּתוֹךְ הַדָּבְרוֹ (Michah 2:12) he takes as like a flock amid its driving, and כְּדָבְרָם (Yeshayahu 5:17) as according to their driving, akin to the Targum, which renders וַיִּנְהַג, and he drove, as וּדְבַר. The right account, he says, is that the pasture of the flocks is called מִדְבָּר from this, since the shepherd drives the flock there, as וַיִּנְהַג אֶת הַצֹּאן אַחַר הַמִּדְבָּר (Shemos 3:1), and he drove the flock after good pasture to the pasture ground, as its Targum has it. From the same he takes דֹּבְרוֹת, rafts, the great logs tied at their heads and driven along the sea.

more.h: The bee and the inner chamber
more.t: דְּבוֹרָה, a bee, as עֲדַת דְּבוֹרִים (Shoftim 14:8), a swarm of bees; and דְּבִיר, the inner house where the Aron was set, the outer one being called the הֵיכָל.

עבר.sense: To pass or cross over, to transgress a covenant, to outstrip. עֵבֶר is a side and an עִבְרִי is of Ever's family. Also to be angry, and grain; בַּעֲבוּר is because of.

more.t: לְעָבְרְךָ בִּבְרִית (Devarim 29:11), for you to pass into a covenant, which he explains from the practice itself: the slaughtered animal or bird is cut in two and the parties to the covenant pass between the pieces, as אֲשֶׁר עָבַר בֵּין הַגְּזָרִים הָאֵלֶּה (Bereishis 15:17), which passed between these pieces. לַעֲבֹר בְּרִיתוֹ (Devarim 17:2), to transgress His covenant, is not the same: it means to forsake and abandon the covenant and pass over it, as though it said מעל בריתו, away from His covenant.

מַעֲבַר יַבֹּק (Bereishis 32:23), the ford of Yabok, and עָבְרוּ מַעְבָּרָה (Yeshayahu 10:29), they have crossed the ford. Where the verb takes an object it is to bring across or to pass through: הֶעֱבִיר אֶת בְּנוֹ בָּאֵשׁ (Melachim II 21:6), he passed his son through the fire.

עֹבֵר לַסֹּחֵר (Bereishis 23:16), current with the merchant. The silver, he says, is sometimes taken in by the merchant and sometimes paid out by him, so that it is always passing to and from his hand.
וַיַּעֲבֹר אֶת הַכּוּשִׁי (Shmuel II 18:23), he outran the Kushi; and so עָבְרוּ דִבְרֵי רָע (Yirmiyahu 5:28), they did worse than other wicked men had done.

מֵעֵבֶר הַנָּהָר (Shmuel II 10:16), from the side of the river, and מִכָּל עֲבָרָיו (Melachim I 5:4), on all his sides. עִבְרִי אָנֹכִי (Yonah 1:9), I am a Hebrew, he takes as being of the family of Ever.

עֹבֵר מִתְעַבֵּר עַל רִיב לֹּא לוֹ (Mishlei 26:17), one who passes by and grows angry at a quarrel not his own, and וַיִּתְעַבֵּר (Devarim 3:26), and He was angry. The noun is עֶבְרָה, as עֶבְרָה וָזַעַם וְצָרָה (Tehillim 78:49), wrath and indignation and trouble. Their sense, he says, is wrath and burning anger.

מֵעֲבוּר הָאָרֶץ (Yehoshua 5:11), the grain of the land; he suggests that the grain of the year past may be called עבור while that of the year coming is תבואה. And בַּעֲבוּר is because of, as בַּעֲבוּר דָּוִד (Tehillim 132:10), for David's sake. He remarks that the word is not rightly used without its bet, as some of the paytanim use it.

פנה.sense: To turn and look; from it פִּנָּה, a corner, and פָּנִים, the face, which also names anger; before, earlier, within, in one's lifetime; and in another sense, to clear.

more.t: כִּי פָנָה אֶל אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים (Devarim 31:18), he turned to other gods, and פְּנוּ לָכֶם צָפֹנָה (Devarim 2:3), turn yourselves northward. לִפְנוֹת עָרֶב (Bereishis 24:63) he glosses as when the evening turns and comes on.

הַשַּׁעַר הַפֹּנֶה (Yechezkel 46:12), the gate that faces, is like שַׁעַר הַפִּנָּה (Melachim II 14:13), the corner gate: the corner is called פונה, facing, because it looks upon the wall and its beauty. And from this, he says, the face is called פָּנִים, because it turns this way and that.

לִפְנֵי, before; מִפְּנֵי, from before; and מִלִּפְנֵי, where both stand together. He asks how the mem, which shows distance, and the lamed, which shows nearness, can be joined in one word, since they are opposites, and answers that it means from the place that is before Hashem, which is the place where prophecy is received.

עַל פְּנֵי he often reads as during a life: וַיָּמָת הָרָן עַל פְּנֵי תֶּרַח אָבִיו (Bereishis 11:28), Haran died in the lifetime of Terach his father, and so עַל פְּנֵי אַהֲרֹן אֲבִיהֶם (Bamidbar 3:4). He reads לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים עַל פָּנָי (Shemos 20:3) the same way, while I endure, which is for ever, and offers beside it that על פני there means לפני, before Me, so that even in secret a thing is before Him. Later in the entry he gives his own view, לפי דעתי, that על פני there is to anger Me.
Where the verb takes an object it is to clear: וְאָנֹכִי פִּנִּיתִי הַבַּיִת (Bereishis 24:31), I have cleared the house, and פַּנּוּ דֶּרֶךְ (Yeshayahu 40:3), clear a way.

In the causative it is turning away: הִפְנָה עֹרֶף מוֹאָב (Yirmiyahu 48:39), Moav has turned the back, לֹא הִפְנוּ אָבוֹת אֶל בָּנִים (Yirmiyahu 47:3), which he glosses as fathers not turning their faces back to their sons, and וּמָנוֹס נָסוּ וְלֹא הִפְנוּ (Yirmiyahu 46:5), they fled and did not turn. Of נֻסוּ הָפְנוּ הֶעְמִקוּ לָשֶׁבֶת יֹשְׁבֵי דְּדָן (Yirmiyahu 49:8) he says it is not a command, as some have thought, since this form has no command, but a past: flee, you who dwell in Dedan, for your enemy has already turned to come upon you and has settled deep in your land to drive you out and exile you. His father reads it of Dedan instead, that when they were told to flee they turned and fled far off and put their dwelling where the enemy's hand would not reach them.

Since anger shows in the face, Scripture names anger by the face: וְנָתַתִּי אֶת פָּנַי בַּנֶּפֶשׁ הַהִוא (Vayikra 20:6), I will set My face against that soul, לוֹא אַפִּיל פָּנַי בָּכֶם (Yirmiyahu 3:12), I will not let My face fall upon you, אֲכַפְּרָה פָנָיו (Bereishis 32:21), appeasing his face, and וּפָנֶיהָ לֹא הָיוּ לָהּ עוֹד (Shmuel I 1:18), her face was hers no longer. On this reckoning he offers וַיּוֹצִאֲךָ בְּפָנָיו (Devarim 4:37) as in His anger, the anger He was angry with at Mitzrayim, having set the same words earlier in the entry among those that mean in a lifetime.

לְפָנִים הָאָרֶץ יָסַדְתָּ (Tehillim 102:26), of old You founded the earth, וְאֶת יְהוּדָה שָׁלַח לְפָנָיו (Bereishis 46:28), sent ahead of him, and וְלִפְנֵי מִזֶּה (Nechemiah 13:4), before this. Inside is the same word: הוּא הַהֵיכָל לִפְנָי (Melachim I 6:17) is the inner Heichal, called inner although it lies outside the Devir because it is inside the Ulam, or else so called because it stood before the Devir as one goes in. So הַבַּיִת הַפְּנִימִי (Yechezkel 41:17) and אֶל הֶחָצֵר הַפְּנִימִית (Esther 4:11), while כָּל כְּבוּדָּה בַת מֶלֶךְ פְּנִימָה (Tehillim 45:14) is a noun, standing within.

חרב.sense: To be dry, or to dry up. A חֶרֶב is anything that cuts, sword, razor or stonecutter's tool, and the verb is to smite with one. Also to lie waste; a חָרְבָּה is a ruin.

more.t: חָרְבוּ פְּנֵי הָאֲדָמָה (Bereishis 8:13), the face of the ground was dry, and וְנָהָר יֶחֱרַב וְיָבֵשׁ (Yeshayahu 19:5), and the river will be parched and dry. The nouns are חָרָבָה, dry land, and חֹרֶב, drought and heat; the adjective is פַּת חֲרֵבָה (Mishlei 17:1), a dry crust. Their sense, he says, is dryness, drying and heat.

Whatever cuts is called a חֶרֶב, whether of iron or of sharpened stone, as חַרְבוֹת צֻרִים (Yehoshua 5:2), which he reads as sharpened flints. It is a general name that is sometimes particular to the sword, and it takes in a razor, קַח לְךָ חֶרֶב חַדָּה תַּעַר הַגַּלָּבִים (Yechezkel 5:1), take a sharp blade, a barbers' razor; the tool that stones are dressed with, כִּי חַרְבְּךָ הֵנַפְתָּ עָלֶיהָ (Shemos 20:22), for you have lifted your tool over it; and the tool that throws towers down, וּמִגְדְּלֹתַיִךְ יִתֹּץ בְּחַרְבוֹתָיו (Yechezkel 26:9), he will break down your towers with his tools.
וְהָעִיר הַזֹּאת תֶּחֱרַב (Yirmiyahu 26:9), this city shall be laid waste, with חָרְבָּה for a ruin and הֶחֳרָבוֹת for ruins.

וְשַׂעֲרוּ חָרְבוּ מְאֹד (Yirmiyahu 2:12), and shudder, be exceedingly dried up, he reads with a chataf kamatz under the ches, a command like שֹׁמּוּ, be astonished, earlier in the pasuk. Rabbi Yonah wrote that some read it like חָרְבוּ פְּנֵי הָאֲדָמָה, the face of the ground was dry, and took it too for a command, of the doubled form, on the pattern of פָּרְקוּ נִזְמֵי הַזָּהָב (Shemos 32:2), break off the golden rings. Rabbi Yonah turned them back from the Mesorah, which marks this חָרְבוּ as the only one of its kind, and the חָרְבוּ of the waters as one of two in a single pasuk.

The same word is used of one who dries a thing out: וְכָל־הַנְּהָרוֹת הֶחֱרִיב (Nachum 1:4), He dried up all the rivers; וְאַחְרִב בְּכַף־פְּעָמַי (Yeshayahu 37:25), I dry up with the sole of my foot; and וְהַחֲרַבְתִּי אֶת־יַמָּהּ (Yirmiyahu 51:36), I will dry up her sea. What has not been dried is אֲשֶׁר לֹא־חֹרָבוּ (Shoftim 16:7), which have not been dried out. וַיָּשֶׂם אֶת־הַיָּם לֶחָרָבָה (Shemos 14:21) is the sea turned to dry ground.

חֹרֶב is the dryness itself: יְהִי נָא חֹרֶב אֶל הַגִּזָּה (Shoftim 6:39), let there be dryness on the fleece, and וְעַל כָּל הָאָרֶץ חֹרֶב (Shoftim 6:37), and dryness on all the ground. Other forms of it are בְּחַרְבֹנֵי קַיִץ (Tehillim 32:4), in the droughts of summer, and וּבַחַרְחֻר וּבַחֶרֶב (Devarim 28:22), with burning heat and with drought. וְלֹא צָמְאוּ בָּחֳרָבוֹת (Yeshayahu 48:21), they did not thirst in the dry places, is the plural.

כְּחֹרֶב בְּצָיוֹן שְׁאוֹן זָרִים תַּכְנִיעַ (Yeshayahu 25:5) he reads as heat in a parched place, a distress that gives no rest, and so will the noise of strangers be brought down past rising again. חֹרֶב בְּצֵל עָב, heat under the shadow of a cloud, he reads as a man who has lain in a hot place and then comes into a cold one and cannot bear it; so will זמיר עריצים, the song of the tyrants, be humbled until they cannot rise.

From the sword comes a verb of putting to the sword: חִרְבוּ כָּל פָּרֶיהָ (Yirmiyahu 50:27), put all her bullocks to the sword, and חֲרֹב וְהַחֲרֵם אַחֲרֵיהֶם (Yirmiyahu 50:21), smite and destroy after them. In הָחֳרֵב נֶחֶרְבוּ הַמְּלָכִים (Melachim II 3:23), the kings have surely smitten one another, both words are this verb: נֶחֶרְבוּ in another of its forms, and הָחֳרֵב its infinitive, of the form that names no doer.

The act has its own forms: הֶחֱרִיבוּ מַלְכֵי אַשּׁוּר (Yeshayahu 37:18), the kings of Ashur laid waste, and מְהָרְסַיִךְ וּמַחֲרִבַיִךְ מִמֵּךְ יֵצֵאוּ (Yeshayahu 49:17), those who tear you down and lay you waste go out from you. The ruin left is וְחִדְּשׁוּ עָרֵי חֹרֶב (Yeshayahu 61:4), they will renew the waste cities, and וְעָרֵיכֶם יִהְיוּ חָרְבָּה (Vayikra 26:33), your cities will be a ruin. The place so left is described חָרֵב הוּא מֵאֵין אָדָם (Yirmiyahu 33:10), waste without a man, and אֲשֶׁר יְרוּשָׁלַם חֲרֵבָה (Nechemiah 2:17), that Yerushalayim lies waste. He allows that וְשַׂעֲרוּ חָרְבוּ מְאֹד (Yirmiyahu 2:12) may belong to this sense rather than to dryness.

נצב.sense: What is set up or stands: נְצִיב, a mound of salt or a governor; מַצֵּבָה, a stone set up to be worshipped; הַנִּצָּב, a knife's handle. Most of it may belong to יָצַב.

more.t: נְצִיב מֶלַח (Bereishis 19:26) he glosses as a mound of salt. The stone set up to be served is a מַצֵּבָה; and the man set over a people is a נְצִיב, as נְצִיב פְּלִשְׁתִּים (Shmuel I 13:3), the governor of the Pelishtim, and שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר נִצָּבִים (Melachim I 4:7), twelve officers set over the people.

וּמֶלֶךְ אֵין בֶּאֱדוֹם נִצָּב מֶלֶךְ (Melachim I 22:48), and there was no king in Edom, a governor was king: in Yehoshafat's day Edom had no king of its own, and the governor whom the kings of David's house set over them served them as king. The pasuk tells it here, he says, because Yehoshafat walked in the way of Hashem, so that Edom did not rebel under him; under his son Yehoram, who did evil, Edom rebelled at once and set a king over itself.

הַנִּצָּבָה לֹא יְכַלְכֵּל (Zecharyah 11:16), the one that stands he will not sustain: the sick ewe standing in her place and unable to stir. And הַנִּצָּב (Shoftim 3:22) is the haft of the knife, which holds the blade so that there is a handle to cut with.
Most of what is written here may belong to the root יָצַב, where he has set down their like; nothing decides between the two.

חיה.sense: To live, and to keep alive; health; חַי, of meat, is raw. חַיָּה is the neshamah, which lives for ever, and the animal soul; an animal; a company; a cluster of houses.

more.t: וְחָיְתָה נַפְשִׁי בִּגְלָלֵךְ (Bereishis 12:13), that my soul may live on your account. Likewise the name חַוָּה, for הִוא הָיְתָה אֵם כָּל חָי (Bereishis 3:20), she was the mother of all living, the yud turned to a vav so that it should not be confused with זֹאת הַחַיָּה אֲשֶׁר תֹּאכְלוּ, the chayah that you shall eat. It is also health: עַד חֲיוֹתָם (Yehoshua 5:8), until they were well, and וְיִמְרְחוּ עַל הַשְּׁחִין וְיֶחִי (Yeshayahu 38:21), let them rub it on the boil, and he will be well. Where the verb takes an object it is to keep alive or to let live, as מְכַשֵּׁפָה לֹא תְחַיֶּה (Shemos 22:17), you shall not let a sorceress live.

more.h: The wild animal and the tame
more.t: On זֹאת הַחַיָּה אֲשֶׁר תֹּאכְלוּ (Vayikra 11:2), this is the chayah that you shall eat, he says the behemah is taken in under chayah. But אֲשֶׁר יָצוּד צֵיד חַיָּה אוֹ עוֹף (Vayikra 17:13), who hunts a chayah or a bird, is of the chayah alone and not the behemah, since the behemah has no covering of its blood.

The neshamah is called חַיָּה, he says, because it lives for ever and is not as the body is; and the animal soul is called חַיָּה too, as וְזִהֲמַתּוּ חַיָּתוֹ לָחֶם (Iyov 33:20), his soul makes him loathe bread.

more.h: Raw, and this time next year
more.t: Of meat חַי is raw: וְלֹא יִקַּח מִמְּךָ בָּשָׂר מְבֻשָּׁל כִּי אִם חָי (Shmuel I 2:15), he will not take cooked meat from you, only raw. כָּעֵת חַיָּה (Bereishis 18:14) he reads as this same time in the coming year, when it will be living. Chazal call a midwife a חַיָּה (Kiddushin 74a), where they say three are believed about a firstborn, his father, his mother and the midwife; on their usage, Radak says, כִּי חָיוֹת הֵנָּה (Shemos 1:19) may be read as midwives: they need no other midwives, being midwives themselves. Chazal also call a woman giving birth a חַיָּה (Yoma 73b), from which, Radak says, it is good to read כָּעֵת חַיָּה as meaning that at this time she will be bearing a child.

more.h: A company, and a cluster of houses
more.t: חַיָּתְךָ יָשְׁבוּ בָהּ (Tehillim 68:11), Your company dwelt in it, and וְחַיַּת פְּלִשְׁתִּים (Shmuel II 23:13), the company of the Pelishtim, are a company of men, and חַיַּת קָנֶה he explains as the company that carries reeds, meaning spears. A cluster of houses standing together, unwalled, which could not be built up as a city, is called a חַיָּה as well, as וַיֵּאָסְפוּ פְלִשְׁתִּים לַחַיָּה (Shmuel II 23:11), the Pelishtim gathered at the cluster; and with a vav for the yud, חַוֹּת יָאִיר (Bamidbar 32:41), the clusters of Yair. Rabbi Yonah explains it so, and says the Arabs call such a cluster by the same word.

שׁלח.sense: To send, and to see off; close to it, to let loose; to drive out; to stretch out the hand, and close to it, branches spreading. Also שֶׁלַח, a sword; שֻׁלְחָן, a table.

more.t: שָׁלַח לִפְנֵיהֶם אִישׁ (Tehillim 105:17), He sent a man before them. His father reads יָדָהּ לַיָּתֵד תִּשְׁלַחְנָה (Shoftim 5:26) not as stretching out but as sending: Yael's hands sent for the peg and for the workmen's hammer, and the sending is ascribed to the hands, though Yael is the one who sends, because the hands are the chief part of the deed.

Close to sending is the loosing of a thing with nothing to hold it back. מְשַׁלְּחֵי רֶגֶל הַשּׁוֹר וְהַחֲמוֹר (Yeshayahu 32:20), who let loose the feet of the ox and the donkey: out of the abundance of grain they send the ox and the donkey to graze in the fields of grain and let them go where they will, and do not mind it. נָוֶה מְשֻׁלָּח (Yeshayahu 27:10), a dwelling let loose, is one that stands open and free to whoever wishes to bring anything into it, and וְנַעַר מְשֻׁלָּח מֵבִישׁ אִמּוֹ (Mishlei 29:15), a boy let loose shames his mother, is a boy free to go after his own desire.

Reaching out: שָׁלַח יָדָיו בִּשְׁלֹמָיו (Tehillim 55:21), he put out his hands against those at peace with him, and וְיָד אַל תִּשְׁלְחוּ בוֹ (Bereishis 37:22), do not put out a hand against him. The nouns are מִשְׁלוֹחַ יָדָם (Yeshayahu 11:14), the putting out of their hand, and בְּכֹל מִשְׁלַח יֶדְכֶם (Devarim 12:7), in all that you put your hand to.

Close to stretching out: שְׁלֻחוֹתֶיהָ נִטְּשׁוּ (Yeshayahu 16:8), the spreading of boughs and branches. A garden of fruit trees is called so as well, because its boughs and branches spread out this way and that, as בְּרֵכַת הַשֶּׁלַח לְגַן הַמֶּלֶךְ (Nechemiah 3:15), the pool of the Shelach at the king's garden, and שְׁלָחַיִךְ פַּרְדֵּס רִמּוֹנִים (Shir HaShirim 4:13), your gardens are an orchard of pomegranates. So too בְּשַׁלְחָהּ תְּרִיבֶנָּה (Yeshayahu 27:8), in her spreading out You contend with her; תְּשַׁלַּח קְצִירֶהָ עַד־יָם (Tehillim 80:12), she sent out her boughs to the sea; and יְשַׁלַּח שָׁרָשָׁיו (Yirmiyahu 17:8), it sends out its roots. The river beside Yerushalayim may be called Shiloach for the same reason, אֵת מֵי הַשִּׁלֹחַ (Yeshayahu 8:6), the waters of the Shiloach, because it spreads out to the gardens to water them.

more.h: Driving out, the sword, the table
more.t: To drive out: וַיְשַׁלְּחֵהוּ (Bereishis 3:23), Hashem sent him out of Gan Eden, and אֶל מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה תְּשַׁלְּחוּם (Bamidbar 5:3), you shall send them outside the camp; all of these, he says, are close in sense. In another sense שֶׁלַח is a sword, as וַיַּעַשׂ שֶׁלַח לָרֹב וּמָגִנִּים (Divrei HaYamim II 32:5), and he made swords in abundance, and shields. And from this root is the שֻׁלְחָן, the table, as הַשֻּׁלְחָן אֲשֶׁר לִפְנֵי י"י (Yechezkel 41:22), the table that is before Hashem.

הֹלֵךְ עִמָּם לְשַׁלְּחָם (Bereishis 18:16), going with them to see them off, וַיְשַׁלְּחֵם יִצְחָק (Bereishis 26:31), and Yitzchak saw them off, and וַיְשַׁלְּחוּ אֶת רִבְקָה אֲחֹתָם (Bereishis 24:59), and they saw off Rivkah their sister. This accompanying, he says, is all one sense with the first.

וְהִשְׁלַחְתִּי בָכֶם (Vayikra 26:22) and הִנְנִי מַשְׁלִיחַ בְּךָ (Shemos 8:17), with the noun מִשְׁלַחַת מַלְאֲכֵי רָעִים (Tehillim 78:49), suit the sense of letting loose, he says: I will let loose among you, I am letting loose upon you, and a letting loose of evil messengers. Chazal speak the same way of משלחת זאבים, a letting loose of wolves, in Bava Metzia 93b.

לָכֵן תִּתְּנִי שִׁלּוּחִים (Michah 1:14), therefore you shall give gifts, and אַחַר שִׁלּוּחֶיהָ (Shemos 18:2), after her gifts: he takes שִׁלּוּחִים as gifts. The second can also be read as after he had sent her and she returned to her father's house.

שֻׁלַּח בְּרַגְלָיו (Shoftim 5:15), sent on his feet: he asked for no beast to ride on, and the pasuk says sent although nobody sent him, because out of his great desire to go he is as one sent. In כִּי שֻׁלַּח בְּרֶשֶׁת בְּרַגְלָיו (Iyov 18:8) he says the words may be read either way, a net for his feet or his feet in a net.

Some take וַיְשַׁלְּחוּ אֶת כְּתֹנֶת הַפַּסִּים (Bereishis 37:32) from the sword: they tore the striped coat so that their father would believe the beasts had torn him. His own reading is that they sent the coat by the hand of some of them, who went to their father and brought it to him. Some take וַיְשַׁלְּחֵם בְּיַד פִּשְׁעָם (Iyov 8:4), which he lists under driving out, He sent them away by the hand of their transgression, from the sword as well. מִשְׁלַחַת מַלְאֲכֵי רָעִים can be read this way too, their sense being a sword; and רַגְלַי שִׁלֵּחוּ (Iyov 30:12) is put here too: they set thorns and briars where I walk, to cut my feet. אִישׁ שִׁלְחוֹ הַמָּיִם (Nechemiah 4:17) is of this sense: as they went to the water, each man had his sword in his hand. It can also be read from the Targum, which renders וְהִפְשִׁיט (Vayikra 1:6), and he shall strip, by וְיַשְׁלַח: none of them put off his clothes by day or by night, and no man put off his clothes to wash them in the water.

more.h: His father on contending by the sword
more.t: His father reads בְּשַׁלְחָהּ תְּרִיבֶנָּה (Yeshayahu 27:8) from the sword too: by her sword You wished to contend with her, that is, by the measure she measured, as the pasuk says בְּסַאסְּאָה, in measure. You wished to kill her, judging her by fire as Sodom was judged, since her deeds were theirs, as it says of her קְצִינֵי סְדֹם, rulers of Sodom (Yeshayahu 1:10); and so You would have judged her, had Hashem not had pity on them and turned the fire aside with the strong east wind after it had been cast upon the city, as Yechezkel sets out.

חבל.sense: Six senses: a pledge, mostly taken, sometimes given; ruin and corruption; pangs and pains; a rope, and so a portion or district; counsels and thoughts; a company.

more.t: לֹא יַחֲבֹל רֵחַיִם וָרָכֶב (Devarim 24:6), he shall not take a mill or an upper millstone in pledge. Most of the uses are the taking of a pledge, some the giving of one. יַחְבְּלוּ שׁוֹר אַלְמָנָה (Iyov 24:3) he reads as taking a widow's ox for a debt owed them, a thing forbidden because of her helplessness, or else as seizing it where no debt is owed at all, as כִּי תַחְבֹּל אַחֶיךָ חִנָּם (Iyov 22:6), for you take pledges from your brothers for nothing.

חָבַלְנוּ לָךְ (Nechemiah 1:7), we have dealt corruptly toward You; and where the verb takes an object, מְחַבְּלִים כְּרָמִים (Shir HaShirim 2:15), spoiling the vineyards, and לְחַבֵּל כָּל הָאָרֶץ (Yeshayahu 13:5), to destroy the whole land.
חֶבְלֵי יוֹלֵדָה (Hoshea 13:13), the pangs of a woman in labour, and צִירִים וַחֲבָלִים יֹאחֵזוּ (Yeshayahu 13:8), pangs and throes take hold. All of them together, he says, are pangs and pains.

more.h: A rope, and land divided by it
more.t: וַתּוֹרִדֵם בַּחֶבֶל (Yehoshua 2:15), she let them down by a rope. Because an inheritance is divided by the rope, as וְאַדְמָתְךָ בַּחֶבֶל תְּחֻלָּק (Amos 7:17), your land shall be divided by the rope, a region is itself called a חֶבֶל: כָּל חֶבֶל אַרְגֹּב (Devarim 3:4), all the region of Argov. רַב הַחֹבֵל (Yonah 1:6) is the chief man of the ship, set over her ropes to work her as she should go.

more.h: What a man lies on at sea
more.t: On וּכְשֹׁכֵב בְּרֹאשׁ חִבֵּל (Mishlei 23:34) Rabbi Yonah says it is a thing made of ropes that floats on the water to mark where ships may anchor, so that a man lying on it is in danger; or else it is the chief of the ship himself, who lies at the head of the ropes and must watch them in great anxiety. Others say חִבֵּל is the mast, from which all the ropes hang. And the Gaon, Rav Saadiah, says the ship herself is called חבל, since she is worked by drawing the ropes and letting them go.

כִּי בְתַחְבֻּלוֹת תַּעֲשֶׂה לְּךָ מִלְחָמָה (Mishlei 24:6), which he glosses as the counsels and thoughts a man turns over in his heart to choose the straight one. And חֶבֶל נְבִיאִים (Shmuel I 10:5) is a company or a gathering. He suggests the two may be one thing, since thoughts are themselves a gathering of matters in the heart.

צפן.sense: To hide or store away. צָפוֹן, the north, is named for it, as though hidden: from men, since little of it is settled, or from the sun, whose path runs on the south.

more.t: אֲשֶׁר צָפַנְתָּ לִּירֵאֶיךָ (Tehillim 31:20), what You have stored up for those who fear You, and וּמִצְוֹתַי תִּצְפֹּן אִתָּךְ (Mishlei 2:1), and store up my commandments with you. The sense of all of them, he says, is concealing and putting away.

His father reads נִצְפְּנָה לְנָקִי חִנָּם (Mishlei 1:11) and יִצְפְּנוּ לְנַפְשֹׁתָם (Mishlei 1:18) as verbs that take no object: let us lie hidden for the innocent without cause, and they lie hidden for their own lives. Of the same kind, יִצְפּוֹנוּ (Tehillim 56:7) means they lie in wait, setting themselves in a hidden place; and so עֵינָיו לְחֵלְכָה יִצְפֹּנוּ (Tehillim 10:8), his eyes lie in wait for the helpless.

וּצְפוּנְךָ תְּמַלֵּא בִטְנָם (Tehillim 17:14), You fill their belly with Your hidden store, the good stored with You to give to whom You please. The good of this world is called hidden, he says, because a man's hand does not reach it as he wishes but only as the Creator wills, so that what is good in his eyes is kept from him as though stored away. וְיִתְיָעֲצוּ עַל צְפוּנֶיךָ (Tehillim 83:4), they take counsel against Your hidden ones, he reads of Yisrael, hidden and sheltered under Your wings.

more.h: Why the north is called צפון
more.t: The north is the left-hand quarter, named so for one of two reasons. Either because the settled world reaches only a little way into that quarter, so that it is as though hidden and unseen by men; or because the sun's path does not run on that side but on the southern one, so that the north is as it were hidden from the sun.

more.h: She hid him, in the singular
more.t: On אֶת שְׁנֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים וַתִּצְפְּנוֹ (Yehoshua 2:4), the two men, and she hid him, he notes the singular: she did not hide the two men together in one place but each by himself, so that nobody should notice them. Or the singular may refer back to the word את, which takes in them both.

חבר.sense: To join; חֶבֶר, a gathering; חָבֵר, a companion; from joining too, the charmer who whispers and gathers beasts; חַבּוּרָה, a cut, or a blow where the blood is joined.

more.t: כָּל אֵלֶּה חָבְרוּ (Bereishis 14:3), all these joined together, and שְׁתֵּי כְתֵפֹת חֹבְרֹת (Shemos 28:7), two shoulder pieces joining. The nouns are חֶבֶר, a gathering, as חֶבֶר כֹּהֲנִים (Hoshea 6:9), a gathering of kohanim, and מַחְבֶּרֶת, a joining.

חָבֵר אָנִי לְכָל אֲשֶׁר יְרֵאוּךָ (Tehillim 119:63), I am a companion to all who fear You, and כְּאִישׁ אֶחָד חֲבֵרִים (Shoftim 20:11), companions as one man. The feminine is חֲבֶרֶת, as וְהִיא חֲבֶרְתְּךָ (Malachi 2:14), and she is your companion.

וְחֹבֵר חָבֶר (Devarim 18:11), the charmer, is from this sense. Chazal say that it takes in a great charmer and a small one alike (Sanhedrin 65a), and Radak explains that the great one whispers and gathers troops of large beasts, and the small one whispers and gathers troops of small ones, such as snakes and scorpions.

חַבּוּרָה תַּחַת חַבּוּרָה (Shemos 21:25), wound for wound. A חבורה is a scratch or a cut; from Chazal's words (Shabbos 106b), Radak says, it appears to be the blow in which the blood is bound up without coming out, and it is called חבורה because the blood is joined together at the place of the blow. Since the חבורה lies in the flesh like a stain, the leopard's spots are called חברבורות, as וְנָמֵר חֲבַרְבֻּרֹתָיו (Yirmiyahu 13:23), or a leopard its spots.

שֹרף.sense: To burn. The serpents called שְׂרָפִים are named for burning with their breath; the שְׂרָפִים who stand are angels of fire.

more.t: וְשָׂרַף אֶת־הַפָּרָה (Bamidbar 19:5), and he shall burn the cow. וַיִּשְׂרֹף בָּאֵשׁ (Shemos 32:20), and he burned it in the fire, means that he melted the calf in the fire to undo its form, and afterwards ground it with a file, for gold does not burn but melts.

וּֽבְמִשְׂרְפוֹת אֲבוֹתֶיךָ (Yirmiyahu 34:5), and as with the burnings of your fathers, is the burning for kings of their bed and the vessels they used. So Chazal say (Sanhedrin 52b) that one burns for kings and it is not of the ways of the Emori, and that what is burnt for them is their bed and the vessels they used. Some explain the burning as a burning of incense, made for the dead so that the flesh should not stink.

עֲשֵׂה לְךָ שָׂרָף (Bamidbar 21:8), make yourself a burning serpent, and הַנְּחָשִׁים הַשְּׂרָפִים (Bamidbar 21:6), the burning serpents, are named so because they burn with the breath of their mouth. שָׂרָף מְעוֹפֵֽף (Yeshayahu 14:29), a flying serpent: it is said that serpents are found in the land of Kush that have wings and fly with them; or מְעוֹפֵֽף means leaping far off, as though it were a bird.
שְׂרָפִים עֹֽמְדִים (Yeshayahu 6:2), serafim standing, are מלאכי אש, angels of fire.

הדר.sense: To honour; הָדָר, splendour; to make oneself fine and show a pleasant face; and הֲדוּרִים, crooked and winding ways.

more.t: וְהָדַרְתָּ פְּנֵי זָקֵן (Vayikra 19:32), you shall honour the face of an elder, and וְדָל לֹא תֶהְדַּר בְּרִיבוֹ (Shemos 23:3), nor shall you honour a poor man in his cause.

הָדוּר בִּלְבוּשׁוֹ (Yeshayahu 63:1), splendid in his garment; as an adjective, פְּרִי עֵץ הָדָר (Vayikra 23:40), the fruit of a splendid tree; and the noun, הוֹד וְהָדָר לְפָנָיו (Tehillim 96:6), glory and splendour are before Him. In the reflexive it is to make oneself fine: אַל תִּתְהַדַּר לִפְנֵי מֶלֶךְ (Mishlei 25:6), do not make yourself fine before a king, which he glosses as adorning and beautifying oneself and showing a pleasant face.

In וַהֲדוּרִים (Yeshayahu 45:2), and the הֲדוּרִים, which I will make straight, the word means crooked and winding ways. It is like what Chazal said (Chullin 113a), הדרא דכנתא, the bowels, which are crooked and wind round and round.

אדר.sense: Greatness and mighty strength, in all that comes from this root: אַדִּיר, mighty, and אַדֶּרֶת, a mantle, called so for its worth and greatness.

more.t: מָה אַדִּיר שִׁמְךָ (Tehillim 8:2), how mighty is Your name. Everything found from this root, he says, is a language of greatness and the strength of might, as יַגְדִּיל תּוֹרָה וְיַאְדִּיר (Yeshayahu 42:21), He will make the Torah great and mighty.

בְּסֵפֶל אַדִּירִים (Shoftim 5:25), in a bowl of the אַדִּירִים, he reads as a bowl fit for great and honoured men to drink from, or else of the great shepherds, as אַדִּירֵי הַצֹּאן (Yirmiyahu 25:34), the mighty ones of the flock.

נֶאְדָּרִי בַּכֹּחַ (Shemos 15:6), made mighty in strength, has an added yud. Rabbi Yonah offers, among his explanations, that the tav of the feminine has fallen and the word is really נאדרית. Radak holds the first account the right one: נאדרי goes with the right hand, spoken of in the masculine, or else its sense goes with Hashem.
כְּאַדֶּרֶת שֵׂעָר (Bereishis 25:25), like a mantle of hair, and אַדֶּרֶת שִׁנְעָר (Yehoshua 7:21), a mantle of Shinar. It was called an אדרת, he says, for its worth and its greatness.

אגר.sense: To gather; and אִגֶּרֶת, a letter, is also from gathering. But in אֲגוֹרַת כֶּסֶף, a silver coin, the alef is added, and the word is like גרה.

more.t: אָגְרָה בַקָּצִיר מַאֲכָלָהּ (Mishlei 6:8), she gathers her food in the harvest, and וְיַיִן לֹא תִשְׁתֶּה וְלֹא תֶאֱגֹר (Devarim 28:39), and wine you shall not drink nor gather: its sense is gathering, and so is everything from this root in Tanach.

וְאִגֶּרֶת פְּתוּחָה (Nechemiah 6:5), and an open letter: its sense is known, the document that is sent, and it too is from the sense of gathering: because many matters are gathered into it, the scroll is called אגרת. The plural is וְגַם אִגְּרוֹת כָּתַב עַל אֶפְרַיִם וּמְנַשֶּׁה (Divrei HaYamim II 30:1), and he also wrote letters to Ephraim and Menasheh.

But in לַאֲגוֹרַת כֶּסֶף (Shmuel I 2:36), for a coin of silver, the alef is added, and the word is like גרה, and its sense is a silver coin; so the Targum renders it, לְמָעָה דִכְסַף, for a maah of silver.

סלע.sense: A rock; high fortresses are called so too, since most of them are built on rock; and figuratively, Hashem as a rock.

more.t: וְדִבַּרְתֶּם אֶל־ הַסֶּלַע (Bamidbar 20:8), speak to the rock, and סְלָעִים מַחְסֶה לַֽשְׁפַנִּֽים (Tehillim 104:18), the rocks are a refuge for the shefanim: the sense of rock is known.

High fortresses are called סלע because most of them are built on rock, as it says וְשִׂים בַּסֶּלַע קִנֶּֽךָ (Bamidbar 24:21), and set your nest in the rock, which the Targum renders וְשַׁוִּי בִכְרַךְ תַּקִּיף מְדוֹרָךְ, and set your dwelling in a strong city. So too וְתָפַשׂ אֶת־ הַסֶּלַע בַּמִּלְחָמָה (Melachim II 14:6 in his edition), and he seized the stronghold in battle, which the Targum renders וּכְבַשׁ יַת כְּרַכָּא, and he conquered the city.

Figuratively, י"י סַלְעִי וּמְצוּדָתִי (Tehillim 18:3), Hashem is my rock and my fortress, after the manner of מִגְדַּל־עֹז שֵׁם י"י (Mishlei 18:10), the name of Hashem is a tower of strength. וְסַלְעוֹ מִמָּגוֹר יַֽעֲבוֹר (Yeshayahu 31:9) the Targum explains as his king, rendering וְשִׁלְטוֹנוֹהִי מִן קֳדָם דַחֲלָא יֶעְדוּן, and his rulers shall pass away before fear. It can also be taken as it sounds, with a lamed understood: to his rock he will pass for terror, that is, he will flee to his rock and his strong towers from great terror. Radak's father explains that the way of the world is that a man who flees his enemy and reaches his stronghold fears no more; but before the waving of Hashem's hand he will pass beyond even his rock and his fortresses in terror and dread, and fear still, and not trust that he will live.

עגל.sense: Round; from it מַעְגָּל, a camp, pitched in a ring, and עֲגָלָה, a wagon, which is round. Also מַעְגָּל, a way; עָגִיל, an earring; and עֵגֶל, a calf.

more.t: עָגֹל סָבִיב (Melachim I 7:35), round about, and מְרֻבָּעוֹת לֹא עֲגֻלּוֹת (Melachim I 7:31), square and not round.

The noun is וְשָׁאוּל שֹׁכֵב בַּמַּעְגָּל (Shmuel I 26:5), and Shaul lay in the מַעְגָּל, which is the place of the camp; with a heh added, וַיָּבֹא הַמַּעְגָּלָה (Shmuel I 17:20), and he came to the camp. It is called so because in a camp they encamp around, in a ring. In יָשָׁר מַעְגַּל צַדִּיק תְּפַלֵּס (Yeshayahu 26:7), You level the straight way of the righteous, and the plural בְמַעְגְּלֵי צֶדֶק (Tehillim 23:3), in ways of righteousness, the sense is the way and the highway.

more.h: The earring, the calf, the wagon
more.t: עָגִיל is an ear ornament: טַבַּעַת עָגִיל (Bamidbar 31:50), ring, earring, and so וַעֲגִילִים עַל אָזְנָיִךְ (Yechezkel 16:12), and earrings on your ears. עֵגֶל בֶּן בָּקָר (Vayikra 9:2), a calf of the herd. עֶגְלָה מְשֻׁלֶּשֶׁת (Bereishis 15:9), a heifer, threefold, is three heifers; it cannot mean one three years old, since at three years she would be called a פרה, a cow. עֲגָלָה חֲדָשָׁה (Shmuel I 6:7), a new wagon: the wagon is called so because it is round.

גזר.sense: To cut and to cut off; and it is said of a firm matter that will not turn back, the matter being cut through.

more.t: גִּזְרוּ אֶת הַיֶּלֶד הַחַי (Melachim I 3:25), cut the living child, and לְגֹזֵר יַם סוּף לִגְזָרִים (Tehillim 136:13), to Him who cut the Yam Suf into pieces. The noun is בֵּין הַגְּזָרִים הָאֵלֶּה (Bereishis 15:17), between these pieces. The sense, he says, is cutting off and cutting.

אֶל אֶרֶץ גְּזֵרָה (Vayikra 16:22), to a land cut off, cut off from settlement and from growing things. The chamber called הַגִּזְרָה, in וְהַגִּזְרָה וְהַבִּנְיָה (Yechezkel 41:13), and the gizrah and the building, he explains as the chamber cut off from the house. And סַפִּיר גִּזְרָתָם (Eichah 4:7), their cutting was sapphire, he reads as though they had been cut out of sapphire, so clear were they.
וּבְמַגְזְרֹת הַבַּרְזֶל (Shmuel II 12:31), and with the iron cutters: the saws with which wood is cut, or iron tools like them that cut.

more.h: A matter that will not turn back
more.t: Said of a firm thing that will not turn back: וְתִגְזַר אֹמֶר וְיָקָם לָךְ (Iyov 22:28), you shall decree a thing and it shall stand for you, and אֲשֶׁר נִגְזַר עָלֶיהָ (Esther 2:1), what had been cut concerning her, that is, the matter was cut through so that it would not turn back again.

ערב.sense: To mingle, and from it עֶרֶב, evening, when things blur together, and מַעֲרָב, the west. Also to be pleasing, to stand surety, עֲרָבָה, wilderness, and willows.

more.t: וַיִּתְעָרְבוּ בַגּוֹיִם (Tehillim 106:35), they mingled among the nations, with the noun עֵרֶב רַב (Shemos 12:38), the mixed multitude. The sense, he says, is the mingling and joining of things one with another.

The time after sunset is עֶרֶב because it is the time of darkness, when things mingle so that a man cannot tell one from another or set them apart. And since the evening divides the night from the day, the night itself is called ערב. בֵּין הָעַרְבָּיִם (Shemos 12:6), between the evenings, runs from the sun's turning westward, from the sixth hour on, until night: two evenings, he says, the first when the sun begins to turn and the second after it has set. The quarter where the sun sets is מַעֲרָב.

more.h: The woof, the raven, the swarm
more.t: הָעֵרֶב (Vayikra 13:52) is the woof, named because it mingles with the warp, the warp thread being fine and the woof thicker than it. עֹרֵב is the raven. And הֶעָרֹב (Shemos 8:17) he explains as gatherings of wild creatures of many kinds together.

מִנְחַת יְהוּדָה (Malachi 3:4) shall be עָרְבָה, pleasing and acceptable before Him; כִּי קוֹלֵךְ עָרֵב (Shir HaShirim 2:14), your voice is sweet. From this, he says, the heavens are called עֲרָבוֹת, because they are good and honoured: לָרֹכֵב בָּעֲרָבוֹת (Tehillim 68:5), to Him who rides upon the heavens. Some put וְאֵת בְּנֵי הַתַּעֲרֻבוֹת (Melachim II 14:14) here, and he takes their reading to mean the sons of the nobles and the honoured, as the Targum said, יַת בְּנֵי רַבְרְבַיָא, the sons of the great ones.

כִּי עַבְדְּךָ עָרַב אֶת הַנַּעַר (Bereishis 44:32), your servant went surety for the boy, and the pledge itself, עֵרָבוֹן (Bereishis 38:17). וְאֶת עֲרֻבָּתָם תִּקָּח (Shmuel I 17:18), and take their pledge, he holds belongs here: soldiers are used to pawning things against their expenses, having no ready money with them, and the pledge was to be taken back from whoever held it. And בְּנֵי הַתַּעֲרֻבוֹת, to his mind, are the sons of the princes, whom they gave into the king's house as a pledge that they should not rebel against him.

more.h: Trade, and who the עֹרְבִים were
more.t: From the sense of surety, he says, trade is called מַעֲרָב, since merchants are used to giving pledges to one another in their dealings. On וְאֶת הָעֹרְבִים צִוִּיתִי לְכַלְכֶּלְךָ שָׁם (Melachim I 17:4), and I have commanded the עֹרְבִים to sustain you there, three readings stand. Rabbi Yonah wrote that they may belong to the pleasing sense; on that reading, Radak explains, צִוִּיתִי means Hashem stirred their spirits to sustain him. Radak's father takes them from trade. And Radak holds it right that they are ravens in plain fact, the black unclean birds.

עֲרָבָה is wilderness, as בַּמִּדְבָּר בָּעֲרָבָה (Devarim 1:1), in the wilderness, in the desert, and בְּעַרְבוֹת מוֹאָב (Bamidbar 22:1), in the deserts of Moav. זְאֵב עֲרָבוֹת (Yirmiyahu 5:6), the wolf of the deserts, and זְאֵבֵי עֶרֶב, wolves of the desert, are of this sense too, though both can be read from עֶרֶב, the night, since wolves come to the city at night to tear, which is how Yonasan renders it, דֵיבֵי רַמְשָׁא, wolves of the evening. עֲרָב is Arabia, whose people dwell in the desert. And וְעַרְבֵי נָחַל (Vayikra 23:40) are willows of the brook.

קרב.sense: To draw near, and to bring near; קָרוֹב, near; קָרְבָּן, the thing brought near on the mizbeach. Close to it, קֶרֶב, the inward part. In another sense, קְרָב, war.

more.t: וְלֹֽא־ קָרַב זֶה אֶל־זֶה כָּל־הַלָּֽיְלָה (Shemos 14:20), and the one did not come near the other all night, and קָֽרְבָה שְׁנַת־הַשֶּׁבַע (Devarim 15:9), the seventh year has drawn near.

The adjective is קָרוֹב, near: וְאִישׁ אֶת־ קְרֹבֽוֹ (Shemos 32:27), and each man his kinsman, and בִּקְרֹבַי אֶקָּדֵשׁ (Vayikra 10:3), through those near Me I will be sanctified. The noun is in קִֽרֲבַת אֱלֹהִים לִי־טוֹב (Tehillim 73:28), the nearness of Hashem is good for me.

Where the verb takes an object it is to bring near or to offer: וְהִקְרִיב הַכֹּהֵן אֶת־הַכֹּל (Vayikra 1:13), and the kohen shall offer it all, and וּפַרְעֹה הִקְרִיב (Shemos 14:10), and Pharaoh brought near, which he reads as Pharaoh bringing his camp near. What is brought near upon the mizbeach is called a קָרְבָּן (Vayikra 1:2).

A sense close to this: קֶרֶב is what is within. וַתִּצְחַק שָׂרָה בְּקִרְבָּהּ (Bereishis 18:12), and Sarah laughed within her, that is, within her heart; כִּֽי־יָקוּם בְּקִרְבְּךָ נָבִיא (Devarim 13:2), if a navi arises in your midst. The entrails are called so because they are within: וְהַקֶּרֶב וְהַכְּרָעַיִם (Vayikra 1:13), and the entrails and the legs.

כְּיוֹם הִלָּֽחֲמוֹ בְּיוֹם קְרָֽב (Zecharyah 14:3), as on the day He fought, on a day of war, and טוֹבָה חָכְמָה מִכְּלֵי קְרָב (Koheles 9:18), wisdom is better than implements of war. וּֽקֲרָב ־לִבּוֹ (Tehillim 55:22), and his heart is war, he explains: his mouth is smooth and his heart is war. The sense of all of them, he says, is war, and the Targum of מִלְחָמָה (Bereishis 14:2), war, is קְרָבָא.

גלל.sense: To roll and go round, all one sense, he says: גַּלְגַּל, a wheel; מְגִלָּה, a rolled letter; גַּל, a heap; גָּלָל, dung; גְּלִילוֹת, districts; בִּגְלַל, because of.
