more.t: וְגָלֲלוּ אֶת הָאֶבֶן (Bereishis 29:3), they rolled the stone away. גֹּל אֶל י"י יְפַלְּטֵהוּ (Tehillim 22:9) he reads as whoever turns his ways toward Hashem, He will deliver him.

From the sense of going round, the heavens are called גלגלים, with the first letter doubled, because they go round the world continually. A wagon's wheel is a גַּלְגַּל, as וְהָמַם גִּלְגַּל עֶגְלָתוֹ (Yeshayahu 28:28), the wheel of his wagon; and straw and stubble are called גַּלְגַּל because they roll for their lightness, as שִׁיתֵמוֹ כַגַּלְגַּל כְּקַשׁ לִפְנֵי רוּחַ (Tehillim 83:14), make them like the stubble, like straw before the wind.

more.h: The scroll, the skull, the heap
more.t: A letter is called a מְגִלָּה because it is rolled up, as מְגִלָּה עָפָה (Zecharyah 5:1), a flying scroll. The head is a גֻּלְגֹּלֶת for its roundness, as עֹמֶר לַגֻּלְגֹּלֶת (Shemos 16:16), an omer a head. A pile of stones is a גַּל for the same reason, as עֵד הַגַּל הַזֶּה (Bereishis 31:52), this heap is witness; and the sea's waves are גַּלִּים because they roll as they move.

Dung is called גָּלָל because it rolls, as כְּגֶלְלוֹ לָנֶצַח יֹאבֵד (Iyov 20:7), like his dung he will perish for ever, and from this, he says, the idols are called גלולים, for their worthlessness and their filth. כַּאֲשֶׁר יְבַעֵר הַגָּלָל (Melachim I 14:10), as one clears away dung, is dung too; Chazal (Bava Kamma 3a) take its גלל as the tooth, and the tooth is called גלל, Radak explains, because it is like the stone called אֶבֶן גְּלָל, which is marble.

גְּלִילוֹת הַיַּרְדֵּן (Yehoshua 22:10), the districts of the Yarden, and גְּלִיל הַגּוֹיִם (Yeshayahu 8:23), the district of the nations, which he takes as like a border, a region or a province. Everything that falls under this root, he says, is one sense, though each word is explained according to its own place and the context nearest it. Likewise בִּגְלַל הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה (Devarim 15:10), on account of this thing.

שׁבל.sense: שְׁבִיל, a way, and from it שֹׁבֶל, the leg; שִׁבֹּלֶת, an ear of grain, and the rush of water; and שַׁבְּלוּל, a creeping thing, the snail.

more.t: שְׁבִילֵי עוֹלָם (Yirmiyahu 18:15), the ancient ways, and וּשְׁבִילְךָ בְּמַיִם רַבִּים (Tehillim 77:20), Your way in the great waters: it is the way.

From it the leg, or the shin, is called שֹׁבֶל: חֶשְׂפִּי שֹׁבֶל (Yeshayahu 47:2), bare the leg, as the pasuk goes on גַּלִּי שׁוֹק עִבְרִי נְהָרוֹת, uncover the shin, cross rivers. The Midrash Chazis explains it from שבולת, the current of the river: חשפי שובל is קלופי שבלתא דנהרא, strip off the current of the river. Rabbi Yonah wrote it from the ear of grain, uncover the locks of your hair, by way of likeness.

more.h: The ear of grain, and the stream
more.t: וָאֲלַקֳטָה בַשִּׁבֳּלִים (Rus 2:2), let me glean among the ears of grain, whose sense is known. The rush of water, the place where water runs down with force, is called שִׁבֹּלֶת as well: אַל תִּשְׁטְפֵנִי שִׁבֹּלֶת מַיִם (Tehillim 69:16), let not the rush of water sweep me away. That is why the test was אֱמָר נָא שִׁבֹּלֶת וַיֹּאמֶר סִבֹּלֶת (Shoftim 12:6), say now shibboles, and he said sibboles: at that place there was a rush of water, running there with force, and they tried a man by what was there where they stood.

שַׁבְּלוּל תֶּמֶס יַהֲלֹךְ (Tehillim 58:9), a snail that melts as it goes: it is a creeping thing, the snail. Chazal say (Shabbos 77b) that of all the Holy One created in His world He created nothing for nothing, and He created the snail for the כתית, a wound; that is, the snail is crushed and laid on the wound, and it is a remedy for it. The כתית is the wound called סמיטא in the language of Chazal (Avodah Zarah 28a), and it is known.

עצם.sense: Strength, force and greatness; עֶצֶם, a bone, so called as stronger than flesh; from it the body, and likewise the body of any thing. Another sense: to close the eyes.

more.t: כִּי עָצַמְתָּ מִמֶּנּוּ (Bereishis 26:16), for you have grown mightier than we, and רַב וְעָצוּם (Shemos 1:9), many and mighty. The nouns are עֹצֶם, as כֹּחִי וְעֹצֶם יָדִי (Devarim 8:18 in his edition), my strength and the might of my hand, and עָצְמָה, strength. The sense of them all, he says, is strength, force and greatness.

It is said of the strength of a quarrel as well: וּבֵין עֲצוּמִים יַפְרִיד (Mishlei 18:18), it parts the strong, that is, those who stand strong in a quarrel, and הַגִּישׁוּ עֲצֻמוֹתֵיכֶם (Yeshayahu 41:21), bring forward your strong points, the force of your suit and your proofs. Chazal use it so (Sanhedrin 31b): שנים שנתעצמו בדין, two who pressed one another at law.
עֶצֶם מֵעֲצָמַי (Bereishis 2:23), bone of my bones, with a masculine plural, עֲצָמִים, and a feminine one, עַצְמוֹת. The bone is called so, he says, because it is stronger and firmer than the flesh.

more.h: The body, and the body of any thing
more.t: Since the bone is the strength of the body and holds it up, the body itself is called עֶצֶם: אַךְ עַצְמִי וּבְשָׂרִי אָתָּה (Bereishis 29:14), surely you are my bone and my flesh. Where flesh is named beside it, he says, the bone does not mean bone alone but the body, and the flesh after it says the same thing twice; Chazal use עצם for the body often. Likewise any thing is called עֶצֶם: בְּעֶצֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה (Bereishis 7:13), which he glosses בגופו של יום, in the body of this day, and וּכְעֶצֶם הַשָּׁמַיִם לָטֹהַר (Shemos 24:10), כגוף השמים, like the body of the heavens for purity.

וְעֹצֵם עֵינָיו מֵרְאוֹת בְּרָע (Yeshayahu 33:15), and shuts his eyes from looking on evil, and וַיְעַצֵּם אֶת עֵינֵיכֶם (Yeshayahu 29:10), and He has shut your eyes. Their sense, he says, is closing.

שׁור.sense: To sing; to look and observe; to go, from which a gift is called תְּשׁוּרָה, since one brings it; שׁוּר, a wall; and שׁוֹר, an ox.

more.t: שָׁרִים וְשָׁרוֹת (Koheles 2:8), men singers and women singers, and אָז יָשִׁיר מֹשֶׁה (Shemos 15:1), then Moshe sang. The nouns are שִׁיר and שִׁירָה, a song.

אֲשׁוּרֶנּוּ וְלֹא קָרוֹב (Bamidbar 24:17), I behold him but not near. יָשׁוּר כְּשַׁךְ יְקוּשִׁים (Yirmiyahu 5:26) he glosses: he watches as a man who sets a trap watches the birds when they settle, and so do they watch and lie in wait for men. Their sense, he says, is looking and observing, and from it אֱלֹהִים יַרְאֵנִי בְשֹׁרְרָי (Tehillim 59:11), Elokim will let me see those who watch me, means my enemies, since an enemy watches his enemy and observes him for harm.

וּתְשׁוּרָה אֵין לְהָבִיא (Shmuel I 9:7), and there is no present to bring, תְּשׁוּרָה being as a minchah, a gift. Rabbi Yonah writes that וַתָּשֻׁרִי לַמֶּלֶךְ בַּשֶּׁמֶן (Yeshayahu 57:9) is of this sense, that you offered a minchah before him, and Rav Saadiah Gaon explains it so too. Radak holds that the right reading is that ותשורי is as ותלכי, and you went to the king with oil; and so תָּשׁוּרִי מֵרֹאשׁ אֲמָנָה, you shall go from the top of Amanah, and יָשֹׁר עַל אֲנָשִׁים, he goes to men and confesses before them. From this sense of going, he says, a gift is called תשורה, because a man brings it.

Of going too: אֳנִיּוֹת תַּרְשִׁישׁ שָׁרוֹתַיִךְ (Yechezkel 27:25), the ships of Tarshish were your caravans, which he explains as the caravans that travel in trade; the Targum renders אֹרְחַת יִשְׁמְעֵאלִים, a caravan of Yishmaelim, by שְׁיָרַת עֲרָבָאֵי, a caravan of Arabs. Those who go by sea are called a caravan too, since many ships go together. It may also be read as those that encamp by you, from the Targum's וּשְׁרָא for וַיִּחַן (Shemos 19:2), and he encamped.

בָּנוֹת צָעֲדָה עֲלֵי שׁוּר (Bereishis 49:22), daughters stride upon the wall, where שׁוּר is a wall, as the Targum of חוֹמָה is שׁוּרִין. עִקְּרוּ שׁוֹר (Bereishis 49:6), spelled with a cholam, he puts under the wall as well: they uprooted a wall. And שׁוֹר אוֹ כֶשֶׂב אוֹ עֵז (Vayikra 17:3), an ox or a sheep or a goat, is the ox. Rabbi Yaakov ben Elazar puts עִקְּרוּ שׁוֹר under the ox, as a figure for a ruler, as Tanach calls great princes rams and he-goats; some take it as a real ox, that they hamstrung the cattle.

שֹור.sense: שָׂרִים, princes, and to rule as a prince; in another sense, מְשׂוּרָה, a measure, but a very small one.

more.t: שָׂרִים עָצְרוּ בְמִלִּים (Iyov 29:9), princes held back their words, and וַיָּשַׂר אֲבִימֶלֶךְ (Shoftim 9:22), Avimelech ruled. Where the verb takes an object it is to set someone in rule: הֵשִׂירוּ וְלֹא יָדָעְתִּי (Hoshea 8:4), they made princes and I did not know, that is, they set a prince over themselves and not by My leave. Two he reads here are written with a samech: יָסֹר בַּמַּשָּׂא (Divrei HaYamim I 15:22), he was chief in the מַשָּׂא, which Radak says is that he was a prince and eminent in prophecy, or in the raising of the voice in song; and כֻּלָּם סָרֵי סוֹרְרִים (Yirmiyahu 6:28), all of them are סָרֵי סוֹרְרִים, which he reads as שרים סוררים, rebellious princes, and so the Targum, כָּל רַבְרְבֵיהוֹן מָרְדִין, all their great ones rebel. Radak says he has explained that pasuk at the root נחשׁ.

בַּמִּשְׁקָל וּבַמְּשׂוּרָה (Vayikra 19:35), in weight and in measure. A מְשׂוּרָה is a measure, but a very small one, as Chazal say (Bava Metzia 61b) that it is a thirty-third part of a log. וּמַיִם בִּמְשׂוּרָה תִשְׁתֶּה (Yechezkel 4:11), and you shall drink water by measure, does not mean that the measure is a sixth of a hin: he is to drink no more than a sixth of a hin in a day, and to drink it little by little, by the measure. In וּלְכָל מְשׂוּרָה וּמִדָּה (Divrei HaYamim I 23:29), and for every measure, small and large, משורה is said of the small measures and מדה of the large.

In וְשָׂם חִטָּה שׂוֹרָה (Yeshayahu 28:25), and he sets the wheat שׂוֹרָה, some take the last word from ruling: fine and choice wheat. Rabbi Yonah sets it with the measures instead, like what the pasuk says next, וּשְׂעֹרָה נִסְמָן וְכֻסֶּמֶת גְּבֻלָתוֹ, and barley in its marked place and spelt at its border.

הלך.sense: To go and to walk, the sense of every form, he says, being known; its nouns include הֲלִיכָה, a going, מַהֲלַךְ יוֹם, a day's walk, and הֵלֶךְ, a traveller.

more.t: הֹלֵךְ לִקְרָאתְךָ (Bereishis 32:7), going to meet you, and וַתִּהֲלַךְ אֵשׁ (Shemos 9:23), and fire went. The noun is הֲלִיכָה, a going, with the plural הֲלִיכוֹת עוֹלָם לוֹ (Chavakuk 3:6), the everlasting goings are His.

more.h: A day's walk, and the traveller
more.t: מַהֲלַךְ יוֹם (Yonah 3:4), a day's walk; and הֵלֶךְ, a traveller, וַיָּבֹא הֵלֶךְ לְאִישׁ הֶעָשִׁיר (Shmuel II 12:4), a traveller came to the rich man.

הִתְהַלֵּךְ לְפָנַי וֶהְיֵה תָמִים (Bereishis 17:1), walk before Me and be whole, as of Noach (Bereishis 6:9) and of the avos, אֲשֶׁר הִתְהַלְּכוּ אֲבֹתַי לְפָנָיו (Bereishis 48:15), before whom my fathers walked. Walking here, he says, means occupying oneself in the service of Hashem.

חפץ.sense: To desire and to delight in, with the noun חֵפֶץ, desire; one pasuk, of a tail like a cedar, has been explained as swift movement.

more.t: כִּי חָפֵץ בְּבַֽת־יַֽעֲקֹב (Bereishis 34:19), for he delighted in Yaakov's daughter, and וְאִם־לֹא יַחְפֹּץ הָאִישׁ (Devarim 25:7), and if the man does not wish. The noun is חֵפֶץ, and in the plural וְכָל־ חֲפָצֶיךָ לֹא יִֽשְׁווּ־בָֽהּ (Mishlei 3:15), all your desires cannot equal her.

On דְּרוּשִׁים לְכָל־חֶפְצֵיהֶֽם (Tehillim 111:2), sought out by all חֶפְצֵיהֶֽם, he holds the right reading is that חֶפְצֵיהֶֽם is an adjective, formed like זִקְנֵיהֶם, their elders: they are sought out by all who desire them.

יַחְפֹּץ זְנָבוֹ כְמוֹ־אָרֶז (Iyov 40:17), he יַחְפֹּץ his tail like a cedar, has been explained as a sense of movement, the tzadi exchanged for a zayin, the two coming from one place in the mouth, as in לֹא יַחְפּוֹז (Iyov 40:23), he does not hasten, a word of quick movement. On this reading his tail, great as a cedar, he moves swiftly.

חפר.sense: To dig, and in a sense close to it, to search out; another sense is shame.

more.t: כִּי חָפַרְתִּי אֶת הַבְּאֵר הַזֹּאת (Bereishis 21:30), that I dug this well, and חֲפָרוּהָ שָׂרִים (Bamidbar 21:18), princes dug it. On וְחָפַרְתָּ לָבֶטַח תִּשְׁכָּב (Iyov 11:18), you shall dig, and lie down in safety, he explains that you will need only to dig round your buildings and will not have to wall them or raise them up, since you will lie down in safety.

כִּי לַחְפֹּר אֶת כָּל הָאָרֶץ בָּאוּ (Yehoshua 2:2 in his edition), for they have come to search out the whole land, and מִשָּׁם חָפַר אֹכֶל (Iyov 39:29), from there it searches out food. It is searching and seeking, he says, because one who searches for a thing is like one who digs for it.

לַחְפֹּר פֵּרוֹת (Yeshayahu 2:20) he takes as the name of a bird; Rabbi Yonah explained that it is called so for its much pecking at fruit, and Radak says that is right, since the pasuk names וְלָעֲטַלֵּפִים, and to the bats, beside it, and men made images of birds and bats to bow down to. It may also be read, he says, as two words meaning to dig diggings: men would come to dig holes to hide in, as bats hide by day in holes, and so the next pasuk says לָבוֹא בְּנִקְרוֹת הַצֻּרִים (Yeshayahu 2:21), to go into the clefts of the rocks.

וְחָפְרָה הַלְּבָנָה (Yeshayahu 24:23), the moon shall be ashamed, and וּבֹשׁוּ הַחֹזִים וְחָפְרוּ הַקֹּסְמִים (Michah 3:7), the seers shall be put to shame and the diviners ashamed. All of these, he says, are shame. הֶחְפִּיר לְבָנוֹן (Yeshayahu 33:9), Levanon is ashamed, is said by way of figure, after the manner of הַגֶּפֶן הוֹבִישָׁה (Yoel 1:12), the vine is put to shame.

יבל.sense: To bring; יוּבַל, a stream; יְבוּל, crops and all that comes out of the land; יוֹבֵל, a ram, the shofar and the fiftieth year named for it; and יַבֶּלֶת, a wart.

more.t: מִי יֹבִלֵנִי עִיר מָצוֹר (Tehillim 60:11), who will bring me to the fortified city, and יוּבַל שַׁי (Yeshayahu 18:7), a gift will be brought: the sense is bringing. The Targum renders bringing with this root: for וַיָּבֵא אוֹתָם אֵלָיו בָּבֶלָה (Yechezkel 17:12), and he brought them to him to Bavel, it has וְאוֹבִיל יַתְהוֹן לְוָתֵה לְבָבֶל, the same words in Aramaic; and for וְהוֹלֵךְ מְהֵרָה (Bamidbar 17:11), and bring it quickly, וְאוֹבִיל בִּפְרִיעַ, and bring quickly.

וְעַל יוּבַל יְשַׁלַּח שָׁרָשָׁיו (Yirmiyahu 17:8), and it sends out its roots by a יוּבַל, which is a stream of water; and so פְּלָגִים יִבְלֵי מָיִם (Yeshayahu 30:25), streams, יִבְלֵי of water, where it says streams first and then explains that they are streams of water. So too וַאֲנִי הָיִיתִי עַל אוּבַל אוּלָי (Daniel 8:2), and I was by the stream of Ulai, the alef in place of the yud.

וְנָתְנָה הָאָרֶץ יְבוּלָהּ (Vayikra 26:4), the land shall give its produce, and וְאֵין יְבוּל בַּגְּפָנִים (Chavakuk 3:17), and there is no produce on the vines. Their sense, he says, is crops and fruit and all that comes out of the land.

more.h: Why the year is called יובל
more.t: For שׁוֹפְרוֹת הַיּוֹבְלִים (Yehoshua 6:8), the shofros of the יובלים, the Targum has שׁוֹפָרַיָא דְקֶרֶן דִכְרַיָא, shofros of rams' horn. Chazal (Rosh Hashanah 26a) ask what shows that this יובל is the word for a ram, and answer from a braisa: Rabbi Akiva said, when I went to Arabia they called a ram יובלא. The shofar itself is called יובל because it is of a ram, and so the fiftieth year is called יובל because a ram's shofar was blown in it: יוֹבֵל הִוא תִּהְיֶה לָכֶם (Vayikra 25:10), it shall be a yovel for you.

אוֹ חָרוּץ אוֹ יַבֶּלֶת (Vayikra 22:22), or cut, or with a wart. The Mishnah (Eruvin 10:13) has חותכין יבלת במקדש אבל לא במדינה, a wart is cut off in the Mikdash but not in the country. But the יבלת written in the Torah describes an animal that has one, as חרוץ is a description, while the one written in the Mishnah is the name of the wart itself.

סתר.sense: To be hidden, and to hide; the noun סֵתֶר, a hiding place or secrecy.

more.t: נִסְתְּרָה דַרְכִּי (Yeshayahu 40:27), my way is hidden, and אִם יִסָּתֵר אִישׁ בַּמִּסְתָּרִים (Yirmiyahu 23:24), if a man hide himself in secret places.

אַסְתִּירָה פָנַי מֵהֶם (Devarim 32:20), I will hide My face from them, and בְּאַשְׁפָּתוֹ הִסְתִּירָנִי (Yeshayahu 49:2), in His quiver He hid me. On וְחַטֹּאותֵיכֶם הִסְתִּירוּ פָנִים מִכֶּם מִשְּׁמוֹעַ (Yeshayahu 59:2), and your sins have hidden the face from you, from hearing, he notes that the verb there carries two objects.
אַתָּה סֵתֶר לִי מִצַּר (Tehillim 32:7), You are a hiding place for me from trouble, and בַּמִּסְתָּרִים יַהֲרֹג נָקִי (Tehillim 10:8), in the hiding places he kills the innocent.

more.h: A word written with a sin
more.t: וַיִּשָּׂתְרוּ לָהֶם (Shmuel I 5:9), and they were hidden on them: though it is written with a sin, he says it is all one sense, and explains that the tumours were covered over within them.

וְסֵתֶר מַיִם יִשְׁטֹפוּ (Yeshayahu 28:17) stands among the nouns: waters will sweep away the hiding place. Or סתר may stand in construct with the water, and be taken in the sense Chazal use often, of pulling down, as הסותר את כותלו (Bava Kamma 30a, 6b), one who pulls down his wall, and many other words of theirs in this sense.

נסך.sense: To cover, and a מַסֵּכָה is a covering. To pour or to cast, as a libation is poured and an idol cast. And in a third sense, to install a ruler.

more.t: כִּי נָסַךְ עֲלֵיכֶם, for Hashem has spread over you, רוּחַ תַּרְדֵּמָה, a spirit of deep sleep (Yeshayahu 29:10), and וְהַמַּסֵּכָה הַנְּסוּכָה (Yeshayahu 25:7), the covering that is spread over. All of these, he says, are hiding and covering. הַמַּסֵּכָה and הַמַּסָּכֶת (Shoftim 16:14) he takes as the name of the cloth spread over a bed.

הַפֶּסֶל נָסַךְ חָרָשׁ (Yeshayahu 40:19), the craftsman overlaid the image, and כִּי שֶׁקֶר נִסְכּוֹ (Yirmiyahu 10:14), his overlaid idol is a falsehood, may be read from the covering sense, he says, because they made the image of wood and overlaid it with gold and silver. Under pouring and casting, נִסְכּוֹ is a molten image, as in מִֽי־יָצַר אֵל וּפֶסֶל נָסָךְ (Yeshayahu 44:10), who fashioned a god or cast an image, and פֶּסֶל וּמַסֵּכָה (Nachum 1:14), a carved image and a molten one.

וְאֵת קְשׂוֹת הַנָּסֶךְ (Bamidbar 4:7) he explains as the tubes with which it is covered: they were like hollow half reeds set over each loaf so that air should pass between them and the bread not go mouldy, and so the tubes were a cover over the bread.
וְנֵסֶךְ לֹא תִסְּכוּ עָלָיו (Shemos 30:9), you shall pour no libation upon it, and וְהִסִּכוּ נְסָכִים (Yirmiyahu 32:29), and they poured libations. All of these, he says, are pouring and melting.

וַאֲנִי נָסַכְתִּי מַלְכִּי (Tehillim 2:6), I have installed My king, and נְסִיכֵי סִיחוֹן (Yehoshua 13:21), the princes of Sichon. All of these, he says, are greatness, rule and princedom. He allows that וְלִנְסֹךְ מַסֵּכָה וְלֹא רוּחִי (Yeshayahu 30:1) may be read in this sense too, to install rulers, and not by My spirit: they set rulers over themselves without His leave, seeking help from Pharaoh. It may also be read in the first sense, to spread a covering, as a figure for taking counsel.

ירח.sense: יָרֵחַ, the moon; and יֶרַח, a month, since the moon renews itself each month.

more.t: עָשָׂה יָרֵחַ לְמוֹעֲדִים (Tehillim 104:19), He made the moon for appointed times, and וְיָרֵחַ לֹא יַגִּיהַ אוֹרוֹ (Yeshayahu 13:10), which he glosses: the moon shall not give its light.

Because the moon renews itself every month, the month is called יֶרַח: בְּיֶרַח הָאֵתָנִים (Melachim I 8:2), in the month of Eisanim, and מִי יִתְּנֵנִי כְיַרְחֵי קֶדֶם (Iyov 29:2), would that I were as in the months of old. And because the moon renews itself many times, it is spoken of in the plural although it is only one: גֶּרֶשׁ יְרָחִים (Devarim 33:14), the yield of the moons, meaning that the moon ripens the fruits.

ירשׁ.sense: To inherit, from a father or by taking what another held; to drive out, as it always is when bound with מ; in a sense close by, to make poor; and תִּירוֹשׁ, new wine.

more.t: וְיָרַשְׁנוּ אֹתָהּ (Bamidbar 13:30), we shall take possession of it, and וִֽירִשְׁתֶּם אֹתָהּ וִֽישַׁבְתֶּם־בָּֽהּ (Devarim 11:31), and you shall take possession of it and dwell in it. All of them are one sense, he says, inheritance: some are a son's inheritance from his father, and some the taking of a thing out of another's hand, that is, taking his inheritance and what was in his holding, as a son takes his father's estate.

וּבְנֵי עֵשָׂו יִֽירָשׁוּם (Devarim 2:12) he reads: and the sons of Esav took their inheritance. There is no need, he says, to take these words out of the sense of inheriting, which Rabbi Yonah did, explaining them as sending away.

In the sense of driving out and sending away: מוֹרִישׁ אוֹתָם מִפָּנֶֽיךָ (Devarim 18:12), drives them out before you, and וְאִם־לֹא תוֹרִישׁוּ אֶת־יֹֽשְׁבֵי הָאָרֶץ מִפְּנֵיכֶם (Bamidbar 33:55), and if you do not drive out the inhabitants of the land before you. The rule, he says, is that wherever the word is bound to a מ it is driving out and sending away. The simple form has this sense too, in לָרֶשֶׁת אוֹתָם מִפָּנֶיךָ (Devarim 12:29), to drive them out before you; but it may be read as inheriting, with מפניך, before you, joined to כִּי יַכְרִית, when He cuts off, and not to לרשת, to inherit, and if so no simple form of the verb means driving out at all.

more.h: Making poor, and being made poor
more.t: In another sense close to it: מוֹרִישׁ וּמַֽעֲשִׁיר (Shmuel I 2:7), makes poor and makes rich, and תּֽוֹרִישֵׁמוֹ יָדִֽי (Shemos 15:9), my hand shall make them poor, though that may instead be from driving out. Likewise פֶּן־ תִּוָּרֵשׁ (Bereishis 45:11), lest you be made poor, and וּפֶֽן־ אִוָּרֵשׁ וְגָנַבְתִּי (Mishlei 30:9), lest I be made poor and steal: the sense of poverty and want. Targum Yonasan renders הַלְיָרְשֵׁנוּ קְרָאתֶם לָנוּ (Shoftim 14:15) from this sense, הַלְמַסְכְּנוּתָנָא קְרֵיתוּן יָתָנָא, have you called us to make us poor. Radak's own reading of it is: have you called us to take possession of our money, and if not, why have you called us? For it looked as though they had been called to have their money taken.

From this same root, he says, comes a noun that belongs to none of those senses, הַתִּירוֹשׁ, the new wine: כַּֽאֲשֶׁר יִמָּצֵא הַתִּירוֹשׁ בָּֽאֶשְׁכּוֹל (Yeshayahu 65:8), as the new wine is found in the cluster.

שֹרק.sense: שׂוֹרֵק, the choicest of the kinds of vine; and שְׂרֻקִּים, patterned in colours, or, as some explain, groomed with a comb.

more.t: נְטַעְתִּיךְ שׂוֹרֵק (Yirmiyahu 2:21), I planted you a choice vine, and וְלַשֹּׂרֵקָה בְּנִי אֲתֹנוֹ (Bereishis 49:11), and to the choice vine his donkey's foal. It is the choicest of the kinds of vine. Rav Ibn Giat writes that it is the good kind whose grapes have no stone in them, and Targum Yonasan (Yeshayahu 5:2) renders it כְּמַצַב גֶפֶן בְּחִירָא, like the planting of a choice vine. Some explain עֹבְדֵי פִשְׁתִּים שְׂרִיקוֹת (Yeshayahu 19:9) the same way, workers of flax of the choicest kind, and so, it is said, in Arabic א"ל שר"ק is the name for the fine sort in silk.

שְׂרֻקִּים וּלְבָנִים (Zecharyah 1:8), שְׂרֻקִּים and white, he explains as patterned: their colour red and white and black, as though they were speckled or patched. So עֹבְדֵי פִשְׁתִּים שְׂרִיקוֹת (Yeshayahu 19:9), on this reading, is workers of flax dotted with colours, and Chazal speak of לובשי סריקין של זהב (Kiddushin 31a), wearers of סריקין of gold, which he explains as a garment figured with gold. Some explain שְׂרֻקִּים as groomed with a comb, and so Chazal (Moed Katan 10b), רבא שרא לסרוקי סוסיא, Rava permitted combing a horse, which Radak explains as combing it with a comb of iron.

שׁרק.sense: To whistle or hiss: the moving of the lips with a sound.

more.t: וְשָׁרַק לוֹ מִקְצֵה הָאָרֶץ (Yeshayahu 5:26), He will whistle to him from the end of the earth, and אֶשְׁרְקָה לָהֶם וַאֲקַבְּצֵם (Zecharyah 10:8), I will whistle to them and gather them.

שָׁרְקוּ וַיָּנִעוּ רֹאשָׁם (Eichah 2:15), they hissed and wagged their head. The nouns are שְׁרִקוֹת עֲדָרִים (Shoftim 5:16), the whistlings of the flocks, and וְיֹשְׁבֶיהָ לִשְׁרֵקָה (Michah 6:16), and her inhabitants for a hissing.

סוס.sense: סוּס, a horse, with סוּסָה for the mare; and a bird of the same name.

more.t: כִּי בָא סוּס פַּרְעֹה (Shemos 15:19), for Pharaoh's horse came, and the feminine, סוּסָה, as in לְסֻסָתִי בְּרִכְבֵי פַרְעֹה (Shir HaShirim 1:9), to my mare among Pharaoh's chariots. On דָּרַכְתָּ בַיָּם סוּסֶיךָ (Chavakuk 3:15), You trod the sea with Your horses, he says the horses are a figure for the clouds.

A bird carries the same name: כְּסוּס עָגוּר כֵּן אֲצַפְצֵף (Yeshayahu 38:14), like a sus, a crane, so do I chirp, which he explains as כסוס ועגור, like a sus and a crane, after the manner of שֶׁמֶשׁ יָרֵחַ (Chavakuk 3:11), sun, moon, where two are named without an and between them. Elsewhere the name is said with a yud in place of the vav, וְסִיס, standing between the turtledove and the crane (Yirmiyahu 8:7), and that too is a bird's name.

נהר.sense: To run toward the thing desired; from this the river, נָהָר, is named, as the place where water runs. A second sense is light, with the noun נְהָרָה.

more.t: וְנָהֲרוּ אֵלָיו כָּל הַגּוֹיִם (Yeshayahu 2:2), and all the nations shall run to it, and וְלֹא יִנְהֲרוּ אֵלָיו עוֹד גּוֹיִם (Yirmiyahu 51:44), and nations shall no longer run to it. Their sense is running toward the thing desired.

From this sense the river is named, since it is the place where the water runs: נָהָר פְּלָגָיו (Tehillim 46:5), a river, its streams, and בְּעֵבֶר הַנָּהָר (Yehoshua 24:2), beyond the river. The plural is נְהָרִים, and the feminine plural נַהֲרוֹת, as in עַל נַהֲרוֹת בָּבֶל (Tehillim 137:1), by the rivers of Bavel.

Another sense: הִבִּיטוּ אֵלָיו וְנָהָרוּ (Tehillim 34:6), they looked to Him and were lit up, and אָז תִּרְאִי וְנָהַרְתְּ (Yeshayahu 60:5), then you will see and be lit up; the noun is in וְאַל תּוֹפַע עָלָיו נְהָרָה (Iyov 3:4), and let no light shine upon it. Their sense is light, and the Targum of אוֹר (Bereishis 1:3), light, is נְהוֹרָא. Some take וְנָהֲרוּ אֵלָיו (Yeshayahu 2:2) from this sense rather than the first.

From this sense, הַמִּנְהָרוֹת אֲשֶׁר בֶּהָרִים (Shoftim 6:2), the מִנְהָרוֹת that are in the mountains, are caves. They are called by a word of light because of the window through which the light comes in, just as the viper's den is called by the same kind of word in מְאוּרַת צִפְעוֹנִי (Yeshayahu 11:8), the viper's den.

אבל.sense: To mourn, and אֵבֶל is mourning. It also means to lie waste, and always does beside אֻמְלַל. The word אֲבָל, 'not only this but also' or 'truly', is of this root too.

more.t: כִּי אָבַל עָלָיו עַמּוֹ (Hoshea 10:5), his people mourned over him, and וַיִּתְאַבֵּל עַל בְּנוֹ (Bereishis 37:34), he mourned for his son. The noun is אֵבֶל כָּבֵד זֶה לְמִצְרָיִם (Bereishis 50:11), this is a heavy mourning for Egypt. On כַּאֲבֶל אֵם (Tehillim 35:14), as one who mourns a mother, his father explains the figure: as an infant whose mother nursed him and died, who weeps and is darkened because he has nobody to nurse him, his mother's breasts having been his life, so קודר שחותי, I went bowed down in gloom.

more.h: How to tell the second sense
more.t: Some uses are desolation and ruin rather than mourning: עַל כֵּן תֶּאֱבַל הָאָרֶץ וְאֻמְלַל כָּל יוֹשֵׁב בָּהּ (Hoshea 4:3), therefore the land is laid waste and all who dwell in it languish. Whenever you find the word bound to אֻמְלַל, he says, it is ruin and waste and destruction, as אָבַל תִּירוֹשׁ אֻמְלְלָה גָפֶן (Yeshayahu 24:7), the new wine is laid waste, the vine languishes; and all the rest are mourning. Yet he allows that וְנַפְשׁוֹ עָלָיו תֶּאֱבָֽל (Iyov 14:22), and his soul mourns over him, which he first explains as the soul mourning while the man still lives, until the body perishes, may also be read as ruin and loss: soul and flesh are destroyed and lost.

more.h: The great Avel: plain or stone
more.t: וְעַד אָבֵל הַגְּדוֹלָה אֲשֶׁר הִנִּיחוּ עָלֶיהָ (Shmuel I 6:18), as far as the great Avel on which they set it down, some explain as the great plain, like אָבֵל מְחוֹלָה (Shoftim 7:22), Avel Mecholah, which the Targum renders מֵישַׁר, a plain; another explains that the lamed stands for a nun and it is the great stone on which they set the Aron, which is how Targum Yonasan renders it. Radak gives his own view: the great stone on which they set the Aron was named אָבֵל, called so for the mourning that was made at it, as the threshing floor of Atad was called אָבֵל מִצְרַיִם (Bereishis 50:11), Avel Mitzrayim, for the mourning.

One word of this root falls outside verb and noun: it is a particle that shifts among many senses. The first is not this alone but this also, or not this but that, in אֲבָל שָׂרָה אִשְׁתְּךָ (Bereishis 17:19), but also Sarah your wife, and אֲבָל בֵּן אֵין לָהּ (Melachim II 4:14), but she has no son. Hashem had told Avraham that He would bless Sarah and give him a son from her, and Avraham said לוּ יִשְׁמָעֵאל יִחְיֶה לְפָנֶֽיךָ (Bereishis 17:18), if only Yishmael might live before You; Hashem answered, true, Yishmael will live, and this too shall be, that Sarah your wife bears you a son. Elisha asked the Shunamis הֲיֵשׁ לְדַבֶּר־לָךְ אֶל־הַמֶּלֶךְ (Melachim II 4:13), is there a word to be spoken for you to the king, and she answered בְּתוֹךְ עַמִּי אָֽנֹכִי יֹשָֽׁבֶת, I dwell among my own people: her family would speak for her to the king when she needed it, and she did not need it. Elisha asked what was to be done for her, and Geichazi's answer means: what you asked her she does not need, but this she does, for she has no son and her husband is old. The second sense is truly: אֲבָל אֲשֵׁמִים אֲנַחְנוּ (Bereishis 42:21), truly we are guilty, and אֲבָל אִשָּׁה אַלְמָנָה אָנִי (Shmuel II 14:5), truly I am a widow woman. Which of the two is meant, he says, a reader can tell from what is written above it.

אסר.sense: To bind; all of it is the sense of binding: אָסִיר, one bound, a prisoner; בֵּית הָאֵסוּר, the prison; and the harnessing of a chariot.

more.t: וַיֶּאְסֹר אֶת רִכְבּוֹ (Shemos 14:6), he harnessed his chariot, and וַאֲסַרְנֻהוּ לְעַנֹּתוֹ (Shoftim 16:5), and we will bind him to afflict him. All of them are the sense of binding, and מִי יֶאְסֹר הַמִּלְחָמָה (Melachim I 20:14), who shall bind the battle, is the harnessing of the chariot.
וְאָסְרָה אִסָּר (Bamidbar 30:4), and she binds a bond.

אֶנְקַת אָסִיר (Tehillim 79:11), the groaning of the prisoner, with the plural הָאֲסִירִם אֲשֶׁר בְּבֵית הַסֹּהַר (Bereishis 39:22), the prisoners who were in the prison house. The prison is בֵּית הָאֵסוּר (Yirmiyahu 37:15), and מִבֵּית הָסוּרִים (Koheles 4:14), from the prison house, is the prison where the bound are put, its alef silent and left out of the writing. אֲסוּרִים יָדֶיהָ (Koheles 7:26), her hands are bonds: one caught in her hands is like a man shut up in the prison house.
Rabbi Yehudah says that בְּמָסֹרֶת הַבְּרִית (Yechezkel 20:37), in the bond of the covenant, belongs to this root, the word being properly בְּמַאֲסֹרֶת.

נגד.sense: To tell; נֶגֶד, over against or in front of, and with a mem before it, at a distance; from it, נָגִיד, the head of the people, to whom all turn.

more.t: מִי הִגִּיד לְךָ (Bereishis 3:11), who told you. The sense of all these forms is relating, except that telling, הגדה, is said of new things as well, while relating, סיפור, is said only of a thing that was done or said.

נֶגֶד is over against and in front of. אֶעֱשֶׂה לּוֹ עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ (Bereishis 2:18), I will make him a helper over against him, is one who will be before him and over against him always, to serve him. With a mem before it the word means at a distance: וַתֵּשֶׁב לָהּ מִנֶּגֶד (Bereishis 21:16), and she sat down at a distance, and מִנֶּגֶד נִגְעִי יַעֲמֹדוּ (Tehillim 38:12), they stand at a distance from my affliction, that is, far off, over against me and in front of me, not drawing near to visit me.

more.h: Why a ruler is called נגיד
more.t: From this sense, he says, the head of the people is called נָגִיד, as וְאַתָּה תִּהְיֶה לְנָגִיד (Shmuel II 5:2), and you shall be ruler, because the people set their faces toward him always and turn to him in all their affairs. From it too good words and matters of wisdom are called נְגִידִים, because all turn toward them for their worth: שִׁמְעוּ כִּי נְגִידִים אֲדַבֵּר (Mishlei 8:6), hear, for I will speak good and wise things.

more.h: A pasuk with a word left out
more.t: On נָגִיד חֲסַר תְּבוּנוֹת וְרַב מַעֲשַׁקּוֹת (Mishlei 28:16) he says the end of the pasuk teaches the meaning of its beginning: the word ימות is missing and left for the understanding reader, as Tanach often leaves out of a pasuk what is understood from it, so that the pasuk runs נָגִיד חֲסַר תְּבוּנוֹת וְרַב מַֽעֲשַׁקּוֹת ימות בקוצר ימים ושונא בצע יאריך ימים, a ruler lacking understanding and great in oppressions dies in the shortness of his days, and one who hates unjust gain lengthens his days. His father reads it through the language of the Targum, in two ways. One is from נְגִידוּ, the Targum of מִשְׁכוּ (Shemos 12:21), draw out: that is, the man great in oppressions is drawn out of the world, but one who hates unjust gain lengthens his days. Better than that is the other, from וְאִיתְנְגִיד, the Targum of וַיִּגְוַע (Bereishis 49:33), and he expired: that is, he dies before his time.

בער.sense: To burn, said of the fire itself even where nothing else is burnt; to cut off and remove; to graze a field. בְּעִיר, a beast, and near it בַּעַר, the brutish man.

more.h: How burning differs from burning up
more.t: וְהִנֵּה הַסְּנֶה בֹּעֵר בָּאֵשׁ (Shemos 3:2), and behold, the bush was burning in the fire, which he glosses דולק, alight; and מדוע לא יִבְעַר הסנה (Shemos 3:3), why is the bush not burnt, which he glosses לא ישרף, is not burnt up. All of these, he says, mean kindling and burning up, except that הבערה, burning, is said of the fire itself even where its working does not pass on to another, while השרפה, burning up in fire, always has its working pass to something else.

Some take every form of בוער as carrying an object, and Radak asks what they will do with כַּפִּשְׁתִּים אֲשֶׁר בָּעֲרוּ בָאֵשׁ (Shoftim 15:14), like flax that burned in the fire, where the flax is itself what burned. The right account, he says, is that all of these are simple forms and intransitive, and כְּאֵשׁ תִּבְעַר יָעַר (Tehillim 83:15) is like fire that burns in the forest, תבער ביער.

וּבִעַרְתָּ הָרָע מִקִּרְבֶּךָ (Devarim 13:6), you shall remove the evil from your midst, and בִּעַרְתִּי הַקֹּדֶשׁ מִן הַבַּיִת (Devarim 26:13), I have removed the holy portion from the house. The sense of these and all like them is cutting off and removal, he says, and it lies near the first.

כִּי יַבְעֶר אִישׁ שָׂדֶה אוֹ כֶרֶם (Shemos 22:4), when a man grazes a field or a vineyard, which he glosses כי ירעה, and בִּעַרְתֶּם הַכֶּרֶם (Yeshayahu 3:14), you have grazed the vineyard. This too lies near the first, he says, since grazing and eating are a consuming and a finishing off.

טַעֲנוּ אֶת בְּעִירְכֶם (Bereishis 45:17), load your beasts, which he glosses בהמתכם, and the Targum of בהמה is בְּעִירָא. Another sense is brutishness: וּבְאַחַת יִבְעֲרוּ וְיִכְסָלוּ (Yirmiyahu 10:8), in one thing they are brutish and foolish, and בִּינוּ בֹּעֲרִים בָּעָם (Tehillim 94:8), understand, you brutish among the people. וּנְתַתִּיךְ בְּיַד אֲנָשִׁים בֹּעֲרִים (Yechezkel 21:36), and I will give you into the hand of brutish men, can also be read of the first sense, burning men, and that seems to be the view of the masters of the Mesorah, who count בוערים twice in two senses. אִישׁ בַּעַר לֹא יֵדָע (Tehillim 92:7), a brutish man does not know, has a known sense, and it lies near בְּעִירְכֶם, because the fool is like a beast.

גבר.sense: Strength, firmness and victory: to prevail; גְּבוּרָה, might; גִּבּוֹר, a mighty man; גְּבִיר, a lord; and גֶּבֶר, a man, so called for his strength over the woman.

more.t: גָּבַר חַסְדּוֹ עַל יְרֵאָיו (Tehillim 103:11), His kindness prevailed over those who fear Him, and וְהַמַּיִם גָּבְרוּ (Bereishis 7:19), the waters prevailed. All of them, he says, are strength, firmness and victory.

more.h: Why a man is called גבר
more.t: A man is called גֶּבֶר, he says, because he has strength over the woman: וְדֶרֶךְ גֶּבֶר בְּעַלְמָה (Mishlei 30:19), and the way of a man with a maiden. Of the locusts too the pasuk says גֶּבֶר בִּמְסִלָּתוֹ יֵלֵכוּן (Yoel 2:8), each man in his highway they go, because it likens them to men and mighty ones.

הֵן גְּבִיר שַׂמְתִּיו לָךְ (Bereishis 27:37), behold, I have made him a גְּבִיר over you, which he glosses as master and head; and the feminine, שָׂרַי גְּבִרְתִּי (Bereishis 16:8), Sarai my mistress, and גְּבֶרֶת מַמְלָכוֹת (Yeshayahu 47:5), mistress of kingdoms.

וַחֲיָלִים יְגַבֵּר (Koheles 10:10), he must put forth more strength, he reads of a blunt axe: if the axe is blunt, the one cleaving with it must add strength and force. טַלְטֵלָה גָּבֶר (Yeshayahu 22:17), a man's tossing about, Chazal explain (Kesubos 28a): the tossing about of a man is harder than the tossing about of a woman.

קצר.sense: Shortness and straitness, the opposite of length; in another sense קָצִיר is a branch; and in another again, to reap, with קָצִיר the harvest.

more.t: כִּֽי־ קָצַר הַמַּצָּע (Yeshayahu 28:20), for the bed is too short, and קָֽצְרָה יָדִי מִפְּדוּת (Yeshayahu 50:2), is My hand too short to redeem. The noun is מִקֹּצֶר רוּחַ (Shemos 6:9), for shortness of spirit, and the adjective קְצַר יָמִים וּֽשְׂבַע־רֹֽגֶז (Iyov 14:1), short of days and full of trouble, and קְֽצַר ־אַפַּיִם יַֽעֲשֶׂה אִוֶּלֶת (Mishlei 14:17), one short of temper does folly. The sense of all of it, he says, is straitness and shortness, which is the opposite of length.

In another sense, וְעָשָׂה קָצִיר כְּמוֹ־נָֽטַע (Iyov 14:9), and it puts forth branches like a sapling, and תְּשַׁלַּח קְצִירֶהָ עַד־יָם (Tehillim 80:12), it sent out its branches to the sea. The sense of all of them and their like, he says, is a branch.
In another sense again, וּקְצַרְתֶּם אֶת־ קְצִירָהּ (Vayikra 23:10), and you reap its harvest, with the noun בֶּֽחָרִישׁ וּבַקָּצִיר (Shemos 34:21), in plowing time and in harvest.

רעה.sense: To graze, and to shepherd; to keep company, and רֵעַ, a friend, may be of this root; רַעְיוֹן, will and thought; and to break.

more.t: וְרָעוּ כְבָשִׂים (Yeshayahu 5:17), and lambs shall graze; and where the verb takes two objects, הָֽאֱלֹהִים הָֽרֹעֶה אֹתִי (Bereishis 48:15), Hashem who has shepherded me. In כָּל־ רֹעַיִךְ תִּרְעֶה־רוּחַ (Yirmiyahu 22:22), all your shepherds the wind shall graze, רֹעַיִךְ is that verb of two objects, and the wind will graze on them and eat them. The noun מַרְעִית is a name for the flock itself, as וְכָל־ מַרְעִיתָם נָפֽוֹצָה (Yirmiyahu 10:21), and all their flock is scattered. In כִּֽי־שֹׁדֵד י"י אֶת־ מַרְעִיתָֽם (Yirmiyahu 25:36), for Hashem is plundering their flock, it may instead be the place of pasture, as the words after it say, וְנָדַמּוּ נְאוֹת הַשָּׁלוֹם, and the peaceful pastures are silenced. The noun for the place of pasture is מִרְעֶה, as מִרְעֶה שָׁמֵן וָטוֹב (Divrei HaYamim I 4:40), fat and good pasture.

וְרֹעֶה כְסִילִים (Mishlei 13:20), one who keeps company with fools, and וְרֹעֶה זוֹנוֹת (Mishlei 29:3), one who keeps company with harlots. In the heavy form, אֲשֶׁר רֵעָה לֽוֹ (Shoftim 14:20), who had been his companion. The noun is מֵרֵעַ, a companion, as וַתְּהִי אֵשֶׁת שִׁמְשׁוֹן לְמֵרֵעֵהוּ (Shoftim 14:20), and Shimshon's wife became his companion's, and וַֽאֲחֻזַּת מֵֽרֵעֵהוּ (Bereishis 26:26), and Achuzas his companion; on another pattern the feminine רַעְיָה, as רַעְיָתִי יָפָתִי (Shir HaShirim 2:10), my companion, my fair one; and on another again, וְאִשָּׁה רְעוּתָהּ (Yirmiyahu 9:19), and each woman her companion.

וּבְרַעְיוֹן לִבּוֹ (Koheles 2:22), and in the will of his heart, and בַּנְתָּה לְרֵעִי (Tehillim 139:2), You understand my will. The sense of all of them is will and thought, after the Targum's word for will. וְלִי מַה־יָּקְרוּ רֵעֶיךָ (Tehillim 139:17), and to me how precious are Your thoughts, is read against בַּנְתָּה לְרֵעִי מֵרָחֽוֹק earlier in the mizmor: You understand my will and my thought from afar, before ever I think it and it becomes my will, but Your will and Your thoughts are precious to me, since I cannot know them.

רֹעֶה עֲקָרָה לֹא תֵלֵד (Iyov 24:21), he breaks the barren woman who does not bear, and יִרְעוּךְ קָדְקֹֽד (Yirmiyahu 2:16), they will break your crown. כָּל־ רֹעַיִךְ תִּרְעֶה־רוּחַ (Yirmiyahu 22:22) may belong here too: the wind they chase after will break all your shepherds. Their sense is breaking.

וּרְעוּת רֽוּחַ (Koheles 1:14), a will of wind, is filed under will and thought, as another pattern of that word. Some explain it and רַעְיוֹן רֽוּחַ (Koheles 1:17) from grazing, a grazing on wind, in the manner of אֶפְרַיִם רֹעֶה רוּחַ (Hoshea 12:2), Ephraim grazes on wind, that is, a grazing that neither profits nor satisfies; some from keeping company; and some from breaking.

נשֹא.sense: To carry and lift, one sense, he says, through the whole root, with taking close to it; מַשָּׂא, a burden and a prophecy; נָשִׂיא, a great man. Another sense: burning.

more.t: וְלֹא נָשָׂא אֹתָם הָאָרֶץ (Bereishis 13:6), which he glosses as the land not bearing them. Everything that enters this root, he says, enters one sense, carrying and lifting, and it is easy to tell them apart a little, each by its place, so there is no need to set the senses out one by one. Among them are וַיִּשָּׂא עֵינָיו וַיַּרְא (Bereishis 18:2), he lifted his eyes and saw, and וַיִּשָּׂא יַעֲקֹב רַגְלָיו (Bereishis 29:1), Yaakov lifted his feet. In marriage it is taking: וַיִּשְׂאוּ לָהֶם נָשִׁים מֹאֲבִיּוֹת (Rus 1:4), they took themselves Moabite wives, the sense of carrying, he says, being close to that of taking; and so the Mishnah's בתולה נשאת (Kesubos 1:1), a maiden who is married.

more.h: The great man, and the clouds
more.t: A great man is called נָשִׂיא: וְנָשִׂיא בְעַמְּךָ לֹא תָאֹר (Shemos 22:27), a great man among your people you shall not curse. The clouds are called נְשִׂיאִים for their rising up, מַעֲלֶה נְשִׂאִים (Tehillim 135:7), He brings up the clouds.

וּמַשֹּׂא פָנִים (Divrei HaYamim II 19:7), and lifting of faces. One who sins and is ashamed, he explains, has his face fall, as וְלָמָּה נָפְלוּ פָנֶיךָ (Bereishis 4:6), why has your face fallen, and one who shows him a pleasant face is as though lifting up the face that had fallen.

שָׂא נָא חַטָּאתִי (Shemos 10:17), lift my sin, I pray, and אַשְׁרֵי נְשׂוּי פֶּשַׁע (Tehillim 32:1), happy is he whose transgression is lifted. The forgiving of a transgression, he says, is its being lifted and taken off the man.

more.h: Why a prophecy is a burden
more.t: A prophecy is called מַשָּׂא because it is carried in a man's mouth. Yisrael would say to Yirmiyahu מַה מַשָּׂא (Yirmiyahu 23:33), what is the burden, and the sense of those pesukim, he says, is this: when they asked the navi that, they did not mean prophecy but heaviness and load, as in מַשָּׂא בְנֵי קְהָת (Bamidbar 4:15), the burden of the sons of Kehas, the word of Hashem having become a heavy load to them. He who knows what is hidden revealed their thought to the navi, and therefore it says, כִּי הַמַּשָּׂא יִהְיֶה לְאִישׁ דְּבָרוֹ (Yirmiyahu 23:36), for the burden shall be each man's word: a man's word will be a burden, since the word is carried in his mouth, and that is why prophecy is called מַשָּׂא, while you turn the words of Hashem about and mean heaviness by it.

וַיִּשָּׂאֵם דָּוִד וַאֲנָשָׁיו (Shmuel II 5:21) he glosses וישרפם: David and his men burned them. So too וְהַמַּשְׂאֵת הֵחֵלָּה (Shoftim 20:40), and the burning began, and וְעַל בֵּית הַכֶּרֶם שְׂאוּ מַשְׂאֵת (Yirmiyahu 6:1), over Beis HaKerem raise a burning. It may be, he suggests, that burning is called so for the flame that rises up; and so the Mishnah (Rosh Hashanah 2:2), משיאין משואות, they kindle fires.

וַתִּשֶּׂנָה קוֹלָן וַתִּבְכֶּינָה (Rus 1:14), they lifted their voice and wept, and וַיִּשָּׂא עֵשָׂו קֹלוֹ וַיֵּבְךְּ (Bereishis 27:38), Esav lifted his voice and wept. יִשְׂאוּ כְּתֹף וְכִנּוֹר (Iyov 21:12) he glosses as raising their voice like the sound of drum and harp, or as pipers raise their voice along with the drum and the harp. וְנָשָׂאתָ תְפִלָּה (Yeshayahu 37:4), you shall lift up prayer, he reads as lifting the prayer to Hashem, or lifting the voice, or the hands, in prayer; and so יִשְׂאוּ מִדְבָּר וְעָרָיו (Yeshayahu 42:11), the wilderness and its cities shall lift, is lifting the voice.

וַיִּשָּׂא מְשָׁלוֹ (Bamidbar 23:7), he took up his mashal, which he glosses as bearing the mashal in his mouth, and יִשָּׂא מִדַּבְּרֹתֶיךָ (Devarim 33:3), he shall bear of Your words, that what You commanded him he carries always in his mouth. יִשָּׂא בַיּוֹם הַהוּא לֵאמֹר (Yeshayahu 3:7), he shall lift up on that day, saying, is lifting the Name in an oath. Also לֹא תִשָּׂא שֵׁמַע שָׁוְא (Shemos 23:1), you shall not take up a false report.

אִם יַעֲלֶה לַשָּׁמַיִם שִׂיאוֹ (Iyov 20:6), if his loftiness goes up to the heavens, שִׂיאוֹ being his greatness and his loftiness. The same gloss closes a run that holds שְׂאֵתוֹ תבעת אתכם (Iyov 13:11), his loftiness will terrify you, and מְשֵׂתוֹ יגורו אילים (Iyov 41:17), the mighty dread his loftiness. From this, יֶתֶר שְׂאֵת (Bereishis 49:3) was explained as the excess of greatness and strength that would have been fitting for you had you not gone up on your father's bed. הֲלוֹא אִם תֵּיטִיב שְׂאֵת (Bereishis 4:7) he glosses himself: if you better your deeds you will have atonement. His father, of blessed memory, explained יֶתֶר שְׂאֵת (Bereishis 49:3) from this, and read so, the words are a prayer to Hashem that He make the atonement prevail over the sin, and that is the blessing given there.

הָרָמִים וְהַנִּשָּׂאִים (Yeshayahu 2:13), the high and the lifted up, and וְעַל כָּל גִּבְעָה נִשָּׂאָה (Yeshayahu 30:25), and on every raised hill. A man lifts himself, מִתְנַשֵּׂא לֵאמֹר (Melachim I 1:5), lifting himself up, saying; others lift him, מְנַשְּׂאִים אֶת הַיְּהוּדִים (Esther 9:3), lifting up the Jews, and יְנַשְּׂאוּהוּ אַנְשֵׁי מְקֹמוֹ (Ezra 1:4), the men of his place shall lift him up; a kingdom is raised, וְתִנַּשֵּׂא מַלְכֻתוֹ (Bamidbar 24:7), and his kingdom shall be lifted up. In חִירָם מֶלֶךְ צֹר נִשָּׂא אֶת שְׁלמֹה בַּעֲצֵי אֲרָזִים (Melachim I 9:11), Chiram king of Tzor bore Shlomo up with cedar wood, it is bearing another: Chiram carried him and bore him and provided for him with these things.

The noun for a gift is מַשְׂאַת: וַתֵּצֵא אַחֲרָיו מַשְׂאַת הַמֶּלֶךְ (Shmuel II 11:8), and the king's gift went out after him; with a tzeirei, אֲרֻחָה וּמַשְׂאֵת (Yirmiyahu 40:5), an allowance and a gift; and the plural, וַיִּשָּׂא מַשְׂאֹת (Bereishis 43:34), he carried gifts. So too the offering to Hashem: אֶת מַשְׂאַת מֹשֶׁה (Divrei HaYamim II 24:6), the offering of Moshe, and וְאֶת רֵאשִׁית מַשְׂאוֹתֵיכֶם (Yechezkel 20:40), and the first of your offerings.

שְׂאֵת אוֹ סַפַּחַת (Vayikra 13:2), a שְׂאֵת or a סַפַּחַת, and שְׂאֵת הַמִּכְוָה הִוא (Vayikra 13:28), it is the שְׂאֵת of the burn, may belong with burning, he allows, since the pasuk says צרבת המכוה היא (Vayikra 13:28), it is the searing of the burn, and searing is a matter of burning; but he holds the right view to be the first sense, raising. So Chazal explained in Sifra: a שְׂאֵת is raised, like the look of shade, which stands higher than the look of the sun, and deep is like the look of the sun, which lies lower than the look of shade, while ספחת is something secondary, as it says, סְפָחֵנִי נא אל אחת הכהנות (Shmuel I 2:36), attach me, please, to one of the priestly posts.

נשׁא.sense: To incite and to entice; and a second sense, ruin and desolation.

more.t: הַנָּחָשׁ הִשִּׁיאַנִי (Bereishis 3:13), the serpent enticed me, and אַל־ יַשִּׁיא לָכֶם חִזְקִיָּהוּ (Melachim II 18:29), let not Chizkiyahu entice you. All of these, he says, mean inciting and enticing.

הַשֵּׁאת וְהַשָּֽׁבֶר (Eichah 3:47), the ruin and the breaking; הִפַּלְתָּם לְמַשּׁוּאֽוֹת (Tehillim 73:18), You cast them down into ruins; and תִּכַּסֶּה שִׂנְאָה בְּמַשָּׁאוֹן (Mishlei 26:26), hatred is covered over in ruin. Their sense, he says, is ruin and desolation.

כסה.sense: To cover; its nouns are כְּסוּי and כְּסוּת, a covering or a garment, and מִכְסֶה, a covering.

more.t: כִּסָּה הֶֽעָנָן (Bamidbar 9:15), the cloud covered, and כִּֽי־תִרְאֶה עָרֹם וְכִסִּיתוֹ (Yeshayahu 58:7), when you see the naked, cover him. In the reflexive, וַתִּקַּח הַצָּעִיף וַתִּתְכָּֽס (Bereishis 24:65), she took the veil and covered herself.

כְּסוּי עוֹר תַּחַשׁ (Bamidbar 4:6), a covering of tachash skin. On another pattern כְּסוּת, as עַל־אַרְבַּע כַּנְפוֹת כְּסֽוּתְךָ (Devarim 22:12), on the four corners of your garment, and כִּי הִוא כְסוּתֹה לְבַדָּהּ (Shemos 22:26), for it alone is his covering. On another again, וְעָשִׂיתָ מִכְסֶה לָאֹהֶל (Shemos 26:14), you shall make a covering for the tent.

אָדָם עָרוּם כֹּסֶה דָּעַת (Mishlei 12:23), a prudent man covers knowledge. אֵלֶיךָ כִסִּֽתִי (Tehillim 143:9), to You I have covered, means: to You I cried in secret, in concealment from men. The whole pasuk is explained so: הַצִּילֵנִי מֵאֹיְבַי, save me from my enemies, Hashem, for I did not uncover my quarrel to men, since the salvation of man is vain, but covered it from them and uncovered it to You alone.

קנה.sense: To acquire, the counterpart of selling; מִקְנֶה, cattle, a man's possession. A second sense: קָנֶה, a reed, and things so called, a measuring rod, a branch, a spear.

more.t: אֲשֶׁר קָנָה אַבְרָהָם (Bereishis 25:10), which Avraham acquired, and כִּי תִקְנֶה עֶבֶד עִבְרִי (Shemos 21:2), if you acquire a Hebrew servant. It stands against selling, and is well known; but there is an acquiring where there is no sale and no money paid, as קֹנֵה שָׁמַיִם וָאָרֶץ (Bereishis 14:22), the One who acquired heaven and earth, and the like. In מִקְנֶה וְקִנְיָן (Yechezkel 38:12), cattle and goods, the one word is of the animals and the other of the rest of a man's goods.
The larger and smaller beasts are called מִקְנֶה because they are a man's possession and his money and his business: וּמִקְנֶה רַב הָיָה (Bamidbar 32:1), and there was very much cattle.

more.h: The reed, and other things so called
more.t: כַּאֲשֶׁר יָנוּד הַקָּנֶה (Melachim I 14:15), as the reed shakes. Because a measure is made from the reed, a measuring rod is a קָנֶה, בִּקְנֵה הַמִּדָּה (Yechezkel 42:17), with the measuring reed. The thin rods in the likeness of a reed are called קָנִים as well, וְשִׁשָּׁה קָנִים (Shemos 25:32), and six branches. The limb from the arm's joint to the shoulder's joint is also called קָנֶה: וְאֶזְרֹעִי מִקָּנָה תִשָּׁבֵר (Iyov 31:22), and let my arm be broken from its קָנֶה. Spears are called so because they are in the likeness of a reed: גְּעַר חַיַּת קָנֶה (Tehillim 68:31), rebuke the band of the reed, that is, the company that fights with spears. The beam of a balance, from which the pans hang by cords on either side, is called קָנֶה too: וְכֶסֶף בַּקָּנֶה יִשְׁקֹלוּ (Yeshayahu 46:6), and they weigh silver on the beam. So is the spice that is in the likeness of a reed, וּקְנֵה בֹשֶׂם (Shemos 30:23), and a reed of spice.

חלק.sense: To divide, with חֵלֶק, a portion, and from it חֶלְקָה, a holding of fields. A second sense is smoothness, and likewise of words, soft and enticing speech and deceit.

more.t: וַיַּחְלְקוּ אֶת הָאָרֶץ (Yehoshua 14:5), they divided the land, and חִלְקוּ שְׁלַל אֹיְבֵיכֶם (Yehoshua 22:8), divide the spoil of your enemies. וַיֵּחָלֵק עֲלֵיהֶם לַיְלָה (Bereishis 14:15), and the night was divided over them, he explains: at the middle of the night he overtook them. The nouns are חֵלֶק, a portion, and מַחֲלֹקֶת, a division.

From this a holding of fields is called a חֶלְקָה, because this is one portion and that another: הַֽחֶלְקָה אֲשֶׁר־לִי (Shmuel II 14:31), the plot that is mine, and חֶלְקַת הַשָּׂדֶה (Rus 4:3), the plot of the field.

וְאָנֹכִי אִישׁ חָלָק (Bereishis 27:11), and I am a smooth man, and מִן הָהָר הֶחָלָק (Yehoshua 11:17), from the smooth mountain, which he explains as the mountain that had no trees on it; Yonasan renders that one from the first sense, טוּרָא פְּלִיגָא, a divided mountain. From smoothness the river stones are named as well, חַלֻּקֵי אֲבָנִים מִן הַנַּחַל (Shmuel I 17:40), smooth stones from the brook, because they are smooth.

חָלְקוּ מַחְמָאֹת פִּיו (Tehillim 55:22), the butter of his mouth was smooth, and לְשׁוֹנָם יַחֲלִיקוּן (Tehillim 5:10), they make their tongue smooth. The nouns are מֵחֶלְקַת לָשׁוֹן נָכְרִיָּה (Mishlei 6:24), from the smoothness of a strange tongue, and דַּבְּרוּ לָנוּ חֲלָקוֹת (Yeshayahu 30:10), speak to us smooth things, and with the letters doubled וַחֲלַקְלַקֹּת (Tehillim 35:6), and smooth places. All of them, he says, are softness and smoothness, and likewise of words, the softening and enticing of the tongue and its deceit.

לַחֲלִק מִשָּׁם בְּתוֹךְ הָעָם (Yirmiyahu 37:12), to slip away from there among the people, he takes as ענין השמטה, slipping away, which lies close to the sense of slipperiness: Yirmiyahu wished to slip out from there. He allows that it may be read from the first sense instead.

חמר.sense: Of wine, to be red; mortar and clay, and water made turbid like clay; a heap; the measure חֹמֶר, a kor; and חֲמוֹר, the donkey.

more.t: וְיַיִן חָמַר (Tehillim 75:9), and the wine is red. The Targum of יַיִן, wine, is חַמְרָא, and the verb from it is said of the wine itself, to say that the wine is very red, that being its nature; in many places wine is likened to blood, וְדַם־עֵנָב תִּשְׁתֶּה־ חָֽמֶר (Devarim 32:14), and the blood of the grape you drank as wine. So too כֶּרֶם חֶמֶד (Yeshayahu 27:2), a vineyard of wine, said so for the great worth and redness of its wine; the word in that pasuk is חמר, pointed with six dots. In Arabic, red is אחמא"ר.

וַתַּחְמְרָה בַֽחֵמָר (Shemos 2:3), she daubed it with חֵמָר, which is a mortar made of lime and sand, to build with and to plaster with. Some say it is a kind of pitch. In וְהַחֵמָר הָיָה לָהֶם לַחֹֽמֶר (Bereishis 11:3), and the lime mortar served them for clay, the one is the opposite of the other, חֵמָר lime mortar and חֹמֶר earthen clay; that חֵמָר is the lime mortar appears from its standing against stone in the account, and this holds where both stand in one account. Earthen clay is what is meant in תִּתְהַפֵּךְ כְּחֹמֶר חוֹתָם (Iyov 38:14), it turns about like the clay of a seal, and in אֲנַחְנוּ הַחֹמֶר (Yeshayahu 64:7), we are the clay; and so בֶּֽאֱרֹת חֵמָר (Bereishis 14:10), pits of clay.

The verb from it is יֶהֱמוּ יֶחְמְרוּ מֵימָיו (Tehillim 46:4), its waters roar and grow turbid, since turbid water is like clay. So too with the second and third root letters doubled, פָּנַי חֳמַרְמְרֻה (Iyov 16:16), my face has grown turbid from weeping, and מֵעַי חֳמַרְמָרוּ (Eichah 1:20), my innards have grown turbid.

וְחֹמֶר שְׂעֹרִים (Hoshea 3:2), a chomer of barley, and לָשֵׂאת מַעְשַׂר הַחֹמֶר (Yechezkel 45:11), to hold a tenth of the chomer: the measure is a kor, ten ephahs, which are thirty se'ah. It is also a heap: חֹמֶר מַיִם רַבִּֽים (Chavakuk 3:15), a heap of many waters, and חֳמָרִם חֳמָרִם (Shemos 8:10), heaps upon heaps; in another form, חֲמוֹר חֲמֹרָתָיִם (Shoftim 15:16), a heap, two heaps.

חֲמוֹר לֶחֶם (Shmuel I 16:20) may be a heap of bread; or it is a donkey, as in חֲמֹר גָּרֶם (Bereishis 49:14), and is short a word, meaning a donkey carrying bread. חֲמֹר גָּרֶם is a strong donkey, a donkey of bones. On אֶחְבְּשָׁה־לִּי הַֽחֲמוֹר וְאֶרְכַּב עָלֶיהָ (Shmuel II 19:27), let me saddle the donkey and ride upon her, the feminine עָלֶיהָ may be because it was a she-donkey, or it is said with a beast, בהמה, in mind.

more.h: A donkey's head, and the yachmur
more.t: עַד הֱיוֹת רֹֽאשׁ־ חֲמוֹר בִּשְׁמֹנִים כֶּסֶף (Melachim II 6:25), until a donkey's head was sold for eighty of silver, is meant plainly, as Targum Yonasan renders it רֵישָׁא דַחֲמְרָא, a donkey's head; some read the word there as the measure, as in מַעְשַׂר הַחֹמֶר (Yechezkel 45:11), a tenth of the chomer. Of אַיָּל וּֽצְבִי וְיַחְמוּר (Devarim 14:5), the hart and the gazelle and the יַחְמוּר, Rabbi Yonah wrote that Arabic calls it by that name, and that it is a beast like a large goat.

שֹכר.sense: To hire, with שָׂכִיר, a hired man, and שָׂכָר, a wage. In another sense, שֶׂכֶר goes with stopping up, under the samech, or it may be a net.

more.t: כִּי שָׂכֹר שְׂכַרְתִּיךָ (Bereishis 30:16), for I have surely hired you, and בְּיוֹמוֹ תִתֵּן שְׂכָרוֹ (Devarim 24:15), on his day you shall give him his wage. A hired man is שָׂכִיר: אִם שָׂכִיר הוּא (Shemos 22:14), if he is a hired man; the nouns are שָׂכָר and שֶׂכֶר, a wage, and מַשְׂכֻּרְתֶּךָ, your wages. שְׂבֵעִים בַּלֶּחֶם נִשְׂכָּרוּ (Shmuel I 2:5), those who were sated hired themselves out for bread. From this too, though written with a samech, is וְסֹכְרִים עֲלֵיהֶם יוֹעֲצִים (Ezra 4:5), and hiring counsellors against them.

וְשֹׂכֵר כְּסִיל וְשֹׂכֵר עֹבְרִים (Mishlei 26:10), and one who hires a fool and hires עֹבְרִים. Rabbi Yonah explains: the רב of the pasuk, the great man of the people, is מחולל to all and rules them; he pays the fool and forces him into his service, and likewise hires the עוברים, who are the refusers. Of the same kind is מַדּוּעַ אַתָּה עוֹבֵר אֵת מִצְוַת הַמֶּלֶךְ (Esther 3:3), why do you transgress the king's command. Radak's brother Rabbi Moshe joins it to the pasuk above it, חוֹחַ עָלָה בְיַד שִׁכּוֹר וּמָשָׁל בְּפִי כְסִילִים (Mishlei 26:9), a thorn goes up into a drunkard's hand, and a proverb in the mouth of fools, and takes רב as many: the fool who tells many proverbs is מחולל to everyone, like a thorn in a drunkard's hand; and one who hires the fool for his proverbs and pays the עוברים, the refusers who transgress the commandments and whom he has no power to compel, are one, this like that. Radak has written another explanation besides these under the root חול. Rav Saadiah Gaon also joins it to the pasuk before: when a word of wisdom comes into the fool's hand he is מתחולל with it and turns it over and does not understand it, like the drunkard with a thorn in his hand who drives it into his nails and between his fingers and does not feel it; and for all that he begrudges that word to one who does not know it, and pains everyone with it, which is רב מחולל כל, since he angers people's hearts with it, and he shuts his mouth from teaching it to the fool and to the wayfarers who ask him. Rav Saadiah takes שוכר from כִּי יִסָּכֵר פִּי דוֹבְרֵי שָׁקֶר (Tehillim 63:12), for the mouth of those who speak falsehood will be stopped.

גַּם שְׂכִרֶיהָ בְקִרְבָּהּ (Yirmiyahu 46:21), her hired men too in her midst: even the troops hired to fight for them were like fatted calves that cannot fight, for they too turned and fled together; the navi likens them to fatted calves because one who is fat and pampered with food and pleasures cannot fight. Some explain שכיריה as גמליה ונכבדיה, her camels and her honoured ones, and so the Targum renders it, אַף רַבְרְבָהָא בְגַוָהּ, even her great ones in her midst.
בְּתַעַר הַשְּׂכִירָה (Yeshayahu 7:20), with the hired razor, because the razor a man hires is the good and sharpened one. In the same way, בתער השכירה is also explained as the great razor.

Another sense: כָּל עֹשֵׂי שֶׂכֶר (Yeshayahu 19:10), all who make שֶׂכֶר. Radak has explained it already under the letter samech, with וַיִּסָּכְרוּ מַעְיְנֹת תְּהוֹם (Bereishis 8:2), the fountains of the deep were stopped up. It may also be read as a net, עושי שכר being men who make nets to catch fish. In the words of Chazal (Sanhedrin 95a), יומא חד נפק לשכר בזאי, one day he went out לשכר בזאי; Radak explains: שכר is a net, and בזאי is the name of a bird with which nobles hunt other birds, a hawk or the like, so that he went out to hunt with a net. And so the Baal HaAruch explains it.

שׁכר.sense: To be drunk, with שִׁכָּרוֹן, drunkenness, and שִׁכּוֹר, a drunkard; שֵׁכָר, wine, called so because it makes drunk, and any drink that does; and אֶשְׁכָּר, a gift.

more.t: וַיֵּשְׁתְּ מִן־הַיַּיִן וַיִּשְׁכָּר (Bereishis 9:21), he drank of the wine and became drunk. But שָׁכְרוּ וְלֹא־יַיִן (Yeshayahu 29:9) is that they are drunk and not from wine, and וּשְׁכֻרַת וְלֹא מִיָּיִן (Yeshayahu 51:21) is one drunk with troubles and not with wine. Where the verb takes an object it is to make drunk: וְהִשְׁכַּרְתִּים לְמַעַן יַעֲלֹזוּ (Yirmiyahu 51:39), I will make them drunk that they may exult, and אַשְׁכִּיר חִצַּי מִדָּם (Devarim 32:42), I will make My arrows drunk with blood.

Being drunk with wine, he says, is to drink what being sated is to food; but a man may drink until he neither feels nor understands. וְהוּא שִׁכֹּר עַד־מְאֹד (Shmuel I 25:36), he was very drunk, and וַיַּחְשְׁבֶהָ עֵלִי לְשִׁכֹּרָה (Shmuel I 1:13), Eli took her for a drunken woman.

Wine is called שֵׁכָר because it makes drunk: שֵׁכָר יִרְדֹּפוּ (Yeshayahu 5:11), they run after intoxicating drink. A drink made from fruit that makes drunk carries the name as well. In יַיִן וְשֵׁכָר אַל־תֵּשְׁתְּ (Vayikra 10:9), drink no wine or intoxicating drink, the word takes in everything that intoxicates, even what is not wine, as Chazal say (Nazir 4a): one who ate pressed figs of Keilah, or drank milk or honey, and entered the Mikdash is liable.

בַּקֹּדֶשׁ הַסֵּךְ נֶסֶךְ שֵׁכָר (Bamidbar 28:7), in the holy place pour a libation of intoxicating drink: a libation of wine that makes drunk, and it is חי, undiluted, as the Sifri says on Pinchas: the quarter of a hin, undiluted you pour it and not the mixed. So too the Midrash on מִיַּיִן וְשֵׁכָר יַזִּיר, from wine and intoxicating drink he shall abstain: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar says יַיִן is the mixed and שֵׁכָר the undiluted; the reverse is raised, and the pasuk of the quarter of a hin, poured undiluted, settles it the first way and not the other.

אֶשְׁכָּר יַקְרִיבוּ (Tehillim 72:10), they shall bring a gift, and הֵשִׁיבוּ אֶשְׁכָּרֵךְ (Yechezkel 27:15), they brought back your gift. He glosses it a מנחה, an offering, and says the word may have four root letters.

מור.sense: מֹר, myrrh, a spice. Some took it for musk; Ibn Ezra makes it a spice of the gathered plants, and Rabbeinu Hai the resin of a sweet-smelling tree.

more.t: מָר־דְּרוֹר (Shemos 30:23), pure myrrh, and בְּשֶׁמֶן הַמֹּר (Esther 2:12), with oil of myrrh. Ibn Ezra writes that some explained it as musk. Against that, were it musk the pasuk would not say אָרִיתִי מוֹרִי (Shir HaShirim 5:1), I have gathered my myrrh, since musk is no plant to be gathered; and Ibn Ezra explained it as a spice of the kinds of plants that are gathered. Rabbeinu Hai explains it as the resin of a sweet-smelling tree, which has a name of its own in Arabic, and on that explanation too one can say אָרִיתִי מוֹרִי.

From Midrash Chazis, on צְרוֹר הַמּוֹר, the bundle of myrrh: as myrrh is the chief of all the spices, so Avraham Avinu is the chief of all the tzaddikim; as whoever gathers myrrh has his hands made bitter, so Avraham Avinu made himself bitter; and as myrrh gives off its scent only in fire, so Avraham Avinu made his good deeds known only in the fiery furnace.

שֹבר.sense: To think a matter over, known from Chazal's word סברא, reasoning; and in a second sense, to hope.

more.t: וָאֱהִי שׂבֵר בְּחוֹמֹת יְרוּשָׁלַם (Nechemiah 2:13), and I was thinking over the walls of Yerushalayim: the sense is one who thinks, from the סברא, the reasoning, of Chazal's language.

In the second sense it is to hope: לֹא־יְשַׂבְּרוּ יוֹרְדֵי־בוֹר אֶל־אֲמִתֶּךָ (Yeshayahu 38:18), those who go down to the pit do not hope for Your truth; עֵינֵי כֹל אֵלֶיךָ יְשַׂבֵּרוּ (Tehillim 145:15), the eyes of all hope to You; and הֲלָהֵן תְּשַׂבֵּרְנָה (Rus 1:13), would you hope for them. The noun is שִׂבְרוֹ (Tehillim 146:5), his hope.

שׁבר.sense: To break; מִשְׁבָּר, the breaking of the sea's waves; מַשְׁבֵּר, the womb; a dream's breaking, its interpretation; and שֶׁבֶר, grain or any food, bought and sold.

more.t: וְלֹא שָׁבַר אֶת־הַחֲמוֹר (Melachim I 13:28), it did not break the donkey, and וּשְׁבָרָהּ כְּשֵׁבֶר נֵבֶל יוֹצְרִים (Yeshayahu 30:14), he shall break it as a potter's jar is broken; וְעֶצֶם לֹא תִשְׁבְּרוּ־בוֹ (Shemos 12:46), you shall not break a bone in it. The nouns are שֵׁבֶר, a breaking, as וּמִשֵּׁבֶר רוּחַ תְּיֵלִילוּ (Yeshayahu 65:14), you shall howl for breaking of spirit, and שִׁבְרוֹן, as הֵאָנַח בְּשִׁבְרוֹן מָתְנַיִם (Yechezkel 21:11), groan with breaking of loins.

אַחַת מֵהֵנָּה לֹא נִשְׁבָּרָה (Tehillim 34:21), not one of them was broken, is a passing form, the verb in the past, since it is stressed on the earlier syllable; רוּחַ נִשְׁבָּרָה (Tehillim 51:19), a broken spirit, is a standing form, not a past, since it is stressed on the last.

כָּל־מִשְׁבָּרֶיךָ וְגַלֶּיךָ עָלַי עָבָרוּ (Yonah 2:4), all Your breakers and Your waves passed over me, is the breaking of the sea's waves in the storm; and from it, carried over, מִשְׁבְּרֵי־מָוֶת (Shmuel II 22:5), the breakers of death. עַד־הַשְּׁבָרִים (Yehoshua 7:5), as far as ha-Shevarim, is a place called so because they were broken there.

וָאֶשְׁבֹּר עָלָיו חֻקִּי, and I broke My statute upon it, means I cut a covenant and decreed My statute upon it, that it shall not pass it; breaking is said of this as cutting is said of a covenant. From this same sense is derived הַאֲנִי אַשְׁבִּיר וְלֹא אוֹלִיד (Yeshayahu 66:9), shall I bring to the מַשְׁבֵּר and not deliver, that is, I bring the woman to the מַשְׁבֵּר. The womb is called מַשְׁבֵּר for the breaking of the woman in labour and her pangs: כִּי בָאוּ בָנִים עַד־מַשְׁבֵּר (Yeshayahu 37:3), for the children have come to the womb, and כִּי־עֵת לֹא־יַעֲמֹד בְּמִשְׁבַּר בָּנִים (Hoshea 13:13), for at the time he will not stand in the womb of children.

more.h: The breaking open of a dream
more.t: אֶת־מִסְפַּר הַחֲלוֹם וְאֶת־שִׁבְרוֹ (Shoftim 7:15), the telling of the dream and its breaking, where its breaking is its interpretation: until it is interpreted the dream is like a thing sealed up, and the interpretation breaks it open and lays it bare.

more.h: Grain, and the buying of it
more.t: כִּי יֶשׁ־שֶׁבֶר בְּמִצְרָיִם (Bereishis 42:1), there is grain in Mitzrayim, and וַיִּשְׂאוּ אֶת־שִׁבְרָם (Bereishis 42:26), they loaded their grain: grain and any food. It may be called so, he suggests, because it breaks hunger, as יִשְׁבְּרוּ פְרָאִים צְמָאָם (Tehillim 104:11), the wild donkeys break their thirst. The buyer of it is himself called שׁוֹבֵר, one who breaks: לְכוּ שִׁבְרוּ וֶאֱכֹלוּ (Yeshayahu 55:1), go, buy and eat. So is the seller, וַיִּשְׁבֹּר לְמִצְרַיִם (Bereishis 41:56), he sold to Mitzrayim; and where the verb takes an object, הוּא הַמַּשְׁבִּיר לְכָל־עַם הָאָרֶץ (Bereishis 42:6), he it was who sold to all the people of the land.

עלם.sense: To be hidden, and to hide; עֶלֶם and עַלְמָה, a youth and a young woman; and עוֹלָם, a long span, as until Yovel or all one's life; עוֹלָמִים, this world and the next.

more.t: וְנֶעְלַם דָּבָר (Vayikra 4:13), the matter is hidden, and וְנֶעֶלְמָה מֵעֵינֵי כָל־חָי (Iyov 28:21), hidden from the eyes of all living. תְּהִי נַעֲלָמָה (Nachum 3:11) he glosses as though you had never been at all. To hide oneself is וְהִתְעַלַּמְתָּ מֵהֶם (Devarim 22:1), and you hide yourself from them, and to hide is אַל־תַּעְלֵם אָזְנְךָ (Eichah 3:56), do not hide Your ear.

וְאַעְלִים עֵינַי בּוֹ (Shmuel I 12:3), and I hid my eyes at him, he reads two ways: that a man took a ransom and hid his eyes from the judgment, so as not to judge as he should; or that he hid his eyes at the giver of the ransom, covering him and not uncovering his crime. His father read it that he was ashamed to speak before the man from whom he took it, and hid his eyes from looking at him.

עֲלֻמֵנוּ לִמְאוֹר פָּנֶיךָ (Tehillim 90:8) he glosses as our errors, since a man's errors are hidden from him, and תַּעֲלֻמוֹת לֵב (Tehillim 44:22) are the heart's hidden things. So too עַל־עֲלָמוֹת שִׁיר (Tehillim 46:1), which he reads as the hidden part of the song and its secrets. Some would read וְהוּא יְנַהֲגֵנוּ עַל־מוּת (Tehillim 48:15) from hiding as well; but the Masoretic note has it as two words, עַל מוּת, and so the accurate sefarim, and then it means עַד מָוֶת, until death: He will lead us until our dying.

more.h: Whether a young woman is a virgin
more.t: וְהָיָה הָעַלְמָה הַיֹּצֵאת לִשְׁאֹב (Bereishis 24:43) is the young woman, and he allows that the word may cover the virgin and the one who has known a man alike, as נערה, a girl, does. הִנֵּה הָעַלְמָה הָרָה (Yeshayahu 7:14), behold, the young woman is with child, he takes of one who had known a man, the wife of the navi or the wife of Achaz (printed אחו), and says on clear proofs that Immanuel is not Chizkiyahu. וְדֶרֶךְ גֶּבֶר בְּעַלְמָה (Mishlei 30:19) cannot be a virgin either, because the pasuk after it says כן דרך אִשָּׁה מְנָאפֶת, so is the way of an adulterous woman, she eats and wipes her mouth and says I have done no wrong; and the things wondered at there leave no trace, the eagle's way in the sky and the snake's upon the rock, and so a man's way with an almah, where the act is not to be told; with a virgin it would be plain beyond doubt. His father brought further proofs in Sefer HaBris: were almah a virgin, there would be no עֶלֶם, a young man, formed from it, just as there is no masculine formed from בתולה, a virgin.

more.h: The youth, and why Shaul asked
more.t: בֶּן־מִי־זֶה הָעָלֶם (Shmuel I 17:56) is the youth. Shaul was not asking who he was, having already sent for him to play before him; but seeing his might as he came back from striking the Pelishti, he asked whether he was the son of a mighty man. So at בֶּן־מִי אַתָּה הַנָּעַר (Shmuel I 17:58) David understood the question, and answered בֶּן־עַבְדְּךָ יִשַׁי בֵּית הַלַּחְמִי, that is, he is from Beis Lechem, and he was a man of מלחמה, of war, famous and known for his might, and that is why they called him Beis HaLachmi, the one word carrying both senses at once. Of the same sense are the days of youth, הִקְצַרְתָּ יְמֵי עֲלוּמָיו (Tehillim 89:46), You have shortened the days of his youth.

לְעֹלָם וָעֶד (Shemos 15:18), for ever and ever, and תְּשׁוּעַת עוֹלָמִים (Yeshayahu 45:17), which he reads as this world and the world to come, or else as long stretches of time, since the word is used of many days that are some part of the long עוֹלָם, world. וַעֲבָדוֹ לְעֹלָם (Shemos 21:6) is all the days until the Yovel; כִּי מֵעוֹלָם שָׁבַרְתִּי עֻלֵּךְ (Yirmiyahu 2:20) is from long ago; and לְעוֹלָם לֹא־אֶשְׁכַּח פִּקּוּדֶיךָ (Tehillim 119:93) is all the days of my life.

כפר.sense: To coat, and from it the כַפֹּרֶת, the aron's cover; to remove, as anger or sin, and atonement is from this; also a village, a young lion, frost, and pans of gold.

more.t: אֲכַפְּרָה פָנָיו (Bereishis 32:21), I will remove his anger; לֹא תֽוּכְלִי כַּפְּרָהּ (Yeshayahu 47:11), you will not be able to remove it and annul it. Atonement is from this sense too, since atonement is the removing of sins: וְכִפֶּר אַֽהֲרֹן (Shemos 30:10), and Aharon shall atone: by putting the blood on the horns of the mizbeach he removes the sins of Yisrael, so that they find favour before Hashem. The noun is in יוֹם כִּפֻּרִים (Vayikra 23:28), the day of atonement.

more.h: What Chazal show of the word
more.t: Chazal say מִזְבֵּחַ מזיח מכפר (Kesubos 10b), the mizbeach dislodges and atones. The question is asked whether dislodging and atoning are not one thing, and the answer is מזיח גזירות, it dislodges decrees, מכפר עונות, it atones for sins. Both are words of removal, since מזיח is from וְלֹֽא־יִזַּח הַחֹשֶׁן מֵעַל הָֽאֵפֽוֹד (Shemos 28:28), and the choshen shall not come loose from the ephod. Chazal use the word for removing in many places, as when they say מכפר ליה בבליתא דפרסא (Chullin 8b), which means one takes off its fat, passing it over a coarse cloth to wipe it.

אִישׁ כֹּפֶר נַפְשׁוֹ (Shemos 30:12), each man the redemption of his soul, which he explains as the removing of his soul's sin, that is, his redemption; so too אִם־ כֹּפֶר יוּשַׁת עָלָיו (Shemos 21:30), if a redemption is laid upon him.

וּכְפַר הָֽעַמֹּנָי (Yehoshua 18:24), and the village of the Ammonite, and נָלִינָה בַּכְּפָרִֽים (Shir HaShirim 7:12), let us lodge in the villages. The Targum renders העיר ובנותיה, the city and its daughter towns, with וְכַפְרָנָהָא, and its villages, which are houses outside the city, for villagers and for those who work the land.

אֶשְׁכֹּל הַכֹּפֶר (Shir HaShirim 1:14), a cluster of kofer, is what is called אלחנ"א in Arabic, and so כְּפָרִים עִם־נְרָדִֽים (Shir HaShirim 4:13), kefarim with nard. Some hold that כְּפָרִים עִם־נְרָדִֽים is a spice of its own and not the same as אֶשְׁכֹּל הַכֹּפֶר. Ibn Ezra wrote that אֶשְׁכֹּל הַכֹּפֶר is the cluster of the date palm, since the palm has names that change as its season changes, and it has a season whose Arabic name is this one, and it has a good scent.

more.h: The young lion, the frost, the pans
more.t: כְּפִיר אֲרָיוֹת (Shoftim 14:5), a young lion, and הַכְּפִירִים שֹֽׁאֲגִים לַטָּרֶף (Tehillim 104:21), the young lions roaring for prey: these are the young in days among the lions and the wild beasts, and a כְּפִיר is bigger than a גור, a cub. By way of figure, כְּפִיר גּוֹיִם נִדְמֵיתָ (Yechezkel 32:2), you were likened to a young lion of the nations, means their great and mighty one. דַּק כַּכְּפֹר עַל־הָאָֽרֶץ (Shemos 16:14), fine as the frost on the ground: the frost is what falls at dawn in the days of cold. וְלִכְפוֹרֵי הַזָּהָב (Divrei HaYamim I 28:17), and for the golden pans: these are כפות זהב, pans of gold. Chazal explained them as basins, saying (Zevachim 25a): the blood of the knife, with what does one wipe it? On the rim of the basin, as it is written כפורי זהב. They are called so because the knife is wiped clean of blood on them, as in מכפר ליה בבליתא דפרסא, whose sense is wiping, as explained above.

שֹער.sense: To dread, with the noun שְׂעָרָה, a storm. Also שָׂעִיר, a he-goat, and the demons called שְׂעִירִם; fine rain; hair, and a hairy man; and barley.

more.t: לֹא שְׂעָרוּם אֲבֹתֵיכֶם (Devarim 32:17), your fathers did not dread them: that is, they did not fear them and did not serve them. The noun is בְּסוּפָה וּבִשְׂעָרָה דַּרְכּוֹ (Nachum 1:3), His way is in whirlwind and in storm.

שְׂעִיר עִזִּים (Bamidbar 7:16), a he-goat, is known. וּשְׂעִירִים יְרַקְּדוּ שָׁם (Yeshayahu 13:21), and שעירים will dance there, and לַשְּׂעִירִם אֲשֶׁר הֵם זֹנִים אַחֲרֵיהֶם (Vayikra 17:7), to the שעירים after whom they stray, are the demons; they are called so because they appear in the likeness of goats to those who believe in them.
כִּשְׂעִירִם עֲלֵי דֶשֶׁא (Devarim 32:2), like שעירים upon the grass: the fine rain is called so.

more.h: Hair, the hairy man, and barley
more.t: לַשֵּׂעָר הַצָּהֹב (Vayikra 13:36), for the yellow hair; שַׂעְרֵךְ כְּעֵדֶר הָעִזִּים (Shir HaShirim 4:1), your hair is like a flock of goats, that is, like the hair of a flock of goats; הֵן עֵשָׂו אָחִי אִישׁ שָׂעִר (Bereishis 27:11), Esav my brother is a hairy man; and וְהַפִּשְׁתָּה וְהַשְּׂעֹרָה (Shemos 9:31), the flax and the barley. These last two, he says, are known.

שׁער.sense: To reckon and estimate; in another sense, foul and filthy, said of figs; and שַׁעַר, a gate, a whole land being called by its gate, its entrance.

more.t: כְּמֽוֹ־ שָׁעַר בְּנַפְשׁוֹ כֶּן־הוּא (Mishlei 23:7), as he reckons in his soul so is he, on the pattern פָּעַל; the noun is שַׁעַר, accented on its first syllable, and in the plural מֵאָה שְׁעָרִים (Bereishis 26:12), a hundred measures; the sense is measure and estimate, and is known. Some take שַֽׁעֲרֽוּרִיָּה in בְּבֵית יִשְׂרָאֵל רָאִיתִי (Hoshea 6:10), in the house of Yisrael I have seen a שַֽׁעֲרֽוּרִיָּה, from this sense, so that the pasuk says: what I reckoned of them I saw in them.

more.h: Another sense, and the foul figs
more.t: Another sense: שַׁמָּה וְשַֽׁעֲרוּרָה (Yirmiyahu 5:30), an astonishment and a שַֽׁעֲרוּרָה, and רָאִיתִי שַֽׁעֲרוּרָה (Yirmiyahu 23:14), I have seen a שַֽׁעֲרוּרָה, and in another form שַֽׁעֲרֻרִת עָֽשְׂתָה מְאֹד (Yirmiyahu 18:13), she has done a שַֽׁעֲרֻרִת exceedingly. Then כַּתְּאֵנִים הַשֹּׁעָרִים (Yirmiyahu 29:17), like the foul figs, an adjective, whose sense is filth and foulness. Whether that sense is given for the whole run or for this last word alone, his text does not mark.

more.h: The gate, and the land's entrance
more.t: שַׁעַר הַשָּׁמָֽיִם (Bereishis 28:17), the gate of heaven, and the verb from it, שֹׁעֵר הָעִיר (Melachim II 7:10), the gatekeeper of the city. A whole land is called by its gate, after its entrance, as וְיִרַשׁ זַֽרְעֲךָ אֵת שַׁעַר אֹֽיְבָֽיו (Bereishis 22:17), your seed shall possess the gate of its enemies: a strong and fortified land is strong at its entrance, having mountains or seas about it, and once enemies have come in and passed those gates the whole land is taken before them. So פָּתוֹחַ נִפְתְּחוּ שַֽׁעֲרֵי אַרְצֵךְ (Nachum 3:13), the gates of your land are thrown wide open, and וְהֵצַר לְךָ בְּכָל־ שְׁעָרֶיךָ (Devarim 28:52), he will press you in all your gates.

קהל.sense: To be gathered together, and to gather others; קָהָל, a congregation, with קְהִלָּה and מַקְהֵלִים for an assembly.

more.t: וַיִּקָּהֵל הָעָם עַל אַהֲרֹן (Shemos 32:1), the people gathered against Aharon, and הַנִּקְהָלִים עָלֶיךָ (Yechezkel 38:7), those gathered to you; where the verb takes an object, הַקְהֵל אֶת הָעָם (Devarim 31:12), assemble the people. The noun, for a congregation, is וְקָהָל וְעַם רָב (Yechezkel 26:7), and a congregation and a great people; another form is קְהִלָּה, as וָאֶתֵּן עֲלֵיהֶם קְהִלָּה גְדוֹלָה (Nechemiah 5:7), and I set a great assembly against them, and קְהִלַּת יַעֲקֹב (Devarim 33:4), the congregation of Yaakov; and בְּמַקְהֵלִים (Tehillim 26:12), in assemblies, with בְּמַקְהֵלוֹת (Tehillim 68:27) for the feminine plural.

In הַקָּהָל חֻקָּה אַחַת לָכֶם (Bamidbar 15:15) the heh is the heh of address, O assembly, one statute for you; the same heh as in הֶאָמוּר בֵּית יַעֲקֹב (Michah 2:7), O you who are called the house of Yaakov, and הַדּוֹר אַתֶּם רְאוּ (Yirmiyahu 2:31), O generation, you, see.

שׁמר.sense: To keep and to guard. Close to it, the watches of the night. In other senses, the lees of wine; שָׁמִיר, a hard stone; and שָׁמִיר, a kind of thorn.

more.t: וְאָבִיו שָׁמַר אֶת־הַדָּבָֽר (Bereishis 37:11), and his father kept the matter, and וּשְׁמָרוֹ כְּרֹעֶה עֶדְרֽוֹ (Yirmiyahu 31:10), and he will guard him as a shepherd his flock. A guarding can also keep others off: אֲנִי שָׁמַרְתִּי אָרְחוֹת פָּרִֽיץ (Tehillim 17:4), I guarded the paths of the robber, is that I guarded them so that no man should walk in them, because of בִּדְבַר שְׂפָתֶיךָ, the word of Your lips, that You had said; and in the same way לִשְׁמֹר אֶת־דֶּרֶךְ עֵץ הַֽחַיִּֽים (Bereishis 3:24), to guard the way to the tree of life.

וְרַק־אַתֶּם שִׁמְרוּ מִן־הַחֵרֶם (Yehoshua 6:18), and only you, guard from the cherem: each man is to guard his fellow from it, for if one takes, all of you are punished for not having guarded. That is what it says there, וְשַׂמְתֶּם אֶת־מַֽחֲנֵה יִשְׂרָאֵל לְחֵרֶם, and you will make the camp of Yisrael a cherem; and that is why Yisrael were punished over Achan, and why it says חָטָא יִשְׂרָאֵל (Yehoshua 7:11), Yisrael has sinned, because they did not guard that no man take from it.

לֹֽא־תִשְׁמוֹר עַל־חַטָּאתִֽי (Iyov 14:16) can mean that You watch over nothing but my sin, as אֵֽין־טוֹב בָּֽאָדָם שֶׁיֹּאכַל וְשָׁתָה (Koheles 2:24), there is no good in man that he eat and drink, where the sense is only that he eat. Or it means You will not wait: You punish me at once and give me no time. Like it are Chazal's words (Berachos 3a) שמור לי על הפתח, keep for me at the door, which Radak explains as wait for me.
