more.t: כִּנּוֹר וְעוּגָֽב (Bereishis 4:21), kinnor and ugav, and וַיְהִי לְאֵבֶל כִּנֹּרִי (Iyov 30:31), my kinnor is turned to mourning. The plural is וְקוֹל כִּנּוֹרַיִךְ לֹא יִשָּׁמַע עֽוֹד (Yechezkel 26:13), the sound of your kinnoros will be heard no more, and in the feminine form וּבְכִנֹּרוֹת וּבִנְבָלִים (Shmuel II 6:5), with kinnoros and nevalim, and תָּלִינוּ כִּנֹּרוֹתֵֽינוּ (Tehillim 137:2), we hung up our kinnoros. Of all of them he says only ידוע, it is known.

יין.sense: Wine, which he calls known. In יַיִן תַּרְעֵלָה and the like he reads a bound word as left out: wine, the wine of reeling.

more.h: Where a word is left out
more.t: The word stands alone in וְיַיִן לַנֶּסֶךְ רְבִיעִית הַהִין (Bamidbar 15:5), wine for a drink offering, a quarter of a hin, and binds as יֵין: יִשְׁתּוּ יֵין נְסִיכָם (Devarim 32:38), let them drink the wine of their offering. In מיין הרקח (Shir HaShirim 8:2), of the wine, the spice, in אֶת־כּוֹס הַיַּיִן הַֽחֵמָה (Yirmiyahu 25:15), the cup of the wine, the wrath, and in הִשְׁקִיתָנוּ יַיִן תַּרְעֵלָֽה (Tehillim 60:5), You gave us wine of reeling to drink, the bound word is missing, and one reads מיין יֵין הרקח, of the wine, the wine of the spice, היין יֵין החמה, the wine, the wine of wrath, and יין יֵין התרעלה, wine, the wine of reeling. It can also be read that in מיין הרקח the second word describes the wine, and then nothing is left out.

כְּיֵין הַטּוֹב (Shir HaShirim 7:10), like the good wine, where the bound form is joined to the description itself, as בְּחֵיל כָּבֵד (Yeshayahu 36:2), with a heavy army, and אֶל־מֵי הַמָּרִֽים (Bamidbar 5:23), to the bitter water.
He finds the plural in the feminine in the words of Chazal, in the Mishnah (Shekalim 4:3): יינות, wines, שמנים וסלתות, oils and fine flours.

ינה.sense: To wrong a man in his money, taking what is another's in buying and selling or otherwise, whether he knows of it or not.

more.t: וְלֹא תוֹנוּ אִישׁ אֶת־עֲמִיתוֹ (Vayikra 25:17), you shall not wrong one another, הוֹנוּ בָֽךְ (Yechezkel 22:7), they wronged in you, and וְהַֽאֲכַלְתִּי אֶת־ מוֹנַיִךְ (Yeshayahu 49:26), I will feed those who wrong you. The sense of wronging is known: taking other men's money in a sale or in some other way, with their knowledge or without it.

From the light form, הָעִיר הַיּוֹנָֽה (Tzefaniah 3:1), the city that wrongs, מִפְּנֵי חֶרֶב הַיּוֹנָֽה (Yirmiyahu 46:16), before the sword that wrongs, and מִפְּנֵי חֲרוֹן הַיּוֹנָה (Yirmiyahu 25:38), before the fury of the one that wrongs. In Rabbi Yonah's view נִינָם יָחַד (Tehillim 74:8), we will wrong them together, is of this root, on the pattern of נִירָם. Targum Yonasan renders מוֹנַיִךְ in this sense, and so too נִינָם יָחַד, חֶרֶב הַיּוֹנָֽה and הָעִיר הַיּוֹנָֽה.

וְלֹֽא־ יוֹנוּ עוֹד נְשִׂיאַי אֶת־עַמִּי (Yechezkel 45:8), my princes will no more wrong my people, which he reads as their not taking the people's inheritance by force, and so לְהֽוֹנֹתָם מֵֽאֲחֻזָּתָם (Yechezkel 46:18), to wrong them out of their holding. Targum Yonasan renders it so, that the ruler shall not take of the people's inheritance to wrong them out of their own.

Chazal (Bava Metzia 58b) said there is wronging in words as well, and that this is what וְגֵר לֹֽא־ תוֹנֶה (Shemos 22:20), you shall not wrong a ger, means: לֹֽא־תוֹנֶה, do not wrong him, in words, and וְלֹא תִלְחָצֶנּוּ, do not oppress him, in money. One is not to say to a ger, remember your earlier deeds; nor to the son of gerim, remember your fathers' deeds; nor to a Jew who has come back in teshuvah, remember your earlier deeds.
Rabbi Yehudah put וְאַֽחֲרִיתוֹ יִהְיֶה מָנֽוֹן (Mishlei 29:21), and in the end he will be מָנֽוֹן, in this root and this sense. Radak holds it more correct to take it from the root נִין.

אכל.sense: To eat; and fire consuming, destroying, the sword cutting down, and מַאֲכֶלֶת, the knife: all one sense, since eating any food is itself consuming and destroying it.

more.t: וְאָֽכַלְתָּ וְשָׂבָֽעְתָּ (Devarim 11:15), you will eat and be satisfied, and by way of figure אָֽכְלָה וּמָחֲתָה פִיהָ (Mishlei 30:20), she ate and wiped her mouth. The noun is וַיִּתֶּן־ אֹכֶל בֶּֽעָרִים (Bereishis 41:48), he put food in the cities, and in other forms בְּכֹחַ הָֽאֲכִילָה הַהִיא (Melachim I 19:8), by the strength of that eating, and וּמַֽאֲכַל שֻׁלְחָנוֹ (Melachim I 10:5), the food of his table. מַכֹּלֶת לְבֵיתוֹ (Melachim I 5:25), food for his house, is missing its alef, its full form being מַֽאֲכֹלֶת. The sense of all these, eating a thing that is food, is a known one.

אֵשׁ אֹֽכְלָה הוּא (Devarim 4:24), He is a consuming fire; in the passive וְנֶֽאֱכַל גָּדִישׁ (Shemos 22:5), and a stack of grain is consumed, אֻכְּלוּ כְּקַשׁ יָבֵשׁ (Nachum 1:10), they were consumed like dry stubble, and וְהַסְּנֶה אֵינֶנּוּ אֻכָּֽל (Shemos 3:2), the bush was not consumed. The noun is מַֽאֲכֹלֶת אֵֽשׁ (Yeshayahu 9:4), food for the fire, and וַיְהִי הָעָם כְּמַֽאֲכֹלֶת אֵשׁ (Yeshayahu 9:18), and the people became like food for the fire.

In the sense of destroying and making an end: וְאָֽכַלְתָּ אֶת־כָּל־הָֽעַמִּים, and you shall consume all the peoples; עַל־כֵּן אָלָה אָכְלָה אֶרֶץ (Yeshayahu 24:6), therefore a curse has devoured the land; and אֶרֶץ אֹכֶלֶת יֽוֹשְׁבֶיהָ (Bamidbar 13:32), a land that eats its dwellers. In the sense of the sword cutting down, הֲלָנֶצַח תֹּאכַל חֶרֶב (Shmuel II 2:26), shall the sword devour for ever: the tav of תֹּאכַל goes with the sword, as if to say, if your sword eats for ever, as in וְחַרְבִּי תֹּאכַל בָּשָׂר (Devarim 32:42), and my sword shall eat flesh. Or else these mean eating in earnest, said by way of figure, as it says אשׁכיר חצי מדם, I will make My arrows drunk with blood, and likewise it says that the sword of Hashem is filled with blood and made fat with fat (Yeshayahu 34:6).

חֶרֶב תְּאֻכְּלוּ (Yeshayahu 1:20), which he reads as בחרב תאכלו, by the sword you will be eaten: if you listen you will eat the good of the land, and if you refuse you will not be eaters but eaten by the sword.

כִּֽי־ יֽוֹכְלוּ אַתִּיקִים מֵהֵנָה (Yechezkel 42:5), for the אַתִּיקִים took from them, which he explains as the corners taking up space from them, and so Targum Yonasan renders. So too in the words of Chazal (Bava Basra 14a), כמה לוחות אוכלות בארון ששה, how much do the luchos take up in the Aron? Six.

more.h: The knife, and all one sense
more.t: The knife too is called מאכלת, for its eating and making an end: וַיִּקַּח אֶת־ הַֽמַּֽאֲכֶלֶת (Bereishis 22:10), he took the knife, and in the plural וּֽמַֽאֲכָלוֹת מְֽתַלְּעֹתָיו (Mishlei 30:14), his jaw teeth are knives. All that come from the root אכל are one sense, he says, since the eating of bread and of any food is itself consuming, burning away and destroying. His father wrote that לְהָכִיל לְמַעַן בָּרָֽק (Yechezkel 21:33), to devour, so that it may flash, is of this root and this sense, its proper form being להאכיל.

סכן.sense: To be of use, to profit. In other senses, to be accustomed; the one set over the treasury, and storehouses; to warm; and מִסְכֵּן, poor.

more.t: הוֹכֵחַ בְּדָבָר לֹא יִסְכּוֹן (Iyov 15:3), arguing with a word that does not profit, and כִּי־תֹאמַר מַה־יִּסְכָּן־לָךְ (Iyov 35:3), for you say, what does it profit you. הַלְאֵל יִסְכָּן־גָּבֶר (Iyov 22:2) he reads as, can a man profit Hashem by his righteousness and the uprightness of his deeds? For a man profits himself alone and not Hashem. The sense of all of them is benefit. Ibn Ezra takes the same words in the sense of reproof, that is, can a man reprove Hashem, or will a wise man reprove between the two of them.

הַסְכֶּן־נָא עִמּוֹ וּשְׁלָם (Iyov 22:21), where Radak says the verb takes an object with the word דְּרָכֶיךָ, your ways, understood: let your ways profit with Him, and be at peace. So too וְכָל־דְּרָכַי הִסְכַּנְתָּה (Tehillim 139:3), and all my ways You have made to profit: he glosses it הועלת, You profited, that is, You put profit in them.

In another sense, הַהַסְכֵּן הִסְכַּנְתִּי (Bamidbar 22:30), which he glosses ההרגל הרגלתי, have I ever been accustomed. הַסְכֶּן־נָא עִמּוֹ can be read of this sense too: be accustomed with Him, so as to be with Him always; and some read וְכָל־דְּרָכַי הִסְכַּנְתָּה so as well, You are accustomed to my ways, that is, You know them always.

more.h: Stores, and the one set over them
more.t: In another sense, בֹּא אֶל־הַסֹּכֵן הַזֶּה (Yeshayahu 22:15), go to this סֹכֵן, which he glosses as the one appointed over the treasury; and so עָרֵי מִסְכְּנוֹת (Shemos 1:11), cities of stores, their sense being storehouses. Rabbi Yonah put וּתְהִי־לוֹ סֹכֶנֶת (Melachim I 1:2), and let her be a סֹכֶנֶת to him, here as well, in the sense of stores. What is correct and straight in Radak's eyes is that סוכנת means one who is of use, as מַה־יִּסְכָּן־לָךְ, what does it profit you: she is to be of use to him against the cold, which is what the pasuk says, וְשָׁכְבָה בְחֵיקֶךָ, and she will lie in your bosom.

It is also read as מחממת, one who warms, and what points to it is וְשָׁכְבָה בְחֵיקֶךָ וְחַם לַאדֹנִי הַמֶּלֶךְ, she will lie in your bosom and my lord the king will be warm. That is, the king did not know her, but she warmed him and lay with him, since she was forbidden to him by לא ירבה לו נשים, he shall not take many wives, and he already had eighteen. So too, in Radak's own view, בּוֹקֵעַ עֵצִים יִסָּכֶן בָּם (Koheles 10:9) is one who splits wood warming himself by it in his labour over it; and in Arabic a hot thing is called א"ל סכו"ן.

Some read יִסָּכֶן בם from סכנה, danger, on the strength of how much Chazal use the word: in the Mishnah, המפרש והיוצא בשיירא (Gittin 6:5), one who sets out to sea and one who goes with a caravan, and והמסוכן, the man in danger; and again, השוחט את המסוכנת (Chullin 2:6), one who slaughters a beast at the point of death. הַמְסֻכָּן תְּרוּמָה (Yeshayahu 40:20) Rabbi Yonah put with the storehouses. Radak himself takes it from טוֹב יֶלֶד מִסְכֵּן (Koheles 4:13), better a poor youth, and הָאִישׁ הַמִּסְכֵּן (Koheles 9:15), the poor man, מִסְכֵּן meaning poor; and so the Targum renders עָנִי (Devarim 24:12), poor, מִסְכֵּן. So the pasuk speaks of the poor man who cannot make his idol of silver and gold as the rich do (Yeshayahu 40:19), and so seeks out for his offering the choicest wood, that will not rot. The noun of this sense is אֶרֶץ אֲשֶׁר לֹא בְמִסְכֵּנֻת (Devarim 8:9), a land where there is no poverty.

חלד.sense: Time: a man's span, or the men of the age; and הַחֹלֶד, a creature named beside the mouse, which Chazal call חולדה, the chuldah.

more.t: מִֽמְתִים מֵחֶלֶד (Tehillim 17:14), from men, from the age, pointed בשש נקודות, with six dots, which he glosses as מאנשי הזמן, from the men of the age; וְחֶלְדִּי כְאַיִן נֶגְדֶּךָ (Tehillim 39:6), my time is as nothing before You; זְכָר־אֲנִי מֶה־ חָלֶד (Tehillim 89:48), remember, as for me, what time is, that is, what my time is; הַֽאֲזִינוּ כָּל־ישְׁבֵי חָֽלֶד (Tehillim 49:2), give ear, all who dwell in the age, the men of the age; and וּֽמִצָּהֳרַיִם יָקוּם חָלֶד (Iyov 11:17), which he reads as your time rising and growing brighter than noon.
הַחֹלֶד וְהָֽעַכְבָּר (Vayikra 11:29), the choled and the mouse. It is the one Chazal (Pesachim 9a) call חולדה, the chuldah, and in la'az מושתיל"א.

חדל.sense: To cease and leave off; and חָדֶל, the age, as though חֶלֶד, time, were turned about.

more.t: עַד כִּֽי־ חָדַל לִסְפֹּר (Bereishis 41:49), until he ceased counting; חָֽדְלוּ גִבּוֹרֵי בָבֶל לְהִלָּחֵם (Yirmiyahu 51:30), the mighty men of Bavel ceased fighting; הַקֹּלוֹת יֶחְדָּלוּן (Shemos 9:29), the thunder will cease; חֲדַל מִמֶּנּוּ וְנַֽעַבְדָה אֶת־מִצְרָיִם (Shemos 14:12), leave us be and let us serve Mitzrayim; and מֵֽחֲדֹל לְהִתְפַּלֵּל בַּֽעַדְכֶם (Shmuel I 12:23), from ceasing to daven for you. חָדְלוּ רֹגֶז (Iyov 3:17) he reads as חדלו מעשות רוגז, they ceased from making agitation.

The description is חָדֵל, ceasing, as וַֽחֲדַל אִישִׁים (Yeshayahu 53:3), ceasing of men; and where the verb takes an object, הֶֽחֳדַלְתִּי אֶת־דִּשְׁנִי (Shoftim 9:9), shall I leave off my fatness, where the chet takes a kamatz for the beauty of the thing.

עִם־יוֹשְׁבֵי חָֽדֶל (Yeshayahu 38:11), which he glosses as יושבי הזמן, the dwellers of the age; it is as it were מִֽמְתִים מֵחֶלֶד (Tehillim 17:14), from men of the age, turned about. The description from it is מֶה־ חָדֵל אָֽנִי (Tehillim 39:5), what my span is; and some read וְיֶחְדָּל in שְׁעֵה מֵעָלָיו וְיֶחְדָּל (Iyov 14:6), turn away from him, in this sense.

טוב.sense: Good; also rich and full, and fair to look at; to do well; and the noun, goodness.

more.t: מַה־ טֹּבוּ אֹֽהָלֶיךָ יַֽעֲקֹב (Bamidbar 24:5), how good are your tents, Yaakov; וַיַּרְא אֱלֹהִים אֶת־הָאוֹר כִּי־ טוֹב (Bereishis 1:4), Hashem saw the light, that it was good; הֲטוֹבָה הִוא אִם־רָעָה (Bamidbar 13:19), is it good or bad; צַדִּקִים וְטֹבִים מִמֶּנּוּ (Melachim I 2:32), more righteous and better than he; and הֱטִיבוֹתָ כִּי הָיָה עִם־לְבָבֶֽךָ, you did well that it was in your heart.

וַנִּשְׂבַּֽע־לֶחֶם וַנִּֽהְיֶה טוֹבִים (Yirmiyahu 44:17), we had our fill of bread and were good, which he glosses as עשירים ומלאים, rich and full. כִּי טֹבֹת הֵנָּה (Bereishis 6:2), that they were good, he glosses as יפות, beautiful, and שֶׁבַע פָּרֹת הַטֹּבֹת (Bereishis 41:26), the seven good cows, as שמנות ויפות, fat and fair. So too בָּחוּר וָטוֹב (Shmuel I 9:2), a young man and fair, and וְאֵין אִישׁ מִבְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל טוֹב מִמֶּנּוּ (Shmuel I 9:2), no man of Yisrael fairer than he, which he glosses as fair of appearance, as Targum Yonasan renders שַׁפִּיר, fair.

טוֹבָתִי בַּל־עָלֶֽיךָ (Tehillim 16:2), my good is not upon You, and without the heh וְהָיָה הַטּוֹב הַהוּא (Bamidbar 10:32), and that good will be. When it is bound the cholam turns to a shuruk: וְרַב־ טוּב לְבֵית יִשְׂרָאֵל (Yeshayahu 63:7), great goodness to the house of Yisrael, טוּב הָאָרֶץ תֹּאכֵֽלוּ (Yeshayahu 1:19), you will eat the good of the land, and אֲנִי אַֽעֲבִיר כָּל־ טוּבִי עַל־פָּנֶיךָ (Shemos 33:19), I will pass all My goodness before you.

One can also say that טוֹב with the cholam is an adjective and טוּב with the shuruk a noun, the same whether bound or standing alone, and he calls this the right account, since מִבְחַר וְטֽוֹב ־לְבָנוֹן (Yechezkel 31:16), the choice and the good of Levanon, is bound and still keeps the cholam.

שׁפר.sense: To be fair, as the Targum renders יְפֵה תֹאַר by שַׁפִּיר; the shofar; and אֶשְׁפָּר, a portion of meat, which may be a fair portion.

more.t: אַף־נַֽחֲלָת שָֽׁפְרָה עָלָֽי (Tehillim 16:6), my inheritance is fair to me, and הַנֹּתֵן אִמְרֵי־ שָֽׁפֶר (Bereishis 49:21), who gives fair words. The Targum of יְפֵה־תֹאַר (Bereishis 39:6), fair of form, is שַׁפִּיר בְּרֵיוָא, fair in appearance, and so in Aramaic מִלְכִּי יִשְׁפַּר עֲלָיךְ (Daniel 4:24), let my counsel be fair in your sight.

Like them is בְּרוּחוֹ שָׁמַיִם שִׁפְרָה (Iyov 26:13), by His wind the heavens were made fair. As to its form, either the beis of ברוחו is added, or the heh of שפרה is; or the word is of four letters, on the pattern of מְתַֽחֲרֶה בָאָרֶז (Yirmiyahu 22:15), vying with the cedar. Some explain שִׁפְרָה as He spread them like a tent, from שַׁפְרִירוֹ (Yirmiyahu 43:10), his tent, the heh standing in place of the doubled letter, as בָּֽזְאוּ נְהָרִים (Yeshayahu 18:2), rivers have plundered, is like בזזו.

שׁוֹפַר תְּרוּעָה (Vayikra 25:9), a shofar of teruah, and שֽׁוֹפְרוֹת הַיּֽוֹבְלִים (Yehoshua 6:4), the shofros of the yovel: the word is known. כַּשּׁוֹפָר הָרֵם קוֹלֶךָ (Yeshayahu 58:1), like the shofar raise your voice: as you would blow on a shofar, so raise your voice.

וְאֶשְׁפָּר אֶחָד (Shmuel II 6:19), and one אֶשְׁפָּר: the alef is added, and the word means a portion of meat. It may be drawn from the first sense, that is, a fair portion. Chazal (Pesachim 36b) made it a word compounded of three, saying אחד מששה בפר, one of six in a bull.

ריח.sense: To smell, a sense he calls known, and by extension to sense a thing; רֵחַיִם, millstones, may be of this root as well.

more.t: אַף לָהֶם וְלֹא יְרִיחֽוּן (Tehillim 115:6), they have a nose and do not smell; אֶת־רֵיחַ הַנִּיחֹחַ (Bereishis 8:21), the pleasing scent, which Hashem smelled; and וְלֹא אָרִיחַ בְּרֵיחַ נִיחֹֽחֲכֶֽם (Vayikra 26:31), I will not smell the scent of your sweet savours. Of the sense itself he says only that it is known.

וּמֵרָחוֹק יָרִיחַ מִלְחָמָה (Iyov 39:25), from afar he smells the battle, is said by way of extension, that is, he senses it; so too בַּהֲרִיחוֹ אֵשׁ (Shoftim 16:9), when it senses fire, and וַֽהֲרִיחוֹ (Yeshayahu 11:3), his smelling in the fear of Hashem, that is, by the least hint he will recognize that one is righteous. That is what it says there, that he will not judge by the sight of his eyes, for smell is the lightest of the senses.

רחים, millstones, may be of this root: לֹא־יַֽחֲבֹל רֵחַיִם וָרָכֶב (Devarim 24:6), he shall not take the millstones or the upper stone in pledge, and קְחִי רֵחַיִם וְטַֽחֲנִי קָמַח (Yeshayahu 47:2), take the millstones and grind meal. Since they are two stones the word is said in the dual. The lower stone alone is called רחים, since it is the main part of the work of the two and the larger, and the upper is called רֶכֶב, the upper stone; that is why the pasuk names both.

It can further be read that the word is said of the two together and not of the lower alone, since the lower by itself is called שֶׁכֶב, the lower stone, as the upper is called רֶכֶב, the upper stone, as the Mishnah says (Bava Basra 2:1) that the millstones are kept three from the lower stone, which is four from the upper. The pasuk then means that one may not take the millstones in pledge, which are the two, and not even the upper alone, since the work is not done but by both together; and it names the upper alone and not the lower because the upper is the easier to take, the lower being fixed in place.

תמר.sense: The palm, even and straight, with no branches until its crown; from it, carved palm figures, and columns of smoke, a tall straight thing being likened to the palm.

more.t: זֹאת קֽוֹמָתֵךְ דָּֽמְתָה לְתָמָר (Shir HaShirim 7:8), your stature is like a palm, גַּם־ תָּמָר וְתַפּוּחַ (Yoel 1:12), the palm and the apple too, and וְשִׁבְעִים תְּמָרִים (Shemos 15:27), and seventy palms: the tree, he says, is known.

From it, כְּתֹמֶר מִקְשָׁה (Yirmiyahu 10:5), which he explains as like a palm that is even and straight, since the palm puts out no branches until high up at its crown, and all its trunk below is even and straight. And with a cholam, וְהִיא יוֹשֶׁבֶת תַּֽחַת־ תֹּמֶר (Shoftim 4:5), she sat under a palm.

From it too, וְתִֽמֹרָה בֵּין־כְּרוּב לִכְרוּב (Yechezkel 41:18), a palm figure between keruv and keruv, מִקְלְעוֹת כְּרוּבִים וְתִמֹרֹת (Melachim I 6:29), carvings of keruvim and palm figures, and וְאֶל־אַיִל תִּֽמֹרִֽים (Yechezkel 40:16), palm figures on the post. Some of them Targum Yonasan renders צורת דקלים, the form of palms, and some כוֹתְרָן, crowns.

Likewise וְתִֽימְרוֹת עשׁן (Yoel 3:3), columns of smoke: because the palm is a tall straight tree, a tall straight thing is likened to it. So too עַמּוּד עָשָׁן (Shoftim 20:40), a pillar of smoke, and Chazal's words of smoke (Chullin 112a; Berachos 43a), משתעלה העשן תמרתו, once the smoke raises its column. They said too (Yoma 38a) that the house of Avtinas were expert in compounding the ketores and would not teach it, and craftsmen brought from Alexandria of Mitzrayim could compound as they did but could not raise the smoke as they did: theirs went up in a column, straight as a stick, while the others' scattered this way and that.

ענג.sense: Taking delight: delighting oneself, and pleasantness in the soul's enjoyment.

more.t: וְהִתְעַנַּגְתֶּם מִזִּיז כְּבוֹדָֽהּ (Yeshayahu 66:11), you will delight in the abundance of her glory; וְהִתְעַנְּגוּ עַל־רֹב שָׁלֽוֹם (Tehillim 37:11), they will delight in abundant peace; וְתִתְעַנַּג בַּדֶּשֶׁן נַפְשְׁכֶֽם (Yeshayahu 55:2), let your soul delight in fatness; and מֵֽהִתְעַנֵּג וּמֵרֹךְ (Devarim 28:56), from delighting herself and from tenderness.

בְּהֵיכְלֵי עֹנֶג (Yeshayahu 13:22), palaces of delight; with a tav added, לֹֽא־נָאוֶה לִכְסִיל תַּֽעֲנוּג (Mishlei 19:10), delight is not fitting for a fool, and in the feminine plural וְתַֽעֲנֻגוֹת בְּנֵי הָאָדָם (Koheles 2:8), the delights of men. The adjective is וְהֶֽעָנֹג מְאֹד (Devarim 28:54), the one who lives in great delight, and הָֽרַכָּה בְךָ וְהָֽעֲנֻגָּה (Devarim 28:56), the tender woman among you and the one who lives in delight. Its sense is delighting oneself, and pleasantness in the soul's enjoyment.

פנק.sense: To pamper, מענגו ומעדנו, giving one delight and indulgence: מְפַנֵּק מִנֹּעַר עַבְדּוֹ (Mishlei 29:21), one who pampers his servant from his youth.

more.t: One line. He glosses מְפַנֵּק as מענגו ומעדנו, giving him delight and delicacy, and notes that the Targum of מַֽעֲדַנֵּי־מֶֽלֶךְ (Bereishis 49:20), royal delicacies, is תַפְנוּקֵי מַלְכִין, the delights of kings.

זבל.sense: To dwell with, for a dwelling is called זבול, as in בֵּית זְבֻל, a house of dwelling.

more.t: הַפַּעַם יִזְבְּלֵנִי אִישִׁי (Bereishis 30:20), this time my husband will dwell with me: its sense is ידור עמי, he will dwell with me, for a dwelling is called זבול. בָּנֹה בָנִיתִי בֵּית זְבֻל לָךְ (Melachim I 8:13), I have built You a house of dwelling; and with a heh added, שֶׁמֶשׁ יָרֵחַ עָמַד זְבֻלָה (Chavakuk 3:11), the sun and the moon stood in their dwelling.

ארם.sense: אַרְמוֹן, the great and high house, a palace; its alef may be an added letter, and he takes the word up again at the root רום.

more.t: כִּֽי־ אַרְמוֹן נֻטָּשׁ (Yeshayahu 32:14), for the palace is forsaken, and וְאַרְמוֹן עַל־מִשְׁפָּטוֹ יֵשֵֽׁב (Yirmiyahu 30:18), and the palace will sit in its rightful place, on the pattern of פַּֽעֲמוֹן, a bell. The plural is feminine, אַרְמְנוֹת בֶּן־הֲדָֽד (Amos 1:4), the palaces of Ben Hadad, and וְאָכְלָה אַרְמְנֹתֶֽיהָ (Amos 1:7), and it will devour her palaces, where the cholam falls away. That is either because the word is bound, since unbound one says אַרְמוֹנוֹת, palaces, or, and this he holds right, because it is another pattern altogether, one that does not change when bound; and indeed עַל־ אַרְמְנוֹת בְּאַשְׁדּוֹד (Amos 3:9), on the palaces in Ashdod, is not bound and still has the sheva, unless such forms are bound to the serving letter, as the language does in places.

וְהִשְׁלַכְתֶּנָה הַֽהַרְמוֹנָה (Amos 4:3), and you shall be cast to the palace, with a heh in place of the alef. Its sense is the great and high house; the alef in the word may itself be added, and he will bring it again at the root רום. Targum Yonasan renders that phrase וְיִגְלוּן יַתְהוֹן לְהָלְאָא מִן טוּרֵי חַרְמִינֵי, they will exile them beyond the mountains of Charmini; Yonasan renders מִנִּי וְאַשְׁכְּנָז (Yirmiyahu 51:27), Minni and Ashkenaz, as הוּרְמִינֵי, Hurmini; and he renders וּלְמִנִּי מָצוֹר וְעַד־נָהָר (Michah 7:12), and from Matzor up to the river, with חוּרְמִינִי רַבְּתָא, great Churmini.

פכה.sense: Coming out, of water; and from this the flask of oil is called פַּךְ, since the oil is brought out and emptied from it.

more.t: וְהִנֵּה־מַיִם מְפַכִּים (Yechezkel 47:2), and behold, water coming out: he glosses the word יוצאים, coming out. From this the flask is called פַּךְ השמן, the cruse of oil, since the oil is brought out and emptied from it.

אפל.sense: Darkness; since the pasuk says חשֶׁךְ וַֽאֲפֵלָה, darkness and gloom, the אֲפֵלָה seems more than the darkness. אֲפִילֹת: dark and hidden underground, or late.

more.t: חשֶׁךְ וַֽאֲפֵלָה (Yoel 2:2), darkness and gloom; בַּֽאֲפֵלוֹת נְהַלֵּֽךְ (Yeshayahu 59:9), we walk in gloom; and the adjective וְאָפֵל וְלֹֽא־נֹגַֽהּ לֽוֹ (Amos 5:20), dark, with no brightness to it. Since it says darkness and אֲפֵלָה together, it seems that the אֲפֵלָה is more than the darkness. Another pattern is וַתֹּפַע כְּמוֹ־ אֹֽפֶל (Iyov 10:22), and it shines like the dark, and a third is מַֽאֲפֵל, as וַיָּשֶׂם מַֽאֲפֵל בֵּינֵיכֶם וּבֵין הַמִּצְרִים (Yehoshua 24:7), and He put darkness between you and the Egyptians.

אֶרֶץ מַאְפֵּלְיָה (Yirmiyahu 2:31), a land of deep darkness: in all books it is one word, but its sense is two, and some exact books point it מְאַפֵּלְיָה. The divine Name is joined to מאפל for the greatness of the darkness, as in שַׁלְהֶבֶתְיָֽה (Shir HaShirim 8:6) it is joined for the greatness of the flame; and so anything that is to be made great is joined to the Name: כְּֽהַרְרֵי־אֵל (Tehillim 36:7), like the mountains of Hashem, עִיר־גְּדוֹלָה לֵֽאלֹהִים (Yonah 3:3), a city great to Hashem, and וַתְּהִי לְחֶרְדַּת אֱלֹהִֽים (Shmuel I 14:15), and it became a trembling of Hashem. Or מאפליה is an adjective for the land, and its yud is a yud of relation, like the yud of תחתיה, lower, and שׁלישׁיה, third.

כִּי אֲפִילֹת הֵֽנָּה (Shemos 9:32), for they are אֲפִילֹת: dark and hidden under the ground, or else late. So in the words of Chazal (Taanis 3b), הא בחרפי הא באפלי, this of the early and this of the late, and they spoke (Shekalim 1:3) of a year that was אפלה, a late year, in which the growths could not be made out.

מות.sense: To die, or to be dead, and מָוֶת is death. Where the verb takes an object, it means to put a man to death.

more.h: Death that may fall short of dying
more.t: וַיָּמָת לִבּוֹ בְּקִרְבּוֹ (Shmuel I 25:37), his heart died within him: he was struck dumb and was as a dead man, or else he died outright. וַיָּמָת תַּחְתָּיו מִפְּנֵי הָֽרָעָב (Yirmiyahu 38:9), and he died where he was because of the famine, means near to death. And לָמָּה נָמוּת לְעֵינֶיךָ גַּם־אֲנַחְנוּ גַּם־אַדְמָתֵנוּ (Bereishis 47:19), why should we die before your eyes, both we and our land: for ground lying waste is like a dead thing, not bringing out grass and fruit trees as it should.

more.h: Death as tzaraas, as Chazal read it
more.t: בִּשְׁנַת־ מוֹת הַמֶּלֶךְ עֻזִּיָּהוּ (Yeshayahu 6:1), in the year of the death of King Uziyahu: Chazal explained it, in the Yalkut in the name of the Yelamdenu, as the year he was struck with tzaraas, as אַל־נָא תְהִי כַּמֵּת (Bamidbar 12:12), let her not be as one dead; and so Targum Yonasan, בְּשַׁתָּא דְאִתְנַגַע בָּהּ מַלְכָּא, in the year the king was stricken.

more.h: Why death comes in the plural
more.t: The plural: מוֹתֵי עֲרֵלִים תָּמוּת בְּיַד־זָרִים (Yechezkel 28:10), you shall die the deaths of the uncircumcised by the hand of strangers; מְמוֹתֵי תַֽחֲלֻאִים יָמֻתוּ (Yirmiyahu 16:4), they shall die deaths of sicknesses; מְמוֹתֵי חָלָל בְּלֵב יַמִּֽים (Yechezkel 28:8), the deaths of the slain in the heart of the seas. Death is spoken of in the plural because a man is sometimes put to death by many stabs, or by hard sufferings; and in the heart of the seas because one who drowns does not die all at once. בְּנֵי תְמוּתָֽה (Tehillim 79:11), sons of death, is another form of the noun.

Targum Yonasan renders וּכְבוֹדוֹ מְתֵי רָעָב (Yeshayahu 5:13) as וְיַקִירֵהוֹן מִיתוּ בְכַפְנָא, their honoured men died of hunger, taking it in this sense, of dying. By the way of grammar that is not sound, because of the sheva under the mem.

more.h: Chastening a son, as some read it
more.t: Some explain וְאֶל־ הֲמִיתוֹ אַל־תִּשָּׂא נַפְשֶֽׁךָ (Mishlei 19:18), and do not set your soul on putting him to death, from this root; Radak gives their reading as: chasten your son gently, not so as to kill him with blows. He has already explained the pasuk himself at the root הָמָה.

פטר.sense: Sending away and opening: to slip away, to dismiss, to be exempt; the firstborn, פֶּטֶר כָּל־רֶחֶם, is so called as the sending out and first opening of the womb.

more.t: וַיִּפְטַר מִפְּנֵי שָׁאוּל (Shmuel I 19:10), and he slipped away from before Shaul, is intransitive. Transitive, it is to dismiss: כִּי לֹֽא־ פָטַר יְהֽוֹיָדָע הַכֹּהֵן אֶת־הַמַּחְלְקֽוֹת (Divrei HaYamim II 23:8), for Yehoyada the kohen did not dismiss the divisions, meaning that he did not send them away nor let them go but held them back, as it says there, באי השבת עם יוצאי השבת, those coming in on Shabbos with those going out on Shabbos.

The word is common in the Mishnah as פטור, exempt, whose opposite is חייב, liable. So פְּטוּרִים (Divrei HaYamim I 9:33) is explained: exempt from other work, since they were busy with the work of song day and night and sat in the chambers.

פּוֹטֵֽר מַיִם רֵאשִׁית מָדוֹן (Mishlei 17:14), one who lets out water is the beginning of strife: like one who sends the water out and opens it first, and it runs so that no man can bring it back; so is the beginning of strife. And יַפְטִירוּ בְשָׂפָה (Tehillim 22:8), they send the words out with the lip and open them.

פֶּטֶר כָּל־רֶחֶם (Shemos 13:2), the opening of every womb, and in the feminine, in construct, פִּטְרַת כָּל־רֶחֶם (Bamidbar 8:16), are ענין השלוח והפתיחה, a sense of sending out and of opening. The Targum renders וְהָֽאֲנָשִׁים שֻׁלְּחוּ (Bereishis 44:3), and the men were sent away, as וְגֻבְרַיָּא אִתְפַּטָּרוּ, and the men were sent off, and וְשַׁלַּח רְצוּצִים חָפְשִׁים (Yeshayahu 58:6), and to send the crushed away free, as וּפַטָרוּ דַהֲווֹ אֲנוּסִין בְּנֵי חוֹרִין, and release those who were oppressed as free men. The firstborn is called so because he is the sending out of the womb, its opening and its first breaking through; and so וּפְטוּרֵי צִצִּים (Melachim I 6:18), openings of buds, where the buds and blossoms opened out.

בושׁ.sense: To be ashamed, with בוּשָׁה and בֹשֶׁת, shame; and another sense, lateness, being long in coming.

more.t: בְּךָ בָטְחוּ וְלֹא־ בֽוֹשׁוּ (Tehillim 22:6), in You they trusted and were not ashamed; כִּי בְֹשְׁתִּי לִשְׁאוֹל מִן־הַמֶּלֶךְ (Ezra 8:22), for I was ashamed to ask of the king; and the reflexive, וְלֹא יִתְבּשָֽׁשׁוּ (Bereishis 2:25), and they were not ashamed. בּוֹשָׁה וְחָפֵרָה (Yirmiyahu 15:9), she is ashamed and disgraced, is stressed on the earlier syllable, and וּבוֹשָׁה הַֽחַמָּה (Yeshayahu 24:23), and the sun shall be ashamed, on the last. In the heavy form: וּמְשַׂנְאֵינוּ הֱבִישֽׁוֹתָ (Tehillim 44:8), and our haters You have put to shame; עֲצַת־עָנִי תָבִישׁוּ (Tehillim 14:6), you would shame the counsel of the poor; הֱבִשֹׁתָה כִּֽי־אֱלֹהִים מְאָסָֽם (Tehillim 53:6), You have put them to shame, for Hashem has rejected them; מֵבִישׁ וּמַחְפִּֽיר (Mishlei 19:26), one who shames and disgraces; and וּכְרָקָב בְּעַצְמוֹתָיו מְבִישָֽׁה (Mishlei 12:4), and she who shames is as rot in his bones.

more.h: Shame, and with an added nun
more.t: The nouns are תְּכַסְּךָ בוּשָׁה (Ovadiah 1:10), shame shall cover you, and וּבשֶׁת פָּנַי כִּסָּֽתְנִי (Tehillim 44:16), and the shame of my face has covered me; and with a nun added, בָּשְׁנָה אֶפְרַיִם יִקָּח (Hoshea 10:6), Ephraim shall take shame. Rabbi Yonah wrote that the nun was added to disgrace the Baal, that it should be called בשנה, as in וְהַבֹּשֶׁת אָֽכְלָה אֶת־יְגִיעַ אֲבוֹתֵינוּ (Yirmiyahu 3:24), the shameful thing devoured our fathers' toil. It can also be taken at its plain sense, as the same pasuk says וְיֵבוֹשׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל מֵֽעֲצָתֽוֹ, Yisrael will be ashamed of its counsel.

וְהֶֽחֱזִיקָה בִּמְבֻשָֽׁיו (Devarim 25:11), and she takes hold of his testicles, which are the place of shame. So עֶרְיָה־ בֹשֶׁת (Michah 1:11), nakedness of shame, is nakedness uncovered, as וַֽחֲשׂוּפַי שֵׁת (Yeshayahu 20:4), with their nakedness bared.

וַיָּחִילוּ עַד־ בֹּוֹשׁ (Shoftim 3:25), and they waited until it was late, and וַיִּפְצְרוּ־בוֹ עַד־ בֹּשׁ (Melachim II 2:17), and they pressed him until it was late; בֹשֵׁשׁ מֹשֶׁה (Shemos 32:1), Moshe was late, and מַדּוּעַ בֹּשֵׁשׁ רִכְבּוֹ לָבוֹא (Shoftim 5:28), why is his chariot late in coming. The sense is ענין איחור, lateness.

אחר.sense: Behind and after: אָחוֹר, the back, and also the west; אַֽחֲרִית, the end, and so a deed's reward; also those who remain after a man; אַחֵר, another; the verb, to tarry.

more.t: וַיֵּֽלְכוּ אֲחֹרַנִּית (Bereishis 9:23), they went backwards. On וְאַתָּה הֲסִבֹּתָ אֶת־לִבָּם אֲחֹֽרַנִּֽית (Melachim I 18:37) Rav Saadiah reads: You have turned their heart, which until now was backward. Radak's father reads it of turning their heart back from the faith of the Baal, since they recognized that its molten image was falsehood.

טוֹב אַֽחֲרִית דָּבָר מֵרֵֽאשִׁיתוֹ (Koheles 7:8), the end of a matter is better than its beginning. Reward is called אַֽחֲרִית because it is the close of the deed: כִּי אִם־יֵשׁ אַֽחֲרִית וְתִקְוָתְךָ לֹא תִכָּרֵֽת (Mishlei 23:18), for surely there is an end, and your hope will not be cut off, and לָתֵת לָכֶם אַֽחֲרִית וְתִקְוָֽה (Yirmiyahu 29:11), to give you an end and a hope.

Men's children are called אַֽחֲרִית because they are left after them, וְאַֽחֲרִיתָם בַּחֶרֶב אֶהֱרֹג (Amos 9:1), which he says is spoken of the people; so וְלֹא לְאַֽחֲרִיתוֹ (Daniel 11:4), that he did not leave the kingship to his son. In וְאַֽחֲרִיתֵךְ בַּחֶרֶב תִּפּוֹל (Yechezkel 23:25) it is your people: the pasuk had said אַפֵּךְ וְאָזְנַיִךְ, your nose and your ears, a figure for the heads, and the head is first to the people, going out and coming in before them, while the people are the end. Targum Yonasan renders עַמִיךְ, your people.

more.h: The back, and so the west
more.t: The western side is called אָחוֹר, as וְאָחוֹר וְֽלֹא־אָבִין לֽוֹ (Iyov 23:8), and to the west, and I do not perceive Him; and the western sea is הַיָּם הָאַֽחֲרוֹן (Devarim 11:24), because the face is the east and the back the west, a man's face being toward the rising of the sun. On that same order the south is called ימין, the right, and the north שמאל, the left. And אַחֵר is another than oneself: וְאִישׁ אַחֵר יִקָּחֶֽנָּה (Devarim 20:7), and another man will take her, and בְּגָדִים אֲחֵרִים (Vayikra 6:4), other garments.

Of a man whose doings are at the end and in waiting: לַֽמְאַֽחֲרִים עַל־הַיָּיִן (Mishlei 23:30), those who stay all day until evening over the drinking of wine, as מְאַֽחֲרֵי בַנֶּשֶׁף (Yeshayahu 5:11); and so מְאַֽחֲרֵי ־שֶׁבֶת (Tehillim 127:2), busy at their work all day until evening. His father writes that כִּי־בֹא יָבֹא לֹא יְאַחֵֽר (Chavakuk 2:3) is not like these, but means it will not come at the end, from אַֽחֲרִית which is the end, and so Targum Yonasan renders לְאָחֽוֹר (Yeshayahu 42:23) as לְסוֹפָא, at the end.

Rabbi Yonah brought a further sense into this root for יִרְבּוּ עַצְּבוֹתָם אַחֵר מָהָרוּ (Tehillim 16:4), reading it as a prayer that the sorrows of those who hurry to strife may increase. Radak holds that wrong, since the root מהר is not found in the light form in the sense of haste, only in the sense of a marriage payment, מָהֹר יִמְהָרֶנָּה לּוֹ לְאִשָּֽׁה (Shemos 22:15). The right reading in his eyes is from the second sense, another: the sorrows of those who pay a marriage price to another god will increase, that is, they give gifts to another god and offer and pour out to it; the close of the pasuk proves it, בַּל־אַסִּיךְ נִסְכֵּיהֶם מִדָּם, I will not pour out their libations of blood.

נכר.sense: To recognize. A second sense, its opposite: denial and strangeness, and from it נֵכָר and נָכְרִי, the foreign. A third: to hand over.

more.t: וְלֹא נִכַּר ־שׁוֹעַ לִפְנֵי־דָל (Iyov 34:19), and the noble is not recognized before the poor; לֹא נִכְּרוּ בַּחוּצוֹת (Eichah 4:8), they were not recognized in the streets. וְלֹא הִכִּירוֹ כִּֽי־הָיוּ יָדָיו (Bereishis 27:23), he did not recognize him because his hands were so; וְאֵינָם מַכִּירִים לְדַבֵּר יְהוּדִית (Nechemiah 13:24), they did not know how to speak Yehudis; לֹֽא־ תַכִּירוּ פָנִים בַּמִּשְׁפָּט (Devarim 1:17), you shall not recognize faces in judgment, and הַֽכֵּר ־פָּנִים לֹֽא־טוֹב (Mishlei 28:21), recognizing faces is not good. The noun is הַכָּרַת פְּנֵיהֶם עָנְתָה בָּם (Yeshayahu 3:9), the recognition of their faces testifies against them. Of all this he says ענין ההכרה ידוע, the sense of recognizing is known.

גַּם בְּמַֽעֲלָלָיו יִתְנַכֶּר ־נָעַר (Mishlei 20:11), even by his doings a lad makes himself known, stands among the forms of recognizing. His father explained it as the reverse of recognizing, which Radak spells out: by his doings the lad makes himself a stranger, for if what he does is clean and upright, people say this is no lad's doing.

The second sense, the opposite of the first: בְּיוֹם נָכְרוֹ (Ovadiah 1:12), on the day of his estrangement, an infinitive; וַֽיְנַכְּרוּ אֶת־הַמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה (Yirmiyahu 19:4), they made this place strange; פֶּן־ יְנַכְּרוּ צָרֵימוֹ (Devarim 32:27), lest their foes deny it; וַיִּתְנַכֵּר אֲלֵיהֶם (Bereishis 42:7), he made himself a stranger to them; וְהִיא מִתְנַכֵּרָֽה (Melachim I 14:5), and she was making herself a stranger. The sense is ענין ההכחשה והזרות, denial and strangeness.

From this sense, the adjective: כָּל־בֶּן־ נֵכָר (Shemos 12:43), any foreigner; אֱלֹהֵי נֵֽכַר ־הָאָרֶץ (Devarim 31:16), the gods of the foreigners of the land; and with a yud, אִישׁ נָכְרִי (Devarim 17:15), a foreign man, מַלְבּוּשׁ נָכְרִֽי (Tzefaniah 1:8), foreign clothing, הֲלוֹא נָכְרִיּוֹת נֶחְשַׁבְנוּ לוֹ (Bereishis 31:15), are we not reckoned to him as strangers. The right account, he holds, is that נֶכֶר is both a noun and an adjective: in לְאֵל נֵכָֽר (Tehillim 81:10), to a foreign god, it is an adjective, and so in כָּל־בֶּן־נֵכָר; those upon which the construct falls are nouns, as וּבְנֵי הַנֵּכָר (Yeshayahu 56:5 in his edition), and the sons of the foreigner, and אֱלֹהֵי הַנֵּכָר (Bereishis 35:2), the gods of the foreigner.
נִכַּר אֹתוֹ אֱלֹהִים בְּיָדִי (Shmuel I 23:7), Elokim has handed him over into my hand, which he glosses מסר והסגיר, gave him over and delivered him up.

זור.sense: To press; a blow is called מָזוֹר because it is pressed, and so is its healing. Another sense, near the first, is to sneeze; another, to be strange or estranged.

more.t: וַיָּזַר אֶת־הַגִּזָּה (Shoftim 6:38), he pressed the fleece; וַתִּשְׁכַּח כִּי־רֶגֶל תְּזוּרֶהָ (Iyov 39:15), and she forgets that a foot may press it; וְהַזּוּרֶה תִּבָּקַע אֶפְעֶֽה (Yeshayahu 59:5), and the pressed one splits open into a viper, where the segol stands in place of a kamatz. Of it he says ענין מעיכה ידוע, the sense of pressing is known.

לֹא־ זֹרוּ וְלֹא חֻבָּשׁוּ (Yeshayahu 1:6), they were not pressed and not bound up: on the view of Rabbi Yehudah the grammarian it is a form whose doer is not named. In Radak's own view it is a past verb standing without an object, on the pattern of מַה־טֹּבוּ אֹֽהָלֶיךָ יַֽעֲקֹב (Bamidbar 24:5), how goodly are your tents, Yaakov; and though this root takes an object in the light form, so we find אָז הָֽלְמוּ עִקְּבֵי־סוּס (Shoftim 5:22), then the horses' hooves hammered, standing without one beside הֲלָמוּנִי בַּל־יָדָעְתִּי (Mishlei 23:35), they struck me, I did not know it, which takes one. On זֹרוּ רְשָׁעִים מֵרָחֶם (Tehillim 58:4), the wicked are estranged from the womb, he says it may be a light past or, on Rabbi Yonah's view, a form whose doer is not named.

more.h: מָזוֹר, the wound and the cure
more.t: A blow is called מָזוֹר because it is pressed: וְלֹֽא־יִגְהֶה מִכֶּם מָזֽוֹר (Hoshea 5:13), and he will not heal the wound from you, and וַיַּרְא אֶפְרַיִם אֶת־חָלְיוֹ וִֽיהוּדָה אֶת־ מְזֹרוֹ (Hoshea 5:13), Efrayim saw his sickness and Yehudah his wound. The healing is called מָזוֹר too, since healing comes by pressing the wound, as לֹא־ זֹרוּ וְלֹא חֻבָּשׁוּ (Yeshayahu 1:6), they were not pressed and not bound up, and אֵֽין־דָּן דִּינֵךְ לְמָזוֹר (Yirmiyahu 30:13), none judges your cause for healing.

וַיְזוֹרֵר הַנַּעַר (Melachim II 4:35), the lad sneezed, which he gives in the vernacular, and the Targum of עֲטִישֹׁתָיו תָּהֶל אוֹר (Iyov 41:10), his sneezes flash forth light, is זְרִירוֹי, his sneezes. This too is near the first sense, since a man in sneezing presses himself.

רוּחִֽי זָרָה לְאִשְׁתִּי (Iyov 19:17), my spirit is strange to my wife; לֹא־ זָרוּ מִתַּֽאֲוָתָם (Tehillim 78:30), they were not estranged from their craving; לְאִישׁ זָר (Vayikra 22:12), to a strange man; מוּזָר הָיִיתִי לְאֶחָי (Tehillim 69:9), I became a stranger to my brothers; נָזֹרוּ אָחֽוֹר (Yeshayahu 1:4), they are estranged, gone backward; and וְהָיָה לָכֶם לְזָרָא (Bamidbar 11:20), and it will be a thing estranged to you, where the alef stands in place of a heh. All of these are ענין התנכרות וזרות, a sense of estrangement and strangeness.

מַיִם זָרִים קָרִים נוֹזְלִֽים (Yirmiyahu 18:14), strange waters, cold and flowing, are waters coming from a strange and distant place, as though strangers to the place they flow in. כְּמַהְפֵּכַת זָרִֽים (Yeshayahu 1:7) is the overturning by strange men from a far land, who when they come on a city and take it overturn and destroy everything, having no mind to stay in it, which neighbours do not do. In וְשִׁלַּחְתִּי לְבָבֶל זָרִים וְזֵרוּהָ (Yirmiyahu 51:2), I will send strangers to Bavel and they will scatter her, one word plays on the other, וְזֵרוּהָ being from זְרֵה ־הָלְאָה (Bamidbar 17:2), scatter afar, and of that root; though it may be of this root, and then: I will send foreigners to Bavel and they will make her a stranger in all she has, taking everything and plundering her.

דלה.sense: To draw water; the דְּלִי is the bucket one draws with. Also to lift up, and דָּלִיּוֹת are boughs, branches raised and high.

more.t: וְגַם־ דָּלֹה דָלָה לָנוּ (Shemos 2:19), and he even drew for us; וַתָּבֹאנָה וַתִּדְלֶנָה (Shemos 2:16), and they came and drew; וְאִישׁ תְּבוּנָה יִדְלֶֽנָּה (Mishlei 20:5), and a man of understanding will draw it out. The noun is in כְּמַר מִדְּלִי (Yeshayahu 40:15), as a drop from a bucket: the דְּלִי is the vessel they draw with.

כִּי דִלִּיתָנִי (Tehillim 30:2), for You have lifted me up, which he glosses רוממתני, You have raised me high. And in לִפְנוֹת דָּֽלִיּוֹתָיו אֵלָיו (Yechezkel 17:6), for its boughs to turn toward him, and בְּצֵל דָּֽלִיּוֹתָיו תִּשְׁכֹּֽנָּה (Yechezkel 17:23), in the shade of its boughs they shall dwell, the דליות are ענפים הרמים והגבוהים, branches raised and high.

יִֽזַּל־מַיִם מִדָּלְיָו (Bamidbar 24:7), water shall flow from his buckets, is the plural, on another pattern; by rule it should carry the short kamatz, on the pattern of חָפְנָיו, his handfuls, and אָזְנָיו, his ears, but it comes with the broad one, as בְּתוֹךְ הַדָּֽבְרוֹ (Michah 2:12), in the midst of its fold. It may also be of the boughs: from under his branches the water flows.

more.h: The legs of the lame man
more.t: דַּלְיוּ (דָּֽלְיוּ) שֹׁקַיִם מִפִּסֵּחַ (Mishlei 26:7): Rabbi Yehudah Chayuj wrote it in the light form, as גבהו, the legs of the lame are raised high. Radak found a patach under the daled, and so Rabbi Yaakov ben Elazar wrote it; if so, it is a command of the doubled form, with the lamed left soft where the rule would double it, and the sense is: lift the legs off the lame man, for what use are they to him; and so is a parable בְּפִי כְסִילִֽים (Mishlei 26:7), in the mouth of fools.

שׁאב.sense: To draw water, with מַשְׁאַבִּים for the places where water is drawn.

more.t: וּשְׁאַבְתֶּם ־מַיִם בְּשָׂשׂוֹן מִמַּֽעַיְנֵי הַיְשׁוּעָֽה (Yeshayahu 12:3), you shall draw water in joy from the springs of salvation; וַתִּשְׁאַב לְכָל־גְּמַלָּֽיו (Bereishis 24:20), she drew for all his camels; יִשְֽׁאֲבוּן הַנְּעָרִֽים (Rus 2:9), the lads draw; לְעֵת צֵאת הַשֹּֽׁאֲבֹֽת (Bereishis 24:11), the time the drawers of water go out; and the places where they draw, בֵּין מַשְׁאַבִּים (Shoftim 5:11), among the drawing places.

שׁתה.sense: To drink, with מִשְׁתֶּה, a feast, and הַשְּׁתִיָּה, the drinking; and in the same letters שְׁתִי, the warp, the thread that runs the length of a garment.

more.t: וּמַיִם לֹא שָׁתָה (Shemos 34:28), and he drank no water; אֲשֶׁר יִשְׁתֶּה אֲדֹנִי בּוֹ (Bereishis 44:5), from which my master drinks; וַיֵּשְׁתְּ מִן־הַיַּיִן (Bereishis 9:21), and he drank of the wine; וּשְׁתוּ בְּיַיִן מָסָֽכְתִּי (Mishlei 9:5), and drink of the wine I have mixed; and בַּל־ יִשְׁתָּיֽוּן (Tehillim 78:44), that they could not drink; and in the passive, וְכָל־מַשְׁקֶה אֲשֶׁר יִשָּׁתֶה (Vayikra 11:34), any drink that is drunk. The word is known.

Chazal said (Eruvin 64a) שָׁתוּי אל יתפלל, one who has drunk should not pray. There שתוי is an adjective and not a passive, for it is the water or the wine that is drunk, שתוי as a passive participle or נשתה as a passive verb; but the שתוי they spoke of is an adjective, like עָצוּם, mighty. They used this word to keep him apart from the שִׁכּוֹר, the drunkard. The שתוי has not drunk as much as the drunkard, so if he prayed his prayer is a prayer, since he could still speak before a king; the drunkard has drunk so much that he could not speak before a king, so if he prayed his prayer is an abomination.

מִשְׁתֶּה וְשִׂמְחָֽה (Esther 9:22), feasting and joy; in the plural, וּמִיֵּין מִשְׁתָּיו (Daniel 1:5), and from the wine of his drinking, and וְיֵין מִשְׁתֵּיהֶם (Daniel 1:16), and the wine of their drinking; and with a heh, וְהַשְּׁתִיָּה כַדָּת (Esther 1:8), and the drinking was according to the law.

בִּגְבוּרָה וְלֹא בַשְּׁתִֽי (Koheles 10:17), in strength and not in drinking: even at the hour they eat, their heart and mind are on strength and not on drinking. In אוֹ בִֽשְׁתִי אוֹ בְעֵרֶב (Vayikra 13:48), either in the warp or in the woof, the שְׁתִי is the thread that runs the length of the garment, and the ערב the one that runs across it. Some explain בִּגְבוּרָה וְלֹא בַשְּׁתִֽי from that word: that is, not in confusion and mixing, as the warp is mixed with the woof, meaning their mind is not muddled with food and delights but clear in strength.
עַד שְׁתֽוֹתֵיהֶם (Shmuel II 10:4) is from this root, on the pattern of בְּנוֹתֵיהֶם, their daughters, and שְׁמוֹתֵיהֶם, their names; Radak has already explained it at the root שׁוּת.

גמא.sense: To give to drink; likewise drinking up the ground, said of great lightness and speed; and גֹּמֶא, a very light wood, which may also be explained from Chazal's גמי.

more.t: הַגְמִיאִינִי נָא מְעַט־מַיִם מִכַּדֵּךְ (Bereishis 24:17), please give me a little water to drink from your pitcher, the word meaning השקיני, give me to drink.
Likewise בְּרַעַשׂ וְרֹגֶז יְגַמֶּא־אָרֶץ (Iyov 39:24), with tumult and fury he drinks up the ground: as though for his great lightness and speed he would drink up the ground.

His father explains מְגַמַּת פְּנֵיהֶם קָדִימָה (Chavakuk 1:9) in the same sense. By his reading it is the heavy form, built as the verbs whose last letter is heh are built, with מְגַמַּת in construct. Radak explains the phrase: the east wind drinks their faces; that is, they come with brazen faces, as though the east wind, which is fierce, had drunk their faces or given them to drink.

הֲיִגְאֶה־גֹּמֶא בְּלֹא בִצָּה (Iyov 8:11), can the gome grow tall without a marsh, תֵּבַת גֹּמֶא (Shemos 2:3), an ark of gome, and וּבִכְלֵי־גֹמֶא (Yeshayahu 18:2), and in vessels of gome: it is a wood exceedingly light. They may also be explained from the word גמי in the words of Chazal (Kelim 10:4), since small boats are made of גמי and coated with pitch so that the water should not come in, and they are light upon the face of the water.

הוה.sense: To be, one in sense with הָיָה. A second sense, as in הוָֹה עַל־הוָֹה, ruin upon ruin, is breaking and evil things.

more.t: וְאַתָּה הוֶֹה לָהֶם לְמֶלֶךְ (Nechemiah 6:6), and you will be a king to them; הֱוֵה גְבִיר לְאַחֶיךָ (Bereishis 27:29), be a lord to your brothers; כִּי מֶֽה־ הוֶֹה לָֽאָדָם (Koheles 2:22), for what is there for a man. In מְקוֹם שֶׁיִּפּוֹל הָעֵץ שָׁם יְהֽוּא (Koheles 11:3), the place where the tree falls, there it will be, the rule would have יֶהְוֶא, and the vav comes at rest as in וַיִּשְׁתַּחוּ, and they bowed; and in כִּי לַשֶּׁלֶג יֹאמַר הֱוֵא אָרֶץ (Iyov 37:6), for to the snow He says, be earth, the alef stands in place of a heh.

more.h: One root with היה, to be, or two
more.t: It is possible that the vav of this root stands in place of the yud of the root הָיָה, or they may be two roots; either way the sense is one.

Another sense: הוָֹה עַל־ הוָֹה (Yechezkel 7:26), ruin upon ruin; and in another form, וְהַוַּת רְשָׁעִים יֶֽהְדֹּֽף (Mishlei 10:3), and the ruin of the wicked He thrusts away, and הַוַּת נַפְשׁוֹ הוּא וַיְעַבְּתֽוּהָ (Michah 7:3), the ruin of his own soul, and they weave it together. In the plural, עַד יַֽעֲבֹר הַוּֽוֹת (Tehillim 57:2), until ruin passes, and הַוּוֹת תַּחְשֹׁב לְשׁוֹנֶךָ (Tehillim 52:4), your tongue devises ruin, meaning that you devise it in your heart and bring it out with your tongue. The sense of them all, and of those like them, is breaking and evil things. It may be that תְּהֽוֹתְתוּ עַל־אִישׁ (Tehillim 62:4), you devise ruin against a man, is of this root and this sense.

more.h: Strong in his ruin, or his wealth
more.t: יָעֹז בְּהַוָּתֽוֹ (Tehillim 52:9), he grew strong in his ruin, means ברעתו, in the evil he does to others. Rav Saadiah reads בהותו as בממונו, in his wealth; on that reading it is from the first sense, the wealth that is his. And it may be the same in וְהַוַּת רְשָׁעִים יֶֽהְדֹּֽף (Mishlei 10:3), and the wealth of the wicked He thrusts away, the opposite of what the same pasuk says, that Hashem does not let the soul of the righteous hunger.

גזם.sense: The gazam, a kind of locust.

more.t: One line, on יֶתֶר הַגָּזָם (Yoel 1:4), what the gazam left, of which he says הוא מין ארבה, it is a kind of locust.

שׁמן.sense: Oil, and close to it, growing fat; שָׁמֵן, fat, and of land, rich. Another sense is eight, שְׁמֹנֶה.

more.t: שֶׁמֶן זַיִת (Shemos 27:20), olive oil; כַּשֶּׁמֶן הַטּוֹב עַל־הָרֹאשׁ (Tehillim 133:2), like the good oil upon the head. וְלֹא רֻכְּכָה בַּשָּֽׁמֶן (Yeshayahu 1:6), nor softened with oil, means the salve fit for a wound, called so because oil is put in it. שֶׁמֶן תּוּרַק שְׁמֶךָ (Shir HaShirim 1:3), your name is oil poured out, is oil poured from vessel to vessel so that its scent spreads; perfumer's oil is meant, and it is spoken of in the feminine. It may be that תּוּרַק is an adjective on the pattern of תּוֹשָׁב, the one with a cholam and the other with a shuruk being all one.

Close to this is growing fat: שָׁמַנְתָּ עָבִיתָ כָּשִׂיתָ (Devarim 32:15), you grew fat and thick and gorged; וַיִּשְׁמַן יְשֻׁרוּן (Devarim 32:15), Yeshurun grew fat; and וַיִּשְׂבְּעוּ וַיַּשְׁמִינוּ (Nechemiah 9:25), they were sated and grew fat, which he calls intransitive. The transitive is הַשְׁמֵן לֵֽב־הָעָם הַזֶּה (Yeshayahu 6:10), fattening the heart of this people, which his father takes as an infinitive, מקור; Radak spells out the meaning, that they themselves made their heart fat and their ear heavy and shut their eyes, so as not to see and not to understand.

The adjective: וְהָיָה דָשֵׁן וְשָׁמֵן (Yeshayahu 30:23), and it shall be rich and fat; מִרְעֶה שָׁמֵן וָטוֹב (Divrei HaYamim I 4:40), fat and good pasture; שְׁמֵנָה לַחְמוֹ (Bereishis 49:20), his bread shall be fat, meaning his land that brings out his bread; and וַֽאֲדָמָה שְׁמֵנָה (Nechemiah 9:25), and fat soil. His father writes that in אוֹצָר נֶחְמָד וָשֶׁמֶן בִּנְוֵה חָכָם (Mishlei 21:20), a treasure desirable and rich in the dwelling of the wise, וָשֶׁמֶן is an adjective like שָׁמֵן. By way of borrowing, כָּל־ שָׁמֵן וְכָל־אִישׁ חָיִל (Shoftim 3:29), every שָׁמֵן and every man of valour, means sound and strong, and Targum Yonasan renders כָּל אֵימְתָן, every formidable one.

more.h: The fat hill, and the yoke broken
more.t: בְּקֶרֶן בֶּן־ שָֽׁמֶן (Yeshayahu 5:1), on a horn, a son of fatness: the place is called a horn because it was high ground, and בן שמן, a son of fatness, because it was fat and rich; his father writes that Yerushalayim is called so because an anointed king and an anointed kohen were there, by the horn of the oil of anointing. וְחֻבַּל עֹל מִפְּנֵי־ שָֽׁמֶן (Yeshayahu 10:27), and the yoke shall be broken because of fatness, Radak reads as: through the fatness and strength of Chizkiyahu the yoke of Sancheriv will be broken; some explain the same words of the oil, of Chizkiyahu who was anointed with the oil of anointing.

Said from this are עֲצֵי־ שָׁמֶן (Melachim I 6:31), wood of the oil tree, and וַֽעֲלֵי־עֵץ שֶׁמֶן (Nechemiah 8:15), and leaves of the oil tree: the tree called in the vernacular pine, because it is oily. Targum Yonasan renders אֲעֵי זֵיתָא, olive trees.

more.h: Eight, and a word for the graves
more.t: Another sense: וּשְׁמֹנָה נְסִיכֵי אָדָֽם (Michah 5:4), and eight princes of men; שְׁמֹנֶה שָׁנִֽים (Shoftim 12:14), eight years; and וּשְׁמֹנִים שָׁנָה (Bereishis 5:28), and eighty years; which is known. בָּֽאַשְׁמַנִּים כַּמֵּתִֽים (Yeshayahu 59:10), in graves like the dead, as Radak explains it by its place, has an added alef; one can also say it is a four-letter word. His father writes that the alef is of the root and the nun added, and its sense is from תֶּאְשַׁם שֹֽׁמְרוֹן (Hoshea 14:1), Shomron shall be desolate, a word of desolation, a place with no settlement, which is the graves.

צהר.sense: Noon, when the day's light is strong; צֹהַר, a window the light comes in by; and יִצְהָר, oil fresh from the treading, called by a word of light for its great clearness.

more.t: כִּי אִתִּי יֹֽאכְלוּ הָֽאֲנָשִׁים בַּֽצָּֽהֳרָֽיִם (Bereishis 43:16), for the men will eat with me at noon; עֶרֶב וָבֹקֶר וְצָהֳרַיִם (Tehillim 55:18), evening and morning and noon; וּֽמִצָּהֳרַיִם יָקוּם חָלֶד (Iyov 11:17), and a lifetime will rise above noon. The word is known: it is the time when the day's light is strong. It is said in the dual because the day is divided in its light into two, from morning to midday going on and growing light, and from midday onward going on toward evening, and noon is the time when the light is strong on both sides.
צֹהַר תַּֽעֲשֶׂה לַתֵּבָה (Bereishis 6:16), you shall make a צֹהַר for the ark: a window through which the light comes in.

דָּגָן תִּירוֹשׁ וְיִצְהָר (Devarim 28:51), grain, wine and oil, and אֶרֶץ זֵית יִצְהָר וּדְבַשׁ (Melachim II 18:32), a land of olive oil and honey: oil is called so at the time of its newness, after the treading. It is called by a word of light for its great clearness, as it is also called gold in another place. The verb from it is בֵּין־שֽׁוּרֹתָם יַצְהִירוּ (Iyov 24:11), between their rows they make oil, that is, they tread the olives and make the oil.

שְׁנֵי בְנֵֽי הַיִּצְהָר (Zecharyah 4:14), the two sons of the oil, are Zerubavel ben Shealtiel and Yehoshua ben Yehotzadak, who were anointed with the oil of anointing, the one for kingship and the other for the kehunah.

להט.sense: Burning, as fire burns. לַהַט הַחֶרֶב is the flame of the sword, and the sorcerers' בְּלַֽהֲטֵיהֶם may be of the same, some sorcery being done with a sword's flame.

more.t: אֵשׁ לֹהֵֽט (Tehillim 104:4), burning fire; אֶשְׁכְּבָה לֹֽהֲטִים (Tehillim 57:5), I lie down, בתוך להטים, in the midst of burning ones. וְלִהַט אֹתָם הַיּוֹם הַבָּא (Malachi 3:19), the day that comes will burn them; וְלֶהָבָה לִֽהֲטָה (Yoel 1:19), and a flame has burned; וַתְּלַהֵט מֽוֹסְדֵי הָרִֽים (Devarim 32:22), and sets the foundations of the mountains burning; וַתְּלַֽהֲטֵהוּ מִסָּבִיב (Yeshayahu 42:25), and it set him burning round about. All of them are ענין שריפה, a sense of burning.
וְאֵת לַהַט הַחֶרֶב (Bereishis 3:24), and the flame of the sword, is in the sense of וְלַהַב חֶרֶב וּבְרַק חֲנִית (Nachum 3:3), the flame of a sword and the flash of a spear.
בְּלַֽהֲטֵיהֶם (Shemos 7:11) may be of this root and this sense, with their flames, since some of the work of sorcery is done with the flame of the sword.

לאט.sense: To cover, as the king covered his face; and of the sorcerers' arts, done in hiding and in covering from men.

more.t: וְהַמֶּלֶךְ לָאַט אֶת־פָּנָיו (Shmuel II 19:5), and the king covered his face.

בְּלַֽהֲטֵיהֶם (Shemos 7:11) and בְּלָֽטֵיהֶם (Shemos 8:3), with their arts: the alef of לאט has turned to heh in the one and fallen silent in the other. What they do is done by hiding it and covering it from people, by contrivance and by illusion. He allows that בְּלַֽהֲטֵיהֶם may instead be from the root לָהַט, and of its sense.
Rabbi Yehudah sets לָאַט under the root לוּט, the vav exchanged for an alef, so that the word stands whole; and Radak says that is correct.

הלם.sense: To be broken and crushed, or to strike; the הַלְמוּת is a hammer. A second sense is הֲלֹם, here.

more.t: אָז הָלְמוּ עִקְּבֵי־סוּס (Shoftim 5:22), then the horses' heels were broken, that is, נשברו ונכתתו, broken and crushed, the form standing alone as though it had said נהלמו; and so וְהִנֵּה הֶֽהָמוֹן נָמוֹג וַיֵּלֶךְ וַֽהֲלֹֽם (Shmuel I 14:16), and behold, the multitude melted away and went on and was broken, meaning it went on going and being broken. Transitive are הֲלָמוּנִי בַּל־יָדָעְתִּי (Mishlei 23:35), they struck me and I did not know it, בְּכַשִּׁיל וְכֵֽילַפֹּת יַֽהֲלֹמֽוּן (Tehillim 74:6), with hatchet and hammers they strike, and הֲלוּמֵי יָיִן (Yeshayahu 28:1), men struck down by wine. The noun is הוֹלֶם פָּעַם (Yeshayahu 41:7), the one who strikes the anvil, and with a mem added, לְמַֽהֲלֻמוֹת (Mishlei 18:6), for blows.
לְהַלְמוּת עֲמֵלִים (Shoftim 5:26), to the הַלְמוּת of the workmen: the name of a tool, which is the מַקֶּבֶת, the hammer.
אַל־תִּקְרַב הֲלֹם (Shemos 3:5), do not come near here, and כִּי הֲבִיאֹתַנִי עַד־הֲלֹם (Shmuel II 7:18), that You have brought me this far: their sense is as הנה, here.

Radak takes יָשׁוּב עַמּוֹ הֲלֹם (Tehillim 73:10), His people return here, in this second sense: they come back again and again here, to this matter, to weigh and consider why the wicked have their ease, and why the waters of a full cup are drained out to them, that is, that they are sated with every good of this world. Rabbi Yonah puts the pasuk in the first sense, of being broken. Radak takes that to mean that the people come back broken at seeing the ease of the wicked, and that the waters of the full cup are then the tears of their weeping.

In נֹפֶךְ סַפִּיר וְיָהֲלֹם (Shemos 28:18), a nofech, a sapphire and a yahalom, the yud may be an addition, and the word is a precious stone. Rabbi Avraham ben Ezra writes there that a great Sephardi sage said it is the one called in Arabic אל מא"ס, which breaks every stone and pierces crystal, and that the name comes from הוֹלֶם פָּעַם (Yeshayahu 41:7), the one who strikes.

הן.sense: הֵן and הִנֵּה point to what is ready at hand; הֵן can stand for אִם, if; עַד־ הֵֽנָּה is until now and הֵנָּה here; and הֵן, הֵנָּה are they, of women.

more.t: הֵן ־אֲנִי כְפִיךָ לָאֵל (Iyov 33:6), see, I am as your own mouth before Hashem. With a heh added it is הִנֵּה, as וְהִנֵּה אָֽנֹכִי עִמָּךְ (Bereishis 28:15), and here I am with you; and with the pronouns הִנְנִי and הִנֶּנִּי, here I am, הִנְנוּ and הִנֶּנּוּ, here we are. The sense of them all is the thing that stands ready.

הֵן הָֽיְתָה כָּזֹֽאת (Yirmiyahu 2:10), has there been such a thing, and הֵן נִזְבַּח (Shemos 8:22), shall we slaughter: though the sense of these two is a question, הֵן keeps its own meaning, since a question can come without the interrogative heh, as אַתָּה זֶה בְּנִי עֵשָׂו (Bereishis 27:24), are you he, my son Esav, and the like. The same two are where it stands in place of אִם, if: וּרְאוּ הֵן הָֽיְתָה כָּזֹֽאת, and see if there has been such a thing, and הֵן נִזְבַּח אֶת־תּֽוֹעֲבַת מִצְרַיִם לְעֵֽינֵיהֶם וְלֹא יִסְקְלֻֽנוּ, if we slaughter the abomination of Mitzrayim before their eyes, will they not stone us?

עַד־ הֵֽנָּה is of time, until now: כִּי לֹֽא־שָׁלֵם עֲוֹן הָֽאֱמֹרִי עַד־ הֵֽנָּה (Bereishis 15:16), for the sin of the Emori is not complete until now, and וְלֹא רְאִיתִיו עַד־ הֵֽנָּה (Bereishis 44:28), and I have not seen him until now. Some explain אֲשֶׁר־ עֲדֶן לֹא הָיָה (Koheles 4:3), who has not yet been, as properly עד הן, until now, and אֲשֶׁר הֵמָּה חַיִּים עֲדֶֽנָה (Koheles 4:2), who are still alive, as עד הנה, until now. הֵנָּה comes also in a sense close to this one, except that this one points to time, until this time, and the other to place, this place: וְהֽוֹרַדְתֶּם אֶת־אָבִי הֵֽנָּה (Bereishis 45:13), and you shall bring my father down here.

It also serves as the pronoun for women spoken of: וְהַֽעֲבַרְתָּ אֶת־נַֽחֲלַת אֲבִיהֶן לָהֶֽן (Bamidbar 27:7), and you shall pass their father's inheritance to them. With a heh added it is הֵנָּה: אֶת־בְּנוֹת הָֽאָדָם כִּי טֹבֹת הֵנָּה (Bereishis 6:2), the daughters of man, that they were fair, and כָּל־הַיּוֹצֵא מֵהֵנָּה (Yirmiyahu 5:6), whoever goes out from them, that is, from the cities. The form with the nun comes for men too: הֲלָהֵן תְּשַׂבֵּרְנָה (Rus 1:13), would you wait for them?

כבד.sense: Heaviness, and with it burden, great numbers and wealth, since abundance is heaviness. Close to it, כָּבוֹד, honour, which also names the soul; הַכָּבֵד, the liver.

more.t: כָּבְדָה מְאֹד יַד הָאֱלֹהִים שָׁם (Shmuel I 5:11), the hand of Hashem was heavy there; וַיִּכְבַּד לֵב פַּרְעֹה (Shemos 9:7), Paroh's heart grew heavy; וְעֵינֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כָּבְדוּ מִזֹּקֶן (Bereishis 48:10), his eyes were dim with age. A man is כָּבֵד in cattle, silver and gold (Bereishis 13:2), heavy with wealth.

יִכְבְּדוּ בָנָיו וְלֹא יֵדָע (Iyov 14:21), his sons grow many, or come to great and heavy wealth, and he does not know it; he reads it so because its opposite in the same pasuk is וְיִצְעֲרוּ, and they are made small. So too וְהִכְבַּדְתִּים וְלֹא יִצְעָרוּ (Yirmiyahu 30:19), I will make them heavy and they will not be made small, which he glosses as their having great and heavy wealth. He holds all of it one sense, for the abundance of anything is its heaviness.
וְלֹא נִכְבַּד עָלֶיךָ (Shmuel II 13:25), we will not be a load and a burden on you, and תִּכְבַּד הָעֲבֹדָה עַל־הָאֲנָשִׁים (Shemos 5:9), let the work lie heavy on the men.

הִתְכַּבֵּד כַּיֶּלֶק (Nachum 3:15) he takes as multiplying like the locust. Others read it as sweeping away, in the sense of וְטֵאטֵאתִיהָ (Yeshayahu 14:23), I will sweep her, and from Chazal's מכבדין בין המטות (Beitzah 22b), they sweep between the couches, and מכבדות של תמרה (Sukkah 13b), palm sweepers, these being the יעים, with which the house is swept; and they read כָּבֹד מִכֹּל כְּלִי חֶמְדָּה (Nachum 2:10) the same way, a sweeping out of every precious vessel.

כִּי־מְכַבְּדַי אֲכַבֵּד וּבֹזַי יֵקָלּוּ (Shmuel I 2:30), those who honour Me I honour and those who scorn Me are made light. Giving כָּבוֹד to Hashem (Yirmiyahu 13:16) he reads as honouring Him with praise and with confessing one's sins before Him.

The higher soul is called כָּבוֹד because it is the honour and worth of the body, שָׂמַח לִבִּי וַיָּגֶל כְּבוֹדִי (Tehillim 16:9), my heart is glad and my soul rejoices. וּכְבוֹדִי לֶעָפָר יַשְׁכֵּן סֶלָה (Tehillim 7:6), and let him make my soul dwell in the dust, selah, he takes as a figure, since the soul does not dwell in dust, like דָּבְקָה לֶעָפָר נַפְשִׁי (Tehillim 119:25), my soul cleaves to the dust. At the end stands the organ, יֹתֶרֶת הַכָּבֵד (Vayikra 8:16), the lobe of the liver, which he calls known.

יקר.sense: To be precious and honoured; the word serves for weight as well as honour, so אֲבָנִים יְקָרוֹת are heavy stones. The noun is יְקָר, honour.

more.t: וְלִי מַה־יָּקְרוּ רֵעֶיךָ אֵל (Tehillim 139:17), and to me how precious are Your thoughts, O Kel: they are precious, and too great to be grasped. אֲשֶׁר יָקַרְתִּי מֵעֲלֵיהֶם (Zecharyah 11:13) he reads as, I was precious in myself and drew away from them, because I was not precious in their eyes.

מַה־יָּקָר חַסְדְּךָ אֱלֹהִים (Tehillim 36:8), how precious is Your kindness, Elokim: Rabbi Yehudah recorded יָּקָר as a past verb, and perhaps his copy had the kuf with a patach; in our books it is all kamatz, so it is rightly an adjective. Of וְאֶת־יְקָר תִּפְאֶרֶת גְּדוּלָּתוֹ (Esther 1:4), and the honour of the glory of his greatness, Rabbi Yehudah wrote that the word is patach and Rabbi Yonah that it is kamatz, and Radak found it kamatz in some of the careful books and patach in others. It may be a construct though kamatz, as כְּתָב, writing, is kamatz whether joined or not; or it may be absolute, the vav of וְאֶת serving twice, the sense being ואת יקר ותפארת גדולתו, the honour and the glory of his greatness.

אֲבָנִים יְקָרוֹת לְיַסֵּד הַבָּיִת (Melachim I 5:31), heavy stones to lay the foundation of the house, for יְקָרוֹת here means heavy: as a word is used in the sense of כבדות, weight, and in the sense of כבוד, honour, so יקר is used in both senses, for they are alike in sense.

לֹא־יִהְיֶה אוֹר יְקָרוֹת (Zecharyah 14:6), there shall not be the light of יְקָרוֹת, which is the clear light, nor the light of קפאון, which is the thick light, but something between, as it says, לֹא־יוֹם וְלֹא־לָיְלָה (Zecharyah 14:7), neither day nor night. It is a figure for the salvation and for the troubles that will come at its start. Targum Yonasan renders it, there will be no light but cold and ice.

בְּנוֹת מְלָכִים בִּיקְּרוֹתֶיךָ (Tehillim 45:10), kings' daughters among your honoured ones. So Ben Naftali reads it, and Radak gives two accounts of the dagesh: the first letter of the root is swallowed in the dagesh of the kuf though it is written; or the dagesh is for grace in reading, and the yud rests and its vowel is thrown back onto the servile beis, the proper form being בְּיִקְּרוֹתֶיךָ. Ben Asher reads the beis with a sheva and the yud with a chirik, as is proper. The word is an adjective: among your honoured women were kings' daughters.

אגם.sense: אֲגַם, a pool, a place where water gathers; and אַגְמוֹן, the rush, and a fish hook named so because its head is bent like the rush.

more.t: לַאֲגַם־מַיִם (Tehillim 107:35), into a pool of water, and וְהָיָה הַשָּׁרָב לַאֲגָם (Yeshayahu 35:7), the parching heat shall become a pool, that is, the place of it. אַגְמֵי־נָפֶשׁ (Yeshayahu 19:10) are the pools in which fish are caught. The sense of these and their like is a place where water gathers.

הֲתָשִׂים אַגְמֹן בְּאַפּוֹ (Iyov 40:26), can you set an agmon in his nose: it is a tool like an iron needle with which fish are caught, and the words beside it point to that, וּבְחוֹחַ תִּקֹּב לֶחֱיוֹ, or pierce his jaw with a thorn. It is called so because its head is bent like the גומא, the rush.

הֲלָכֹף כְּאַגְמֹן רֹאשׁוֹ (Yeshayahu 58:5), is it to bow his head like an agmon: the word here is as גומא, the rush, which Chazal call גמי. So too וְאֶת־הָאֲגַמִּים שָׂרְפוּ בָאֵשׁ (Yirmiyahu 51:32), and they burned the rushes with fire, that is, all the rush growing along the rivers, so that its great mass should not keep them from coming into the lands. Rabbi Yonah explained that word as fortresses, likening it to the Arabic name for fortresses.

In כִּפָּה וְאַגְמוֹן the agmon is the rush: it says כפה of the strong and אגמון of the weak, who are like the rush. Or אגמון may be a name for a ruler, as Chazal say, מצא אותו הגמון, a hegmon found him (Berachos 32b), and הגמון וקומון (Shabbos 145b), the hegmon and the komon, הגמון meaning a ruler.

כְּדוּד נָפוּחַ וְאַגְמֹן (Iyov 41:12), like a pot blown upon, and agmon: some explained אגמון here as the rush, some by the run of the pasuk as a pot, and one said it keeps its plain sense, from אגם, a pool, a hint at the vapour that rises off water in the winter.

שׁפת.sense: To set in place, which he glosses תערוך: peace set for us, a pot set on the שְׁפַתַּיִם, the hearth it stands on; and the מִשְׁפְּתָיִם, two loads, one on each side.

more.t: תִּשְׁפֹּת שָׁלוֹם לָנוּ (Yeshayahu 26:12), You will set peace for us, and וְלַֽעֲפַר־מָוֶת תִּשְׁפְּתֵֽנִי (Tehillim 22:16), and in the dust of death You set me; he glosses them תערוך, תערכני, You will set in order, You set me in order.

שְׁפֹת הַסִּיר שְׁפֹת (Yechezkel 24:3), set the pot, set it: set it on the שְׁפַתַּיִם, which are the hearth on which the pots stand, or the iron frame. The word is dual because it is the place where two pots are set. Also וְהַֽשְׁפַתַּיִם טֹפַח אֶחָד (Yechezkel 40:43), and the shefatayim, one handbreadth. אִם־תִּשְׁכְּבוּן בֵּין שְׁפַתָּיִם (Tehillim 68:14), if you lie among the shefatayim, he reads as: in a place as low as this, you will yet be overlaid with silver. Yonasan renders וְהַֽשְׁפַתַּיִם טֹפַח אֶחָד as וְעָנְקְלִין נַפְקִין פְּשַׁח חָד, and hooks projecting one handbreadth; these are the hooks on the pillars, on which the korbanos are hung and flayed.

רֹבֵץ בֵּין הַֽמִּשְׁפְּתָֽיִם (Bereishis 49:14), lying between the mishpesayim: between the two sets, which are the two loads they put on him, one on this side and one on that; and he is so strong that he lies between them and rises with them.

שֹפה.sense: The lip itself in some places and a side or edge in others; and language, as שָׂפָה אֶחָת, one language, with lips of song read as words of song.

more.t: שָׂפָה לְפִיו סָבִיב (Shemos 39:23), a lip round its opening; עַל שְׂפַת הַיְרִיעָה (Shemos 26:4), on the edge of the curtain; עַל־שְׂפַת הַיְאֹֽר (Shemos 2:3), on the bank of the river; כְּמַֽעֲשֵׂה שְׂפַת־כּוֹס (Melachim I 7:26), like the work of the brim of a cup; שְׂפָתַיִם יִשָּׁק (Mishlei 24:26), he kisses the lips; וְשִׂפְתֵי חֲכָמִים תִּשְׁמוּרֵם (Mishlei 14:3), and the lips of the wise guard them; שִׂפְתֵי חֲכָמִים יְזָרוּ דָעַת (Mishlei 15:7), the lips of the wise scatter knowledge; and in the feminine plural, שִׂפְתוֹתָיו שֽׁוֹשַׁנִּים (Shir HaShirim 5:13), his lips are lilies. Of these, he says, some are the lip itself and some a side.

שָׂפָה אֶחָת (Bereishis 11:1) is לשון אחת, one language; and so וְשִׂפְתֵי רְנָנוֹת יְהַלֶּל־פִּֽי (Tehillim 63:6), and with words of song my mouth will praise, which he explains as ודברי רננות, and words of song.

שׁפה.sense: To break and crush, as also in the Targum and in Chazal; another sense, height; and שְׁפוֹת בָּקָר, cheeses of milk, or as some say, the cows' udder.

more.t: וְשֻׁפּוּ עַצְמֹתָיו (Iyov 33:21), his bones are broken and crushed. The Targum of וָאֶכֹּת אֹתוֹ טָחוֹן (Devarim 9:21), and I crushed it, grinding it, is וְשָׁפִית יָתֵהּ בְּשׁוּפִינָא, and I filed it with a file; and so in the words of Chazal (Avodah Zarah 42a), גוי ששפה עבודה זרה, a gentile who filed down an idol.

In another sense, וַיֵּלֶךְ שֶׁפִי (Bamidbar 23:3), and he went to a high place; אֶפְתַּח עַל־שְׁפָיִים נְהָרוֹת (Yeshayahu 41:18), I will open rivers on the heights; רוּחַ צַח שְׁפָיִם (Yirmiyahu 4:11), a clear wind of the heights; and from it עַל הַר־נִשְׁפֶּה (Yeshayahu 13:2), on a lofty mountain, whose sense is high. Rabbi Yehudah put וַיֵּלֶךְ שֶׁפִי with ושפו עצמותיו, his bones are broken and crushed; that is, שֶׁפִי means broken: he went with a broken spirit.

וּשְׁפוֹת בָּקָר (Shmuel II 17:29), and שְׁפוֹת of the herd, has the sense of חריצי חלב, cheeses of milk, and so Targum Yonasan renders וְגוּבְנִין דַחֲלַב תּוֹרִין, cheeses of cows' milk. Chazal said of these cheeses of cows' milk that a fly could not stand on them but fell off at once, so smooth and fat were they, and it seems it was the word שפות that led them to it. It may be drawn from the first sense, as cheeses are also called חריצים, from the sense of חרוץ, cutting, which he explains under that root; and some explain it as the udder of the cows.

שְׁפִיפֹן עֲלֵי־אֹרַח (Bereishis 49:17), a שְׁפִיפֹן on the path, may be of this root, the middle root letter doubled as in הֲגִיגִי (Tehillim 5:2), my meditation, from הָגָה. It would then be so called because it crushes other living creatures, from הוּא יְשׁוּפְךָ רֹאשׁ (Bereishis 3:15), he will crush your head, so that שׁוּף and שָׁפָה are of one sense, the sense of וְשֻׁפּוּ עַצְמֹתָיו, his bones are broken and crushed. יָשְׁפֵה too, in תַּרְשִׁישׁ וְשֹׁהַם וְיָֽשְׁפֵה (Shemos 28:20), the tarshish, the shoham and the yashfeh, may be of this root, with the yud added. It is said to be the stone called in Arabic אליס"ף, and that name is close to the Hebrew.

לשׁן.sense: לָשׁוֹן, the tongue, and in the plural the tongues of the nations; the verb, to denounce and slander; and by borrowing, a tongue of gold, of fire, of sea, or of rock.

more.t: The plural takes the feminine form, and its sense is plain: לְקַבֵּץ אֶת־כָּל־הַגּוֹיִם וְהַלְּשֹׁנוֹת (Yeshayahu 66:18), to gather all the nations and the tongues, and לִלְשֹֽׁנֹתָם בְּאַרְצֹתָם (Bereishis 10:20), by their tongues in their lands.
אַל־ תַּלְשֵׁן עֶבֶד (Mishlei 30:10), do not denounce a servant to his master, and מְלָשְׁנִי בַסֵּתֶר רֵעֵהוּ (Tehillim 101:5), one who slanders his fellow in secret.

more.h: A tongue of gold, of fire, of sea
more.t: וּלְשׁוֹן זָהָב אֶחָד (Yehoshua 7:21), one tongue of gold, is a bar of gold shaped like a tongue; and by the same borrowing לְשׁוֹן אֵשׁ (Yeshayahu 5:24), a tongue of fire, לְשׁוֹן יָם (Yeshayahu 11:15), a tongue of sea, and מִן־ הַלָּשֹׁן הַפֹּנֶה נֶֽגְבָּה (Yehoshua 15:2), from the tongue that faces south, a rock in the shape of a tongue. So Yonasan renders it, מִן כֵּיפָא, from the rock.

צחק.sense: To laugh; and to make sport, whether in amusement and rejoicing, in mockery, or in abuse. All of them, he says, come under the sense of laughter.

more.t: וַתִּצְחַק שָׂרָה בְּקִרְבָּהּ (Bereishis 18:12), and Sarah laughed within herself: that is, she laughed and said it within herself, and brought no word out of her mouth, which is why she denied it, out of fear. Or it means that she laughed by herself, with nobody seeing her laugh. The noun, צְחֹק עָשָׂה לִי אֱלֹהִים (Bereishis 21:6), God has made laughter for me, is laughter in the mouth.

In the heavy form, וַיְצַחֵק לִפְנֵיהֶם (Shoftim 16:25), and he made sport before them, מְצַחֵק אֵת רִבְקָה אִשְׁתּֽוֹ (Bereishis 26:8), sporting with Rivkah his wife, and וַיָּקֻמוּ לְצַחֵֽק (Shemos 32:6), and they rose up to make merry: this is amusement and rejoicing.

לְצַחֶק־בי (Bereishis 39:17) is להתעולל בי, to deal abusively with me; and in אֲשֶׁר־יָֽלְדָה לְאַבְרָהָם מְצַחֵֽק (Bereishis 21:9), whom she had borne to Avraham, mocking, the word is מלעיג, mocking. All of them, he says, come under the sense of laughter.

שֹחק.sense: Laughter, which is sometimes a matter of joy and sometimes of mockery.

more.t: שָֽׂחֲקוּ עַל מִשְׁבַּתֶּֽהָ (Eichah 1:7), they laughed at her ceasing; לִשְׂחוֹק עֹשִׂים לֶחֶם (Koheles 10:19), bread is made for laughter; הָרֹאִים בִּשְׂחוֹק שִׁמְשֽׁוֹן (Shoftim 16:27), those who watched Shimshon's sport; and in another pattern, וְרֹֽזְנִים מִשְׂחָק לוֹ (Chavakuk 1:10), and rulers are a laughing matter to him.

וְשִֽׂחַקְתִּי לִפְנֵי י"י (Shmuel II 6:21), and I will make merry before Hashem; קִרְאוּ לְשִׁמְשׁוֹן וִישַֽׂחֶק־לָנוּ (Shoftim 16:25), call Shimshon that he may make sport for us; מְשַֽׂחֲקִים לִפְנֵי י"י (Shmuel II 6:5), making merry before Hashem. Another heavy form: וַיִּֽהְיוּ מַשְׂחִיקִים עֲלֵיהֶם (Divrei HaYamim II 30:10), and they were laughing them to scorn.

שׁחק.sense: To grind, a known sense, and more than treading; the noun שַׁחַק is dust, as the dust on the scales; of בַשַּׁחַק and שְׁחָקִים, skies, he says only that they are known.

more.t: וְשָׁחַקְתָּ מִמֶּנָּה הָדֵק (Shemos 30:36), and you shall grind some of it fine; אֲבָנִים שָׁחֲקוּ מַיִם (Iyov 14:19), water wears stones away; and וְאֶשְׁחָקֵם כְּעָפָר עַל־פְּנֵי־רוּחַ (Tehillim 18:43), and I ground them like dust before the wind. The sense of grinding is known, and it is more than treading.

The noun from it is וּכְשַׁחַק מֹאזְנַיִם (Yeshayahu 40:15), and like the dust of the scales, which he glosses as אבק, dust. Of כִּי מִי בַשַּׁחַק יַעֲרֹךְ לַי"י (Tehillim 89:7), for who in the skies can compare to Hashem, and וּבְגַאֲוָתוֹ שְׁחָקִים (Devarim 33:26), and in His majesty the skies, he says only that they are known.

צרע.sense: To be stricken with צָרַעַת, tzaraas, a thing he calls known. The צִרְעָה some said was a flying creature that struck the eyes with venom; Ibn Ezra takes it from צרעת.

more.t: וְהוּא צָרוּעַ אוֹ זָב (Vayikra 22:4), and he is stricken with tzaraas or has a flow; זָב וּמְצֹרָע (Shmuel II 3:29), one with a flow and one stricken with tzaraas; וְהִנֵּה־הוּא מְצֹרָע בְּמִצְחוֹ (Divrei HaYamim II 26:20), and behold, he was stricken with tzaraas in his forehead; and מְצֹרַעַת כַּשָּׁלֶג (Bamidbar 12:10), stricken with tzaraas, like snow. The noun is נֶגַע צָרַעַת (Vayikra 13:9), an affliction of tzaraas, and he says it is known.

וְשָׁלַחְתִּי אֶת־הַצִּרְעָה (Shemos 23:28), and I will send the tzirah: some said it is a kind of flying swarming creature, which struck them in their eyes and cast its venom into them, and they died. Ibn Ezra explained the word from the sense of צרעת.

נגע.sense: Reaching and bringing near: touching, at times to do harm, reaching a place, and bringing one thing to another. A second sense is being stricken, with נֶגַע, a plague.

more.t: כַּאֲשֶׁר לֹא נְגַעֲנוּךָ (Bereishis 26:29), as we have not touched you, is touching to do harm; so too לְבִלְתִּי נָגְעֵךְ (Rus 2:9), not to touch you, and הַנֹּגֵעַ בָּאִישׁ הַזֶּה (Bereishis 26:11), whoever touches this man, to do him harm.

Without an object it is reaching: עַד לַשָּׁמַיִם הִגִּיעַ (Divrei HaYamim II 28:9), it reached to heaven, and עֵת הַזָּמִיר הִגִּיעַ (Shir HaShirim 2:12), the time of singing has come; though on fine analysis, he adds, every form of this kind takes an object. With an object it is bringing one thing up to another: וְהִגַּעְתֶּם אֶל־הַמַּשְׁקוֹף (Shemos 12:22), and you shall bring it to the lintel, and וַיַּגַּע עַל־פִּי (Yeshayahu 6:7), and he brought it to my mouth, that is, the angel brought the coal to my mouth. The sense of the whole is reaching and bringing near.

וְאִם־לֹא תַגִּיעַ יָדוֹ (Vayikra 5:7), and if his hand does not reach, is that his hand does not reach to money with which to buy a lamb. Chazal explained it in the Sifra: he has no means to borrow, nor to work at his craft; and even one who had the lamb or its price but not the cost of the road brings the poor man's korban, as the pasuk says, דֵּי שֶׂה, enough for a lamb.

A second sense is being stricken: נָגוּעַ מֻכֵּה (Yeshayahu 53:4), stricken and smitten; and the noun, נֶגַע צָרַעַת (Vayikra 13:3), a plague of tzaraas, and אִישׁ נֶגַע לְבָבוֹ (Melachim I 8:38), each man the plague of his own heart.

וַיִּנָּגְעוּ יְהוֹשֻׁעַ וְכָל־יִשְׂרָאֵל (Yehoshua 8:15), and Yehoshua and all Yisrael were stricken, means that they made themselves out as men struck and beaten, since they were fleeing before them to draw them away from the city. It can also be read that they were stricken in truth, since men who flee and do not turn to fight back at their pursuers cannot but be struck; and had the sense been that they made a show of being stricken without being so, it would have said ויתנגעו, they made themselves out as stricken, in the form for what one does to himself, for that is the rule.

כן.sense: כִּנִּים, lice, in Shemos 8: the single one is כִּנָּה, in the words of Chazal, and הַכִּנָּם takes in the whole kind. The word כֵן, so, he files under כּוּן.

more.t: וַיַּעֲשׂוּ־כֵן הַחַרְטֻמִּים (Shemos 8:3), and the magicians did so: that word he has set down under the root כּוּן, and there too וְכַנָּה אֲשֶׁר־נָטְעָה יְמִינֶךָ (Tehillim 80:16), and the kanah that Your right hand planted.

וְהָיָה לְכִנִּם (Shemos 8:12), and it shall become lice, and הָיָה כִנִּים (Shemos 8:13), it became lice, are the many. The single one is found in the words of Chazal, with the feminine heh (Shabbos 12a): ההורג כִּנָּה בשבת, one who kills a louse on Shabbos. But וַתְּהִי הַכִּנָּם (Shemos 8:14), and the lice came, takes in the whole kind.

לחך.sense: To lick up, as an ox licks up the green of the field; the sense, he says, is known.

more.t: כִּלְחֹךְ הַשּׁוֹר אֵת יֶרֶק הַשָּׂדֶה (Bamidbar 22:4), as the ox licks up the green of the field; and in the heavy form הַמַּיִם אֲשֶׁר־בַּתְּעָלָה לִחֵֽכָה (Melachim I 18:38), it licked up the water in the trench; עַתָּה יְלַֽחֲכוּ הַקָּהָל (Bamidbar 22:4), now the company will lick up; עָפָר יְלַחֵֽכוּ (Tehillim 72:9), they will lick the dust. The sense of licking, he says, is known.
