טעה.sense: Leading astray is the only form in the pesukim, yet to stray is Biblical all the same; in the Mishnah it is an unwitting error. It is one sense with תָּעָה.

more.h: Only the form with an object
more.t: In the pesukim there is הִטְעוּ אֶת־עַמִּי (Yechezkel 13:10), they led my people astray, and not the plain verb. The plain verb is Biblical language all the same, without doubt, since הִטְעוּ is transitive to עַמִּי, and a people led astray are טועים, straying.
It is found besides in the Mishnah (Berachos 34a): העובר לפני התיבה וטעה, one who passes before the teivah and errs; and it is the sense of שגגה, an unwitting error.

תָּעָה with a tav and טָעָה with a tet are one sense, since the two letters come from one place in the mouth; and so Onkelos renders וַתֵּלֶךְ וַתֵּתַע (Bereishis 21:14), and she went and strayed, as וַאֲזָלַת וְטָעַת, and she went and strayed.

ירק.sense: Two senses: to spit; and green, of growing herbage and of the herb people eat. The doubled form is a deep green, and a face turns green at sudden trouble.

more.t: יָרֹק יָרַק בְּפָנֶיהָ (Bamidbar 12:14), spitting in her face, and וְיָרְקָה בְּפָנָיו (Devarim 25:9), she shall spit in his face, are the plain use. But רֻקִּי, my spittle, and יָרֹק הַזָּב (Vayikra 15:8), the spitting of the zav, belong to the root רָקַק, even if the matter is one.

יֶרֶק עֵשֶׂב (Bereishis 1:30), the green of herbage, יֶרֶק בָּעֵץ (Shemos 10:15), the green on the tree, and in another form וִירַק דֶּשֶׁא (Yeshayahu 37:27), and the green of grass. The adjective is יָרוֹק (Iyov 39:8), and כָּל יָרוֹק there is every green herb.

לְגַן־יָרָק (Melachim I 21:2), for a garden of herbs, and אֲרֻחַת יָרָק (Mishlei 15:17), a meal of herbs, use the word for the plant that is food for a man. So Chazal call such a plant ירק, and the plural is ירקות.

The doubled form is for a deep green: יְרַקְרַק אוֹ אֲדַמְדָּם (Vayikra 13:49), deep green or deep red. בִּירַקְרַק חָרוּץ (Tehillim 68:14) is gold whose colour leans a little towards green, or else the word names the saffron shade. In another form, יֵרָקוֹן (Yirmiyahu 30:6) is the green a face turns when trouble comes on a man suddenly.

כרפס.sense: One of the colours, and they say it is green.

more.t: חוּר כַּרְפַּס וּתְכֵלֶת (Esther 1:6), white, karpas and techeiles: the word is one of the colours, and they say it is green.

צעף.sense: A veil, the wrap in which women wrap their faces.

more.t: וַתְּכַס בַּצָּעִיף (Bereishis 38:14), and she covered herself with the veil, and וַתָּסַר צְעִיפָהּ מֵֽעָלֶיהָ (Bereishis 38:19), and she took her veil off herself: it is the wrap in which women wrap their faces.

רדד.sense: Spreading out and beating flat, as gold over the keruvim and palm figures; of the same sense, beating nations down. Also the רְדִיד, something like a veil or wrap.

more.t: The heavy form, with an object: וַיָּרֶד עַל־הַכְּרוּבִים וְעַל־הַתִּמֹרוֹת אֶת־הַזָּהָֽב (Melachim I 6:32), he spread the gold over the keruvim and over the palm figures. The noun is מַֽעֲשֵׂה מוֹרָֽד (Melachim I 7:29), beaten work, and its sense is spreading and beating out. The Targum renders וַֽיְרַקְּעוּ אֶת־פַּחֵי הַזָּהָב (Shemos 39:3), they beat out the plates of gold, with וְרַדִּידוּ יָת טַסֵּי דַהֲבָא, they beat out the plates of gold.

הָרוֹדֵד עַמִּי תַחְתָּֽי (Tehillim 144:2), who beats my people down under me. Of this root and of the same sense of spreading and beating out is לְרַד־לְפָנָיו גּוֹיִם (Yeshayahu 45:1), to beat nations down before him, which is an infinitive of the plain form.

נָשְׂאוּ אֶת־רְדִידִי מֵֽעָלַי (Shir HaShirim 5:7), they took my redid from upon me. The redidim are something like veils or wraps, called in Arabic al-arda; and some explain them as silk braids that women make to bind up the head.

מה.sense: What: a question after what a thing is or how it is. It can mean 'when'; with a lamed, 'for what reason'; it also magnifies, belittles, leaves unsaid, or laments.

more.t: The word asks what a thing is or how it is: מַה־תָּאֳרוֹ, what is his appearance, and מַה־זֶּה מִהַרְתָּ לִמְצֹא בְּנִי (Bereishis 27:20), what is this, that you found it so quickly, my son. It does not ask after a living, speaking being; מִי, who, is the word for that.

It sometimes stands for מָתַי, when, as עַד־מָה (Tehillim 79:5), until when. With a lamed it asks the reason: לָמָּה זֶּה שְׁלַחְתָּנִי (Shemos 5:22), which he glosses for what did you send me in this way. A shin may join the lamed, שַׁלָּמָה (Shir HaShirim 1:7), for what reason; and the lamed may drop away with the sense of 'for what' still standing, as וּמֶה לֹֽא־תִשָּׂא פִשְׁעִי (Iyov 7:21), and why do you not bear my transgression.

more.h: A reading of Rabbi Yonah refused
more.t: Rabbi Yonah read לָמָה אֶשְׁכַּל גַּם־שְׁנֵיכֶם (Bereishis 27:45), why should I be bereaved of you both, and its like as 'lest'. Radak finds no ground for that reading: they mean what their fellows mean, for what reason, and לָמָה אֶשְׁכַּל is why would you want me to be bereaved; and so all of them.

The word magnifies a thing, מָה רַב טוּבְךָ (Tehillim 31:20), how great is Your goodness, and equally belittles it, מָה־אֱנוֹשׁ כִּי־תִזְכְּרֶנּוּ (Tehillim 8:5), what is man that You remember him. In וְאַֽהֲרֹן מַה־הוּא (Bamidbar 16:11), and Aharon, what is he, the sense is that their complaints are against one greater than he, against Hashem; but Aharon, what is he, that you complain against him?

וִיהִי מָה אָרֻצָה (Shmuel II 18:22), let be what will be, I will run, leaves the thing unsaid: whatever will be, I do not care, I will run and tell. So too וְיַעֲבֹר עָלַי מָה (Iyov 13:13), let come upon me what may, and I do not care. In some places it is a cry of grief, מָה אֲמֻלָה לִבָּתֵךְ (Yechezkel 16:30), how faint is your heart.

With a kaf it asks quantity, כַּמָּה יְמֵי שְׁנֵי חַיֶּיךָ (Bereishis 47:8), how many are the days of the years of your life; it also magnifies, זֶה כַּמֶּה שָׁנִים (Zecharyah 7:3), meaning many years. אֵיךְ, how, asks after the manner of a thing, and כַּמָּה after the thing itself.

מדע.sense: Why: the word's sense, he says, is like למה; some say it is two words, מַה דַּוּעַ, what knowledge, from יָדַע, knowing.

more.t: וּמַדּוּעַ תִּתְנַשְּׂאוּ עַל־קְהַל י"י (Bamidbar 16:3), and why do you raise yourselves over the congregation of Hashem: the word's sense is like למה, why. Some say it is two words, מַה דַּוּעַ, from יָדַע, to know. Radak spells their reading out: what knowledge is in this thing, what is its matter.

ידע.sense: To know, and in places to recognize or to feel a thing; also of a man knowing his wife. Making a thing known; and מוֹדָע, a kinsman, so called because he knows a man.

more.t: All of these are knowing, and among them are recognizing and feeling a thing in oneself: לֹא יָדַעְתִּי נַפְשִׁי שָׂמַתְנִי (Shir HaShirim 6:12), I did not know, my soul set me, is that I did not feel it in myself until my soul set me there, and הַמַּעְתִּיק הָרִים וְלֹא יָדָעוּ (Iyov 9:5), who moves mountains and they did not know, is that the mountains did not feel it until He moved them.

וְהָאָדָם יָדַע אֶת־חַוָּה (Bereishis 4:1), and Adam knew Chava, and אֲשֶׁר לֹא־יָדְעוּ אִישׁ (Bereishis 19:8), who have not known a man: these are knowing too, and all of it is a sense that follows on the sense of knowing.

דֵּעָה and דַּעַת are the knowledge itself. מַדָּע is thought: וּמְבִינֵי מַדָּע (Daniel 1:4), those who understand thought, are those who understood what was in a man's heart from a slight hint, and בְּמַדָּעֲךָ (Koheles 10:20) is in your thought. Its root may be נָדַע, on the evidence of the Aramaic מִנְדַּע תִּנְדַּע, to know you shall know, forms of knowing written with a nun, or else יָדַע.

Because a man's near relative, one of his own family, knows him and recognizes him, the member of the family is called מוֹדָע. In הֲלֹא בֹעַז מֹדַעְתָּנוּ (Rus 3:2), is not Boaz of our family, a mem of connection is missing: it stands for ממודעתנו, of our family.

Rabbi Yehudah put וַיֹּדַע בָּהֶם אֵת אַנְשֵׁי סֻכּוֹת (Shoftim 8:16) under another sense, and Rabbi Yonah likewise, who put וּבְקֶרֶב כְּסִילִים תִּוָּדֵֽעַ (Mishlei 14:33) there with it. The sense they explain them by is breaking and destroying, and so they read וִידוּעַ חֹלִי (Yeshayahu 53:3) as broken by sickness; so too וַיֵּדַע אַלְמְנוֹתָיו וְעָֽרֵיהֶם הֶחֱרִיב (Yechezkel 19:7), and he laid waste their cities, where Targum Yonasan renders the first words וְאַצְדֵי בִּרְנְיָתֵיהּ, and he laid waste its palaces; and so וּמְעַקֵּשׁ דְּרָכָיו יִוָּדֵֽעַ (Mishlei 10:9), and one who twists his ways, on their reading, will be broken. Radak answers that there is no need to take these words out of their sense. וַיֹּדַע בָּהֶם, and with them he made the men of Sukkos know, is that he made their sin and their guilt known to them, and on the name of Sukkos, the city there that they trusted in as fortified, he chastised them with thorns whose name is סכות, as הַֽתְמַלֵּא בְשֻׂכּוֹת עוֹרוֹ (Iyov 40:31), can you fill his skin with thorns. וּבְקֶרֶב כְּסִילִים תִּוָּדֵֽעַ, and in the midst of fools it is made known, is the reverse of the pasuk's first half: the wisdom in the heart of a man of understanding rests in him, and he does not make himself known as wise or bring it out wherever he is, only at need; but a word of wisdom among fools they make known to every man, that they know such and such. It is like Chazal's saying (Bava Metzia 85b), אסתירא בלגינא קיש קיש קריא, a single coin in a jar cries out kish, kish. וִידוּעַ חֹלִי is one known and marked to all as a man of sicknesses.
Chazal explained יִדְּעֹנִי as one who puts the bone of a yadua in his mouth and it speaks of itself. Radak glosses their word: ידוע is a beast whose name is ידוע.

הוֹדִיעוּ בָעַמִּים (Tehillim 105:1), make it known among the peoples, and הוֹדַע אֶת יְרוּשָׁלַם (Yechezkel 16:2), make known to Yerushalayim. וּמוֹדִיעִים לְהַלֵּל (Divrei HaYamim II 23:13), and those making known to praise, are those who knew how to sing and to praise well and made it known to the rest of their brothers the Leviim.

לֹא נוֹדַע מִי הִכָּהוּ (Devarim 21:1), it was not known who struck him, and כִּי נוֹדַע דָּוִד (Shmuel I 22:6), that David had become known, which is that word got out and spread of where they were. On וּמְעַקֵּשׁ דְּרָכָיו יִוָּדֵעַ (Mishlei 10:9), and one who twists his ways will become known, he sets the halves of the pasuk against each other: whoever walks in innocence walks secure and fears no man, while one who twists his ways becomes known to men, cannot keep his evil deeds hidden from them and cannot be secure. וְאַחֲרֵי הִוָּדְעִי סָפַקְתִּי עַל יָרֵךְ (Yirmiyahu 31:19), and after I came to know I struck upon my thigh, is after I recognized it in myself and recognized the evil deeds I had done, I regretted them and struck upon my thigh.
מָה אָדָם וַתֵּדָעֵהוּ (Tehillim 144:3), what is man that You should know him, he glosses as Your watching over him and turning to his sin.

On יִוָּדַע כְּמֵבִיא לְמָעְלָה (Tehillim 74:5), he would be known as one bringing up on high, his father has the building of the House in view, built for glory and splendour: whoever brought an axe into the thicket of the cedars of Levanon to hew them and bring them for the building was known as though he were bringing them up before the Throne of Glory, and now the enemies hammer the gold carvings on its walls with hatchet and axes and profane the dwelling of Your Name, in the heat of Your anger against Your people. Radak later says the pasuk is to be read as explained here. His father explains וְגָבֹהַּ מִמֶּרְחָק יְיֵדָע (Tehillim 138:6), and exalted, from afar He knows, together with the words before it, that Hashem is high and sees the low: that is, He is high in heaven and sees the low upon earth, and exalted, from heaven He knows hidden things and makes them known to whom He wishes. On וַיֵּדַע אַלְמְנוֹתָיו וְעָרֵיהֶם הֶחֱרִיב (Yechezkel 19:7) his father writes וַיֵּדַע אָדָם עוֹד אֶת אִשְׁתּוֹ (Bereishis 4:25), and Adam knew his wife again: that is, he would kill the men and lie with their widows, and this is what and he laid waste their cities means, not that he pulled their cities down with his hands, but that what he did was the ruin of the world. So too Divrei HaYamim says of him וְתֹעֲבֹתָיו אֲשֶׁר־עָשָׂה (Divrei HaYamim II 36:8), and his abominations that he did.

Rabbi Yonah reads לִמְנוֹת יָמֵינוּ כֵּן הוֹדַע (Tehillim 90:12), to count our days so make known, from that sense of breaking; that is, chasten us according to the days of our life, said as a request: my God, do not multiply our chastening, for the days of our life are few, but chasten us according to them. Radak keeps the words in knowing: according to the number of our days, which are short and have shrunk from a thousand years to seventy, as it is written יְמֵי שְׁנוֹתֵינוּ בָּהֶם שִׁבְעִים שָׁנָה (Tehillim 90:10), the days of our years in them are seventy years, help us in the learning of wisdom and make its ways known to us, and then we shall acquire a heart of wisdom with Your help, as it says דְּרָכֶיךָ י"י הוֹדִיעֵנִי (Tehillim 25:4), make Your ways known to me, Hashem.

אלם.sense: To bind sheaves; to be dumb, from which, Rabbi Yonah explains and Radak approves, the widow is named; and אוּלָם, truly, and a building like a side chamber.

more.t: מְאַלּמִים אֲלֻּמִים (Bereishis 37:7), binding sheaves, means tying bundles together, and the noun in the feminine is נֹשֵׂא אֲלֻמֹּתָֽיו (Tehillim 126:6), carrying his sheaves. From this sense is אֵלֶם צֶדֶק תְּדַבֵּרוּן (Tehillim 58:2), you speak righteousness, where אֵלֶם is a noun meaning a multitude; it may also be explained from אִלֵּם, one who is dumb.

אִלֵּם (Shemos 4:11) is one who cannot speak, and כְּלָבִים אִלְּמִים (Yeshayahu 56:10) are dumb dogs; נֶאֱלַמְתִּי דוּמִיָּה (Tehillim 39:3), I was struck dumb in silence, and תֵּֽאָלַמְנָה שִׂפְתֵי שָׁקֶר (Tehillim 31:19), let lying lips be struck dumb.

more.h: Why the widow is called so
more.t: Rabbi Yonah explained well, Radak says, that a woman whose husband has died is called אלמנה from this sense, because she cannot speak and contend with those who contend with her. The nun in אלמנה is an addition. Under the root too are כִּי לֹֽא־ אַלְמָן יִשְׂרָאֵל (Yirmiyahu 51:5), for Israel is not widowed; the noun שְׁכוֹל וְאַלְמֹן (Yeshayahu 47:9), bereavement and widowhood; and אַלְמְנוּת חַיּֽוּת (Shmuel II 20:3), a widowhood in life.

In פְּלֹנִי אַלְמֹנִי (Rus 4:1), so-and-so, the man is called אַלְמֹנִי because his name is not spoken; and likewise פלוני, from פָלָא, to be hidden, meaning his name is covered. The first is correct, Radak says, rather than that he is called אלמוני because he may have had a wife who died, since a place whose name is not given is called so as well, אל מקום פְּלֹנִי אַלְמוֹנִֽי (Shmuel I 21:3), to such and such a place; though it may be said that there the words are said not of the place but of its owner.

וְאוּלָם חַי־אָנִי (Bamidbar 14:21), but truly, as I live, and its like mean truly. וְהָֽאוּלָם עַל־פְּנֵי הֵיכַל הַבַּיִת (Melachim I 6:3), and the ulam before the Heichal of the House, is a building like a side chamber, or else a vault, called in the vernacular volta. Another form is וְאֵֽלַמָּו (Yechezkel 40:21), and its ulams, and in the feminine וְאֵֽלַמּוֹת סָבִיב (Yechezkel 40:30), and ulams round about.

In וְעָנָה אִיִּים בְּאַלְמְנוֹתָיו (Yeshayahu 13:22), and wild creatures shall cry out in its אלמנות, Rabbi Yonah read בְּאַלְמְנוֹתָיו as ארמנותיו, its palaces. It may be as Rabbi Yonah says, Radak allows, but not by an interchange of lamed and resh, for only the letters אהו"י, alef, heh, vav and yud, interchange. What is right in Radak's eyes is that the word means what it says, from the widow: ruined cities are called widows, as in הָיְתָה כְּאַלְמָנָה (Eichah 1:1), she has become like a widow, since a city full of people is like a married woman and when ruined is like a widow.

כרמל.sense: The ear of grain while still soft and moist; a colour, said to be scarlet; and land of fruit trees and grain fields, for which the mountain is named.

more.t: וְכַרְמֶל בְּצִקְלֹנוֹ (Melachim II 4:42), and karmel in his sack, and וְלֶחֶם וְקָלִי וְכַרְמֶל (Vayikra 23:14), and bread and parched grain and karmel: the ear of grain is called so while it is soft and still moist. The Sifra reads the word as רַךְ מָל, that is, soft and full; the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught כַּר מָלֵא, a full cushion, that is, the ear is full like a cushion full of down.

His father takes it as a compound, כר מל: כר as in the language of Chazal, כרים וכסתות (Kilayim 9:2), cushions and covers, and מל also from the language of Chazal, מילתא (Shabbos 10b), which is a garment of silk.

רֹאשֵׁךְ עָלַיִךְ כַּכַּרְמֶל (Shir HaShirim 7:6), your head upon you is like karmel, is a colour, and they say it is the colour of שָׁנִי, scarlet; so too with a yud, וְכַרְמִיל וּתְכֵלֶת (Divrei HaYamim II 2:6), and karmil and blue.

אֶל־הַר הַכַּרְמֶל (Melachim I 18:19), to Har HaKarmel, is a known mountain in Eretz Yisrael by that name, called so because it was a place of fields and trees, for כַּרְמֶל is the name anywhere for a place of fruit trees and fields of grain. וְשָׁב לְבָנוֹן לַכַּרְמֶל וְהַכַּרְמֶל לַיַּעַר יֵחָשֵֽׁב (Yeshayahu 29:17), and Levanon shall turn to karmel and the karmel be counted a forest, is a parable: those high now like the lofty cedars of Levanon will be like the trees of the karmel, which are low, and those low now like the trees of the karmel will be high like the trees of the forest of Levanon; the prophecy is about the kingdom of Chizkiyahu. So in another prophecy, וְהָיָה מִדְבָּר לַכַּרְמֶל (Yeshayahu 32:15), and the wilderness shall become karmel: the cities that are like a wilderness with no trees will be like the karmel with its fruit trees and sown fields, and the karmel like a forest of cedars and tall trees; that is to say, Yisrael will rise from level to level.

נשׁה.sense: To forget; and in another sense, to lend and to be a creditor, where נֹשֶׁה may name the lender and the borrower alike.

more.t: נָשִׁיתִי טוֹבָה (Eichah 3:17), I have forgotten good, and צוּר יְלָדְךָ תֶּשִׁי (Devarim 32:18), the Rock that bore you, you forgot. יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא תִנָּשֵׁנִי (Yeshayahu 44:21), Yisrael, you will not be forgotten, he explains לא תנשה ממני, you will not be forgotten by Me. From this sense is בְּאֶרֶץ נְשִׁיָּה (Tehillim 88:13), in the land of forgetting, which is the place of the dead, for they are forgotten.

Another sense: לֹא־נָשִׁיתִי וְלֹא־נָשׁוּ־בִי (Yirmiyahu 15:10) is a doubled saying, either I asked nothing of them and they gave me nothing of themselves, or I did not lend to them and they did not lend to me, the verb of the lender being bound with a bet and that of the borrower without one.

It is not far-fetched, he says, that נושה should name both the borrower and the lender, since the bond of the bet tells them apart, and where the bond is missing the context shows which is meant; so שובר is said of the buyer and of the seller, the bond and the context telling them apart. The word comes without the bet in וְכָל־אִישׁ אֲשֶׁר־לוֹ נֹשֶׁא (Shmuel I 22:2), and every man who had a creditor; and of the lender without it, the context showing which is meant, in וְהַנֹּשֶׁה בָּא לָקַחַת (Melachim II 4:1), and the creditor has come to take, and in אוֹ מִי מִנּוֹשַׁי (Yeshayahu 50:1), or which of my creditors, which he explains מנושים בי, those who hold a debt against me. In the Targum's view the adjective from this root is נָשָׁה, and in the plural נָשִׁים, since it renders וְנָשִׁים מָשְׁלוּ בוֹ (Yeshayahu 3:12) as וּכְמָרי חוֹבָא שַׁלִיטוּ בֵּיהּ, and like masters of debt they ruled over him.

The heavy form is כִּי־תַשֶּׁה בְרֵעֲךָ מַשַּׁאת מְאוּמָה (Devarim 24:10), when you lend your fellow a loan of anything. One can explain from this sense כִּי־יַשֶּׁה לְךָ אֱלוֹהַ מֵעֲוֹנֶךָ (Iyov 11:6), which Radak also sets under forgetting, as Hashem holding you liable for your iniquity. And וְנָשָׁא־בוֹ אָלָה (Melachim I 8:31) is that the judge lays an oath on him. לֹא־יַשִּׁא אוֹיֵב בּוֹ (Tehillim 89:23) is that no enemy will be to him as a creditor who takes his money, and likewise יַשִּׁי מות (Tehillim 55:16), let death be to them as a creditor who takes them.

גִּיד הַנָּשֶׁה (Bereishis 32:33): Chazal said it is called so because it slipped from its place and went up (Chullin 91a); that is, Radak explains, as though it forgot its place and turned away from it. It would be right, Radak says, to explain it as the sinew that is severed, from נָשְׁתָה גְבוּרָתָם (Yirmiyahu 51:30), their might has failed, and then that too would be of this root; but it is better to join נָשְׁתָה גְבוּרָתָם with וְנִשְּׁתוּ־מַיִם (Yeshayahu 19:5), and the waters shall fail, under the root נָשַׁת.
נָשִׁים, women, and נְשֵׁיהֶם, their women, are not treated here but under the root אָנַשׁ.

דמה.sense: To be like, and to liken one thing to another; to be cut off and brought to an end; to think; and silence.

more.t: לֹא־דָמָה אֵלָיו בְּיָפְיוֹ (Yechezkel 31:8), none was like him in his beauty; and, transitive, הַנָּוָה וְהַמְּעֻנָּגָה דָּמִיתִי בַּת־צִיּוֹן (Yirmiyahu 6:2), to the comely and delicate one I have likened the daughter of Tzion. The noun is דְּמוּת, a likeness.

In אִמְּךָ כַגֶּפֶן בְּדָמְךָ (Yechezkel 19:10), your mother is like a vine in your likeness, בְּדָמְךָ is like בדמותך, as אֵצֶל פִּנָּהּ (Mishlei 7:8), near her corner, is like פנתה, and וְצוּרָם לְבַלּוֹת שְׁאוֹל (Tehillim 49:15), and their form for the grave to wear away, is like וצורתם, and their form. Or else it is another pattern, דַּם, on the measure of צַו and קַו. Rav Hai wrote that it means the moisture of nature, since whatever comes out of another thing and blossoms from it holds some of the moisture of its nature. Some take it instead from the sense of cutting off.

וְדָמִיתִי אִמֶּךָ (Hoshea 4:5), and I will cut off your mother, and נִדְמְתָה אַשְׁקְלֹון, Ashkelon is cut off: the sense of all of them is cutting off and destruction, and בִּדְמִי יָמַי אֵלֵכָה (Yeshayahu 38:10), in the cutting off of my days I shall go, is the noun. עֵינִי נִגְּרָה וְלֹא תִדְמֶה, my eye runs and does not cease, is of this sense too.

וְהוּא לֹא־כֵן יְדַמֶּה (Yeshayahu 10:7), but he does not think so: its sense is יחשוב, he will think. Likewise אַל־תְּדַמִּי בְנַפְשֵׁךְ (Esther 4:13), do not think in yourself. דִּמִּינוּ אֱלֹהִים חַסְדֶּךָ (Tehillim 48:10), we thought, Elokim, of Your kindness, is of this sense too, and may also be read in the sense of hope and expectation: we hoped, Elokim, for Your kindness.

אַל־דֳּמִי־לָךְ (Tehillim 83:2), let there be no silence for You, and דוּמִיָּה in its several places are all שתיקה, silence. לְךָ דֻמִיָּה תְהִלָּה (Tehillim 65:2), to You silence is praise, means that praise falls silent before Your mighty deeds, since praise does not reach You. Some read אוֹי־לִי כִּי־נִדְמֵיתִי (Yeshayahu 6:5), woe is me, for נִדְמֵיתִי, from this sense, that is, I have been silenced, I cannot speak a word; Radak lists it with the words of cutting off.

אנשׁ.sense: אֱנוֹשׁ, man, a name that takes in all people; and אָנוּשׁ, pain, breaking and grievous sickness, which may be why man is called אֱנוֹשׁ, all his days being pains.

more.t: אֱנוֹשׁ כֶּחָצִיר יָמָיו (Tehillim 103:15), man, his days are as grass: a name that takes in all people. Sometimes it is said of one man in particular, וְאַתָּה אֱנוֹשׁ כְּעֶרְכִּי (Tehillim 55:14), and you, a man of my own rank.

Sometimes אנשים, men, comes bare, and what men are meant is read from the pasuk. In כֻּלָּם אֲנָשִׁים (Bamidbar 13:3), all of them men, we would not know whether great men or lesser were meant, until the end of the pasuk says ראשי בני ישראל המה, they are heads of Bnei Yisrael, and then we know it means great men. In וְכָל־מַרְבִּית בֵּֽיתְךָ יָמוּתוּ אֲנָשִֽׁים (Shmuel I 2:33), and all the increase of your house shall die as men, it has just said there will be no old man in your house, so it means young men. זָקֵן בָּא בַֽאֲנָשִֽׁים (Shmuel I 17:12), old, come among men, means old men. And in זֶרַע אֲנָשִׁים (Shmuel I 1:11), seed of men, after she said she would give him to Hashem all the days of his life, she meant worthy men, whose seed is fit for blessing and to be given to Hashem.

אִשָּׁה, woman, may be of this root, the dagesh standing for a missing nun, properly אנשה, and so the plural אִשֹּׁת הַזִּמָּֽה (Yechezkel 23:44), the lewd women; he has already written of them under the root אישׁ. For women the alef falls away: נָשִׁים בְּקִרְבֵּךְ (Nachum 3:13), women in your midst, and נְשֵׁי אֲדֹנֶיךָ (Shmuel II 12:8), your master's wives.

אָנוּשׁ חִצִּי בְלִי־פָֽשַׁע (Iyov 34:6), my arrow is grievous without transgression, and כִּי אֲנוּשָׁה מַכּוֹתֶיהָ (Michah 1:9), for her wounds are grievous: all of them are pain, breaking and heavy sickness. Or they are an ill in the heart's thought, by a borrowing, as in מִכְּאֵב לֵב וּמִשֵּׁבֶר רוּחַ (Yeshayahu 65:14), from pain of heart and breaking of spirit; so it says עָקֹב הַלֵּב מִכֹּל וְאָנֻשׁ הוּא (Yirmiyahu 17:9), the heart is crooked above all and it is sick, and חֶרְפָּה שָֽׁבְרָה לִבִּי וָֽאָנוּשָׁה (Tehillim 69:21), reproach has broken my heart and I am sick. It may be that man is called אֱנוֹשׁ for this, since all his days are pains, and in this sense it says יֵדְעוּ גוֹיִם אֱנוֹשׁ הֵמָּה סֶּֽלָה (Tehillim 9:21), let the nations know that they are men, Selah.

ידד.sense: Beloved, and the noun, the love of one's soul; and יַדּוּ גוֹרָל, they cast lots, its root disputed: יָדַד to Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Yonah, יָדָה to Radak's father.

more.t: יְדִיד (Devarim 33:12), the beloved of Hashem, may keep the same form in construct and absolute alike, like גְּבִיר, a lord. מֶה לִֽידִידִי בְּבֵיתִי (Yirmiyahu 11:15), what is My beloved doing in My house: their sense is beloved, my beloved. מַה־ יְּדִידוֹת מִשְׁכְּנוֹתֶיךָ (Tehillim 84:2), how beloved are Your dwellings. The noun is נָתַתִּי אֶת־ יְדִדוּת נַפְשִׁי (Yirmiyahu 12:7), I have given the love of My soul.

יַדּוּ גוֹרָל (Yoel 4:3), they cast lots, on the pattern of רַבּוּ מִשַּֽׂעֲרוֹת רֹאשִׁי (Tehillim 69:5), they are more than the hairs of my head, and רַכּוּ דְבָרָיו מִשֶּׁמֶן (Tehillim 55:22), his words are softer than oil; its meaning is השליכו, they threw. So Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Yonah wrote it, taking its root as יָדַד, on the pattern of קַלּוּ מִנְּשָׁרִים (Yirmiyahu 4:13), they are swifter than eagles. Radak's father wrote that its root is יָדָה, in the added form, as in וַיַּדּוּ ־אֶבֶן בִּֽי (Eichah 3:53), and they cast a stone at me.

קוא.sense: To vomit, a sense he calls well known, and the noun קִיא, vomit; the land too is said to vomit out those in it.

more.t: כַּֽאֲשֶׁר קָאָה (Vayikra 18:28), as it vomited, on the pattern of הִנְנִי אַֽחֲרֵיכֶם בָּאָה (Shmuel I 25:19), here I am coming after you; or it may be from a root whose last letter is heh, on the pattern of עָשָֹה, בָּנָה, he made, he built. With an object, וְלֹֽא־ תָקִיא אֶתְכֶם הָאָרֶץ (Vayikra 20:22), that the land not vomit you out, and וַיָּקֵא אֶת־יוֹנָה (Yonah 2:11), and it vomited Yonah out.

קִיא צֹאָה (Yeshayahu 28:8) he explains as vomit and filth. The word is compounded with קלון, disgrace, in וְקִֽיקָלוֹן עַל־כְּבוֹדֶֽךָ (Chavakuk 2:16), and vomit of disgrace upon your glory. With a tzere, כְּכֶלֶב שָׁב עַל־ קֵאוֹ (Mishlei 26:11), like a dog returning to its vomit.

עלק.sense: The עֲלוּקָה: in his own view the leech of Chazal, the river worm that sucks blood until it swells and never says enough. Rav Saadiah Gaon read it as privation.

more.t: Rav Saadiah Gaon explained לַֽעֲלוּקָה שְׁתֵּי בָנוֹת (Mishlei 30:15), the alukah has two daughters, as a matter of privation. Radak spells out what that means: privation in living things is of two kinds, the passing of what exists, when it dies, which is the שְׁאוֹל of the pasuk (Mishlei 30:16), the grave; and the not coming to be of what is not, which is עֹצֶר רָחַם, a closed womb. So too in plants: ארץ לא שבעה מים (Mishlei 30:16), the earth not sated with water, that has brought forth no plants; and the second, the destroying of plants after they have come to be, which is ואש לא אמרה הון (Mishlei 30:16), and fire that has not said enough.

The root of the word, it seems to him, is the very word Chazal use in מפני סכנת עלוקה, because of the danger of the leech (Avodah Zarah 12b): the worm that grows in rivers and fastens on the feet of man and beast as they cross the rivers, and sucks their blood until it is full and swells, and drops off. The pasuk likens the matter it names to the leech, which never says enough in drinking blood.

חבת.sense: The מַֽחֲבַת, a pan, whose tav may be a root letter, though he had filed it under חָבָה; and the Kohen Gadol's daily pan offering, Chazal's חבתי כהן גדול.

more.h: Why the tav may be a root letter
more.t: עַֽל־ מַֽחֲבַת בַּשֶּׁמֶן (Vayikra 6:14), on a pan with oil, he had treated under the root חָבָה; but because of בֶּאֱמוּנָה עַל מַֽעֲשֵׂה הַֽחֲבִתִּֽים (Divrei HaYamim I 9:31), in trust over the making of the pan offerings, he allows that the tav may be a root letter.

Chazal speak of חבתי כהן גדול (Menachos 96a), the Kohen Gadol's pan offerings, whose kneading and shaping are done inside. Radak explains that the Kohen Gadol offered a tenth of an eifah in a pan every day, half in the morning and half in the evening, as it is written זֶה קָרְבַּן אַֽהֲרֹן וּבָנָיו (Vayikra 6:13), this is the offering of Aharon and his sons.

נדר.sense: To vow, with the noun נֶדֶר, a vow; the sense, he says, is known.

more.t: כִּֽי־ נֵדֶר נָדַר עַבְדְּךָ (Shmuel II 15:8), for your servant vowed a vow; אִישׁ כִּֽי־ יִדֹּר נֶדֶר (Bamidbar 30:3), a man who vows a vow; וַיִּדַּר יַֽעֲקֹב נֶדֶר לֵאמֹר (Bereishis 28:20), and Yaakov vowed a vow, saying; וַיִּדְּרוּ נְדָרִֽים (Yonah 1:16), and they vowed vows; and וְכִי תֶחְדַּל לִנְדֹּר (Devarim 23:23), and if you refrain from vowing. Of all of them, ענינם ידוע, their sense is known. Of the word נדר he says that five are pointed with five dots and the rest with six, as he wrote in the part of his work on grammar.

נדב.sense: To give willingly, where the heart moves a man to it. The נָדִיב is one whose soul is broad to give of his own in the fitting place, and a נְדָבָה is a freewill gift.

more.t: וענין הנדיבות ידוע, the sense of generosity is known: the generous man is the one whose soul is broad to give of his own in the fitting place and as befits him. The verb: אֲשֶׁר נָדַב לִבָּם אֹתָם (Shemos 35:29), whose heart made them willing; אֲשֶׁר נָֽדְבָה רוּחוֹ אֹתוֹ (Shemos 35:21), whose spirit made him willing; and אֲשֶׁר יִדְּבֶנּוּ לִבּוֹ (Shemos 25:2), whose heart makes him willing.

more.h: The noble man and his qualities
more.t: וְנָדִיב נְדִיבוֹת יָעָץ (Yeshayahu 32:8), the noble man counsels noble things; כֹּל נְדִיב לֵב (Shemos 35:22), everyone generous of heart; לְהוֹשִׁיבִי עִם־ נְדִיבִים (Tehillim 113:8), to seat him with princes. In וְהוּא עַל־נְדִיבוֹת יָקֽוּם (Yeshayahu 32:8), and for the sake of noble things he stands, the נְדִיבוֹת are מעלות נדיבות, noble qualities, and it is for their sake that he stands.

more.h: The freewill gift, and giving willingly
more.t: The noun is the freewill gift: גֶּשֶׁם נְדָבוֹת (Tehillim 68:10), a rain of bounty, and נִדְבוֹת פִּי רְצֵה (Tehillim 119:108), accept the freewill offerings of my mouth. Another form is הַמִּֽתְנַדְּבִים בָּעָם (Shoftim 5:9), those among the people who came forward willingly, and אֲנִי בְּיֹשֶׁר לְבָבִי הִתְנַדַּבְתִּי (Divrei HaYamim I 29:17), in the uprightness of my heart I have given willingly.

לְבַד עַל־כָּל־ הִתְנַדֵּֽב (Ezra 1:6), besides all that was freely offered, carries two particles where one would have done: either לְבַד, apart from, or עַל, over, would have sufficed on its own, and the second is added to make the sense plain. Lashon Hakodesh does this in many places, as הֲמִבְּלִי אֵין־קְבָרִים (Shemos 14:11), is it for want of there being no graves.

תִּרְדֹּף כָּרוּחַ נְדִֽבָתִי (Iyov 30:15), it pursues my nobility like the wind. It may be explained of the soul, as it says elsewhere וְרוּחַ נְדִיבָה תִסְמְכֵֽנִי (Tehillim 51:14), and let a generous spirit uphold me, since it is the soul that possesses generosity; or it may be said of a high station beyond the ordinary that was due to come to him, as the pasuk goes on, וּכְעָב עָֽבְרָה יְשֻֽׁעָתִֽי (Iyov 30:15), and my deliverance has passed like a cloud.

מלץ.sense: Sweet, and strongly so: he reads מַה־ נִּמְלְצוּ as how sweet and how forceful, the sweetness at its full strength. The words for spokesmen may belong here too.

more.t: מַה־ נִּמְלְצוּ לְחִכִּי אִמְרָתֶךָ (Tehillim 119:103), how sweet Your word is to my palate, he glosses מה נמתקו ומה נמרצו, how sweet they are and how forceful, meaning that the sweetness was at its full strength.

He allows that the noun מְלִיצָה, which he does not gloss, may be of this root, and with it בִּמְלִיצֵי שָׂרֵי בָבֶל (Divrei HaYamim II 32:31), with the spokesmen of the princes of Bavel, and וּמְלִיצֶיךָ פָּשְׁעוּ בִֽי (Yeshayahu 43:27), and your spokesmen rebelled against Me. Then מליצי and מְלִיצֶיךָ, formed like שָֹרֵי, the princes of, and שָֹרֶיךָ, your princes, would be from this root.

לוץ.sense: To scoff, a sense he calls known, the לֵץ being the scoffer; and a separate sense, of the מֵלִיץ and the מְלִיצָה, meaning the substance of a matter and the plea for it.

more.t: וְלַצְתָּ לְֽבַדְּךָ תִשָּֽׂא (Mishlei 9:12), if you scoff, you alone will bear it; אִם־לַלֵּצִים הוּא יָלִיץ (Mishlei 3:34), if it is the scorners, He scorns them; זֵדִים הֱלִיצֻנִי (Tehillim 119:51), the insolent have scorned me; and וְעַתָּה אַל־ תִּתְלוֹצָצוּ (Yeshayahu 28:22), and now do not scoff. Of the thing itself he says only ענין הליצנות ידוע, the sense of scoffing is known.

לֵץ תַּכֶּה וּפֶתִי יַעְרִם (Mishlei 19:25), strike a scoffer and the simple grows shrewd; זֵד יָהִיר לֵץ שְׁמוֹ (Mishlei 21:24), proud and haughty, scoffer is his name. לֵץ הַיַּין (Mishlei 20:1), the scoffer of the wine, he explains as the one who drinks the wine.

מָשַׁךְ יָדוֹ אֶת־ לֹֽצְצִֽים (Hoshea 7:5), he stretched out his hand with scoffers. With its last letter doubled the word is an adjective, a word of description, and not a verb, for were it a verb it would have to come from a root whose last letter doubles.

כִּי הַמֵּלִיץ בֵּֽינֹתָֽם (Bereishis 42:23), for the one who put the case was between them; אִם־יֵשׁ עָלָיו מַלְאָךְ מֵלִיץ (Iyov 33:23), if there is an angel to speak for him; מְלִיצַי רֵעָי (Iyov 16:20), my friends are the ones who plead for me; אֱוִלִים יָלִיץ אָשָׁם (Mishlei 14:9), for fools guilt makes the plea; and the noun לְהָבִין מָשָׁל וּמְלִיצָה (Mishlei 1:6), to understand a parable and the substance of a matter. Of all of them: ענינם תוכן הדבר והטענה, their sense is the substance of the matter and the plea made for it.

עֵד בְּלִיַּעַל יָלִיץ מִשְׁפָּט (Mishlei 19:28), a worthless witness sets out a case in judgment: the worthless witness dresses his testimony up in his best words, and false though it is, sets it out in judgment as though it were true. So the pasuk goes on, וּפִי רְשָׁעִים יְבַלַּע־אָֽוֶן, the mouth of the wicked swallows iniquity, that is, he covers the lie over with his finest arguments.

לוז.sense: To turn aside, to incline away; נָלוֹז is what is bent aside. And the לוּז, called avellanier in the vernacular, which Rav Saadiah Gaon took for the almond.

more.t: אַל־ יָלֻזוּ מֵעֵינֶיךָ נְצֹר תֻּשִׁיָּה (Mishlei 3:21), let them not turn aside from your eyes, keep sound wisdom, which he explains as let them not depart and not incline away from before your eyes. In the heavy form, אַל־ יַלִּיזוּ מֵֽעֵינֶיךָ שָׁמְרֵם בְּתוֹךְ לְבָבֶֽךָ (Mishlei 4:21), let them not turn aside from your eyes, keep them within your heart, where the dagesh stands in place of the quiescent letter, as it does also in וַיַּלִּינוּ (Bamidbar 14:36), and they stirred up complaint.

כִּי תֽוֹעֲבַת י"י נָלוֹז (Mishlei 3:32), for the crooked one is an abomination to Hashem. So too וַתִּבְטְחוּ בְּעֹשֶׁק וְנָלוֹז (Yeshayahu 30:12), you trusted in oppression and in what is crooked, which he explains as in a crooked thing, that is, in perverted judgment, in the way of וְהָעִיר מָֽלְאָה מֻטֶּה (Yechezkel 9:9), the city is full of perversion. Rabbi Yonah explained the וְנָלוֹז of that pasuk as a noun. And וּנְלוֹזִים בְּמַעְגְּלוֹתָֽם (Mishlei 2:15), crooked in their paths.

more.h: The noun from the root לָזָה
more.t: From this sense, he says, is the noun from the root לָזָה: וּלְזוּת שְׂפָתַיִם הַרְחֵק מִמֶּֽךָּ (Mishlei 4:24), put crookedness of lips far from you.

more.h: The לוּז, and whether it is the almond
more.t: וְלוּז וְעַרְמוֹן (Bereishis 30:37), and luz and armon: the לוּז is what the vernacular calls avellanier. Rav Saadiah Gaon explained לוז as שְׁקֵדִים, almonds, because almonds are called so in the language of Yishmael; and so Targum Yerushalmi renders שְׁקֵדִֽים (Bamidbar 17:23), almonds, as לוזים, the plural of לוז.

שׁקד.sense: To be quick, diligent and constant at a thing. The almond, שָׁקֵד, takes its name from this sense, since its tree hastens to blossom before the other trees.

more.t: שָׁוְא שָׁקַד שׁוֹמֵֽר (Tehillim 127:1), in vain the watchman is diligent; נָמֵר שֹׁקֵד עַל־עָרֵיהֶם (Yirmiyahu 5:6), a leopard intent upon their cities; לִשְׁקֹד עַל־דַּלְתֹתַי (Mishlei 8:34), to be constant at my doors; וְנִכְרְתוּ כָּל־ שֹׁקְדֵי אָֽוֶן (Yeshayahu 29:20), and all who are quick after iniquity will be cut off; שִׁקְדוּ וְשִׁמְרוּ (Ezra 8:29), be diligent and keep guard. Their sense is ענין המהירות וההשתדלות וההתמדה על הדבר, speed, effort, and staying constantly at the thing.

more.h: Why the almond carries the name
more.t: מַקֵּל שָׁקֵד (Yirmiyahu 1:11), an almond rod, וּשְׁקֵדִֽים (Bereishis 43:11), and almonds, and וַיִּגְמֹל שְׁקֵדִֽים (Bamidbar 17:23), and it ripened almonds, are known; and this too is taken from the first sense, because the almond tree hastens to blossom before the other trees. So it was said to the prophet, הֵיטַבְתָּ לִרְאוֹת כִּֽי־ שֹׁקֵד אֲנִי עַל־דְּבָרִי (Yirmiyahu 1:12), you have seen well, for I am quick over My word: it appears that שָׁקֵד is of the language of שוקד, one who is quick.
שְׁלֹשָׁה גְבִעִים מְשֻׁקָּדִים (Shemos 25:33), three cups made almond-shaped, which he glosses as carved in the likeness of almonds.
וְיָנֵאץ הַשָּׁקֵד (Koheles 12:5), the almond blossoms, he takes by way of figure for white hair, which is white like the almond's blossom.

more.h: Two other readings of that pasuk
more.t: Some read הַשָּׁקֵד there as the member of intercourse, and then וְיָנֵאץ is like וַיִנְאַץ בְּזַֽעַם־אַפּוֹ (Eichah 2:6), He spurned in the heat of His anger. Radak explains that reading as a man coming to loathe the bed out of his great weakness, as the pasuk goes on, וְתָפֵר הָֽאֲבִיּוֹנָה (Koheles 12:5), and desire fails. Chazal (Shabbos 152a) explain הַשָּׁקֵד as קליבוסתא. On that reading וְיָנֵאץ means it grows large: that bone, which is above the buttocks, grows and shows in old age as the flesh wastes and the moisture dries.

שֹקד.sense: Bound or joined: that is the sense its place gives נִשְׂקַד עֹל פְּשָׁעַי (Eichah 1:14), the yoke of my transgressions is bound fast.

more.t: One pasuk, whose sense in its place is bound or joined. On מלמדך להועיל, who teaches you for your benefit, the midrash has (Vayikra Rabbah 29) מסקדנא לך כהדין מססא דמסקיד לתורתא, I will be joined to you as this goad is joined to the cow; that is, in Radak's words, I will be with you always to lead you, as the מלמד, the goad, cleaves always to the cow to drive her. Rabbeinu Hai brought a proof for the sense from the words of Chazal (Bava Kamma), כלבא בסקדא וגדיא בסרכא, a dog in its sekda and a kid in its sirka.

כסא.sense: A throne, and the heavens are called Hashem's throne. כֶּסֶא, pointed with six dots, is a time, and it is also written with a heh, כֵּסֶה.

more.t: כִּסֵּא כָבוֹד (Yirmiyahu 17:12), a throne of glory. Shlomo sat on the throne of Hashem (Divrei HaYamim I 29:23), that is, for judgment, since judgment belongs to Hashem. הַיֹּשֵׁב עַל־ כִּסְאוֹ (Shemos 11:5), the one who sits on his throne; הַשָּׁמַיִם כִּסְאִי (Yeshayahu 66:1), the heavens are My throne. The plural takes the feminine form, כִסְאוֹת לְמִשְׁפָּט כִּסְאוֹת לְבֵית דָּוִֽד (Tehillim 122:5), thrones for judgment, thrones of the house of David.

more.h: Written with a heh, and shortened
more.t: שֵׁשׁ מַֽעֲלוֹת לַכִּסֵּה (Melachim I 10:19), six steps to the throne, and וְרֹאשׁ־עָגֹל לַכִּסֵּה, and a round top to the throne, in the same pasuk, are written with a heh. In Shemos 17:16 the word stands as כֵּס, a throne, without its alef, because it is joined to the name after it and the two are one word.

more.h: Grasping the face of the throne
more.t: מְאַחֵז פְּנֵי־ כִסֵּה (Iyov 26:9): Hashem holds fast the face of the heavens, which are called a throne, that is, by His power they stand, and He spreads His cloud over them.

לְיוֹם הַכֶּסֶא יָבֹא בֵיתֽוֹ (Mishlei 7:20), he will come home on the day of the כֶּסֶא, which he glosses as time; and so בַּכֵּסֶה לְיוֹם חַגֵּֽנוּ (Tehillim 81:4), at the time, for the day of our festival. The heh stands in place of an alef.

כרשֹ.sense: The belly: מִלָּא כְרֵשֹׂו מֵֽעֲדָנָי (Yirmiyahu 51:34), he filled his belly with my delicacies. The word, he says, is known from the language of Chachamim.

more.t: One pasuk, and the word as Chachamim use it (Chullin 3:1, 42a), where they speak of the inner כרס, the belly, being pierced, or most of the outer one torn, and much else besides.

ילד.sense: To bear a child and to beget one; יֶלֶד is a child. A day's events are called its children, as are the heart's thoughts; תולדות is a man's offspring or what befell him.

more.t: For the most part the light form is used of the woman, and the heavy form that gives וְהוֹלִיד is used of the man: וְיָֽלְדָה ־לּוֹ בָנִים אוֹ בָנוֹת (Shemos 21:4), she bears him sons or daughters, against וְהוֹלִיד בֵּן־פָּרִיץ (Yechezkel 18:10), he begets a violent son. Sometimes the light form is used of the man too: וְכוּשׁ יָלַד (Bereishis 10:8), and Kush begot, and שְׁמַע לְאָבִיךָ זֶה יְלָדֶךָ (Mishlei 23:22), listen to your father who begot you. אֲנִי הַיּוֹם יְלִדְתִּֽיךָ (Tehillim 2:7), I have begotten you this day, means as though I had begotten you today to be king.

The male child is יֶלֶד, הַיֶּלֶד אֵינֶנּוּ (Bereishis 37:30), the boy is gone; the female קַח־לִי אֶת־ הַיַּלְדָּה הַזֹּאת (Bereishis 34:4), take me this girl. With a vav for the yud, אֵין לָהּ וָלָֽד (Bereishis 11:30), she had no child; and in another pattern יְלִיד בָּיִת (Bereishis 17:12), one born in the house. The days of youth are יַלְדוּת, כִּֽי־ הַיַּלְדוּת וְהַֽשַּֽׁחֲרוּת הָֽבֶל (Koheles 11:10), for youth and the prime of life are vanity.

more.h: The midwife, and the day of birth
more.t: הַֽמְיַלֶּדֶת (Bereishis 38:28) is the midwife, so called because she helps the woman in labour to give birth. יוֹם הֻלֶּדֶת אֶת־פַּרְעֹה (Bereishis 40:20) is either the day a son was born to Pharaoh, or the day he himself was born, on which he made a feast every year.

more.h: Born in the house or outside it
more.t: מוֹלֶדֶת בַּיִת אוֹ מוֹלֶדֶת חוּץ (Vayikra 18:9), born at home or born outside, is a noun, or else an adjective, and the adjective is correct. By the plain sense of the pasuk it explains the daughter of your father or the daughter of your mother: whether born to your father from another woman, which is מוֹלֶדֶת בַּיִת, or born to your mother from another man, which is מוֹלֶדֶת חוּץ; and so Onkelos renders it. Chazal expounded it (Yevamos 23a) as whether your father is told to keep her mother, which is מוֹלֶדֶת בַּיִת, or told to send her mother away, as with the daughter of a mamzeres or of a nesinah, which is מוֹלֶדֶת חוּץ.

more.h: What a day gives birth to
more.t: Because time gives birth to events, the events of time are called its children: כִּי לֹא־תֵדַע מַה־ יֵּלֶד יֽוֹם (Mishlei 27:1), for you do not know what a day will bear. In another pattern, אֵלֶּה תֹּֽלְדוֹת יַֽעֲקֹב (Bereishis 37:2) means these are the events that befell Yaakov in the matter of Yosef and the cause of his going down to Mitzrayim, while אֵלֶּה תּֽוֹלְדֹת נֹחַ (Bereishis 6:9) takes in both the children Noach begot and what befell him, since the pasuk tells that Noach begot three sons and afterwards recounts what befell him. Wherever תולדות stands, its place shows whether it means the begetting itself or the events.

Because the heart gives birth to thoughts and counsels, they are called its children: וּבְיַלְדֵי נָכְרִים יַשְׂפִּֽיקוּ (Yeshayahu 2:6), and they content themselves with the children of strangers. Some read that of men contenting themselves with outside wisdoms and busying themselves with those rather than with the statutes of Hashem and His teachings; and some read it further of idols made new every day.

טלא.sense: Spotted with broad spots, where נָקֹד has small ones; likewise patched, a patch; and the lamb, טָלֶה, may belong here, since its plural is written with an alef.

more.t: נָקֹד וְטָלוּא בָּֽעִזִּים (Bereishis 30:33), speckled and spotted among the goats, and הָֽעֲקֻדִּים וְהַטְּלֻאִים (Bereishis 30:35), the streaked and the spotted. טָלוּא marks the large spots, while נָקֹד marks the small ones, dots upon dots; the spotted one is the one whose spots are broad.

וּנְעָלוֹת בָּלוֹת וּמְטֻלָּאוֹת (Yehoshua 9:5), worn and patched shoes: mended with pieces of leather set on where they wore through. Likewise Chachamim say of a piece of leather טלאי על גבי טלאי, patch upon patch (Shabbos 114a), and of a piece of cloth מטלית, a rag (Niddah 56a). So too spots of colour look like pieces upon pieces: וַתַּֽעֲשִׂי־לָךְ בָּמוֹת טְלֻאוֹת (Yechezkel 16:16), and you made yourself high places טְלֻאוֹת, which he explains as garments of many colours.

It may be that זְאֵב וְטָלֶה (Yeshayahu 65:25), wolf and lamb, and טְלֵה חָלָב אֶחָד (Shmuel I 7:9), one suckling lamb, are of this root, though written with a heh, since the plural is found with an alef: בִּזְרֹעוֹ יְקַבֵּץ טְלָאִים (Yeshayahu 40:11), He gathers lambs in His arm. By rule the lamed of טְלָאִים should carry a tzeirei, as in the other words ending in alef, צָמֵא צְמֵאִים, thirsty, and טָמֵא טְמֵאִים, unclean; it carries a kamatz instead, as נְכָאִֽים (Yeshayahu 16:7), the stricken, does, from נְכֵה רַגְלָיִם (Shmuel II 4:4), stricken in the feet. טְלֵה חָלָב he explains as one still sucking milk that had not yet eaten grass, and that is the choicest.

more.h: Against a root ending in heh
more.t: One might say the root is טָלָה, ending in heh, and that the alef of טְלָאִים replaces a yud, as the alef does in וְעַמִּי תְלוּאִים (Hoshea 11:7), and My people are hung; he calls that far-fetched. The root with alef is found in many words and with heh is not found, and טְלָאִים is not formed as the plural of a root ending in heh, which would have given טָלִים, lambs, as קָנֶה, a reed, gives קָנִים, reeds.

וַֽיִּפְקְדֵם בַּטְּלָאִים (Shmuel I 15:4), he counted them by the lambs. Chachamim (Yoma 22b) explained the word as a place name; the right reading, he holds, is the plain one, from טָלֶה, a lamb: their number was known by each man's bringing a lamb, the season being Pesach. So Targum Yonasan renders it בְּאִימְרֵי פִסְחַיָא, with the Pesach lambs.

קור.sense: To come as far as the source of the waters, and מְקוֹר, a spring; and, of this root, the spider's קוּרֵי, which he explains as sheets.

more.t: אֲנִי קַרְתִּי וְשָׁתִיתִי מַיִם (Melachim II 19:24), I came as far as the source and drank water: that is, the speaker drank all the waters of the rivers and the streams until he came to their sources and drank their water. Targum Yonasan renders it אֲנָא הֲוֵיתִי חָפֵיר גוּבִין וְשָׁתֵי מַיְן, I was digging pits and drinking water.

more.h: The spring, and making water flow
more.t: מְקוֹר מַֽיִם־חַיִּים (Yirmiyahu 2:13), a spring of living water; and כְּהָקִיר, as a well makes its waters flow, כֵּן הֵקֵרָה רָעָתָהּ, so she makes her evil flow (Yirmiyahu 6:7).

Of this root, וְקוּרֵי עַכָּבִישׁ יֶאֱרֹגוּ (Yeshayahu 59:5), they weave the spider's sheets, and קֽוּרֵיהֶם לֹא־יִהְיוּ לְבֶגֶד (Yeshayahu 59:6), their sheets will not serve for a garment: קוּרֵי, he says, are sheets. His father explains them as like קֹרוֹת בָּתֵּינוּ (Shir HaShirim 1:17), the beams of our houses; Radak takes him to mean that the spider weaves to make a covering, as the beams do.

צנן.sense: Coldness; in another sense a thorn; and in a third the צִנָּה, a weapon of war like a shield.

more.t: כְּצִנַּת ־שֶׁלֶג בְּיוֹם קָצִיר (Mishlei 25:13), like the cold of snow in the day of harvest, whose sense is coldness. Chachamim use the doubled form of it: so that it should not cool, hot into cold (Pesachim 76a), and one separates from the warm for the cold and from the cold for the warm (Mishnah Demai).

וְלִצְנִינִם בְּצִדֵּיכֶם (Bamidbar 33:55), and for thorns in your sides, and וְלִצְנִנִים בְּעֵֽינֵיכֶם (Yehoshua 23:13), and for thorns in your eyes: the sense is a thorn, explained as a hedge of thorns set round about to shut you in, so that none goes out and none comes in; or else it is a figure, like לְשִׂכִּים בְּעֵינֵיכֶם (Bamidbar 33:55), for pricks in your eyes.

וְאֶל־ מִצִּנִּים יִקָּחֵהוּ (Iyov 5:5), and even from among the thorns he takes it, and צִנִּים פַּחִים בְּדֶרֶךְ עִקֵּשׁ (Mishlei 22:5), thorns and snares in the crooked way; and in the feminine וְנִשָּׂא אֶתְכֶם בְּצִנּוֹת (Amos 4:2), and he will carry you off with thorns. The Mishlei phrase may also be read from the cold: the cold is like snares in a crooked way.

וְנֹשֵׂא הַצִּנָּה הֹלֵךְ לְפָנָֽיו (Shmuel I 17:7), the bearer of the shield went before him; עֹֽרְכֵי צִנָּה וָרֹמַח (Divrei HaYamim I 12:8 in his edition), men handling shield and spear; צִנָּה וְֽסֹחֵרָה אֲמִתּֽוֹ (Tehillim 91:4), His truth is a shield and a buckler; and the plural צִנּוֹת וּרְמָחִים (Divrei HaYamim II 11:12), shields and spears. It is a weapon of war like a shield, targa in the vernacular and al-daraqa in Arabic.

וְנִשָּׂא אֶתְכֶם בְּצִנּוֹת (Amos 4:2), he will carry you off in צנות, may belong here as well: the small boats made like a shield and a צִנָּה. So Chachamim read וְאַֽחֲרִֽיתְכֶן בְּסִירוֹת דּוּגָֽה, and your remnant in fishing boats (Bava Basra 73a): Sumchos says that one who sells a ship has sold its dugis, the small boat, and they said that Sumchos, being of Eretz Yisrael, calls it dugis, as it is written, and your remnant in fishing boats. Targum Yonasan takes בְּצִנּוֹת from the shield: the nations will carry you off on their shields, and your daughters in fishermen's boats.

כרת.sense: To cut: to cut a covenant, to be cut off from one's people, and to cut off; סֵפֶר כְּרִיתֻת, a bill of divorce; and cedar beams cut and well hewn.

more.t: וַיִּכְרְתוּ בְרִית בִּבְאֵר שָׁבַע (Bereishis 21:32), they made a covenant at Be'er Sheva; הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי כֹּרֵת בְּרִית (Shemos 34:10), I am making a covenant; כְּרָת ־לָנוּ בְרִית (Shmuel I 11:1), make a covenant with us; and אָלוֹת שָׁוְא כָּרֹת בְּרִית (Hoshea 10:4), swearing falsely in making a covenant. Also וְכָתַב לָהּ סֵפֶר כְּרִיתֻת (Devarim 24:1), he writes her a bill of divorce, and its plural, וָאֶתֵּן אֶת־סֵפֶר כְּרִֽיתֻתֶיהָ אֵלֶיהָ (Yirmiyahu 3:8), I gave her her bill of divorce.

more.h: A dispute over one word in Yirmiyahu
more.t: כָּרְתוּ יַעְרָהּ (Yirmiyahu 46:23) is read two ways. Some read it with kamatz chatuf and say it is a command, cut down her forest; others read it with the first vowel held, and so the accurate books have it, the kaf held with a ga'ya. That, he holds, is right, and it is then a past standing for a future, יִכְרְתוּ יַעְרָהּ, they will cut down her forest, as Scripture does in many places and very often in prophecy. נְאֻם, the declaration, is joined here to a past verb, though that is not the usual way in prophecy; יָֽרְדוּ לַטָּבַח (Yirmiyahu 48:15), they have gone down to the slaughter, is one like it, and so with a past verb in words of rebuke, כֻּלְּכֶם פְּשַׁעְתֶּם בִּי (Yirmiyahu 2:29), all of you have rebelled against Me.

more.h: Being cut off, and cutting off
more.t: וְנִכְרַת מֵֽעַמָּֽיו (Shemos 30:33), he is cut off from his people; וְנִכְרְתָה הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַהִוא (Vayikra 7:20), that soul is cut off; הִכָּרֵת תִּכָּרֵת (Bamidbar 15:31), it is surely cut off; אַֽחֲרִית רְשָׁעִים נִכְרָֽתָה (Tehillim 37:38), the end of the wicked is cut off. Where another does the cutting, וְהִכְרַתִּי לְאַחְאָב (Melachim II 9:8), I will cut off from Achav, and לְהַכְרִית הַֽצְפַרְדְּעִים (Shemos 8:5), to cut off the frogs. וְלוֹא נַכְרִית מֵהַבְּהֵמָה (Melachim I 18:5) is that we not cut the city off from the beasts.
וּכְרוּת שָׁפְכָה (Devarim 23:2) is one whose member has been cut, so that it no longer shoots the stream of seed like an arrow but pours and dribbles, and he does not beget.

וְהַכְּרֵתִי וְהַפְּלֵתִי (Melachim I 1:38), the Kereisi and the Peleisi, were two families in Yisrael whose name was so, and Targum Yonasan renders them as archers and slingers. But נֶגֶב הַכְּרֵתִי (Shmuel I 30:14), the Negev of the Kereisi, is of the Pelishtim, as it says of them גּוֹי כְּרֵתִים (Tzefaniah 2:5), the nation of the Kereisim.
כְּרֻתֹת אֲרָזִֽים (Melachim I 6:36), which he explains as beams of cedar, cut and well hewn; and כִּרְתוּ עֵצָה (Yirmiyahu 6:6), cut down timber, has a chirik under its first root letter.

ערר.sense: Childless: the עֲרִירִי is a man alone, with no children.

more.t: וְאָֽנֹכִי הוֹלֵךְ עֲרִירִי (Bereishis 15:2), and I go childless, which he glosses as alone, without children; and likewise כִּתְבוּ אֶת־הָאִישׁ הַזֶּה עֲרִירִי (Yirmiyahu 22:30), write this man down childless. On עֲרִירִים יִֽהְיֽוּ (Vayikra 20:21), they shall be childless, Chazal said (Yevamos 55a) that even if he has children he buries them, and they are left without children. עֲרִירִים יָמֻֽתוּ (Vayikra 20:20), they shall die childless, is read as their having no children.

חשֹך.sense: To hold back, to withhold: וְלֹֽא־ חָשַׂךְ מִמֶּנִּי מְאוּמָה, he withheld nothing from me.

more.t: וְלֹֽא־ חָשַׂךְ מִמֶּנִּי מְאוּמָה (Bereishis 39:9), he withheld nothing from me; וְאֶת־עַבְדּוֹ חָשַׂךְ מֵֽרָעָה (Shmuel I 25:39), He kept His servant back from evil; גַּם מִזֵּדִים חֲשׂךְ עַבְדֶּךָ (Tehillim 19:14), keep Your servant back from the insolent too; וְחוֹשֵׂךְ שְׂפָתָיו מַשְׂכִּֽיל (Mishlei 10:19), one who holds his lips back is wise. מֻרְדָּף בְּלִי חָשָֽׂךְ (Yeshayahu 14:6), pursued without holding back, means that the pursuer did not hold back from pursuing him. And the passive, לֹא־ יֵֽחָשֵׂךְ כְּאֵבִי (Iyov 16:6), my pain is not held back. All of them are ענין מניעה, holding back.

קְרָא בְגָרוֹן אַל־ תַּחְשֹׂךְ (Yeshayahu 58:1), call with the throat, do not hold back, means do not hold back the call; so too וְצַדִּיק יִתֵּן וְלֹא יַחְשֹֽׂךְ (Mishlei 21:26), the righteous gives and does not hold back, means he does not hold back the gift: all of them are verbs that carry an object. But וְנִיד שְׂפָתַי יַחְשֹֽׂךְ (Iyov 16:5), and the moving of my lips would hold back, seems to be a verb that stands on its own. חָשַׂכְתָּֽ לְמַטָּה מֵֽעֲוֹנֵנוּ (Ezra 9:13) means You held back from our iniquities, from bringing us low and from repaying us as they deserved.

וּבִתְחַפְנְחֵס חָשַׂךְ הַיּוֹם (Yechezkel 30:18), and in Techafneches the day held back. Rabbi Yonah explained it as חָשַֹך השׁמשׁ, the sun grew dark; Radak answers that such an exchange of letters is not found in Lashon Hakodesh, and the word means what it says, holding back, with a word left unsaid, אוֹרוֹ, its light: the day held back its light. The pasuk says it for the greatness of the trouble that was to come upon them.

חשׁך.sense: To grow dark, and to make dark; חשֶׁךְ is darkness and מַחְשָׁךְ a dark place. The lowly of men, who are in darkness, are called the dark ones, חֲשֻׁכִּים.

more.t: חָשַׁךְ הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ בְּצֵאתוֹ (Yeshayahu 13:10), the sun is darkened as it goes forth; וַתֶּחְשַׁךְ הָאָרֶץ (Shemos 10:15), the land was darkened; וְחָשְׁכָה לָכֶם מִקְּסֹם (Michah 3:6), it will be dark for you, with no divining; and תֶּחְשַׁכְנָה עֵינֵיהֶם מֵרְאוֹת (Tehillim 69:24), let their eyes grow too dark to see.

וְחשֶׁךְ עַל־פְּנֵי תְהוֹם (Bereishis 1:2), darkness on the face of the deep, and יַגִּיהַּ חָשְׁכִּֽי (Tehillim 18:29), He lights up my darkness. With a mem added, וְהָיָה בְמַחְשָׁךְ מַֽעֲשֵׂיהֶם (Yeshayahu 29:15), their deeds are in the dark, and מְֽיֻדָּעַי מַחְשָֽׁךְ (Tehillim 88:19), my friends are a dark place, meaning that my friends are as though in a dark place, where I cannot see them and they do not come to visit me in my illness. Also בְּמַֽחֲשַׁכִּים הוֹשִׁיבַנִי (Eichah 3:6), He has set me in dark places. In another pattern, כַּֽחֲשֵׁיכָה כָּאוֹרָֽה (Tehillim 139:12), the dark as the light, with its construct חֶֽשְׁכַת ־מַיִם (Tehillim 18:12), a darkness of waters, and its plural in the masculine, אֲשֶׁר הָלַךְ חֲשֵׁכִים (Yeshayahu 50:10), who has walked in darkness.

כִּי־מָלְאוּ מַֽחֲשַׁכֵּי ־אֶרֶץ (Tehillim 74:20), for the dark ones of the land are full: these are the lowly of men, who are in darkness. So too בַּל־יִתְיַצֵּב לִפְנֵי חֲשֻׁכִּֽים (Mishlei 22:29), he will not stand before dark ones, that is, lowly men, where the word is an adjective on the pattern of עֲרֻמִּים, naked. The Targum renders וּמִן־הָעָם הַדַּלִּים (Yirmiyahu 39:10), and of the poor of the people, as וּמִן עַמָא חֲשִׁיכַיָא, and of the people, the dark ones; and דַּלּוֹת וְרָעוֹת (Bereishis 41:19), poor and bad, as חֲסִיכָן וּבִישָׁן, poor ones and bad ones.

גַּם־חשֶׁךְ לֹֽא־ יַחְשִׁיךְ מִמֶּךָ (Tehillim 139:12), even darkness does not darken from You, meaning it darkens nothing from You; שָׁלַֽח חשֶׁךְ וַיַּחְשִׁךְ (Tehillim 105:28), He sent darkness and made it dark; and בְּטֶרֶם יַחְשִׁךְ (Yirmiyahu 13:16), before He brings darkness.

פרעשׁ.sense: פַּרְעֹשׁ, the flea, a known word; before the king the one speaking calls himself a dog and a flea, for his lowliness and weakness. It is also a man's name.

more.h: A flea, and why he calls himself one
more.t: אַֽחֲרֵי פַּרְעֹשׁ אֶחָֽד (Shmuel I 24:15), after a single flea: the word is known. For his lowliness and his weakness against the king, the one speaking called himself a dog and a flea. Yonasan renders בָּתַר חֲלַשׁ חָד בָּתַר הֶדְיוֹט חָד, after one weak man, after one commoner; and at לְבַקֵּשׁ אֶת־ פַּרְעֹשׁ אֶחָד (Shmuel I 26:20), to seek a single flea, he renders יַת חֲלָשׁ חַד, the one weak man. It is also a man's name (Ezra 2:3).

קרן.sense: A horn, and as a figure, might; the horns of the mizbeach, which are its corners; and in another sense close to the first, brightness, as Moshe's face shone.

more.h: The horn, and the horn as might
more.t: הַקֶּרֶן הַגְּדֹלָה (Daniel 8:8), the great horn, and נֶֽאֱחַז בַּסְּבַךְ בְּקַרְנָיו (Bereishis 22:13), caught in the thicket by its horns. As a figure, וְכָל־ קַרְנֵי רְשָׁעִים אֲגַדֵּעַ (Tehillim 75:11), and all the horns of the wicked I will cut off; so too רָמָה קַרְנִי (Shmuel I 2:1), my horn is lifted, and וְיָרֵם קֶרֶן מְשִׁיחֽוֹ (Shmuel I 2:10), and He will raise the horn of His anointed. The sense in all of them is might, תוקף.

more.h: His father on the sprouting horn
more.t: אַצְמִיחַ קֶרֶן לְבֵית יִשְׂרָאֵל (Yechezkel 29:21), I will make a horn sprout for the house of Yisrael, his father sets within the seventy years that the kingdom of Nevuchadnetzar, his son and his son's son stood. On his reading the horn is Koresh, born fifty years into the exile, the fifty years of עַד־מָשִׁיחַ נָגִיד שָֽׁבֻעִים שִׁבְעָה (Daniel 9:25), until an anointed prince, seven weeks. Koresh is called a horn as the pasuk says לִמְשִׁיחוֹ לְכוֹרֶשׁ (Yeshayahu 45:1), to His anointed, to Koresh, for he was the horn of Yisrael and their anointed, and by him they came out of exile; and וּלְךָ אֶתֵּן פִּתְחֽוֹן־פֶּה (Yechezkel 29:21), and to you I will give an opening of the mouth, is that Yisrael will see your prophecies come true.

עַל קַרְנֹת הַמִּזְבֵּחַ (Shemos 29:12), on the corners of the mizbeach, and וְעָשִׂיתָ קַרְנֹתָיו (Shemos 27:2), you shall make its corners: these are angles, and in the vernacular too a corner is named by the word for a horn.

כִּי קָרַן עוֹר פְּנֵי מֹשֶׁה (Shemos 34:35), for the skin of Moshe's face shone, is another sense, with the noun קֶרֶן and its dual, קַרְנַיִם מִיָּדוֹ לוֹ (Chavakuk 3:4), He has brightness from His hand: ענין זהר, the sense of brightness. It is close to the first sense, for when a man looks hard at the sun or at any light, it seems to him that the brightness makes horns. Of this sense too is וְעֹלַלְתִּי בֶעָפָר קַרְנִֽי (Iyov 16:15), I have laid my horn in the dust, that is, my brightness and my honour.

חצר.sense: Blowing trumpets; a courtyard, and the unwalled villages that are like one; and in a second sense חָצִיר, grass, which in one pasuk is the leek.

more.t: וַיְהִי כְאֶחָד לַֽמְחַצְּצרִים (Divrei HaYamim II 5:13), and it was as one for the trumpeters, and מַחְצְרִים בַּֽחֲצֹֽצְרֽוֹת (Divrei HaYamim II 5:12), sounding the trumpets; the regular form would be מַֽחֲצִירִים. Their sense is blowing the trumpets, since the tzadi is doubled in חֲצֹצְרוֹת, trumpets. The tzadi is written doubled in לַֽמְחַצְּצרִים as well, and the second one is not read though it is written, like the second shin of Yissachar.

הֶחָצֵר הַפְּנִימִית (Yechezkel 10:3), the inner court, and הֶחָצֵר הַחִיצֹנָה (Yechezkel 10:5), the outer. Most of them are feminine, but some are masculine: הֶחָצֵר הַפְּנִימִי (Yechezkel 40:19), the inner court, and בֶּחָצֵר הָעֶלְיוֹן (Yirmiyahu 36:10), in the upper court. The plural is masculine in רְמֹס חֲצֵרָי (Yeshayahu 1:12), to trample My courts, and feminine in בְּחַצְרוֹת בֵּית (Tehillim 116:19), in the courts of the house. Another form, חָצִיר, means the same as חָצֵר, a court: חָצִיר לִבְנוֹת יַעֲנָה (Yeshayahu 34:13), a court for ostriches, and חָצִיר לְקָנֶה וָגֹמֶא (Yeshayahu 35:7), a court for reed and rush.

וּבָתֵּי הַחֲצֵרִים (Vayikra 25:31), the houses of the villages, בְּחַצְרֵיהֶם וּבְטִירֹתָם (Bereishis 25:16), in their villages and encampments, and חֲצֵרִים תֵּשֵׁב קֵדָר (Yeshayahu 42:11), the villages where Kedar dwells: these and the like are the hamlets and open places with no wall around them, which are like a courtyard.

A second sense is grass: חָצִיר כַּבָּקָר יֹאכֵל (Iyov 40:15), he eats grass like an ox, and מַצְמִיחַ חָצִיר לַבְּהֵמָה (Tehillim 104:14), who makes grass grow for the cattle. Rabbi Yonah explained וְצָמְחוּ בְּבֵין חָצִיר (Yeshayahu 44:4), and they shall spring up among the חָצִיר, in the first sense instead, like חָצֵר, a court. And וְאֶת הֶחָצִיר וְאֶת הַבְּצָלִים (Bamidbar 11:5), the leeks and the onions, is what is called in the language of Chazal (Berachos 9b) כרתי, the leek, which he names in the vernacular; and so Targum Yonasan has it, וכרתי בָּצְלַיָא, the leeks and the onions.

מנע.sense: To withhold, to keep a thing back from someone; and to be withheld, or to hold back. The sense of withholding, he says, is known.

more.t: אֲשֶׁר מָנַע מִמֵּךְ פְּרִי בָטֶן (Bereishis 30:2), who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb; לֹא יִמְנַע טוֹב לַהֹלְכִים בְּתָמִים (Tehillim 84:12), He withholds no good from those who walk whole; מֹנֵעַ בָּר יִקְּבֻהוּ לְאוֹם (Mishlei 11:26), the people curse one who withholds grain; וָאֶמְנַע נַהֲרוֹתֶיהָ (Yechezkel 31:15), I held back its rivers.

כִּי נִמְנַע מִבֵּית אֱלֹהֵיכֶם (Yoel 1:13), for it is withheld from the house of your God, and וַיִּמָּנְעוּ רְבִבִים (Yirmiyahu 3:3), the showers were withheld. The sense of withholding, ענין המניעה, he calls known.

כלא.sense: To withhold and restrain, which he says the verb, the prison and the sheepfold all mean; and כִּלְאַיִם: wool and linen mixed, two kinds of seed, grafting.

more.t: כָּֽלְאוּ שָׁמַיִם מִטָּל וְהָאָרֶץ כָּֽלְאָה יְבוּלָֽהּ (Chaggai 1:10), the heavens have held back from dew and the earth has held back her produce; הִנֵּה שְׂפָתַי לֹא אֶכְלָא (Tehillim 40:10), behold, I do not hold back my lips; and וַיִּכָּלֵא הַגֶּשֶׁם (Bereishis 8:2), the rain was held back. All of these, with the prison and the fold, he calls the sense of withholding and restraining.

בֵּית הַכֶּֽלֶא (Yirmiyahu 37:18), the prison house, אֵת בִּגְדֵי כִלְאֹו (Yirmiyahu 52:33), his prison clothes, and וּבְבָתֵּי כְלָאִים הָחְבָּאוּ (Yeshayahu 42:22), they are hidden away in prison houses.

גָּזַר מִמִּכְלָה צֹאן (Chavakuk 3:17), the flock is cut off from the fold: the place where the sheep are held within the fences around it, so that they cannot go out but by the opening. The heh there stands for an alef, as its plural מִמִּכְלְאֹת צֹֽאן (Tehillim 78:70), from the sheepfolds, shows.

וּבֶגֶד כִּלְאַיִם (Vayikra 19:19), and a garment of kilayim, is cloth mixed of wool and linen; לֹֽא־תִזְרַע כַּרְמְךָ כִּלְאָיִם (Devarim 22:9), do not sow your vineyard with kilayim, is two kinds of seed together with the grape pip; שָֽׂדְךָ לֹֽא־תִזְרַע כִּלְאָיִם (Vayikra 19:19), do not sow your field with kilayim, is two kinds of seed, and the grafting of a tree is included in it.

כלם.sense: Disgrace: to be disgraced, and to disgrace another. It is more than shame, and always a matter of disrepute, where shame can come from humility.

more.t: He holds it more than בושה, shame, and the proof is the pesukim that pair the two: בּוֹשׁוּ וְגַם־ נִכְלְמוּ (Yeshayahu 45:16), they were ashamed and disgraced besides, and בֹּשְׁתִּי וְגַם־ נִכְלַמְתִּי (Yirmiyahu 31:19), I was ashamed and disgraced besides.
כְּלִמָּה is always from the side of disrepute, while shame is at times from the side of praise, coming from a man's humility.

כִּסְּתָה כְלִמָּה פָנָֽי (Tehillim 69:8), disgrace has covered my face, and in the plural מִכְּלִמּוֹת וָרֹֽק (Yeshayahu 50:6), from disgrace and spitting; in another pattern וּכְלִמּוּת עוֹלָם אֲשֶׁר לֹא תִשָּׁכֵֽחַ (Yirmiyahu 23:40), everlasting disgrace that is not forgotten.
גַּם־ הַכְלִים לֹא יָדָעוּ (Yirmiyahu 6:15), nor did they know disgrace: they did not feel it when a man disgraced them for the evil of their deeds.

חרף.sense: To lay open and make known: exposing oneself to death; a maidservant designated and known as a man's; reviling, which lays blemishes open. In another sense, winter.

more.t: עַם חֵרֵף נַפְשׁוֹ לָמוּת (Shoftim 5:18), a people that laid its life open to death: they revealed and showed themselves in the battle, to die. So too בְּחָֽרְפָם בַּפְּלִשְׁתִּים (Shmuel II 23:9), when they laid themselves open against the Pelishtim. Some take בחרפם as sharpening, like וְכִלְיוֹתַי אֶשְׁתּוֹנָֽן (Tehillim 73:21), I was sharpened in my reins: their heart grew hot and sharp against the Pelishtim. The Targum renders אֲשֶׁר חִצָּיו שְׁנוּנִים (Yeshayahu 5:28), whose arrows are sharpened, and כְּחֶרֶב חַדָּה (Yeshayahu 49:2), like a sharp sword, with words of these letters, and Chazal speak of סכינא חריפא, a sharp knife (Menachos 74a). In the Targum's view בְּחָֽרְפָם בַּפְּלִשְׁתִּים is of reviling, since it renders it with a word of reviling, and its word for חֶרְפָּה (Bereishis 34:14), disgrace, is of the same kind.

It serves for reviling too, since reviling is the laying open of a man's blemishes and the publishing of them: חֵרַפְתִּי אֶת־מַֽעַרְכוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל (Shmuel I 17:10), I have taunted the ranks of Yisrael, אֶת־מִי חֵרַפְתָּ וְגִדַּפְתָּ (Yeshayahu 37:23), whom have you taunted and blasphemed, and כִּי לֹֽא־אוֹיֵב יְחָֽרְפֵנִי (Tehillim 55:13), it is no enemy who taunts me. The noun is חֶרְפָּה שָֽׁבְרָה לִבִּי (Tehillim 69:21), disgrace has broken my heart.

וְהִוא שִׁפְחָה נֶֽחֱרֶפֶת לְאִישׁ (Vayikra 19:20), and she is a maidservant נֶֽחֱרֶפֶת to a man, that is, designated for him and known to be his, and Chazal use the word this way (Kiddushin 6a). They read the pasuk of a Canaanite maidservant, half slave and half free, betrothed to an eved ivri, and that is the meaning of וְהָפְדֵּה לֹא נִפְדָּתָה (Vayikra 19:20), redeemed and not redeemed.

לֹא־יֶחֱרַף לְבָבִי (Iyov 27:6), my heart will not revile, he counts in the light form of reviling, with וְחֶרְפּוֹת חוֹרְפֶיךָ נָפְלוּ עָלָֽי (Tehillim 69:10), the taunts of those who taunt You have fallen on me. Some take it from the sense of בִּימֵי חָרְפִּי (Iyov 29:4), which means in the days of my youth. Radak's father explains it as drawing back: my heart will not go back on what I said, that I have not sinned. In Arabic a thing that draws back is called מנחרא"ף.

In another sense, וְכָל־בֶּהֱמַת הָאָרֶץ עָלָיו תֶּחֱרָֽף (Yeshayahu 18:6), every beast of the land will winter upon it, which he explains as staying there through the days of winter. And וְקַיִץ וָחֹרֶף (Bereishis 8:22), summer and winter, בֵֽית־ הַחֹרֶף (Amos 3:15), the winter house, and מֵחֹרֶף עָצֵל לֹא־יַֽחֲרֹשׁ (Mishlei 20:4), which he explains: the sluggard will not plough for the cold of the winter.

כרה.sense: To dig. A second sense is eating, as כֵּרָה גְדוֹלָה is a great meal; a third is acquiring, as by purchase.

more.t: בּוֹר כָּרָה וַיַּחְפְּרֵהוּ (Tehillim 7:16), he dug a pit and hollowed it out; כִּי יִכְרֶה אִישׁ בֹּר (Shemos 21:33), if a man digs a pit; כֹּרֶה שַּׁחַת (Mishlei 26:27), one who digs a pit. אָזְנַיִם כָּרִיתָ לִּי (Tehillim 40:7), ears You have dug for me, means You dug ears for me to hear, and burnt offering and sin offering You did not ask; it is in the way of הִנֵּה שְׁמֹעַ מִזֶּבַח טוֹב (Shmuel I 15:22), behold, to listen is better than sacrifice.

בְּקִבְרִי אֲשֶׁר כָּרִיתִי לִי (Bereishis 50:5), in my grave that I dug for myself: it may be that Yaakov Avinu dug and hollowed out his grave in his lifetime. Some take it from the sense of buying, the grave I bought for myself: though Avraham bought the place, it is as though Yaakov had bought it; or because Yaakov bought Esav's share for a pot of lentils.

וּמִכְרֵה מֶלַח (Tzefaniah 2:9), a pit of salt, and נְוֹת כְּרֹת רֹעִים (Tzefaniah 2:6), the place shepherds dig so that their flocks will be penned there. All of these are digging. וּמִכְרֵה מֶלַח can also be read as a mound of salt, like the word כרי that Chazal use for a heap of grain, in the blessing said by one who begins to measure it (Bava Metzia 42a): ברוך השולח ברכה בכרי הזה, blessed is He who sends blessing on this heap.

וַיִּכְרֶה לָהֶם כֵּרָה גְדוֹלָה (Melachim II 6:23), and he made them a great meal, and יִכְרוּ עָלָיו חַבָּרִים (Iyov 40:30), companions make a meal over him: their sense is eating. לְהַכְרוֹת אֶת־דָּוִד (Shmuel II 3:35), to give David to eat, is written so with a kaf but read לְהַבְרוֹת, with a beis, and so Chazal say (Sanhedrin 20a): it is written לְהַכְרוֹת and read לְהַבְרוֹת, at first להברותו and at the end להכרותו. Menachem ben Saruk wrote that the kaf is what is written, and so did Rabbi Yehudah; but Radak found it so in none of the accurate sefarim he had seen, and Rabbi Yonah wrote that he found להכרות written in no accurate sefer, nor in the Mesorah. Radak's father writes in Sefer HaGalui that כָּרָה is a large meal and בָרָה a small one. Radak reads Chazal's words by this: at first they pressed him to eat a little, which is להברותו, as in וְאֶבְרֶה מִיָּדָהּ (Shmuel II 13:6), and I will eat from her hand, the little a man eats when he is sick; and at the end להכרותו, to make him eat much once he had begun to eat a little.

וְגַם מַיִם תִּכְרוּ מֵאִתָּם (Devarim 2:6), and water too you shall buy from them, and וָאֶכְּרֶהָ לִּי (Hoshea 3:2), so I bought her for myself; the nouns are וְנָתַתִּי מִכְרָם (Bamidbar 20:19), I will give their price, and וְרָחֹק מִפְּנִינִים מִכְרָהּ (Mishlei 31:10), her price is far above pearls. Their sense is acquiring. עַל מִכְרָם בַּכֶּסֶף צַדִּיק (Amos 2:6), for their buying the righteous for silver, may be from this too, as it says elsewhere לִקְנוֹת בַּכֶּסֶף דַּלִּים (Amos 8:6), to buy the poor for silver.

חצב.sense: Cutting, of the kind done in carving: to hew out a winepress, cisterns or a grave; and, as a figure, Hashem's many words spoken through the prophets.

more.t: וְגַם־יֶקֶב חָצֵב בּוֹ (Yeshayahu 5:2), and he also hewed out a winepress in it; וּבֹרֹת חֲצוּבִים (Devarim 6:11), hewn cisterns; כִּֽי־ חָצַבְתָּ לְּךָ פֹּה קָבֶר (Yeshayahu 22:16), that you have hewn yourself a grave here; and תַּחְצֹב נְחֽשֶׁת (Devarim 8:9), you may hew out copper. In the passive, לָעַד בַּצּוּר יֵחָֽצְבֽוּן (Iyov 19:24), that they be hewn in the rock forever, and הַבִּיטוּ אֶל־צוּר חֻצַּבְתֶּם (Yeshayahu 51:1), look to the rock you were hewn from.
עַל־כֵּן חָצַבְתִּי בַּנְּבִיאִים (Hoshea 6:5), therefore I have hewn by the prophets, is a figure: He spoke through them so much that it was as though He were beating them to pieces with His words.

more.h: The heavy form, and the noun
more.t: In the heavy form, הַמַּחְצֶבֶת רַהַב (Yeshayahu 51:9), that hewed Rahav down. The noun is וְאַבְנֵי מַחְצֵב (Melachim II 12:13), and hewn stones. The sense of it all is cutting, of the kind done in carving.

ישׁב.sense: To sit; to stay and tarry, even standing on one's feet; a man's long remaining where he is, to dwell; and being established and enduring.

more.t: אַבְרָם יָשַׁב בְּאֶרֶץ כְּנָעַן (Bereishis 13:12), Avram dwelt in the land of Canaan; וְעֵלִי הַכֹּהֵן יֹשֵׁב עַל הַכִּסֵּא (Shmuel I 1:9), Eli the kohen sitting on the seat; and בַּסֻּכֹּת תֵּשְׁבוּ (Vayikra 23:42), in booths you shall dwell.

אָנֹכִי אֵשֵׁב עַד שׁוּבֶךָ (Shoftim 6:18), I will stay until you return, that is, I will tarry; and וַתֵּשְׁבוּ בְקָדֵשׁ יָמִים, you stayed at Kadesh for days, that is, you tarried. It is tarrying even when a man is standing on his feet, as אַשְׁרֵי יוֹשְׁבֵי בֵיתֶךָ (Tehillim 84:5), happy are those who stay in Your house, and וַיֵּשֶׁב תַּחַת הָאֵלָה (Shoftim 6:11), and he stayed under the terebinth. The sense of the word is known: some of them are sitting itself, some tarrying, some a man's long remaining in the place where he is, and some being established and enduring.

לָכֵן קָרָאתִי לָזֹאת רַהַב הֵם שָׁבֶת (Yeshayahu 30:7), therefore I have called this one: strong are they in sitting. Since Yisrael go to Egypt and ask help of Egypt, which will not avail them, therefore I have called this one, Yerushalayim, so; that is, those who sit in her will be strong, and will trust in Hashem and not go to seek help, for sitting is more strength and might to them than going.

more.h: The resident and the hired man
more.t: The word for one whose stay in a place has been long: כְּשָׂכִיר כְּתוֹשָׁב (Vayikra 25:40), as a hired man and as a resident, and תּוֹשַׁב כֹּהֵן (Vayikra 22:10), a kohen's resident. This תּוֹשָׁב is one acquired as a possession forever, the servant who was pierced; this שָׂכִיר is one acquired for a term of years, the one who goes out at the end of six. The resident and hired man spoken of at the Pesach are gentiles and uncircumcised.

מוֹשִׁיב יְחִידִים בַּיְתָה (Tehillim 68:7), He settles the solitary in a house; הוֹשֵׁב אֶת אָבִיךָ וְאֶת אַחֶיךָ (Bereishis 47:6), settle your father and your brothers; and the land itself is spoken of as settled, אֶל אֶרֶץ נוֹשָׁבֶת (Shemos 16:35), to an inhabited land. Rabbi Yonah writes that in וְכֹל מוֹשַׁב בֵּית צִיבָא עֲבָדִים (Shmuel II 9:12) the word מוֹשַׁב is descriptive; Radak explains, all who sat and dwelt in the house of Tziva were servants.

דור.sense: Dwelling, like מגור; in another sense, a great burning; and דּוֹר, a generation, a word from the span of a man's life.

more.t: מִדּוּר בְּאָהֳלֵי־רֶֽשַׁע (Tehillim 84:11), than to dwell in the tents of wickedness, is like מגור, dwelling, as the Targum renders גּוּר (Bereishis 26:3), sojourn, with דּוּר. So too דּוֹרִי נִסַּע וְנִגְלָה (Yeshayahu 38:12), that is, my dwelling in this world has been pulled up and carried off.

Another sense: וְגַם דּוּר הָֽעֲצָמִים תַּחְתֶּיהָ (Yechezkel 24:5), and also kindle the bones beneath it, is a command, formed like שׁוּב, return, and קוּם, rise. The noun is אַגְדִּיל הַמְּדוּרָֽה (Yechezkel 24:9), I will make the burning great, and מְדֻרָתָהּ אֵשׁ וְעֵצִים הַרְבֵּה (Yeshayahu 30:33), its burning is fire and much wood. The sense of all of it is the great burning.

דּוֹר הֹלֵךְ וְדוֹר בָּא (Koheles 1:4), a generation goes and a generation comes. The masculine plural is וְלִפְנֵי יָרֵחַ דּוֹר דּוֹרִֽים (Tehillim 72:5), and before the moon, a generation of generations; the feminine is דֹּרוֹת בְּנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵל (Shoftim 3:2), the generations of Bnei Yisrael, דּוֹרוֹת עוֹלָמִים (Yeshayahu 51:9), generations of old, and לְדֹֽרֹתָם בְּרִית עוֹלָֽם (Shemos 31:16), for their generations, an everlasting covenant. The word is from the span of a man's life. דּוֹרִי נִסַּע וְנִגְלָה may also be of this sense, the time of my life; and it is of the first sense, since all the days a man dwells in the world are a דור.

פתח.sense: To open; from it פֶּתַח, a doorway, and the key one opens with. Close to it: to loose and set free, as a sword is drawn; and to engrave, from which swords are named.

more.t: וְדַלְתֵי שָׁמַיִם פָּתָח (Tehillim 78:23), He opened the doors of heaven; פּוֹתֵחַ אֶת יָדֶךָ (Tehillim 145:16), You open Your hand; וְאִגֶּרֶת פְּתוּחָה בְּיָדוֹ (Nechemiah 6:5), an open letter in his hand; and וּכְפִתְחוֹ עָמְדוּ כָל הָעָם (Nechemiah 8:5), and when he opened, all the people stood, that is, when he opened his mouth to read in the Torah.

From this the doorway is called פֶּתַח: לַפֶּתַח חַטָּאת רֹבֵץ (Bereishis 4:7), sin crouches at the doorway. The פֶּתַח is what lies outside the doors of the gate, and it carries the name because it is always open, staying open even when the doors are shut. So too the tool one opens with: וַיִּקְחוּ אֶת הַמַּפְתֵּחַ וַיִּפְתָּחוּ (Shoftim 3:25), they took the key and opened; and, unchanged in construct, מַפְתֵּחַ בֵּית דָּוִד (Yeshayahu 22:22), the key of the house of David, which Targum Yonasan renders the key of the Beis HaMikdash and the rule of the house of David.

Some explain מַגְבִּיהַּ פִּתְחוֹ מְבַקֶּשׁ שָׁבֶר (Mishlei 17:19), one who raises his פֶּתַח seeks ruin, from the mouth's opening: that is, one who speaks lofty things over people; and so it is explained in the words of Chazal, in Esther Rabbah. Taken of the doorway, it is one who busies himself with great buildings, in the way Chazal said (Sotah 11a), whoever busies himself with building grows poor.

The sense of loosing is close to the sense of opening: וַיְפַתַּח הַגְּמַלִּים (Bereishis 24:32), he loosed the camels; פַּתֵּחַ חַרְצֻבּוֹת רֶשַׁע (Yeshayahu 58:6), loose the bonds of wickedness; אַל יִתְהַלֵּל חֹגֵר כִּמְפַתֵּחַ (Melachim I 20:11), let one girding himself not boast like one loosing; and אֲסִירָיו לֹא פָתַח בָּיְתָה (Yeshayahu 14:17), he did not release his prisoners homeward. הִנְנִי מְפַתֵּחַ פִּתֻּחָהּ (Zecharyah 3:9), behold, I loose its loosing, is as though the stone had been in confinement all the days the work stood idle, and now He will release it and it will be set into the building.

Digging and engraving are also close to these: וּפִתַּחְתָּ עֲלֵיהֶם (Shemos 28:9), and you shall engrave upon them; פִּתּוּחֵי חֹתָם תְּפַתַּח אֶת שְׁתֵּי הָאֲבָנִים (Shemos 28:11), with the engravings of a seal you shall engrave the two stones. הִנְנִי מְפַתֵּחַ פִּתֻּחָהּ may also be read in this sense, behold, I engrave its engraving: since what completes the form of a fine stone is the figures and flowers and knobs engraved and drawn on it, the pasuk says so by way of a figure, meaning, I am completing it for the building in all its form.

From this sense of engraving swords are called פְתִחוֹת: וְהֵמָּה פְתִחוֹת (Tehillim 55:22), and they are swords, and וְאֶת אֶרֶץ נִמְרֹד בִּפְתָחֶיהָ (Michah 5:5), and the land of Nimrod with her swords.
