From this a man's near relatives are called שְׁאֵר, אִישׁ אִישׁ אֶל־כָּל־ שְׁאֵר בְּשָׂרוֹ (Vayikra 18:6), any man to any near of kin, and שַֽׁאֲרָה הֵנָּה (Vayikra 18:17), they are near kin, as though to say they are one flesh. A man's relative is like his own flesh, as it says אַךְ עַצְמִי וּבְשָׂרִי אָתָּה (Bereishis 29:14), you are my bone and my flesh.

The word is used of food at large, שְׁאֵרָהּ כְּסוּתָהּ וְעֹֽנָתָהּ (Shemos 21:10), her food, her covering and her conjugal right, which the Targum renders זִיּוּנַהּ, her provisioning. Another sense: בָּרוּךְ טַנְאֲךָ וּמִשְׁאַרְתֶּֽךָ (Devarim 28:5), blessed is your basket and your kneading trough, the trough in which the dough is kneaded; but in מִשְׁאֲרֹתָם צְרֻרֹת בְּשִׂמְלֹתָם (Shemos 12:34), bound up in their garments, it is the dough itself. It may be called so for food, since bread is a man's chief food.

פדר.sense: הַפָּדֶר, which he glosses as fat, as the Targum renders it.

more.t: וְאֶת־הַפָּדֶר (Vayikra 1:8), and the fat, and וְאֶת־רֹאשׁוֹ וְאֶת־פִּדְרוֹ (Vayikra 1:12), and its head and its fat: the meaning is fat, and so the Targum renders it, וְיָת תַּרְבֵּיהּ, and its fat. Chazal say (Chullin 26b) that this teaches that the place of the slaughter was covered with the fat and so brought up, and that this is the way of honour due to the One above.

רבה.sense: To be many, to increase, with הַרְבֵּה, much; a second sense close to it, rearing; a third, the archer; and the locust may be named for being a numerous kind.

more.t: וְחָיִיתָ וְרָבִיתָ (Devarim 30:16), and you shall live and multiply; אֶסְפְּרֵם מֵחוֹל יִרְבּוּן (Tehillim 139:18), were I to count them they would be more than the sand; פְּרֵה וּרְבֵה (Bereishis 35:11), be fruitful and multiply. In the heavy form, הִרְבָּה אַשְׁמָֽה (Divrei HaYamim II 33:23), he multiplied guilt, עַד כָּל־ מַרְבֵּה רַגְלַיִם (Vayikra 11:42), every many-footed creature, and וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים (Devarim 17:17), he shall not take many wives.

הֶֽרֶב כַּבְּסֵנִי (Tehillim 51:4), wash me thoroughly, is an imperative with a letter missing, or else a noun; and so הַרְבֵּה: אֵשׁ וְעֵצִים הַרְבֵּה (Yeshayahu 30:33), fire and wood in plenty; וְלִבִּי רָאָה הַרְבֵּה חָכְמָה וָדָֽעַת (Koheles 1:16), my heart has seen much wisdom and knowledge; וְהַרְבֵּה עִמּוֹ פְדֽוּת (Tehillim 130:7), and with Him is much redemption. Other patterns are לְמַרְבֵּה הַמִּשְׂרָה (Yeshayahu 9:6), for the increase of the dominion, which takes a tzeirei because it leans on the word after it, and כִּי מַרְבִּית הָעָם (Divrei HaYamim II 30:18), for the multitude of the people.

Rabbi Yehudah set וְלֹא־רִבִּיתָ בִּמְחִירֵיהֶֽם (Tehillim 44:13), and You did not raise their price, with וּבְמַרְבִּית לֹֽא־תִתֵּן אָכְלֶֽךָ (Vayikra 25:37), you shall not give your food at increase, and וְתַרְבִּית לֹא יִקָּח (Yechezkel 18:8), he takes no increase, in a sense of its own. Radak holds there is no need for that, and that they belong to this same sense, as they plainly sound.

A second sense, close to the first, is bringing up: רִבְּתָה גוּרֶֽיהָ (Yechezkel 19:2), she reared her cubs, and אֲשֶׁר־טִפַּחְתִּי וְרִבִּיתִי (Eichah 2:22), those I nursed and reared. The nouns are תַּרְבּוּת אֲנָשִׁים חַטָּאִים (Bamidbar 32:14), a brood of sinful men, and וְכָל־ מַרְבִּית בֵּֽיתְךָ (Shmuel I 2:33), all those reared in your house, the sense being the raising of them.

A third sense is רֹבֶה קַשָּֽׁת (Bereishis 21:20), one who shoots arrows with a bow. Some take it instead from the Targum of נַּעַר (Bereishis 21:12), רַבְיָא, a lad. It may be that אֶת־הָֽאַרְבֶּה לְמִינוֹ (Vayikra 11:22), the locust after its kind, is from this root, called so because it is a numerous kind.

ציץ.sense: Flowers coming out and being seen; other senses are the plate of gold, צִיץ, and a wing; and צִיצִת, the loose end that hangs from a garment.

more.t: צָץ הַמַּטֶּה (Yechezkel 7:10), the staff has blossomed; וַיָּצֵֽץ צִיץ (Bamidbar 17:23), and it put forth a blossom; יָצִיץ וּפָרַח יִשְׂרָאֵל (Yeshayahu 27:6), Yisrael shall bud and blossom. וּפְטוּרֵי צִצִּים (Melachim I 6:18) are figures like flowers and blossoms, the yud swallowed in the dagesh. And וְֽהָיְתָה צִיצַת נֹבֵל (Yeshayahu 28:4), and the fading blossom shall be, takes the feminine tav though נֹבֵל, fading, is masculine. The sense of all of them is the flowers coming out and being seen.

Close to this sense is מֵצִיץ מִן־הַֽחֲרַכִּֽים (Shir HaShirim 2:9), showing himself from the lattices, which is to say he reveals himself and is seen and looks out from the windows. Some read from it וְעָלָיו יָצִיץ נִזְרֽוֹ (Tehillim 132:18), and upon him his crown shall be seen: in the place where I make a horn sprout for David, there his crown will be seen. Or it may mean that the crown on his head will flower and blossom, that is, his greatness and glory will grow day by day.

Another sense is a plate of gold: וְעָשִׂיתָ צִּיץ זָהָב (Shemos 28:36), and you shall make a plate of gold, and צִיץ נֶֽזֶר־הַקֹּדֶשׁ (Shemos 39:30), the plate of the holy crown. The verb from it is the יָצִיץ of Tehillim 132:18, upon him his crown, which makes a third way of reading that pasuk; what the verb means on this reading he does not say.

Another sense is תְּנוּ־ צִיץ לְמוֹאָב (Yirmiyahu 48:9), give a wing to Moav, a wing to fly with. The Targum renders סְנַפִּיר (Vayikra 11:9), a fin, as צִיצִין, and Chazal said (Chullin 66b) that fins are what the fish flies with.

וְעָשׂוּ לָהֶם צִיצִת (Bamidbar 15:38), and they shall make themselves fringes. The loose end of a garment, what is left over from the weave and hangs from it, is called ציצית, and so the threads that the Torah commands to be hung on the corner of the garment are called ציצית. Hanging locks of hair are the same, וַיִּקָּחֵנִי בְּצִיצִת רֹאשִׁי (Yechezkel 8:3), and he took me by a lock of my head, and some read מֵצִיץ מִן־הַֽחֲרַכִּֽים this way too, showing the locks of his head from the lattices. It is called ציצית after the loose end that hangs from it, since most of the threads of the ציצית are loose end, as Chazal said (Menachos 39a), a third is the twisted cord and two thirds the loose end; and they said (Menachos 62a) there is no ציצית but a loose end. In the same sense they speak (Shabbos 19:6) of the ציצין, the hanging shreds, that hold back the milah.

גדל.sense: To be great: in honour and standing, in years, or in any increase, of quality or of quantity; to grow, and to make grow; מִגְדָּל, a tower; and גְּדִלִים, fringes.

more.h: Great in honour, great in years
more.t: מַה־גָּדְלוּ מַעֲשֶׂיךָ (Tehillim 92:6), how great are Your works, and גִּדַּל הַמֶּלֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ (Esther 3:3 in his edition), King Achashverosh made great, are greatness in honour and standing. וַיִּגְדַּל הַיֶּלֶד (Bereishis 21:8), the child grew, and וַיִּגְדְּלוּ הַנְּעָרִים (Bereishis 25:27), the lads grew, are the adding of years. The adjective goes both ways: גַּם הָאִישׁ מֹשֶׁה גָּדוֹל מְאֹד (Shemos 11:3), the man Moshe too was very great, is great in honour and standing, and אֲחִי יֶפֶת הַגָּדוֹל (Bereishis 10:21), the brother of Yefes the great, is great in years, as Chazal explained it (Sanhedrin 69b), that Yefes was the eldest of his brothers.

אֶת־שְׁנֵי הַמְּאֹרֹת הַגְּדֹלִים (Bereishis 1:16), the two great lights, are great in light; אִשָּׁה גְדוֹלָה (Melachim II 4:8), a great woman, is one of importance and honour; הַמַּסֹּת הַגְּדֹלֹת (Devarim 7:19), the great trials, are great in wonder. חַיִל גָּדוֹל מְאֹד (Yechezkel 37:10), a very great host, means a great number, and likewise זְבָחִים גְּדוֹלִים (Nechemiah 12:43), great sacrifices, since the word is used of every kind of increase, whether in quality or in quantity.

רַק הַכִּסֵּא אֶגְדַּל מִמֶּךָּ (Bereishis 41:40), only in the throne will I be greater than you, he explains as greater in the matter of the throne, since here too the verb takes no object, as Rabbi Yonah wrote.

עַל־פְּרִי־גֹדֶל (Yeshayahu 10:12), upon the fruit of the greatness; כְּגֹדֶל חַסְדֶּךָ (Bamidbar 14:19), according to the greatness of Your kindness; הַלְלוּהוּ כְּרֹב גֻּדְּלוֹ (Tehillim 150:2), praise Him according to the abundance of His greatness. Another pattern is הַגְּדֻלָּה, the greatness, as in וְלִגְדֻלָּתוֹ אֵין חֵקֶר (Tehillim 145:3), and His greatness is unsearchable; and another is בִּגְדֹל זְרוֹעֲךָ (Shemos 15:16), by the greatness of Your arm.

כִּי מִנְּעוּרַי גְּדֵלַנִי כְאָב (Iyov 31:18), for from my youth he grew up with me as a father: Radak takes the verb as intransitive, גדל עמי, he grew with me, said of the orphan named just before; Rabbi Yonah wrote that גְדֵלַנִי is transitive. The doubled verb: מַיִם גִּדְּלוּהוּ (Yechezkel 31:4), the waters made it grow, וְגֶשֶׁם יְגַדֵּל (Yeshayahu 44:14), and the rain makes it grow, and גַּדֵּל פֶּרַע שְׂעַר רֹאשׁוֹ (Bamidbar 6:5), letting the locks of the hair of his head grow.

מִגְדָּל is a tower, the tall and large building: וַיִּבֶן מִגְדָּל בְּתוֹכוֹ (Yeshayahu 5:2), and he built a tower in it, and אֶתֹּץ אֶת־הַמִּגְדָּל הַזֶּה (Shoftim 8:9), I will pull down this tower. The plural is בִּנְפֹל מִגְדָּלִים (Yeshayahu 30:25), when towers fall, and in the feminine וּמִגְדְּלֹתַיִךְ יִתֹּץ (Yechezkel 26:9), he will pull down your towers. מִגְדְּלוֹת מֶרְקָחִים (Shir HaShirim 5:13) he takes as the flowers that grow among the spices.

גְּדִלִים תַּעֲשֶׂה־לָּךְ (Devarim 22:12), you shall make yourself גְּדִלִים: the fringes hanging from a garment that are not woven are called גדילים. גְּדִלִים מַעֲשֵׂה שַׁרְשְׁרוֹת (Melachim I 7:17) are cords of chain work, and the Targum renders מַעֲשֵׂה עֲבֹת (Shemos 28:22), cord work, as עוֹבַד גְּדִילוּ, work of cords. The pasuk is about the tzitzis commanded elsewhere (Bamidbar 15:38); it says גדיל here and ציצית there because the mitzvah of tzitzis is that a third be גדיל, cord, and two thirds ענף, branch.

פתל.sense: Twisting and turning about, which he holds is the one sense of the whole root: crooked conduct, a thread doubled and twisted, and פָּתִיל, a small piece of cloth.

more.t: אֵין בָּהֶם נִפְתָּל וְעִקֵּֽשׁ (Mishlei 8:8), there is nothing twisted or crooked in them; וַֽעֲצַת נִפְתָּלִים נִמְהָֽרָה (Iyov 5:13), the counsel of the twisted is rushed; וְעִם־עִקֵּשׁ תִּתְפַּתָּֽל (Tehillim 18:27), and with the crooked You show Yourself twisted. The sense of all of them is turning about and distortion, and the adjective with the letters doubled is דּוֹר עִקֵּשׁ וּפְתַלְתֹּֽל (Devarim 32:5), a crooked and twisted generation.

נַפְתּוּלֵי אֱלֹהִים נִפְתַּלְתִּי (Bereishis 30:8) he reads as I turned about and strove with my sister to overcome her, and I have prevailed. נפתולי is joined to the word אלהים for the greatness of the wrestlings and their might, on the model of מַאְפֵּלְיָה (Yirmiyahu 2:31), a great darkness, שַׁלְהֶבֶתְיָֽה (Shir HaShirim 8:6), a great flame, עִיר־גְּדוֹלָה לֵֽאלֹהִים (Yonah 3:3), an exceedingly great city, and כְּֽהַרְרֵי־אֵל (Tehillim 36:7), like great mountains. Some explain the phrase from the twisted thread: that is, I grew strong with my sister, since a thread doubled and twisted is the stronger for it.

In אֲשֶׁר אֵין־צָמִיד פָּתִיל (Bamidbar 19:15), which has no covering of פָּתִיל, he explains פָּתִיל as a small piece of cloth, and like it in the words of the Mishnah (Shabbos 2:3), פתילת הבגד שקפלה ולא הבהבה, a wick of cloth that one folded and did not singe. To his mind חֹתָֽמְךָ וּפְתִילֶךָ (Bereishis 38:18), your seal and your פְּתִיל, is the same, meaning the cloak of the one addressed or the turban on his head; and that is the view of the Targum, which renders it שׁוֹשִׁפָּךְ, your wrap, as it renders וַיָּלֶט פָּנָיו בְּאַדַּרְתּוֹ (Melachim I 19:13), and he wrapped his face in his mantle, בְּשׁוֹשִׁיפֵיהּ. Some of the commentators read חותמך ופתילך as a thread doubled and twisted, but Radak holds that what he wrote is correct.

פְּתִֽיל־הַנְּעֹרֶת (Shoftim 16:9), a thread of tow, and פְּתִיל תְּכֵלֶת (Shemos 39:31), a thread of techeiles, are a cord doubled and twisted, and so Chazal said (Sifrei, Shelach) פתיל שיהיה טווי ושזור, that a פתיל be spun and twisted. Everything that falls under this root is one sense, distortion and turning about, since a thread doubled and twisted is distorted, and so is cloth made from twisted threads.

גפן.sense: גֶּפֶן, the vine; and גֶּפֶן שָׂדֶה, a vine of the field, which some take for a tree like a vine that the gourds grow on.

more.t: וְהִנֵּה־ גֶפֶן לְפָנָֽי, and behold a vine before me; לְגֶפֶן אַדָּֽרֶת (Yechezkel 17:8), a splendid vine; גֶּפֶן בּוֹקֵק יִשְׂרָאֵל (Hoshea 10:1), Yisrael is an emptied vine; and the plural, וְהַגְּפָנִים סְמָדַר (Shir HaShirim 2:13), the vines are in blossom.

וַיִּמְצָא גֶּפֶן שָׂדֶה (Melachim II 4:39), and he found a vine of the field, from which he gathered wild gourds. Some explain גפן שדה as a particular tree on which the gourds grow; it is like a vine, and is called a vine of the field.

לקשׁ.sense: The late rain and the late grass: the מַלְקוֹשׁ is the later rain, where the יוֹרֶה comes first; the לֶקֶשׁ is late grass; and the verb is to leave a vineyard late.

more.h: The first rain and the last
more.t: יוֹרֶה וּמַלְקוֹשׁ (Devarim 11:14), the early rain and the late rain: the yoreh is the rain that comes first and the malkosh is the later one.

Likewise the late grass: בִּתְחִלַּת עֲלוֹת הַלָּקֶשׁ (Amos 7:1), at the beginning of the coming up of the late grass, and in that same pasuk וְהִנֵּה־ לֶקֶשׁ אַחַר גִּזֵּי הַמֶּֽלֶךְ, and behold, late grass after the king's mowings. The noun carries six points.

The heavier verb from it: וְכֶרֶם רָשָׁע יְלַקֵּֽשׁוּ (Iyov 24:6), and they leave a vineyard late for the wicked man. His father gave it a correct reading: they hold the vineyard back for the wicked man's need. That is, the grapes are left on the vines after the other vineyards have been picked, so that they ripen well on the vines and make the finest wine; and for dread of the wicked man they are afraid, and no one touches them, though the other vineyards have been picked.

מרד.sense: To rebel, against a king or against Hashem; and in another sense, poverty and lowliness: מְרוּדִים, the lowly poor, and the days of her affliction and lowliness.

more.t: וְגַם בַּמֶּלֶךְ נְבֽוּכַדְנֶאצַּר מָרָד (Divrei HaYamim II 36:13), and he also rebelled against king Nevuchadnetzar; and וּשְׁלשׁ־עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה מָרָֽדוּ (Bereishis 14:4), thirteen years they rebelled, which he reads as, and in the thirteenth year.
אַל־ תִּמְרֹדוּ (Bamidbar 14:9), do not rebel, said of rebelling against Hashem, and וְאֹתָנוּ אֶל־ תִּמְרֹדוּ (Yehoshua 22:19), and do not rebel against us.

הֵמָּה הָיוּ בְּֽמֹרְדֵי ־אוֹר (Iyov 24:13), they were among those who rebel against the light, that is, they rebel against the light and do not know it. He allows a second reading, that the mem is added and the root is יָרַד, to go down, so that they were in the going down of the light: they go about at evening and dig through the walls of houses in the dark.

אִם־ בְּמֶרֶד וְאִם־בְּמַעַל (Yehoshua 22:22), whether in rebellion or in treachery, which carries six points; and in another pattern בֶּֽן־נַֽעֲוַת הַמַּרְדּוּת (Shmuel I 20:30), son of a perverse rebelliousness.

מְרוּדִים תָּבִיא בָיִת (Yeshayahu 58:7), bring the lowly poor into your house; and the noun יְמֵי עָנְיָהּ וּמְרוּדֶיהָ (Eichah 1:7), the days of her affliction and her lowliness, which he reads as, in the days of her affliction; and זְכָר־עָנְיִי וּמְרוּדִי (Eichah 3:19), remember my affliction and my lowliness. Their sense, he says, is ענין דלות ושפלות, poverty and lowliness, and he will write of them again under the root רוּד.

מרה.sense: To defy a word or a command, which in all its forms he calls changing and altering it; מְרִי, defiance. מוֹרָה is a razor.

more.t: אֲשֶׁר מָרָה אֶת־פִּי (Melachim I 13:26), who defied the mouth of Hashem; כִּי מָרוּ בָֽךְ (Tehillim 5:11), for they rebelled against You; and כִּֽי־אֹתִי מָרָתָה (Yirmiyahu 4:17), for she defied Me.

more.h: They did not defy His word
more.t: וְלֹֽא־ מָרוּ אֶת־דְּבָרֹֽיו (Tehillim 105:28), and they did not defy His words: the signs He set among them were as He commanded, and likewise the frogs and the swarm came. Or it is read that Moshe and Aharon, whom He sent over the plagues, did not defy His word.
כִּי מָרוֹ מָרִיתִי (Eichah 1:20), for I have grievously defied; סוֹרֵר וּמוֹרֶה (Devarim 21:18), wayward and defiant; and שִׁמְעוּ־נָא הַמֹּרִים (Bamidbar 20:10), hear now, you defiant ones.

מֹרַת רוּחַ (Bereishis 26:35), a defiance of spirit: each one of them was defying their spirit, that is, altering and changing their will. Or it is a noun on the pattern of תּוֹעָה, error (Yeshayahu 32:6).

כִּי בֵּית מְרִי הֵמָּה (Yechezkel 2:5), for they are a house of defiance; גַּם־הַיּוֹם מְרִי שִׂחִי (Iyov 23:2), even today my complaint is defiance; אֶֽת־ מֶרְיְךָ (Devarim 31:27), your defiance, with a segol under the mem; and לָשׁוּב לְעַבְדֻתָם בְּמִרְיָם (Nechemiah 9:17), to return to their bondage in their defiance, with a chirik under the mem.

The describing word is on the pattern of the noun: וְאָמַרְתָּ אֶל־ מֶרִי (Yechezkel 44:6), and you shall say to the defiant. So too אַל־תְּהִי־ מֶרִי כְּבֵית הַמֶּרִי (Yechezkel 2:8), do not be defiant like the house of defiance, where the first מֶרִי describes, on the pattern of פֶּתִי, a simpleton, and the second is a noun; or the first is a noun too and is short a word, the right reading being, do not be a man of defiance. So too וַֽאֲנִי תְפִלָּֽה (Tehillim 109:4), and I am prayer, meaning I am a man of prayer; and so אַךְ־ מְרִי יְבַקֶּשׁ־רָע (Mishlei 17:11), a defiant man seeks only evil, a describing word or a noun short the word man.

כִּֽי־ הִמְרוּ אֶת־רוּחוֹ (Tehillim 106:33), for they defied His spirit: Moshe and Aharon defied the word of Hashem, His spirit here being His word, and it was Hashem who pronounced with His lips that they should not enter the land. So וַיַּמְרוּ ־בִי (Yechezkel 20:13), and they defied Me; מַמְרִים הֱיִתֶם (Devarim 31:27), you have been defiant; כַּמָּה יַמְרוּהוּ בַמִּדְבָּר (Tehillim 78:40), how often they defied Him in the wilderness; and וַתֶּמֶר אֶת־מִשְׁפָּטַי לְרִשְׁעָה (Yechezkel 5:6), and she changed My laws into wickedness.
לַמְרוֹת עֵנֵי כְבוֹדֽוֹ (Yeshayahu 3:8), to defy the eyes of His glory, whose proper form is לְהַמְרוֹת; and so לַמְרוֹת עֶלְיוֹן בַּצִּיָּֽה (Tehillim 78:17), to defy the Most High in the desert.
עַל־הָאָרֶץ מְרָתַיִם (Yirmiyahu 50:21), against the land of Merasayim: Targum Yonasan renders it from this sense, עַל אַרְעָא דְעַמָא סַרְבָן, against the land of a defiant people.

אֶת־עֳנִי יִשְׂרָאֵל מֹרֶה מְאֹד (Melachim II 14:26), the affliction of Yisrael, greatly altered, is from this sense too, that is, much changed and altered. And in וּמוֹרָה לֹא־יַעֲלֶה עַל־רֹאשׁוֹ (Shoftim 13:5), and no מוֹרָה shall come upon his head, the מוֹרָה is the razor.

מרר.sense: Bitter and bitterness, in taste and in soul; the gall; and in other senses, exchange, as of a scent unchanged, and height, as the tall markers, תַּמְרוּרִים.

more.h: Bitter in taste and in soul
more.t: מַר ־נֶפֶשׁ (Shmuel I 22:2), bitter of soul; כִּי מָרִים הֵם (Shemos 15:23), for they are bitter, said of the waters; צְעָקָה גְּדֹלָה וּמָרָה (Bereishis 27:34), a great and bitter cry; and מָרָה כַלַּֽעֲנָה (Mishlei 5:4), bitter as wormwood. In קְרֶאןָ לִי מָרָא (Rus 1:20), call me Mara, the alef comes in place of the hei. Further, וְהִיא מָרַת נָפֶשׁ (Shmuel I 1:10), and she was bitter of soul, and כִּי־רַע וָמָר עָזְבֵךְ (Yirmiyahu 2:19), that your forsaking is evil and bitter.

כִּֽי־ מָרָה נֶפֶשׁ כָּל־הָעָם (Shmuel I 30:6), for the soul of all the people was bitter, is a past verb, since its stress falls on the first syllable and it carries two pashta accents. כִּֽי־ מַר ־לִי מְאֹד מִכֶּם (Rus 1:13), for it is far more bitter for me than for you, may likewise be a past verb, since it has a patach; or it may be a noun rather than an adjective, for though patach is found in adjectives of doubled roots, they are few.

עַל־ מַר נַפְשִֽׁי (Yeshayahu 38:15), over the bitterness of my soul, is a noun, that is, that You saved me from the bitterness of my soul; and so Targum Yonasan renders it, דְאוֹסִיף עַל חַיַי וְשֵׁיזֵיב מִמְרִיר נַפְשִׁי, who added to my life and saved me from the bitterness of my soul. So also הִנֵּה לְשָׁלוֹם מַר ־לִי מָר (Yeshayahu 38:17), behold, for peace I had bitter bitterness; and with the feminine hei, bound to the next word, לֵב יוֹדֵעַ מָרַּת נַפְשׁוֹ (Mishlei 14:10), the heart knows the bitterness of its soul, the resh taking a dagesh.

Rabbi Yonah brought מֹרַת רוּחַ (Bereishis 26:35), a bitterness of spirit, under this root; but then it ought to have had a dagesh, and a hurried vowel under the mem. The right view is that it belongs to the root מָרָה.

The noun in its full form is מָרוֹר, bitterness; in the plural, עַל־מַצּוֹת וּמְרֹרִים (Bamidbar 9:11), with matzos and bitter herbs, and הִשְׂבִּיעַנִי בַמְּרוֹרִים (Eichah 3:15), He has sated me with bitterness; in the feminine plural, כִּֽי־תִכְתֹּב עָלַי מְרֹרוֹת (Iyov 13:26), for You write bitter things against me, and אַשְׁכְּלֹת מְרֹרֹת (Devarim 32:32), clusters of bitterness.

בְּשִׁבְרוֹן מָתְנַיִם וּבִמְרִירוּת (Yechezkel 21:11), with breaking of loins and with bitterness; בְּכִי תַמְרוּרִים (Yirmiyahu 31:15), bitter weeping; וּמֶמֶר לְיֽוֹלַדְתּֽוֹ (Mishlei 17:25), and bitterness to her who bore him; and כִּי יַשְׂבִּעַנִי מַמְּרֹרִֽים (Iyov 9:18), for He fills me with bitterness.

more.h: The adjective, and the bitter of day
more.t: The adjective is וְקֶטֶב מְרִירִי (Devarim 32:24), and a bitter ketev, whose sense is the force of the heat, which is like a deadly poison. כִּמְרִירֵי יֽוֹם (Iyov 3:5) he reads as, like those who are bitter of day and ill starred: may they terrify that day with their curse. Some take the kaf as added, as in כַּֽחֲצֹת הַלַּיְלָה (Shemos 11:4), at midnight, and כְּמַסִּיגֵי גְּבוּל (Hoshea 5:10), movers of a boundary.

יֵמַר שֵׁכָר לְשֹׁתָֽיו (Yeshayahu 24:9), strong drink turns bitter to those who drink it; אֲמָרֵר בַּבֶּכִי (Yeshayahu 22:4), I will embitter with weeping, that is, embitter my soul, or those who hear me; וַיְמָֽרֲרוּ אֶת־חַיֵּיהֶם (Shemos 1:14), and they made their lives bitter; and כִּי־ הֵמַר שַׁדַּי לִי (Rus 1:20), for Shakai has made it bitter for me.

אַל־ תַּמֵּר בּוֹ (Shemos 23:21) is another sense in this verb; because it is joined with a beis, its sense is like תְּמָרֵר: do not embitter him. In yet another sense, וְרֵיחֹו לֹא נָמָֽר (Yirmiyahu 48:11), and its scent was not changed, is like לא נתחלף, was not exchanged. His father writes that אֶדַּדֶּה כָל־שְׁנוֹתַי עַל־ מַר נַפְשִֽׁי (Yeshayahu 38:15) is of this sense; Radak explains it: I shall take my delight all my years over what He exchanged for me, adding to my years; and עֲלֵיהֶם יִֽחְיוּ (Yeshayahu 38:16), upon them they live, is: now I know that to the years allotted to men You add, at Your will, as You added to mine.

שִׂמִי לָךְ תַּמְרוּרִים (Yirmiyahu 31:21), set up markers for yourself, are the tall markers; so too הִכְעִיס אֶפְרַיִם תַּמְרוּרִים (Hoshea 12:15), Ephraim provoked with markers, that is, with the markers he made he provoked Hashem, though it may be of the first sense, that Ephraim provoked a provocation of bitterness. Of this sense, with the mem doubled, וַיִּתְמַרְמַר אֵלָיו (Daniel 8:7), he rose up against him, that is, grew high and lifted himself up against him. And the right view is that כְּמַר מִדְּלִי (Yeshayahu 40:15), like a drop from a bucket, is from this root and this sense, the sense of height; the bucket's drop is so called because it falls from a height.

יִשְׁפֹּךְ לָאָרֶץ מְרֵֽרָֽתִי (Iyov 16:13), He pours out my gall on the ground; מְרוֹרַת פְּתָנִים בְּקִרְבּֽוֹ (Iyov 20:14), the gall of asps within him; and וּבָרָק מִמְּרֹֽרָתוֹ יַֽהֲלֹךְ (Iyov 20:25), and a glittering point comes out of his gall. This is the gall bladder, and some read אַשְׁכְּלֹת מְרֹרֹת (Devarim 32:32) the same way, clusters of gall. In the heavy form, וַֽיְמָֽרֲרֻהוּ וָרֹבּוּ (Bereishis 49:23), they struck him to the gall and shot, that is, they shot their arrows as far as the gall.

קדד.sense: Bowing: the lowering and bending of the קָדְקֹד, the crown of the head, a word of this root with its first letter doubled. Also the spice קִדָּה.

more.t: וַיִּקֹּד דָּוִד אַפַּיִם (Shmuel I 24:8 in his edition), and David bowed his face, and וַֽיִּקְּדוּ וַיִּֽשְׁתַּֽחֲוֻֽ (Bereishis 43:28), and they bowed and prostrated themselves. Their sense is the lowering and bending of the crown of the head.

קדקד is from the root קָדַד with its first letter doubled: וְטָרַף זְרוֹעַ אַף־קָדְקֹֽד (Devarim 33:20), and he tears the arm, yes, the crown of the head; וּלְקָדְקֹד נְזִיר אֶחָֽיו (Bereishis 49:26), and on the crown of the head of him who was set apart from his brothers; וְעַֽל־קָדְקֳדוֹ חֲמָסוֹ יֵרֵֽד (Tehillim 7:17), and his violence comes down on his own crown; and וְעַד קָדְקֳדֶֽךָ (Devarim 28:35), and to the crown of your head. קָדְקֹד שֵׂעָר (Tehillim 68:22) is the crown of hair, for at the crown the hair of the head divides, half to the right and half to the left.

וְקִדָּה חֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת (Shemos 30:24), and of kidah five hundred, Onkelos renders וּקְצִיעֲתָא, cassia. So it is named in the words of Chazal (Kerisos 6a) in the compounding of the ketores, myrrh and cassia; and so it is called in Arabic and in Greek, קציעה. Rav Saadiah Gaon wrote that it is costus.

כרע.sense: To kneel or crouch, and to bring another low; from this, כְּרָעַיִם, a beast's legs, named for their bending in kneeling.

more.t: כָּרַע רָבַץ כְּאַרְיֵה (Bereishis 49:9), he crouched, he lay down like a lion; כָּֽרְעוּ עַל־בִּרְכֵיהֶם (Shoftim 7:6), they knelt on their knees; מִכְּרֹעַ עַל־בִּרְכָּיו (Melachim I 8:54), from kneeling on his knees; וּבִרְכַּיִם כֹּֽרְעוֹת תְּאַמֵּֽץ (Iyov 4:4), you strengthened the buckling knees; and וְכֻלְּכֶם לַטֶּבַח תִּכְרָעוּ (Yeshayahu 65:12), and all of you shall bow down to the slaughter.

בִּלְתִּי כָרַע תַּחַת אַסִּיר (Yeshayahu 10:4), without bowing under the prisoner. Ibn Ezra explains that none escapes except one who bows and hides himself beneath a prisoner, and beneath the slain they fall so as to escape. Radak's brother Rabbi Moshe explains it otherwise: apart from this bowing they now have in their own land, where the nations bring them low, they shall go as prisoners and fall as slain; and תַּחַת here means in the place of, as in שְׁבוּ אִישׁ תַּחְתָּיו (Shemos 16:29), let every man stay in his place.

וּבַחוּרֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הִכְרִֽיעַ (Tehillim 78:31), and He brought low the young men of Yisrael; תַּכְרִיעַ קָמַי תַּחְתָּֽי (Tehillim 18:40), You bring low beneath me those who rise against me; and הַכְרֵעַ הִכְרַעְתִּנִי (Shoftim 11:35), you have brought me very low. Their sense is humbling.

From this the legs of a beast are called כרעים, because they bend in kneeling: שְׁתֵּי כְרָעַיִם אוֹ בְדַל־אֹזֶן (Amos 3:12), two legs or a piece of an ear, and וְהַקֶּרֶב וְהַכְּרָעַיִם יִרְחַץ בַּמָּיִם (Vayikra 1:13), and the innards and the legs he washes in water.

But כְרָעַיִם מִמַּעַל לְרַגְלָיו (Vayikra 11:21), כרעים above its legs, are the extra digits of the legs, above the four legs that the locust has near its head, with which it braces itself when it wants to spring; and that is what the pasuk means by לְנַתֵּר בָּהֵן עַל־הָאָֽרֶץ, to leap with them upon the ground.

סגד.sense: To bow down. His entry gives no gloss of its own: two pesukim, and the Targum's use of the word for bowing oneself down.

more.t: יִסְגָּד ־לוֹ וְיִשְׁתַּחוּ (Yeshayahu 44:17), he bows to it and prostrates himself, and לְבוּל עֵץ אֶסְגּֽוֹד (Yeshayahu 44:19), shall I bow down to a block of wood. The Targum renders וַיִּשְׁתַּחוּ (Bereishis 18:2), and he bowed himself, with וּסְגִיד, and he bowed. That is the whole of the entry.

צעק.sense: To cry out, and the noun צְעָקָה, a cry; their sense, he says, is like that of זעקה, spelled with a zayin.

more.t: צָעַק לִבָּם (Eichah 2:18), their heart cried out; צָעֲקוּ וַי"י שָׁמֵעַ (Tehillim 34:18), they cried out and Hashem heard; עַל־כֵּן הֵם צֹעֲקִים (Shemos 5:8), therefore they cry out; and עֲלִי הַלְּבָנוֹן וּצְעָקִי (Yirmiyahu 22:20), go up to Levanon and cry out, where the first root letter takes a chataf kamatz. And כִּי אִם־צָעֹק יִצְעַק (Shemos 22:22), for if he cries out at all.

וַיִּצְעַק צְעָקָה גְּדֹלָה (Bereishis 27:34), and he cried a great cry; הַכְּצַעֲקָתָהּ הַבָּאָה אֵלַי (Bereishis 18:21), whether according to its cry that has come to Me; and וְאֶת־צַעֲקָתָם שָׁמַעְתִּי (Shemos 3:7), and I have heard their cry.

Another form, וַיִּצָּעֲקוּ מִכֹּל חֹגֵר חֲגֹרָה (Melachim II 3:21), and they were called out, everyone who could gird on armour, and וַיִּצָּעֵק אִישׁ־יִשְׂרָאֵל (Shoftim 7:23), and the men of Israel were called together; and the heavy form, וְהוּא מְצַעֵק אָבִי אָבִי (Melachim II 2:12), and he was crying, my father, my father. Their sense is like that of זעקה, with a zayin.

זעק.sense: To cry out, calling in a loud voice; and the gathering of a people, which belongs to the same sense, since a crowd gathers at a cry.

more.t: אֵלֶיךָ זָֽעֲקוּ וְנִמְלָטוּ (Tehillim 22:6), to You they cried out and were delivered; וַתֵּלֶךְ הָלוֹךְ וְזָעָֽקָה (Shmuel II 13:19), and she went on and cried out, where the past stands for the present, that is, she was going and crying; לִי יִזְעָקוּ אֱלֹהַי יְֽדַֽעֲנוּךָ (Hoshea 8:2), to Me they cry, my God, we know You; זְעַק וְהֵילֵל בֶּן־אָדָם (Yechezkel 21:17), cry out and wail, son of man; and וַיָּשׁוּבוּ וַיִּזְעָקוּךָ (Nechemiah 9:28), and they turned back and cried out to You, the suffix meaning ויזעקו לך, and they cried out to You.

וּזְעָקָה בַּגּוֹיִם נִשְׁמָֽע (Yirmiyahu 50:46), and a cry is heard among the nations; וְאֶת־ זַֽעֲקָתָם שָׁמַעְתָּ עַל־יַם־סֽוּף (Nechemiah 9:9), and You heard their cry at the Sea of Reeds; and וְֽאַל־יְהִי מָקוֹם לְזַֽעֲקָתִֽי (Iyov 16:18), and let there be no place for my cry. זעקה, crying out, is calling in a loud voice.

more.h: His father on a double object
more.t: His father sets מֵרֹב עֲשׁוּקִים יַזְעִיקוּ (Iyov 35:9), for the many oppressions they make cry out, under this sense, as a verb governing two objects: the wicked and the robbers make the poor cry out, and the poor cry out to Hashem.

הַזְעֶק ־לִי אֶת־אִֽישׁ־יְהוּדָה (Shmuel II 20:4), summon the men of Yehudah for me, and וַיַּזְעֵק בָּרָק אֶת־זְבוּלֻן וְאֶת־נַפְתָּלִי (Shoftim 4:10), and Barak summoned Zevulun and Naftali. In the form where the men are the ones gathered: נִֽזְעֲקוּ וַיַּדְבִּיקוּ אֶת־בְּנֵי־דָֽן (Shoftim 18:23 in his edition), they gathered and overtook the sons of Dan; מַה־לְּךָ כִּי נִזְעָֽקְתָּ (Shoftim 18:23), what ails you that you have gathered; and וַיִּזָּֽעֲקוּ כָּל־הָעָם (Yehoshua 8:16), and all the people were gathered.

more.h: Why a cry gathers a crowd
more.t: בְּזַֽעֲקֵךְ יַצִּילֻךְ קִבּוּצַיִךְ (Yeshayahu 57:13), when you cry out, let your gathered ones save you. Their sense is the gathering and assembling of the people, and these too belong to the first sense, since a people is not gathered without a herald who goes about and cries to them to assemble; or when a man cries out at a wrong done him, the people gather at the sound of his cry, so that he is the one who summons them.

שׁוע.sense: To cry out, and the cry; from this root, to shut the eyes, and in the Targum, to plaster; and שׁוֹעַ, the honoured man who gives freely of his money.

more.t: הִנֵּה־קוֹל שַֽׁוְעַת בַּת־עַמִּי (Yirmiyahu 8:19), behold the sound of the cry of the daughter of my people, and וְשַׁוְעָתִי לְפָנָיו תָּבוֹא בְאָזְנָֽיו (Tehillim 18:7), and my cry before Him came into His ears. The verb: שִׁוַּעְתִּי שָׁמַעְתָּ קוֹלִֽי (Yonah 2:3), I cried out and You heard my voice; יְשַׁוְּעוּ וְאֵין מוֹשִׁיעַ (Tehillim 18:42), they cry out and there is none to save; and קַמְתִּי בַקָּהָל אֲשַׁוֵּֽעַ (Iyov 30:28), I stood up in the assembly and cried out. Their sense is crying out.

Some explain הֲיַֽעֲרֹךְ שׁוּֽעֲךָ לֹא בְצָר (Iyov 36:19), will your cry avail you without distress, in this sense; and Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Yonah brought alongside them אִם־בְּפִידוֹ לָהֶן שֽׁוּעַ (Iyov 30:24), whether in his calamity there is a cry for them. The two of them also brought under this root and this sense הַנּוֹתֵן תְּשׁוּעָה לַמְּלָכִים (Tehillim 144:10), who gives salvation to kings.

more.h: His father on the word for salvation
more.t: His father too wrote it so in Sefer HaGalui, and said that the sense of תשועה, salvation, in Arabic is א"ל גאת"ה, which is the receiving of a cry. Radak has written of it already under the root יָשַׁע.

From this root, וְעֵינָיו הָשַׁע (Yeshayahu 6:10), and shut his eyes, that is, close his eyes so that he not see. The Targum of וְטָח אֶת־הַבָּֽיִת (Vayikra 14:42), and he shall plaster the house, is וִישׁוּעַ יָת בֵּיתָא, the same words in Aramaic.

His father takes וּבְמַיִם לֹֽא־רֻחַצְתְּ לְמִשְׁעִי (Yechezkel 16:4), and in water you were not washed לְמִשְׁעִי, from this sense, its sense being like anointing, since the plastering of a house is done by drawing the hand over it as anointing is; the yod stands for a hei. It may instead carry the sense of smoothness, the yod in לְמִשְׁעִי standing for the doubled letter and the root being שָׁעַע, from the Targum of חֶלְקַת צַוָּארָֽיו (Bereishis 27:16), the smooth of his neck, which is שְׁעִיעוּת צַוְרֵיהּ, and of וְאָֽנֹכִי אִישׁ חָלָֽק (Bereishis 27:11), and I am a smooth man, which is גבר שעיע; so the pasuk would mean, to make your flesh smooth, since washing in water smooths the flesh and makes it soft. His father writes a further reading, for cleansing, since in Arabic טהרה, cleanness, is א"ל תמשי"ע.

more.h: Shut your eyes from me, or let me go
more.t: Rabbi Yonah explains הָשַׁע מִמֶּנִּי וְאַבְלִיגָה (Tehillim 39:14), הָשַׁע from me and I will recover, from the sense of shutting the eyes: shut your eyes from me, as though it said, cease from me. Others read it as, let go of me, like שְׁעֵה מֵעָלָיו וְיֶחְדָּל (Iyov 14:6), let go of him that he may cease; שוע and שעה are one sense.

הִשְׁתַּֽעַשְׁעוּ וָשֹׁעוּ (Yeshayahu 29:9) is from this root and from the first sense, that is, they cried out and cried aloud; and so וְשׁוֹעַ אֶל־הָהָֽר (Yeshayahu 22:5), and crying out to the mountain. His father explains them from the sense of וְעֵינָיו הָשַׁע, shutting the eyes, as the pasuk after it says, וַיְעַצֵּם אֶת־עֵֽינֵיכֶם, and He has closed your eyes, which is said of the false prophet. On that reading הִשְׁתַּֽעַשְׁעוּ is past tense, and so is וְשֹׁעוּ, on the pattern of מַה־ טֹּבוּ אֹֽהָלֶיךָ (Bamidbar 24:5), how goodly are your tents; and the meaning is that the false prophets blinded themselves and blinded others.

Another sense: וּלְכִילַי לֹא יֵֽאָמֵר שֽׁוֹעַ (Yeshayahu 32:5), and of the churl it shall not be said, open handed. This is the honoured man, very open handed with his money, who gives more than is fitting for him. The noun from this is הֲיַֽעֲרֹךְ שׁוּֽעֲךָ לֹא בְצָר (Iyov 36:19), that is, will your money arrange that you not be in distress, and וְכֹל מַֽאֲמַצֵּי־כֹֽחַ, and all the forces of strength: money and strength cannot save you from the trouble that is due to come upon you.

גאל.sense: To redeem, the near kinsman being called גואל because the right of redemption is his; and a second sense, of filth and soiling, to defile and be defiled.

more.t: גְּאַל ־לְךָ אַתָּה אֶת־גְּאֻלָּתִי (Rus 4:6), redeem for yourself my right of redemption; וּבָא גֹֽאֲלוֹ הַקָּרֹב אֵלָיו (Vayikra 25:25), and his redeemer who is near to him shall come; and מִֽגֹּֽאֲלֵנוּ הֽוּא (Rus 2:20), he is one of our redeeming kinsmen: because the right of redemption belongs to the near relative, he is called גואל. Hashem redeeming His servant Yaakov is the same verb at Yeshayahu 48:20.

אֽוֹ־הִשִּׂיגָה יָדוֹ וְנִגְאָֽל (Vayikra 25:49), or if his means suffice, he is redeemed; וְאִם־לֹא יִגָּאֵל בְּאֵלֶּה (Vayikra 25:54), and if he is not redeemed by these; and the noun וּלְךָ הַגְּאֻלָּה (Yirmiyahu 32:8), and the right of redemption is yours.

more.h: Buying from a Levi, or redeeming
more.t: Some explain וַֽאֲשֶׁר יִגְאַל מִן־הַֽלְוִיִּם (Vayikra 25:33) as אשר יקנה, what one buys from the Leviim; that is, if a man buys a house in a walled city from the Leviim, it is not made his outright after a year as one bought from an Israel would be, but goes out at the yovel if he did not redeem it. It may also be read as redemption, since the pasuk says גְּאֻלַּת עוֹלָם תִּהְיֶה לַֽלְוִיִּֽם (Vayikra 25:32), the Leviim shall have a perpetual right of redemption. One might have thought the pasuk speaks only of an Israel who took from a Levi, so that a Levi may redeem forever but a Levi who took from a Levi could not; therefore it says that a Levi redeems from the hand of a Levi with a perpetual redemption, and if he did not redeem it, the sale of the house and of the city of his holding goes out at the yovel.

Another sense: הוֹי מֹֽרְאָה וְנִגְאָלָה (Tzefaniah 3:1), woe to her that is filthy and defiled; בַּמֶּה גֵֽאַלְנוּךָ (Malachi 1:7), wherein have we defiled You, and in that same pasuk לֶחֶם מְגֹאָל, defiled bread; וַיְגֹֽאֲלוּ מִן־הַכְּהֻנָּֽה (Nechemiah 7:64), and they were put out of the priesthood as defiled; נְגֹֽאֲלוּ בַדָּם (Yeshayahu 59:3), they are defiled with blood; גָּֽאֳלֵי הַכְּהֻנָּה (Nechemiah 13:29), those who defiled the priesthood; and אֲשֶׁר לֹֽא־ יִתְגָּאַל בְּפַת־בַּג הַמֶּלֶךְ (Daniel 1:8), that he would not defile himself with the king's food. All of them are a matter of filth and befouling.

יִגְאָלֻהוּ חשֶׁךְ וְצַלְמָוֶת (Iyov 3:5), in the sense of filth, means, let darkness and the shadow of death defile it. Some read it from מִֽגֹּֽאֲלֵנוּ הֽוּא (Rus 2:20), he is one of our kinsmen; that is, let darkness and the shadow of death be its near kin. And some read וַיְגֹֽאֲלוּ מִן־הַכְּהֻנָּֽה (Nechemiah 7:64) from that sense of kinship turned to its opposite, as מַשְׁרִישׁ, taking root, stands against מִשָׁרֵשׁ, uprooting: a גואל is the near kinsman and a מגאל one put far from kinship and family, and these were put far from the priesthood because they did not find their record of lineage.
וְכָל־מַלְבּוּשַׁי אֶגְאָֽלְתִּי (Yeshayahu 63:3), and I have stained all my raiment, whose proper form is הִגְאָלְתִּי, the alef standing in place of the hei of the form.

פדה.sense: To redeem, with its nouns for redemption and ransom. The פְדֻת set between My people and yours is that they are redeemed and saved, which sets the two apart.

more.t: פָּדָה בְשָׁלוֹם נַפְשִׁי (Tehillim 55:19), He has redeemed my soul in peace, and וְהוּא יִפְדֶּה אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל (Tehillim 130:8), and He will redeem Israel.

פְּדוּת שָׁלַח לְעַמּוֹ (Tehillim 111:9), He sent redemption to His people; in another pattern וְיֵקַר פִּדְיוֹן נַפְשָׁם (Tehillim 49:9), and the ransom of their soul is costly; with a mem, אֵת כֶּסֶף הַפִּדְיוֹם (Bamidbar 3:49), the ransom money; and in another pattern again, וְאֵת פְּדוּיֵי הַשְּׁלֹשָׁה (Bamidbar 3:46), the redemption of the three, whose singular is פְּדוּי, a redemption, formed like כְּסוּי עוֹר תַּחַשׁ (Bamidbar 4:6), a covering of tachash skin.

לֹא נִפְדָּתָה (Vayikra 19:20), she was not redeemed; and יְעָדָהּ וְהֶפְדָּהּ (Shemos 21:8), he designated her, and let her be redeemed. וְהֶפְדָּהּ is that the one who designated her helps in her redemption, that is, he takes off her redemption price for the years she was with him, as though she had been hired to him, and she pays him the rest and goes free. The infinitive of the passive is וְהָפְדֵּה לֹא נִפְדָּתָה (Vayikra 19:20), and she was not redeemed at all.

וְשַׂמְתִּי פְדֻת בֵּין עַמִּי וּבֵין עַמֶּךָ (Shemos 8:19), and I will set a redemption between My people and your people: the redemption is that they are redeemed and saved from the wild beasts, and that is the separation and the distinction between My people and your people.

פדע.sense: To redeem: its one word, פְּדָעֵהוּ, he glosses as פדהו, redeem him.

more.t: פְּדָעֵהוּ מֵרֶדֶת שָׁחַת (Iyov 33:24), redeem him from going down to the pit, which he glosses as פדהו, redeem him. That is the whole of the entry.

בזה.sense: To despise, and בִּזָּיוֹן, contempt; in another sense, which he holds is of this root too, with an alef in place of the final heh, to plunder.

more.t: כִּי דְבַר־ י"י בָּזָה (Bamidbar 15:31), for he despised the word of Hashem, and מַדּוּעַ בָּזִיתָ אֶת־דְּבַר י"י (Shmuel II 12:9), why have you despised the word of Hashem. In the passive, נִבְזֶה בְּֽעֵינָיו נִמְאָס (Tehillim 15:4), a vile man is despised in his eyes; and causing contempt, לְהַבְזוֹת בַּעְלֵיהֶן בְּעֵינֵיהֶן (Esther 1:17), to make their husbands contemptible in their eyes. The noun is בִּזָּיוֹן וָקָֽצֶף (Esther 1:18), contempt and wrath, and the sense of contempt is plain.

From this sense, לִבְזֹה ־נֶפֶשׁ (Yeshayahu 49:7), to him whom souls despise, is an adjective or an infinitive on the pattern of קְֽנֹה־חָכְמָה מַה־טּוֹב (Mishlei 16:16), to get wisdom, how good it is; the meaning is, to one whom every soul is ready to despise and every nation to abhor. Or it stands in place of the passive, as though it said לבזוי נפש, despised of soul. From this sense also is נְמִבְזָה וְנָמֵס (Shmuel I 15:9), despised and worthless, with an added nun and mem.

אֲשֶׁר־ בָּֽזְאוּ נְהָרִים אַרְצֽוֹ (Yeshayahu 18:2), whose land the rivers have spoiled. In his view it is from this root, the alef standing in place of the heh that is the last root letter, as a yud came in place of that heh in the word חֲסָיוּ, they took refuge; its sense is plunder and spoil, and they are two roots with one sense. Most of the grammarians say the alef stands for the doubled letter, and that it is like בזזו, they plundered.

קלה.sense: To parch or roast in fire; and in another sense to hold cheap and be held cheap, with the noun קָלוֹן, disgrace.

more.t: אֲשֶׁר־ קָלָם מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶל (Yirmiyahu 29:22), whom the king of Bavel roasted; אָבִיב קָלוּי בָּאֵשׁ (Vayikra 2:14), fresh ears parched with fire; and מַצּוֹת וְקָלוּי (Yehoshua 5:11), matzos and parched grain. The adjective: וְלֶחֶם וְקָלִי וְכַרְמֶל (Vayikra 23:14), and bread and parched grain and fresh ears; and it is written with an alef in אֵיפַת הַקָּלִיא הַזֶּה (Shmuel I 17:17), this ephah of parched grain.

His father explains כִּֽי־כְסָלַי מָלְאוּ נִקְלֶה (Tehillim 38:8) from this sense, for my loins are filled with burning, and so מַלֵּא פְנֵיהֶם קָלוֹן (Tehillim 83:17), fill their faces with burning. Read so, their sense is burning and roasting.

Another sense: מַקְלֶה אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ (Devarim 27:16), he who holds his father and his mother cheap. In the passive, וְנִקְלָה כבוד מואב (Yeshayahu 16:14), and the glory of Moav shall be held cheap, and אִישׁ־רָשׁ וְנִקְלֶֽה (Shmuel I 18:23), a poor man and lightly esteemed. Radak reads כִּֽי־כְסָלַי מָלְאוּ נִקְלֶה (Tehillim 38:8) here too, as נגע נקלה, a contemptible affliction: for my loins are filled with a contemptible affliction.

שָׂבַעְתָּ קָלוֹן מִכָּבוֹד (Chavakuk 2:16), you are sated with disgrace instead of honour, and in that same pasuk וְקִֽיקָלוֹן עַל־כְּבוֹדֶֽךָ, and vomit of disgrace upon your glory, a word compounded of קיא, vomit, and קלון, disgrace. Their sense is contempt.

נחם.sense: Consolation: comforting, being comforted and taking comfort, with the nouns for it; and in another sense, regret.

more.t: מֵֽאֲנָה לְהִנָּחֵם עַל־בָּנֶיהָ (Yirmiyahu 31:15), she refused to be comforted for her children; נַֽחֲמוּ עַמִּי (Yeshayahu 40:1), comfort My people; כְּאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר אִמּוֹ תְּנַֽחֲמֶנּוּ (Yeshayahu 66:13), as a man whom his mother comforts. All of these are of the sense of consolation, and it is well known.

כּוֹס תַּנְחוּמִים (Yirmiyahu 16:7), a cup of consolations; תַּנְחוּמֶיךָ יְֽשַֽׁעַשְׁעוּ נַפְשִֽׁי (Tehillim 94:19), Your consolations delight my soul; זֹאת נֶחָמָתִי בְעָנְיִי (Tehillim 119:50), this is my comfort in my affliction. דְּבָרִים נִֽחֻמִֽים (Zecharyah 1:13), comforting words, lacks the word in construct: in full it would be דברים דברי ניחומים, words, words of consolation.

more.h: Against Rabbi Yonah on a form
more.t: הוֹי אֶנָּחֵם מִצָּרַי (Yeshayahu 1:24), ah, I will be consoled over My foes. Rabbi Yonah wrote, as a possibility, that the proper form is אֶתְנָחֵם, I will console Myself. Radak holds otherwise: the nun carries a kamatz, and so the word is of the passive form; had it been the reflexive, the nun would carry a patach, since with a ches the missing doubling is not made up.

נִחָם כִּֽי־הִמְלִיךְ אֶת־שָׁאוּל (Shmuel I 15:35), Hashem regretted that He had made Shaul king; אֵין אִישׁ נִחָם עַל־רָעָתוֹ (Yirmiyahu 8:6), no man regrets his wickedness; וְנִחָם עַל־הָֽרָעָֽה (Yonah 4:2), and regrets the evil; כִּי נִחַמְתִּי כִּי עֲשִׂיתִֽם (Bereishis 6:7), for I regret that I made them; and the noun, יַחַד נִכְמְרוּ נִֽחוּמָֽי (Hoshea 11:8), My regrets are turned over together. All of these are of the sense of regret. נכמרו ניחומי means נתגלגלו חרטותי, My regrets rolled over, when I had thought to overturn them and destroy them.

חלב.sense: Milk, חָלָב; and חֵלֶב, fat, which by way of borrowing names the choicest of anything; also חֶלְבְּנָה, a spice whose smell is foul.

more.t: וּבְלוֹא מְחִיר יַיִן וְחָלָֽב (Yeshayahu 55:1), and without price wine and milk; לֹֽא־תְבַשֵּׁל גְּדִי בַּֽחֲלֵב אִמּֽוֹ (Shemos 34:26), you shall not cook a kid in its mother's milk; וְהֵמָּה יִשְׁתּוּ חֲלָבֵֽךְ (Yechezkel 25:4), and they shall drink your milk. The word, he says, is known.

וְחֵלֶב נְבֵלָה וְחֵלֶב טְרֵפָה (Vayikra 7:24), the fat of a carcass and the fat of a torn beast, and in the plural עַל אִשֵּׁי הַֽחֲלָבִים (Vayikra 10:15), upon the fire offerings of the fats. It is right, he says, that וּמֵֽחֶלְבֵהֶן (Bereishis 4:4), and of the fat ones among them, be a describing noun, as the Targum renders it וּמִשַּׁמִּנְהוֹן, and of their fat ones; what is fat is called חֵלֶב, on the pattern of מֶלֶךְ, a king, and עֶבֶד, a servant, which are describing nouns.

By way of borrowing, as the fat is the choicest of the flesh, the choicest of anything came to be called חֵלֶב: כֹּל חֵלֶב יִצְהָר וְכָל־ חֵלֶב תִּירוֹשׁ וְדָגָן (Bamidbar 18:12), all the best of the oil and all the best of the wine and the grain, and וְאִכְלוּ אֶת־ חֵלֶב הָאָֽרֶץ (Bereishis 45:18), and eat the best of the land.

וּשְׁחֵלֶת וְחֶלְבְּנָה (Shemos 30:34), onycha and galbanum: he describes it as a spice whose smell is foul, the resin of a tree found in the cities of Greece, like a black honey, and in Arabic מיעה. And בְּיֵין חֶלְבּוֹן (Yechezkel 27:18), with wine of Chelbon, which Targum Yonasan renders בַּחֲמַר חֵילַת מְבַשֵׁל, with cooked wine of Cheilas.

צחר.sense: White: אֲתֹנוֹת צְחֹרוֹת (Shoftim 5:10), white she-donkeys, and וְצֶמֶר צָֽחַר (Yechezkel 27:18), white wool.

גנן.sense: To shield; the magen, so called because it shields its bearer, and great men, called shields because they shield the people; a separate sense, sorrow of heart.

more.t: וְגַנּוֹתִי עַל־הָעִיר הַזֹּאת (Melachim II 20:6), and I will shield this city, and גָּנוֹן וְהִצִּיל (Yeshayahu 31:5), shielding and rescuing.

מָגֵן גִּבֹּרֵיהוּ מְאָדָּם (Nachum 2:4), the shield of his mighty men is reddened; אֶלֶף הַמָּגֵן תָּלוּי עָלָיו (Shir HaShirim 4:4), a thousand shields hung upon it; and in the feminine וְאֶת־ הַמָּגִנּוֹת (Divrei HaYamim II 23:9), and the shields. It is called magen, he says, because it shields the one who bears it. So מָגִנֵּנוּ רְאֵה אֱלֹהִים (Tehillim 84:10), which he reads as: You who are a shield and a buckler to us, see our affliction and our distress.

The great men of a people are called shields as well, because they shield the people, as the pasuk says כִּי לֵֽאלֹהִים מָֽגִנֵּי ־אֶרֶץ (Tehillim 47:10), for the shields of the earth are Hashem's, and אָֽהֲבוּ הֵבוּ קָלוֹן מָֽגִנֶּֽיהָ (Hoshea 4:18), her shields have loved, give shame.

תִּתֵּן לָהֶם מְגִנַּת ־לֵב (Eichah 3:65), You will give them meginas lev, is another sense, like דאבון, sorrow. Radak allows that it may belong with the first sense, meaning a covering of the heart, on the model of הַשְׁמֵן לֵֽב־הָעָם הַזֶּה (Yeshayahu 6:10), make the heart of this people fat; and his father explains a covering of the heart as a known sickness among the sicknesses of the brain, called in Arabic gashit al kalb.

פרדס.sense: A garden of fruit trees, as he glosses it: פַּרְדֵּס רִמּוֹנִים (Shir HaShirim 4:13), an orchard of pomegranates.

רעב.sense: To be hungry; the noun רָעָב, famine, also in the form רְעָבוֹן; and to make someone go hungry.

more.t: רָשׁוּ וְרָעֵבוּ (Tehillim 34:11), they wanted and were hungry; לֹא יִרְעָבוּ וְלֹא יִצְמָאוּ (Yeshayahu 49:10), they shall not hunger nor thirst; the noun וַיְהִי רָעָב בָּאָרֶץ (Bereishis 12:10), and there was a famine in the land; and in another form וּבִימֵי רְעָבוֹן יִשְׂבָּֽעוּ (Tehillim 37:19), in days of famine they shall be satisfied.

רַֽעֲבוֹן בָּֽתֵּיכֶם (Bereishis 42:33), the hunger of your households, in smichus, he reads two ways. Either a word is missing, and the sense is the grain for the hunger of your households; or it means just what it says, take what is the hunger of your households and go, that is, the bread they are hungry for, which is then their hunger.
וַֽיְעַנְּךָ וַיַּרְעִבֶךָ (Devarim 8:3), and He afflicted you and let you hunger.

כפן.sense: Gathering, as of roots gathered in; and כָּפָן, the Targum's word for famine, which his father explains instead as lack of the purse.

more.t: כָּֽפְנָה שָֽׁרֳשֶׁיהָ עָלָיו (Yechezkel 17:7), it gathered its roots toward him: אספה, it gathered. The word has its letters turned about from its like in the words of Chazal, who call a gathering of people כנופיא (Yoma 51a).

לְשֹׁד וּלְכָפָן תִּשְׂחָק (Iyov 5:22), at destruction and at kafan you shall laugh. The Targum renders רָעָב (Bereishis 12:10), famine, as כַפְנָא. His father explained it well, Radak says: חסרון הכיס, lack of the purse; Radak takes him to mean want of money at a time when money is dear, since there is no need to mention famine twice, famine having been named already at the head of them all, in בְּרָעָב פָּֽדְךָ מִמָּוֶת (Iyov 5:20), in famine He redeemed you from death.

רחשׁ.sense: To bring out and set moving, as Chazal use it of lips that move; and from it the מַרְחֶשֶׁת, a deep vessel in which the meal offering moves about.

more.t: רָחַשׁ לִבִּי דָּבָר טוֹב (Tehillim 45:2), my heart brought forth a good word. He glosses הוציא והניע, brought out and set moving, since in the words of Chazal this is the language of the moving of the lips, רחושי מרחשן שפוותיה (Sanhedrin 90b), his lips were moving.

From this sense is derived וְאִם־מִנְחַת מַרְחֶשֶׁת (Vayikra 2:7), and if a meal offering of the marcheshes, which is a deep vessel. So Chazal explain (Menachos 5:8): the marcheshes is deep and what is made in it moves about, while the machavas is flat and what is made in it is hard. Radak explains that because the marcheshes was deep its oil gathered in it and the fire did not burn it, so the meal offerings made inside it moved and stirred.

גשׁם.sense: Rain, and it is the strong rain. At one pasuk some take it for the name of a tree or for a body; he holds it is rain there too.

more.t: הַגֶּשֶׁם וְהַשֶּׁלֶג (Yeshayahu 55:10), the rain and the snow; גֶּשֶׁם שׁוֹטֵף (Yechezkel 13:11), an overflowing rain; וַיּוֹרֶד לָכֶם גֶּשֶׁם (Yoel 2:23), and He brought down rain for you. It is the strong rain. In the plural, וְנָֽתַתִּי גִשְׁמֵיכֶם בְּעִתָּם (Vayikra 26:4), and I will give your rains in their season.

On נָטַע אֹרֶן וְגֶשֶׁם יְגַדֵּֽל (Yeshayahu 44:14), he planted an oren and the rain makes it grow, the Targum says וּמִטְרָא יְרַבֵּי, and the rain makes it grow. Some explain geshem here as the name of a tree, and some as a body, from the Aramaic גִּשְׁמֵהּ יִצְטַבַּע (Daniel 4:30), his body was drenched. Radak holds the right reading is rain.

more.h: Why the pasuk says the rain grows it
more.t: It is plain that rain makes everything grow, so the pasuk comes to say that although a man plants the tree for avodah zarah, the rain grows it; and though the rain comes on Hashem's errand and by His will, the world goes on in its way. As Chazal said on this matter (Avodah Zarah 54b), one who stole a se'ah of wheat and sowed it, by right it should not sprout, but the world goes on in its way, and the fools who acted corruptly will in time give account.

לֹא גֻשְׁמָהּ בְּיוֹם זָֽעַם (Yechezkel 22:24) he takes as a noun of another pattern, since the heh carries a mappik: alone it would be גֹּֽשֶׁם, rain, on the pattern of גֹּֽרֶל, a lot, and with a suffix joined it takes a shuruk, as כְּרֹב גֻּדְּלֽוֹ (Tehillim 150:2), according to His abundant greatness. The pasuk then means that its rain did not come down in the day of wrath. It may also be a passive verb, it was not rained upon, with the mappik there for the beauty of the reading and not out of need, like וְתַֽעֲלֻמָהּ יֹצִא אֽוֹר (Iyov 28:11), and He brings the hidden thing out to light.

שׁנה.sense: To change. A second sense: second, two, and doing a thing again; and from it שָׁנָה, the year, named for the sun's return a second time. Scarlet he treats under shen.

more.t: לֹא שָׁנִיתִי (Malachi 3:6), I have not changed; עִם־ שׁוֹנִים אַל־תִּתְעָרָֽב (Mishlei 24:21), do not mix with those who change; וְדָתֵיהֶם שֹׁנוֹת מִכָּל־עָם (Esther 3:8), their laws are different from every people; וְשִׁנָּא אֵת בִּגְדֵי כִלְאוֹ (Melachim II 25:29), and he changed his prison garments; קוּמִי נָא וְהִשְׁתַּנִּית (Melachim I 14:2), rise now and change yourself. The sense of change, he says, is known.

יוֹם שֵׁנִֽי (Bereishis 1:8), a second day. On וּפַר הַשֵּׁנִי שֶׁבַע שָׁנִים (Shoftim 6:25), and the second bull of seven years, some explain second to the womb, while Radak holds the right reading is second to the bull just named, קַח אֶת־פַּר־הַשּׁוֹר אֲשֶׁר לְאָבִיךָ, take the bullock of the ox that is your father's. The seven years Targum Yonasan renders דְאִתְפַּטִים שְׁבַע שְׁנִין, that had been fattened seven years. Chazal (Temurah 28b) take them as years it had been set aside for idolatry: Reish Lakish said nothing counts as muktzeh, set aside, for idolatry unless it was set aside for seven years, as the pasuk says; some of them said it had been worshipped seven years; and they said eight things were permitted that night. מִדָּה שֵׁנִי (Nechemiah 3:30), a second measure, Rabbi Yonah said is like שֵׁנִית, second in the feminine; Radak sees no need for that, since many nouns come both masculine and feminine.

more.h: Mishneh, a second of a thing
more.t: וְכֶסֶף מִשְׁנֶה (Bereishis 43:12), and second money, מִשְׁנֶה being like שני, second. וְהַבָּקָר וְהַמִּשְׁנִים (Shmuel I 15:9), the cattle and the mishnim: the mishnim are lambs second to the womb, perhaps choice ones, or two years old; Rabbi Yaakov ben Elazar explained it from שָׁנָה, a year, an adjective for lambs a year old. כִּי מִשְׁנֶה שְׂכַר שָׂכִיר (Devarim 15:18) means a second hired man's wage that you owe him, since he served you six full years by day and by night, while a hired man who works by day does not work by night, and one who works by night does not work by day. אֶת־ מִשְׁנֵה הַתּוֹרָה הַזֹּאת (Devarim 17:18), the mishneh of this Torah, written with a tzeirei, Radak reads as writing it a second time, so that the king has two, and Chazal learned from here (Sanhedrin 21b) that a king needs two, one that goes out and comes in with him and one laid up in his treasury. Some explain it instead as repetition, from וְשִׁנַּנְתָּם לְבָנֶיךָ (Devarim 6:7), and you shall repeat them to your children; and likewise וְהִיא יֹשֶׁבֶת בִּירֽוּשָׁלַם בַּמִּשְׁנֶה (Melachim II 22:14), and she dwelt in Yerushalayim in the mishneh, meaning in the house of study, as Yonasan rendered it, בְּבֵית אוּלְפָנָא, in the house of teaching. כֹּֽהֲנֵי הַמִּשְׁנֶה (Melachim II 23:4) are the deputies of the kohanim, second to the kohanim gedolim.

From the sense of second, שָׁנָה תְמִימָה (Vayikra 25:30), a full year, is called so because the sun has returned a second time to the point from which it began. שְׁנָתַיִם יָמִים (Bereishis 41:1) he explains as two full years. On וַֽיְהִי דָּֽנִיֵּאל עַד־ שְׁנַת אַחַת לְכוֹרֶשׁ הַמֶּֽלֶךְ (Daniel 1:21), and Daniel was until the first year of Koresh the king, Ibn Ezra wrote that the construct is used because it was not a full year, the sense being within the year; Radak answers that this reason will not serve for the other constructs on a number, as בִּשְׁנַת שְׁתַּיִם (Melachim I 15:25), in the second year.

The verb of the same sense, a second time, is doing a thing again: וְלֹֽא־ שָׁנָה לוֹ (Shmuel II 20:10), and he did not do it to him again; פַּעַם אַחַת וְלֹא אֶשְׁנֶה לֽוֹ (Shmuel I 26:8), once, and I will not do it to him a second time; שְׁנוּ וַיִּשְׁנוּ (Melachim I 18:34), do it a second time, and they did it a second time. From it Rav Saadiah Gaon explained עִם־ שׁוֹנִים אַל־תִּתְעָרָֽב (Mishlei 24:21) of those who say there are שְׁנַיִם אלהים, two gods, in the world; and he gave a second explanation, better than that one, that the shonim are men who go back a second time to their wickedness after they have done teshuvah. Radak counts the same pasuk with כְּסִיל שׁוֹנֶה בְאִוַּלְתּֽוֹ (Mishlei 26:11), a fool repeating his folly, where the sense is time after time, many times.

כִּי כָל־בֵּיתָהּ לָבֻשׁ שָׁנִֽים (Mishlei 31:21), for all her household is clothed in shanim. His father explained it from this root, which Radak spells out: בגדים שונים, garments of different kinds, and so she does not fear the snow for her household.

וְתוֹלַעַת שָׁנִי (Shemos 25:4), scarlet worm, and אִם־יִֽהְיוּ חֲטָֽאֵיכֶם כַּשָּׁנִים (Yeshayahu 1:18), though your sins be as scarlet, come from this root, and he says he has already written of them under the root shen.

אמץ.sense: To be strong, and to strengthen; in another sense אֲמֻצִּים, red, a second shade of red beside the reds already named.

more.t: כִּי אָֽמְצוּ מִמֶּֽנִי (Tehillim 142:6 in his edition), for they are stronger than I; חֲזַק וֶֽאֱמָץ (Yehoshua 1:6), be strong and firm; וּלְאֹם מִלְאֹם יֶֽאֱמָץ (Bereishis 25:23), one people shall be stronger than the other; וְאַמִּיץ כֹּחַ (Iyov 9:4), mighty in strength. All of these and their like, he says, are the matter of strength.

וְאִמֵּץ אֶת־לְבָבוֹ (Devarim 2:30), and He made his heart strong; וּבִרְכַּיִם כֹּֽרְעוֹת תְּאַמֵּֽץ (Iyov 4:4), and you strengthen bowing knees; וְיַֽאֲמֵץ לְבַבְכֶם (Tehillim 31:25), and He will strengthen your heart; and of a man gathering his own strength, הִתְאַמֵּץ לַֽעֲלוֹת בַּמֶּרְכָּבָה (Melachim I 12:18), he strengthened himself to go up into the chariot.

בְּרֻדִּים אֲמֻצִּֽים (Zecharyah 6:3), speckled amutzim. The word is as חמוצים, from חֲמוּץ בְּגָדִים (Yeshayahu 63:1), of reddened garments; that is, amutzim are red; and although reds had been named already, there were two shades of redness, one truly red and one not strong in its redness. Some explain amutzim as the look of ashes, and so Yonasan renders קִטְמָנִין, ash-coloured.

חום.sense: חוּם, said of a lamb: black. The correct view, he holds, is that the word is from the root חָמַם, and he will explain it there.

more.t: וְכָל־שֶֽׂה־חוּם בַּכְּשָׂבִים (Bereishis 30:32), and every black lamb among the sheep, which he glosses שחור, black. The correct view in his own eyes is that חוּם comes from the root חָמַם, and he says he will explain it there.

יסף.sense: To add, and to do a thing again; and to be added to something. All of it, he holds, is one sense.

more.t: וְלֹא־ יָֽסְפָה שׁוּב־אֵלָיו עֽוֹד (Bereishis 8:12), and it did not again return to him any more; לֹא אֹסֵף לִשְׁמֹעַ (Devarim 18:16), I will not again hear. קוֹל גָּדוֹל וְלֹא יָסָף (Devarim 5:22 in his edition), a great voice, and it did not add, means that no other great voice like it came again.

וַיִּֽתְנַבְּאוּ וְלֹא יָסָֽפוּ (Bamidbar 11:25), and they prophesied and did not add, which he explains as they did not prophesy again, as Chazal said in Maseches Sanhedrin that they prophesied that day alone. The Targum took the words in another sense, rendering וְלָא פָּסְקָן, and they did not cease.

יָסַפְתָּ עַל־הַשְּׁמוּעָה אֲשֶׁר שָׁמָֽעְתִּי (Divrei HaYamim II 9:6), you have added to the report that I heard; אַל־ תּוֹסְףְ עַל־דְּבָרָיו (Mishlei 30:6), do not add to His words; and in the passive וְנוֹסַף גַּם־הוּא עַל־שֹׂנְאֵינוּ (Shemos 1:10), and he too will be added to our enemies.

כִּי לֹא תוֹסִיפִי יִקְרְאוּ־לָךְ רַכָּה וַֽעֲנֻגָּֽה (Yeshayahu 47:1), for you shall no more be called tender and delicate, and כִּי לֹא תוֹסִיפִי יִקְרְאוּ־לָךְ גְּבֶרֶת מַמְלָכֽוֹת (Yeshayahu 47:5), for you shall no more be called mistress of kingdoms, both carry the stress on the last syllable, with a single pashta, and the Mesorah marks the two so. The sense of all of it is known. Rabbi Yonah separated them; Radak says there is no need, and all of it is one sense.

ברך.sense: To bless, and a blessing; the word can mean a gift or a greeting of peace, and stands in place of a curse. Other senses: kneeling, and the knee; and בְּרֵכָה, a pool.

more.t: בְּרָכָה בְּקֶרֶב הָאָֽרֶץ (Yeshayahu 19:24), a blessing in the midst of the earth; בְרָכוֹת לָעַד (Tehillim 21:7), blessings for ever; בִּרְכֹת שָׁמַיִם מֵעָל בִּרְכֹת תְּהוֹם רֹבֶצֶת תָּחַת (Bereishis 49:25), blessings of heaven above, blessings of the deep couching beneath; בֵּרַךְ אֶת־אַבְרָהָם בַּכֹּֽל (Bereishis 24:1), He blessed Avraham in all. The forms בְּרוּכָה and בְּרוּכִים, blessed, and their like are all describing words, he says, since the simple verb was not built from this root. Where created beings bless Hashem it is like praise, as בָּֽרֲכִי נַפְשִׁי אֶת־י"י (Tehillim 103:22), bless Hashem, my soul.
בֵּרַךְ נָבוֹת אֱלֹהִים (Melachim I 21:13), Navos blessed Hashem, and בָּרֵךְ אֱלֹהִים וָמֻֽת (Iyov 2:9), bless Hashem and die, and their like, are a way of speaking around a curse.

קַח־נָא אֶת־ בִּרְכָתִי (Bereishis 33:11), take my berachah, he glosses מנחתי, my gift; likewise קַח־נָא בְרָכָה מֵאֵת עַבְדֶּֽךָ (Melachim II 5:15), take a gift from your servant. It may be that מְבָרֵֽךְ אָוֶן (Yeshayahu 66:3) is of this sort too, the מְבָרֵךְ being one who brings the gift, and אָוֶן iniquity. So too לִשְׁאָל־לוֹ לְשָׁלוֹם וּלְבָֽרֲכוֹ, to ask after his peace and to bring him a gift, as he explains the last word.

וְאָֽרוֹתִי אֶת־ בִּרְכֽוֹתֵיכֶם (Malachi 2:2), and I will curse your blessings, is not of that sort, against what Rabbi Yonah wrote. Radak says it is blessing in the plain sense, and the proof is that the pasuk says וְאָֽרוֹתִי, and I will curse, since the curse is the opposite of the blessing: a blessing adds to the good and a curse takes from it.

עֲשׂוּ־אִתִּי בְרָכָה (Yeshayahu 36:16), make a berachah with me, he glosses פשרה ושלום, a settlement and peace. Like it are וַיְבָרֶךְ יַֽעֲקֹב אֶת־פַּרְעֹֽה (Bereishis 47:7), and Yaakov greeted Pharaoh, and כִּי תִמְצָא־אִישׁ לֹא תְבָֽרֲכֶנּוּ (Melachim II 4:29), if you meet a man do not greet him, which are the asking after another's peace; and all of them, he says, are the sense of blessing.

Another sense is kneeling: וַיִּבְרַךְ עַל־ בִּרְכָּיו (Divrei HaYamim II 6:13), and he knelt upon his knees, and נִבְרְכָה לִפְנֵֽי־י"י עֹשֵֽׂנוּ (Tehillim 95:6), let us kneel before Hashem our Maker. The heavy form is וַיַּבְרֵךְ הַגְּמַלִּים (Bereishis 24:11), he made the camels kneel, and with it he sets וַיִּקְרְאוּ לְפָנָיו אַבְרֵךְ (Bereishis 41:43), and they called before him אַבְרֵךְ: the alef stands in place of the heh of הַבְרֵך, or else it is the alef of one speaking of himself, each one calling אַבְרֵךְ before him. The noun is the knee: תִּכְרַע כָּל־ בֶּרֶךְ (Yeshayahu 45:23), every knee shall bow; כָּֽרְעוּ עַל־ בִּרְכֵיהֶם (Shoftim 7:6), they knelt upon their knees, which the Mesorah marks as one of the two places where the word is left soft.

הַבְּרֵכָה הָֽעֶלְיוֹנָה (Yeshayahu 7:3), the upper pool. Some explain bereichah as a spring; the truth, he says, is that it is water gathered together and not a spring. So too in the words of Chazal (Moed Katan 4a): the pesakos and the berechos that filled with water before yom tov may not be used for watering on chol hamoed. He explains their two words himself: the pesakos are ditches not built up with stones, and the berechos ditches built with stones and plaster, into which rainwater is gathered, or water is gathered, or water is drawn to them from the spring. So בְּרֵכוֹת מָיִם (Koheles 2:6), pools of water. It may be that גַּם־ בְּרָכוֹת יַעְטֶה מוֹרֶֽה (Tehillim 84:7), the early rain covers it with pools too, is like them, and so הָֽבָה־לִּי בְרָכָה כִּי אֶרֶץ הַנֶּגֶב נְתַתָּנִי (Shoftim 1:15), give me a pool, for you have given me the land of the Negev, though the resh there has a kamatz, a kamatz in place of a tzeirei as in many words; or it is blessing proper.

רכך.sense: Soft or tender: a soft heart, words softer than oil, a tender child; a heart grown faint, and the noun מֹרֶךְ, faintness.

more.t: יַעַן רַךְ ־לְבָבְךָ (Melachim II 22:19), because your heart was soft; רַכּוּ דְבָרָיו מִשֶּׁמֶן (Tehillim 55:22), his words were softer than oil; רַךְ וָטוֹב (Bereishis 18:7), tender and good; כִּֽי־הַיְלָדִים רַכִּים (Bereishis 33:13), that the children are tender; וְעֵינֵי לֵאָה רַכּוֹת (Bereishis 29:17), and Leah's eyes were tender.
רַךְ וּמָשׁוּחַ מֶלֶךְ (Shmuel II 3:39), soft and an anointed king, he explains to mean that in the matter of kingship he was still soft, as a lad is soft.

אַל־ יֵרַךְ לְבַבְכֶם (Devarim 20:3), let not your heart grow faint; וְאֵל הֵרַךְ לִבִּי (Iyov 23:16), and Hashem made my heart faint; וְלֹא רֻכְּכָה בַּשָּֽׁמֶן (Yeshayahu 1:6), nor softened with oil; and the noun וְהֵבֵאתִי מֹרֶךְ (Vayikra 26:36), and I will bring faintness.

שׁדם.sense: Vines, as he glosses it, and in Chavakuk perhaps a sown field; by Kidron the Targum makes it a plain; and once it is like שְׁדֵפָה, blighted.

more.t: וּמִשַּׁדְמֹת עֲמֹרָה (Devarim 32:32), and of the vines of Amorah, which he glosses as vines; and so כִּי שַׁדְמוֹת חֶשְׁבּוֹן אֻמְלָל (Yeshayahu 16:8), for the vines of Cheshbon are withered, and וּשְׁדֵמוֹת לֹא־עָשָׂה אֹכֶל (Chavakuk 3:17), the vines have yielded no food.
In Chavakuk the sense may be a field of seed, since the pasuk has already said וְאֵין יְבוּל בַּגְּפָנִים, and there is no yield in the vines.

For בְּשַׁדְמוֹת קִדְרוֹן (Melachim II 23:4), in the plains of Kidron, the Targum renders נַחְלָא בְמֵישַׁר קִדְרוֹן, the wadi in the plain of Kidron; and Radak reads הַשְּׁדֵמוֹת עַד־נַחַל קִדְרוֹן (Yirmiyahu 31:39 in his edition), the plains as far as the wadi of Kidron, the same way, though the Targum renders that pasuk otherwise.

But וּשְׁדֵמָה לִפְנֵי קָמָֽה (Yeshayahu 37:27), blighted before it stands grown, is like וּשְׁדֵפָה, from שִׁדָּפוֹן, blight, the mem and the peh coming from one place in the mouth; and so the pasuk in Melachim II 19:26 reads וּשְׁדֵפָה לִפְנֵי קָמָֽה.

שֹרג.sense: שָׂרִיגִם, branches of the vine; as a verb, to become entangled; and the Targum and the Mishnah use the word of lattice work and interlacing.

more.t: וּבַגֶּפֶן שְׁלֹשָׁה שָֽׂרִיגִם (Bereishis 40:10), and on the vine were three branches, which he glosses שעפים, branches; and הִלְבִּינוּ שָֽׂרִיגֶֽיהָ (Yoel 1:7), its branches have turned white.

The reflexive form יִשְׂתָּרְגוּ עָלוּ עַל־צַוָּארִי (Eichah 1:14), they are entangled, they have come up upon my neck, he explains as יסתבכו, they become entangled; and so, in the passive of the heavy form, גִּידֵי פַֽחֲדָו [פַֽחֲדָיו] יְשׂרָֽגוּ (Iyov 40:17), the sinews of his thighs are entangled.

The Targum renders שְׂבָכִים מַֽעֲשֵׂה שְׂבָכָה (Melachim I 7:17), nets of lattice work, as סְרִיגַן עוֹבַד סְרִיגָא, lattices of lattice work; and the Mishnah has ומסרגין את המטות (Moed Katan 1:8, 8b), and one may interlace the beds.

סוד.sense: Counsel and a hidden matter, and from this sense the counsel of those who join together. Rabbi Yonah made two senses of it; Radak holds it is all one sense.

more.t: Their sense is counsel and a hidden thing, ענין עצה ודבר סתר: כִּי אִם־גָּלָה סוֹדוֹ (Amos 3:7), unless He has revealed His secret, and וְסוֹד אַחֵר אַל־תְּגָֽל (Mishlei 25:9), do not reveal another man's secret.

From this sense, לֹֽא־יָשַׁבְתִּי בְסוֹד־מְשַֽׂחֲקִים (Yirmiyahu 15:17), I have not sat in the counsel of merrymakers, which he explains בעצתם, in their counsel, when they join together for play and for the vanities of the world; and so וְעַל סוֹד בַּחוּרִים יַחְדָּו (Yirmiyahu 6:11), upon the counsel of young men together, and בְּסוֹד יְשָׁרִים וְעֵדָֽה (Tehillim 111:1), in the counsel of the upright and the congregation.
Rabbi Yonah divided these into two senses. Radak holds the correct view is that the whole of it is one sense.

הוּסַד שְׁלֹמֹה לִבְנוֹת אֶת־בֵּית הָֽאֱלֹהִים (Divrei HaYamim II 3:3), Shlomo took counsel to build the house of God, is from this root and this sense: נתיעץ ועמד בסוד בנין עם דוד אביו, he took counsel and stood in the counsel of the building with Dovid his father, as it says, ויתן דוד לשלמה את תבנית האולם, and Dovid gave Shlomo the pattern of the porch.
וְתָשֵׂם בַּסַּד רַגְלַי (Iyov 13:27), and You put my feet in the סַּד: some explain it as the wood in which the feet of prisoners are set, the stocks.

כמס.sense: Stored away: he glosses כָּמֻס עִמָּדִי (Devarim 32:34), laid up with Me, as גנוז, put away in store.

רזם.sense: To hint with the eyes; he takes it as רמז turned about, the word Chazal use for hinting.

more.t: וּמַה־יִּרְזְמוּן עֵינֶיךָ (Iyov 15:12), and what do your eyes hint, is רמז with its letters turned about, as Chazal use it: חרש רומז ונרמז (Gittin 5:7, 59b), a deaf man hints and is hinted to, and מרמוזי רמוזי להדדי (Bava Kamma 24b), they hint one to another.

קֹרֵֽץ עַיִן (Mishlei 10:10), he who winks the eye, the Targum renders דְרָמֵז בְּעַיְנוֹהִי, who hints with his eyes, and שְׁלַח אֶצְבַּע (Yeshayahu 58:9), the pointing of the finger, it renders מִרְמַז בְּאֶצְבַּע, hinting with the finger.

דון.sense: To judge; דִּין is a judgment and דַּיָּן a judge. The noun of strife, מָדוֹן, is of the root as well.

more.t: דָּן דִּין־עָנִי וְאֶבְיוֹן (Yirmiyahu 22:16), he judged the cause of the poor and needy, דָּנַנִּי אֱלֹהִים (Bereishis 30:6), Hashem has judged me, and לֹֽא־יָדוֹן רוּחִי (Bereishis 6:3), My spirit shall not judge.

The noun is a judgment: לֹא־דָנוּ דִּין יָתוֹם (Yirmiyahu 5:28), they did not judge the cause of the orphan; and the adjective, a judge: אֲבִי יְתוֹמִים וְדַיַּן אַלְמָנוֹת (Tehillim 68:6), father of orphans and judge of widows.

The noun for strife is here too: אִישׁ חֵמָה יְגָרֶה מָדוֹן (Mishlei 15:18), a man of wrath stirs up strife, and מִדְיָנִים יְשַׁלֵּֽחַ (Mishlei 6:14), he sends out quarrels. וַיְהִי אִישׁ מָדֹין (Shmuel II 21:20) can be explained from this: and there was a man of strife, איש ריב ומלחמה, a man of quarrel and of war.

more.h: A sheath, on a second reading
more.t: לֹֽא־יָדוֹן רוּחִי may bear another sense: that it lacks its first root letter, a nun, the vowel letter standing in place of the dagesh, and the root is נָדַן, as in וַיָּשֶׁב חַרְבּוֹ אֶל־נְדָנָֽהּ (Divrei HaYamim I 21:27), he returned his sword to its sheath.

more.h: A sense of quarrel on its own
more.t: The chacham Rabbi Yehudah brought לֹֽא־יָדוֹן רוּחִי, and כָל־הָעָם נָדוֹן, all the people were at strife, together with יְגָרֶה מָדוֹן, stirs up strife, and מִדְיָנִים יְשַׁלֵּֽחַ, he sends out quarrels, as a sense standing on its own, that of strife. Radak's father explained it so: My higher spirit, which I blew into man, shall not be at strife with the body forever, since the spirit takes no pleasure in the body's desires while the body is drawn after the desires of a beast, for he is flesh, and in the nature of flesh the desires are sunk and fixed; I will lengthen his days a hundred and twenty years if they repent, and if not, I will destroy them from the world.

תקע.sense: To blow the shofar; in another sense to pitch, set or drive a thing in place; and, near to that, to strike palm on palm in surety or in joy.

more.t: וְשָׁאוּל תָּקַע בַּשּׁוֹפָר (Shmuel I 13:3), and Shaul blew the shofar, with the noun בְּתֵקַע שׁוֹפָר (Tehillim 150:3), with the blast of the shofar. The shofar itself is called תָּקוֹעַ, as in תָּֽקְעוּ בַתָּקוֹעַ (Yechezkel 7:14), they have blown on the takoa.

But וּבִתְקוֹעַ תִּקְעוּ שׁוֹפָר (Yirmiyahu 6:1), in Tekoa blow the shofar, he takes as a place name, said as a turn of speech with one word falling on another, as in וְעֶקְרוֹן תֵּֽעָקֵֽר (Tzefaniah 2:4), and Ekron shall be uprooted.

Another sense: ויעקב תָּקַע אֶת־אָֽהֳלוֹ (Bereishis 31:25), Yaakov pitched his tent, and וְלָבָן תָּקַע אֶת־אֶחָיו (Bereishis 31:25), Lavan stationed his brothers there. So וְאֶת־גְּוִיָּתוֹ תָּֽקְעוּ בְּחוֹמַת בֵּית שָֽׁן (Shmuel I 31:10), they fastened his body to the wall of Beis Shan, with nails or otherwise, and וַתִּתְקַע אֶת־הַיָּתֵד בְּרַקָּתוֹ (Shoftim 4:21), she drove the peg into his temple.

Near to this is אַל־תְּהִי בְתֹֽקְעֵי־כָף (Mishlei 22:26), be not of those who strike hands, which he explains as הכות כף האדם אל כף חבירו בערבון, a man striking his palm against his fellow's in surety; and for joy תָּקְעוּ כַף עָלֶיךָ (Nachum 3:19), they have clapped hands over you.

רוע.sense: Bad, evil, whether it comes from a man or upon him from Hashem; so too a body run down and a face changed. Other senses: a shout, a friend, and breaking.

more.t: וּבְעֵינֵי מֹשֶׁה רָֽע (Bamidbar 11:10), and it was evil in the eyes of Moshe, כַּדָּבָר הָרָע הַזֶּה (Devarim 19:20), like this evil thing, and the noun רֹעַ לֵב (Nechemiah 2:2), badness of heart. Radak holds there is no dividing this from רַבּוֹת רָעוֹת צַדִּיק (Tehillim 34:20), many are the evils of the righteous, for an evil that comes from a man and an evil that comes upon him from Hashem are alike evil, with no difference between them.

הֵרֵעוּ מַֽעַלְלֵיהֶֽם (Michah 3:4), they made their deeds evil, and לָמָה הֲרֵֽעֹתֶם לִי (Bereishis 43:6), why did you deal ill with me. In זֶרַע מְרֵעִים (Yeshayahu 1:4), a seed of evildoers, he says the word is said not of the fathers but of the sons, a seed who are your evildoers and children who corrupt their doings.

more.h: A body run down, a face changed
more.t: So too of a body run down and a face changed: וְרָעוֹת תֹּאַר מְאֹד (Bereishis 41:19), and very bad of form, רָעוֹת הַמַּרְאֶה (Bereishis 41:4), bad of appearance, and מַדּוּעַ פְּנֵיכֶם רָעִים (Bereishis 40:7), why are your faces bad. So וְלֹא הָיִיתִי רַע לְפָנָיו (Nechemiah 2:1), and I had not been bad before him: until that day I had not been so before him, but glad and of good heart, and that day, when he saw me so, he asked me why my face was bad. All of them are the sense of evil, and it is known.

Another sense: תִּתְקְעוּ וְלֹא תָרִֽיעוּ (Bamidbar 10:7), you shall blow but not sound a teruah, with the noun וּתְקַעְתֶּם תְּרוּעָה, and you shall blow a teruah. All of them are the sense of teruah, the sounding of the voice in a teruah, whether for joy or for mourning, as לָמָּה תָרִיעִי רֵעַ (Michah 4:9), why do you raise a shout. יִתְרוֹעֲעוּ אַף יָשִׁירוּ (Tehillim 65:14), they shout, indeed they sing, is said of the ears of grain, which strike one another when the wind blows through them, as though they shouted and sang.
A noun of the same sense in another form is יַגִּיד עָלָיו רֵעוֹ (Iyov 36:33), its noise tells of it, that is, the thunder tells of the rain and points to it.
Another sense is a companion: אִישׁ רֵעִים לְהִתְרוֹעֵעַ (Mishlei 18:24), a man of friends to keep company with, and וְרֵעַ אָבִיךָ (Mishlei 27:10), and your father's friend.

Another sense is breaking: תְּרֹעֵֽם בְּשֵׁבֶט בַּרְזֶל (Tehillim 2:9), You shall break them with a rod of iron, and רֹעוּ עַמִּים וָחֹתּוּ (Yeshayahu 8:9), be broken, you peoples, and be dismayed. הֲיָרֹעַ בַּרְזֶל בַּרְזֶל מִצָּפוֹן וּנְחֹשֶׁת (Yirmiyahu 15:12), will iron break the iron from the north, and copper: the iron and copper from the north is Nevuchadnetzar, and will their iron break it? If they are strong, one stronger than they will come upon them to break them and crush them. In Radak's view this whole sense belongs to the doubled roots, and so in the words of the Chachamim (Bava Kamma 30a), בכותל רעוע שנו, they taught it of a crumbling wall.

חנן.sense: To show favour, חֵן, which in places comes close to a gift, and to plead for favour, with תְּחִנָּה, a plea; all of it one sense. And חִנָּם, free, as though by favour.

more.t: וְחַנֹּתִי אֶת־אֲשֶׁר אָחֹן (Shemos 33:19), which he explains אתן חִנִּי, I will give My favour to whom I will favour; likewise כִּֽי־חַנַּנִי אֱלֹהִים (Bereishis 33:11), for Hashem has favoured me.

אֲשֶׁר־חָנַן אֱלֹהִים אֶת־עַבְדֶּֽךָ (Bereishis 33:5) he explains of the children: with them, the children, Hashem has favoured your servant. חָנּוּנוּ אוֹתָם (Shoftim 21:22) he explains חנו אותנו מהם, favour us with them. These, he says, are close to the sense of מתנה, a gift.

וָֽאֶתְחַנַּן (Devarim 3:23), I pleaded, he explains בקשתי מלפניו שיחנני, I asked before Him that He favour me; and כִּֽי־יְחַנֵּן קוֹלוֹ (Mishlei 26:25), when he raises his voice in the manner of supplication, as he explains it, ישא קולו בדרך תחינה. These he calls close to the sense of תפלה ובקשה, prayer and request, and with them go תְּחִנָּה, a plea, as מַפִּיל־אֲנִי תְחִנָּתִי לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ (Yirmiyahu 38:26), I lay my plea before the king.

He holds כלם ענין חֵן, that all of them are the sense of favour, adding that one who understands can tell a little between each of them according to its place; and he closes that for one who understands all of them come into one sense.

more.h: Free, which is to say in favour
more.t: וְיָֽצְאָה חִנָּם (Shemos 21:11), she shall go out free: the mem is an addition, like the mem of רֵיקָם, empty, and the sense is ותצא בחן מאין כסף, she goes out in favour, without money; that is, since she leaves without money, it is as though she goes out by the favour she found in her master's eyes. Every חנם in Scripture, he says, is to be explained as favour.

חוס.sense: To have pity: the sense of them all, he says, is compassion, ענין חמלה. At וַתָּחָס עָלֶיךָ, which names no eye, he reads it as my eye, or my soul, had pity on you.

more.t: אַתָּה חַסְתָּ עַל־הַקִּיקָיוֹן (Yonah 4:10), you had pity on the kikayon, לֹֽא־חָסָה עָלַיִךְ עַיִן (Yechezkel 16:5), no eye pitied you, and יָחֹס עַל־דַּל וְאֶבְיוֹן (Tehillim 72:13), he shall have pity on the poor and the needy.

more.h: Where the eye is left out
more.t: וַתָּחָס עֵינִי עֲלֵיהֶם מִשַּֽׁחֲתָם (Yechezkel 20:17), my eye had pity on them, from destroying them; and where the pasuk says only וַתָּחָס עָלֶיךָ (Shmuel I 24:11), and it had pity on you, he reads ותחס עיני או נפשי, my eye or my soul had pity.

These forms all come with cholam, as לֹא תָחוֹס עֵינֶֽךָ (Devarim 25:12), your eye shall not pity, and וְלֹא־תָחוֹס עֵינִי (Yechezkel 5:11), and my eye shall not pity. One alone comes with shuruk, לֹֽא־תָחוּס עֵינָֽם (Yeshayahu 13:18), their eye shall not pity, and so does every אָחוּס (Yirmiyahu 13:14; Yechezkel 24:14; Yonah 4:11), I will pity.

חמל.sense: To have pity. Some read two pesukim as rejoicing; Radak holds there is no need to take them out of the sense of pity (חמלה).

more.h: Pity, the verb and the noun
more.t: וְעַל אֲשֶׁר לֹֽא־חָמָֽל (Shmuel II 12:6), and because he had no pity; מִֽי־יַחְמֹל עָלַיִךְ יְרוּשָׁלַם (Yirmiyahu 15:5), who will pity you, Yerushalayim; וְלֹֽא־תַחְמֹל וְלֹֽא־תְכַסֶּה עָלָֽיו (Devarim 13:9), you shall not pity him nor cover for him. The noun is בְּחֶמְלַת י"י עָלָיו (Bereishis 19:16), in Hashem's pity on him, and in another measure וּמַחְמַל נַפְשְׁכֶם (Yechezkel 24:21), that on which your soul has pity.
