Some explain וַיַּחְמֹל הַמֶּלֶךְ עַל־מְפִיבֹשֶׁת (Shmuel II 21:7), and the king had pity on Mefiboshes, as וישמח, he rejoiced, and they take וְחָֽמַלְתִּי עֲלֵיהֶם כַּֽאֲשֶׁר יַחְמֹל אִישׁ עַל־בְּנוֹ (Malachi 3:17), and I will pity them as a man pities his son, the same way. Radak says there is no need to take them out of the sense of pity. The meaning of וַיַּחְמֹל is that he did not take him with the others; or it is as Chazal explained (Yevamos 79a), that he asked mercy for him, that the aron should not take him in. So too וְחָֽמַלְתִּי, and I will pity, and כאשר יחמול, as he pities, are plainly in the sense of pity.

לְחֻמְלָה עָלָיִךְ (Yechezkel 16:5), to have pity on you, is an infinitive whose first root letter carries shuruk, and another infinitive comes in that same measure, מִלּוּשׁ בָּצֵק עַד־חֻמְצָתֽוֹ (Hoshea 7:4), from the kneading of the dough until it is leavened.

אהב.sense: To love. He gives no gloss, since the sense of every word of this root is known. The noun is אַהֲבָה, love, and in the masculine אַהַב.

more.t: וְיִשְׂרָאֵל אָהַב אֶת־יוֹסֵף (Bereishis 37:3), and Yisrael loved Yosef, וַיֶּֽאֱהַב יִצְחָק אֶת־עֵשָׂו (Bereishis 25:28), and Yitzchak loved Esav, and וָֽאֹהַב אֶֽת־יַֽעֲקֹֽב (Malachi 1:2), and I loved Yaakov.

לְזֶרַע אַבְרָהָם אֹֽהַבְךָ (Divrei HaYamim II 20:7), to the seed of Avraham, who loves You, carries its suffix as בֹּרַֽאֲךָ יַֽעֲקֹב (Yeshayahu 43:1), He who created you, Yaakov, and חֲמוֹר שֹׂנַֽאֲךָ (Shemos 23:5), the donkey of one who hates you, do.
וְרִדְּפָה אֶת־מְאַֽהֲבֶיהָ (Hoshea 2:7 in his edition), and she shall pursue her lovers, and תְּֽאֵֽהֲבוּ פֶתִי (Mishlei 1:22), you love simplicity, where the tzeirei stands in place of a patach.

The noun אַהֲבָה: אִם־תָּעִירוּ וְֽאִם־תְּעֽוֹרְרוּ אֶת־הָאַֽהֲבָה (Shir HaShirim 2:7), that you not stir up nor awaken love. In the masculine the noun is אַהַב, whose plural is in אַיֶּלֶת אֲהָבִים (Mishlei 5:19), a hind of loves. On another pattern, with a chataf kamatz under the alef, is נִתְעַלְּסָה בָּֽאֳהָבִֽים (Mishlei 7:18), let us delight ourselves with loves, whose singular is אֹהֶב, on the pattern of אֹהֶל, a tent.
In אָֽהֲבוּ הֵבוּ (Hoshea 4:18), they loved 'give', the הבו is not of this root but of יהב, to be explained in its own place.

חבב.sense: Love and affection: He loves the peoples, and לִטְמוֹן בְּחֻבִּי עֲוֹֽנִי, to hide my sin out of my love for it. Chazal use the word often.

more.t: אַף חֹבֵב עַמִּים (Devarim 33:3), He loves the peoples, and לִטְמוֹן בְּחֻבִּי עֲוֹֽנִי (Iyov 31:33), to hide my sin out of my love for it: their sense, he says, is ענין אהבה וחיבה, love and affection.

Chazal use this word a great deal, as they said (Avos 3:18), חביבין ישראל שנקראו בנים למקום, beloved are Yisrael, who are called sons of the Omnipresent; חיבה יתירה נודעת להם, an extra affection was made known to them.

more.h: Hiding a sin out of love
more.t: לִטְמוֹן בְּחֻבִּי עֲוֹֽנִי he explains לטמן עוני באהבתי אותו, to hide my sin out of my love for it, and continues רק גליתי אותו ושנאתיו והרחקתיו ממני, rather I uncovered it and hated it and put it far from me.

עגב.sense: Love and words of desire; and עוּגָב, one of the instruments of music, from which Yonasan renders כְּשִׁיר עֲגָבִים, like a song of love, as the music of pipes.

more.t: וּבְכֹל אֲשֶׁר־עָגְבָה (Yechezkel 23:7), and with all whom she loved; מָאֲסוּ־בָךְ עֹגְבִים (Yirmiyahu 4:30), your lovers despise you; וַתַּשְׁחֵת עַגְבָתָהּ (Yechezkel 23:11), and she corrupted her love; כְּשִׁיר עֲגָבִים (Yechezkel 33:32), like a song of love; and וַתַּעְגַּב עַל־מְאַהֲבֶיהָ (Yechezkel 23:5), and she desired her lovers. Their sense is ענין אהבה ודברי חשק, love and words of desire.

כִּי־עֲגָבִים בְּפִיהֶם הֵמָּה עֹשִׂים (Yechezkel 33:31), for they make desire with their mouths, Radak explains: מדמים בפיהם ובדבריהם כי דברי חשק להם דבריך ולא כן לבם, with their mouths and their words they make it seem that your words are words of desire to them, but their heart is not so. Targum Yonasan renders it as mockery and derision: אֲרֵי תּוּלְעָבָא בְּפוּמְהוֹן אִינוּן עָבְדִין, for they make mockery with their mouths.

בְּמִנִּים וְעוּגָב (Tehillim 150:4), with strings and ugav, and וְעֻגָבִי לְקוֹל בֹּכִים (Iyov 30:31), and my ugav to the voice of those who weep. Targum Yonasan takes כְּשִׁיר עֲגָבִים (Yechezkel 33:32) from this, rendering it כִּזְמַר אֲבּוּבִין, like the music of pipes; and it is one of the instruments of music.

מטר.sense: Rain; and to rain, of Hashem raining bread or snares down, and of the cloud that rains, or does not rain, upon a field.

more.t: יַֽעֲרֹף כַּמָּטָר לִקְחִי (Devarim 32:2), my teaching shall drop as the rain, and וְנָֽתַתִּי מְטַֽר־אַרְצְכֶם בְּעִתּוֹ (Devarim 11:14), I will give the rain of your land in its season; the plural in the feminine is מִטְרוֹת עֻזּֽוֹ (Iyov 37:6), the rains of His strength.

more.h: Bound to the word for shower
more.t: וּמְטַֽר־גֶּשֶׁם יִתֵּן לָהֶם (Zecharyah 10:1), He will give them the rain of the shower: מָטָר set in construct with גֶּשֶׁם, as in אַדְמַת עָפָר (Daniel 12:2), the ground of dust, and מִטִּיט הַיָּוֵן (Tehillim 40:3), from the mud of the mire.

The heavier form takes a further object: וְהִמְטַרְתִּי עַל־עִיר אֶחָת (Amos 4:7), I will cause rain upon one city, הִנְנִי מַמְטִיר לָכֶם לֶחֶם (Shemos 16:4), I will rain down bread for you, and יַמְטֵר עַל־רְשָׁעִים פַּחִים (Tehillim 11:6), He will rain snares upon the wicked.

In וְחֶלְקָה אֲשֶֽׁר־לֹֽא־תַמְטִיר עָלֶיהָ תִּיבָֽשׁ (Amos 4:7), and the field on which it does not rain shall wither, the one that does not rain upon it is the cloud. Read so, the verb there passes to a second, where וְהִמְטַרְתִּי, I will cause rain, and its fellows pass to a third. The verb is used of the clouds likewise in וְעַל הֶֽעָבִים אֲצַוֶּה מֵֽהַמְטִיר עָלָיו מָטָֽר (Yeshayahu 5:6), and I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it.

זהם.sense: Filth, זוהמא, the loathsome sweat of a man's body or of food, as when a man's soul reckons his bread filth; Chazal use the word of food and of the body.

more.t: וְזִהֲמַתּוּ חַיָּתוֹ לָחֶם (Iyov 33:20), his soul makes bread filth to him: that is, his soul reckons the food as zuhama, filth.
The zuhama is הזיעה המאוסה, the loathsome sweat, whether it comes off a man's body or off the food.

more.h: The word in Chazal, of food
more.t: Chazal use it of food, להעביר הזהומה, to take off the filth (Chullin 105a), and בידים מזהמות, with filthy hands (Berachos 47b).

more.h: The word in Chazal, of the body
more.t: Of the body, ישֹראל שעמדו על הר סיני פסקה זוהמתן (Avodah Zarah 22b), of Yisrael who stood at Har Sinai, that their filth ceased.

טנף.sense: To soil, to dirty: אֲטַנְּפֵם is אלכלכם, I shall dirty them. Chazal use the word of dirt, as in the filthy alleyways, and there are many more.

more.t: אֵיכָכָה אֲטַנְּפֵֽם (Shir HaShirim 5:3), how shall I soil them. Radak glosses it אלכלכם, I shall dirty them.
Chazal speak of dirt in this word, במבואות המטונפות, in the filthy alleyways (Berachos 24b). Radak adds that there are many more like it.

אלח.sense: To stink; the word is the letters of חֶלְאָתָה, the scum in a pot, turned about.

more.t: אַף כִּֽי־נִתְעָב וְֽנֶאֱלָח (Iyov 15:16), all the more one abhorrent and stinking, and יַחְדָּו נֶאֱלָחוּ (Tehillim 14:3), together they have come to stink. Radak gives the sense of both as נבאש, stinking.
Radak holds the word a transposition of the letters in סִיר אֲשֶׁר חֶלְאָתָה בָהּ (Yechezkel 24:6), a pot whose scum is in it.

בהן.sense: The thumb, which he glosses גודל, the thumb; the plural takes in the thumbs of the hands and the big toes of the feet.

more.t: וְעַל־ בֹּהֶן יָדוֹ הַיְמָנִית (Vayikra 14:17), and on the thumb of his right hand. Radak glosses the word גודל, the thumb.

בְּֽהֹנוֹת יְדֵיהֶם וְרַגְלֵיהֶם מְקֻצָּצִים (Shoftim 1:7), the thumbs of their hands and the big toes of their feet cut off. Radak allows that this plural may stand on a different pattern of the noun.

זקף.sense: To raise, מרים: Hashem raises those who are bent over; and the Targum renders lifting the eyes with this word.

more.t: זֹקֵף כְּפוּפִים (Tehillim 146:8), Hashem raises up those who are bent over. Radak gives the sense as מרים, lifting.

The Targum renders וַיִּשָּׂא עֵינָיו וַיַּרְא (Bereishis 18:2), he lifted his eyes and saw, as וּזְקַף עֵינוֹהִי וַחֲזָא, and he raised his eyes and saw, putting this root where the pasuk has lifting.

רבב.sense: Many, much, great; also enough. As a number, ten thousand; a man of standing is called rav, his merits being many; heavy rain; and, a sense apart, shooting arrows.

more.t: רַבּוּ מִשַּֽׂעֲרוֹת רֹאשִׁי (Tehillim 69:5), they are more than the hairs of my head, and as a description, עוֹד הָעָם רָב (Shoftim 7:4), the people are still too many.

In some places the word is enough: רַב ־לָכֶם בְּנֵי לֵוִֽי (Bamidbar 16:7), enough for you, sons of Levi, and רַב עַתָּה הֶרֶף יָדֶךָ (Shmuel II 24:16), it is enough, now stay your hand. Radak glosses the group די, sufficient.
As a number the word is ten thousand, which Radak calls the great reckoning: רִֽבֲבוֹת אַלְפֵי יִשְׂרָאֵֽל (Bamidbar 10:36), the ten thousands of the thousands of Yisrael.

A man of standing is called rav because his merits are many: עַל כָּל־ רַב בֵּיתוֹ (Esther 1:8), over every officer of his house. Radak reads קִרְיַת מֶלֶךְ רָֽב (Tehillim 48:3), the city of a great king, of Dovid.
From the same root and sense, וְכִרְבִיבִים עֲלֵי־עֵֽשֶׂב (Devarim 32:2), like heavy rains upon the grass, which Radak explains as המטר החזק, the hard rain.

Another sense, which he closes with ענין הורות החצים, the shooting of arrows: וּבְרָקִים רָב וַיְהֻמֵּֽם (Tehillim 18:15), and lightnings He shot and confounded them, a past verb, or a description where some of the Mesorah has it with kamatz; וַֽיְמָֽרֲרֻהוּ וָרֹבּוּ (Bereishis 49:23), they embittered him and shot; the description רַב, an archer, in the plural in הַשְׁמִיעוּ אֶל־בָּבֶל רַבִּים (Yirmiyahu 50:29), summon archers against Bavel; and יָסֹבּוּ עָלַי רַבָּיו (Iyov 16:13), his archers surround me.

טטף.sense: Totafos: a thing tied on the forehead, like a tzitz, and at times on the arm; the totefes written in the Torah is what Chazal call tefillin.

more.t: וְהָיוּ לְטֽוֹטָפֹת בֵּין עֵֽינֵיכֶֽם (Devarim 11:18), they shall be for totafos between your eyes. The word, he explains, is like a ציץ, a tzitz, that is tied on the forehead.

As Chazal say, לא בטוטפת ולא בסנביטין, not with a totefes and not with sanbitin (Shabbos 57a); and they ask מאי טוטפת, what is a totefes (Shabbos 57b), and Rabbi Abahu answers, המקפת מאזן לאזן, the one that goes round from ear to ear.

A totefes is at times tied on the arm, as the Targum renders וְאֶצְעָדָה אֲשֶׁר עַל־זְרֹעוֹ (Shmuel II 1:10), and the armlet that was on his arm, as וְטוֹטַפְתָּא דְעַל דַרְעֵיהּ, and the totefes that was on his arm.

The totefes written in the Torah is known: it is what Chazal call tefillin. It is Chazal who said that the head tefillin are four batim, and, following the received tradition, they rested this on the word read as טט פת, tat and pat, as they said, טט בכתפי שתים פת באפרקי שתים, tat is two in Katfi and pat is two in Afriki (Menachos 34b).

Chazal explain בין עיניך, between your eyes, as בגובה הראש, on the height of the head, the place where an infant's brain is soft, which lies opposite the space between the eyes (Menachos 36a); and לֹֽא־תָשִׂימוּ קָרְחָה בֵּין עֵֽינֵיכֶם (Devarim 14:1), you shall not make a bald patch between your eyes, is explained the same way.

תפל.sense: Tafel: a building that has no standing, and raw meat or fish, not eaten without much salt; and תִּפְלָה, a poor thing with no sense to it.

more.t: וְהִנָּם טָחִים אֹתוֹ תָּפֵֽל (Yechezkel 13:10), and they daub it with tafel, that is, a building that has no standing. The Targum says of it טִין פַּטִיר דְלָא תֲבָן, plain clay with no straw in it.
הֲיֵֽאָכֵל תָּפֵל מִבְּלִי־מֶלַח (Iyov 6:6), can what is tafel be eaten without salt. Radak explains it as raw meat or raw fish, which is not eaten raw unless it is heavily salted.
נְבִיאַיִךְ חָזוּ לָךְ שָׁוְא וְתָפֵל (Eichah 2:14), your prophets saw for you emptiness and tafel.

more.h: Tiflah, a thing of no worth
more.t: וְלֹֽא־נָתַן תִּפְלָה לֵֽאלֹהִֽים (Iyov 1:12 in his edition), and he ascribed no tiflah to Hashem, and וֶאֱלוֹהַּ לֹא־יָשִׂים תִּפְלָֽה (Iyov 24:12), and Hashem sets no tiflah. Radak glosses tiflah as דבר גרועה שאין לו טעם, a poor thing with no sense to it, and reads the second pasuk as saying that Hashem sets them no curtailing and no hindrance upon their deeds.

פסח.sense: Lame; and in a sense close to it, to skip over, as Hashem skipped over the doorways and over Yerushalayim; the offering is called pesach for that skipping.

more.t: אִישׁ עִוֵּר אוֹ פִסֵּחַ (Vayikra 21:18), a blind man or a lame one, and פִּסֵּחַ שְׁתֵּי רַגְלָֽיו (Shmuel II 9:13), lame in both his legs. In the plural, פִּסְחִים בָּזְזוּ בַֽז (Yeshayahu 33:23), the lame plunder spoil; and וַיִּפֹּל וַיִּפָּסֵחַ (Shmuel II 4:4), he fell and was made lame.

A sense close to it is skipping over: וּפָסַח י"י עַל־הַפֶּתַח (Shemos 12:23), and Hashem will skip over the doorway. Radak explains that He skips over the doorway when He sees the blood, and the destroyer does not come in. So too וּפָֽסַחְתִּי עֲלֵכֶם (Shemos 12:13), and I shall skip over you.

Therefore that offering is called pesach: וַֽאֲמַרְתֶּם זֶֽבַח־ פֶּסַח הוּא (Shemos 12:27), you shall say that it is a pesach offering, with a segol under the peh, because He passed over the houses of Bnei Yisrael and jumped and skipped over them. The plural is נָֽתְנוּ לַפְּסָחִים (Divrei HaYamim II 35:8), they gave for the pesach offerings.

And so the pasuk גָּנוֹן וְהִצִּיל (Yeshayahu 31:5), shielding and saving, goes on פָּסוֹחַ וְהִמְלִֽיט, skipping over and rescuing, because He passed over and skipped Yerushalayim when the destroying angel came upon the camp of Ashur.

עַד־מָתַי אַתֶּם פֹּֽסְחִים עַל־שְׁתֵּי הַסְּעִפִּים (Melachim I 18:21), how long will you skip over the two boughs. Radak explains that they do not stand firm on either one but skip and leap over both.

וַיְפַסְּחוּ עַל־הַמִּזְבֵּחַ אֲשֶׁר עָשָֽׂה (Melachim I 18:26), and they skipped upon the mizbeach that he had made. Radak says they passed over it in skips, since their minds were not settled and steady upon it. Targum Yonasan renders וְאִשְׁתַּטוּ עַל אֱגוֹרָא דַעֲבָד, and they danced upon the altar that he made, which Radak takes to mean that they were dancing after their custom on their altars. And in אֲשֶׁר עָשָֽׂה, that he made, he is the one who made it for the Baal, Achav or another.

דלג.sense: To leap; its sense is like מקפץ, springing: the lame man leaping like a deer, one leaping over the mountains or over the threshold.

more.t: עַל כָּל־ הַדּוֹלֵג עַל־הַמִּפְתָּן (Tzefaniah 1:9), upon everyone who leaps over the threshold. Targum Yonasan renders it עַל כָּל דִמְהַלְכִין בְּנִימוּסֵי פְּלִשְׁתָּאֵי, upon all who walk in the customs of the Pelishtim.
Radak explains the Targum by the pasuk עַל־כֵּן לֹֽא־יִדְרְכוּ כֹֽהֲנֵי דָגוֹן, therefore the priests of Dagon do not tread, and עַל־מִפְתַּן דָּגוֹן (Shmuel I 5:5), on the threshold of Dagon.

אָז יְדַלֵּג כָּֽאַיָּל פִּסֵּחַ (Yeshayahu 35:6), then the lame man will leap like a deer, and מְדַלֵּג עַל־הֶהָרִים (Shir HaShirim 2:8), leaping over the mountains. Its sense, he says, is like מקפץ, springing.

קפץ.sense: To close and withhold, of a hand or a mouth shut; in another form, skipping and hurrying along; and of men, coming quickly to an end, like one who skips away.

more.t: וְלֹא תִקְפֹּץ אֶת־יָדְךָ (Devarim 15:7), you shall not close your hand; יִקְפְּצוּ מְלָכִים פִּיהֶם (Yeshayahu 52:15), kings will shut their mouths; אִם־ קָפַץ בְּאַף רַֽחֲמָיו סֶֽלָה (Tehillim 77:10), has He in anger shut up His mercies; וְעֹלָתָה קָפְצָה פִּֽיהָ (Iyov 5:16), wrongdoing shuts its mouth. Radak gives the sense of all of them as סתימה ומניעה, closing and withholding.
מְקַפֵּץ עַל־הַגְּבָעֽוֹת (Shir HaShirim 2:8), springing over the hills, which Radak takes as leaping and hurrying along.
כַּכֹּל יִקָּפְצוּן (Iyov 24:24), like all others they spring away: that is, they come quickly to an end and their place is not known, like one who skips away.
Chazal use the word too: קפץ ונשבע, he leapt and swore (Yevamos 32b).

כלה.sense: Wasting away and ruin; completion, a sense close to it; desire and longing; holding back. From this root too come the kidneys, and kli, any article of use.

more.t: כִּי לֹא־ כָלוּ רַֽחֲמָֽיו (Eichah 3:22), His mercies are not spent, and כָּלוּ עֵינַי מְיַחֵל (Tehillim 69:4), my eyes are spent with waiting. The sense of these and all like them is כליון והשחתה, wasting away and ruin.

A sense near the first is completion: כָּלָה הַבַּיִת לְכָל־דְּבָרָיו (Melachim I 6:38), the house was finished in all its details, that is, the house was completed, and וַתְּכַל לְהַשְׁקֹתוֹ (Bereishis 24:19), she finished giving him drink.

לְֽכָל תִּכְלָה רָאִיתִי קֵץ (Tehillim 119:96) means: to the completion of all things I have seen an end, but Your commandment is very broad and has no end, since though the mitzvos have an end and a known count, their branches are broad without end. Whoever derives תִּכְלָה from וְכָל בַּשָּׁלִשׁ (Yeshayahu 40:12), and measured in a measure, on the pattern of מִתִּגְרַת יָדְךָ (Tehillim 39:11), from the blow of Your hand, has erred in both, since by the rules of grammar both come from roots ending in heh. It is also explained that רְחָבָה מִצְוָתְךָ מְאֹֽד, Your commandment is exceedingly broad, speaks of the mitzvos of the heart, while the mitzvos of the body have an end; and Radak says that explanation is the true one.

נִכְסְפָה וְגַם־ כָּלְתָה נַפְשִׁי (Tehillim 84:3), my soul yearned and longed. וַתְּכַל דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ (Shmuel II 13:39), and King Dovid longed, means the soul of Dovid longed. Ibn Ezra explained the word as carrying an object, said of Avshalom's mother, who longed for Dovid until Dovid wished to go out from his place to his son. The pasuk does not name her, as it does not name the mother in אֲשֶׁר יָֽלְדָה אֹתָהּ לְלֵוִי (Bamidbar 26:59), whom she bore to Levi, or in וְאֹתוֹ יָֽלְדָה אַֽחֲרֵי אַבְשָׁלֽוֹם (Melachim I 1:6), and she bore him after Avshalom. The sense of these and all like them is desire and longing.

Another sense, like that of the word spelled with an alef: וְאֶת־בְּנֵיהֶם כָּלוּ בַבָּֽיִת (Shmuel I 6:10), they shut their young up in the house, and לֹֽא־ יִכְלֶה מִמְּךָ (Bereishis 23:6), will not withhold from you. All of these mean מניעה ועצירה, holding back and restraining.

From this root וְאֵת שְׁתֵּי הַכְּלָיֹת (Vayikra 3:4), the two kidneys, which Radak calls well known. Some say they are named so because they have power in desire, from the sense of כָּלְתָה נַפְשִׁי, my soul longed. By way of borrowing, כִּלְיוֹת חִטָּה (Devarim 32:14), kidneys of wheat, since the grains of wheat resemble kidneys.

From this root כָּל־ כְּלִי יוּצַר עָלַיִךְ (Yeshayahu 54:17), every weapon formed against you. The word serves for any article of use, for weapons, and for clothing, as in וְכַכַּלָּה תַּעְדֶּה כֵלֶֽיהָ (Yeshayahu 61:10), as a bride adorns herself with her things, which he explains as her garments and her jewellery.

עצה.sense: To shut the eyes; and הֶעָצֶה, the end of the spine, which Chazal took instead from the root יעץ, counsel.

more.t: עֹצֶה עֵינָיו לַחְשֹׁב תַּהְפֻּכוֹת (Mishlei 16:30), he shuts his eyes to devise perverse things. Radak glosses it סותם, closing, and explains that a man thinks better with his eyes shut than open, since he does not turn this way and that and his heart is on nothing but the matter he is thinking about.
לְעֻמַּת הֶֽעָצֶה יְסִירֶנָּה (Vayikra 3:9), he shall remove it opposite the atzeh, which Radak says is the end of the spine.
Chazal put this word under the root of counsel, saying מקום שהכליות יועצות, the place where the kidneys give counsel (Chullin 11a), and that it was taken off above the kidneys.

טוח.sense: To plaster: daubing the walls of a house with lime or clay, and eyes smeared over from seeing. The טֻּחוֹת of two pesukim he explains as the kidneys.

more.t: וְטָח אֶת־הַבָּֽיִת (Vayikra 14:42), he shall plaster the house, and אַיֵּה הַטִּיחַ אֲשֶׁר טַחְתֶּֽם (Yechezkel 13:12), where is the daubing you daubed. Radak explains the tiach as plastering the walls of a house with lime or clay, between one stone and the next on the outside, or over the whole wall.

כִּי טַח מֵֽרְאוֹת עֵֽינֵיהֶם (Yeshayahu 44:18), for their eyes are smeared over from seeing. Radak allows that טַח here may stand without an object, or carry one like its fellows, the smearer being the false prophet or the heart, as it says לֵב הוּתַל הִטָּהוּ (Yeshayahu 44:20), a deluded heart has turned him aside.

וְהִנָּם טָחִים אֹתוֹ תָּפֵֽל (Yechezkel 13:10), and they daub it with tafel, untempered plaster, and אֱמֹר אֶל־ טָחֵי תָפֵל וְיִפֹּל (Yechezkel 13:11), say to those who daub with tafel that it shall fall.

הֵן־אֱמֶת חָפַצְתָּ בַטֻּחוֹת (Tehillim 51:8), You desire truth in the tuchos, and מִי־שָׁת בַּטֻּחוֹת חָכְמָה (Iyov 38:36), who put wisdom in the tuchos. Radak explains both as the kidneys; and it has been said that they are called so because they are plastered over and covered with fat.

סחר.sense: To go round about. From this a trader is socher, going round the lands and back, and a round shield is sochera; also trade, wares, and a gem perhaps named for traders.

more.t: סָֽחֲרוּ אֶל־אֶרֶץ וְלֹא יָדָֽעוּ (Yirmiyahu 14:18), which Radak glosses סבבו, they went round, to a land they did not know. And לִבִּי סְחַרְחַר (Tehillim 38:11), my heart goes round and round and will not settle, from the weight of troubles.
The Targum renders סָבִיב סָבִיב (Yechezkel 37:2), round about, as סְחוֹר סְחוֹר, and וַיִּסֹּב מֵֽעֲלֵיהֶם (Bereishis 42:24), he turned away from them, as וְאִסְתַּחַר מֵעִלָּוֵיהוֹן.

more.h: Why a trader is a socher
more.t: From this sense the dealer is called socher, because he is always going round the lands, out and back: אֲנָשִׁים מִדְיָנִים סֹֽחֲרִים (Bereishis 37:28), Midianite traders, and אֲשֶׁר סֹֽחֲרֶיה שָׂרִים (Yeshayahu 23:8), whose merchants are princes.

שְׁבוּ וּסְחָרוּהָ (Bereishis 34:10), settle and trade in the land, and תַּרְשִׁישׁ סֹֽחַרְתֵּךְ (Yechezkel 27:12), Tarshish was your merchant, which Radak reads as bringing the wares to you. As a noun, אִיִּים רַבִּים סְחֹרַת יָדֵךְ (Yechezkel 27:15), many islands were the market of your hand, and טוֹב סַחְרָהּ (Mishlei 3:14), her trade is better.
From the same sense the shield that is round on every side is called sochera: צִנָּה וְֽסֹחֵרָה אֲמִתּֽוֹ (Tehillim 91:4), His truth is a shield and a buckler.

וְדַר וְסֹחָֽרֶת (Esther 1:6), dar and sochares, is a precious stone; perhaps it is called sochares because it is always in the hands of traders. As Chazal say of that pasuk (Megillah 12a), it is one stone, which proclaims dror, freedom, to all who deal in wares.

פתה.sense: The heart leaning aside, off the way of truth and reason; to entice; פֶּתִי, the fool who leans to anything; from it פִּתְאֹם, suddenly; a second sense, to make wide.

more.h: A heart leaning where it should not
more.t: פֶּן־ יִפְתֶּה לְבַבְכֶם (Devarim 11:16), lest your heart lean aside, and וַיִּפְתְּ בַּסֵּתֶר לִבִּי (Iyov 31:27), and my heart leaned aside in secret: the sense is the heart inclining toward another, not by the way of truth and reason. So too וּלְפֹתֶה שְׂפָתָיו לֹא תִתְעָרָֽב (Mishlei 20:19), do not mix with one who leans toward you with his lips, that is, the man who speaks smooth things to you while his heart is not right with you. וּפֹתֶה תָּמִית קִנְאָֽה (Iyov 5:2): the one who leans toward every thing he sees and desires it, envy will kill him, for he envies every desirable thing he sees another have.

more.h: Why a fool is called פתי
more.t: The fool is called פתי because he leans toward every thing, as פֶּתִי יַֽאֲמִין לְכָל־דָּבָר (Mishlei 14:15), a fool believes every word. So כְּיוֹנָה פוֹתָה אֵין לֵב (Hoshea 7:11), like a dove that leans aside, without heart: as the dove leans toward the food and has no heart to understand that the net is spread to take her as she leans to it, so Ephraim leaned where his desire drew him, to Egypt and Ashur to seek help, with no heart to know that the Maker of all will trip them up as they go to seek help from any but Him. So the next pasuk says, כאשר יֵלֵכוּ אֶפְרוֹשׂ עֲלֵיהֶם רִשְׁתִּי (Hoshea 7:12), when they go, I will spread My net over them.

From this same sense and root comes the word פתאום, the alef standing in place of the hei at the end of the root: וּפִתְאֹם יָבוֹא אֶל־הֵֽיכָלוֹ (Malachi 3:1), and suddenly he will come to his Heichal, and עַל־כֵּן פִּתְאֹם יָבוֹא אֵידוֹ (Mishlei 6:15), therefore his ruin will come suddenly. The sense is speed and suddenness, a thing a man does not feel until it is upon him, since the פתי does what he does in haste, as וַֽעֲצַת נִפְתָּלִים נִמְהָֽרָה (Iyov 5:13), the counsel of the twisted is hasty.

To press the suddenness further the word is doubled with פתע, an instant: בְּפֶתַע פִּתְאֹם (Bamidbar 6:9), in an instant, all at once, and אֲשֶׁר־ פִּתְאֹם לְפֶתַע (Yeshayahu 30:13), which comes suddenly, in a moment.

In the heavy form it is enticing another: פִּתִּיתַנִי י"י (Yirmiyahu 20:7), You enticed me, Hashem; פִּתֵּיתִי אֵת הַנָּבִיא הַהוּא (Yechezkel 14:9), I enticed that prophet; מִי יְפַתֶּה אֶת־אַחְאָב (Melachim I 22:20), who will entice Achav; and הִנֵּה אָֽנֹכִי מְפַתֶּיהָ (Hoshea 2:16), behold, I will entice her.

Another sense is יַפְתְּ אֱלֹהִים לְיֶפֶת (Bereishis 9:27), Hashem will make wide for Yefes; and the Targum renders כִּֽי־יַרְחִיב (Devarim 12:20), when He widens, as אֲרֵי יַפְתֵּי, using this root. Some explain וּלְפֹתֶה שְׂפָתָיו (Mishlei 20:19) in this sense, that is: do not join with the man who opens his mouth wide to speak empty words and insults and revilings of people. Or it is read with what the pasuk says before it, גּֽוֹלֶה־סּוֹד הוֹלֵךְ רָכִיל, a talebearer reveals secrets, so that the one who opens his lips wide is the man who uncovers a secret: do not mix with him.

more.h: His brother on a false witness
more.t: His brother Rabbi Moshe takes וַֽהֲפִתִּיתָ בִּשְׂפָתֶֽיךָ (Mishlei 24:28) from here, the hei standing for אם, if, as though it said, and if you have enticed with your lips. Radak explains the pasuk so: אַל־תְּהִי עֵֽד־חִנָּם בְּרֵעֶךָ, do not be a witness against your fellow without cause, and even though you enticed someone with your lips and he bore false witness for you, do not bear false witness for him on that account. That is what it says after it, אל תאמר כאשר עשה לי כן אעשה לו, do not say, as he did to me so I will do to him.

פלט.sense: Rescue and escape: to get away and to deliver, the פָּלִיט being one who got away; and in another sense close to it, a casting out, as of the unborn child at birth.

more.h: Escape, and the one who escaped
more.t: וּפָֽלְטוּ פְּלִיטֵיהֶם (Yechezkel 7:16), and their escaped ones shall get away; as an adjective, וַיָּבֹא הַפָּלִיט (Bereishis 14:13), and the one who escaped came, and וְזָֽכְרוּ פְלִֽיטֵיכֶם (Yechezkel 6:9), and your escaped ones shall remember. The whole of it, he says, is rescue and escape. וְיַפְלִיט וְאֵין מַצִּֽיל (Yeshayahu 5:29), and he carries it off and none rescues, he explains as taking spoil and plunder, with none to rescue from his hand.

כִּי אָמְרוּ פְּלִיטֵי אֶפְרַיִם (Shoftim 12:4), for the lesser men of Ephraim said, as he explains it: the lesser men of Ephraim used to say, you Gilead, what are you reckoned among Ephraim and among Menasheh? The lesser are called פלטים because they are like the escaped leavings of the great and the honoured. In his own view פְּלִיטֵי הַגּוֹיִם (Yeshayahu 45:20) likewise means the lesser of the nations.

פַּלְּטָה נַפְשִׁי מֵרָשָׁע חַרְבֶּֽךָ (Tehillim 17:13), deliver my soul from the wicked, Your sword, and תְּפַלְּטֵנִי מֵרִיבֵי עָם (Tehillim 18:44), You deliver me from the strivings of the people. רָנֵּי פַלֵּט תְּסוֹבְבֵנִי סֶֽלָה (Tehillim 32:7), You surround me with songs of rescue, Selah, he explains as praise and thanks for the rescue: when I am saved from the enemy I will sing and give thanks to You.

In another sense close to it, וְלֹא תַפְלִיט וַֽאֲשֶׁר תְּפַלֵּט לַחֶרֶב אֶתֵּֽן (Michah 6:14), you will not cast forth, and what you cast forth I will give to the sword, is the casting out of the unborn child at birth; and so עַל־אָוֶן פַּלֶּט ־לָמוֹ (Tehillim 56:8), for iniquity cast them out, that is, a casting away and a putting far from them. Like it are Chazal's words (Berachos 3:6), נדה שפלטה שכבת זרע, a niddah who cast out seed; and the Targum of וַיָּקֵא אֶת־יוֹנָה (Yonah 2:11), and it spewed out Yonah, is וּפְלֵט יַת יוֹנָה, and it cast out Yonah.
For עַל־אָוֶן פַּלֶּט ־לָמוֹ, though, Radak holds the right reading to be from the first sense, escape, with the pasuk put as a question of wonder: for iniquity shall they escape?

שֹרד.sense: Survivors, a sense he calls known; also the carpenter's marking thread, and בִּגְדֵי הַשְּׂרָד, cloths that covered the mizbeach, shulchan and menorah on the march.

more.h: Those left when the rest are gone
more.t: וְהַשְּׂרִידִים שָֽׂרְדוּ מֵהֶם (Yehoshua 10:20), the survivors who were left of them, פָּלִיט וְשָׂרִיד (Eichah 2:22), a fugitive or a survivor, and שְׂרִידֵי חָרֶב (Yirmiyahu 31:2), those left over from the sword. Radak says the sense is known and gives no gloss of his own.
In יְתָֽאֲרֵהוּ בַשֶּׂרֶד (Yeshayahu 44:13), he marks it out with the sered, the שרד is the coloured thread with which the carpenter marks what he wants to cut away from the wood.

וְאֵת בִּגְדֵי הַשְּׂרָד (Shemos 31:10) are the garments of the service, and Radak says they are not priestly garments but cloths made to cover the mizbeach, the shulchan and the menorah when the camp travelled. Rashi wrote that they are called בגדי שרד because they are made like hangings, which the Targum renders סרדין.

קלט.sense: Taking in and gathering: the cities of refuge took in those who fled there, a קָלוּט has a foot gathered in and narrow, and dye is taken in and gathered.

more.t: שָׂרוּעַ וְקָלוּט (Vayikra 22:23), the limb overgrown and the limb drawn in: the קָלוּט is one whose foot is gathered in and narrow, and Chazal explained (Bechoros 40a) that its hooves are closed, like the feet of a horse or a donkey.

more.h: The cities that take a man in
more.t: עָרֵי מִקְלָט (Bamidbar 35:11), cities of refuge, which took in and gathered within them those who fled there.
And in the Mishnah (Shabbos 1:6, Shabbos 17b), כדי שיקלוט את העין, so that it takes up the colour: that is, so that it takes the dye and gathers it in.

עיף.sense: Weary: עָיֵף וְיָגֵעַ, faint and weary, and my soul is faint. He gives no gloss here, having set these pesukim down already under the root עוף.

more.t: עָיֵף וְיָגֵעַ (Devarim 25:18), faint and weary, and כִּי־ עָֽיְפָה נַפְשִׁי (Yirmiyahu 4:31), for my soul faints. Radak adds only that he has already mentioned them under the root עוף, and gives no gloss here at all.

יעף.sense: Weariness: to tire, and the weary man. מֻעָף בִּיעָף is of the sense of flying; and in another sense, תּֽוֹעָפוֹת is strength.

more.t: לֹא יִיעַף וְלֹא יִיגָע (Yeshayahu 40:28), he neither tires nor wearies, and וְיִֽעֲפוּ נְעָרִים וְיִגָעוּ (Yeshayahu 40:30), youths will tire and weary. As a description, לִשְׁתּוֹת הַיָּעֵף (Shmuel II 16:2), for the weary man to drink; Radak says the sense of weariness is known.

more.h: The weary man thirsty to hear
more.t: לָעוּת אֶת־ יָעֵף דָּבָר (Yeshayahu 50:4), to hold up the weary with a word, and Radak says this is the man thirsty to hear the word of Hashem.

מֻעָף בִּיעָף (Daniel 9:21), made to fly in flight, is of the sense of flying, מֻעָף being a passive form and בִּיעָף a noun. The pasuk means: Gavriel, whom Daniel had seen in the earlier vision flying above, he now saw touching him.

Another sense: וְתֽוֹעֲפוֹת הָרִים לֽוֹ (Tehillim 95:4), the strength of the mountains is His, כְּתֽוֹעֲפֹת רְאֵם לֽוֹ (Bamidbar 23:22), he has as it were the strength of a re'em, and וְכֶסֶף תּֽוֹעָפוֹת לָֽךְ (Iyov 22:25), silver of strength will be yours. Their sense is strength.

יגע.sense: To toil; the sense of toil, he says, is known, like the sense of weariness. The noun is labour, and the adjective, weary.

more.h: Toil that wears a man out
more.t: יָגַעְתִּי בְקָרְאִי נִחַר גְּרוֹנִי (Tehillim 69:4), I am worn out with calling, my throat is dry, עַד כִּי־יָגְעָה יָדוֹ (Shmuel II 23:10), until his hand was weary, and לֹא יִיגְעוּ לָרִיק (Yeshayahu 65:23), they will not toil for nothing. Radak says the sense of toil is known, like the sense of weariness.

Turned on another the verb is wearying him: הוֹגַעְתַּנִי בַּעֲוֹנֹתֶיךָ (Yeshayahu 43:24), you have wearied me with your sins, and אַל־תְּיַגַּע־שָׁמָּה אֶת־כָּל־הָעָם (Yehoshua 7:3), do not weary the whole people there.

The noun: יְגִיעַ מִצְרַיִם (Yeshayahu 45:14), the labour of Mitzrayim, and וְכָל־יְגִיעֲךָ (Devarim 28:33), and all your labour; and in another pattern, all kamatz, מֵשִׁיב יָגָע וְלֹא יִבְלָע (Iyov 20:18), he gives back the labour and does not swallow it.

The adjective: עָיֵף וְיָגֵעַ (Devarim 25:18), faint and weary, and כָּל־הַדְּבָרִים יְגֵעִים (Koheles 1:8), all things are wearying, which are described in the language of toil because there is labour and toil for anyone occupied with them. In another pattern, וְשָׁם יָנוּחוּ יְגִיעֵי כֹחַ (Iyov 3:17), there those worn out of strength are at rest, the singular of which would be יָגִיעַ.

דנג.sense: Wax: כַּדּוֹנַג מִפְּנֵי הָאֵשׁ (Michah 1:4), like wax before the fire; דונג, he says, is השעוה, wax.

קיר.sense: A wall: the wall of the mizbeach or of a house, and by borrowing the walls of the heart; the doubled verb from it is tearing a wall down.

more.t: קִיר הַמִּזְבֵּֽחַ (Vayikra 1:15), the wall of the mizbeach, and נֹגַעַת בַּקִּיר הַשֵּׁנִי (Melachim I 6:27), touching the second wall; Radak says it is the כותל known from the Mishnah. In the feminine plural, בְּקִירוֹת הַבָּֽיִת (Melachim I 6:6), in the walls of the house, and וְקִֽירֹתָיו עֵץ (Yechezkel 41:22), and its walls of wood.

more.h: An upper room built of stone
more.t: On נַֽעֲשֶׂה־נָּא עֲלִיַּת־ קִיר (Melachim II 4:10), let us make a walled upper room, Radak says the upper room is joined to קיר to tell that it is to be built with walls, a building of stones, and not with partitions of reeds.
By way of borrowing, קִירוֹת לִבִּי הֹֽמֶה־לִּי (Yirmiyahu 4:19), the walls of my heart moan within me; Radak says it is said of the heart because a heart has sides and hollows.

The doubled verb is the pulling down of a wall: וְקַרְקַר כָּל־בְּנֵי־שֵֽׁת (Bamidbar 24:17), and he will break down all the sons of Shes, and מְקַרְקַר קִר (Yeshayahu 22:5), pulling down the wall. As מְשָׁרֵשׁ is taking out the root, so מקרקר is pulling down the wall, and קִר is added for more clearness, since מקרקר alone would have done, as in לִצְבֹא צָבָא (Bamidbar 4:23), to serve the service, and וַיִּקְסְמוּ קְסָמִים (Melachim II 17:17), and they divined divinations.

נכת.sense: נְכֹאת, a desirable thing (Bereishis 37:25); some explain it as carob fruit, and Bereishis Rabbah as wax.

more.t: נְכֹאת וּצְרִי וָלֹט (Bereishis 37:25), nechos, tzari and lot: the alef stands in for a lengthening vav, and the meaning is a desirable thing. So too אֶת־בֵּית נְכֹתֹה (Yeshayahu 39:2), the house of his desirable things, and so the Targum renders it, יַת כֹּל בֵּית גִנְזוֹהִי, the whole house of his treasuries.
Some explain נכאת in נכאת וצרי ולט, nechos, tzari and lot, as the fruit of the carob tree. Bereishis Rabbah, at the end of parashah 91, explains נכאת as שעוה, wax, and it is known.

more.h: Verbs that may share the root
more.t: וַיַּכּוּם וַֽיַּכְּתוּם (Bamidbar 14:45), and they struck them and beat them down, may be of this root; its regular form would be וַיַּכִּיּתוּם, just as וַיַּדְבְּקוּ גַם־הֵמָּה (Shmuel I 14:22), and they too clung on, would regularly be וַיַּדְבּיקוּ. So too וָֽאֶכֹּת אֹתוֹ טָחוֹן (Devarim 9:21), and I beat it, grinding, may be of this root. Their sense he explains under the root כָּתַת.

הלל.sense: Praise, lauding and thanks, with rejoicing close to it; a second sense, madness, going out from the mind's understanding; and a third, shining and light.

more.h: Praise, and thanks along with it
more.t: שֶׁבַע בַּיּוֹם הִלַּלְתִּיךָ (Tehillim 119:164), seven times a day I praise You; with a tav added, the noun תְּהִלָּה לְדָוִד (Tehillim 145:1), a praise of David, and in the plural יוֹשֵׁב תְּהִלּוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵֽל (Tehillim 22:4), He who sits enthroned on the praises of Yisrael. The reflexive is בִּקְדוֹשׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל תִּתְהַלָּֽל (Yeshayahu 41:16), in the Holy One of Yisrael you will glory.

Some explain לְהִתְהַלֵּל עִם־נַֽחֲלָתֶֽךָ (Tehillim 106:5), to glory with Your inheritance, as rejoicing, from קֹדֶשׁ הִלּוּלִים (Vayikra 19:24), a holy thing of rejoicing. Radak says there is no need to take them out of the sense of praise, which is lauding and thanks; rather, rejoicing is close to its sense. So too וּבְתוּלֹתָיו לֹא הוּלָּֽלוּ (Tehillim 78:63), his maidens were not celebrated, that is, they never came to the time of rejoicing and celebration, meaning they did not become men's wives. And in the language of Chazal the wedding chamber is called בי הלולא (Bava Metzia 36a), the house of celebration.

more.h: הֽוֹלֵלוֹת, going out of one's mind
more.t: A second sense is madness: אָמַרְתִּי לַֽהוֹלְלִים אַל־ תָּהֹלּוּ (Tehillim 75:5), I said to the raving, do not rave, כִּי הָעֹשֶׁק יְהוֹלֵל חָכָם (Koheles 7:7), oppression drives a wise man mad, and the nouns וְדַעַת הֹֽלֵלוֹת וְשִׂכְלוּת (Koheles 1:17), the knowing of madness and folly. Radak says they are all madness, the going out from the mind's understanding and from the way of what is right and straight.

more.h: מְהוֹלָלַי, and Rabbi Yonah on the oath
more.t: מְהוֹלָלַי בִּי נִשְׁבָּֽעוּ (Tehillim 102:9), those mad in my eyes swear by me: מְהוֹלָלַי are those who are mad in my eyes. On בִּי נִשְׁבָּֽעוּ, they swear by me, Rabbi Yonah wrote that the speaker stood so low in their eyes that they would say, may Hashem make me like so-and-so if such and such comes about.

יִתְהֽוֹלְלוּ הָרֶכֶב יִשְׁתַּקְשְׁקוּן בָּֽרְחֹבוֹת (Nachum 2:5), the chariots rave and clatter in the open places: Radak says that from the greatness of their running in joy it is as though they were mad with much joy. So too עַל־כֵּן יִתְהֹֽלְלוּ גוֹיִֽם (Yirmiyahu 51:7), therefore the nations rave, at the sight of Bavel's fall.

בְּהִלּוֹ נֵרוֹ עֲלֵי רֹאשִׁי (Iyov 29:3), when his lamp shone over my head; אִם־אֶרְאֶה אוֹר כִּי יָהֵל (Iyov 31:26), if I saw the light when it shone, and לֹא יָהֵלּוּ אוֹרָם (Yeshayahu 13:10), they will not let their light shine: in יהל the shining is set on the light itself, and in יהלו on the stars. From this sense the morning star is called הֵילֵל בֶּן־שָׁחַר (Yeshayahu 14:12), the shining one, son of the dawn; the sense of all of them is brightness and light.

שׁבח.sense: To praise, a sense he calls known; and in another sense, to quiet and settle, as waves and the roar of the seas are stilled.

more.t: יְשַׁבַּח מַֽעֲשֶׂיךָ (Tehillim 145:4), shall praise Your works, and שְׂפָתַי יְשַׁבְּחֽוּנְךָ (Tehillim 63:4), my lips will praise You; with the reflexive, לְהִשְׁתַּבֵּחַ בִּתְהִלָּתֶֽךָ (Tehillim 106:47), to glory in Your praise. The sense, he says, is known.

בְּשׂוֹא גַלָּיו אַתָּה תְשַׁבְּחֵֽם (Tehillim 89:10), when its waves rise You still them, וְחָכָם בְּאָחוֹר יְשַׁבְּחֶֽנָּה (Mishlei 29:11), a wise man holds it back and quiets it, and מַשְׁבִּיחַ שְׁאוֹן יַמִּים (Tehillim 65:8), who stills the roaring of the seas. Radak says the sense of all of these is ההשקט וההנחה, quieting and setting at rest.

פאר.sense: Glory, praise and beauty: to take glory to oneself, and to glorify; הַפְּאֵרִים are caps, a glory on the head. פֻּארָה, a bough, may belong here.

more.t: הֲיִתְפָּאֵר הַגַּרְזֶן עַל הַחֹצֵב בּוֹ (Yeshayahu 10:15), shall the axe take glory over the one hewing with it, and אֲשֶׁר־בְּךָ אֶתְפָּאָֽר (Yeshayahu 49:3), in whom I will be glorified. On הִתְפָּאֵר עָלַי (Shemos 8:5) Radak says it is: take the glory and the praise to yourself over me, that you should say when I am to entreat for you, and so I will do.

וְאֶת־ פַּֽאֲרֵי הַמִּגְבָּעֹת (Shemos 39:28), and the adornments, the caps; פַּֽאֲרֵי פִשְׁתִּים יִֽהְיוּ עַל־רֹאשָׁם (Yechezkel 44:18), linen headdresses will be on their head; and הַפְּאֵרִים וְהַצְּעָדוֹת (Yeshayahu 3:20), the headdresses and the ankle chains. These are the caps, which are a glory to a man while they are on his head, and Radak says the sense of all of them is praise and beauty.

On כָּל־פָּנִים קִבְּצוּ פָארֽוּר (Yoel 2:6), all faces gather a פארור, Menachem explains that they gathered in their glory so that none was left them, in the way of וְכֽוֹכָבִים אָסְפוּ נָגְהָֽם (Yoel 2:10), the stars gathered in their brightness. Dunash explains it from וּבִשְּׁלוּ בַּפָּרוּר (Bamidbar 11:8), and they cooked it in the pot, the alef added, so that they gathered all the blackness of the pot.

His father holds that Menachem cannot be right, since there is a difference between אסיפה, taking in, and קיבוץ, gathering: gathering is said only of scattered things brought to one place, so one cannot say that all faces gathered their glory, which is not seen, while taking in can be said so, as וַיֶּֽאֱסֹף רַגְלָיו (Bereishis 49:33), he drew in his feet, and אֱסֹף יָדֶֽךָ (Shmuel I 14:19), draw back your hand; and one does not say קְבוֹץ ידיך, gather your hands, or ויקבוץ רגליו, he gathered his feet.

It may be from this root that a branch is called so: מְסָעֵף פֻּארָה (Yeshayahu 10:33), lopping off a bough, with a shuruk, and וַתֶּאֱרַכְנָה פֹארֹתָו (Yechezkel 31:5), its boughs grew long, with a cholam, like סעיף, a branch, and סעפותיו, its branches. Radak says the great high branch may be called פארה because it is the glory and the beauty of the tree.

more.h: Not stripping the boughs behind you
more.t: The verb from it is לֹא תְפַאֵר אַֽחֲרֶיךָ (Devarim 24:20), you shall not go over the boughs after you, pointed with a patach to set the sense apart; it means that you shall not take what is left in the boughs. The Chachamim explained it (Chullin 131a) from the word פאר, glory: that you shall not take its glory from it.

The root of פֻּארָה and פֹֽארֹתָיו may be פרה, as Rabbi Yehudah wrote, the alef before the resh standing like a lengthening vav, and פֻּארָה a noun of a root ending in heh, on the pattern of תּוֹעָה, error; its shuruk is no bar, since shuruk and cholam weigh the same. The alef before the resh is no proof that they are of the root פאר, for it comes first in only a few of them: וַתְּשַׁלַּח פֹּארֽוֹת (Yechezkel 17:6), and it sent out boughs, puts the resh first, and so do most of the פֹֽארֹתָיו, the Mesorah noting two written with the alef first and the rest with the resh first.

קלס.sense: Mockery and contempt; sometimes this word is said of praise, and in that sense Kaddish says ויתקלס, though Rav Amram Gaon wrote that it is not fitting to say it.

more.t: לַעַג וָקֶלֶס (Tehillim 44:14), derision and scorn, לְחֶרְפָּה וּלְקֶלֶס כָּל־הַיּֽוֹם (Yirmiyahu 20:8), a reproach and a mocking all the day, and in another form וְקַלָּסָה לְכָל־הָֽאֲרָצֽוֹת (Yechezkel 22:4), a mockery to all the lands. Radak says the sense is mocking and contempt.

more.h: The form that falls on the mocker
more.t: The reflexive falls on the one doing the mocking and is bound with a bet: יִתְקַלְּסוּ ־בָךְ (Yechezkel 22:5), they will mock at you, and וַיִּתְקַלְּסוּ ־בוֹ וַיֹּאמְרוּ לוֹ עֲלֵה קֵרֵחַ (Melachim II 2:23), they mocked at him and said to him, go up, baldhead. Radak says that since the mocking is kept up against them, the form shows the mocker taken up with it.

more.h: The same word used for praise
more.t: Sometimes this word falls on praise: כַּזּוֹנָה לְקַלֵּס אֶתְנָֽן (Yechezkel 16:31), like a harlot praising the hire she takes. Radak allows that וְהוּא בַּמְּלָכִים יִתְקַלָּס (Chavakuk 1:10) may be of this sense, that he glories in kings, though from what follows it, וְרֹזְנִים מִשְׂחָק לוֹ, and rulers are a laughing matter to him, it looks more like the first sense; and so Targum Yonasan renders it, וְהוּא עַל מַלְכַיָא מִתְלַעַב, and he mocks at kings.

more.h: ויתקלס in Kaddish, and an objection
more.t: In the sense of praise, Radak says, they said in Kaddish ויתעלה ויתקלס, may He be exalted and praised; but Rav Amram Gaon wrote in the siddur of prayers that he composed that it is not fitting to say ויתקלס.

Radak also allows explaining לְקַלֵּס אֶתְנָֽן from mocking and contempt, so that every use of the word is mockery and contempt: the harlot mocks at the hire once she has taken it, and mocks at the man who comes after her and despises him in her heart for letting himself be enticed by her words and led astray by the sweetness of her lips. Or she mocks at the hire itself before him, and despises it, so that he will raise it for her. And you, not only were you not like the harlot in this, but you gave your own gifts.

אפס.sense: To come to an end; the noun is the want of a thing, and it stands for 'except'; אַפְסֵי אָרֶץ, the ends of the earth. All are close to one sense, ending and what is not.

more.t: אָפֵס הַמֵּץ (Yeshayahu 16:4), the oppressor is at an end, and כִּי אָפֵס כָּסֶף (Bereishis 47:15), for the money is at an end, are a past verb, on the pattern of חָפֵץ; so too הֶאָפֵס לָנֶצַח חַסְדּוֹ (Tehillim 77:9), has His kindness come to an end forever. Their sense, Radak says, is known: כלה המץ, the oppressor is finished, כלה הכסף, the money is finished, and so all of them.

more.h: The noun: none of it, without it
more.t: בְּאֶפֶס עֵצִים תִּכְבֶּה־אֵשׁ (Mishlei 26:20) is, without wood the fire goes out; הַאֶפֶס עוֹד אִישׁ (Shmuel II 9:3) is הלא עוד איש, is there not still a man; עַד אֶפֶס מָקוֹם (Yeshayahu 5:8) is עד לא מקום, until there is no room; and בְּאֶפֶס עֲשָׁקוֹ, oppressed him for nothing, is בחנם בלא משפט, for nothing, without justice.

It comes in place of בלתי, except, only: אֶפֶס כִּי־נִאֵץ נִאַצְתָּ (Shmuel II 12:14), only that you have greatly blasphemed; אֶפֶס כי עז העם (Bamidbar 13:28), only that the people is strong; and אֲנִי וְאַפְסִי עוֹד (Tzefaniah 2:15), which he glosses אני ואין בלתי עוד, I am, and there is none besides me.

אַפְסֵי אָרֶץ (Shmuel I 2:10) is קצות הארץ, the ends of the earth. Radak says they are all close to one sense, כליון ודבר שאינו, an ending and a thing that is not, only that each is explained by the sense nearest to it.

Radak reads מֵי אָפְסָיִם (Yechezkel 47:3) as מי כליון, waters of ending, with only a little in them. Rabbi Yonah explained it as מי פסים with an added alef, waters of the palms, since in Aramaic the palm of the hand is called פס ידא; that is, the waters covered only the soles of his feet. Our Rabbis explained it (in Shekalim, chapter 6, halachah 3) as water a man crosses up to his ankles, and so Targum Yonasan renders מֵי קַרְסוּלִין, ankle water.

תהה.sense: Desolation: הָֽיְתָה תֹהוּ וָבֹהוּ (Bereishis 1:2), it was tohu and vohu; he has explained it already at the root בָּהָה.

בלם.sense: To muzzle, לחסום; Chazal read בְּלִימָה of one who muzzles himself in strife, and by the plain sense it is two words, the earth hung on nothing.

more.t: עֶדְיוֹ לִבְלוֹם (Tehillim 32:9), his trappings, to muzzle him, is לחסום, to muzzle. Chazal say (Chullin 89a) on תֹּלֶה אֶרֶץ עַל־ בְּלִימָֽה (Iyov 26:7), He hangs the earth upon בלימה, that the world endures only in the merit of one who muzzles himself, בולם עצמו, in a time of strife. That is, Radak explains, he closes his mouth and is silent, hears himself reviled and does not answer.

more.h: The plain sense: hung on nothing
more.t: By the plain sense בלימה is two words: the earth is תלויה על לא דבר, hung upon no thing, since it hangs in the middle of the spheres at a great distance from them on every side.

כתר.sense: The crown, כֶּתֶר, and the capitals that sat on the pillars like one; since a crown is round, to surround; and in another sense, to wait.

more.t: כֶּֽתֶר ־מַלְכוּת (Esther 2:17), a royal crown. בִּי יַכְתִּרוּ צַדִּיקִים, the righteous will crown themselves with me, which he explains as יחשבוני עליהם לכתר, they will count me a crown upon them. וַֽעֲרוּמִים יַכְתִּרוּ דָֽעַת (Mishlei 14:18), and the prudent crown themselves with knowledge: they set knowledge like a crown on their head.

הַכֹּתֶרֶת הָאֶחָת (Melachim I 7:16), the one capital, and וּשְׁתֵּי כֹֽתָרֹת עָשָׂה (Melachim I 7:16), and he made two capitals: they were called so, he says, because they sat on the head of the pillars like a crown.

Since a crown is round all about, he says, the language came to be used for surrounding: אַבִּירֵי בָשָׁן כִּתְּרֽוּנִי (Tehillim 22:13), the mighty of Bashan surrounded me; כִּתְּרוּ אֶת־בִּנְיָמִן (Shoftim 20:43), they surrounded Binyamin, so that he could not flee this way or that; and כִּי רָשָׁע מַכְתִּיר אֶת־הַצַּדִּיק (Chavakuk 1:4), for the wicked surrounds the righteous and encompasses him.
But כַּֽתַּר ־לִי זְעֵיר וַֽאֲחַוֶּךָּ (Iyov 36:2) is another sense, and by its context, he says, it means המתן לי מעט, wait for me a little, and be still until I show you.

Yonasan renders וּלְתוֹרָתוֹ אִיִּים יְיַחֵֽילוּ (Yeshayahu 42:4), and the islands shall wait for his teaching, with יְכַתְּרוּן, they shall wait; and the Targum of וְלַיְלָה וְֽלֹא־דֽוּמִיָּה לִֽי (Tehillim 22:3), and by night, and there is no stillness for me, is ולא אכתר לי, with this word for the stillness. From this his father explained כִּתְּרוּ אֶת־בִּנְיָמִן, and Radak spells that reading out: they waited for them until they came out and chased after them, as it says וּֽנְתַקְּנֻהוּ מִן־הָעִיר (Shoftim 20:32), and let us draw him away from the city. That is why it says הִרְדִיפֻהוּ (Shoftim 20:43), they made him give chase, and not רדפוהו, they pursued him: Yisrael did it of their own will, fleeing so that Binyamin would pursue after them, saying they are fleeing as at the first. And that is מנוחה הדריכוהו, at ease they led him on: in their flight Yisrael led Binyamin on at ease after them, and did not hurry until they turned back upon them.

עטר.sense: The crown, whose sense he calls known. The plain verb, from the noun, is to surround a man like a crown; the heavy forms are to give a crown and to crown.

more.t: לַֽעֲטֶרֶת צְבִי (Yeshayahu 28:5), a crown of beauty; וְהָרִים הָֽעֲטָרָה (Yechezkel 21:31), take off the crown; תָּשִׁית לְרֹאשׁוֹ עֲטֶרֶת פָּֽז (Tehillim 21:4), You set a crown of fine gold on his head; and the plural וְעָשִׂיתָ עֲטָרוֹת (Zecharyah 6:11), you shall make crowns. Radak says the sense is known.

The plain verb from this noun: עֹֽטְרִים אֶל־דָּוִד וְאֶל־אֲנָשָׁיו (Shmuel I 23:26), surrounding David and his men, which Radak explains as מסובבים אותו, surrounding him, lying in wait about him on every side like a crown, to seize them.

The heavy form: עַל־צֹר הַמַּֽעֲטִירָה (Yeshayahu 23:8), upon Tzor that crowns: she gives a crown and honour to her men. Radak says רָצוֹן תַּעְטְרֶֽנּוּ (Tehillim 5:13), encircling him with favour, may be of this form, as though it were תעטירנו, on the pattern of יַעְשְׁרֶנּוּ הַמֶּלֶךְ (Shmuel I 17:25), the king will enrich him; and its meaning is תסובבנו רצון סביביו, that he is surrounded with favour on every side, like a shield, which is round like a crown. He says it may also be of the plain form.

Another heavy form: עִטַּרְתָּ שְׁנַת טוֹבָתֶךָ, You have crowned the year of Your goodness; בָּֽעֲטָרָה שֶׁעִטְּרָה־לּוֹ אִמּוֹ (Shir HaShirim 3:11), with the crown his mother crowned him with; הַֽמְעַטְּרֵכִי חֶסֶד וְרַֽחֲמִֽים (Tehillim 103:4), who crowns you with kindness and mercy; וְכָבוֹד וְהָדָר תְּעַטְּרֵֽהוּ (Tehillim 8:6), and with honour and splendour You crown him.

נזר.sense: Keeping apart: the nazir keeps himself apart from wine, and the growth of his hair is called נֶזֶר. In another sense, נֵזֶר is a crown.

more.t: אֲשֶׁר נָזֹרוּ מֵֽעָלַי בְּגִלּֽוּלֵיהֶם כֻּלָּֽם (Yechezkel 14:5), who have all turned away from Me through their idols, and נָזֹרוּ אָחֽוֹר (Yeshayahu 1:4), they have turned backward: he has written them at the root זוּר, and they may be of this root. הַנָּזֵר כַּֽאֲשֶׁר עָשִׂיתִי זֶה כַּמֶּה שָׁנִֽים (Zecharyah 7:3) he explains as אם אנזר, shall I keep myself apart from food, from drink and from pleasures, as I have done these many years.

כֹּל יְמֵי נִזְרוֹ (Bamidbar 6:4), all the days of his keeping apart, and the growth of hair is itself called נֶזֶר, as שְׂעַר רֹאשׁ נִזְרוֹ (Bamidbar 6:18), the hair of his head's growth. Because the nazir does not shave the hair of his head, long hair is spoken of so: גָּזִּי נִזְרֵךְ וְֽהַשְׁלִיכִי (Yirmiyahu 7:29), shear your long hair and cast it away.

more.h: All of it is keeping apart
more.t: מִיַּיִן וְשֵׁכָר יַזִּיר (Bamidbar 6:3), from wine and strong drink he shall keep apart, which Radak explains as יזיר עצמו, he shall keep himself apart, for this verb too takes an object; and כָּל־יְמֵי הַזִּירוֹ (Bamidbar 6:6), all the days of his keeping apart. All of them, he says, are the matter of הפרישות, keeping apart. And וְאֶת־עִנְּבֵי נְזִירֶךָ (Vayikra 25:5), the grapes of your keeping apart, are the grapes you kept apart from and did no work upon.

Another sense, which he glosses as עטרה, a crown: צִיץ נֶֽזֶר ־הַקֹּדֶשׁ (Shemos 39:30), the plate of the holy crown, and so נֵזֶר שֶׁמֶן מִשְׁחַת אֱלֹהָיו (Vayikra 21:12), the crown of the anointing oil of his God. וּלְקָדְקֹד נְזִיר אֶחָֽיו (Bereishis 49:26), and upon the head of the נְזִיר of his brothers, is the one who is head of his brothers and crowned, and מִנְּזָרַיִךְ כָּֽאַרְבֶּה (Nachum 3:17), your crowned ones are like the locust, are the princes who wear the crowns. It may be, Radak adds, that נזיר אחיו belongs to the first sense, since he was set apart from them.

כלל.sense: Wholeness: כָּלִיל, the whole of a thing; beauty made whole; the bride, כַּלָּה, with all her beauty upon her; and כֹּל, all, which he holds is of this root.

more.t: כְּלִילַת יֹפִי (Eichah 2:15), whole in beauty, is an adjective: she is all beauty. מִכְלַל ־יֹפִי (Tehillim 50:2) is a noun: Tzion is the whole of beauty, the beauty of all the lands. The verb is כָּֽלְלוּ יָפְיֵֽךְ (Yechezkel 27:11), they made your beauty whole.

From this sense too, he says, come אַֽהֲבַת כְּלוּלֹתָיִךְ (Yirmiyahu 2:2), the love of your bridal days, and כַּלָּה קִשֻּׁרֶיהָ (Yirmiyahu 2:32), a bride her sashes, for in the days of her chuppah a woman has all her beauty and all her ornaments upon her. Even after the chuppah she is called כַּלָּה to her father in law and mother in law, as in עֶרְוַת כַּלָּֽתְךָ (Vayikra 18:15), the nakedness of your daughter in law, just as a man is called חתן, bridegroom, to his father in law and mother in law all his days by reason of his chuppah.

וְהָאֱלִילִים כָּלִיל יַֽחֲלֹֽף (Yeshayahu 2:18), and the idols He will wholly cut off, that is, all of them He will cut off. כָּלִיל תָּקְטָֽר (Vayikra 6:15), it shall be burnt whole, and וְכָלִיל עַל־מִזְבְּחֶֽךָ (Devarim 33:10), and whole offerings upon Your altar: the olah, which is burnt entire. כְלִיל ־הָעִיר (Shoftim 20:40), the whole of the city, he explains as the smoke of the burnings of all the city. So too וְאֶת־כָּל־שְׁלָלָהּ כָּלִיל (Devarim 13:17), and all its spoil, whole, and so the Targum renders it, גְּמִיר, complete; and so כְּלִיל תְּכֵֽלֶת (Shemos 28:31), all of blue, is that all of it is blue.

The word כֹּל, all, everywhere belongs to this root, he says, missing its doubled letter, and its forms with suffixes prove it: כֻּלּוֹ, all of it, and כֻּלָּם, all of them, carry a dagesh for the letter that is missing. It is a word that gathers the particulars, and sometimes it comes as an overstatement of number: וְכָל ־הָאָרֶץ בָּאוּ מִצְרַיְמָה (Bereishis 41:57), and all the earth came to Egypt.

וְלָרָשׁ אֵֽין־ כֹּל (Shmuel II 12:3), and the poor man had nothing, כֹּל here meaning מאומה, anything at all; and so אֵין לְשִׁפְחָֽתְךָ כֹל בַּבַּיִת (Melachim II 4:2), your maidservant has nothing in the house. In these places, he says, it means even one thing out of the whole.

רקד.sense: To skip or dance, as the mountains skipped like rams; and to make another skip.

more.t: הֶהָֽרִים רָקְדוּ כְאֵילִים (Tehillim 114:4), the mountains skipped like rams, and עֵת סְפוֹד וְעֵת רְקֽוֹד (Koheles 3:4), a time to mourn and a time to dance. In the heavier form וּשְׂעִירִים יְרַקְּדוּ־שָֽׁם (Yeshayahu 13:21), and se'irim will skip there; עַל־רָאשֵׁי הֶֽהָרִים יְרַקֵּדוּן (Yoel 2:5), they skip on the mountain tops; and וּמֶרְכָּבָה מְרַקֵּדָֽה (Nachum 3:2), and a chariot that leaps.
Another heavy form, and a transitive verb: וַיַּרְקִידֵם כְּמוֹ־עֵגֶל (Tehillim 29:6), He makes them skip like a calf.

כרכר.sense: To dance. From it camels, or beasts light in their going, are called כרכרות, since in their lightness and speed they seem to dance.

more.t: מְכַרְכֵּר בְּכָל־עֹז (Shmuel II 6:14), dancing with all his might: מְכַרְכֵּר is מרקד, dancing.

From this, Radak says, camels, or the beasts light in their going, were called כרכרות: וּבַצַּבִּים וּבַפְּרָדִים וּבַכִּרְכָּרוֹת (Yeshayahu 66:20), with litters, with mules and with these beasts, since in their great lightness and speed they seem to be dancing.
Targum Yonasan renders מְכַרְכֵּר as מְשַׁבַּח, praising, and וּבַכִּרְכָּרוֹת as וּבְתוּשְׁבְּחָן, with songs of praise.

פזז.sense: Growing strong: וַיָּפֹזּוּ, they grew strong; מְפַזֵּז, bracing oneself as dancers do; and פָּז, the good refined gold, since the refined is the stronger.

more.t: וַיָּפֹזּוּ זְרֹעֵי יָדָיו (Bereishis 49:24) is ויתחזקו: the arms of his hands grew strong. מְפַזֵּז וּמְכַרְכֵּר (Shmuel II 6:16) is מתחזק ורוקד, bracing himself and dancing, for it is the way of dancers to tighten the girdle of their loins when they dance.

תָּשִׁית לְרֹאשׁוֹ עֲטֶרֶת פָּֽז (Tehillim 21:4), You set on his head a crown of פָּז: it is the good refined gold, for the refined is the stronger. The verb from it is זָהָב מוּפָֽז (Melachim I 10:18), refined gold, that is, refined and made strong; and with an added alef, וּמָתְנָיו חֲגֻרִים בְּכֶתֶם אוּפָֽז (Daniel 10:5), and his loins girded with refined gold. From this too וַיָּפֹזּוּ זְרֹעֵי יָדָיו can be explained.

רצד.sense: תְּרַצְּדוּן (Tehillim 68:17): some explain it as skipping, or by its context as lowering yourselves; Rabbeinu Hai, as looking and hoping.

more.t: לָמָּה תְּֽרַצְּדוּן הָרִים גַּבְנֻנִּים (Tehillim 68:17), why do you תְּרַצְּדוּן, you many-peaked mountains: some explain it like תרקדון, why do you skip; or, by its context, its sense is תשפילו עצמכם, why do you lower yourselves.

Under the letter dalet, Rabbeinu Hai explains it as לשון עיון ותוחלת, a word of looking and hoping, as though to say מה אתם מעיינים ומיחלים לכך, why are you looking to this and hoping for it; it is close to the Arabic, which calls looking into a thing אלרצ"ד.

עפר.sense: Dust and anything fine; one in sense with אֲדָמָה, ground, אֶרֶץ, earth, תֵּבֵל, world, differing a little; עוֹפֶרֶת, lead, gaining in dust; עֹפֶר, a young hart or deer.

more.h: Dust, and the dust of gold
more.t: עָפָר מִן־הָאֲדָמָה (Bereishis 2:7), dust from the ground; עַד אֲשֶׁר־דַּק לְעָפָר (Devarim 9:21), until it was ground fine as dust. וְעַפְרֹת זָהָב לֽוֹ (Iyov 28:6), and it has dusts of gold, means the dusts out of which the gold is taken; or else the ground gold is itself called dust, as it is written וָֽאַשְׁלִךְ אֶת־ עֲפָרוֹ (Devarim 9:21), and I cast away its dust, and as Chazal said (Avodah Zarah 44a). Ash too is called dust, מֵֽעֲפַר שְׂרֵפַת הַֽחַטָּאת (Bamidbar 19:17), from the dust of the burning of the chatas.

The four are of one sense and are set beside one another, as עַפְרוֹת תֵּבֵל, the dusts of the world, אַדְמַת־עָפָר (Daniel 12:2), the ground of dust, and עַל־ עֲפַר ־אֶרֶץ (Amos 2:7), on the dust of the earth; yet Radak says there is a small difference between them. עפר is mostly said of what is fine, and so is אדמה, as וַֽאֲדָמָה עַל־רֹאשֽׁוֹ (Shmuel I 4:12), and earth upon his head, though אדמה is seldom said of the fine. Between ארץ and תבל too there is a small difference: ארץ takes in the whole, settled land and wilderness together, and תבל takes in the settled part only.

Radak says fine things are named by dust: וַיָּדֶק לְעָפָר (Melachim II 23:6), he ground it to dust, and וְנָשָׂא אֶת־ עֲפָרָם (Melachim II 23:4), he carried away their dust. The heavy verb taken from it is וְעִפַּר בֶּעָפָֽר (Shmuel II 16:13), and he dusted with dust.

צָֽלֲלוּ כַּֽעוֹפֶרֶת (Shemos 15:10), they sank like lead, is the metal אבר, as the Targum has it. It is rightly named על שם האפר, after the ash, since dust eats away all metals and lessens them while they lie in it, but lead gains in dust. And לְעֹפֶר הָֽאַיָּלִים (Shir HaShirim 2:9), to a young hart, and כִּשְׁנֵי עֳפָרִים (Shir HaShirim 4:5), like two young ones: the עֹפֶר is the young of the hart or of the deer.

אפר.sense: Ash; אֲפֵר, a veil, its letters turned about from the פאר of headgear; and Ofir, a man's name given to his place, one of the places of gold.

more.t: וְאָֽנֹכִי עָפָר וָאֵֽפֶר (Bereishis 18:27), and I am dust and ash: pointed with five dots, a tzeirei and a segol, its sense is דשן, ash.

וַיִּתְחַפֵּשׂ בָּֽאֲפֵר (Melachim I 20:38), he disguised himself בצעיף, with a veil; the word has the letters of the פאר of וְאֶת־פַּֽאֲרֵי הַמִּגְבָּעֹת (Shemos 39:28), and the headgear of the caps, turned about.

וְאֶת־ אוֹפִר וְאֶת־חֲוִילָה (Bereishis 10:29), Ofir and Chavilah, are men's names, Radak says, and their places were called after them. They are the places of the gold, as it says, אֵת כָּל־אֶרֶץ הַֽחֲוִילָה אֲשֶׁר־שָׁם הַזָּהָֽב (Bereishis 2:11), all the land of Chavilah where the gold is, and so it is written, זָהָב מֵֽאוֹפִיר (Melachim I 10:11), gold from Ofir. In וּבְצוּר נְחָלִים אוֹפִֽיר (Iyov 22:24), and Ofir among the rocks of the streams, אוֹפִיר means the gold of Ofir.

אבק.sense: Fine dust; spices ground fine, אַבְקַת רוֹכֵל; and of two men striving together, raising dust with their feet.

more.t: אָבָק וְעָפָר (Devarim 28:24), dust and earth, and וּפִרְחָם כָּאָבָק יַּעֲלֶה (Yeshayahu 5:24), and their blossom shall go up like dust. Fine earth, Radak says, is called אבק.

more.h: Against Ibn Ezra on the pointing
more.t: Radak says כָּאָבָק of Yeshayahu 5:24 is wholly with kamatz and is not in the construct, against what the sage Rabbi Avraham Ibn Ezra wrote there, and that Ibn Ezra confused it with כְּאָבָק דַּק (Yeshayahu 29:5), like fine dust, which in some books has the alef with sheva and patach and is in the construct; כאבק there is said of fine things, since it does not mean earth alone.

In most books, Radak says, that word too has a kamatz under the alef but the kaf with sheva, and the Mesorah notes on it לית, that it is unique. Radak found another note, on וְהָיָה לְאָבָק (Shemos 9:9), and it shall become dust, which says כל אבקא קמץ, every אבקא has a kamatz; and it forgot, he says, וְעָנָן אֲבַק רַגְלָיו (Nachum 1:3), and the cloud is the dust of His feet, unless perhaps it reckoned the word together with its prefixed letter.

Spices ground fine are called so too: מִכֹּל אַבְקַת רוֹכֵל (Shir HaShirim 3:6), of all the powders of the merchant. And וַיֵּאָבֵק אִישׁ עִמּוֹ (Bereishis 32:25), and a man raised dust with him, means that they raised dust with their feet as each strove with the other.

דשׁן.sense: To be fat and rich, and to make fat; the noun דֶּשֶׁן is fatness. In another sense דֶּשֶׁן is ash, and the verb is to clear away the ash, or to turn a thing to ash.

more.t: וְאָכַל וְשָׂבַע וְדָשֵׁן (Devarim 31:20), and he will eat and be full and grow fat, he marks as a verb, and וְהָיָה דָשֵׁן וְשָׁמֵן (Yeshayahu 30:23), and it will be rich and fat, as an adjective; so too דְּשֵׁנִים וְרַֽעֲנַנִּים יִהְיֽוּ (Tehillim 92:15), they will be full of sap and fresh. The noun is in וְתִתְעַנַּג בַּדֶּשֶׁן נַפְשְׁכֶֽם (Yeshayahu 55:2), and your soul shall delight in fatness.

דִּשַּׁנְתָּ בַשֶּׁמֶן רֹאשִׁי (Tehillim 23:5), You have made my head rich with oil, and שְׁמוּעָה טוֹבָה תְּדַשֶּׁן ־עָֽצֶם (Mishlei 15:30), good news puts fat on the bone. Where the doer is not named, נֶֽפֶשׁ־בְּרָכָה תְדֻשָּׁן (Mishlei 11:25), a soul of blessing will be made fat, and וַֽעֲפָרָם מֵחֵלֶב יְדֻשָּֽׁן (Yeshayahu 34:7), their dust will be made fat with fat.

In another sense, אֶל־שֶׁפֶךְ הַדֶּשֶׁן (Vayikra 4:12), to the place where the דֶּשֶׁן is poured out, pointed with six points, is the ash, and so וְכָל־הָעֵמֶק הַפְּגָרִים וְהַדֶּשֶׁן (Yirmiyahu 31:39 in his edition), and all the valley of the corpses and of the ash. That is the place where the ash was poured out, which lay outside Yerushalayim, and the pasuk says that place will be added to the city in time to come: the whole valley will be an addition to the city, and all the fields up to Nachal Kidron.

Targum Yonasan renders וְכָל־הָעֵמֶק הַפְּגָרִים, and all the valley of the corpses, as the plain where the corpses of the camp of Ashur fell. Radak says Yonasan either did not render וְהַדֶּשֶׁן, and the ash, at all, or rendered it by משרית אתורא, the camp of Ashur, since they were fat and rich, as it says of him וּמִשְׁמַן בְּשָׂרוֹ יֵרָזֶֽה (Yeshayahu 17:4), and the fat of his flesh will grow lean.

וְדִשְּׁנוּ אֶת־הַמִּזְבֵּחַ (Bamidbar 4:13), which Radak glosses יסירו דשנו, they shall take away its ash, and וְעָשִׂיתָ סִּֽירֹתָיו לְדַשְּׁנוֹ (Shemos 27:3), and you shall make its pots for clearing away its ash. וְעוֹלָתְךָ יְדַשְּׁנֶה סֶֽלָה (Tehillim 20:4), and your burnt offering He will make ash, selah, he reads as ישימה דשן, He will turn it to ash: that is, He will send His fire down from heaven to consume it and to accept it with favour.

כרב.sense: A keruv, a winged figure. Ibn Ezra holds the word covers any form; Chazal take the kaf as a prefix, כרביא, like a youth. A king is called a keruv by borrowing.

more.t: כְּרוּב אֶחָד מִקָּצָה מִזֶּה (Shemos 25:19), one keruv at this end, and וְהָיוּ הַכְּרֻבִים פֹּֽרְשֵׂי כְנָפַיִם (Shemos 25:20), the keruvim shall spread their wings.

more.h: Ibn Ezra: the word covers any form
more.t: Ibn Ezra explains that keruv takes in every figure: the keruvim of the Torah were explained as a human form, while the face of the keruv in Yechezkel's visions seems to be the ox's, since in one pasuk it says וּפְנֵי־שׁוֹר מֵֽהַשְּׂמֹאול לְאַרְבַּעְתָּן (Yechezkel 1:10), and the face of an ox on the left for all four, and in another פְּנֵי הָֽאֶחָד פְּנֵי הַכְּרוּב (Yechezkel 10:14), the face of the one the face of the keruv, in the place where the first said the face of an ox.

more.h: Chazal: the kaf is a prefix
more.t: Chazal took the kaf as the prefix "like" (Chagigah 13b), keruv being כרביא, like a youth, for they were in the likeness of youths. They asked from these pesukim in Yechezkel, and answered that Yechezkel begged mercy over the ox's face and it was turned into a keruv, for he said, Master of the world, אין קטיגור נעשה סניגור, an accuser is not made a defender. They asked further from פְּנֵי הָֽאֶחָד פְּנֵי הַכְּרוּב וּפְנֵי הַשֵּׁנִי פְּנֵי אָדָם, the face of the one the face of the keruv and the face of the second the face of a man, since a man and a keruv are then two different things, and answered אפי רברבי ואפי זוטרי, large faces and small faces.
יַֽעֲשֶׂה אֹתָהּ כְּרֻבִֽים (Shemos 26:31), he shall make it keruvim: that is, the paroches is to be made embroidered with the figures of keruvim.
The king is called a keruv by way of borrowed speech, for greatness: אַתְּ־ כְּרוּב מִמְשַׁח הַסּוֹכֵךְ (Yechezkel 28:14), you are the anointed covering keruv.

אפן.sense: A wheel. A word spoken עַל־אָפְנָיו, on its wheels, is a figure for a word settled in its place; Rabbi Yonah reads it as על פניו, upon its face.

more.t: וַיָּסַר אֵת אֹפַן מַרְכְּבֹתָיו (Shemos 14:25), he removed the wheel of his chariots; כַּֽאֲשֶׁר יִהְיֶה הָֽאוֹפַן (Yechezkel 10:10), as the ofan would be; לָאֽוֹפַנִּים לָהֶם (Yechezkel 10:13), as for the ofanim, to them. The sense of them all is a wheel.

דָּבָר דָּבֻר עַל־ אָפְנָֽיו (Mishlei 25:11), a word spoken on its wheels, על גלגליו, is another vowel pattern and is said as a figure: that is, a word settled in its place. Its pattern is that of חָפְנָיו, his two handfuls, one of the duals whose single is חֹפֶן, a handful; so the single here is אֹפֶן, and it is dual because it holds the hidden and the revealed.

more.h: Rabbi Yonah: the alef is added
more.t: Rabbi Yonah explained it as על פניו, upon its face, the alef being an addition. He wrote that נָשָׂאתִי אֵמֶיךָ אָפֽוּנָה (Tehillim 88:16), I have borne your terrors a long time, is of this root as well, and said that time is called in Arabic אִפַּא"ן, with a chirik under the alef and a dagesh in the peh. Radak has also written אָפֽוּנָה under the root פון, in the pattern of אָקוּמָה, I shall arise, as Rabbi Yehudah mentioned it.

אראל.sense: אֶרְאֶלָּם, their angel, אראל being a name of greatness, as Chazal call the angels; others read it as I will show them, or as Yerushalayim.

more.h: Their angel, and a name of greatness
more.t: הֵן אֶרְאֶלָּם צָֽעֲקוּ חֻצָה (Yeshayahu 33:7), behold their erelam cried outside, is their angel; arel is a name of greatness, as Radak explained at the word אריאל. He is close to saying that it is all one root, even though the yud has dropped out in אֶרְאֶלָּם.

Chazal also named the holy angels with this term for their great standing (Kesubos 104a): אראלים ומצוקים אחזו בארון הקדש, the arelim and the metzukim seized the holy ark, and נצחו אראלים את המצוקים, the arelim prevailed over the metzukim. Arelim is said of the angels for their greatness, metzukim of men of weight and standing, as in מְצֻקֵי אֶרֶץ וַיָּשֶׁת עֲלֵיהֶם תֵּבֵֽל (Shmuel I 2:8), the pillars of the earth, and He set the world upon them, which Chazal expounded (Yoma 38b) of the pious and the great, upon whom the world stands.

Rabbi Adonim read אֶרְאֶלָּם as a word compounded of אֶרְאֶה לָהֶם, I will show them, as בִּשְּׁלָם הַבָּשָׂר (Melachim I 19:21), he cooked the meat for them, stands for בשל להם, he cooked for them. Radak's father wrote the same and explained it so: the navi says, I will show Yisrael troubles, so that they cry outside, and the messengers of peace who used to come with words of peace מר יבכיון נשמו מסילות, weep bitterly, the highways lie desolate.
Ibn Ezra took it as Yerushalayim, which is called הוֹי אֲרִיאֵל אֲרִיאֵל (Yeshayahu 29:1), woe, Ariel, Ariel. The sense is then that when they see their arel torn down, they cry outside.

חשׁמל.sense: The chashmal of Yechezkel's vision: an angel of that name, or, as Radak allows, it may be the name of a hue close to the hue of fire.

more.t: כְּעֵין הַֽחַשְׁמַל (Yechezkel 1:4), like the look of the chashmal, is an angel so called, and it was the like of his hue that the navi saw out of the fire.

more.h: Chazal: the child and the fire
more.t: So Chazal said (Chagigah 13a) of the child who was expounding the workings of the merkavah and understood the chashmal, and fire came out of the chashmal and consumed him.

They further said (Chagigah 13b) that the word is a compound: what is chashmal? חש מל, silent, speaking. Rabbi Yehudah said חיות אש ממללות, creatures of fire that speak. A braisa taught עתים חשות עתים ממללות, at times they are silent and at times they speak: silent when the word goes out from the mouth of Hakadosh Baruch Hu, speaking when it does not. That speaking, Radak says, is praising and lauding Hashem.

more.h: Radak: perhaps the name of a hue
more.t: Radak says chashmal may be the name of the hue itself, one close to the hue of fire, since the pasuk says כְּעֵין הַֽחַשְׁמַל מִתּוֹךְ הָאֵשׁ, like the look of the chashmal out of the midst of the fire; and כְּעֵין חַשְׁמַל כְּמַרְאֵה־אֵשׁ בֵּֽית־לָהּ סָבִיב (Yechezkel 1:27), like the look of chashmal, like the appearance of fire with a housing round about it; and in the second vision כְּמַרְאֵה־זֹהַר כְּעֵין הַחַשְׁמַֽלָה (Yechezkel 8:2), like the appearance of brightness, like the look of the chashmalah.

חזק.sense: To be strong, or stronger than another; to make strong; with a beis, to take firm hold of a thing, like seizing; and of a vessel, what it holds.

more.t: וַיְהִי כִּֽי־ חָזַק יִשְׂרָאֵל (Shoftim 1:28), when Yisrael grew strong; אִם־ תֶּחֱזַק אֲרָם מִמֶּנִּי (Shmuel II 10:11), if Aram is too strong for me; חֲזַקְתַּנִי וַתּוּכָל (Yirmiyahu 20:7), meaning you were stronger than I, and you prevailed. The describing form is הֶֽחָזָק הוּא הֲרָפֶה (Bamidbar 13:18), whether it is strong or weak, and בְּחָזָק יָבוֹא (Yeshayahu 40:10), he comes with a strong force, his force being his arm.

more.h: Achaz and the king of Ashur
more.t: וַיָּצַר לוֹ וְלֹא חֲזָקֽוֹ (Divrei HaYamim II 28:20), he distressed him and did not strengthen him, a transitive use of the simple form. It can also be read as not stronger than him, or not strong before him, with Achaz the one who was not strong. Read as transitive, it is either that Hashem did not strengthen Achaz before him, or that the king of Ashur did not strengthen him: Achaz had sent to the kings of Ashur to help him, and the pasuk says that not only did he not strengthen him, he came against him and distressed him. Radak holds this last reading the right one.

חִזְּקוּ פְנֵיהֶם מִסֶּלַע (Yirmiyahu 5:3), they made their faces harder than rock; לֹֽא־ חִזְּקוּ הַכֹּֽהֲנִים אֶת־בֶּדֶק הַבָּֽיִת (Melachim II 12:7), the kohanim did not strengthen the breach of the house.

more.h: Where the object is left unsaid
more.t: וְעַל־יָדָם הֶֽחֱזִיקוּ (Nechemiah 3:5), and beside them they strengthened, meaning they strengthened the work; הַֽחֲזִיקִי מַלְבֵּֽן (Nachum 3:14), strengthen the brick mould, that is, the work of the mould; כִּי הֶֽחֱזִיק עַד־לְמָֽעְלָה (Divrei HaYamim II 26:8), for he strengthened to the very top, meaning he strengthened his kingship.

Where it is bound to a beis the sense is that a man fastens himself on a thing to grip it with strength, and it is like seizing, אחיזה: וְהַֽחֲזִיקִי אֶת־יָדֵךְ בּוֹ (Bereishis 21:18), hold your hand fast on him; וַיַּֽחֲזִיקוּ הָֽאֲנָשִׁים בְּיָדוֹ (Bereishis 19:16), the men took hold of his hand; אֲשֶׁר הֶחֱזַקְתִּיךָ מִקְצוֹת הָאָרֶץ (Yeshayahu 41:9), whom I took hold of from the ends of the earth, meaning I took hold of you. At times it comes without the beis, as the word אחיזה comes with a beis and without, as in Tehillim, הַֽחֲזֵק מָגֵן וְצִנָּה, take hold of shield and buckler; and with a lamed in the beis's place, וְהֶחֱזִיק לוֹ וְנָשַׁק־לֽוֹ (Shmuel II 15:5), he took hold of him and kissed him.

There is also the sense of what a vessel contains, מַֽחֲזִיק בַּתִּים שְׁלֹשֶׁת אֲלָפִים יָכִֽיל (Divrei HaYamim II 4:5), holding three thousand bath in capacity. Chazal made this usage common (Berachos 40a): כלי ריקן מחזיק מלא אינו מחזיק, an empty vessel holds, a full one does not hold.

עזז.sense: To be strong and to hold sway; oz, strength, and maoz, a stronghold; az, strong or fierce; and the ozniyah, a bird named for its great fierceness.

more.h: The verb, and a dispute over it
more.t: וַתָּעָז יַד־מִדְיָן (Shoftim 6:2), the hand of Midyan grew strong. הַֽחָכְמָה תָּעֹז לֶחָכָם (Koheles 7:19), wisdom is strong for the wise, also stands alone, taking no object, as the sage Rabbi Yehudah wrote; Radak spells it out: wisdom will be strong and ruling for him. The sage Rabbi Yonah holds that it takes an object.

עוּזָּה אֱלֹהִים (Tehillim 68:29), be strong, Elokim, written with a vav and a dagesh, is a command: be strong for our sake against the enemy, as You have wrought for us many times. The word זוּ there, as in זוּ חָטָאנוּ לוֹ (Yeshayahu 42:24), zu we have sinned against Him, is either in the sense of "which" or in the sense of "this".

עֹז לְעַמּוֹ יִתֵּן (Tehillim 29:11), He will give strength to His people; עָזִּי וְזִמְרָת יָהּ (Shemos 15:2), my strength and song is Kah; and in the fuller form וֶעֱזוּז מִלְחָמָה (Yeshayahu 42:25), the might of war, and וֶעֱזוּז נוֹרְאֹתֶיךָ יֹאמֵרוּ (Tehillim 145:6), they shall tell the might of Your awesome deeds.

With an added mem and the doubled letter dropped: לָעוֹז בְּמָעוֹז פַּרְעֹה (Yeshayahu 30:2), to be strong in the stronghold of Pharaoh, and עַל רֹאשׁ הַמָּעוֹז הַזֶּה (Shoftim 6:26), on the top of this stronghold, said of the rock, since it is a place of strength.
וּמֶלֶךְ עַז יִמְשָׁל־בָּם (Yeshayahu 19:4), a fierce king shall rule over them; כִּי־ עַז הָעָם (Bamidbar 13:28), the people is strong; חֵמָה עַזָּֽה (Mishlei 21:14), fierce wrath.

From this sense also וְאֶת־הַפֶּרֶס וְאֵת הָֽעָזְנִיָּֽה (Vayikra 11:13), the peres and the ozniyah, so named for its great fierceness. It is found in the Mishnah too, called עוז, in חוץ מכנף העוז (Keilim 17:14), except for the wing of the oz, which has been explained as the ozniyah. Rabbi Yonah explained עֲזָאזֵל as from this sense, and Radak spells out his view: it was hard and fierce. Radak has written of it already under the root עַז.

כבר.sense: כַּבִּיר, mighty and great, in quantity or in quality; also a sieve, a cushion, and כְּבָר, already, of time gone by. In כִּבְרַת, a stretch, the kaf is a prefix.

more.t: הֶן־אֵל כַּבִּיר וְלֹא יִמְאָס (Iyov 36:5), behold, Hashem is mighty and does not reject; וּשְׁאָר מְעַט מִזְעָר לוֹא כַבִּֽיר (Yeshayahu 16:14), and the remnant shall be small and slight, not great; כִּשְׁאוֹן מַיִם כַּבִּירִים (Yeshayahu 17:12), like the roaring of mighty waters. The noun, with an added mem, is יִֽתֶּן־אֹכֶל לְמַכְבִּֽיר (Iyov 36:31), He gives food in abundance. The sense of them all is might and greatness, whether of quantity or of quality. And the verb from it, בִּבְלִי־דַעַת מִלִּין יַכְבִּֽר (Iyov 35:16), without knowledge he multiplies words, that is, he makes them many and great.

In וְאוֹרִיד כַּאבִּיר (Yeshayahu 10:13), and I brought down, כַּאבִּיר, the alef is an addition to כַּבִּיר, mighty; or else the word is compounded of כַּבִּיר and אַבִּיר, mighty and strong, and this is for magnifying.

כַּֽאֲשֶׁר יִנּוֹעַ בַּכְּבָרָה (Amos 9:9), as it is shaken in a כְּבָרָה, means in a sieve; and so, in another pattern, וְעָשִׂיתָ לּוֹ מִכְבָּר (Shemos 27:4), and you shall make for it a מִכְבָּר, a thing of the same kind. כְּבִיר הָֽעִזִּים (Shmuel I 19:13) is a cushion of goats' wool, and so, in another pattern, וַיִּקַּח הַמַּכְבֵּר וַיִּטְבֹּל בַּמַּיִם (Melachim II 8:15), and he took the cushion and dipped it in water. Targum Yonasan renders it גוּנְבָא, as he renders וַתְּכַסֵּהוּ בַּשְּׂמִיכָֽה (Shoftim 4:18), and she covered him with the blanket; it is a thick cloth.

וַיֵּלֶךְ מֵֽאִתּוֹ כִּבְרַת ־אָֽרֶץ (Melachim II 5:19), he went from him a stretch of land, and בְּעוֹד כִּבְרַת ־אֶרֶץ לָבֹא אֶפְרָתָה (Bereishis 48:7), while there was yet a stretch of land to come to Efras. It was explained as a mil, since they say the way from Rachel's burial place to Efras is a mil. Radak's own view, as he wrote at the root בָּרָה, is that the kaf here is a prefix and not part of the root.

שֶׁכְּבָר מֵתוּ (Koheles 4:2), who have already died; כְּבָר הָיָה לְעֹֽלָמִים (Koheles 1:10), it has already been, for ages; מַה־שֶּֽׁהָיָה כְּבָר נִקְרָא שְׁמוֹ (Koheles 6:10), what has already been, its name was called. Everywhere this word is of time gone by. מַה־שֶּֽׁהָיָה כְּבָר הוּא (Koheles 3:15), what has already been is, means that what was already in the days of old is now. On בְּשֶׁכְּבָר הַיָּמִים הַבָּאִים הַכֹּל נִשְׁכָּח (Koheles 2:16) Radak explains that neither in what has already been nor in the days to come is there remembrance of the wise man with the fool, though over length of days all is forgotten; and some read it: in what has already been and in what will be in the days to come, all is forgotten, the memory of the fool.
