תקף.sense: To overpower, and to take hold of a man; תֹּקֶף, power; and תָּקִיף, strong, which is the Targum's word for חָזָק.

more.h: The verb, the noun, the adjective
more.t: וְאִֽם־ יִתְקְפוֹ הָֽאֶחָד (Koheles 4:12), and if one overpowers him. The noun is אֶת־כָּל־ תֹּקֶף (Esther 9:29), all the force, and וְכָל־מַֽעֲשֵׂה תָקְפּוֹ (Esther 10:2), every act of his power; the adjective, שֶׁתַּקִּיף מִמֶּנּוּ (Koheles 6:10), one who is stronger than he. The Targum for חָזָק (Shemos 10:19), strong, is תָּקִיף.

So too תִּתְקְפֵהוּ לָנֶצַח (Iyov 14:20), You take hold of him forever, and תִּתְקְפֵהוּ כְּמֶלֶךְ עָתִיד לַכִּידֽוֹר (Iyov 15:24), it takes hold of him like a king ready for battle: the word means תחזיק בו, takes hold of him.

פסל.sense: To hew, said mostly of stone and also of wood; the nouns פֶסֶל and פְּסִילִים, carved images; and הַפְּסִילִים, a place where stones were hewn.

more.t: פְּסָל ־לְךָ שְׁנֵֽי־לֻחֹת אֲבָנִים (Shemos 34:1), hew for yourself two tablets of stone, and וַיִּפְסֹל שְׁנֵֽי־לֻחֹת (Shemos 34:4), and he hewed two tablets. The noun is פְּסִילֵי אֱלֹֽהֵיהֶם (Devarim 7:25), the carved images of their gods, and in another pattern פֶסֶל וּמַסֵּכָה (Devarim 27:15), a carved and a molten image.

The term falls for the most part on the hewing of stones, and likewise on wood: הַנֹּֽשְׂאִים אֶת־עֵץ פִּסְלָם (Yeshayahu 45:20), who carry the wood of their carved image, and וּשְׁאֵרִיתוֹ לְאֵל עָשָׂה לְפִסְלוֹ (Yeshayahu 44:17), and the rest of it he made into a god, into his carved image. וְהוּא עָבַר אֶת־ הַפְּסִילִים (Shoftim 3:26), and he passed the pesilim, is a place where they used to hew stones.

חרת.sense: Engraved: חָרוּת on the luchos has the sense of חקוק, cut in, as he explained חֲרוּשָׁה, engraved on the tablet of their heart.

more.t: חָרוּת עַל־הַלֻּחֹת (Shemos 32:16), engraved upon the tablets, has the sense of חקוק, cut in, as Radak explained חֲרוּשָׁה עַל־לוּחַ לִבָּם (Yirmiyahu 17:1), engraved upon the tablet of their heart.

חרט.sense: חֶרֶט, a scribes' pen, in both of its pesukim, though some take one of them as a mould; and חֲרִטִים, purses.

more.t: וַיָּצַר אֹתוֹ בַּחֶרֶט (Shemos 32:4), he formed it with a stylus, and וּכְתֹב עָלָיו בְּחֶרֶט אֱנוֹשׁ (Yeshayahu 8:1), write upon it with a man's stylus. It is a scribes' pen. Some explain the first as done with a mould.

For בְּחֶרֶט אֱנוֹשׁ, with a man's stylus, Targum Yonasan renders כְּתַב מְפָרַשׁ, plain script, that any man can read. Radak holds the correct reading to be that it says a man's stylus to show that the navi was to do the deed in fact, and not think this writing he was commanded to write would be in the vision of prophecy alone, as most of the acts shown to the nevi'im are: עָרוֹם וְיָחֵֽף (Yeshayahu 20:2), naked and barefoot, commanded to Yeshayahu; אֵשֶׁת זְנוּנִים (Hoshea 1:2), a wife of harlotry, to Hoshea; the shaving of head and beard to Yechezkel (Yechezkel 5:1); and the like, for all these acts were only in the vision of prophecy.

בִּשְׁנֵי חֲרִטִים (Melachim II 5:23) is in two purses, and so וְהַמִּטְפָּחוֹת וְהָֽחֲרִיטִֽים (Yeshayahu 3:22), the cloaks and the purses. So too a purse is called in Arabic כרט"ה, the ches standing in for the Arabic kaf, as it does in many places.

רשׁם.sense: הָֽרָשׁוּם, what is marked down in writing: a word from Aramaic, of the sense of רושם, a mark, which is like a sign and a token.

more.t: אֶת־ הָֽרָשׁוּם בִּכְתָב אֱמֶת (Daniel 10:21), what is marked down in the writing of truth, is from the Aramaic tongue, as כְתָבָא דִּי רְשִׁים (Daniel 5:25), the writing that was inscribed; and the word is of the sense of רושם, a mark, which is like the sense of a sign and a token.

רחב.sense: To be broad, and to widen or give room. רֹחַב is breadth, רְחוֹב an open square, and מֶרְחָב open ground; a heart grown broad is glad; Shlomo's, wide in understanding.

more.h: The verb, and a heart made broad
more.t: רָחַב פִּי עַל־אוֹיְבַי (Shmuel I 2:1), my mouth is opened wide over my enemies. On וּפָחַד וְרָחַב לְבָבֵךְ (Yeshayahu 60:5), your heart shall fear and grow broad, Radak explains that they will fear the honoured Name when they see the abundance of good, as at Hoshea 3:5, where they come trembling to Hashem and to His goodness; and broad after the troubles they were in at first, for now the heart will be broad and glad.

וְרֹחַב לֵב כַּחוֹל (Melachim I 5:9), breadth of heart like the sand, means that in everything needing understanding he had a broad heart. Radak argues that כַּחוֹל, like the sand, does not describe the breadth of heart itself, since what describes breadth is a measure and not a number, as in וּרְחָבָה מִנִּי־יָֽם (Iyov 11:9), broader than the sea. Rather the sand describes all the things that need understanding, which are as the sand on the seashore, and Shlomo had breadth of heart for them all. So too לִתְבוּנָתוֹ אֵין מִסְפָּֽר (Tehillim 147:5), of His understanding there is no number, means that the things He understands are without number, since what describes understanding itself is searching, as in אֵין חֵקֶר לִתְבוּנָתֽוֹ (Yeshayahu 40:28), His understanding is past searching.

וְחָמֵשׁ אַמּוֹת רֹחַב (Shemos 27:1), five amos broad; לְאָרְכָּהּ וּלְרָחְבָּהּ (Bereishis 13:17), to its length and to its breadth. וְאֶתְהַלְּכָה בָרְחָבָה (Tehillim 119:45), I shall walk in a wide place, is a name for the broad ground; כִּי בָֽרְחוֹב נָלִֽין (Bereishis 19:2), we shall spend the night in the square; the plural, in the feminine form, בְּתוֹךְ רְחֹבוֹת אֵֽרָצֵֽחַ (Mishlei 22:13), I shall be slain in the streets; and וַיּוֹצִיאֵנִי לַמֶּרְחָב (Tehillim 18:20), He brought me out to open ground.

more.h: Broad of hands, broad of soul
more.t: וּרְחַב יָדָיִם (Tehillim 104:25), broad of hands; רְחַב ־נֶפֶשׁ יְגָרֶה מָדוֹן (Mishlei 28:25), the broad of soul stirs up strife; for the feminine רְחָבָה מִצְוָתְךָ מְאֹֽד (Tehillim 119:96), Your mitzvah is exceedingly broad, and וְהָאָרֶץ רַֽחֲבַת יָדַיִם (Divrei HaYamim I 4:40), the land was broad of hands.

הִרְחִיבָה שְּׁאוֹל נַפְשָׁהּ (Yeshayahu 5:14), she'ol has widened her appetite; בַּצָּר הִרְחַבְתָּ לִּי (Tehillim 4:2), in straits You gave me room; הַרְחֶב ־פִּיךָ וַֽאֲמַלְאֵֽהוּ (Tehillim 81:11), open your mouth wide and I shall fill it.

צָרוֹת לְבָבִי הִרְחִיבוּ (Tehillim 25:17), the troubles of my heart have widened, is also a verb that takes an object: the troubles of my heart have widened their place and border within my heart by their number, pressing on my heart and widening their place and border in it. Radak notes that the pasuk speaks with elegance here, joining two words in one matter, the one being the opposite of the other.

נתב.sense: Nasiv and nesivah, a path; its sense is that of derech, a way.

more.t: יְפַלֵּס נָתִיב לְאַפּוֹ (Tehillim 78:50), He levelled a path for His anger; נָתִיב לֹֽא־יְדָעוֹ עָיִט (Iyov 28:7), a path the bird of prey has not known; הַדְרִיכֵנִי בִּנְתִיב מִצְוֹתֶיךָ (Tehillim 119:35), lead me in the path of Your mitzvos.

וְדֶרֶךְ נְתִיבָה אַל־מָֽוֶת (Mishlei 12:28), and the way of her path is no death, where the heh is weak though it should have carried a mappik. With the feminine heh: וּבְמַיִם עַזִּים נְתִיבָֽה (Yeshayahu 43:16), a path in mighty waters, and מְנַע רַגְלְךָ מִנְּתִֽיבָתָֽם (Mishlei 1:15), keep your foot from their path. The plural is בִּנְתִיבוֹת לֹא־יָדְעוּ אַדְרִיכֵם (Yeshayahu 42:16), in paths they have not known I shall lead them. Its sense is as a way.

סלל.sense: Raising and lifting high, all one sense on his view: lifting stones off a road, so the road is a מְסִלָּה; the siege work, סֹלְלָה; extolling. Another sense: a thorn.

more.t: Rabbi Yonah set down under this root several different senses: one for סֹלּוּ סֹלּוּ הַֽמְסִלָּה (Yeshayahu 62:10), clear, clear the highway; another for סֹלּוּ לָרֹכֵב בָּֽעֲרָבוֹת (Tehillim 68:5), extol Him who rides in the plains, and עֽוֹדְךָ מִסְתּוֹלֵל (Shemos 9:17), you still exalt yourself; and another for the mesillos of the house of Hashem (Divrei HaYamim II 9:11). Radak holds that they are all one sense, that of raising and lifting high.

more.h: Lifting the stones off a road
more.t: On his own reading, סֹלּוּ סֹלּוּ הַֽמְסִלָּה is lift the stones and the stumbling blocks out of the way; and because it is usual to clear the stones and lift the obstacles from a road, the road itself came to be called מְסִלָּה. So דֶּרֶךְ לֹא סְלוּלָֽה (Yirmiyahu 18:15), a way not cleared, is one whose obstacles have not been lifted from it.

more.h: His father: a road built up
more.t: Radak's father explains מְסִלָּה as a road raised with stones laid into it, and brings סַקְּלוּ מֵאֶבֶן (Yeshayahu 62:10) with it, the sense being that they built the road of strong stones. So too it says וּמְסִלֹּתַי יְרֻמֽוּן (Yeshayahu 49:11), and My highways shall be raised, and in the same way סֹלּוּ סֹלּוּ is that they should raise the highway.

The timber on which stones are lifted and thrown into a city is called סֹלְלָה: כִּרְתוּ עֵצָה וְשִׁפְכוּ עַל־יְרֽוּשָׁלַם סֹֽלְלָה (Yirmiyahu 6:6), cut down her trees and pour out a mound against Yerushalayim, and הַסֹּֽלְלוֹת בָּאוּ הָעִיר לְלָכְדָהּ (Yirmiyahu 32:24), the mounds have reached the city to take it. Yonasan renders וְצָבְרִין מִלֵיתָא, and they heap up a mound, מליתא being a heap of earth in the words of Chazal (Bava Basra 54a), and every סֹלְלָה he renders so. At הַנְּתֻצִים אֶל־הַסֹּֽלְלוֹת (Yirmiyahu 33:4), the houses torn down for the mounds, he renders that they tear them down and heap up mounds to strengthen the wall against those who kill with the sword; that is, the townsmen would pull down the houses and make heaps of the stones against the wall from within to strengthen it. Radak says Yonasan's explanation is correct. Of the same matter is וַיִּצְבֹּר עָפָר וַיִּלְכְּדָֽהּ (Chavakuk 1:10), he heaped up earth and took it.

סֹלּוּ לָרֹכֵב בָּֽעֲרָבוֹת, extol Him who rides in the plains, is exalt Him and magnify Him, and so מְסִלּוֹת בִּלְבָבָֽם (Tehillim 84:6), exaltations in their heart. So too the four-letter word with its first root letter doubled, סַלְסְלֶ֥הָ וּתְרֽוֹמְמֶ֑ךָּ (Mishlei 4:8), exalt her and she will raise you, and מִסְתּוֹלֵל בְּעַמִּי (Shemos 9:17), exalting yourself over My people, that is, lifting himself up over them and taking pride against them so as not to send them out.

more.h: The mesillos of the Beis Hamikdash
more.t: The mesillos of the house of Hashem (Divrei HaYamim II 9:11) can be read as ceilings, called so for their height, or as steps, called so because they are like a road that men tread always. But since Melachim has מסעד, a support, for the house of Hashem where this has מְסִלּוֹת, Radak explains מסילות in the sense of a support: the ceiling, as he said, being a support too, or else some other structure, like pillars, made for support and strength.
Another sense altogether is סִלּוֹן מַמְאִיר (Yechezkel 28:24), a pricking thorn, and כִּי סָֽרָבִים וְסַלּוֹנִים (Yechezkel 2:6), for briers and thorns, whose sense is like a thorn.

Radak says at the outset that וַיָּסֹלּוּ may be another sense, though Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Yonah brought it under this root, where וַיָּסֹלּוּ עָלַי דַּרְכָּם (Iyov 19:12) is they raised up their way against me, and וַיָּסֹלּוּ עָלַי אָרְחוֹת אֵידָֽם (Iyov 30:12), they raised up against me the paths of their ruin. Radak himself counts both pesukim as the simple verb of the thorn sense, and so wrote the sage Rabbi Avraham Ibn Ezra, Rabbi Yehudah ben Balaam, and Radak's father.

רכל.sense: A merchant, and רכלה, merchandise. רָכִיל is talebearing, a sense close to the first: the talebearer passes words along as the merchant passes goods.

more.t: בְּעִיר רֹֽכְלִים שָׂמֽוֹ (Yechezkel 17:4), he set it in a city of merchants, and בְּנֵי דְדָן רֹֽכְלַיִךְ (Yechezkel 27:15), the sons of Dedan your traders: these are the merchants. The noun for the merchandise is רכלה, as in בְּרֹב רְכֻלָּֽתְךָ (Yechezkel 28:16), in the abundance of your merchandise, and וּבָֽזְזוּ רְכֻלָּתֵךְ (Yechezkel 26:12), they plundered your merchandise. Another pattern of it is וַֽאֲרֻזִים בְּמַרְכֻלְתֵּֽךְ (Yechezkel 27:24), and cedars in your merchandise.

more.h: Targum Yonasan on Ashur and Kilmad
more.t: On אַשּׁוּר כִּלֽמַד רֹֽכַלְתֵּֽךְ (Yechezkel 27:23), Ashur and Kilmad your traders, Targum Yonasan has מְדִינַן אַתּוּר וּמָדַי אִינוּן תַּגָרֵיךְ, the provinces of Ashur and Madai, they are your merchants. Radak has already given all of these another explanation at the root לָמַד.

At times the word is said of the spice seller alone, one sort among the merchants: מִכֹּל אַבְקַת רוֹכֵֽל (Shir HaShirim 3:6), from all the powders of the spice seller, and הֶֽחֱזִיקוּ הַצֹּֽרְפִים וְהָרֹֽכְלִֽים (Nechemiah 3:32), the goldsmiths and the spice sellers made repairs. וַיָּלִינוּ הָרֹֽכְלִים וּמֹֽכְרֵי כָל־מִמְכָּר (Nechemiah 13:20), the merchants and the sellers of every ware lodged, may be of that kind too.

רָכִיל is a name for talebearing: לֹֽא־תֵלֵךְ רָכִיל (Vayikra 19:16), you shall not go about as a talebearer; הֹֽלְכֵי רָכִיל (Yirmiyahu 6:28), goers of talebearing; אַנְשֵׁי רָכִיל הָיוּ בָךְ (Yechezkel 22:9), men of talebearing were in you. The word is joined with going, since the talebearer goes about in his fellow's house, and what he heard in his house he goes and tells another.

more.h: Why the two senses are close
more.t: This sense too is close to the first, for the talebearer is like the רוכל, the merchant who has many kinds of goods in hand, and like the spice seller called רוכל, who has many kinds of spices, as it says מִכֹּל אַבְקַת רוֹכֵֽל, from all the powders of the spice seller. So the talebearer gathers words from this one and that one and tells them to this one and that one; or, as the trader moves goods along, buying from one and selling to another, so the talebearer moves words along, hearing from one and telling another.

כנע.sense: Lowering: to be humbled, and to bring another low. כְּנַעַן is also a trader, a merchant.

more.t: כִּֽי־ נִכְנַע אַחְאָב (Melachim I 21:29), that Achav humbled himself; וַיִּכָּנַע מִדְיָן לִפְנֵי בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (Shoftim 8:28), Midyan was subdued before Bnei Yisrael; כְּהִכָּנַע מְנַשֶּׁה אָבִיו (Divrei HaYamim II 33:23), as Menasheh his father humbled himself. Where the word acts on another it is to subdue: הוּא יַשְׁמִידֵם וְהוּא יַכְנִיעֵם לְפָנֶיךָ (Devarim 9:3), He will destroy them and He will subdue them before you; וַיַּכְנַע אֱלֹהִים בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא (Shoftim 4:23), Hashem subdued on that day; וַיַּכְנַע בֶּעָמָל לִבָּם (Tehillim 107:12), He brought their heart low with toil. All of them are the matter of lowering.

more.h: Gather your humbling from the land
more.t: אִסְפִּי מֵאֶרֶץ כִּנְעָתֵךְ (Yirmiyahu 10:17), gather your humbling from the land, which Radak explains as: gather in from the world the humbling you used to work on them, for you are destined to sit under siege. אִסְפִּי here is like אֱסֹף יָדֶֽךָ (Shmuel I 14:19), withdraw your hand.

כְּנַעַן בְּיָדוֹ מֹֽאזְנֵי מִרְמָה (Hoshea 12:8), a trader in whose hand are scales of deceit, and וַיְבִיאֵהוּ אֶל־אֶרֶץ כְּנַעַן בְּעִיר רֹֽכְלִים שָׂמֽוֹ (Yechezkel 17:4), he brought it to a land of trade, in a city of merchants he set it; the nun of the word is an added letter. So too וַֽחֲגוֹר נָֽתְנָה לַֽכְּנַֽעֲנִֽי (Mishlei 31:24), she gave a belt to the merchant, and in another form כִּנְעָנֶיהָ נִכְבַּדֵּי־אָֽרֶץ (Yeshayahu 23:8), her כנענים are the honoured of the earth, which he explains as סוחריה, her merchants.

אִסְפִּי מֵאֶרֶץ כִּנְעָתֵךְ can be read from this second sense, of trade, and so the Targum says: כְּנוּשִׁי מֵאַרְעָא סְחוֹרְתִּיךְ, gather your merchandise from the land. By the Targum's view so too וַיַּרְא־שָׁם יְהוּדָה בַּת־אִישׁ כְּנַֽעֲנִי (Bereishis 38:2), Yehudah saw there the daughter of a merchant, and יֶחֱצוּהוּ בֵּין כְּנַֽעֲנִֽים (Iyov 40:30), they will divide him among merchants.

כִּי נִדְמָה כָּל־עַם כְּנַעַן (Tzefaniah 1:11), for all the people of כנען are cut off, may be from this sense as well: the rich men who hold the trade, as the pasuk goes on, נכרתו כל נטילי כסף, all who are laden with silver are cut off. And so וְלֹֽא־יִהְיֶה כְנַֽעֲנִי עוֹד (Zecharyah 14:21), there will be no merchant any more: so many will dedicate vessels to the Beis Hamikdash that they will have no need of a merchant to sell to them.

His father writes that the כנעני there is a Canaanite in fact, from the nation of Canaan. Since the hewers of wood and drawers of water were Canaanites, the Chivim whom Yehoshua made hewers of wood and drawers of water for the Beis Hamikdash, the pasuk means that they will no longer be the hewers and the drawers, for men from among the great of the nations will come to the service of the Beis Hamikdash, as it says וְגַם־מֵהֶם אֶקַּח לַכֹּֽהֲנִים לַֽלְוִיִּם (Yeshayahu 66:21), and from them too I will take for kohanim and leviim.

רצח.sense: To murder, and to be murdered, with רֶצַח, murder. Over תְּרָצְּחוּ Ben Naftali and Ben Asher differ: you are all murderers, or may you all be murdered.

more.t: וְרָצַח גֹּאֵל הַדָּם אֶת־ הָרֹצֵחַ (Bamidbar 35:27), the redeemer of the blood kills the murderer; וּרְצָחוֹ נֶפֶשׁ (Devarim 22:26), and he murders him, a life; הֲרָצַחְתָּ וְגַם־יָֽרָשְׁתָּ (Melachim I 21:19), have you murdered and also taken possession; לֹא תִרְצַח (Shemos 20:13), you shall not murder; הֲגָנֹב רָצֹחַ (Yirmiyahu 7:9), stealing, murdering.
לִפְתֹּחַ פֶּה בְּרֶצַח (Yechezkel 21:27), to open the mouth with murder, and בְּרֶצַח בְּֽעַצְמוֹתַי (Tehillim 42:11), with murder in my bones, both pointed with a segol.

הָאִשָּׁה הַנִּרְצָחָה (Shoftim 20:4), the murdered woman, and בְּתוֹךְ רְחֹבוֹת אֵֽרָצֵֽחַ (Mishlei 22:13), I shall be murdered in the midst of the streets. The heavy form gives דֶּרֶךְ יְרַצְּחוּ שֶׁכְמָה (Hoshea 6:9), they murder on the way to Shechem; בֶּן־ הַֽמְרַצֵּחַ הַזֶּה (Melachim II 6:32), this son of the murderer; וְעַתָּה מְרַצְּחִֽים (Yeshayahu 1:21), and now murderers.

The two of them divided over תְּרָצְּחוּ כֻלְּכֶם (Tehillim 62:4). Ben Naftali reads it with a patach under the resh, so that עַד־אָנָה תְּהֽוֹתְתוּ עַל־אִישׁ, how long will you set upon a man, means that you devise ruin against men, and you are all murderers. Ben Asher reads it with a kamatz under the resh, תְּרָצְּחוּ, which makes the word a passive of the heavy form, and then the pasuk is put as a prayer: may you all be murdered, and be always כְּקִיר נָטוּי, a leaning wall, a pushed fence that is close to falling, so that you stand in fear continually.

הרג.sense: To kill and slay; the nouns הֲרֵגָה and הֶרֶג are killing and slaughter.

more.t: כִּי הָרַג שָׁאוּל (Shmuel I 22:21), for Shaul killed; יַֽהֲרֹג בַּבָּרָד גַּפְנָם (Tehillim 78:47), He killed their vines with hail; הִרְגוּ אִישׁ אֲנָשָׁיו (Bamidbar 25:5), let each man kill his men; הָרֹג בָּקָר וְשָׁחֹט צֹאן (Yeshayahu 22:13), slaying cattle and slaughtering sheep; וְיוֹאָב וַֽאֲבִישַׁי אָחִיו הָֽרְגוּ לְאַבְנֵר (Shmuel II 3:30), Yoav and Avishai his brother killed Avner. The slain are הֲרֻגֵי מָוֶת (Yirmiyahu 18:21), slain of death, and בַּֽהֲרוּגִים הָאֵלֶּה (Yechezkel 37:9), these slain ones.

עֵת לַֽהֲרוֹג וְעֵת לִרְפּוֹא (Koheles 3:3), a time to kill and a time to heal. Although healing is not the opposite of killing, the pasuk says healing because the reviving of the dead is not a time that runs by the way of the world as the other times do, even though it comes by way of a miracle and is destined to be. Some explain לַֽהֲרוֹג as like לִמְחוֹץ, to smite.

גֵּיא הַֽהֲרֵגָה (Yirmiyahu 7:32), the valley of the killing, and לְיוֹם הֲרֵגָֽה (Yirmiyahu 12:3), for a day of slaughter. Without the feminine hei: בְּיוֹם הֶרֶג רָב (Yeshayahu 30:25), on a day of great slaughter, pointed with segols, and מַכַּת־חֶרֶב וְהֶרֶג וְאַבְדָן (Esther 9:5), a blow of the sword and killing and destruction.

אִם־ כְּהֶרֶג הֲרֻגָיו הֹרָֽג (Yeshayahu 27:7), was he slain as his slain were slain, and כִּֽי־עָלֶיךָ הֹרַגְנוּ כָל־הַיּוֹם (Tehillim 44:23), for Your sake we are killed all the day. Another passive form is בַּחֶרֶב תֵּֽהָרַגְנָה (Yechezkel 26:6), they shall be killed by the sword, and בֵּהָרֵג הֶרֶג בְּתוֹכֵךְ (Yechezkel 26:15), when slaughter is done in your midst, which stands in the measure of בֵּֽעָטֵף עוֹלֵל וְיוֹנֵק (Eichah 2:11), when infant and suckling faint, though by rule the two would be בְּהֵהָרֵג and בְּהֵעָטֵף.

קטל.sense: Killing, the sense of the verb and of its noun alike.

more.t: אִם־תִּקְטֹל אֱלוֹהַּ רָשָׁע (Tehillim 139:19), if You would slay the wicked, O Eloka, and הֵן יִקְטְלֵנִי (Iyov 13:15), though He slay me. The noun is in מֵהַר עֵשָׂו מִקָּֽטֶל (Ovadiah 1:9), from the mount of Esav, by killing, whose kamatz stands because of the pause. Their sense is killing.

רסן.sense: The bridle, set in a beast's mouth to lead it as the rider wishes; to send the bridle away before a man is to have no fear or shame of him.

more.t: וְרֶסֶן מַתְעֶה (Yeshayahu 30:28), a bridle that leads astray, and וְרֶסֶן מִפָּנַי שִׁלֵּֽחוּ (Iyov 30:11), they have cast off the bridle before me, pointed with segols.

Radak explains וְרֶסֶן מִפָּנַי שִׁלֵּֽחוּ to mean that they had no fear and no shame before the speaker, as though until then he had kept their mouths shut with a bridle, as is done to beasts, as the pasuk says בְּמֶתֶג וָרֶסֶן עֶדְיוֹ לִבְלוֹם (Tehillim 32:9), with bit and bridle, his trappings, to hold him in, the bridle being set in the mouths of beasts to lead them as the rider wishes; and now they have sent the bridle away from before him, meaning that they do not fear him.
בְּכֶפֶל רִסְנוֹ מִי יָבֽוֹא (Iyov 41:5), who can come within his double bridle, is said by way of likeness.

מתג.sense: The מֶתֶג: the iron goad that pricks a donkey, and the long iron put in a beast's mouth to lead it, all one sense, he says. Also Meseg HaAmah, taken from the Pelishtim.

more.t: בְּמֶתֶג וָרֶסֶן עֶדְיוֹ לִבְלוֹם (Tehillim 32:9), with bit and bridle to curb his trappings; מֶתֶג לַֽחֲמוֹר (Mishlei 26:3), a goad for the donkey, pointed with six dots; וּמִתְגִּי בִּשְׂפָתֶיךָ (Yeshayahu 37:29), my bit in your lips: all three are one sense. מֶתֶג לַֽחֲמוֹר is the iron goad fixed in the end of a stick, with which the donkey is pricked to hurry him. In the other two it is the long iron put in the beast's mouth to lead it, called in the vernacular פְּרֵי"ן, and it is like the bridle except that it is not made in its fashion.

וַיִּקַּח דָּוִד אֶת־ מֶתֶג הָֽאַמָּה מִיַּד פְּלִשְׁתִּֽים (Shmuel II 8:1), David took Meseg HaAmah from the hand of the Pelishtim, which Targum Yonasan renders תִּקוּן אַמְתָא, the setting in order of the amah. In Divrei HaYamim, in its place, the pasuk runs וַיִּקַּח אֶת־גַּת וּבְנֹתֶיהָ מִיַּד פְּלִשְׁתִּֽים (Divrei HaYamim I 18:1), he took Gat and her daughter towns from the hand of the Pelishtim; Radak offers that Meseg HaAmah may be a name covering Gat and her daughter towns together.

זמם.sense: To think, and the nouns are thought; in another sense, filth, abomination and evil deed. Some say it is all one sense, thought for good or for evil.

more.t: אֲשֶׁר זָמָם (Eichah 2:17), what He had thought, and כַּֽאֲשֶׁר זָמַם לַֽעֲשׂוֹת לְאָחִיו (Devarim 19:19), as he thought to do to his brother. עַל כִּֽי־דִבַּרְתִּי זַמֹּתִי (Yirmiyahu 4:28), because I have spoken, I have thought it, is accented on the syllable before the last, while זַמֹּתִי בַּל־יַֽעֲבָר־פִּֽי (Tehillim 17:3), my thought shall not pass my mouth, is accented on the last.

זְמָמוֹ אַל־תָּפֵק (Tehillim 140:9), do not let his thought come about; the plural, זִמֹּתַי נִתְּקוּ (Iyov 17:11), my thoughts are torn away; and with an added mem, מְזִמָּה תִּשְׁמֹר עָלֶיךָ, thought shall guard over you. All of these and their like are the matter of thinking.

זִמַּת אִוֶּלֶת חַטָּאת (Mishlei 24:9), the thought of folly is sin: whoever thinks upon matters of folly, it brings him to sin. וְתֽוֹעֲבַת לְאָדָם לֵֽץ (Mishlei 24:9), and the scorner is an abomination to man: one who thinks upon the words of the scorner, who is no fool but mocks people and whose dealings are evil, and who runs after him, is brought to be an abomination to man, so that people loathe him.

more.h: Not setting your heart to it
more.t: Where the pasuk says you did not do אֶת־ הַזִּמָּה עַל כָּל־תּֽוֹעֲבֹתָֽיִךְ (Yechezkel 16:43), the thought upon all your abominations, the sense is: you did not set your heart to it and did not think what you had done, upon all your abominations.

In another sense: כִּי זִמָּה עָשֽׂוּ (Hoshea 6:9), for they have done foulness, and זִמָּה הִֽוא (Vayikra 18:17), it is foulness. The plural is הוּא זִמּוֹת יָעָץ (Yeshayahu 32:7), he counsels foul things, and with an added mem, אֲשֶׁר יֹאמְרֻךָ לִמְזִמָּה (Tehillim 139:20), who speak of You for foulness, and עֲשׂוֹתָהּ הַֽמְזִמָּתָה הָֽרַבִּים (Yirmiyahu 11:15), her working foulness with the many. Their sense is filth and abomination and evil deed.

more.h: Some say it is all one sense
more.t: Some say that they are all one sense, since every זמה is a thought, whether for good or for evil, and each is explained according to its place.

נוא.sense: Breaking words and thoughts, and making them void.

more.t: וְאִם־הֵנִיא אָבִיהָ אֹתָהּ (Bamidbar 30:6), and if her father voids her words; וְלָמָּה תְנִואוּן (Bamidbar 32:7), and why would you break the purpose in the heart of Bnei Yisrael; שֶׁמֶן רֹאשׁ אַל־יָנִי רֹאשִׁי (Tehillim 141:5), oil for the head, let my head not void it, where the word is written without an alef.

וִֽידַעְתֶּם אֶת־תְּנֽוּאָתִֽי (Bamidbar 14:34), and you shall know My voiding, and תְּנוּאוֹת עָלַי יִמְצָא (Iyov 33:10), He finds breakings-off against me. Their sense is the breaking of words and thoughts, and making them void.

פרר.sense: His entry under these letters is only פָּרוּר, the pot in which food is cooked.

more.t: וּבִשְּׁלוּ בַּפָּרוּר (Bamidbar 11:8), and they cooked it in the pot, and אוֹ בַפָּרוּר (Shmuel I 2:14), or in the pot: it is the cauldron in which one cooks. Some explain כָּל־פָּנִים קִבְּצוּ פָארֽוּר (Yoel 2:6) from this word, which is to say blackness: all faces have gathered blackness. Radak has explained that word at the root פָּאַר.

בטל.sense: Of the grinders in Koheles 12:3, with a one-word gloss printed ושבחו, and they praised, that does not fit the pasuk; Chazal use the word a great deal.

more.t: וּבָטְלוּ הַטֹּֽחֲנוֹת (Koheles 12:3), and the grinders cease. His whole gloss is one word, printed ושבחו, and they praised, which does not answer to the pasuk and reads as a slip of the press. Chazal used this word a great deal, the light form where it stands of itself and the doubled form where it acts on something else.

אות.sense: A sign, which he explains as a mark, סימן; he writes of it further at the root יפת.

more.t: וְנָתַן אֵלֶיךָ אוֹת אוֹ מוֹפֵֽת (Devarim 13:2), and he gives you a sign or a wonder; וּבָא הָאוֹת וְהַמּוֹפֵת (Devarim 13:3), and the sign and the wonder come about; זֹאת אוֹת ־הַבְּרִית (Bereishis 9:12), this is the sign of the covenant; וְהָיָה הַדָּם לָכֶם לְאֹת (Shemos 12:13), the blood shall be a sign for you; אִישׁ עַל־דִּגְלוֹ בְאֹתֹת (Bamidbar 2:2), each man by his banner with signs. Its explanation is a mark, and Radak writes further on it under the root יפת.

יפת.sense: מוֹפֵת, whose sense is like אוֹת, a sign; but a מוֹפֵת is shown so that one believe in something like it yet to come, where an אוֹת can be a bare mark.

more.h: Like a sign, and how it differs
more.t: תְּנוּ לָכֶם מוֹפֵת (Shemos 7:9), give a sign for yourselves; אֲנִי מוֹפֶתְכֶם (Yechezkel 12:11), I am your sign; אֶת־כָּל־הַמֹּפְתִים הָאֵלֶּה (Shemos 11:10), all these signs. Its sense is like אוֹת, a sign, except that אוֹת falls in places where מוֹפֵת does not: אִישׁ עַל־דִּגְלוֹ בְאֹתֹת (Bamidbar 2:2), each man by his banner, with the signs, and וְהָיְתָה לְאוֹת בְּרִית (Bereishis 9:13), and it shall be for a sign of a covenant. In those places and their like מוֹפֵת does not fall, for a מוֹפֵת is a thing shown so that one may believe through it in something of its kind that is yet to be shown; אוֹת comes in that sense too, except that at times it comes for a mark alone, and מוֹפֵת does not.

פלא.sense: To be wondrous, or too wondrous for someone, with פֶּלֶא, a wonder. Another sense, close to it, is setting apart, as with a vow; in that sense the root is פָּלָה.

more.t: כִּי יִפָּלֵא מִמְּךָ דָבָר (Devarim 17:8), if a matter is too wondrous for you; לֹֽא־ נִפְלֵאת הִוא מִמְּךָ (Devarim 30:11), it is not too wondrous for you; נִפְלְאַתָה אַֽהֲבָֽתְךָ לִי (Shmuel II 1:26), your love to me was wondrous, carrying two feminine endings, like כִּי הֶחְבְּאַתָה (Yehoshua 6:17), for she hid; נִפְלָאִים מַֽעֲשֶׂיךָ (Tehillim 139:14), Your works are wondrous; בִּגְדֹלוֹת וּבְנִפְלָאוֹת מִמֶּֽנִּי (Tehillim 131:1), in great things and in things too wondrous for me; שִׂיחוּ בְּכָל־ נִפְלְאוֹתָֽיו (Tehillim 105:2), speak of all His wonders. It is also written like the roots that end in heh: נוֹרָאוֹת נִפְלֵיתִי (Tehillim 139:14), I am made fearfully wondrous.

עֹשֵׂה פֶֽלֶא (Shemos 15:11), doer of wonder, pointed with segols; וַתֵּרֶד פְּלָאִים (Eichah 1:9), she came down wondrously. The feminine plural is פְּלָאוֹת עֵדְוֹתֶיךָ (Tehillim 119:129), Your testimonies are wonders, and קֵץ הַפְּלָאֽוֹת (Daniel 12:6), the end of the wonders; with an added mem, מִפְלְאוֹת תְּמִים דֵּעִֽים (Iyov 37:16), the wonders of Him who is perfect in knowledge. The adjective is פְּלִאָֽיה (Tehillim 139:6), wondrous, said of דַעַת מִמֶּנִּי, knowledge too wondrous for me, formed as שְֹרִידָה is from שָֹרִיד and פְּלִיטָה from פָּלִיט. The adjective also takes the form פֶּלֶא, with segols: פֶּלֶא יוֹעֵץ (Yeshayahu 9:5), a wondrous counsellor.

הִפְלִיא עֵצָה (Yeshayahu 28:29), He made counsel wondrous; כִּֽי־ הִפְלִיא חַסְדּוֹ לִי (Tehillim 31:22), for He made His kindness wondrous to me; אֲשֶׁר־עָשָׂה עִמָּכֶם לְהַפְלִיא (Yoel 2:26), who dealt wondrously with you; הַפְלֵא וָפֶלֶא (Yeshayahu 29:14), wonder upon wonder; and וְתָשֹׁב תִּתְפַּלָּא ־בִֽי (Iyov 10:16), and again You show Yourself wondrous against me. The sense of wonder is well known.

From this sense, וְהוּא־ פֶֽלִאי (Shoftim 13:18), and it is wondrous, is an adjective for the wondrous name, as though to say: my name is wondrous and too lofty to be made known to you. So too with Yaakov Avinu, where the angel would not make his own name known to him and said לָמָּה זֶּה תִּשְׁאַל לִשְׁמִי (Bereishis 32:30), why is it that you ask my name. This was because the angels appeared to them in the likeness of men and did not reveal that they were angels, and so did not mention their names. So too פְּלֹנִי אַלְמֹנִי (Melachim II 6:8), so-and-so: a man whose name is hidden from the one who mentions him is called פלוני, and even where he is known to the one who mentions him, if he does not wish to call him by name he says פלוני of him. Chazal use it often in their language.

Another sense, close to this one: כִּי יַפְלִא לִנְדֹּר נֶדֶר נָזִיר (Bamidbar 6:2), when a man sets himself apart to vow a nazir's vow, and לְפַלֵּא ־נֶדֶר (Bamidbar 15:3), to set apart a vow. Their sense is separating, and in this sense the root is פָּלָה, with a heh.

פתע.sense: Suddenly: his gloss is פתאום בלא כוונה, suddenly, without intent.

more.t: פֶּתַע יִשָּׁבֵר (Mishlei 6:15), suddenly he will be broken, the pei pointed with a segol; בְּפֶתַע פִּתְאֹם (Bamidbar 6:9), in sudden suddenness; וְאִם־בְּפֶתַע בְּלֹא־אֵיבָה (Bamidbar 35:22), and if suddenly, without enmity. His gloss is: suddenly, without intent.

אגד.sense: Gathering things and tying them together; so too a band of one agreement, and in Amos His counsel, or in Radak's own view the elements, bound one upon another.

more.t: אֲגֻדַּת אֵזוֹב (Shemos 12:22), a bundle of hyssop, and הַתֵּר אֲגֻדּוֹת מוֹטָה (Yeshayahu 58:6), to loose the bands of the yoke: the sense of these and their like is the gathering of things and the tying of them together.
Chazal say (Parah 11:9) that the mitzvah of hyssop is שלשה קלחין, three stalks, ובהם שלשה גבעולין, with three stems in them.

So too וַיִּֽהְיוּ לַֽאֲגֻדָּה אֶחָת (Shmuel II 2:25), and they became one band, that is, one gathering and one agreement; and so וַֽאֲגֻדָּתוֹ עַל־אֶרֶץ יְסָדָהּ (Amos 9:6), and His band He founded upon the earth, that is, His counsel and His agreement.

In Radak's own view it is the three elements that are upon the earth that it calls an agudah, since they are one bundle, one upon the other, upon the earth; that is why it says וַֽאֲגֻדָּתוֹ עַל־אֶרֶץ יְסָדָהּ, and He founded His bundle upon the earth.

עוד.sense: Three matters: to plunder, and the spoil; to testify, a witness and his testimony; and continuance and the present time: while, still, yet, further, for ever.

more.t: חֶבְלֵי רְשָׁעִים עִוְּדֻנִי (Tehillim 119:61), the bands of the wicked plundered me: he explains עודוני as שללוני ובזוני, they plundered me and despoiled me. The noun is יֹאכַל עַד (Bereishis 49:27), he devours spoil, and אָז חֻלַּק עַד ־שָׁלָל מַרְבֶּה (Yeshayahu 33:23), then plunder and much spoil were divided, which he reads as עד ושלל, plunder and spoil, two nouns side by side as in שֶׁמֶשׁ יָרֵחַ (Chavakuk 3:11), sun, moon.

Of לְיוֹם קוּמִי לְעַד (Tzefaniah 3:8), for the day I rise up to the spoil, and the like, he says that although they were brought under the root עד, the right filing is this root, since we find the verb, עודונו, of plundering.

הַֽעִידֹתִי בָכֶם הַיּוֹם (Devarim 4:26), I have called witness against you this day, and הָעֵד הֵעִד בָּנוּ הָאִישׁ לֵאמֹר (Bereishis 43:3), the man solemnly warned us, saying. Some of them, this last among them, are close to warning, and are put in the language of testimony because one who warns a man warns before witnesses, so that he cannot deny it afterwards.

From this the Torah and the mitzvos are called תעודה and עדות, testimony, to Israel, who took His mitzvos upon themselves: לְתוֹרָה וְלִתְעוּדָה (Yeshayahu 8:20), to the Torah and to the testimony. Likewise אֲרוֹן הָֽעֵדֻת (Shemos 25:22), the ark of the testimony, the testimony being the luchos within it, which are testimony to Israel.

בְּעוֹד שְׁלֹשֶׁת יָמִים (Bereishis 40:19) he explains as at the end: at the end of three days from this time. כִּֽי־כָל־ עוֹד נִשְׁמָתִי בִי (Iyov 27:3) is for as long as the soul is in me; and עוֹלָם וָעֶד (Tehillim 104:5) is all the days the world endures.

more.h: Not yet, as it may be read
more.t: אֲשֶׁר לֹא זְכַרְתָּם עוֹד (Tehillim 88:6) can be read so, whom You have not yet remembered, and on that reading it is a sign that a time will come when the dead are remembered.

Rabbi Yehudah separates מָֽה־ אֲעִידֵךְ מָה אֲדַמֶּה־לָּךְ (Eichah 2:13), what shall I אֲעִידֵךְ, what shall I liken to you, from this sense. Radak says it may be read within it: what nation can I bring to testify to you, to show you that they were stricken as you were and that evil came on them like yours.

פנג.sense: Pannag, named with wheat and honey: some say it is a place; the Targum renders it kulya, a field herb in Chazal's usage; and Yosef ben Gurion says it is balsam.

more.t: בְּחִטֵּי מִנִּית וּפַנַּג וּדְבַשׁ (Yechezkel 27:17), with wheat of Minnis and pannag and honey. Some say pannag is the name of a place, and so is מִנִּית, Minnis.
The Targum gives וְקוֹלְיָא, and kulya, and kulya in the words of Chazal is a herb among the field greens that are eaten, as they said (Eruvin 28b), מערבין בקוליא, an eruv may be made with kulya.

Yosef ben Gurion said that pannag is balsam, and that it was found in Yericho. Yet the same pasuk says וצרי, and tzori, and the tzori is explained as the oil of afarsemon, which is what is called balsam.

צרה.sense: Tzori, balm, which he takes to be the נטף among the spices of the ketores; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel calls it sap that drips from the ketaf trees.

more.t: מְעַט צֳרִי (Bereishis 43:11), a little balm, הַצֳרִי אֵין בְּגִלְעָד (Yirmiyahu 8:22), is there no balm in Gilad, and עֲלִי גִלְעָד וּקְחִי צֳרִי (Yirmiyahu 46:11), go up to Gilad and take balm.

In וּדְבַשׁ וָשֶׁמֶן וָצֹרִי (Yechezkel 27:17), and honey and oil and balm, the vowel is a cholam; in the three above it is a chataf kamatz; and in וּצְרִי וָלֹט (Bereishis 37:25), balm and lot, it carries a sheva alone.
Radak identifies it with the נטף, literally a drop, that the pasuk names among the spices of the ketores.

So too in the words of Chazal (Kerisos 6a), Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says הצרי אינו אלא שרף הנוטף מעצי הקטף, tzori is nothing but the sap that drips from the ketaf trees, which are scored so that the tzori comes out of them. It is the one called balsamo in la'az.

נטף.sense: Flowing and melting: hands dripping myrrh, mountains dripping sweet wine; by borrowing, speech that drops; neck pendants; and נָטָף, a spice said to be tzori.

more.t: וְיָדַי נָֽטְפוּ ־מוֹר (Shir HaShirim 5:5), my hands dripped myrrh, and יִטְּפוּ הֶֽהָרִים עָסִיס (Yoel 4:18), the mountains shall drip sweet wine. The noun is נִטְפֵי ־מָיִם (Iyov 36:27), drops of water. The sense of the whole is flowing and melting.

By way of borrowing, of speech: וְעָלֵימוֹ תִּטֹּף מִלָּתִֽי (Iyov 29:22), and my word dropped upon them, like תִּזַּל כַּטַּל אִמְרָתִי (Devarim 32:2), my speech shall distil as the dew. The heavy form is of speech too: אַטִּף לְךָ לַיַּיִן וְלַשֵּׁכָר (Michah 2:11), I will preach to you of wine and strong drink. אַל־ תַּטִּפוּ יַטִּיפוּן (Michah 2:6), do not preach, they preach, means that Yisrael were preaching and saying to the true prophets, do not preach.

הַנְּטִיפוֹת וְהַשֵּׁירוֹת (Yeshayahu 3:19), the pendants and the bracelets, and וְהַנְּטִפוֹת (Shoftim 8:26), and the pendants, are הענקים, neck ornaments; and they say that clear bdolach is called by this name in Arabic.

נָטָף וּשְׁחֵלֶת (Shemos 30:34), nataf and shecheles: they said the nataf is tzori, and it is called so because it drips from the ketaf trees, as Chazal say, tzori is nothing but the sap that drips from the ketaf trees (Kerisos 6a); balsamo in the vernacular. Some explain הַנְּטִיפוֹת וְהַשֵּׁירוֹת, the netifos and the bracelets, from this, the netifos being a vessel in which the tzori is put.

בשֹם.sense: Spice. His entry gives no gloss, only the word's three vowel patterns and a plural formed from one of them.

more.t: וּקְנֵה־ בֹשֶׂם (Shemos 30:23), and cane of spice, and לֹא־בָא כַבֹּשֶׂם הַהוּא (Melachim I 10:10), there came none like that spice; a second pattern in וְקִנְּמָן־ בֶּשֶׂם מַֽחֲצִיתוֹ (Shemos 30:23), and cinnamon of spice, half as much; a third in אָרִיתִי מוֹרִי עִם־ בְּשָׂמִי (Shir HaShirim 5:1), I have gathered my myrrh with my spice.
The plural is בְּשָׂמִים רֹאשׁ (Shemos 30:23), chief spices, and it is formed from one of the three patterns. The account of their grammar is found in the section on the grammar of nouns.

להב.sense: A flame. The sword too is called lahav, since it looks like a flame as it blazes; and the לַהֶבֶת of a spear is its iron.

more.t: וַיְהִי בַעֲלוֹת הַלַּהַב (Shoftim 13:20), as the flame went up, and its plural in פְּנֵי לְהָבִים פְּנֵיהֶֽם (Yeshayahu 13:8), their faces are faces of flames; in the feminine לֶֽהָבָה מִקִּרְיַת סִיחֹן (Bamidbar 21:28), a flame from the city of Sichon, and in another form לַהֶבֶת שַׁלְהֶבֶת (Yechezkel 21:3), a blazing flame; its plural in אֵשׁ לֶהָבוֹת בְּאַרְצָֽם (Tehillim 105:32), fire of flames in their land, and in the construct לַֽהֲבוֹת אֵֽשׁ (Tehillim 29:7), flames of fire.

Since the sword resembles a flame as it blazes, it too is called a lahav: וַיָּבֹא גַם־הַנִּצָּב אַחַר הַלַּהַב (Shoftim 3:22), the haft too went in after the blade. So the pasuk likens it to flame and to lightning together, וְלַהַב חֶרֶב וּבְרַק חֲנִית (Nachum 3:3), the flame of the sword and the lightning of the spear; and in the feminine, וְלַהֶבֶת חֲנִיתוֹ (Shmuel I 17:7), the lahevet of his spear, is the iron that is in the spear.

אור.sense: Light, and to shine or give light; light also stands for abundant good. Other senses: to set ablaze, greens, rain, mangers; and אוּר may be a valley.

more.t: הַבֹּקֶר אוֹר (Bereishis 44:3), the morning was light, and וְלַיְלָה אוֹר בַּעֲדֵנִי (Tehillim 139:11), and night is light about me, are past verbs, while הוֹלֵךְ וָאוֹר (Mishlei 4:18) is a participle, which he glosses הולך ומאיר, going on and giving light. רְאוּ־נָא כִּי־ אֹרוּ עֵינַי (Shmuel I 14:29), see how my eyes have brightened, and קוּמִי אוֹרִי (Yeshayahu 60:1), arise and shine. Of making something else light: הֵאִירוּ בְרָקָיו תֵּבֵל (Tehillim 97:4), His lightnings lit up the world, and יָאֵר פָּנָיו אִתָּנוּ סֶֽלָה (Tehillim 67:2), may He make His face shine with us, selah.

The noun: בְּאֽוֹר ־פְּנֵי־מֶלֶךְ חַיִּים (Mishlei 16:15), in the light of a king's face is life; the plural לְעֹשֵׂה אוֹרִים גְּדֹלִים (Tehillim 136:7), who made the great lights; and with a mem set in front, כָּל־ מְאוֹרֵי אוֹר בַּשָּׁמַיִם (Yechezkel 32:8), all the bright lights of heaven.

Some of them stand for abundant good: אֽוֹר ־צַדִּיקִים יִשְׂמָח (Mishlei 13:9), the light of the righteous rejoices, and לַיְּהוּדִים הָֽיְתָה אוֹרָה (Esther 8:16), the Jews had light. Darkness in the same way stands for abundant trouble.

אֵי־זֶה הַדֶּרֶךְ יִשְׁכָּן־ אוֹר (Iyov 38:19), where is the way where light dwells: Rav Saadiah Gaon explained it of a place on earth that is light the whole year but for one day, and its opposite, a place all darkness but for one day, which is וחשׁך אי זה מקומו, and darkness, where is its place.

Some derive אֶת ־הָֽאוּרִים וְאֶת־הַתֻּמִּים (Vayikra 8:8), the Urim and the Tumim, from light. Radak writes that what they are has not become clear to us, since it seems from the pesukim that they are something other than the stones of the choshen. Rashi explained them as the writing of the Shem HaMeforash, placed within the folds of the choshen, by which it lit up its words and made its words whole; Radak closes that the truth is not known.

וְלֹֽא־ תָאִירוּ מִזְבְּחִי חִנָּם (Malachi 1:10), and you shall not light My altar for nothing, he glosses ולא תלהיבו, and you shall not set it ablaze. Likewise לְכוּ בְּאוּר אֶשְׁכֶם (Yeshayahu 50:11), walk in the flame of your fire, and נָשִׁים בָּאוֹת מְאִירוֹת אוֹתָהּ (Yeshayahu 27:11), women come and light it, which he reads of men weak as women who come and burn it.

more.h: Ur: fire, or a valley; a hole
more.t: אֲשֶׁר הֽוֹצֵאתִיךָ מֵאוּר כַּשְׂדִּים, who brought you out of Ur Kasdim, belongs with the fire on the reading Chazal gave it, a sense close to the first; or אוּר כַּשְׂדִּֽים may be the valley of the Kasdim, as עַל־כֵּן בָּֽאֻרִים כַּבְּדוּ (Yeshayahu 24:14 in his edition), therefore give honour in the valleys, where the word is glossed בעמקים, in the valleys. So too מְאוּרַת צִפְעוֹנִי (Yeshayahu 11:8) is חור צפעוני, the viper's hole.

לְלַקֵּט אֹרֹת (Melachim II 4:39), to gather orot, he glosses ירקות, greens, and the Targum renders יֵרוֹקָנִין, greens. In the words of Chazal (Yoma 18b), it was taught in Rabbi Meir's name that orot is gargir, and Rabbi Yochanan said it is called ארת, orot, because it lights up the eyes. One reading takes טַל אוֹרֹת טַלֶּךָ (Yeshayahu 26:19), the dew of orot is Your dew, in this sense, which is to say dew fit for greens; or else אוֹרֹת there is like the light of day.

כְּחֹם צַח עֲלֵי־ אוֹר (Yeshayahu 18:4), like clear heat upon rain, and יָפִיץ עֲנַן אוֹרֽוֹ (Iyov 37:11), He scatters the cloud of His rain: the sense of these is rain. In the words of Chazal (Bereishis Rabbah, end of parsha 26), Rabbi Yochanan said that every orah in Elihu's words is nothing but the coming down of rain; and some say rain is called or on account of the lesser luminary, since by its movements the rain comes at the Creator's command. With these stands הֵן־פָּרַשׂ עָלָיו אוֹרוֹ (Iyov 36:30), behold, He spread His rain over it; one explains אוֹרוֹ there as His sun, and so צַר וָאוֹר חָשַׁךְ בַּעֲרִיפֶיהָ (Yeshayahu 5:30) as the moon and the sun grown dark in its skies, and on that reading they are of the first sense.
וַֽעֲדָרִים לַֽאֲוֵרֽוֹת (Divrei HaYamim II 32:28), and flocks for the mangers: the אֲוֵרוֹת are the mangers, the letters turned about from אֻרְוֹת סוּסִים (Melachim I 5:6), mangers for horses.

שׁלהב.sense: A blaze, like לְהֶבֶת, a flame; and שַׁלְהֶבֶתְיָה, one word with the sense of two, a great blaze, since Scripture magnifies a thing by setting it beside the Name.

more.t: יֹנַקְתּוֹ תְּיַבֵּשׁ שַׁלְהָבֶת (Iyov 15:30), a blaze shall dry up his shoot, and לֹא־תִכְבֶּה לַהֶבֶת שַׁלְהֶבֶת (Yechezkel 21:3), the flame of the blaze shall not be quenched.

Likewise שַׁלְהֶבֶתְיָה (Shir HaShirim 8:6): though it is one word, its sense is two words, a great blaze. It is the way of Scripture, when it would magnify a thing, to set it in construct with the Name, may He be exalted, as with מַאְפֵּלְיָה (Yirmiyahu 2:31), a great darkness, and the like, of which he has written under the root אָפַל.

שלהבת, a blaze, is like לְהֶבֶת, a flame, and להבת is set in construct with שלהבת in the manner of אַדְמַת־עָפָר (Daniel 12:2), the ground of dust, and מִטִּיט הַיָּוֵן (Tehillim 40:3), from the mud of the mire.

The Targum renders פְּנֵי לְהָבִים פְּנֵיהֶם (Yeshayahu 13:8), their faces are faces of flame, as אַפֵּי שַׁלְהוֹבִין אַפֵּיהוֹן, faces of blazes are their faces, and בְּלַבַּת־אֵשׁ (Shemos 3:2), in a flame of fire, as בְּשַׁלְהוֹבִית אֶשָּׁתָא, in a blaze of fire.

לפד.sense: לַפִּיד, the burning wood, called so only once alight; Eishes Lapidos is the wife of Barak, and ברק, lightning, and לפיד, a torch, are close in sense.

more.t: כְּלַפִּיד יִבְעָר (Yeshayahu 62:1), it shall burn like a torch, and לַפִּיד בּוּז (Iyov 12:5), a torch of contempt: a lapid is the wood that is alight.
אֵשֶׁת לַפִּידוֹת (Shoftim 4:4), the wife of Lapidos, is אשת ברק, the wife of Barak, and Radak holds barak, lightning, and lapid, torch, close to one another in sense.

וַיַּבְעֶר־אֵשׁ בַּלַּפִּידִים (Shoftim 15:5), and he set fire to the torches, names them for their end, since before he set the fire in them they were not called torches, only wood. So too וְטַחֲנִי קָמַח (Yeshayahu 47:2), grind meal, and אָפִיתִי עַל־גֶּחָלָיו לֶחֶם (Yeshayahu 44:19), I baked bread on its coals.
אֶת־הַקּוֹלֹת וְאֶת־הַלַּפִּידִם (Shemos 20:15), the sounds and the torches, is said by way of likeness, as though they saw torches burning.

פרשֹ.sense: To spread out flat, as a cloud, the hands or a net is spread; close to it, to scatter far apart; and a further sense, which he explains at פרס.

more.t: פָּרַשׂ עָנָן לְמָסָךְ (Tehillim 105:39), He spread a cloud for a covering, וּפָרַשׂ כַּפָּיו אֶל־הַבַּיִת (Melachim I 8:38), he spreads his hands toward the House, and פָּרְשׂוּ רֶשֶׁת לְיַד מַעְגָּל (Tehillim 140:6), they spread a net beside the path: all of them are spreading flat. The noun is מִפְרְשֵׂי ־עָב (Iyov 36:29), the spreading of the clouds.

Close to it: וְהַנִּשְׁאָרִים לְכָל־רוּחַ יִפָּרֵשׂוּ (Yechezkel 17:21), the rest shall be scattered to every wind, and כִּי כְּאַרְבַּע רוּחוֹת הַשָּׁמַיִם פֵּרַשְׂתִּי אֶתְכֶם (Zecharyah 2:10), which he reads: as the four winds of heaven are far one from another, so will I set you far apart in scattering you.

Another sense is in וּפָֽרְשׂוּ כַּֽאֲשֶׁר בַּסִּיר (Michah 3:3), and they break them apart as in the pot, and פֹּרֵשׂ אֵין לָהֶֽם (Eichah 4:4), none breaks bread for them, and in פֵּֽרְשָׂה צִיּוֹן בְּיָדֶיהָ (Eichah 1:17), Tzion spreads out her hands, and תְּפָרֵשׂ כַּפֶּיהָ (Yirmiyahu 4:31), she spreads out her hands; Radak explains these at פרס. Some explain בְּפָרֵשׂ שַׁדַּי (Tehillim 68:15), when the Almighty spreads, which he lists above with the spreading, as belonging to this sense.

פרשׁ.sense: To make plain, and a full account; close to it, separated; another sense, a snake's strike, and from it the horseman, who pricks his horse on; and dung.

more.t: לִפְרשׁ לָהֶם (Vayikra 24:12), to make it plain to them, and לֹא פֹרַשׁ מַה־יֵּֽעָשֶׂה לֽוֹ (Bamidbar 15:34), it had not been made plain what was to be done with him: the sense throughout is explanation and clarification. The noun is וְאֵת פָּרָשַׁת הַכֶּסֶף (Esther 4:7), the full account of the money, and וּפָרָשַׁת גְּדֻלַּת מָרְדֳּכַי (Esther 10:2), the full account of Mordechai's greatness.
Close to it, נִפְרָשׁוֹת (Yechezkel 34:12), said of a flock, means נפרדות, ones that have been separated off.
Another sense: וּכְצִפְעֹנִי יַפְרִֽשׁ (Mishlei 23:32), it strikes like an adder, is the sense of striking, טריקה, in the words of Chazal (Avodah Zarah 27b), as in חויא טרקיא, a snake that strikes.

more.h: Why a rider is a parash
more.t: From that sense the horseman is called a parash, as in בְּרִכְבּוֹ וּבְפָֽרָשָֽׁיו (Shemos 14:17), with his chariot and his horsemen, since he pricks the horse with the boots on his feet to make it run. In פָּרָשׁ מַֽעֲלֶה (Nachum 3:3), a horseman raising, Radak reads the horseman as raising the flame of the sword and the lightning of the spear, the vav of וְלַהַב being an added one; or the phrase is short of a word, meaning raising a spear or a javelin or the like among weapons of war.

Some take the פָּרָשִׁים of סוּסִים וּפָֽרָשִׁים (Yechezkel 27:14) to be a kind of pedigreed horse called by that name. Radak holds there is no need for that: the word is as it sounds, horses and horsemen, and the sense is as it says, המה רכליך בנפש אדם, they traded with you in the souls of men.

Another sense: וְזֵרִיתִי פֶרֶשׁ עַל־פְּנֵיכֶם (Malachi 2:3), I will scatter dung upon your faces, and עַל־ פִּרְשָׁהּ יִשְׂרֹֽף (Bamidbar 19:5), its dung shall be burnt: it is the dung in the animal's belly.

באר.sense: To explain, as in explaining this Torah and explaining it well; and in another sense a well, one whose waters spring up.

more.t: בֵּאֵר אֶת־הַתּוֹרָה הַזֹּאת (Devarim 1:5), he explained this Torah, בַּאֵר הֵיטֵֽב (Devarim 27:8), explaining it well, and וּבָאֵר עַל־הַלֻּחוֹת (Chavakuk 2:2), and explain it upon the tablets. His gloss of the first two is פירש את התורה, פירש היטב, he explained the Torah, he explained well.

The other sense: בְּאֵר מַיִם חַיִּים (Shir HaShirim 4:15), a well of living water, חָפַרְתִּי אֶת־ הַבְּאֵר הַזֹּֽאת (Bereishis 21:30), I dug this well, and the plural וְכָל־ הַבְּאֵרֹת אֲשֶׁר חָֽפְרוּ (Bereishis 26:15), all the wells they had dug. Their sense is known: a well is one whose waters spring up.
In construct the plural sometimes keeps its vowels, בְּאֵרֹת הַמַּיִם (Bereishis 26:18), the wells of water, and sometimes changes them, בֶּֽאֱרֹת חֵמָר (Bereishis 14:10), wells of clay.

פשׁר.sense: Interpreting: פֵּשֶׁר דָּבָר is פתרון דבר, the interpretation of a matter, and the Targum uses the word for the interpretation of a dream.

more.t: וּמִי יוֹדֵעַ פֵּשֶׁר דָּבָר (Koheles 8:1), who knows the interpretation of a thing, pointed with a tzere, though there are seforim that point it with a segol. Its sense is פתרון דבר, the solving of a matter.

The Targum renders אִישׁ כְּפִתְרוֹן חֲלֹמוֹ (Bereishis 41:11), each man according to the interpretation of his dream, as גְּבַר כְּפִשְׁרַן חֶלְמֵהּ, each man according to the solving of his dream, which is this word.

פתר.sense: Interpreting a dream: of verb and noun alike he says the sense is the explaining and clarifying of the dream.

more.t: כַּֽאֲשֶׁר פָּֽתַר־לָנוּ (Bereishis 41:13), as he interpreted for us; וּפֹתֵר אֵין אֹתוֹ (Bereishis 41:15), and there is none to interpret it; תִּשְׁמַע חֲלוֹם לִפְתֹּר אֹתֽוֹ (Bereishis 41:15), you hear a dream to interpret it; אִישׁ כְּפִתְרוֹן חֲלֹמוֹ (Bereishis 41:11), each man according to the interpretation of his dream; הֲלוֹא לֵֽאלֹהִים פִּתְרֹנִים (Bereishis 40:8), do not interpretations belong to Hashem. The sense of them all is the explaining and clarifying of the dream.
The entry breaks off at ואשר הם בני ארבע אותיות, and those that are of four letters, and what he meant to say of them is not in it.

הבל.sense: A thing that is nothing at all; the verb, to become empty or to make others so; and in Chazal, the breath of the mouth, a thing soon gone.

more.t: הֶבֶל הֵמָּה (Yirmiyahu 10:15), they are nothing, and הֲבֵל הֲבָלִים (Koheles 1:2), emptiness of emptinesses: Radak glosses hevel as a thing that is nothing at all.
וַיֵּלְכוּ אַֽחֲרֵי הַהֶבֶל וַיֶּהְבָּלוּ (Yirmiyahu 2:5), they went after emptiness and became empty themselves, and מַהְבִּלִים הֵמָּה אֶתְכֶם (Yirmiyahu 23:16), they are making you empty.

So too Chazal call the vapour that leaves the mouth by this word, בהבל פיו (Shabbos 88b), with the breath of his mouth, and הבל תינוקות (Shabbos 119b), the breath of children, it being a thing that ceases and is soon gone.

שׁעל.sense: A fist, that is, a fistful; מִשְׁעוֹל, the vineyard path, so called because it is no wider than a man needs to walk in; and שׁוּעָל, the fox.

more.h: A fistful of water or of dust
more.t: מִי מָדַד בְּשָׁעֳלוֹ מַיִם (Yeshayahu 40:12), who measured the waters by his fistful. In another pattern לִשְׁעָלִים לְכָל הָעָם (Melachim I 20:10), fistfuls for all the people, and בְּשַׁעֲלֵי שְׂעֹרִים (Yechezkel 13:19), for fistfuls of barley. Their sense is like a fist, that is, a fistful.

more.h: The narrow way through the vineyards
more.t: בְּמִשְׁעוֹל הַכְּרָמִים (Bamidbar 22:24), in the path of the vineyards, is a path. From the sense of this root the vineyard path is called משעול, because it is a narrow road with no more width to it than the measure a man needs to walk along it.

more.h: Yonasan on the dust on their feet
more.t: From this sense Targum Yonasan renders לִשְׁעָלִים לְכָל הָעָם אֲשֶׁר בְּרַגְלָי, fistfuls for all the people at my feet, as לְמֵיסַב בִּשְׁעוֹלֵי פַרְסַת רִגְלֵי עַמָא דְעִמִי, to take up in the hollows of the soles of the feet of the people who are with me. Radak explains this as the dust that clings to the soles of their feet.

more.h: The fox under the same letters
more.t: אִם־יַֽעֲלֶה שׁוּעָל וּפָרַץ (Nechemiah 3:35), if a fox goes up he will breach it, and שֽׁוּעָלִים קְטַנִּים (Shir HaShirim 2:15), little foxes. Radak says the animal is known, and gives it no further gloss.

אבה.sense: To be willing, to desire; the very poor man is called אביון for lacking all and craving all. Filed here too, in a sense of its own, is אָב, father, also said of a chief.

more.t: וְלֹֽא־ אָבָה (Devarim 23:6), and Hashem was not willing, and אִם־יְפַתּוּךָ חַטָּאִים אַל־ תֹּבֵֽא (Mishlei 1:10), if sinners entice you, do not consent. In תֹּבֵֽא the alef stands in place of a hei and the first root letter is hidden, and the sense is one of will and desire.

וְתָפֵר הָֽאֲבִיּוֹנָה (Koheles 12:5) belongs here too, the yud standing as the third root letter in place of the hei of אבה. אֲבִיּוֹנָה is explained as the one that has the will and the craving, the soul that desires, so that the pasuk says the soul breaks its covenant with the body. Some say the word is a name for the organ of relations.

more.h: Why the very poor man is אביון
more.t: The very poor man is called אביון because he lacks everything and his craving and his will go out to all. So too in the midrash (Vayikra Rabbah 34): the אביון sees a thing and does not eat it, sees a thing and does not drink it, and craves everything; and he is harder pressed than the עני, the poor man.

more.h: אָבִי יִבָּחֵן, my wish or my Father
more.t: אָבִי יִבָּחֵן אִיּוֹב עַד־נֶצַח (Iyov 34:36), on his reading: my wish and my will is that Iyov be tested to the end. Some take אָבִי instead from the word for father, as a calling out to Hashem.

חָֽלְפוּ עִם־אֳנִיּוֹת אֵבֶה (Iyov 9:26), they passed like ships of אֵבֶה: on his reading, ships whose wish and will is to go to the place, so that they hurry on; so my days passed quickly. Some explain it as the name of a place or a river, and some take it from the root איב, the sense of enmity, ships of plunderers. Everything of this root is to be explained in the sense of will, except two words. One is לְמִי אוֹי לְמִי אֲבוֹי (Mishlei 23:29), who has woe, who has אֲבוֹי, whose sense is that of אוי, woe; though some take it from אביון, meaning who has poverty.

more.h: אב the father and the chief
more.t: The second word outside that sense is אָב וָאֵם (Esther 2:7), father and mother, whose meaning Radak calls known. The great man and the one who came first is called אב too: וַיְשִׂימֵנִי לְאָב לְפַרְעֹה (Bereishis 45:8), he has made me a father to Pharaoh, meaning an officer and a great man, as a father is officer over a son; and וֶֽהְיֵה־לָנוּ לְאָב וּלְכֹהֵן (Shoftim 18:19), be to us a father and a kohen.

Pupils are called sons, as בְנֵֽי־הַנְּבִיאִים (Melachim II 2:15), the sons of the prophets; and אֲבִי כָּל־תֹּפֵשׂ כִּנּוֹר וְעוּגָֽב (Bereishis 4:21), the father of all who hold harp and pipe, and אֲבִי ישֵׁב אֹהֶל וּמִקְנֶֽה (Bereishis 4:20), the father of those who dwell in tents with cattle, mean that he came first and was a teacher to all of them, as a father comes before a son.

דלל.sense: To dry up; דַּל is poor, and also sick. Another sense is to be raised, as eyes lifted on high; and דַּלַּת of the head is its locks.

more.t: דָּלְלוּ וְחָרְבוּ (Yeshayahu 19:6), they are dried up and laid waste: the sense of דָּלְלוּ is they dried up. So too דַּלּוּ מֵאֱנוֹשׁ נָעוּ (Iyov 28:4), they dried up away from men and wandered off.

וְאִם־דַּל הוּא וְאֵין יָדוֹ מַשֶּׂגֶת (Vayikra 14:21), and if he is poor and his means do not reach: דַּל is a poor man. The plural is in הֹֽלְכִים וְדַלִּֽים (Shmuel II 3:1), going on and growing poorer, and the feminine in דַּלּוֹת וְרָעוֹת תֹּאַר (Bereishis 41:19), poor and ill of form. The noun is וּמִדַּלַּת הָאָרֶץ, and of the poor of the land, or it may be an adjective describing a community. Its plural is וּמִדַּלֹּות הָעָם (Yirmiyahu 52:15), and of the poor of the people.

מַדּוּעַ אַתָּה כָּכָה דַּל בֶּן־הַמֶּלֶךְ (Shmuel II 13:4), why are you so sick, son of the king: here דַּל is sick. So too אַשְׁרֵי מַשְׂכִּיל אֶל־ דָּל (Tehillim 41:2), happy is he who considers the sick man, for the mizmor was made over the psalmist's own illness. מִדַּלָּה יְבַצְּעֵנִי (Yeshayahu 38:12), from sickness He will finish me, means: I thought that this sickness of mine would finish me, that I would die of it.

Another sense: דַּלּוּ עֵינַי לַמָּרוֹם (Yeshayahu 38:14), my eyes are lifted to the height, where the sense is that they were raised. Rabbi Yonah joined נִצְּרָה עַל־ דַּל שְׂפָתָֽי (Tehillim 141:3), keep watch over the דַּל of my lips, to this sense, and Radak says he will take the word up again under the root דָּלַת.
וְדַלַּת רֹאשֵׁךְ כָּאַרְגָּמָן (Shir HaShirim 7:6), and the locks of your head are like purple: דַּלַּת is the tresses of the hair.

מכך.sense: Lowness: to be brought low, as in sin, and to sink, as a roof does. The brother who grows poor may be from it too.

more.t: וַיָּמֹכּוּ בַּֽעֲוֹנָֽם (Tehillim 106:43), they were brought low in their sin. וְכִי־יָמוּךְ אָחִיךָ (Vayikra 25:25), and when your brother grows poor, may come from it, a shuruk standing in for a cholam as in יָרוּן וְשָׂמֵֽחַ (Mishlei 29:6), he sings and rejoices. So too וּמָךְ אָחִיךָ עִמּוֹ (Vayikra 25:47), and your brother grows poor beside him, where the kamatz is not the way of the doubled roots; perhaps the resting letter came here in place of the doubled one.

יִמַּךְ הַמְּקָרֶה (Koheles 10:18), the rafters sink, is the form in which the thing itself is brought low, and וְֽהֻמְּכוּ כַּכֹּל יִקָּפְצוּן (Iyov 24:24), they are brought low and gathered in like all, is the form of being brought low by another. Radak says the word should by rights have been וְהֻמַּכּוּ, and that all of them carry a sense of lowness.

His father writes that the root of וְֽהֻמְּכוּ is נָמַך, and brings as proof the Chachamim's מקום נָמוֹךְ, a low place (Berachos 10b), on the pattern of גָּדוֹל, great; and further, that it should have said והמכו with a dagesh in the kaf were its root מָכַך.

more.h: Radak's answer on the doubled roots
more.t: Radak says there is no proof from יִדְּמוּ כָּאָבֶן (Shemos 15:16), they are still as a stone, or וַֽיִּתְּמוּ יְמֵי בְכִי אֵבֶל (Devarim 34:8), the days of weeping for the mourning came to an end, for on his father's view their roots are נָדַם and נָתַם, while on Radak's own account they belong with the doubled roots, and so does וְֽהֻמְּכוּ along with them. He adds that the low place in the words of the Chachamim may itself be of the doubled roots, like נָגוֹזּוּ וְעָבָר (Nachum 1:12), they were shorn and he passed away.

תכך.sense: A sense of breaking: תֹּךְ וּמִרְמָֽה is breaking a man who trusts in one and deceiving him by mouth. Rav Saadiah Gaon reads אִישׁ תְּכָכִים as a man of middling means.

more.t: רָשׁ וְאִישׁ תְּכָכִים (Mishlei 29:13), the poor man and the man of breaking, with תֹּךְ וּמִרְמָֽה (Tehillim 55:12), breaking and deceit, and מִתּוֹךְ וּמֵחָמָס (Tehillim 72:14), from breaking and from violence, all carry a sense of breaking. Radak explains תוך ומרמה as breaking the man who trusts in him and does not guard himself against him, and deceiving him with his mouth.
Radak says he has already written this word under the root תוּך, except that Rabbi Yehudah Chayuj brought it together with אִישׁ תְּכָכִים, the man of breaking, under one sense.

The Gaon Rav Saadiah explained תככים from תּוֹךְ הַבַּיִת (Shmuel II 4:6), the middle of the house, which is the middling sort. He said that רָשׁ וְאִישׁ תְּכָכִים, a poor man and a man of middling means, are fit to be shown kindness, since there are middling people who hide their poverty and keep up their standing so as to remain in honour; which is why the two are said to be at one rank, and why both need pity.

ירד.sense: To go down, and to bring down; מוֹרָד, a descent; eyes said to go down with water; and מַעֲשֵׂה מוֹרָד, beaten work, close in sense to going down.

more.t: יָרֹד יָרַדְנוּ בַּתְּחִלָּה (Bereishis 43:20), we came down at the first, and רְדוּ־שָׁמָּה וְשִׁבְרוּ־לָנוּ מִשָּׁם (Bereishis 42:2), go down there and buy for us from there. The form that brings a thing down gives הוֹרַדְנוּ בְיָדֵנוּ (Bereishis 43:22), we brought it down in our hand, and וּבִנְסֹעַ הַמִּשְׁכָּן יוֹרִידוּ אֹתוֹ הַֽלְוִיִּם (Bamidbar 1:51), when the Mishkan travels the Leviim take it down.

עֵינִי עֵינִי יֹרְדָה מַּיִם (Eichah 1:16), my eye, my eye goes down with water, is יורדה במים, going down with water, the beis left out; so וְתֵרַדְנָה עֵינֵינוּ דִּמְעָה (Yirmiyahu 9:17) is תרדנה בדמעה, our eyes go down with tears. It may also be read with no beis missing: because so much of the tear flows down from the eyes, the going down is ascribed to the eyes themselves. In the same way, וְהַגְּבָעוֹת תֵּלַכְנָה חָלָב (Yoel 4:18), the hills shall go with milk.

more.h: The ephod that came down in his hand
more.t: Some read אֵפוֹד יָרַד בְּיָדוֹ (Shmuel I 23:6), the ephod came down in his hand, as though it said הוֹרִיד, he brought it down. Radak finds that hard, since this root in its plain form is found only without an object, never taking one. It may be read that when Evyasar went down, he went down with the ephod in his hand. It can also be read that when Evyasar fled and took his vessels and his clothes with him, it was brought about by Hashem that he took the ephod among his vessels without noticing, and he did not know of it until he came to David; so the pasuk does not say הוֹרִידוֹ, that he brought it down knowingly, but יָרַד, that the ephod came down in his hand by chance. That reading, Radak holds, is the right one.

more.h: Rabbi Yonah's reading, and the answer
more.t: Rabbi Yonah explains וְיָרַדְתִּי עַל־הֶֽהָרִים (Shoftim 11:37), and I will go down upon the hills, as and I will go up, and likewise וְלֹא־יֵרֵד עִמָּנוּ בַּמִּלְחָמָה (Shmuel I 29:4), he shall not go down with us to the war, as not going up. Radak says there is no sense in it, since going up is the opposite of going down, and that going down to war is the plain meaning, war being fought in the valley and not on the mountain. He reads Yiftach's daughter as saying: I will go down from the Mitzpeh to walk on the hills, for Yiftach's house was in the Mitzpeh and the Mitzpeh stood higher than the hills, and she said, I will go down and part from people and be alone there and weep over my maidenhood.

מַעֲשֵׂה מוֹרָד (Melachim I 7:29) is in the sense of beaten work, and that is close to the sense of going down. Targum Yonasan renders it עוֹבַד כִּבּוּשׁ, pressed work, as Onkelos renders עַד רֶדֶת חֹמֹתֶיךָ (Devarim 28:52), until your walls come down, and עַד רִדְתָּהּ (Devarim 20:20), until it comes down; and all of it comes under one sense. The word may instead be of the root רָדַד, and then it would join its sense well, from וַיָּרֶד עַל הַכְּרוּבִים (Melachim I 6:32), and he beat it out over the keruvim, and the Targum's וְרַדִּידוּ for וַיְרַקְּעוּ (Shemos 39:3), and they beat out.

גדר.sense: To fence in, and the fence: any wall that is not strong building, as for gardens and vineyards, and the sheepfold; all of it is stopping up and closing off.

more.t: גָּדַר דְּרָכַי בְּגָזִית (Eichah 3:9), He walled my ways with hewn stone, גָּדַר בַּֽעֲדִי וְלֹא אֵצֵא (Eichah 3:7), He fenced me about and I cannot go out, and אָרְחִי גָדַר וְלֹא אֶעֱבוֹר (Iyov 19:8), He fenced my path and I cannot pass. The sense of all of it is stopping up and closing off.

The noun, from which the verb is taken, is גָּדֵר מִזֶּה וְגָדֵר מִזֶּֽה (Bamidbar 22:24), a fence on this side and a fence on that, and פָּרֹץ גְּדֵרוֹ (Yeshayahu 5:5), breaking down its fence. In the plural לָמָּה פָּרַצְתָּ גְדֵרֶיהָ (Tehillim 80:13), why have You broken down her fences, and יוֹם לִבְנוֹת גְּדֵרָיִךְ (Michah 7:11), a day for building your fences. וְגֶדֶר אֲבָנָיו נֶֽהֱרָֽסָה (Mishlei 24:31), its stone wall was thrown down, is another form, or else the first form itself, changed so in the construct, like גָּזֵל, robbery, and כָּתֵף, shoulder.

Radak says that every wall made for gardens and for vineyards, and every wall that is not strong building of the kind houses and city walls are, is called a גדר, as in גֶּדֶר הֶֽחָצֵר (Yechezkel 42:10), the wall of the courtyard.

The closing in made for a sheep pen bears the word too: גִּדְרֹת צֹאן נִבְנֶה לְמִקְנֵנוּ (Bamidbar 32:16), we will build folds of sheep for our cattle, and וּגְדֵרֹת לְצֹנַֽאֲכֶם (Bamidbar 32:24), and folds for your flocks. Radak says this is what the Chachamim call a דיר, in their words about animals entering the pen to be tithed (Bava Metzia 6b).

Rabbeinu Shlomo explained וְהִתְשׁוֹטַטְנָה בַּגְּדֵרֹות (Yirmiyahu 49:3), and make sport in the folds, from this sense, the sheepfolds; Radak himself lists the word among the plurals. His gloss on Rashi's reading is that they will make sport in the dung of the sheepfolds, by way of contempt. Targum Yonasan renders it וְאִתְהַמְמוּן בְּסִיָען, and they shall be confounded among the bands.

קוה.sense: Hope and expectation; in a second sense, gathering, as of waters; and in a third, קַו, the measuring line, which a builder stretches as he builds.

more.t: אֲשֶׁר לֹֽא־יֵבֹשׁוּ קוָֹֽי (Yeshayahu 49:23), those who hope in Me shall not be ashamed. In the strengthened form קִוְּתָה נַפְשִׁי (Tehillim 130:5), my soul hoped, וַיְקַו לַֽעֲשׂוֹת עֲנָבִים (Yeshayahu 5:2), he hoped it would make grapes, and יְקַו־לְאוֹר וָאַיִן (Iyov 3:9), let it hope for light and there be none. All of them are of the sense of hope and expectation.

The noun is מִקְוֵה יִשְׂרָאֵל (Yirmiyahu 14:8), the hope of Yisrael, and in another form וַיִּכְלוּ בְּאֶפֶס תִּקְוָֽה (Iyov 7:6), they came to an end without hope, and וְתִקְוָתִי מִי יְשׁוּרֶֽנָּה (Iyov 17:15), and my hope, who shall see it.

וְנִקְוּוּ אֵלֶיהָ כָל־הַגּוֹיִם (Yirmiyahu 3:17), all the nations shall be gathered to her, and יִקָּווּ הַמַּיִם (Bereishis 1:9), let the waters be gathered. The noun is מִקְוֵה־מַיִם (Vayikra 11:36), a gathering of water, and in the feminine וּמִקְוָה עֲשִׂיתֶם בֵּין הַחֹמֹתַיִם (Yeshayahu 22:11), you made a reservoir between the two walls. Radak gives their sense as gathering.

more.h: The third sense, the measuring line
more.t: קַו הַמִּדָּה (Yirmiyahu 31:39), the measuring line, and וְקָו שְׁלֹשִׁים בָּאַמָּה יָסֹב אֹתוֹ (Melachim I 7:23), and a line of thirty cubits went round it. קַו־קָו וּמְבוּסָה (Yeshayahu 18:2) he explains as: little by little they will trample him down, the way a builder stretches out the line a little at a time. It may be that אִם־אֲקַוֶּה שְׁאוֹל בֵּיתִי (Iyov 17:13) is of this sense, if I build Sheol as my house, since building is done by stretching the line. So too קַו לָקָו (Yeshayahu 28:10) is building after building, the prophets charging them command after command and they building themselves building after building, since a command and a statute are like a building; and from this, counsel is called a foundation. And in בְּכָל־הָאָרֶץ יָצָא קַוָּם (Tehillim 19:5), their קַו has gone out through all the earth, he glosses קַוָּם as their building.

אֶת־תִּקְוַת חוּט הַשָּׁנִי (Yehoshua 2:18), the line of scarlet thread, is another form, joined to the word for thread as אַדְמַת־עָפָר (Daniel 12:2), the ground of dust, is joined. Targum Yonasan renders it תּוֹרָא דְחוּט זְהוֹרִיתָא, the border of the scarlet thread, and the Targum on the hem at the opening of the garment (Shemos 28:32) gives תּוֹרָא יְהֵא מַקַּף לְפוּמֵהּ, a border shall go round its mouth. Radak draws from this that the Targum takes תקות חוט השני as the hem of a red garment. It may be that וַיִּכְלוּ בְּאֶפֶס תִּקְוָה (Iyov 7:6), and they came to an end with no תִּקְוָה, is of this sense too, since the pasuk likens his days to the weaver's tool that holds the thread of the woof.

Of this sense too is וּמִקְוֵה סֹחֲרֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ יִקְחוּ מִקְוֵה בִּמְחִיר (Melachim I 10:28), and מקוה, the king's traders took מקוה at a price. Radak explains that the king's traders brought the horses out of Mitzrayim and took מקוה in Yerushalayim at the horses' price, carrying it to Mitzrayim; and he allows it may be the other way, that they brought the מקוה out of Mitzrayim as they did the horses, since the working of linen is more at home there than in any other land. On that reading, Pharaoh had granted Shlomo the export of the horses, so that the horses went out without payment while the linen went out for money. In Divrei HaYamim II 1:16 the word is written מִקְוֵא with an alef.

זנח.sense: To cast off: Hashem casting off His mizbeach, a soul cast off from peace, the vessels King Achaz cast aside. He gives the word no gloss of its own.

more.t: זָנַח (Eichah 2:7) is Hashem casting off His mizbeach, and כִּי לֹא יִזְנַח לְעוֹלָם (Eichah 3:31), for Hashem will not cast off for ever. The form that takes no object is וַתִּזְנַח מִשָּׁלוֹם נַפְשִׁי (Eichah 3:17), and my soul is cast off from peace.

The added form gives וְאֵת כָּל־הַכֵּלִים אֲשֶׁר הִזְנִיחַ הַמֶּלֶךְ אָחָז (Divrei HaYamim II 29:19), and all the vessels that King Achaz cast aside, and וְהֶֽאֶזְנִיחוּ נְהָרוֹת (Yeshayahu 19:6), and the rivers shall be cast off.

more.h: Rabbi Yonah on the added alef
more.t: Rabbi Yonah wrote that in this word the Hebrews followed the way of Aramaic, which adds an alef, as in אִשְׁתִּיו חַמְרָא (Daniel 5:4), they drank wine, and אֶתְכְּרִיַּת רוּחִי (Daniel 7:15), my spirit was grieved; and that they wrote in it the hei of the form as well. Radak says he has already set out its grammar in the grammar part of his work.

נבט.sense: To look toward, to gaze; and the noun מַבָּט, the thing one looks to. His word for the sense is השגחה, watchful attention.

more.t: וְנִבַּט לָאָרֶץ (Yeshayahu 5:30), and one looks to the earth: the nun is a root letter, and he takes the word as a past verb of the heavy form with the dagesh; some say it is of the passive form. Another heavy form: לֹא־הִבִּיט אָוֶן בְּיַֽעֲקֹב (Bamidbar 23:21), He has not looked on iniquity in Yaakov, וְהִבִּיטוּ אַֽחֲרֵי מֹשֶׁה (Shemos 33:8), they looked after Moshe, and הַבֶּט־נָא הַשָּׁמַיְמָה (Bereishis 15:5), look now toward the heavens.

וְהַבִּיט אֶל־עָמָל לֹא תוּכָל (Chavakuk 1:13), You cannot look upon wrong, מֵֽהַבִּיט אֶל־הָֽאֱלֹהִֽים (Shemos 3:6), from looking toward Hashem, and אַל־תַּבִּיט אַֽחֲרֶיךָ (Bereishis 19:17), do not look behind you.

The noun is הִנֵּה־כֹה מַבָּטֵנוּ (Yeshayahu 20:6), see, such is what we looked to, and מִכּוּשׁ מַבָּטָם (Yeshayahu 20:5), of Kush, what they looked to, with a patach under the mem; and וְעֶקְרוֹן כִּֽי־הוֹבִישׁ מֶבָּטָהּ (Zecharyah 9:5), and Ekron, for what she looked to has withered, with a segol under the mem. Their sense, he says, ענינם ענין ההשגחה, is that of watchful attention.

שׁקף.sense: Watching and peering, as one looks out from a height; the lintel, so called because it is always looked at, or because the door strikes it; and poles set in rows.

more.t: וְצֶדֶק מִשָּׁמַיִם נִשְׁקָֽף (Tehillim 85:12), righteousness looks down from heaven, בְּעַד אֶשְׁנַבִּי נִשְׁקָֽפְתִּי (Mishlei 7:6), I looked out through my lattice, and כִּי רָעָה נִשְׁקְפָה מִצָּפוֹן (Yirmiyahu 6:1), for evil looks out from the north. Their sense is watching and peering. The Targum renders וּבִנְקִיקֵי הַסְּלָעִים (Yeshayahu 7:19), and in the clefts of the rocks, as וּבִשְׁקִיפֵי כֵיפַיָא, in the look-outs of the rocks, and so it renders וּבִסְעִפֵי הַסְּלָעִים (Yeshayahu 2:21), and in the crags of the rocks, because men look out from them for their height.

more.h: Why the word is used passively
more.t: Radak says the word is used in the form of being acted upon because a man who stands in a high place and looks out is himself looked at by those who look toward him. That is why it says הַשְׁקִיפָה מִמְּעוֹן קָדְשְׁךָ מִן־הַשָּׁמַיִם (Devarim 26:15), look down from Your holy dwelling from the heavens, in the active form, since the Holy One looks out and is not looked at.

וַיַּשְׁקֵף אֲבִימֶלֶךְ (Bereishis 26:8), and Avimelech looked out, is so put because he was in a place where he saw them and they did not see him; and וַתַּשְׁקֵף בְּעַד הַחַלּֽוֹן (Melachim II 9:30), and she looked out through the window, likewise, for she saw them and they did not see her until Yehu drew near the gate.

On חַלּוֹנֵי שְׁקֻפִים אֲטֻמִֽים (Melachim I 6:4), windows, שְׁקֻפִים and sealed, the Targum says פְּתִיחָן מִלְגָיו וּסְתִימָן מִלְבָרָא, open within and closed without. Radak notes that in the words of the Chachamim the reverse is found (Menachos 86b): open outside and closed inside, unlike other windows, to show that He has no need of light.

אֶל־ הַמַּשְׁקוֹף וְאֶל־שְׁתֵּי הַמְּזוּזֹת (Shemos 12:22), to the lintel and to the two doorposts: it is the upper threshold above the doorpost of the gate, so called, Radak says, because it is always in view, looked at, or because the door strikes against it continually. The Targum renders וּשְׁדוּפֹת קָדִים (Bereishis 41:6), blighted by the east wind, as וּשְׁקִיפָן קִדּוּם, that is, struck by the east wind, and וַיִּסְפֹּק אֶת־כַּפָּיו (Bamidbar 24:10), and he struck his hands together, as וּשְׁקָפִנּוּן לִידוֹהִי, and he struck them, his hands. Ibn Ezra wrote that the משקוף is a window made above the doorway, from which they look out when a man calls at the gate, to see who is calling, and that this is known in the land of Yishmael, where windows are made above the doorways to look out from.

וּשְׁקֻפִים שְׁלֹשָׁה טוּרִים (Melachim I 7:4), and שְׁקֻפִים in three rows, set one facing the other: Targum Yonasan renders it וּכְלֵנְסָא תְּלַת סִדְרִין, and poles, three rows. So too וְכָל־הַפְּתָחִים וְהַמְּזוּזוֹת רְבֻעִים שָׁקֶף (Melachim I 7:5), and all the doorways and doorposts squared, שָׁקֶף, is rendered מְרַבְּעִין וַחֲפָן כְּלֵנְסָא, squared and covered with poles. The same word is in the words of the Chachamim, מביאין כלונסות של ארז, they bring poles of cedar (Rosh Hashanah 22b), and ומודלה על גבי כלונסות, trained up over poles, in Chullin, and כלונסות means staves.

צפה.sense: To look out and watch, all of it the sense of looking; in the heavy form close to hoping, since one who hopes for another looks out for him. A second sense: to overlay.

more.t: צֹפֶה נְתַתִּיךָ (Yechezkel 3:17), I have set you as a watchman, עֵינָיו בַּגּוֹיִם תִּצְפֶּינָה (Tehillim 66:7), His eyes keep watch on the nations, and צָפֹה הַצָּפִית (Yeshayahu 21:5), set the watch. Radak says הַצָּפִית is either a word describing the watchman, the tav standing for the hei of the third root letter, or else the tav is added to the word.

וְהִשְׁקֵיתִי אֶרֶץ צָפָֽתְךָ מִדָּמְךָ (Yechezkel 32:6), I will water the land of your tzafah from your blood: its sense is the land of your looking out and your gazing, that is, even the high places I will water with your blood. Radak notes that he gave another explanation of the word under the root צוּף.

In the heavy form, בְּצִפִּיָּתֵנוּ צִפִּינוּ (Eichah 4:17), in our watching we watched, בֹּקֶר אֶֽעֱרָךְ־לְךָ וַֽאֲצַפֶּֽה (Tehillim 5:4), in the morning I set it before You and look out, and צַפֵּה ־דֶרֶךְ (Nachum 2:2), watch the road. Radak says that in this form it comes close to the sense of hoping, since one who hopes for another looks out for him.

more.h: Why a high place is a מצפה
more.t: The noun is וַיִּקְרָא אַרְיֵה עַל־ מִצְפֶּה (Yeshayahu 21:8), a lion called out upon the watchtower. A high place is called a מצפה because a man looks out from it far off. All of these, he says, are the sense of looking.

וְצִפָּה רָֽאשֵׁיהֶם (Shemos 36:38), he overlaid their tops, וְצִפִּיתָ אֹתָם (Shemos 27:6), and you shall overlay them, and מְצֻפֶּה עַל־חָרֶשׂ (Mishlei 26:23), laid over earthenware. The noun is צִפּוּי לַמִּזְבֵּֽחַ (Bamidbar 17:4), an overlay for the mizbeach.

Radak allows that וְהַצֶּפֶת אֲשֶׁר־עַל־רֹאשׁוֹ אַמּוֹת חָמֵֽשׁ (Divrei HaYamim II 3:15), and the capital that was on its top was five cubits, may be of this root and this sense, the capital being so called because it was an overlay for the pillar. He adds that he will write צֶפֶת as a root of its own, as Rabbi Yonah did, who said in the name of Rav Saadiah Gaon that the word means a צנצנת, a jar.

שׁגח.sense: To look closely, with attention; that is his sense for all three of his pesukim.

more.t: מִֽמְּכֽוֹן־שִׁבְתּוֹ הִשְׁגִּיחַ (Tehillim 33:14), from the place of His dwelling He looked out closely; רֹאֶיךָ אֵלֶיךָ יַשְׁגִּיחוּ (Yeshayahu 14:16), those who see you look closely at you; מַשְׁגִּיחַ מִן־הַֽחֲלֹּנוֹת (Shir HaShirim 2:9), looking closely in through the windows. Radak gives their sense as looking with close attention.

אסף.sense: To gather: the harvest brought in, a man gathered to his fathers at death, the metzora taken back among people; and a second sense, removal and making an end.

more.t: וְאָסַף אִישׁ טָהוֹר (Bamidbar 19:9), a clean man shall gather up, וַיַּֽאַסְפוּ אֶת־הַשְּׂלָו (Bamidbar 11:32), they gathered the quail, and אָסֹף אֶאֱסֹף יַֽעֲקֹב כֻּלָּךְ (Michah 2:12), I will surely gather all of you, Yaakov. Their sense is that of קבוץ, gathering, though there is a difference between the two words, which he says he will set out under the root קבץ.

more.h: Why the festival is חַג הָאָסִיף
more.t: וְחַג הָֽאָסִיף (Shemos 34:22), the festival of ingathering, is so called, he says, because then they gather the grain harvest and the vintage and all the fruit into the houses on account of the rains.

בַּֽעֲלֵי אֲסֻפּוֹת (Koheles 12:11), masters of collections, means the words of the masters of collections: the pasuk calls the wise who compose books masters of collections because they gather the words of wisdom into their books.

more.h: The crowd that gathered to them
more.t: וְהָֽאסַפְסֻף אֲשֶׁר בְּקִרְבּוֹ (Bamidbar 11:4), the gathered throng in its midst, doubles the second and third root letters, the alef resting, and the doubling strengthens the sense. It means the great crowd of people that had gathered to them, as it is written וְגַם־עֵרֶב רַב עָלָה אִתָּם (Shemos 12:38), and a great mixed multitude went up with them.
