כַּֽאֲשֶׁר נֶֽאֱסַף אַֽהֲרֹן אָחִֽיךָ (Bamidbar 27:13), as Aharon your brother was gathered in, and אֲנִי נֶֽאֱסָף אֶל־עַמִּי (Bereishis 49:29), I am being gathered to my people. Radak says the word is used of dying because the dead man has gone the way his fathers went, as though he were gathered to them.

From the same sense, וְאָסַף הַמְּצֹרָֽע (Melachim II 5:11), and he will gather in the metzora, and עַד־הֵֽאָסֵף מִרְיָֽם (Bamidbar 12:15), until Miriam was gathered in. Radak explains that the metzora's way is to sit outside the camp or the city, parted from people, and when he is healed he is gathered back to them and comes in among them.

עָשִׁיר יִשְׁכַּב וְלֹא יֵאָסֵף (Iyov 27:19), the rich man lies down and is not gathered in, means that if a rich man lies down in sickness he will not die rich, for before he dies they plunder all that he has, since once he has fallen to his bed they no longer fear him. That is why the pasuk says עֵינָיו פָּקַח וְאֵינֶֽנּוּ, he opened his eyes and he is not, meaning that he is no longer in his wealth.

more.h: The other sense, making an end
more.t: אָסֹף אָסֵף כֹּל מֵעַל פְּנֵי הָֽאֲדָמָה (Tzefaniah 1:2), I will utterly make an end of everything from off the face of the earth, and אָסֹף אֲסִיפֵם (Yirmiyahu 8:13), I will make a full end of them, where he writes that אָסֹף and אֲסִיפֵם have the root סוף. So too פֶּן־אֹסִֽפְךָ עִמּוֹ (Shmuel I 15:6), lest I make an end of you with him. All of them, he says, mean removal and destruction.

קבץ.sense: To gather together. Its sense is like that of taking in, אסיפה, but as his father wrote, gathering is said only of what is scattered, and taking in even of what is not.

more.t: וַיִּקְבֹּץ אֶת־כָּל־אֹכֶל (Bereishis 41:48), he gathered all the food, וְקֹבֵץ עַל־יָד יַרְבֶּֽה (Mishlei 13:11), one who gathers little by little increases it, and שְׁלַח קְבֹץ אֵלַי אֶת־כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל (Melachim I 18:19), send and gather all Yisrael to me. The noun is קְבֻצַת כֶּסֶף וּנְחשֶׁת (Yechezkel 22:20), a gathering of silver and copper.

more.h: Being gathered, and the heavy form
more.t: Being gathered: כָּל־צֹאן קֵדָר יִקָּבְצוּ לָךְ (Yeshayahu 60:7), all the flocks of Kedar shall be gathered to you. In the heavy form: וְקִבַּצְתִּים מִיַּרְכְּתֵי־אָרֶץ (Yirmiyahu 31:7 in his edition), I will gather them from the ends of the earth. The noun is בְּזַֽעֲקֵךְ יַצִּילֻךְ קִבּוּצַיִךְ (Yeshayahu 57:13), when you cry out let your gatherings save you, which he glosses as קהליך, your assemblies.

more.h: Rabbi Yonah on קִבָּצָה, and Radak
more.t: On כִּי מֵֽאֶתְנַן זוֹנָה קִבָּצָה (Michah 1:7), for from a harlot's hire קִבָּצָה, Rabbi Yonah wrote that the word is passive, it was gathered, the chirik standing in place of a shuruk, as in וּפִתְּחוּ שְׁעָרַיִךְ תָּמִיד (Yeshayahu 60:11), and your gates shall be opened continually. Radak holds it right that קבצה is of the heavy form, and reads the pasuk as: what Shomron had, she gathered from a harlot's hire, וְעַד־אֶתְנַן זוֹנָה יָשֽׁוּבוּ, and to a harlot's hire they shall return. וּפִתְּחוּ too, he says, is of the heavy form and takes no object, as if it said ונפתחו שעריך, your gates shall be opened.

more.h: His father on the two words
more.t: The sense of gathering is like that of taking in, but there is a difference between them, as his father writes in the Chibbur HaLeket: gathering is said only of what is scattered, while taking in is said even of what is not scattered. One says אסוף ידיך, draw in your hand, and does not say קבוץ ידיך, gather your hand; one says ויאסוף רגליו, he drew in his feet, and ואין איש מאסף אותי, and no man takes me in, but one does not say מקבץ אותי, gathers me.

זלזל.sense: The branches of young plantings: וְכָרַת הַזַּלְזַלִּים (Yeshayahu 18:5), and he shall cut off the branches; he gives the Old French word for them.

רמח.sense: A spear, a word whose sense is known: וַיִּקַּח רֹמַח בְּיָדֽוֹ (Bamidbar 25:7), and he took a spear in his hand.

more.t: מִרְקוּ הָֽרְמָחִים (Yirmiyahu 46:4), polish the spears, is like בקרים, mornings, from בֹּקֶר, morning. Or it is of another pattern: עִם־חַרְבֹֽתֵיהֶם רָמְחֵיהֶם וְקַשְּׁתֹֽתֵיהֶֽם (Nechemiah 4:7), with their swords, their spears and their bows.

more.h: A kamatz in the careful sefarim
more.t: In some exact sefarim רָמְחֵיהֶם is pointed with a kamatz under the resh, keeping to the base form, on the pattern of חָדְשֵׁיכֶם וּמֽוֹעֲדֵיכֶם (Yeshayahu 1:14), your new moons and your appointed times. So too Rabbi Yonah wrote.

כיד.sense: כִּידוֹן, the spear that carries the banner, or perhaps the spear alone; the bronze kidon between the shoulders is a shoulder guard. כִּידוֹ is like אידו, ruin.

more.h: The spear that carries the banner
more.t: נְטֵה בַּכִּידוֹן אֲשֶֽׁר־בְּיָֽדְךָ (Yehoshua 8:18), stretch out the kidon that is in your hand, is the spear on which the banner is. So too וְיִשְׂחַק לְרַעַשׁ כִּידֽוֹן (Iyov 41:21), it laughs at the noise of a kidon, though this one may be the spear by itself without the banner, and the noise of the kidon is the noise the spear makes as it goes, when it is carried along.
Like them is לַהַב חֲנִית וְכִידֽוֹן (Iyov 39:23), the blade of spear and kidon, meaning the blade of the spear and the blade of the kidon.

more.h: Where it is not a spear
more.t: But וְכִידוֹן נְחשֶׁת בֵּין כְּתֵפָֽיו (Shmuel I 17:6), and a bronze kidon between his shoulders, is no spear, for it is a guard for his shoulders, and the Targum renders it וּמְסַחֲפָא דִנְחָשָׁא, a covering of bronze. At קֶשֶׁת וְכִידוֹן יַֽחֲזִיקוּ (Yirmiyahu 6:23), they take hold of bow and kidon, the Targum has קַשְׁתָּן וּתְרֵיסִין, bows and shields.
יִרְאוּ עֵינָו [עֵינָיו] כִּידוֹ (Iyov 21:20), let his eyes see his כִּיד: כִּידוֹ is like אידו, his ruin.

שׁפט.sense: To judge, with the nouns for judgment and for judgments carried out; and, in a sense close to it, the statute, the law and the proper order of a thing.

more.h: Judging a man and his cause
more.t: אֲשֶׁר שָׁפַט הַמֶּלֶךְ (Melachim I 3:28), which the king judged; וּשְׁפָטָנוּ מַלְכֵּנוּ (Shmuel I 8:20), our king shall judge us; וְשָֽׁפְטוּ אֶת־הָעָם (Shemos 18:22), they shall judge the people; וּשְׁפַטְתֶּם צֶדֶק (Devarim 1:16), judge righteously; and כִּֽי־ שְׁפָטוֹ י"י מִיַּד אֹֽיְבָֽיו (Shmuel II 18:19), that Hashem has judged him out of the hand of his enemies.

כַּֽאֲשֶׁר נִשְׁפַּטְתִּי אֶת־אֲבוֹתֵיכֶם (Yechezkel 20:36), as I came to judgment with your fathers; הִנְנִי נִשְׁפָּט אוֹתָךְ (Yirmiyahu 2:35), behold, I enter into judgment with you; נִשָּֽׁפְטָה יָחַד (Yeshayahu 43:26), let us be judged together; בְּהִשָּׁפְטוֹ יֵצֵא רָשָׁע (Tehillim 109:7), when he is judged let him come out guilty. הִיא שֹֽׁפְטָה אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל (Shoftim 4:4), she was judging Yisrael, and לִמְשֹֽׁפְטִי אֶתְחַנָּֽן (Iyov 9:15), I would plead with the one who judges me, stand in the heavy form.

The noun is מִשְׁפַּט ־צֶֽדֶק (Devarim 16:18), righteous judgment, and עַד־הֵנָּה מִשְׁפַּט מוֹאָֽב (Yirmiyahu 48:47), thus far is the judgment of Moav. In other patterns: with a cholam, חֶרֶב שְׁפוֹט וְדֶבֶר (Divrei HaYamim II 20:9), sword, judgment and plague; the plural with a shuruk, וּשְׁפוּטִים עָשׂוּ בָֽהּ (Yechezkel 23:10), they carried out judgments upon her; and עָשָׂה י"י שְׁפָטִֽים (Bamidbar 33:4), Hashem carried out judgments.

more.h: The rule, the law, the manner
more.t: A sense close to this: וְזֶה יִהְיֶה מִשְׁפַּט הַכֹּֽהֲנִים (Devarim 18:3), and this shall be the rule of the kohanim; כַּמִּשְׁפָּט הָֽרִאשׁוֹן (Bereishis 40:13), after the former manner; מִשְׁפַּט הַמֶּלֶךְ אֲשֶׁר יִמְלֹךְ עֲלֵיכֶם (Shmuel I 8:11), the rule of the king who will reign over you; וַיָּסֹבּוּ אֶת־הָעִיר כַּמִּשְׁפָּט הַזֶּה (Yehoshua 6:15), they went round the city in this same manner; וְאַרְמוֹן עַל־ מִשְׁפָּטוֹ יֵשֵֽׁב (Yirmiyahu 30:18), the palace shall stand after its proper order; יְכַלְכֵּל דְּבָרָיו בְּמִשְׁפָּֽט (Tehillim 112:5), he orders his affairs by rule. All of them, he says, are the sense of statute, law and the proper order of a thing.

So too יַסְּרֵנִי י"י אַךְ־ בְּמִשְׁפָּט (Yirmiyahu 10:24), chasten me, Hashem, but in measure, that is, by a measure I can bear; and the pasuk goes on אַל־בְּאַפְּךָ פֶּן־תַּמְעִטֵֽנִי, not in Your anger, lest You diminish me. So too וְיִסַּרְתִּיךָ לַמִּשְׁפָּט, I will chasten you in measure.

חקק.sense: To cut in or engrave, and to write. A man's due is his חֹק because it was set down in writing, and the word also means a fixed law or custom.

more.t: הוֹי הַחֹֽקְקִים חִקְקֵי־אָוֶן (Yeshayahu 10:1), woe to those who inscribe decrees of wrong; חֹֽקְקִי בַסֶּלַע מִשְׁכָּן לֽוֹ (Yeshayahu 22:16), carving himself a dwelling in the rock, where the yud is an addition, as it is in חֹֽצְבִי, hewing, in that same pasuk; חֲקֻקִים בַּשָּׁשַֽׁר (Yechezkel 23:14), engraved in vermilion; וְחַקּוֹתָ עָלֶיהָ עִיר (Yechezkel 4:1), engrave a city upon it; בְּחוּקוֹ חוּג עַל־פְּנֵי תְהֽוֹם (Mishlei 8:27), when He cut a circle on the face of the deep; בְּחוּקוֹ מוֹסְדֵי אָֽרֶץ (Mishlei 8:29), when He cut out the foundations of the earth.

עַל־לוּחַ אִתָּם וְעַל־סֵפֶר חֻקָּהּ (Yeshayahu 30:8), on a tablet with them, and on a book engrave it: the heh has a mappik, and חֻקָּהּ means engrave it. בַּסֵּפֶר וְיֻחָֽקוּ (Iyov 19:23), that they were graven in a book; וְיִשְׁכַּח מְחֻקָּק (Mishlei 31:5), and he forgets what is inscribed.
חִקְקֵי ־לֵֽב (Shoftim 5:15), engravings of the heart: the heart engraves and thinks about them, how they did not come to the war.

more.h: Mechokek as the one who writes
more.t: בִּמְחֹקֵק בְּמִשְׁעֲנֹתָם (Bamidbar 21:18), with the mechokek, with their staves; וּמְחֹקֵק מִבֵּין רַגְלָיו (Bereishis 49:10), and a mechokek from between his feet; חֶלְקַת מְחֹקֵק (Devarim 33:21), the portion of a mechokek; יָֽרְדוּ מְחֹקְקִים (Shoftim 5:14), mechokekim came down. All of these have the sense of writing. וּמְחֹקֵק מִבֵּין רַגְלָיו is explained by the ruler's way, which is to have a scribe sitting at his feet; and חֶלְקַת מְחֹקֵק is explained as the Targum takes it.

more.h: Or the mechokek may be the ruler
more.t: וּמְחֹקֵק מִבֵּין רַגְלָיו and חֶלְקַת מְחֹקֵק may also be read from the statute: the mechokek is then the ruler, so called because he sets the laws of his land. וּמְחֹקֵק מִבֵּין רַגְלָיו is then that a ruler shall not depart from his seed, מִבֵּין רַגְלָיו as in הַיּוֹצֵת מִבֵּין רַגְלֶיהָ (Devarim 28:57), what comes out from between her feet; and חֶלְקַת מְחֹקֵק goes with the opening of the pasuk, וירא ראשית לו, he saw first for himself: he looked and chose first to take his share across the Yarden, for he saw that the portion of kings and rulers was there, בתים ספונים וטובים, houses panelled and good. So too מְחֹֽקְקֵנוּ (Yeshayahu 33:22), Hashem our lawgiver, the one who gave us the statutes.

כִּֽי־ חָקְךָ וְחָק־בָּנֶיךָ נִתְּנוּ (Vayikra 10:14), for your due and your sons' due are given; כִּי חֹק לַכֹּֽהֲנִים מֵאֵת פַּרְעֹה (Bereishis 47:22), for the kohanim had an allowance from Pharaoh; הַטְרִיפֵנִי לֶחֶם חֻקִּֽי (Mishlei 30:8), feed me my allotted bread. In Iyov, כִּי יַשְׁלִים חֻקִּי, for He will complete my portion, is the blows and sores that pain me always, every day, as though they were my fixed portion; and מֵחֻקִּי צָפַנְתִּי אִמְרֵי־פִֽיו (Iyov 23:12) is: it was my practice to store the words of His mouth in my heart. לִבְלִי־ חֹק (Yeshayahu 5:14), without חֹק, is the opposite of rule and of custom.

חֻקָּה אַחַת לָכֶם (Bamidbar 15:15), one statute for you; זֹאת חֻקַּת הַתּוֹרָה (Bamidbar 19:2), this is the statute of the Torah; חֻקּוֹת עוֹלָם תָּמִֽיד (Yechezkel 46:14), lasting statutes always; וְאֶת־ חֻקֹּתַי תִּשְׁמְרוּ (Vayikra 18:4), and you shall keep My statutes.

פלל.sense: To judge: to rule on a case, and to carry out judgment. Prayer, תְּפִלָּה, belongs here because the one who prays asks Hashem to judge him in His mercy.

more.t: רְאֹה פָנֶיךָ לֹא פִלָּלְתִּי (Bereishis 48:11), to see your face I had not judged, means: I had not reached the judgment and ruling in my own mind that I could ever see your face again.
וַיַּֽעֲמֹד פִּֽינְחָס וַיְפַלֵּל (Tehillim 106:30), Pinchas stood up and did judgment, is the judgment he carried out when he ran Zimri and Kozbi bas Tzur through.

more.h: The judge, and the man judged
more.t: On וּפִֽלְלוֹ אֱלֹהִים (Shmuel I 2:25), the judge will judge him, he says: if a man sins against a man, the judge judges him and brings him out clear of his fellow's hand, ordering what is fitting for him to do, or making a settlement between the two; but if a man sins against Hashem, מי יתפלל לו, who will act as judge for him, that is, who will take it on himself to enter into judgment with him and say, let the law between you be thus and thus. The judge is spoken of in the reflexive form, which is the form of one acted on, as also at וְנִשְׁפַּטְתִּי אִתּוֹ בְּדֶבֶר וּבְדָם (Yechezkel 38:22), I will enter into judgment with him with plague and with blood, since a judge goes back over the pleadings and shows each man the other's claim, as though he himself were the one being judged.

אֲשֶׁר פִּלַּלְתְּ לַֽאֲחוֹתֵךְ (Yechezkel 16:52), that you gave judgment on your sister: the pasuk says גַּם־אַתְּ שְׂאִי כְלִמָּתֵךְ, you too bear your shame, for you sat in judgment on her when she first began to do wrong, and now you have done worse than she did, so that by your own sins, more than hers, you have made her out the righteous one.

עָוֹן פְּלִילִי (Iyov 31:28), a wrong for the judges; עָוֹן פְּלִילִֽים (Iyov 31:11), a wrong the judges must deal with; וְנָתַן בִּפְלִלִֽים (Shemos 21:22), he shall pay as the judges assess; פְלִילָה (Yeshayahu 16:3), give a ruling; פָּקוּ פְּלִֽילִיָּֽה (Yeshayahu 28:7), they stumbled in giving judgment. Rabbi Yehudah holds that the verb in וְנִפְֽלַל חָלָל (Yechezkel 28:23), said of the slain, is the passive of this root. Radak gives it no gloss of its own; it stands in the run he closes with ענין הכל המשפט והדין, the sense of all of it is judgment and law.

וַיִּתְפַּלֵּל אַבְרָהָם (Bereishis 20:17), Avraham prayed; וְהִתְפַּלֵּל אֶל־הַבַּיִת (Melachim I 8:42), and he prays toward the house; וְיִתְפַּלֵּל בַּֽעַדְךָ וֶֽחְיֵה (Bereishis 20:7), he will pray for you and you will live; and the noun, תְּפִלָּה לְמֹשֶׁה (Tehillim 90:1), a prayer of Moshe, and שָׁמַעְתִּי אֶת־ תְּפִלָּֽתְךָ (Melachim I 9:3), I have heard your prayer. The reflexive form is used of supplication and request, and it belongs to this root because the one who prays asks Him to judge him in His mercy and not to look to the many wrongs he has done, for the judgment he asks is that He let his sins go and not call them to mind against him at all; as the navi said, יַסְּרֵנִי, chasten me, Hashem, אַךְ־בְּמִשְׁפָּט אַל־בְּאַפְּךָ (Yirmiyahu 10:24), but in judgment, not in Your anger.

בקשׁ.sense: To seek, and to require at someone's hand; the noun is a request. He gives no gloss: the sense of them all, he says, is known.

more.t: בִּקַּשְׁתִּיהוּ וְלֹא מְצָאתִיהוּ (Shir HaShirim 5:6), I sought him and did not find him; יְבַקֵּשׁ אֶת־נַפְשִׁי (Shmuel I 22:23), he seeks my life; וּבִקֵּשׁ י"י מִיַּד אֹֽיְבֵי דָוִֽד (Shmuel I 20:16), and Hashem shall require it at the hand of David's enemies; and מִיָּדִי תְּבַקְשֶׁנָּה (Bereishis 31:39), you would require it at my hand.

וַיְבֻקַּשׁ הַדָּבָר וַיִּמָּצֵא (Esther 2:23), the matter was looked into and found out; וּֽתְבֻקְשִׁי וְלֹֽא־תִמָּצְאִי עוֹד (Yechezkel 26:21), you will be sought and never found again; and the noun, וְלַֽעֲשׂוֹת אֶת־ בַּקָּשָׁתִי (Esther 5:8), and to grant my request.
In תְּבַקְשֶׁנָּה the kuf is light, carrying no strengthening point, and so through most of the pattern: where the kuf takes a sheva, it is light.

מאן.sense: To refuse: מֵאֵן בִּלְעָם הֲלֹךְ עִמָּֽנוּ (Bamidbar 22:14), Bilam refused to go with us; and the adjective, one who refuses, in two patterns.

more.t: מֵֽאֲנוּ קַחַת מוּסָר (Yirmiyahu 5:3), they refused to take correction; אִם־ מָאֵן יְמָאֵן אָבִיהָ (Shemos 22:16), if her father altogether refuses.

The adjective is וְאִם־ מָאֵן אַתָּה לְשַׁלֵּחַ (Shemos 7:27), and if you are one who refuses to let them go, on the pattern of וְשַׁבֵּחַ אֲנִי אֶת־הַמֵּתִים (Koheles 4:2), and I am one who praises the dead. Another pattern is מֵאַן, as in הַמֵּֽאֲנִים לִשְׁמוֹעַ אֶת־דְּבָרַי (Yirmiyahu 13:10), those who refuse to hear My words.

סרב.sense: To refuse and rebel, ממאנים וממרים in his gloss; the Targum uses the word for refusing and for rebellion, and it is known in the language of Chazal.

more.t: כִּי סָֽרָבִים וְסַלּוֹנִים (Yechezkel 2:6) he glosses ממאנים וממרים, refusing and rebelling; his text does not mark whether that is said of סָרָבִים alone or of both words. The Targum of וַיְמָאֵן (Bereishis 37:35), and he refused, is וְסָרֵיב, and he refused; and the Targum of עַם מְרִי (Yeshayahu 30:9), a rebellious people, is סַרְבָן, a refuser.

The word is known in the words of Chazal, as they say, ולא יהיה סרבן באותה שעה (Berachos 5:3, 34a), and let him not be one who refuses at that hour; and besides this, Radak says, there is a great deal more.

חסל.sense: To cut off and make an end of; so the kind of locust that destroys most is called חָסִיל, and from this comes חסלת, said of a seder or masechta when it is finished.

more.t: כִּי יַחְסְלֶנּוּ הָֽאַרְבֶּֽה (Devarim 28:38), for the locust will make an end of it, is יכרתנו ויכלנו, it will cut it off and finish it. That is why the kind of locust that destroys most is called חָסִיל, as in וְהֶֽחָסִיל וְהַגָּזָם (Yoel 2:25), the chasil and the gazam.

Chazal asked why it is called חָסִיל and answered שהוא חוסל הכל, that it makes an end of everything; and of another of its names, גובי דהוא גבי דינא דמריה, that it collects its Master's due. From this comes the way of saying that a thing is done and complete, חסלת סדר פלוני או מסכת פלונית, such a seder is finished, or such a masechta.

חגב.sense: A chagav, one of the kinds of locust: וַנְּהִי בְעֵינֵינוּ כַּֽחֲגָבִים (Bamidbar 13:33), we were like chagavim in our own eyes.

more.h: One of the kinds of locust
more.t: וְאֶת־ הֶֽחָגָב לְמִינֵֽהוּ (Vayikra 11:22), and the chagav after its kind, is one of the kinds of locust.

וְיִסְתַּבֵּל הֶֽחָגָב (Koheles 12:5), the chagav shall be a burden, has been read (Shabbos 152a) as though the word were עגב, as in וַתַּעְגְּבָה עֲלֵיהֶם (Yechezkel 23:16), she lusted after them, so that it hints at the organ of relations. Radak holds the plain meaning is the right one, and says he will explain the word at the root סבל.

צלל.sense: Shade and shadow, and growing shadowed or casting shade. A second sense is the motion of a noise, as in ringing ears, and from it bells and cymbals; a third is sinking.

more.t: יָמָיו כְּצֵל עוֹבֵֽר (Tehillim 144:4), his days are like a passing shadow, is like the shadow that passes quickly as the sunlight spreads. It can also be read as the shadow of a bird passing in its flight, and so it was explained in the Midrash: כהדין עופא דעבר בטוליה וטוליה עבר עמיה, like that bird which passes by with its shadow, and its shadow passes along with it. So כִּי יִנָּטוּ צִלְלֵי ־עָֽרֶב (Yirmiyahu 6:4), for the shadows of evening stretch out; יְסֻכֻּהוּ צֶאֱלִים צִלְלוֹ (Iyov 40:22), the shade trees cover him with their shadow; וְלֹֽא־יַֽאֲרִיךְ יָמִים כַּצֵּל (Koheles 8:13), he will not lengthen his days, like a shadow; בְּצֵל קֹֽרָתִֽי (Bereishis 19:8), in the shade of my roof; סָר צִלָּם מֵֽעֲלֵיהֶם (Bamidbar 14:9), their shadow has turned away from them; וְנָסוּ הַצְּלָלִים (Shir HaShirim 2:17), and the shadows flee.

more.h: In the shade of wisdom and of money
more.t: בְּצֵל הַֽחָכְמָה בְּצֵל הַכָּסֶף (Koheles 7:12), in the shade of wisdom, in the shade of money, means that a man rests in the shade of wisdom when he is also in the shade of money and has enough for his needs: he is better received by others when he has no need of them, and he can occupy himself with wisdom when he has what to live on. So the other pasuk says, טוֹבָה חָכְמָה עִם־נַֽחֲלָה (Koheles 7:11), wisdom is good with an inheritance; and even so, the advantage of knowledge is that wisdom by itself keeps its owner alive.

more.h: A land that shades with wings
more.t: הוֹי אֶרֶץ צִלְצַל כְּנָפָיִם (Yeshayahu 18:1), woe, land that shades with wings, is a land that casts shade over the world with the great number of its wings, a figure for the quantity of goods and wares that go out from it to other lands. Targum Yonasan rendered it דְאָתָן לָהּ בִּסְפִינָן מֵאַרְעָא רְחִיקָא וְקִלְעֵיהוֹן פְּרִיסָן כְּנִשְׁרָא דְטָאִיס בְּכַנְפוֹהִי, that they come to it in ships from a far land, their sails spread like an eagle flying with its wings.

כַּֽאֲשֶׁר צָֽלְלוּ שַֽׁעֲרֵי יְרֽוּשָׁלַם (Nechemiah 13:19), when the gates of Yerushalayim grew shadowed, is that the sun had set; and וְחֹרֶשׁ מֵצַל (Yechezkel 31:3), a thicket casting shade, is the form that means making shade, or else it may be a word of description.

Another sense: לְקוֹל צָֽלְלוּ שְׂפָתַי (Chavakuk 3:16), at the sound my lips quivered; תִּצַּלְנָה שְׁתֵּי אָזְנָֽיו (Melachim II 21:12), both his ears will ring; תִּצַּלְנָה אָזְנָֽיו (Yirmiyahu 19:3), his ears will ring; תְּצִלֶּינָה שְׁתֵּי אָזְנָֽיו (Shmuel I 3:11), both his ears will ring. The sense is the motion of a noise, which he names in the vernacular. The noun is צְלִיל (Shoftim 7:13): the noise of a לֶחֶם שְׂעֹרִים, a barley loaf, which was heard and then seen turning over in the camp of Midian. He takes the word up again under the root צָלָה.

From this come מְצִלּוֹת הַסּוּס (Zecharyah 14:20), the bells of the horse, the jingles hung on a horse that knock against each other. So too, with the first root letter doubled, וּבִמְנַֽעַנְעִים וּבְצֶלְצֶלִֽים (Shmuel II 6:5), with rattles and with cymbals, and בְצִֽלְצְלֵי ־שָׁמַע (Tehillim 150:5), sounding cymbals: two bronze vessels struck one against the other to make a sound, as the Mishnah says, הקיש בן ארזא בצלצל (Shekalim 5:1), ben Arza struck the cymbal. But בְּֽצִלְצְלֵי תְרוּעָֽה (Tehillim 150:5), with the tziltzelim of the blast, speaks of the trumpets. בַּֽמְצִלְתַּיִם (Ezra 3:10), with cymbals, and בִּמְצִלְתַּיִם נְחֹשֶׁת לְהַשְׁמִֽיעַ (Divrei HaYamim I 15:19), with bronze cymbals to sound out, drop the doubled letter, and the word stands in the form of two because they are a pair struck together.

A further sense is sinking: צָֽלֲלוּ כַּֽעוֹפֶרֶת (Shemos 15:10), they sank like lead, and with it כַּֽאֲשֶׁר צָֽלְלוּ שַֽׁעֲרֵי יְרֽוּשָׁלַם (Nechemiah 13:19), when the gates of Yerushalayim sank; Rabbi Yehudah brought the two so too. On that reading the gates of Yerushalayim were sunk away from being entered, which is to say that it was evening. Radak holds that the right reading of that pasuk is the one given above, from צֵל, shade.

וּבְצִלְצַל דָּגִים רֹאשֽׁוֹ (Iyov 40:31), and his head with a fish tziltzal, is a tool with which a fish is speared in the water and lifted out, which he names in the vernacular; and there are those who say it is a vessel made of rods that the fish's head goes into and is caught in.

ישׁע.sense: Deliverance, in the nouns יֵשַׁע and תְּשׁוּעָה; the verb is to save, and to be saved.

more.t: The noun takes a tzere in יָצָאתָ לְיֵשַׁע עַמֶּךָ (Chavakuk 3:13), You went out for the deliverance of Your people; a segol in וְיֶשְֽׁעֲךָ תִּתֶּן־לָֽנוּ (Tehillim 85:8), and grant us Your deliverance; and a chirik under the yud in כִּֽי־כָל־ יִשְׁעִי וְכָל־חֵפֶץ כִּי־לֹא יַצְמִֽיחַ (Shmuel II 23:5), for all my deliverance and all desire, will He not make it grow?

וַֽיְהִי־לִי לִֽישׁוּעָה (Shemos 15:2), and He became my deliverance; אֱמֹר לְנַפְשִׁי יְֽשֻֽׁעָתֵךְ אָֽנִי (Tehillim 35:3), say to my soul, I am your deliverance. With a tav added and the first letter of the root falling away: תְּשׁוּעָה גְדוֹלָה (Shmuel I 19:5), a great deliverance; הַנּוֹתֵן תְּשׁוּעָה לַמְּלָכִים (Tehillim 144:10), who gives deliverance to kings; וּתְשׁוּעָה בְּרֹב יוֹעֵֽץ (Mishlei 11:14), and deliverance in many counsellors; שֶׁקֶר הַסּוּס לִתְשׁוּעָה (Tehillim 33:17), a horse is a false thing for deliverance; and הַתְּשׁוּעָֽה (Mishlei 21:31), deliverance, which the pasuk gives to Hashem.

more.h: His father on a word in Iyov
more.t: His father takes אִם־בְּפִידוֹ לָהֶן שֽׁוּעַ (Iyov 30:24), if in his פיד they have deliverance, from this sense. That is, in the פיד, which is the day of death, there is deliverance for those whose strength was worn out in life, as it says וְשָׁם יָנוּחוּ יְגִיעֵי כֹֽחַ (Iyov 3:17), and there the weary of strength rest. On that reading שֽׁוּעַ is from יָשַׁע with the first letter of the root missing, as בוּל הָרִים (Iyov 40:20), the produce of the hills, is like יְבוּל with its first letter missing.

הוֹשִׁיעַ (Tehillim 20:7), Hashem has saved His anointed; וַיְהִי לָהֶם לְמוֹשִֽׁיעַ (Yeshayahu 63:8), and He became a saviour to them; הוֹשַׁע (Yirmiyahu 31:7), save, Hashem, Your people; הֽוֹשִׁיעֵנוּ אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׁעֵנוּ (Divrei HaYamim I 16:35), save us, God of our deliverance; and the noun מוֹשָׁעָה, deliverance, with the plural in הָאֵל לָנוּ אֵל לְֽמוֹשָׁעוֹת (Tehillim 68:21), God is to us a God of deliverances.

יִשְׂרָאֵל נוֹשַׁע (Yeshayahu 45:17), Israel was saved, and עַם נוֹשַׁע (Devarim 33:29), a people that was saved, take a patach, since they are past verbs; אֵין הַמֶּלֶךְ נוֹשָׁע בְּרָב־חָיִל, the king is not saved by a great army, takes a kamatz, since it is עומד, standing, and not a past verb. וְנֽוֹשַׁעְתֶּם מֵאֹֽיְבֵיכֶֽם (Bamidbar 10:9), and you will be saved from your enemies.

נצל.sense: To be rescued and to rescue, to take away, and to strip. The sense is removal and stripping, and rescue falls under it, as removal from the one who takes a man.

more.t: וַֽאֲמַרְתֶּם נִצַּלְנוּ (Yirmiyahu 7:10), and you say, we are saved; אֲשֶׁר־ יִנָּצֵל אֵלֶיךָ (Devarim 23:16), who escapes to you; לְהִנָּצֵל מִפְּנֵי מֶלֶךְ אַשּׁוּר (Yeshayahu 20:6), to be delivered from the king of Ashur; הֵמָּה בְצִדְקָתָם יְנַצְּלוּ נַפְשָׁם (Yechezkel 14:14), they by their righteousness will deliver their own soul.

וְהַצֵּל לֹֽא־ הִצַּלְתָּ אֶת־עַמֶּֽךָ (Shemos 5:23), and you have not delivered your people at all; וְהִצַּלְתֶּם אֶת־נַפְשֹׁתֵינוּ (Yehoshua 2:13), and you shall save our lives; לְמַעַן הַצִּיל אֹתוֹ (Bereishis 37:22), in order to save him; כְּאוּד מֻצָּל מִשְּׂרֵפָה (Amos 4:11), like a brand pulled out of the burning; הֲלוֹא זֶה אוּד מֻצָּל מֵאֵֽשׁ (Zecharyah 3:2), is this not a brand pulled out of the fire; and the noun רֶוַח וְהַצָּלָה (Esther 4:14), relief and deliverance.

more.h: Taking away, of the stripping sense
more.t: אֲשֶׁר הִצִּיל אֱלֹהִים מֵֽאָבִינוּ (Bereishis 31:16), which Hashem took away from our father, and וַיַּצֵּל אֱלֹהִים אֶת־מִקְנֵה אֲבִיכֶם (Bereishis 31:9), Hashem took away your father's cattle. וְהִצִּיל עֵינֵֽנוּ (Shmuel II 20:6), and take away our eye, he reads as his taking away our sight and the view of our eyes by entering one of the places; and וְאַל־ תַּצֵּל מִפִּי דְבַר־אֱמֶת עַד־מְאֹד (Tehillim 119:43), and do not take the word of truth out of my mouth utterly.

Close in sense to rescue: וְנִצַּלְתֶּם אֶת־מִצְרָֽיִם (Shemos 3:22), and you will strip Egypt, and וַיְנַצְּלוּ לָהֶם לְאֵין מַשָּׂא (Divrei HaYamim II 20:25), they stripped for themselves more than they could carry. וַיִּתְנַצְּלוּ בְנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶת־עֶדְיָם מֵהַר חוֹרֵֽב (Shemos 33:6), the children of Israel stripped themselves of their ornaments from Mount Chorev, he reads as their taking the ornaments off and wearing them no more. The sense is removal and stripping away, and the first sense falls under it too, since a rescue is a removal from the one who takes him.

פרק.sense: Breaking, and parting one thing from another: a yoke off the neck, rings from the ears; and close to it, tearing a man free from his foes.

more.t: וּפָֽרַקְתָּ עֻלּוֹ מֵעַל צַוָּארֶֽךָ (Bereishis 27:40), you will break his yoke off your neck; פֹּרֵק וְאֵין מַצִּֽיל (Tehillim 7:3), tearing with none to rescue; פָּֽרְקוּ נִזְמֵי הַזָּהָב (Shemos 32:2), break off the golden rings; וּפַרְסֵיהֶן יְפָרֵֽק (Zecharyah 11:16), he will tear off their hooves; מְפָרֵק הָרִים (Melachim I 19:11), breaking the mountains. All of it is breaking, and the parting of one thing from another.

הִתְפָּרָקוּ וַיִּתְּנוּ־לִי (Shemos 32:24), they took them off and gave them to me, and וַיִּֽתְפָּֽרְקוּ כָּל־הָעָם (Shemos 32:3), and all the people took them off, mean that they broke themselves free of the golden rings in their ears. The form that turns the act back on the doer is used because they did it with great eagerness, wanting to be rid of their rings and have them no longer. The same form stands in הִתְפָּרְקוּ וְיָבֵשׁוּ (Yechezkel 19:12), they were broken off and dried up.

more.h: Do not stand at the perek
more.t: The noun is a breaking: כַּחַשׁ פֶּרֶק מְלֵאָה (Nachum 3:1), full of lying and of breaking. וְאַֽל־תַּֽעֲמֹד עַל־ הַפֶּרֶק in Ovadiah, do not stand at the perek, means that you should not have stood over the breaking that came upon Yisrael, but should have saved them if you could, in the way of לֹא תַֽעֲמֹד עַל־דַּם רֵעֶךָ (Vayikra 19:16), do not stand by your fellow's blood. Some explain על הפרק as at the head of the roads, the place where the roads part: there you stood and told the Bavliim which way the fugitive had gone.

וַתִּשָּׁבֵר מַפְרַקְתּוֹ (Shmuel I 4:18), his mafrekes was broken, is the bone of the neck. So Chazal say, ודילמא בעצם המפרקה איפגים (Chullin 10b), perhaps it was the neck bone that was nicked. It is called so because it is made of joint upon joint.

A sense close to the first: וַיִּפְרְקֵנוּ מִצָּרֵינוּ (Tehillim 136:24), He tore us free from our foes; פֹּרֵק אֵין מִיָּדָֽם (Eichah 5:8), there is none to tear us out of their hand; and the Targum of וַיּוֹשַׁע (Shemos 14:30), and He saved, is וּפְרַק.

עקד.sense: To tie, which he glosses ויקשור; and the flock called עֲקֻדִּים, so named because their spots were where the foreleg is bent onto the leg and tied.

more.t: וַֽיַּֽעֲקֹד אֶת־יִצְחָק בְּנוֹ (Bereishis 22:9), and he bound Yitzchak his son: ויקשור, and he tied.

וַיִּתֵּן פְּנֵי הַצֹּאן אֶל־ עָקֹד (Bereishis 30:40), and he set the faces of the flock toward the akod, and עֲקֻדִּים נְקֻדִּים (Bereishis 30:39), the ringed and the speckled: their spots were at the place where the foreleg and the leg are tied, for the foreleg is bent onto the leg and tied, and at that very place their spots were; and so they are called akudim.

בֵּֽית־ עֵקֶד הָֽרֹעִים (Melachim II 10:12), Beis Eked of the shepherds: Targum Yonasan renders בֵּית כְּנִישַׁת רַעֲיָא, the shepherds' gathering house. Radak's father explains it as the house where the shepherds sheared their flocks, and at the shearing they tie them by their legs, at the place of binding.

חבשׁ.sense: To bind and fasten: headgear bound on, a wound bound up, a beast tied with its girth; and ruling, since a ruler confines and binds whoever breaks his commands.

more.t: וְחָֽבַשְׁתָּ לָהֶם מִגְבָּעֹת (Shemos 29:9), and you shall bind turbans on them; פְּאֵֽרְךָ חֲבוֹשׁ עָלֶיךָ (Yechezkel 24:17), bind your headdress upon you; סוּף חָבוּשׁ לְרֹאשִֽׁי (Yonah 2:6), weed was bound about my head; פְּנֵיהֶם חֲבֹשׁ בַּטָּמֽוּן (Iyov 40:13), bind their faces in the hidden place; and מִבְּכִי נְהָרוֹת חִבֵּשׁ (Iyov 28:11), he binds up the rivers from weeping. All of them and their like, he says, are tying and binding fast.

It is also the binding of a wound and the wrapping laid over it: וְלַנִּשְׁבֶּרֶת לֹא חֲבַשְׁתֶּם (Yechezkel 34:4), and the broken you did not bind up; כִּי הוּא יַכְאִיב וְיֶחְבָּשׁ (Iyov 5:18), for He wounds and He binds up; וּמְחַבֵּשׁ לְעַצְּבוֹתָֽם (Tehillim 147:3), binding up their sorrows; and in the passive, לֹא־זֹרוּ וְלֹא חֻבָּשׁוּ (Yeshayahu 1:6), they were not pressed out and not bound up.

Because a ruler confines and binds whoever breaks his commands, the word is used of ruling: לֹֽא־אֶהְיֶה חֹבֵשׁ (Yeshayahu 3:7), I will not be a ruler, and האף שֹונא משׁפט יַֽחֲבוֹשׁ (Iyov 34:17), shall even one who hates justice rule?

It is also tying a beast with its girth: וַֽיַּֽחֲבֹשׁ אֶת־חֲמֹרוֹ (Bereishis 22:3), and he girthed his donkey; חִבְשׁוּ ־לִי הַֽחֲמוֹר (Melachim I 13:13), girth the donkey for me; צֶמֶד חֲמוֹרִים חֲבוּשִׁים (Shoftim 19:10), a pair of girthed donkeys. All the words of this root, he says, are one sense.

וַעֲרָפֶל חֲתֻלָּתוֹ (Iyov 38:9), and thick cloud its wrapping; וְהָחְתֵּל לֹא חֻתָּלְתְּ (Yechezkel 16:4), and you were not wrapped at all; לָשׂוּם חִתּול (Yechezkel 30:21), to put on a binding. Their sense is binding up and wrapping.

שׁאג.sense: The lion's cry is called שאגה, a roar; the word is borrowed for a man's moaning and the voice he gives over his troubles.

more.t: אַרְיֵה שָׁאָג (Amos 3:8), a lion has roared; שֹׁאֵג לִקְרָאתוֹ (Shoftim 14:5), roaring toward him; שֹׁאֲגִים לַטָּרֶף (Tehillim 104:21), roaring after prey; עָלָיו יִשְׁאֲגוּ כְפִרִים (Yirmiyahu 2:15), young lions roared over him; and שָׁאֹג יִשְׁאַג עַל נָוֵהוּ (Yirmiyahu 25:30), he shall surely roar over his dwelling.

שָׁאַגְתִּי מִנַּהֲמַת לִבִּי (Tehillim 38:9), I have roared from the groaning of my heart, and וַיִּתְּכוּ כַמַּיִם שַׁאֲגֹתָי (Iyov 3:24), my roarings pour out like water. The lion's cry is called שאגה, and the word is borrowed for a man's moaning and the voice he gives over his troubles.
שְׁאָגָה לוֹ כַּלָּבִיא (Yeshayahu 5:29), he has a roar like a lioness, and in construct שַׁאֲגַת אַרְיֵה וְקוֹל שָׁחַל (Iyov 4:10), the roar of the lion and the voice of the fierce lion.

נהם.sense: Its sense is like that of שאגה, roaring: said of men, of young lions, of the sea, and of the heart.

more.t: וְנָֽהַמְתָּ בְאַֽחֲרִיתֶךָ (Mishlei 5:11), and you will roar at your end, and וּנְהַמְתֶּם אִישׁ אֶל־אָחִֽיו (Yechezkel 24:23), and you shall roar one to another; so too מִנַּֽהֲמַת לִבִּֽי (Tehillim 38:9), from the roaring of my heart.

וִשְׁאַג [יִשְׁאַג] כַּכְּפִירִים וְיִנְהֹם (Yeshayahu 5:29), he roars like the young lions, and he roars; the noun נַהַם כַּכְּפִיר אֵימַת מֶלֶךְ (Mishlei 20:2), the dread of a king is a roaring like a young lion's; and of the sea, כְּנַֽהֲמַת ־יָם (Yeshayahu 5:30), like the roaring of the sea.

הגה.sense: Speech and the chirping sound of the mouth, said also of a lion and of doves; his father holds it all mumbling, not speech. In another sense, removing.

more.h: Speech and the sound of the mouth
more.t: וְהָגִיתִי בְכָל־פָּעֳלֶךָ (Tehillim 77:13), and I will speak of all Your work; לֹֽא־ יֶהְגּוּ בִּגְרוֹנָֽם (Tehillim 115:7), they make no sound in their throat; וּלְשׁוֹנִי אִם־ יֶהְגֶּה רְמִיָּֽה (Iyov 27:4), nor shall my tongue utter deceit; כִּֽי־אֱמֶת יֶהְגֶּה חִכִּי (Mishlei 8:7), for my palate speaks truth; יֶהְגוּ ־רִֽיק (Tehillim 2:1), they utter emptiness. The sense of all of it is speech and the chirping of the mouth.

more.h: Lion, doves, and those who chirp
more.t: כַּֽאֲשֶׁר יֶהְגֶּה הָֽאַרְיֵה (Yeshayahu 31:4), as the lion growls; וְכַיּוֹנִים הָגֹה נֶהְגֶּה (Yeshayahu 59:11), we moan and moan like doves; and הַֽמְצַפְצְפִים וְהַמַּהְגִּים (Yeshayahu 8:19), those who chirp and mutter.

וְהֶגֶה מִפִּיו יֵצֵֽא (Iyov 37:2), and a sound goes out from his mouth; כִּלִּינוּ שָׁנֵינוּ כְמוֹ־ הֶֽגֶה (Tehillim 90:9), we spend our years like a sound; קִנִים וָהֶגֶה וָהִֽי (Yechezkel 2:10), lamentations, moaning and woe. In other patterns, הִגָּיוֹן סֶֽלָה (Tehillim 9:17), utterance, selah; וְהֶגְיוֹן לִבִּי לְפָנֶיךָ (Tehillim 19:15), and the utterance of my heart before You; בִּינָה הֲגִֽיגִי (Tehillim 5:2), consider my utterance; and וְהָגוּת לִבִּי תְבוּנֽוֹת (Tehillim 49:4), and the utterance of my heart is understanding.

more.h: A form pointed to match its neighbour
more.t: הֹרוֹ וְהֹגוֹ מִלֵּב דִּבְרֵי־שָֽׁקֶר (Yeshayahu 59:13), putting forth and uttering words of falsehood from the heart, is an infinitive. His father writes that הֹרוֹ has its cholam by rule, being from יָרָה, like וּלְהוֹרֹת אֶת־בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (Vayikra 10:11), and to teach Bnei Yisrael, and that וְהֹגוֹ came with a cholam too, to pair the two words, as with the pair אֶת־מוֹצָֽאֲךָ וְאֶת־מֹבָואֶךָ (Shmuel II 3:25), your going out and your coming in.

more.h: His father on what it is not
more.t: His father holds the whole root a mumbling and a chirping, with no sense of reading or speaking in it. So וּֽבְתוֹרָתוֹ יֶהְגֶּה (Tehillim 1:2), and in His Torah he mumbles, is not the reading itself: a man reads in Torah so much that at every hour, even when he is not reading, the words come out upon his mouth and appear on his lips. The proof he gives is וְכַיּוֹנִים הָגֹה נֶהְגֶּה (Yeshayahu 59:11), we moan and moan like doves, which is chirping and is like a sound of wailing, and so קִנִים וָהֶגֶה (Yechezkel 2:10), lamentations and moaning.

הָגָה בְּרוּחוֹ הַקָּשָׁה (Yeshayahu 27:8), He removed it with His harsh wind; הָגוֹ סִיגִים מִכָּסֶף (Mishlei 25:4), take the dross away from the silver; and הָגוֹ רָשָׁע לִפְנֵי־מֶלֶךְ (Mishlei 25:5), take the wicked man away from before the king: the sense is removal. His father puts כַּֽאֲשֶׁר הֹגָּה מִן־הַֽמְסִלָּה (Shmuel II 20:13), when he was moved off the highway, in this root and this sense.

שׁוק.sense: Four senses: longing and desire; vats flooding over, as water floods; the street; and the leg.

more.t: וְאֶל אִישֵׁךְ תְּשׁוּקָתֵךְ (Bereishis 3:16), your longing shall be toward your husband; וְאֵלֶיךָ תְּשׁוּקָתוֹ (Bereishis 4:7), its longing is toward you; וְעָלַי תְּשׁוּקָתוֹ (Shir HaShirim 7:11), his desire is upon me. Their sense, he says, is desire and longing; and וְנַפְשׁוֹ שׁוֹקֵקָה (Yeshayahu 29:8), and his soul craves, may be of this sense and this root.

פָּקַדְתָּ הָאָרֶץ וַתְּשֹׁקְקֶהָ (Tehillim 65:10) he reads two ways: You visited the land and longed for it, to sate it; or, as a transitive verb, You had already made it long, decreeing that it crave the rain, and only afterward did You visit it.

וְהֵשִׁיקוּ הַיְקָבִים תִּירוֹשׁ וְיִצְהָר (Yoel 2:24), the vats shall overflow with wine and oil. Its sense is like וְהֵצִיפוּ, they made flood over, from הֵצִיף אֶת מֵי יַם סוּף (Devarim 11:4), He made the waters of the Yam Suf flood over them.

So too in the words of Chazal (Pesachim 34b): waters of the Chag that became tamei, if he השיקן and afterward sanctified them, they are tahor; if he sanctified them and afterward השיקן, they are tamei. Radak explains השיקן as sinking them in the water of a mikveh until the mikveh water floods over them.
וְסָבְבוּ בַשּׁוּק (Koheles 12:5), they go about in the street, and בַּשְּׁוָקִים וּבָרְחֹבוֹת (Shir HaShirim 3:2), in the streets and in the squares. He calls this sense known and does not gloss it.

שׁוֹק הַיָּמִין (Shemos 29:22), the right leg; עַל הַבִּרְכַּיִם וְעַל הַשֹּׁקַיִם (Devarim 28:35), on the knees and on the legs; שׁוֹקָיו עַמּוּדֵי שֵׁשׁ (Shir HaShirim 5:15), his legs are pillars of marble. אֶת הַשּׁוֹק וְהֶעָלֶיהָ (Shmuel I 9:24), the leg and what was upon it: what was upon it is the thigh, which is above the leg. The reflexive of it is יִשְׁתַּקְשְׁקוּן בָּרְחֹבוֹת (Nachum 2:5), they run to and fro in the squares, which he again calls known and leaves unglossed.

וַיַּךְ אוֹתָם שׁוֹק עַל יָרֵךְ (Shoftim 15:8), and he smote them leg upon thigh, he explains as felling them with the blow: a man falling before his pursuer buckles at the knees and drops on his face, so that his leg lies upon his thigh. His father explains otherwise, שׁוֹק being the foot soldier and יָרֵךְ the man riding the horse, and so Targum Yonasan renders פָּרָשִׁין עִם רִגְלָאִין, horsemen with footmen.

נהק.sense: Making a noise, המיה, which is his sense for both pesukim: the wild donkey over grass, and those among the bushes.

more.t: הֲיִנְהַק־פֶּרֶא עֲלֵי־דֶשֶׁא (Iyov 6:5), does the wild donkey make a noise over grass, and בֵּֽין־שִׂיחִים יִנְהָקוּ (Iyov 30:7), among the bushes they make a noise. Their sense is המיה, making a noise.

שׁען.sense: To lean, on a thing or on Hashem. The nouns are a stay and support, and מִשְׁעֶנֶת, a staff.

more.t: וְנִשְׁעַן לִגְבוּל מוֹאָב (Bamidbar 21:15), leaning up against the border of Moav; וְהוּא נִשְׁעָן עַל יָדִי (Melachim II 5:18), he leans on my hand; יִשָּׁעֵן עַל בֵּיתוֹ (Iyov 8:15), he leans on his house. The same word is relying on Hashem, at Yeshayahu 10:20 and Divrei HaYamim II 13:18, and so too לְהִשָּׁעֵן עַל מַכֵּהוּ (Yeshayahu 10:20), leaning on the one who strikes him.

מַשְׁעֵן וּמַשְׁעֵנָה (Yeshayahu 3:1), stay and support, and in construct in that same pasuk כֹּל מִשְׁעַן לֶחֶם וְכֹל מִשְׁעַן מָיִם, every stay of bread and every stay of water. In another form, לְמִשְׁעָן לִי (Tehillim 18:19), Hashem became a support to me; and he allows that כֹּל מִשְׁעַן לֶחֶם may belong to this second form.
עַל מִשְׁעֶנֶת הַקָּנֶה הָרָצוּץ (Yeshayahu 36:6), on the staff of that crushed reed, and עַל מִשְׁעַנְתּוֹ (Shemos 21:19), on his staff.

מַקֵּל שָׁקֵד (Yirmiyahu 1:11), a rod of almond; מַקֵּל תִּפְאָרָה (Yirmiyahu 48:17), a rod of beauty; וּבְמַקֵּל יָד (Yechezkel 39:9), a hand staff; מַקַּל לִבְנֶה (Bereishis 30:37), a rod of livneh; כִּי בְמַקְלִי עָבַרְתִּי (Bereishis 32:11), with my staff I crossed over; וּמַקְלוֹ יַגִּיד לוֹ (Hoshea 4:12), his stick tells him.

The first three carry a tzeirei and מַקַּל לִבְנֶה a patach; with a suffix and in the plural the dagesh falls away, as at כִּי בְמַקְלִי עָבַרְתִּי and וַיַּצֵּג אֶת הַמַּקְלוֹת (Bereishis 30:38), he set up the rods. He allows that the word may belong with the roots whose first letter is a nun, the mem being added.

שׁרב.sense: Heat; and in one pasuk, the place of desert and drought.

more.h: Heat, and the place of drought
more.t: וְלֹֽא־יַכֵּם שָׁרָב וָשָׁמֶשׁ (Yeshayahu 49:10), neither heat nor sun shall strike them: its sense, he says, is the heat. At וְהָיָה הַשָּׁרָב לַֽאֲגָם (Yeshayahu 35:7), the sharav shall become a pool, he reads it as the place of desert and drought. The Targum renders אֲכָלַנִי חֹרֶב (Bereishis 31:40), drought consumed me, with this same word, אֲכַלְנִי שַׁרְבָא, the sharav consumed me.

חטר.sense: A rod, the word the Targum gives for מַטֶּה, a staff; and in Mishlei the rod of pride in the fool's mouth, which he and Rabbi Yonah read differently.

more.t: וְיָצָא חֹטֶר מִגֶּזַע יִשָׁי (Yeshayahu 11:1), a rod shall come out of the stock of Yishai. The Targum renders מַטֶּה (Shemos 4:2), a staff, as חוּטְרָא.

בְּפִי אֱוִיל חֹטֶר גַּאֲוָה (Mishlei 14:3) he reads as the rod of pride in the fool's mouth, since the fool speaks proud and lofty words against men. Rabbi Yonah takes it the other way about: on account of the words the fool speaks, a rod of pride comes upon him. Radak explains this to mean that the fool is struck great blows for what he said.

זקן.sense: To grow old, with the old man, the elder and old age; and, under the same letters, the beard.

more.t: וַיְהִי כִּי זָקֵן יִצְחָק (Bereishis 27:1), and it was when Yitzchak grew old, is a verb, while וְאַבְרָהָם זָקֵן (Bereishis 24:1), and Avraham was old, is an adjective. In construct, זְקַן בֵּיתוֹ (Bereishis 24:2), the elder of his house; and זָקַנְתִּי וָשַׂבְתִּי (Shmuel I 12:2), I am old and grey.

כִּי בֶן זְקֻנִים הוּא לוֹ (Bereishis 37:3), for he was a son of old age to him, and בֵּן לִזְקֻנָיו (Bereishis 21:2), a son to his old age: זְקֻנִים is a plural noun from which no singular comes, like נְעוּרִים, youth, and בְּתוּלִים, maidenhood. In other patterns, וְעֵינֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כָּֽבְדוּ מִזֹּקֶן (Bereishis 48:10), and the eyes of Yisrael were heavy with age; and זִקְנָה, old age, in וְעַד־ זִקְנָה אֲנִי הוּא (Yeshayahu 46:4), even to old age I am He, and אַֽחֲרֵי זִקְנָתָהּ (Bereishis 24:36), after her old age.
אִם יַזְקִין בָּאָרֶץ שָׁרְשׁוֹ (Iyov 14:8), though its root grow old in the ground, and גַּם כִּי יַזְקִין לֹא יָסוּר מִמֶּנָּה (Mishlei 22:6), even when he is old he will not turn from it.

וְגַם אֶת הַזָּקָן תִּסְפֶּה (Yeshayahu 7:20), and the beard too shall be swept away; in construct בִּזְקַן עֲמָשָׂא לִנְשָׁק לוֹ (Shmuel II 20:9), by Amasa's beard, to kiss him, and וְהֶחֱזַקְתִּי בִּזְקָנוֹ (Shmuel I 17:35), and I took hold of his beard. The word comes as a masculine at עַד יְצַמַּח זְקַנְכֶם (Shmuel II 10:5), until your beard grows, and as a feminine at וְכָל זָקָן גְּרֻעָה (Yirmiyahu 48:37), every beard shorn, and again at וְגַם אֶת הַזָּקָן תִּסְפֶּה.

ישׁשׁ.sense: The aged, further on in years than the זָקֵן, the old, or the שָׂב, the grey-haired; he takes it from יֵשׁ, being, which has stood in him many days.

more.t: זָקֵן וְיָשֵׁשׁ (Divrei HaYamim II 36:17), old and aged, with a tzeirei; and with a chirik גַּם שָׂב גַּם יָשִׁישׁ בָּנוּ (Iyov 15:10), among us are both the grey-haired and the aged, and בִּישִׁישִׁים חָכְמָה (Iyov 12:12), wisdom is with the aged. They are the elders, many of days, and he holds the yashish further on in years than the zakein and than the sav.
He holds it right that the word be of the sense of יֵשׁ, there is, and reckons יָשָׁה and יְשַׁשׁ one sense; the old man is called יָשִׁישׁ because being has stood in him many days.

קשׁשׁ.sense: To gather up fine things, straw or thin sticks, the verb being derived from קַשׁ, straw; and likewise of searching out faults and gathering them with care.

more.t: לְקֹשֵׁשׁ קַשׁ (Shemos 5:12), to gather straw, and מְקֹשֵׁשׁ עֵצִים (Bamidbar 15:32), gathering wood. The kash is the fine straw, or the thin sticks, and the verb is derived from it: the picking up of fine things, straw or wood. He gives the vernacular word for it.

The word is used likewise of searching out blemishes and gathering them with care, as with fine things, which need careful searching. הִתְקוֹשְׁשׁוּ וָקוֹשּׁוּ (Tzefaniah 2:1), search yourselves and search, means search yourselves of your own evil blemishes and afterwards search others, as Chazal said from this pasuk (Bava Basra 60a), correct yourself and afterwards correct others. They also said (Yerushalmi Shabbos), נקשש גרמין עד לא נקשש אחרין, let us search ourselves before we search others.

Likewise וְלַמּוֹכִיחַ בַּשַּׁעַר יְקֹשׁוּן (Yeshayahu 29:21), and the one who reproves in the gate they search out, the quiescent letter standing in place of the doubling. It means that they reprove the reprovers, in the manner of what Chazal said (Bava Basra 15b) of a generation that judges its judges: one says to him, take the splinter from between your eyes, and he says back, take the beam from between your eyes.

שׁבט.sense: A tribe, in sense a family but larger than one; a rod, for striking or for chastening; and, since a ruler holds a rod, the head and ruler himself.

more.t: לְשֵׁבֶט וּלְמִשְׁפָּחָה (Shoftim 18:19), for a tribe and for a family; שְׁבָטִים שִׁבְטֵי יָהּ (Tehillim 122:4), the tribes, the tribes of Hashem; בְּכָל שִׁבְטֵי בִנְיָמִן (Shoftim 20:12), through all the tribes of Binyamin; and הִתְעוּ אֶת מִצְרַיִם פִּנַּת שְׁבָטֶיהָ (Yeshayahu 19:13), they led Mitzrayim astray, the cornerstone of her tribes. The sense of them all is family, but the tribe is larger than the family: מִשְׁפְּחוֹת שִׁבְטֵי בִנְיָמִן (Shmuel I 9:21), the families of the tribes of Binyamin, and וַיַּקְרֵב אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל לִשְׁבָטָיו (Yehoshua 7:16), he brought Yisrael near by its tribes, and afterwards וַיַּקְרֵב אֶת מִשְׁפַּחַת יְהוּדָה, he brought near the family of Yehudah.

more.h: One word for all the tribes
more.t: וְיִשְׂרָאֵל שֵׁבֶט נַחֲלָתוֹ (Yirmiyahu 10:16), and Yisrael is the tribe of His inheritance, where the one word covers all the tribes together.

וְכִי יַכֶּה אִישׁ אֶת עַבְדּוֹ אוֹ אֶת אֲמָתוֹ בַּשֵּׁבֶט (Shemos 21:20), and if a man strikes his servant or his maidservant with the rod; תְּרֹעֵם בְּשֵׁבֶט בַּרְזֶל (Tehillim 2:9), You shall break them with a rod of iron; וּפָקַדְתִּי בְשֵׁבֶט פִּשְׁעָם (Tehillim 89:33), I will visit their sin with a rod; שֵׁבֶט מוּסָר יַרְחִיקֶנָּה מִמֶּנּוּ (Mishlei 22:15), the rod of discipline drives it far from him. It is a מטה, a staff, and the family is likewise called a מטה, as he writes at the root נָטָה, since in a family each one is a rod and a staff to his fellow.

more.h: Rain as rod or as kindness
more.t: אִם לְשֵׁבֶט אִם לְאַרְצוֹ (Iyov 37:13), whether for a rod or for His land, is the rod of chastening: sometimes the rain comes as a rod and a chastisement upon the world, sweeping away the seed and ruining everything, and sometimes לְאַרְצוֹ, for His land, that is, for the world's need, because its people do His will; and אם לחסד, whether for kindness, since sometimes He brings it in kindness though the people of the world are guilty.

Since a ruler carries a rod in his hand, and since the rod for chastening the people is in his hand, the head and the ruler are called שֵׁבֶט: שֵׁבֶט מֹשְׁלִים (Yeshayahu 14:5), the rod of rulers; לֹא יָסוּר שֵׁבֶט מִיהוּדָה (Bereishis 49:10), the sceptre shall not depart from Yehudah; שֵׁבֶט מִישֹׁר שֵׁבֶט מַלְכוּתֶךָ (Tehillim 45:7), a sceptre of uprightness is the sceptre of your kingdom. It is also said together with a scribe: מֹשְׁכִים בְּשֵׁבֶט סֹפֵר (Shoftim 5:14), they that handle the scribe's rod.

הֲדָבָר דִּבַּרְתִּי אֶת אַחַד שִׁבְטֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (Shmuel II 7:7), did I speak a word with one of the tribes of Yisrael, means with the heads and the kings; and the parallel pasuk has אֶת אַחַד שֹׁפְטֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (Divrei HaYamim I 17:6), one of the judges of Yisrael.

פשׁת.sense: Flax. The word is feminine, yet its suffix and its plural come in masculine form; פִּשְׁתֵּי הָעֵץ is flax still in its stalk, which is called wood.

more.t: וְהַפִּשְׁתָּה וְהַשְּׂעֹרָה נֻכָּתָה (Shemos 9:31), the flax and the barley were struck, and וּפִשְׁתָּה כֵהָה לֹא יְכַבֶּנָּה (Yeshayahu 42:3), a dim flax he will not put out.

more.h: Masculine forms on a feminine word
more.t: The suffix comes in the masculine although the thing is feminine, צַמְרִי וּפִשְׁתִּי (Hoshea 2:7), my wool and my flax; and so does the plural, כַּפִּשְׁתִּים אֲשֶׁר בָּעֲרוּ בָאֵשׁ (Shoftim 15:14), like flax burnt in fire, and בַּצֶּמֶר אוֹ בַפִּשְׁתִּים (Vayikra 13:52), in the wool or in the linen.

בְּפִשְׁתֵּי הָעֵץ (Yehoshua 2:6), in the flax of the wood, means in the wood of the flax, since it was still in its stalk, and a stalk is called עֵץ, wood. This is found in construct in the holy tongue: at times the governing word becomes the governed and the governed the governing, as תּוֹלַעַת שָׁנִי, worm of scarlet, beside וְאֶת־שְׁנִי הַתּוֹלַעַת (Vayikra 14:6, 14:51), and the scarlet of the worm. It holds where each of the two can stand either way, and everything goes by the sense and the explanation.

כתן.sense: A tunic, כְּתֹנֶת, in several patterns of the noun. A pasuk may name the tunic and the robe together as one, but among the priestly garments they are two.

more.t: פָּשַׁטְתִּי אֶת־ כֻּתָּנְתִּי (Shir HaShirim 5:3), I have taken off my tunic, and of Yosef, וַיַּפְשִׁיטוּ אֶת־יוֹסֵף אֶת־ כֻּתָּנְתּוֹ (Bereishis 37:23), they stripped Yosef of his tunic. The plural is וְהִלְבַּשְׁתָּ אֹתָם כֻּתֳּנֹֽת (Shemos 40:14), and you shall clothe them in tunics, and וַיִּשָּׂאֻם בְּכֻתֳּנֹתָם (Vayikra 10:5), and they carried them in their tunics.
In those two plurals the tav carries a sheva alone, though by rule it should carry a chataf kamatz; in another, exact sefer he found the tav with the chataf kamatz.

One pattern: וַֽיַּֽעֲשׂוּ אֶת־ הַכָּתְנֹת שֵׁשׁ (Shemos 39:26 in his edition), and they made the tunics of linen, and כָּתְנוֹת עוֹר (Bereishis 3:21), tunics of skin. Another: וַיִּטְבְּלוּ אֶת־ הַכֻּתֹּנֶת בַּדָּֽם (Bereishis 37:31), and they dipped the tunic in the blood; אֶת־ כְּתֹנֶת הַפַּסִּים (Bereishis 37:23), the tunic of passim; and וְעָשָׂה לוֹ כְּתֹנֶת פַּסִּֽים (Bereishis 37:3), and he made him a tunic of passim.

At times the tunic and the robe are spoken of as one, since the two seem to be one thing, as it is written וְעָלֶיהָ כְּתֹנֶת פַּסִּים כִּי כֵן תִּלְבַּשְׁןָ בְּנוֹת־הַמֶּלֶךְ הַבְּתוּלֹת מְעִילִים (Shmuel II 13:18), and she had on a tunic of passim, for so the king's maiden daughters were clothed, in robes. But the tunic written among the bigdei kehunah is not the robe, since each of them is a garment in its own right.

קטן.sense: To be small, or a small thing in someone's eyes; קָטֹן, small, the lesser or the youngest; and to make small.

more.t: קָטֹנְתִּי מִכֹּל הַֽחֲסָדִים (Bereishis 32:11), I am too small for all the kindnesses, and וַתִּקְטַן עוֹד זֹאת בְּעֵינֶיךָ (Shmuel II 7:19), and this was still a small thing in Your eyes.

הַמָּאוֹר הַקָּטֹן (Bereishis 1:16), the lesser light; קָטֹן וְגָדוֹל שָׁם הוּא (Iyov 3:19), small and great are there alike; and קָטָנִּי עָבָה (Melachim I 12:10), my little one is thicker, meaning my little finger. With a kamatz, וְדָוִד הוּא הַקָּטָן (Shmuel I 17:14), and David was the youngest.

הַקְּטַנִּים עִם־הַגְּדֹלִֽים (Tehillim 115:13), the small together with the great; לַֽעֲשׂוֹת קְטַנָּה אוֹ גְדוֹלָֽה (Bamidbar 22:18), to do a small thing or a great one; and כִּי מִי בַז לְיוֹם קְטַנּוֹת (Zecharyah 4:10), for who has despised a day of small things. To make small is לְהַקְטִין אֵיפָה (Amos 8:5), to shrink the eifah.
The grammar of קָטָנִּי עָבָה, my little one is thicker, he has set out in the section on grammar that he put before the book, in the gate of nouns.

כיל.sense: The miser, so called in his own view because he lays out his expenses by a fixed measure with nothing over; he stands opposite the open-handed man.

more.t: וּלְכִילַי לֹא יֵאָמֵר שׁוֹעַ (Yeshayahu 32:5), the miser will not be called open-handed, with a chirik; and with a tzeirei, וְכֵלַי כֵּלָיו רָעִים (Yeshayahu 32:7), the miser, his measures are bad. The yud is the yud of relation, like the yud of מוֹכִיחַ אָדָם אַחֲרַי (Mishlei 28:23), one who reproves a man, afterward, and of הוּא הַהֵיכָל לִפְנָי (Melachim I 6:17), that is the Heichal, in front.
The miser stands opposite the שׁוֹעַ, the open-handed man, since the open-handed man is more than the נדיב, the generous one.

more.h: Where he takes the word from
more.t: In his own view the word is cut from the sense of וְכָל בַּשָּׁלִשׁ (Yeshayahu 40:12), he measured out by a measure, and from that root: the man is called a miser because he conducts his affairs and lays out his expenses by a fixed measure, so that nothing is left over.

כֵּלָיו is the noun of miserliness; its singular is כֵּל, on the pattern of גֵּר and כֵּן, and the plural is כֵּלִים. It means that his measures are bad. A fixed and even measure is good in most things, but the miser's measures are bad in all of them, since he adds nothing to the set measure, not in his household outlay and not in giving to the poor, and his eye is grudging over everything he spends.
He explains the word further at the root כלה, from the sense of כְּלִי, a vessel, and כֵּלִים, vessels, with the vernacular avaro set beside it.

כול.sense: To measure; to hold, a vessel's measure being what it holds; to bear. Doubled, to hold and bear, and to feed each by his measure. כִּילַי, the miser, is from it.

more.t: וְכָל בשׁלשׁ (Yeshayahu 40:12), and measured with a shalish: he explains וְכָל as ומדד, and measured. In the heavy form, אַלְפַּיִם בַּת יָכִֽיל (Melachim I 7:26), it held two thousand bath: that was its measure, that is, that much it held; קָטֹן מֵֽהָכִיל אֶת־הָעֹלָה (Melachim I 8:64), too small to hold the olah, its measure not large enough for all the olos and shelamim; and אֲשֶׁר לֹֽא־ יָכִלוּ הַמָּֽיִם (Yirmiyahu 2:13), that do not hold the water, which goes out of them, for they are broken.

more.h: The large cup, and the sword
more.t: מִרְבָּה לְהָכִֽיל (Yechezkel 23:32), much to hold: the cup is large enough to hold much, as the pasuk there calls it deep and wide. לְהָכִיל לְמַעַן בָּרָֽק (Yechezkel 21:33), said of the sword, is: it was whetted to hold and bear the killing, and to make its flash the greater, to put fear in the nations. Radak's father reads that לְהָכִיל as לְהַֽאֲכִיל, to feed, and Radak has written of it at the root אכל.

וּמִי יְכִילֶֽנּוּ (Yoel 2:11), and who can bear it. From this sense and root, doubled: לֹא יְכַלְכְּלוּךָ (Melachim I 8:27), the heavens and the heaven of heavens cannot hold You or bear You; וְנִלְאֵיתִי כַּֽלְכֵל (Yirmiyahu 20:9), I am weary of holding and bearing; וּמִי מְכַלְכֵּל אֶת־יוֹם בּוֹאוֹ (Malachi 3:2), who can hold and bear the day of his coming; and הַנִּצָּבָה לֹא יְכַלְכֵּל (Zecharyah 11:16), the sick one that stands elsewhere he will neither bear nor strengthen.

more.h: The body's illness and the soul's
more.t: רוּחַ אִישׁ יְכַלְכֵּל מַֽחֲלֵהוּ וְרוּחַ נְכֵאָה מִי יִשָּׂאֶֽנָּה (Mishlei 18:14), a man's spirit bears up his illness, but a broken spirit who can carry: it is lighter to bear the sickness of the body than the sickness of the soul.

In another sense close to this, וְכִלְכַּלְתִּי אֹֽתְךָ שָׁם (Bereishis 45:11), I will provide for you there; וַיְכַלְכֵּל יוֹסֵף אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אֶחָיו (Bereishis 47:12), Yosef provided for his father and his brothers; and וְכִלְכְּלָם לֶחֶם וָמָֽיִם (Melachim I 18:4), he sustained them with bread and water. This is food supplied to each one's need by his own measure, and it does not leave the first sense but is included in it.

יְכַלְכֵּל דְּבָרָיו בְּמִשְׁפָּֽט (Tehillim 112:5): he brings out his words with justice and uprightness and measure, and does not multiply words; or דְּבָרָיו is his affairs, that he orders his outlays and his gifts in order and with justice. From this root and this sense comes וּלְכִילַי לֹא יֵֽאָמֵר שֽׁוֹעַ (Yeshayahu 32:5), nor shall the miser be called open-handed, which he takes up again at the root כיל.

נכל.sense: The evil thought hidden away in the heart, and the deed done by guile that comes of it.

more.t: וְאָרוּר נוֹכֵל (Malachi 1:14), cursed be the deceiver; the noun בְּנִכְלֵיהֶם (Bamidbar 25:18), by their wiles, and in the same pasuk אֲשֶׁר־ נִכְּלוּ לָכֶם, with which they plotted against you; וַיִּתְנַכְּלוּ אֹתוֹ לַהֲמִיתוֹ (Bereishis 37:18), they plotted against him to kill him; and לְהִתְנַכֵּל בַּעֲבָדָיו (Tehillim 105:25), to deal craftily with his servants.
The Targum of לְהָרְגוֹ בְעָרְמָה (Shemos 21:14), to kill him by guile, is לְמִקְטְלֵיהּ בִּנְכִילוּ, to kill him with guile, which puts this very root where the Hebrew has guile.

קמץ.sense: Gathering and collecting: the fistful, taken with the fingers gathered in to the palm; and the gathering in of the years of plenty.

more.t: וְקָמַץ מִשָּׁם מְלֹא קֻמְצוֹ (Vayikra 2:2), and he shall take a fistful from there, the fill of his fist. The sense is gathering and collecting, and מְלֹא קֻמְצוֹ is a full fist, the fingers gathered in to the palm of the hand.
Chazal describe it (Menachos 11a): he stretches three fingers over the flat of his hand, and wipes off with his thumb above and with his little finger below.

וַתַּעַשׂ הָאָרֶץ בְּשֶׁבַע שְׁנֵי הַשָּׂבָע לִקְמָצִֽים (Bereishis 41:47), and the land made it into gatherings in the seven years of plenty, is of the same kind: the people of the land gathered the grain into collections, so much produce did they gather in. Or the land is the earth itself, and it put out much produce, handfuls from a single prutah.

גוי.sense: A nation, said also of a swarm of locusts; Chazal call a man who is not of Israel a goy. Rabbi Yonah holds it is said of one man too; Radak reads his proof otherwise.

more.h: A yud dropped from the writing
more.t: וְיֶתֶר גּוֹיִ יִנְחָלֽוּם (Tzefaniah 2:9), and the remnant of My nation will inherit them: the yud of the suffix, my, is missing from the writing and stays in the speaking. In גּוֹיִם רַבִּים (Yeshayahu 52:15), many nations, לִשְׂמֹחַ בְּשִׂמְחַת גּוֹיֶךָ (Tehillim 106:5), to rejoice in the joy of Your nations, and גּוֹיַיִךְ (Yechezkel 36:13), your nations, it is the yud of the plural that has fallen from the writing and stays in the speaking; and so כֵּֽאלֹהֵי גּוֹיֵי הָֽאֲרָצוֹת (Divrei HaYamim II 32:17), like the gods of the nations of the lands.
כִּי־ גוֹי עָלָה עַל־אַרְצִי (Yoel 1:6), for a nation has come up against my land, is said of a gathering of locusts.

more.h: Why a non-Jew is called a goy
more.t: Chazal were accustomed in their speech to call a man who is not of Israel a goy. The usage came about because whenever they wished to say of a man that he was not of Israel but of some other nation, and it was not settled with them which nation he came from, whether Edomite or Ishmaelite or one of the rest, they said goy, meaning that he is of another nation and not of Israel.

more.h: Whether one man is called a goy
more.t: Rabbi Yonah said that גוי falls on a single man, as it says הֲגוֹי גַּם־צַדִּיק תַּֽהֲרֹֽג (Bereishis 20:4), will You slay a גוי, even a righteous one? What seems right to Radak is that Avimelech said it on account of his people, since Hashem's anger was on him and on his people; and so Avimelech said כִּֽי־הֵבֵאתָ עָלַי וְעַל־מַמְלַכְתִּי חֲטָאָה גְדֹלָה (Bereishis 20:9), that you have brought on me and on my kingdom a great sin. Further, וַיִּרְפָּא אֱלֹהִים אֶת־אֲבִימֶלֶךְ וְאֶת־אִשְׁתּוֹ וְאַמְהֹתָיו וַיֵּלֵֽדוּ (Bereishis 20:17), and Hashem healed Avimelech and his wife and his maidservants and they bore children: so it is plain that Avimelech was not stricken alone.

עמם.sense: To cover over and hide. Under the same letters stands עַם, a people, a gathering of men, said also of other creatures such as locusts and ants.

more.t: אֲרָזִים לֹא־עֲמָמֻהוּ (Yechezkel 31:8), the tall cedars did not cover him or hide him, for he rose above them all; כָּל־סָתוּם לֹא עֲמָמוּךָ (Yechezkel 28:3), no hidden thing was covered or concealed from you, none that you did not know; and אֵיכָה יוּעַם זָהָב (Eichah 4:1), how the gold is covered over. The sense of them all is hiding and covering. His father takes עֲמָמוּךָ from עִם, with: that is, the matters were not closed off with you.

more.h: A people, and the gender of the word
more.t: עַם רַב וְעָצוּם (Yoel 2:2), a great and mighty people. The word is mostly masculine and at times feminine: מַדּוּעַ שׁוֹבְבָה הָעָם הַזֶּה (Yirmiyahu 8:5), why has this people turned away; וְחָטָאת עַמֶּךָ (Shemos 5:16), and your people sins; and הָעָם אֲשֶׁר־בְּקִרְבָּהּ יוֹשֶׁבֶת־לָבֶטַח (Shoftim 18:7), the people in its midst dwelling secure. So too חֲבִי כִמְעַט־רֶגַע (Yeshayahu 26:20), hide for a brief moment, for one who reads it as a command.

עַמִּים הַר־יִקְרָאוּ (Devarim 33:19), peoples will call to the mountain; in the fuller form בַּעֲמָמֶיךָ (Shoftim 5:14), among your peoples, and עַמְמֵי הָאָרֶץ (Nechemiah 9:24), the peoples of the land.

As עַם is said of a gathering and assembly of men, so it is said of other things: of the locust, עַם רַב וְעָצוּם כָּמֹהוּ לֹא נִהְיָה מִן־הָעוֹלָם (Yoel 2:2), a people great and mighty whose like has never been; of the ants, עַם לֹא־עָז (Mishlei 30:25), a people not strong; and of the shefanim, עַם לֹא־עָצוּם (Mishlei 30:26), a people not mighty. His father explains עַם־זוּ יָצַרְתִּי לִי תְּהִלָּתִי יְסַפֵּרוּ (Yeshayahu 43:21), this people I formed for Myself, they shall tell My praise, the same way, of the beasts, since the pasuk before it says that the beast of the field shall honour Me.

לאם.sense: לְאֹם, a people, and the plural לְאֻמִּים; his entry gives no gloss, only the pesukim and a note on one spelling.

more.t: וּלְאֹם מִלְאֹם יֶאֱמָץ (Bereishis 25:23), one people will be stronger than the other, and וּשְׁנֵי לְאֻמִּים in the same pasuk, and two peoples; תּוֹכֵחֹת בַּל־אֻמִּים (Tehillim 149:7), rebukes upon the peoples; and וּלְאוּמִּי אֵלַי הַאֲזִינוּ (Yeshayahu 51:4), and My people, give ear to Me, in which the quiescent letter, the vav, is written, and the dagesh with it. Its like, he says, is set out in the section on grammar, and they are like אומים, peoples.

אם.sense: Mostly if, setting a condition; also a question, when, truly, and an oath. On the same letters, אֵם, a mother, אוּמָּה, a family or nation, and אַמָּה, a cubit.

more.t: In most places it sets a condition, as וְאִם־עֵז קָרְבָּנוֹ (Vayikra 3:12), and if his offering is a goat. It also asks a question, as הֲיִנְהַק־פֶּרֶא עֲלֵי־דֶשֶׁא אִם יִגְעֶה־שּׁוֹר (Iyov 6:5), does the wild donkey bray over grass, or will the ox low? The heh of asking can come on it as well: הַאִם תַּמְנוּ לִגְוֹעַ (Bamidbar 17:28), are we to perish to the last?

וְהָיָה אִם־בָּא אֶל־אֵשֶׁת אָחִיו (Bereishis 38:9) is: when he came to his brother's wife. So too אִם־כֶּסֶף תַּלְוֶה אֶת־עַמִּי (Shemos 22:24), when you lend money to my people, since lending is an obligation, as it says וְהַעֲבֵט תַּעֲבִיטֶנּוּ (Devarim 15:8), you shall surely lend to him.

כִּי אִם־תַּם הַכֶּסֶף (Bereishis 47:18), truly the money is gone, and אִם־לַלֵּצִים הוּא יָלִיץ (Mishlei 3:34), truly he scoffs at the scoffers. Every אִם of this kind is to be read as truly, and he holds these are short of the nun of אָמֵן, as אֱמֶת is short a nun, its proper form being אֱמֶנֶת, which the dagesh in אֲמִתּוֹ proves.

אָב וָאֵם (Esther 2:7), father and mother, is plain enough. A family is called אוּם or אוּמָּה, the plural רֹאשׁ אֻמּוֹת (Bamidbar 25:15), head of families, and שְׁנֵים־עָשָׂר נְשִׂיאִם לְאֻמֹּתָם (Bereishis 25:16), twelve princes for their families; and a whole nation is called אוּם, כָּל־הָאֻמִּים (Tehillim 117:1), all the nations. His father writes that the root of אוּם is אָמַם, on the evidence of the Arabic.

more.h: A mother of roads, a mother city
more.t: The middle of the road, where the roads turn to it from this side and that, is called אֵם הַדֶּרֶךְ (Yechezkel 21:26), the mother of the road, since it is like a mother to the roads that turn in to it; and the great city is עִיר וְאֵם בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל (Shmuel II 20:19), a city and a mother in Israel, since it is like a mother to the smaller places, which are themselves called daughters.

וְהָאַמָּה מִזֶּה וְהָאַמָּה מִזֶּה (Shemos 26:13), and the cubit on the one side and the cubit on the other, is the cubit, whose sense is known, and so בְּאַמַּת־אִישׁ (Devarim 3:11), by the cubit of a man. אַמַּת בִּצְעֵךְ (Yirmiyahu 51:13) is the arm of your gain, or the measure of your gain, that is, the measure you measured out. In וַיָּנֻעוּ אַמּוֹת הַסִּפִּים (Yeshayahu 6:4), and the אַמּוֹת of the thresholds moved, the doorposts are called אַמּוֹת. Yonasan renders it אֵילְוַת סִפֵּי, and by that the Targum seems to mean the corners standing on the doorposts on either side, on which the lintel rests. Some explain it that the thresholds moved two or three cubits from their place.

מוט.sense: To tilt and slip, with מוֹט a slipping; and, close to that sense, מוֹט a carrying pole, and מוֹטָה the yoke, or the strap it is tied with.

more.t: וּמָטָה יָדוֹ עִמָּךְ (Vayikra 25:35), and his hand slips beside you; צַדִּיק מָט לִפְנֵֽי־רָשָֽׁע (Mishlei 25:26), a righteous man slipping before a wicked one; וּמָטִים לַהֶרֶג (Mishlei 24:11), those slipping toward the slaughter; and וְהַגְּבָעוֹת תְּמוּטֶינָה (Yeshayahu 54:10), and the hills will tilt. The sense of them all is tilting and slipping.

The noun: לֹא־יִתֵּן לְעוֹלָם מוֹט לַצַּדִּֽיק (Tehillim 55:23), He will never let the righteous slip, and אַל־יִתֵּן לַמּוֹט רַגְלֶךָ (Tehillim 121:3), He will not let your foot slip; and with the verb, וַיְחַזְּקֵהוּ בְמַסְמְרִים לֹא יִמּֽוֹט (Yeshayahu 41:7), and it was fastened with nails, that it should not tilt.

Close to this sense: וַיִּשָּׂאֻהוּ בַמּוֹט (Bamidbar 13:23), they carried it on a pole; וְנָֽתְנוּ עַל־ הַמּֽוֹט (Bamidbar 4:10), they put it on the pole; and אֶשְׁבֹּר מֹטֵהוּ (Nachum 1:13), I will break his bar. The plural is בִּכְתֵפָם בַּמֹּטוֹת (Divrei HaYamim I 15:15), on their shoulder with the poles, and מוֹטֹת עֵץ שָׁבָרְתָּ (Yirmiyahu 28:13), bars of wood you have broken.

more.h: The yoke, and a masculine verb
more.t: וַיִּקַּח חֲנַנְיָה הַנָּבִיא אֶת־ הַמּוֹטָה מֵעַל צַוַּאר יִרְמְיָה הַנָּבִיא וַיִּשְׁבְּרֵֽהוּ (Yirmiyahu 28:12 in his edition), and Chananyah the navi took the מוֹטָה off the neck of Yirmiyahu the navi and broke it. Though מוֹטָה is feminine, the pasuk says וַיִּשְׁבְּרֵֽהוּ, and broke it, in the masculine, agreeing with העול, the yoke, for the מוֹטָה is the yoke; or else the מוֹטָה is the strap by which the yoke is tied.

מֻטּוֹת כְּנָפָיו (Yeshayahu 8:8), the bonds of his wings, he keeps at this root, the quiescent letter swallowed in a dagesh and the cholam turned into a shuruk, its sense being bonds or staves of wood. His father writes the phrase under the root נָטָה, the dagesh standing for a swallowed nun; on that reading it means that the spreading of his camp will fill the breadth of your land. The Midrash of Rabbi Tanchuma asks how great the מוטות of a rooster's wings are, and answers a sixtieth of its wings, a sixtieth of Sancheriv's hosts, the full breadth of the land of Yehudah.

בדד.sense: Alone, solitary: a noun of solitude, not an adjective, used too where security is meant; with a lamed, לְבַד, apart or besides; and as a verb, to keep apart.

more.h: Not an adjective but a noun
more.t: בָּדָד יֵשֵׁב (Vayikra 13:46), he shall dwell alone, that is, solitary. The word is not an adjective for the masculine only, for it serves the feminine and the plural too, אֵיכָה יָשְׁבָה בָדָד (Eichah 1:1), how she sat alone, and בָּדָד יִשְׁכֹּנוּ (Yirmiyahu 49:31), they dwell alone; and it takes a serving lamed in the way of a noun and not of an adjective, שֹׁכְנִי לְבָדָד (Michah 7:14), who dwell alone. Therefore it is not an adjective but the noun of solitude.

It comes in the matter of בֶּטַח, security, since one who dwells secure sits alone and has no need of many men about him to help; therefore it is said of dwelling in the two pesukim above, and וַיִּשְׁכֹּן יִשְׂרָאֵל בֶּטַח בָּדָד (Devarim 33:28), Israel dwelt secure, alone; and so בָּדָד יַנְחֶנּוּ (Devarim 32:12), Hashem led him alone.

בַּד בְּבַד (Shemos 30:34) is one by one, that is, each of the spices is to be ground by itself. Some explain it as weight by weight, and so Onkelos rendered it; that is, each one weighed by itself for exactness, or the weight of one like the weight of another, since there were among them spices of equal weight, the ones the Torah names, nataf, shecheles, chelbenah and levonah. So too Chazal say (Kereisos 6a) that the tzori and the tziporen, the levonah and the chelbenah, weighed seventy manah each.

Most use of the noun is with a lamed: מִשְׁפַּחַת בֵּית־דָּוִיד לְבָד וּנְשֵׁיהֶם לְבָד (Zecharyah 12:12), the family of Beis David apart and their wives apart, pointed with a kamatz, and in construct with a patach, לְבַד מִשָּׂרֵי הַנִּצָּבִים (Melachim I 5:30), apart from the appointed officers. A mem is added on top of that, מִלְּבַד נְשֵׁי בְנֵי־יַעֲקֹב (Bereishis 46:26), apart from the wives of Yaakov's sons; and with suffixes it takes a dagesh for the doubled letter that is missing, וַיִּוָּתֵר יַעֲקֹב לְבַדּוֹ (Bereishis 32:25), Yaakov was left alone, and אֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ (Devarim 4:35), there is none besides Him.

The verb from it is וְאֵין בּוֹדֵד בְּמוֹעָדָיו (Yeshayahu 14:31), and none keeps apart at his appointed times: at the times Nevuchadnetzar sets his troops, this day and this hour, to be ready to go to war, not one of them holds himself apart or stays back, for all come together. Targum Yonasan renders it, and none delays at his times.

The pasuk is read three ways. It may speak of Nevuchadnetzar, as above, since the smoke comes from the north, and Bavel lies north of Pelishtim as it does of Eretz Yisrael, and in the destruction the king of Bavel brought on Pelishtim Israel was saved from the Pelishtim who pressed them. It may speak of Pharaoh, who struck the Pelishtim, as it says בְּטֶרֶם יַכֶּה פַרְעֹה אֶת־עַזָּה (Yirmiyahu 47:1), before Pharaoh struck Gaza. But Radak holds it better, for the parsha as a whole, to read it of Chizkiyahu, who struck the Pelishtim as far as Gaza (Melachim II 18:8): the rod that was broken is Uziyahu, who had struck the Pelishtim (Divrei HaYamim II 26:6), and from his seed came the one who would strike them now.
פֶּרֶא בּוֹדֵד לוֹ (Hoshea 8:9), a wild donkey off by itself, and כְּצִפּוֹר בּוֹדֵד עַל־גָּג (Tehillim 102:8), like a lone bird on a roof, both of them meaning solitary.

נסס.sense: The נֵס, the banner carried high for a whole army to see and follow; the root's core is height and being raised, and a sail is a נֵס too.

more.t: וְנָשָׂא־נֵס לַגּוֹיִם (Yeshayahu 5:26), he will raise a banner to the nations, and נִסִּי (Shemos 17:15), my banner, in Hashem Nissi, Hashem is my banner; the word is known. The root is height and being lifted up, since the man bearing the banner carries it high, so that it is seen over the whole army and they march after it.

כִּמְסֹס נֹסֵס (Yeshayahu 10:18), as a banner-bearer melts away: when the one bearing the banner melts, the whole army melts and flees. Rabbi Yehudah wrote that the phrase has another sense, and Rabbi Yonah put it under another root and another sense.

נֹסְסָה בוֹ (Yeshayahu 59:19), raised itself against him: that is, the spirit of Hashem rose up against him to drive him back. נָתַתָּה לִּירֵאֶיךָ נֵּס לְהִתְנוֹסֵס (Tehillim 60:6), You gave those who fear You a banner to be raised, לְהִתְנוֹסֵס meaning to rise up and be lifted high; and כִּי אַבְנֵי־נֵזֶר מִתְנוֹסְסוֹת עַל־אַדְמָתוֹ (Zecharyah 9:16), for crown stones are raised high on his land.

The sail is called נֵס as well, since they raise it on the mast: בַּל־פָּרְשׂוּ נֵס (Yeshayahu 33:23), they did not spread a sail, and וְכַנֵּס עַל־הַגִּבְעָה (Yeshayahu 30:17), like a sail on the hill.

תרן.sense: The mast, the tall timber on a ship by which the sail is let down and set up.

more.t: כַּתֹּרֶן עַל־רֹאשׁ הָהָר (Yeshayahu 30:17), like a mast on a mountain top; לַעֲשׂוֹת תֹּרֶן עָלָיִךְ (Yechezkel 27:5), to make a mast for you; and בַּל־יְחַזְּקוּ כֵן־תָּרְנָם (Yeshayahu 33:23), they did not hold the base of their mast firm. He closes with the foreign word for it.

עתד.sense: Ready, made ready: what is prepared for someone, of punishment or of treasure; and עַתּוּדִים, the grown he-goats, a name borrowed for the nobles who lead the people.

more.t: כְּמֶלֶךְ עָתִיד לַכִּידוֹר (Iyov 15:24), like a king made ready for the onslaught, and עֲתִידִים (Esther 8:13), that the Jews be ready; הָעֲתִידִים עֹרֵר לִוְיָתָן (Iyov 3:8), those who are ready to rouse their mourning. Of what is made ready to come: וְחָשׁ עֲתִדֹת לָמוֹ (Devarim 32:35), and what is ready for them hastens, which is what is prepared to come upon them of punishment.

עֲתוּדוֹתֵיהֶם (Yeshayahu 10:13) is what is made ready for them of treasure and things desired; or it may mean their borders, since the same pasuk says וְאָסִיר גְּבוּלֹת עַמִּים, I have removed the bounds of peoples, a border and a set time being near to one another in sense.

וְעַתְּדָהּ בַּשָּׂדֶה לָךְ (Mishlei 24:27), and make it ready for yourself in the field, where the heh with a mapik points back to the work just named: understand and make ready your work in the field, and afterwards build your house. And הִתְעַתְּדוּ לְגַלִּים (Iyov 15:28), which are ready for ruin and to become heaps.

הָעֲתֻדִים הָעֹלִים עַל הַצֹּאן (Bereishis 31:10), the he-goats that mounted the flock, are known: they are the males of the goats, called תְּיָשִׁים as well, the grown ones called עַתּוּדִים and תְּיָשִׁים and the young ones שְׂעִירִים.

The nobles and the great men are called by this word by way of borrowing: כָּל־עַתּוּדֵי אָרֶץ (Yeshayahu 14:9), all the he-goats of the earth, since they go before the people and lead them as the he-goats go before the flock.

מצר.sense: Straits, which he reads as fences on either side that leave no way to flee; in Chazal's words, a boundary. The mem may or may not be a root letter.

more.t: כָּל־רֹדְפֶיהָ הִשִּׂיגוּהָ בֵּין הַמְּצָרִֽים (Eichah 1:3), all her pursuers overtook her between the straits, that is, between the fences, a fence on this side and a fence on that, so that she cannot flee one way or the other. In the construct, וּמְצָרֵי שְׁאוֹל מְצָאוּנִי (Tehillim 116:3), the straits of the grave found me.

The singular of them may be מִן־ הַמֵּצַֽר (Tehillim 118:5), out of the strait, so that מֵצַר gives מְצָרִים, straits, as עֵנָב, a grape, gives עֲנָבִים, grapes, except that this one is of the words with a dagesh. Or מִן־הַמֵּצַֽר may be from another root, יָצַר or צָרַר, as he wrote at the root יָצַר.

So too in the words of Chazal, אילן הסמוך למצר (Bava Basra 26b), a tree close to the boundary, and מצרים הרחיב לו (Bava Basra 61b), he widened the boundaries for him. It seems that they hold the mem to be a letter of the root, since they said (Bava Basra 62a) מצר לו מצר ראובן מצר אחד, he set him a boundary, Reuven's boundary, one boundary. It may also be that the root of מצרים is צָרַר, and וּמְצָרֵי שְׁאוֹל מְצָאוּנִי then stands in the pattern of מְמַדֵּי, the measures of, from מִי־שָׂם מְמַדֶּיהָ (Iyov 38:5), who set its measures.

רהב.sense: To grow strong and haughty, as a youth against an elder; Rahav, which is Egypt, so called for its strength and pride; and to strengthen another, putting might in him.

more.t: יִרְֽהֲבוּ הַנַּעַר בַּזָּקֵן (Yeshayahu 3:5), the youth will grow strong and haughty against the elder: יתחזקו ויתגאו, they will strengthen themselves and grow proud. The infinitive is וְרָהְבָּם עָמָל וָאָוֶן (Tehillim 90:10), and their strength is toil and trouble, which stands on the pattern of בְּשָׁמְרָם עֵקֶב רָֽב (Tehillim 19:12), in keeping them there is great reward; or else it is a noun.

לֵךְ הִתְרַפֵּס וּרְהַב רֵעֶֽיךָ (Mishlei 6:3), go, humble yourself and strengthen your fellow, he reads as: bow before him and strengthen him with words of appeasement. Although רעיך is written with a yud and the Mesorah marks it the only one written full, the yud is either added or the word is from a root whose last letter is a heh, the yud being of the root. It can also be read as a plural with a bet missing, ברעיך, that you should set many friends upon him.

רַהַב הֵם שָֽׁבֶת (Yeshayahu 30:7) he glosses החוזק שלהם ישבת ויבטל, their strength will cease and come to nothing, and it is said of Egypt, for it is their strength; he gave it another reading at the root יָשַׁב. אַזְכִּיר רַהַב וּבָבֶל (Tehillim 87:4), I will make mention of Rahav and Bavel, is Egypt too, called so because the Egyptians were possessed of strength and pride.

הַמַּחְצֶבֶת רַהַב (Yeshayahu 51:9), that hewed Rahav, and מָחַץ רָֽהַב (Iyov 26:12), He smote Rahav, are all of strength and might. וְרָהְבָּם עָמָל וָאָוֶן (Tehillim 90:10) he takes as: their vigor is emptiness, since it soon passes away. And וְֽלֹֽא־פָנָה אֶל־ רְהָבִים, and he has not turned to the רְהָבִים, is to those who have strength and pride.

more.h: Chayuj on a word in Yeshayahu
more.t: Radak wonders at what he found in the book of pointing of Rabbi Yehudah Chayuj, who wrote וּפָחַד וְרָחַב לְבָבֵךְ (Yeshayahu 60:5), your heart shall throb and swell, with a heh, and said that the resh is kamatz and the heh patach, so as to keep it apart from רַהַב, which is patach throughout. Radak answers that we have received the reading וְרָחַב with a ches, and that Rabbi Yonah wrote it with a ches as well.

תַּרְהִבֵנִי בְנַפְשִׁי עֹֽז (Tehillim 138:3), You strengthen me with might in my soul, he glosses החזקני, strengthen me, that You put might in my soul to strengthen myself for Your service. שֶׁהֵם הִרְהִיבֻנִי (Shir HaShirim 6:5), for they have strengthened me, is חזקו חשקי ואמצוני עליו, they strengthened my desire and emboldened me over it.

כפתר.sense: כַּפְתֹּר: on the menorah, knobs like apples bulging from its body; in Amos, the lintel over the doorposts, called so for the flowers and kaftorim figured on it.

more.t: וְכַפְתֹּר תַּחַת שְׁנֵי הַקָּנִים (Shemos 25:35), and a kaftor under two of the branches, and כַּפְתֹּֽרֵיהֶם וּקְנֹתָם (Shemos 25:36), their kaftorim and their branches: their meaning is apple, for they were like apples bulging out of the body of the menorah.
