הַךְ הַכַּפְתּוֹר וְיִרְֽעֲשׁוּ הַסִּפִּים (Amos 9:1), strike the kaftor and the posts will shake: the kaftor is the lintel that rests on the two posts, the סִפִּים, which are the doorposts. It is called kaftor because figures of flowers and kaftorim are made on it. So too בְּכַפְתֹּרֶיהָ יָלִינוּ (Tzefaniah 2:14), they will lodge in its kaftorim, on which the Targum has בְּפִתּוּחַ תַּרְעַיָא, in the carved work of the gates.

אלל.sense: Emptiness, a thing of no use, the sense he gives for אֱלִיל and for הָאֱלִילִם; and אַלְלַי, woe, whose sense he likens to אבוי, alas.

more.t: רֹפְאֵי אֱלִל כֻּלְּכֶֽם (Iyov 13:4), you are all worthless healers; רֹעִי הָֽאֱלִיל (Zecharyah 11:17), the worthless shepherd; וְקֶסֶם וֶֽאֱלִול (Yirmiyahu 14:14), and divination and a thing of nought, read וֶֽאֱלִיל; אַל־תִּפְנוּ אֶל־ הָאֱלִילִם (Vayikra 19:4), do not turn to the elilim. Its sense is emptiness and a thing that is of no use, in the vernacular נול"א.

אִם־רָשַׁעְתִּי אַלְלַי לִי (Iyov 10:15), if I am wicked, woe to me, is accented on the last syllable, and accented on the one before it is אַלְלַי לִי כִּי הָיִיתִי כְּאָסְפֵּי־קַיִץ (Michah 7:1), woe to me, for I am like the gatherings of the summer fruit. The sense is like that of אבוי, alas.
His brother Rabbi Moshe wrote that the alef stands in place of a yud, as יִשַׁי, Yishai, is also אִישַׁי, and that the word is from יְלָלָה, wailing, the yud being that of one speaking of himself.

תרף.sense: Terafim: images in which the future would be seen. In Hoshea the eifod is for Hashem and the terafim for idolatry, as the sacrifice and the pillar are.

more.h: Images that show what is coming
more.t: לָֽקְחָה אֶת־ הַתְּרָפִים (Bereishis 31:34), she had taken the terafim; וַתִּקַּח מִיכַל אֶת־ הַתְּרָפִים (Shmuel I 19:13), Michal took the terafim; וְאֵין אֵפוֹד וּתְרָפִֽים (Hoshea 3:4), and no eifod and terafim. They are images through which future things are seen.

He reads וְאֵין אֵפוֹד וּתְרָפִֽים along with וְאֵין זֶבַח וְאֵין מַצֵּבָה (Hoshea 3:4), and no sacrifice and no pillar: the sacrifice is to Hashem and the pillar to idolatry, and so the eifod is to Hashem and the terafim to idolatry.
Targum Yonasan rendered the phrase וְלֵית אֵפוֹד וּמְחַוֵי, there is no eifod and none who declares, and terafim elsewhere he rendered צַלְמָנַיָא, images.

שׁקץ.sense: To hold a thing in abomination, and the abomination itself, in two forms of the noun. The sense of them all, he says, is abomination.

more.t: כִּי לֹֽא־בָזָה וְלֹא שִׁקַּץ (Tehillim 22:25), for He has not despised and not held in abomination; אַל־ תְּשַׁקְּצוּ אֶת־נַפְשֹׁתֵיכֶם (Vayikra 11:43), do not make yourselves abominable; וְאֶת־נִבְלָתָם תְּשַׁקֵּֽצוּ (Vayikra 11:11), and their carcass you shall hold in abomination; שַׁקֵּץ תְּשַׁקְּצֶנּוּ (Devarim 7:26), you shall utterly hold it in abomination.

The noun is וְלָתֵת שִׁקּוּץ שֹׁמֵם (Daniel 12:11), and to set up an abomination that appalls; and in the plural וְעַל כְּנַף שִׁקּוּצִים מְשֹׁמֵם (Daniel 9:27), and upon the wing of abominations one who appalls; וַתִּרְאוּ אֶת־ שִׁקּוּצֵיהֶם (Devarim 29:16), and you saw their abominations; אִישׁ שִׁקּוּצֵי עֵינָיו הַשְׁלִיכוּ (Yechezkel 20:7), let each man cast away the abominations of his eyes.
Another form of the noun is שֶׁקֶץ הוּא לָכֶֽם (Vayikra 11:12), it is an abomination to you, pointed with six dots. The sense of them all is abomination.

חמם.sense: Heat and growing warm: to be warm, to warm another or oneself, hot bread, heat itself; and from this sense the sun is called חַמָּה.

more.t: וְחַם הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ וְנָמָֽס (Shemos 16:21), when the sun grew hot it melted; אִם־יִשְׁכְּבוּ שְׁנַיִם וְחַם לָהֶם (Koheles 4:11), if two lie together they are warm, meaning their flesh is warm; חַמּוֹתִי רָאִיתִי אֽוּר (Yeshayahu 44:16), I have warmed myself, I have seen the fire, with the stress on the last syllable; אַף־ יָחֹם וְיֹאמַר הֶאָח (Yeshayahu 44:16), he even grows warm and says aha. In וַיִּקַּח מֵהֶם וַיָּחָם (Yeshayahu 44:15), and he takes of them and warms himself, the ches has a kamatz chatuf, since the zakef stands on the yud.

The infinitive in its full form is וְשֹׁרֶשׁ רְתָמִים לַחְמָֽם (Iyov 30:4), and the root of the broom shrub for warming, and אֵין־גַּחֶלֶת לַחְמָם (Yeshayahu 47:14), there is no coal for warming, in the pattern of לִשְׁכַּב אֶת־בַּֽת־יַֽעֲקֹב (Bereishis 34:7), to lie with the daughter of Yaakov.

more.h: Hot as a word of description
more.t: חַם ־לִבִּי בְּקִרְבִּי (Tehillim 39:4), my heart was hot within me, and זֶה לַחְמֵנוּ חָם (Yehoshua 9:12), this bread of ours was hot, are words of description; but the first may be a verb of what has happened, since it takes a patach, while לַחְמֵנוּ חָם is a word of description, since it takes a kamatz. The Mesorah notes on it that it is the only one with a kamatz, and that every use of it as a man's name is like it. In the plural, אֲשֶׁר־בְּגָדֶיךָ חַמִּים (Iyov 37:17), you whose garments are warm.

לָשׂוּם לֶחֶם חֹם (Shmuel I 21:7), to set out hot bread, is another form of the word, in the pattern of מָעוֹז לַתֹּם (Mishlei 10:29), a stronghold to the upright, and הַמַּבְלִיג שֹׁד עַל־ עָז (Amos 5:9), who brings ruin upon the strong.

The noun is heat: זֶרַע וְקָצִיר וְקֹר וָחֹם (Bereishis 8:22), seedtime and harvest, cold and heat; לָבוֹשׁ וְאֵֽין־ לְחֹם לוֹ (Chaggai 1:6), clothing, and no warmth for him; בְּחֻמּוֹ נִדְֽעֲכוּ מִמְּקוֹמָֽם (Iyov 6:17), in its heat they are gone from their place.
It may be that וְכָל־שֶֽׂה־ חוּם (Bereishis 30:32), and every black lamb, is of this root: חוּם means black, and blackness comes of heat, with a shuruk standing in place of a cholam.

אֵיךְ יֵחָֽם (Koheles 4:11), how shall one be warm; כֻּלָּם יֵחַמּוּ (Hoshea 7:7), they are all heated; הַנֵּֽחָמִים בָּֽאֵלִים (Yeshayahu 57:5), you that heat yourselves among the terebinths, in the pattern of בַּמְּאֵרָה אַתֶּם נֵֽאָרִים (Malachi 3:9), you are cursed with a curse; or it is from the root יָחַם.

וְֽעַל־עָפָר תְּחַמֵּֽם (Iyov 39:14), and on the dust she warms them, that is, she warms her eggs; and the form that turns the act back on the doer is וּמִגֵּז כְּבָשַׂי יִתְחַמָּֽם (Iyov 31:20), and he warms himself with the fleece of my sheep.

From this sense the sun is called חַמָּה: בָּרָה כַּֽחַמָּה (Shir HaShirim 6:10), clear as the sun, and כְּאוֹר הַֽחַמָּה (Yeshayahu 30:26), like the light of the sun. But וְאֵין נִסְתָּר מֵֽחַמָּתֽוֹ (Tehillim 19:7), and nothing is hidden from its heat, is the noun for heat itself. וְהִכְרַתִּי אֶת־ חַמָּנֵיכֶם (Vayikra 26:30), and I will cut down your chamanim, can be read as of this root and this sense, the nun being added; they would then be called so because sun worshippers made them.

אים.sense: Fear and dread, which he says is the sense of all of them: dreadful, dread and terrors, the Eimim who are the giants, and graven images called eimim.

more.t: אָיֹם וְנוֹרָא (Chavakuk 1:7), dreadful and fearsome, and אֲיֻמָּה כַּנִּדְגָּלוֹת (Shir HaShirim 6:10), terrible as an army with banners.

וְהִנֵּה אֵימָה (Bereishis 15:12), and behold, a dread; in construct אֵימַת מֶלֶךְ (Mishlei 20:2), the dread of a king; in the plural of the feminine וְאֵימוֹת מָוֶת (Tehillim 55:5), the terrors of death. In אֵימָתָה וָפַחַד (Shemos 15:16), dread and fear, the mark of the feminine is doubled, as it is doubled in יְשׁוּעָתָה (Tehillim 3:3), salvation.

In the plural of the masculine: יַהֲלֹךְ עָלָיו אֵמִים (Iyov 20:25), terrors go over him; נָשָׂאתִי אֵמֶיךָ (Tehillim 88:16), I have borne your terrors. הָאֵמִים לְפָנִים (Devarim 2:10), the Eimim of old, are the giants, called so because dread and fear fall upon those who see them.

וּבָאֵימִים יִתְהֹלָלוּ (Yirmiyahu 50:38), and they go mad over the eimim, are the graven images. They are called eimim as a name of contempt, as idols are called עצבים, or else because those who pass by them are afraid of them. The sense of them all is fear and dread.

פחד.sense: To fear, with פַּחַד, fear; פַּחַד יִצְחָק is the One whom Yitzchak fears; and in another sense, at Iyov 40:17, the testicles.

more.t: וּפָחַד וְרָחַב לְבָבֵךְ (Yeshayahu 60:5), your heart shall fear and be enlarged; פָּחֲדוּ בְצִיּוֹן חַטָּאִים (Yeshayahu 33:14), sinners in Tzion are afraid; שָׁם פָּחֲדוּ פָחַד (Tehillim 14:5), there they feared a fear.

וּפָחֲדוּ (Hoshea 3:5), and they shall fear, said toward Hashem וְאֶל־טוּבוֹ, and toward His goodness: that is, they will fear Him and be in awe of Him, and stream to Him and to His good. In the same way, וּפָחֲדוּ וְרָגְזוּ עַל כָּל־הַטּוֹבָה וְעַל כָּל־הַשָּׁלוֹם, and they shall fear and tremble over all the good and all the peace.

The noun: פָּחֲדוּ־פַחַד (Tehillim 53:6), they feared a fear, is, there was no fear like it. Its plural is קוֹל־פְּחָדִים בְּאָזְנָיו (Iyov 15:21), a sound of terrors in his ears, and with the feminine heh, וְלֹא פַחְדָּתִי אֵלַיִךְ (Yirmiyahu 2:19), and My fear was not upon you.

וּפַחַד יִצְחָק הָיָה לִי (Bereishis 31:42), and the Fear of Yitzchak was with me, is: the One whom Yitzchak fears was with me; and so וַיִּשָּׁבַע יַעֲקֹב בְּפַחַד אָבִיו יִצְחָק (Bereishis 31:53), Yaakov swore by the Fear of his father Yitzchak, by the One whom Yitzchak fears. Radak says it is said of Yitzchak because Yitzchak feared Hashem and gave himself over in the matter of the Akeidah.

אַשְׁרֵי אָדָם מְפַחֵד תָּמִיד (Mishlei 28:14), happy is the man who is always afraid, and וַתְּפַחֵד תָּמִיד כָּל־הַיּוֹם מִפְּנֵי חֲמַת הַמֵּצִיק (Yeshayahu 51:13), and you are afraid all the day because of the fury of the oppressor, are in the heavy form; and the form that puts fear into another is וְרֹב עַצְמוֹתַי הִפְחִיד (Iyov 4:14), and it terrified the mass of my bones.
פַֽחֲדָיו יְשׂרָֽגוּ (Iyov 40:17) is another sense: his testicles are knit together. And the Targum of מְרוֹחַ אָשֶׁךְ (Vayikra 21:20), one crushed in the testicle, is מְרִיס פַּחְדִּין.

ירא.sense: To fear, whether Hashem or a man; the nouns for fear and awe; awesome, one who is feared; and to make another afraid.

more.t: וְלֹא יָרֵא אֱלֹהִֽים (Devarim 25:18), and he did not fear Hashem; כִּֽי־ יָֽרְאוּ הַֽמְיַלְּדֹת אֶת־הָֽאֱלֹהִים (Shemos 1:21), because the midwives feared Hashem; לֹא צָחַקְתִּי כִּי יָרֵאָה (Bereishis 18:15), I did not laugh, for she was afraid; סָמוּךְ לִבּוֹ לֹא יִירָא (Tehillim 112:8), his heart is steady, he will not fear; וָֽאִירָא כִּֽי־עֵירֹם אָנֹכִי וָאֵֽחָבֵֽא (Bereishis 3:10), and I was afraid because I was naked, and I hid; וַיִּֽירְאוּ מִגֶּשֶׁת אֵלָֽיו (Shemos 34:30), and they were afraid to come near him; וַיֹּאסֶף שָׁאוּל לֵרֹא מִפְּנֵי דָוִד (Shmuel I 18:29), and Shaul feared David still more.

לְמַעַן יְרָאתֶם (Yehoshua 4:24), so that you may fear, has a kamatz under the resh, and he notes that there is none like it. אַךְ יְראוּ (Shmuel I 12:24), only fear, ought by rule to be יִרְאוּ, but the alef is left at rest so that the word should not look like יִרְאוּ from רָאָה, to see. תִּֽרְאוּ חֲתַת וַתִּירָֽאוּ (Iyov 6:21), you fear a terror and are afraid, are both written with a yud and belong to this root and this sense.

The word of description is אַשְׁרֵי־ אִישׁ יָרֵא (Tehillim 112:1), happy is the man who fears; and in construct אַשְׁרֵי כָּל־ יְרֵא (Tehillim 128:1), happy is every one who fears, יִרְאֵי (Tehillim 22:24), those who fear, and אִשָּׁה יִֽרְאַת (Mishlei 31:30), a woman who fears.

more.h: Awe, and the place of it
more.t: The noun: יֹבִילוּ שַׁי לַמּוֹרָֽא (Tehillim 76:12), they bring a gift to the awe, that is, to the Beis HaMikdash, the place of awe; וְאֶת־ מֽוֹרָאוֹ לֹֽא־ תִֽירְאוּ וְלֹא תַֽעֲרִֽיצוּ (Yeshayahu 8:12), and do not fear what it fears nor be in dread of it; וּמוֹרַֽאֲכֶם וְחִתְּכֶם יִֽהְיֶה (Bereishis 9:2), and the fear of you and the dread of you shall be; מוֹרָה לָהֶם (Tehillim 9:21), set fear upon them, where the heh stands in place of an alef. Or יֹבִילוּ שַׁי לַמּוֹרָֽא may be a description of Hashem Himself, as וְהוּא מוֹרַֽאֲכֶם (Yeshayahu 8:13), and He is your fear.

The noun in another pattern is יִרְאָה: וְיִרְאָה לָהֶם (Yechezkel 1:18), and fear was about them; יִרְאַת י"י רֵאשִׁית דָּעַת (Mishlei 1:7), the fear of Hashem is the beginning of knowledge; וּבַֽעֲבוּר תִּהְיֶה יִרְאָתוֹ (Shemos 20:17), and so that His fear may be upon you.

נוֹרָא מְאֹד (Shoftim 13:6), very awesome; נוֹרָאוֹת בְּצֶדֶק תַּֽעֲנֵנוּ (Tehillim 65:6), with awesome things in righteousness You answer us; לְמַעַן תִּוָּרֵֽא (Tehillim 130:4), so that You may be feared.

more.h: So that You may be feared
more.t: His father explains the pasuk so: Hashem gave the beings above dominion to do His will on earth, but forgiveness is not with them, only with Him. Why? So that men should not say in their hearts, if we sin the angels will be appeased for us and will bear our sins. The pasuk comes to make known that forgiveness is not in them, so that men should fear Hashem, since forgiveness is with Him and with no other. The chacham Rabbi Avraham Ibn Ezra explained that if You did not forgive, sinners would not fear You and would do whatever their soul desires.

more.h: Rabbi Yonah on a distant people
more.t: וּמֵעַם נוָֹרא (Yeshayahu 18:7), from a people feared, and מֵאֶרֶץ נֽוֹרָאָֽה (Yeshayahu 21:1), from a fearsome land, Rabbi Yonah explained as far off, the one and the other. They are not to be taken out of their own sense, even though the plain meaning of the pasuk speaks of a distant people and a distant land, since a man always fears those far from him, whose ways and whose might he does not know, more than those near him, whose ways and might he does know, and the distant ones seem in his eyes mightier and stronger.

כִּי יֵֽרְאֻנִי הָעָם (Shmuel II 14:15), for the people made me afraid, stands in the pattern of גֵּֽרְשׁוּנִי, they drove me out, and he glosses it הפחידוני, they frightened me. So אֲשֶׁר הָיוּ מְיָֽרְאִים אוֹתִֽי (Nechemiah 6:14), who were making me afraid; אִגְּרוֹת שָׁלַח טֽוֹבִיָּה לְיָֽרְאֵנִי (Nechemiah 6:19), Toviah sent letters to make me afraid; לְיָֽרְאָם וּלְבַֽהֲלָם (Divrei HaYamim II 32:18), to make them afraid and to terrify them.

דאג.sense: Fear and sorrow over what is yet to come.

more.t: וְדָאַג לָֽנוּ (Shmuel I 9:5), and he will be anxious for us; עֲוֹנִי אַגִּיד אֶדְאַג מֵֽחַטָּאתִֽי (Tehillim 38:19), I declare my sin, I am anxious over my transgression; וְהָֽרָעָב אֲשֶׁר־אַתֶּם דֹּֽאֲגִים מִמֶּנּוּ (Yirmiyahu 42:16), and the famine that you are anxious about; אֲנִי דֹאֵג אֶת־הַיְּהוּדִים (Yirmiyahu 38:19), I am anxious about the Yehudim; וְאֶת־מִי דָּאַגְתְּ וַתִּֽירְאִי (Yeshayahu 57:11), and of whom were you anxious and afraid.
וּבִשְׁנַת בַּצֹּרֶת לֹ֣א יִדְאָ֔ג (Yirmiyahu 17:8), and in a year of drought it will not be anxious, takes a kamatz with the zakef, and is said by way of borrowing.
וְאִם־לֹא מִדְּאָגָה (Yehoshua 22:24), and if it was not out of anxiety. The sense of them all is fear and sorrow over what is to come.

קמח.sense: Flour. Where a pasuk says to grind flour, it names the thing by what it will become, since no one grinds what is already flour.

more.t: קֶמַח שְׂעֹרִים (Bamidbar 5:15), barley flour, with a segol, and וַתִּקַּח־ קֶמַח וַתָּלָשׁ (Shmuel I 28:24), and she took flour and kneaded it.

קְחִי רֵחַיִם וְטַֽחֲנִי קָמַח (Yeshayahu 47:2), take millstones and grind flour, says flour on account of its end, since a man does not grind flour. So too אָפִיתִי עַל־גֶּחָלָיו לֶחֶם (Yeshayahu 44:19), I baked bread on its coals, since it is not bread until it has been baked, and others besides these, as he wrote at the root אָפָה. And so בְּלִי יַֽעֲשֶׂה־ קֶּמַח (Hoshea 8:7), it shall yield no flour, which he wrote at the root לָחַם.

סלת.sense: Solet, the flour of a coarse grinding; so the Mishnah speaks of a sieve that lets the flour through and holds the solet back.

more.h: The flour of a coarse grinding
more.t: סֹלֶת חִטִּים (Shemos 29:2), solet of wheat, and מִסָּלְתָּהּ וּמִשַּׁמְנָהּ (Vayikra 2:2), of its solet and of its oil: it is the flour ground with a coarse grinding. So the Mishnah has it (Avos 5:15), נפה שהיא מוציאה את הקמח וקולטת את הסולת, a sieve that lets the flour out and holds back the solet.

גרשֹ.sense: Wheat broken and crumbled, as he explains at the root גרס: גֶּרֶשׂ כַּרְמֶל (Vayikra 2:14), fresh ears broken small, and מִגִּרְשָׂהּ (Vayikra 2:16), its broken wheat.

גרשׁ.sense: To drive out and send away, as a wife from her husband; of the sea, to toss and cast up mire. The open land outside a city is named as though driven out of it.

more.t: הִנְנִי גֹרֵשׁ מִפָּנֶיךָ (Shemos 34:11), behold, I drive out before you; וְאִשָּׁה גְּרוּשָׁה מֵֽאִישָׁהּ (Vayikra 21:7), and a woman put away from her husband; גָּרֵשׁ הָֽאָמָה הַזֹּאת (Bereishis 21:10), drive out this maidservant; and with no doer named, כִּי־ גֹֽרְשׁוּ מִמִּצְרַיִם (Shemos 12:39), for they were driven out of Egypt.

הָרִימוּ גְרֻשֹֽׁתֵיכֶם מֵעַל עַמִּי (Yechezkel 45:9), take away your exactions from my people, he reads as the taxes you heap and cast upon them, lift them off them. Targum Yonasan rendered סְלִיקוּ תִקְלַתְכוֹן מִגוֹ עַמִי, remove your burden from among my people.

more.h: The sea that casts up mire
more.t: וַיִּגְרְשׁוּ מֵימָיו רֶפֶשׁ וָטִֽיט (Yeshayahu 57:20), its waters cast up mire and mud, and כַּיָּם נִגְרָשׁ (Yeshayahu 57:20), like the tossing sea, which he reads as a sea shaking with its waves, and they go out to the shore. The same form is in נִגְרַשְׁתִּי מִנֶּגֶד עֵינֶיךָ (Yonah 2:5), I am driven out from before Your eyes, and in וְנִגְרְשָׁה (Amos 8:8), it heaves up, וְנִשְׁקְעָה כִּיאוֹר מִצְרָֽיִם, and sinks like the river of Egypt.

more.h: The moons that drive the fruit out
more.t: גֶּרֶשׁ יְרָחִֽים (Devarim 33:14), the putting forth of the moons, is a noun pointed with six dots, and is the season when the fruits bud and blossom with force, as though the moon were driving them outward.

With a mem added, מִגְרָשׁ: לְמַעַן מִגְרָשָׁהּ לָבַֽז (Yechezkel 36:5) is a noun standing in place of the infinitive, as if it said למען גרוש אותה לבז, so as to drive it out for spoil. The same noun names the open lands that lie outside a city, וּמִגְרָשׁ לֶֽעָרִים (Bamidbar 35:2), and open land for the cities, and וּמִגְרְשֵׁי הֶֽעָרִים (Bamidbar 35:4), the open lands of the cities. In another pattern, לְקוֹל זַֽעֲקַת חֹֽבְלָיִךְ יִרְֽעֲשׁוּ מִגְרֹשֽׁוֹת (Yechezkel 27:28), at the sound of the cry of your pilots the outlying lands shake, called so because they lie outside the city, as though they had been driven out of it.

גרס.sense: To break and pound: a soul broken with longing, teeth broken on gravel; and גֶּרֶשׂ, the wheat broken and crumbled.

more.t: גָּרְסָה נַפְשִׁי לְתַאֲבָה (Tehillim 119:20), my soul is broken with longing: broken and pounded from the greatness of its desire for Your judgments. The heavy form, וַיַּגְרֵס בֶּחָצָץ שִׁנָּי (Eichah 3:17 in his edition), he broke my teeth on gravel, which he glosses וישבר, and he broke.

Written with a sin: גֶּרֶשׂ כַּרְמֶל (Vayikra 2:14), broken grain of fresh ears, pointed with six dots, and מִגִּרְשָׂהּ וּמִשַּׁמְנָהּ (Vayikra 2:16), of its broken grain and of its oil, which is the wheat broken and crumbled, and he gives the Old French word for it. Like it in the words of Chazal (Avodah Zarah 65b), חומץ שנפל לתוך הגריסין, vinegar that fell into the grits.

בוץ.sense: Butz is linen: וְתַכְרִיךְ בּוּץ (Esther 8:15), a robe of butz; and the Targum renders מִֽכְנְסֵי־בַד (Vayikra 6:3), linen breeches, with this word.

זמן.sense: A time, as everything has its time and season; and appointed times, whose sense he calls known.

more.t: וָאֶתְּנָה לוֹ זְמָן (Nechemiah 2:6), and I set him a time; לַכֹּל זְמָן וְעֵת (Koheles 3:1), everything has its time and its season; and יְמֵי הַפֻּרִים הָאֵלֶּה בִּזְמַנֵּיהֶם (Esther 9:31), these days of Purim at their times, which he glosses as year by year.
לְעִתִּים מְזֻמָּנִים (Ezra 10:14) and בְּעִתִּים מְזֻמָּנוֹת (Nechemiah 13:31), at times appointed; of these he says only that their sense is known.

יעד.sense: Summoning, meeting by appointment; מוֹעֵד is a set time, and the place where people gather at a known time; the עֵדָה, the congregation, is those summoned together.

more.t: מִן־הַמּוֹעֵד אֲשֶׁר יְעָדוֹ (Shmuel II 20:5), from the set time he had appointed him, and וְאִם־לִבְנוֹ יִיעָדֶנָּה (Shemos 21:9), and if he appoints her for his son.

וְנוֹעַדְתִּי לְךָ שָׁם (Shemos 25:22), I will meet with you there, and כִּי־הִנֵּה הַמְּלָכִים נוֹעֲדוּ (Tehillim 48:5), for behold the kings had assembled. All of these, and those above, are the sense of summoning.

Rabbi Yehudah set יוֹעִידֶנִּי apart to a sense of its own; Radak says there is no need, since these too are summoning. כִּי מִי כָמוֹנִי וּמִי יֹעִידֶנִּי (Yirmiyahu 49:19) he explains as who will summon for Me one like Me, and וְאִם־לְמִשְׁפָּט מִי יוֹעִידֵנִי (Iyov 9:19), and if for judgment, is read as who will summon me to judgment with Hashem.

בְּמֹעֵד שְׁנַת הַשְּׁמִטָּה (Devarim 31:10), at the set time of the shemittah year; וַיֹּֽאכְלוּ אֶת־ הַמּוֹעֵד שִׁבְעַת הַיָּמִים (Divrei HaYamim II 30:22), they ate the מועד seven days, which he glosses זבחי המועד, the offerings of the set time; מוֹעֵד וְשַׁבָּת (Eichah 2:6), set time and Shabbos; and לַשַּׁבָּתוֹת וְלֶחֳדָשִׁים וְלַמּוֹעֲדוֹת (Divrei HaYamim II 8:13), for the Shabbosos, the new moons and the set times, all of which he says mean time, times.

מֵהַבֹּקֶר וְעַד־עֵת מוֹעֵד (Shmuel II 24:15), from the morning until the time of the מועד, he takes as the time of the offering, which he puts at four hours, and so Targum Yonasan renders it, from when the tamid is slaughtered until it is brought up.

A place where people gather at a known time is called a מוֹעֵד. שָׁאֲגוּ צֹרְרֶיךָ בְּקֶרֶב מוֹעֲדֶךָ (Tehillim 74:4), your foes roared in the midst of your meeting place, he takes of the Beis HaMikdash, where all Yisrael would meet, and so שָׂרְפוּ כָל־מוֹעֲדֵי־אֵל (Tehillim 74:8), they burned all the meeting places of Hashem. קְרִאֵי מוֹעֵד (Bamidbar 16:2), those called to the meeting, are those called when the great men met on some matter, since they were men of standing.
The אהל מועד is so called because Yisrael would gather there, and further because Hashem met with Moshe there, as וְנוֹעַדְתִּי לְךָ שָׁם (Shemos 25:22), I will meet with you there, says.

וְאֵשֵׁב בְּהַר־מוֹעֵד בְּיַרְכְּתֵי צָפוֹן (Yeshayahu 14:13), I will sit on the mount of meeting in the far north, is a place where all the kings gather and meet to him, which he says is Bavel; וּבֵית מוֹעֵד לְכָל־חָי (Iyov 30:23), a meeting house for all the living, is the grave, where all the living meet when their end comes; and עָרֵי הַמּוּעָדָה (Yehoshua 20:9), the cities of meeting, are the cities where anyone who killed by accident was to gather.

The assembly is called an עֵדָה, as קְרִיאֵי הָעֵדָה (Bamidbar 26:9), those called of the congregation, because they are summoned together in their gathering; and so a swarm, וְהִנֵּה עֲדַת דְּבוֹרִים (Shoftim 14:8), a company of bees, gathered as though each had been summoned to the next.

שׁעה.sense: To turn to. Other senses: to trust in; to be alarmed and afraid; to leave off; and delight, or else telling.

more.t: וְאֶל־קַיִן וְאֶל־מִנְחָתוֹ לֹא שָׁעָה (Bereishis 4:5), and to Kayin and his offering He did not turn, while אֶל־הֶבֶל וְאֶל־מִנְחָתוֹ (Bereishis 4:4), to Hevel and his offering, He did turn. Their sense is לא פנה, He did not turn, and ויפן, He turned, in the way of אַל־תֵּפֶן אֶל־מִנְחָתָם (Bamidbar 16:15), do not turn to their offering.

יִשְׁעוּ וְאֵין מֹשִׁיעַ (Shmuel II 22:42) he reads as turning this way and that with none to save; or it is like יְשַׁוְּעוּ (Tehillim 18:42), they cry out, so that שׁוּעַ and שָׁעָה would be one sense.

In another sense, יִשְׁעֶה הָאָדָם עַל־עֹשֵׂהוּ (Yeshayahu 17:7), a man will trust in his Maker; וְלֹא יִשְׁעֶה אֶל־הַמִּזְבְּחוֹת (Yeshayahu 17:8), he will not trust in the altars; וְלֹא שָׁעוּ עַל־קְדוֹשׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל (Yeshayahu 31:1), they did not trust in the Holy One of Yisrael; and וְאַל־יִשְׁעוּ בְּדִבְרֵי־שָׁקֶר (Shemos 5:9), let them not trust in words of falsehood. Their sense is trust; it may be that these too are to be explained from the first sense.

וְלֹא תִשְׁעֶינָה עֵינֵי רֹאִים (Yeshayahu 32:3), the eyes of those who see shall not be alarmed, and אַל־תִּשְׁתָּע כִּי־אֲנִי אֱלֹהֶיךָ (Yeshayahu 41:10), be not alarmed, for I am your God: their sense is alarm and fear. The first can also be read from וְעֵינָיו הָשַׁע (Yeshayahu 6:10), and shut his eyes, and then they would be two roots with one sense.

On אַל־תִּשְׁתָּע, be not alarmed, the midrash says אל תהיה כשעוה, do not be like wax (Bereishis Rabbah 43). The שעוה is the דונג, wax, and the meaning is, do not melt like wax before the fire. And שעוה is beyond doubt from this root.

שְׁעֵה מֵעָלָיו וְיֶחְדָּל (Iyov 14:6), let him alone, that he may cease, and שְׁעוּ מִנִּי אֲמָרֵר בַּבֶּכִי (Yeshayahu 22:4), let me alone, I will weep bitterly: their sense is letting be. His father explains אַל־תִּשְׁתָּע from this sense, which Radak spells out as אל תתרפה, do not go slack.

וְאֶשְׁעָה בְחֻקֶּיךָ תָמִיד (Tehillim 119:117), I will delight in Your statutes always, is of the sense of תּוֹרָתְךָ שַׁעֲשֻׁעָי (Tehillim 119:92), Your Torah is my delight, the kamatz standing in for a segol; or it may be a sense of telling, from the Targum of וַיְסַפֵּר (Bereishis 37:10), and he told, which is וְאִשְׁתָּעֵי. So too וְנִשְׁתָּעָה (Yeshayahu 41:23), and let us tell, where the kamatz again stands where a segol would; but Targum Yonasan renders it וְנִסְתַּכֵּיל, and let us look, and on that it belongs to the first sense.
וּבְמַיִם לֹא־רֻחַצְתְּ לְמִשְׁעִי (Yechezkel 16:4), nor were you washed in water לְמִשְׁעִי, a word he gives no sense here: he has written it under the root שוע.

שׁלל.sense: To take spoil, and the spoil taken; שׁוֹלָל, stripped. Close to this sense is שֹׁל־תָּשֹׁלּוּ, letting ears of grain fall from the bundles.

more.t: וְשָׁלַל שְׁלָלָהּ (Yechezkel 29:19), he will take its spoil; כִּי אַתָּה שַׁלּוֹתָ גּוֹיִם רַבִּים (Chavakuk 2:8), because you plundered many nations; and in the same pasuk יְשָׁלּוּךָ כָּל־יֶתֶר עַמִּים, all the rest of the peoples will plunder you.

As an adjective, שׁוֹלָל וְעָרוֹם (Michah 1:8), stripped and bare. On מוֹלִיךְ יוֹעֲצִים שׁוֹלָל (Iyov 12:17), He leads counsellors away stripped, his reading is that He leads each one of the counsellors away so, and his counsel avails him nothing. Some explain שׁוֹלָל as stripped of understanding, like וְשֹׁפְטִים יְהוֹלֵל in the same pasuk, and He makes fools of judges.

אֶשְׁתּוֹלְלוּ אַבִּירֵי לֵב (Tehillim 76:6), the stout of heart were despoiled, where the alef stands in place of the hei of the reflexive; and וְסָר מֵרָע מִשְׁתּוֹלֵל (Yeshayahu 59:15), and he who turns from evil is despoiled, that is, as though they had despoiled him, so that he is not to be found.

וְאֶת־הַמַּלְקוֹחַ וְאֶת־הַשָּׁלָל (Bamidbar 31:12), the booty and the spoil, and זֶה שְׁלַל דָּוִד (Shmuel I 30:20), this is David's spoil. וְהָיְתָה לְךָ נַפְשְׁךָ לְשָׁלָל (Yirmiyahu 39:18), your life will be yours as spoil, he glosses as gain, as though you had taken it as plunder.
Close to this sense is שֹׁל־תָּשֹׁלּוּ לָהּ (Rus 2:16), let fall for her, that is, let ears of grain drop for her out of the bundles.

בזז.sense: To plunder, and the plunder taken; all of it, he says, is the sense of שלל, spoil.

more.t: וּבָזַז בִּזָּהּ (Yechezkel 29:19), he will plunder its plunder; בָּזְזוּ לָהֶם בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (Yehoshua 11:14), Bnei Yisrael plundered for themselves; בַּזּוֹנוּ לָנוּ (Devarim 3:7), we plundered for ourselves; שְׁאֵרִית עַמִּי יְבָזּוּם (Tzefaniah 2:9), the remnant of My people will plunder them; and וּשְׁלָלָם לָבוֹז (Esther 8:11), their spoil to plunder.
In וְנָבֹזָה בָהֶם עַד־אוֹר הַבֹּקֶר (Shmuel I 14:36), let us plunder among them until the morning light, the zayin is left without its dagesh, which he says belongs to it by right.
וְהִבּוֹז תִּבּוֹז (Yeshayahu 24:3), it shall surely be plundered, and חֶרֶב אֶל־אוֹצְרֹתֶיהָ וּבֻזָּזוּ (Yirmiyahu 50:37), a sword upon her treasuries, and they shall be plundered.

וּבַבִּזָּה לֹא שָׁלְחוּ אֶת־יָדָם (Esther 9:10), they did not put out their hand to the plunder; without the hei, יֶתֶר הַבָּז (Bamidbar 31:32), the rest of the plunder; and בִּזָּהּ in וּבָזַז בִּזָּהּ (Yechezkel 29:19), its plunder, where the hei is as though it carried a mappik.

לקח.sense: To take. Its nouns: מַלְקוֹחַ, spoil; tongs, named for taking hold of a thing; a purchase; and לֶקַח, knowledge.

more.t: וְאֶתְכֶם לָקַח (Devarim 4:20), and you He took. With the first letter dropped, קָח עַל־מַיִם רַבִּים (Yechezkel 17:5), he took it by abundant waters, pointed with a kamatz to keep it apart from the command. From how heavily the word is used, the first letter falls away in most places, and the kuf's dagesh with it, as in וְאֶקְחָה פַת־לֶחֶם (Bereishis 18:5), and let me take a morsel of bread.

וַיִּקַּח קֹרַח (Bamidbar 16:1), and Korach took, is Korach taking himself along with his fellows, and they took counsel in the matter; so too וַיִּקְחוּ שְׁלשִׁים מֵֽרֵעִים וַיִּהְיוּ אִתּֽוֹ (Shoftim 14:11), thirty companions took themselves and were with him, and וְאַבְשָׁלֹם לָקַח (Shmuel II 18:18), and Avshalom took, who took this counsel upon himself. תִּֽקַּֽח ־לָהּ (Bereishis 38:23), let her take them for herself, means let her keep them for herself, and do not go back after them again.

Said of the death of the righteous: כִּֽי־ לָקַח אֹתוֹ אֱלֹהִֽים (Bereishis 5:24), for Hashem took him; כִּי יִקָּחֵנִי סֶֽלָה (Tehillim 49:16), for He will take me, selah; and וְאַחַר כָּבוֹד תִּקָּחֵֽנִי (Tehillim 73:24), and afterward You will take me in honour.

הוּא בַּֽעֲוֹנוֹ נִלְקָח (Yechezkel 33:6), he is taken in his sin; וַֽאֲרוֹן הָאֱלֹהִים נִלְקָֽחָה (Shmuel I 4:17), and the Aron of Hashem was taken; and וְאֵשׁ מִתְלַקַּחַת (Shemos 9:24), fire taking hold of itself.

The noun מַלְקוֹחַ is used in the sense of spoil: אֶת־הַשְּׁבִי וְאֶת־ הַמַּלְקוֹחַ (Bamidbar 31:12), the captives and the spoil, and וּמַלְקוֹחַ עָרִיץ (Yeshayahu 49:25), the spoil of the tyrant. Where it says אֶת־הַשְּׁבִי וְאֶת־הַמַּלְקוֹחַ וְאֶת־הַשָּׁלָל, the captives and the מלקוח and the שלל, he divides them: שבי of people, מלקוח of animals, שלל of clothing and vessels; and so they are read wherever they stand together. One comes in place of another all the same: וְחָצִיתָ אֶת־ הַמַּלְקוֹחַ (Bamidbar 31:27), and you shall halve the spoil, is said of man and beast alike, and זֶה שְׁלַל דָּוִֽד (Shmuel I 30:20), this is David's spoil, of animals.

On another pattern, with the first letter dropped, וּמִקַּח ־שֹֽׁחַד (Divrei HaYamim II 19:7), the taking of a bribe. In the sense of acquisition, הַֽמְבִיאִים אֶת־ הַמַּקָּחוֹת (Nechemiah 10:32), those who bring in the wares, and in the words of Chazal (Bava Metzia 2a) מקח וממכר, buying and selling. From this, לֹֽקְחֵי חִטִּים (Shmuel II 4:6), takers of wheat, means as though buyers of wheat, and so Yonasan renders it, כְּזַבְּנֵי חִטִין, like buyers of wheat; and so too זָֽמְמָה שָׂדֶה וַתִּקָּחֵהוּ (Mishlei 31:16), she considered a field and bought it.

more.h: Tongs, and what takes the food
more.t: The tongs are called מלקחים because they take hold of a thing: בְּמֶלְקָחַיִם לָקַח מֵעַל הַמִּזְבֵּֽחַ (Yeshayahu 6:6), with tongs he took from upon the mizbeach, and וּמַלְקָחֶיהָ וּמַחְתֹּתֶיהָ (Shemos 37:23), its tongs and its pans, named in the pair form since they are two. The menorah's tongs served to lift the wicks out of the oil, set them straight and draw them to the mouths of the lamps. וּלְשׁוֹנִי מֻדְבָּק מַלְקוֹחָי (Tehillim 22:16), and my tongue cleaves to my מלקוחים: what lies above the tongue and beneath it is so called, since they come together and take the food in chewing.

In the sense of knowledge, כִּי לֶקַח טוֹב נָתַתִּי לָכֶם (Mishlei 4:2), for I have given you a good teaching; וְיוֹסֶף לֶקַח (Mishlei 1:5), and he will add learning; יַֽעֲרֹף כַּמָּטָר לִקְחִי (Devarim 32:2), my teaching will fall as the rain; and הִטַּתּוּ בְּרֹב לִקְחָהּ (Mishlei 7:21), she turned him with her much persuading. From this, הַלֹּֽקְחִים לְשׁוֹנָם וַיִּנְֽאֲמוּ נְאֻֽם (Yirmiyahu 23:31), who take their tongue and declare a declaration, like לְשׁוֹנָם יַֽחֲלִֽיקוּן (Tehillim 5:10), they make their tongue smooth.

Rabbi Yonah read וַיִּקְחוּ הָֽאֲנָשִׁים מִצֵּידָם (Yehoshua 9:14), and the men took of their provision, from this sense of learning; Radak spells his reading out as their learning and knowing from the dryness of the provision that the truth was with them. Radak holds there is no need to take it out of the plain sense of taking: the men of Yisrael took of their provision and ate, to confirm the covenant with them. So too וַיִּקַּח וַיִּתֵּן אֶת־הָֽעֵדֻת (Shemos 40:20), and he took and put the testimony, is as it sounds: he took the luchos of the covenant and put them in the Aron.

שׁבה.sense: To take captive; the captive, and captives and captivity in several forms; and of this root too the shevo, one of the precious stones.

more.t: אֲשֶׁר־ שָׁבָה יִשְׁמָעֵאל (Yirmiyahu 41:14), whom Yishmael had taken captive; וַיִּשְׁבְּ מִמֶּנּוּ שֶֽׁבִי (Bamidbar 21:1), he took captives from him; וְשָׁבִיתָ שִׁבְיֽוֹ (Devarim 21:10), and you take his captives; and שֹׁבִים לְשֹֽׁבֵיהֶם (Yeshayahu 14:2), taking their captors captive.

כִּי נִשְׁבָּה אָחִיו (Bereishis 14:14), for his brother had been taken captive, and וּנְשֵׁיהֶם וּבְנֵיהֶם וּבְנֹֽתֵיהֶם נִשְׁבּֽוּ (Shmuel I 30:3), their wives and sons and daughters had been taken captive: their sense, he says, is known.
שְׁבִיָּה בַּת־צִיּֽוֹן (Yeshayahu 52:2), captive daughter of Tzion; for a man, he says, the form would be שָׁבִי, on the weight of עָנִי, a poor man.

קוּמִי שְּׁבִי יְרֽוּשָׁלָם (Yeshayahu 52:2), arise, captive Yerushalayim, is the noun, captivity; Yonasan rendered it instead from יָשַׁב, to sit: קומי תְבִי עַל כּוּרְסֵי יְקָרָא יְרוּשְׁלֵם, arise, sit upon the throne of honour, Yerushalayim.

וְרָאִיתָ בַּשִּׁבְיָה (Devarim 21:11), and you see among the captives; וּבְנֹתָיו בַּשְּׁבִית (Bamidbar 21:29), his daughters in captivity; שְׁבִיתֵנוּ (Tehillim 126:4), our captivity; and with a shuruk, אֶת־ שְׁבֽוּתְךָ (Devarim 30:3), your captivity, and שְׁבוּת אָהֳלֵי יַֽעֲקוֹב (Yirmiyahu 30:18), the captivity of the tents of Yaakov.
Of this root too is לֶשֶׁם שְׁבוֹ (Shemos 28:19), a leshem, a shevo: the shevo is one of the precious stones, and he gives its name in Arabic.

שׁלך.sense: To throw and cast down, the sense of all its verbs; used of casting people out of their dwellings, and of casting a lot.

more.t: הִשְׁלִיךְ מִשָּׁמַיִם אֶרֶץ (Eichah 2:1), He cast down from heaven to earth; וַתַּשְׁלֵךְ אֶת־הַיֶּלֶד (Bereishis 21:15), she cast the child down; הַשְׁלִיכוּ אֹתוֹ אֶל־הַבּוֹר (Bereishis 37:22), throw him into the pit; and מַשְׁלִיךְ קַרְחוֹ כְפִתִּים (Tehillim 147:17), casting His ice like crumbs. All of it is the sense of throwing and casting down.
כִּי הִשְׁלִיכוּ מִשְׁכְּנוֹתֵינוּ (Yirmiyahu 9:18) he reads as they cast us out of our dwellings, in the way of וְלֹא־תָקִיא אֶתְכֶם הָאָרֶץ (Vayikra 20:22), and the land shall not vomit you out.
וּפֹה אַשְׁלִיךְ לָכֶם גּוֹרָל (Yehoshua 18:8), and here I will cast a lot for you.

וְהֻשְׁלַךְ מְכוֹן מִקְדָּשׁוֹ (Daniel 8:11), the place of His Mikdash was cast down; עָלֶיךָ הָשְׁלַכְתִּי מֵרָחֶם (Tehillim 22:11), upon You I was cast from the womb; and וַתֻּשְׁלְכִי אֶל־פְּנֵי הַשָּׂדֶה (Yechezkel 16:5), you were cast out on the open field.

וַיַּשְׁלִכוּ הָרָצִים וְהַשָּׁלִשִׁים וַיֵּלְכוּ (Melachim II 10:25), and the runners and the officers cast and went, is said by way of extension, from their great haste and speed when they were sent to the city of Beis HaBaal to break down the pillars.

וְאֶת־הַשָּׁלָךְ (Vayikra 11:17), and the שָׁלָךְ, our Rabbis explained (Chullin 63a) as the one that draws fish out of the sea, and Onkelos renders it so, וְשָׁלֵינוּנָא. אֲשֶׁר בְּשַׁלֶּכֶת (Yeshayahu 6:13), which at Shalleches, Radak takes as the name of a gate that was in the Beis HaMikdash, the one named in Divrei HaYamim, עִם שַׁעַר שַׁלֶּכֶת (Divrei HaYamim I 26:16), with the gate of Shalleches; Targum Yonasan rendered it as a word of casting.

Targum Yonasan renders the whole pasuk: like the terebinth and the oak, whose leaves fall and look dry while they are still moist, to keep seed from them, so the exile of Yisrael will be gathered in and return to their land, for the holy seed is their planting.

זרק.sense: To throw, as Moshe throws it heavenward and blood is thrown on the mizbeach; מִזְרָק is the vessel that one throws from.

more.t: וּזְרָקוֹ מֹשֶׁה הַשָּׁמַיְמָה (Shemos 9:8), and Moshe shall throw it toward the heavens; וַחֲצִי הַדָּם זָרַק עַל־הַמִּזְבֵּחַ (Shemos 24:6), and half the blood he threw on the mizbeach; and וְזָרַקְתִּי עֲלֵיכֶם מַיִם טְהוֹרִים וּטְהַרְתֶּם (Yechezkel 36:25), I will throw pure water upon you and you will be pure.

גַּם־שֵׂיבָה זָרְקָה בּוֹ (Hoshea 7:9), grey hair too was thrown into him. It is either a verb standing alone, that is, the grey was thrown into him, or it means that nature threw the grey into him, since grey hair comes of a man's nature.
In the form that names no doer, כִּי מֵי נִדָּה לֹא־זֹרַק עָלָיו (Bamidbar 19:13), for the mei niddah was not thrown upon him.

The vessel one throws from is a מִזְרָק: וְיָעָיו וּמִזְרְקֹתָיו (Shemos 27:3), its shovels and its basins; כַּמִּזְרָקִים לִפְנֵי הַמִּזְבֵּחַ (Zecharyah 14:20), like the basins before the mizbeach; and מִזְרְקֵי־כֶסֶף (Bamidbar 7:84), basins of silver.

הַשֹּׁתִים בְּמִזְרְקֵי יַיִן (Amos 6:6), who drink wine in basins: the word that completes the construct is missing, and it means that they drink wine in basins of silver or of gold; or else it is like מזרקים, basins. So too חַלּוֹנֵי שְׁקֻפִים (Melachim I 6:4), windows that are shekufim, and נִטְעֵי נַעֲמָנִים (Yeshayahu 17:10), pleasant plantings, and those like them.

נזה.sense: To sprinkle, of blood and of the water of the niddah; a known sense, like dripping. He reads כֵּן יַזֶּה גּוֹיִם רַבִּים as speaking: so shall he address many nations.

more.t: וַאֲשֶׁר יִזֶּה מִדָּמָהּ עַל־הַבֶּגֶד (Vayikra 6:20), whatever of its blood spatters on a garment, and וַיִּז מִדָּמָהּ אֶל־הַקִּיר (Melachim II 9:33), some of her blood spattered on the wall.

וְהִזָּה אֶל־הַבַּיִת (Vayikra 14:51), and he shall sprinkle toward the house; יַזֶּה שֶׁבַע־פְּעָמִים (Vayikra 16:14), he shall sprinkle seven times; הַזֵּה עֲלֵיהֶם מֵי חַטָּאת (Bamidbar 8:7), sprinkle the waters of the chatas upon them; and וַיַּז מִמֶּנּוּ (Vayikra 8:11), and he sprinkled of it. The sense of הזאה, sprinkling, is known, like the sense of dripping.

more.h: The one who carries the water
more.t: וּמַזֵּה מֵי־הַנִּדָּה (Bamidbar 19:21), and the sprinkling of the water of the niddah: Chazal (Niddah 9a) say that the one who sprinkles stays tahor and the pasuk speaks rather of one who carries it, who takes a severe tumah that makes tamei the clothes upon him, unlike one who only touches it, who need not launder his clothes; and it is put as מִזֵּה to say that he is not tamei until there is enough of it for a sprinkling. On that reading מזה is a noun on the pattern of מַטֶּה, a staff, and the pasuk means that whoever carries the sprinkling of the water of the niddah shall launder his clothes.
כֵּן יַזֶּה גּוֹיִם רַבִּים (Yeshayahu 52:15) he takes in the sense of speaking, a verb that takes an object: so shall he address many nations. The edition sets a vernacular word beside it.

רמה.sense: To cast or throw; in another sense, to deceive, with רְמִיָּה and מִרְמָה, deceit.

more.t: רָמָה בַיָּם (Shemos 15:1), He cast into the sea; פָּרָשׁ וְרֹמֵה קֶשֶׁת (Yirmiyahu 4:29), horseman and one who shoots the bow; נוֹשְׁקֵי רוֹמֵי־קָשֶׁת (Tehillim 78:9), armed men shooting with the bow; and רָמַת לֶחִי (Shoftim 15:17), the casting of the jawbone. The sense of casting is well known. The noun from it is in הָיוּ כְּקֶשֶׁת רְמִיָּה (Hoshea 7:16), they were like a casting bow.
Rabbi Yonah takes וּמִלֵּאתִי הַגֵּאָיוֹת רָמוּתֶךָ (Yechezkel 32:5), and I will fill the valleys with those of you cast down, from this sense: that is, the slain who will fall from your multitude.

Another sense: כֵּן־אִישׁ רִמָּה אֶת־רֵעֵהוּ (Mishlei 26:19), so is a man who deceived his fellow; לָמָּה רִמִּיתָנִי (Shmuel I 28:12), why did you deceive me; הֵמָּה רִמּוּנִי (Eichah 1:19), they deceived me; and וְאִם־לְרַמּוֹתַנִי לְצָרַי (Divrei HaYamim I 12:18), and if it is to deceive me for my foes.

more.h: The nouns and adjective of deceit
more.t: The noun: וְלוֹ תְּדַבְּרוּ רְמִיָּה (Iyov 13:7), will you speak deceit for Him, on the pattern of בִּצְדִיָּה (Bamidbar 35:20), by lying in wait. The adjective: לָשׁוֹן רְמִיָּה (Tehillim 120:3), a deceitful tongue. Another form of the noun: הֶחֱזִיקוּ בַּתַּרְמִית (Yirmiyahu 8:5), they held fast to deceit; another, בְּתָרְמָה לֵאמֹר (Shoftim 9:31), with deceit, saying; and another, מֹאזְנֵי מִרְמָה (Mishlei 11:1), scales of deceit.

more.h: Where his father reads a place
more.t: His father explains בְּתָרְמָה לֵאמֹר (Shoftim 9:31) as the name of a place, in Tormah, saying, since that pattern is not found with an added tav.

כְּקֶשֶׁת רְמִיָּה (Hoshea 7:16) may instead belong to the sense of deceit: a bow that shoots with deceit, so that no one is aware of it. So too כְּתַעַר מְלֻטָּשׁ עֹשֵׂה רְמִיָּה (Tehillim 52:4), like a sharpened razor working deceit.

רטב.sense: To be moist; the sense of both pesukim, he says, is moisture.

more.t: רָטֹב הוּא לִפְנֵי־שָׁמֶשׁ (Iyov 8:16), he is moist before the sun, and מִזֶּרֶם הָרִים יִרְטָבוּ (Iyov 24:8), they are wet from the downpour of the mountains. Their sense is that of moisture.

רען.sense: Fresh with moisture: the sense, he says, is לחות, moistness; an olive tree, a leaf, a couch; and fresh oil, meaning new oil.

more.h: Verb or adjective by the stress
more.t: The verb is found with its last letter doubled. וְכִפָּתוֹ לֹא רַעֲנָנָה (Iyov 15:32), and his branch was not fresh, is a past verb, because the stress falls back; אַף־עַרְשֵׂנוּ רַעֲנָנָה (Shir HaShirim 1:16), our couch too is fresh, is an adjective, because the stress falls at the end.

כְּזַיִת רַעֲנָן (Tehillim 52:10), like a fresh olive tree; וְהָיָה עָלֵהוּ רַעֲנָן (Yirmiyahu 17:8), and its leaf will be fresh; and in the plural, which takes a dagesh, דְּשֵׁנִים וְרַעֲנַנִּים יִהְיוּ (Tehillim 92:15), they will be fat and fresh. Their sense is לחות, moistness.
בְּשֶׁמֶן רַעֲנָן (Tehillim 92:11), with fresh oil, means new oil.

רטפשׁ.sense: Of flesh, grew soft, as he reads it from its place in its one pasuk; some take it as a word made of two.

more.t: רֻטֲפַשׁ בְּשָׂרוֹ מִנֹּעַר (Iyov 33:25), his flesh grew soft beyond a youth's: that the word means it became soft, he says, is to be taken from its place.

Some say it is a word compounded of two words. The two, as he spells them out, are רטוב and פש, that is, moist and be fruitful and multiply, the second from the Targum of פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ (Bereishis 1:28), be fruitful and multiply, which is פּוּשׁוּ וּסְגוּ.

more.h: Read by atbash, and the Targum
more.t: It is also explained that רטפש is רטוב by atbash, the peh standing for a vav and the shin for a beis. The Targum renders it אִתְחֲלִישׁ בִּסְרֵיהּ, his flesh grew weak.

טפח.sense: The tefach, a handbreadth, measured by four fingers held together; and a verb of rearing children, since an infant is patted and his limbs straightened as he is swaddled.

more.t: מִסְגֶּרֶת טֹפַח (Shemos 25:25), a rim a handbreadth wide, and שֵׁשׁ־אַמּוֹת בָּאַמָּה וָטֹפַח (Yechezkel 40:5), six cubits by the cubit and a handbreadth; on another pattern, with a segol, וְעָבְיוֹ טֶפַח (Divrei HaYamim II 4:5), its thickness a handbreadth. In Tanach the plural is feminine, הִנֵּה טְפָחוֹת נָתַתָּה יָמַי (Tehillim 39:6), behold, You have made my days handbreadths, while Chazal (Bava Basra 1:1) use it as a masculine, טפחים.

The tefach is of a kind with the זרת, the span, but not of one size with it: the span is measured by the fingers of the hand spread apart and the tefach by four fingers held together, and the span is three tefachim, as he has written.

הִנֵּה טְפָחוֹת נָתַתָּה יָמַי, You have made my days handbreadths, answers what comes before it, וּמִדַּת יָמַי מַה־הִיא (Tehillim 39:5), and the measure of my days, what it is: as the tefach's measure is small, so is the measure of my days. Even were I to live all a man can live, my days are handbreadths, וְחֶלְדִּי כְאַיִן נֶגְדֶּךָ, and my lifetime is as nothing before You, as it says כִּי אֶלֶף שָׁנִים בְּעֵינֶיךָ כְּיוֹם אֶתְמוֹל (Tehillim 90:4), for a thousand years in Your eyes are as yesterday.

וּמִמַּסַּד עַד־הַטְּפָחוֹת (Melachim I 7:9), from the foundation up to the טְפָחוֹת, is from the foundation up to the wall above, which was built to the handbreadth measure; Targum Yonasan renders it finished by handbreadths.

וִימִינִי טִפְּחָה שָׁמָיִם (Yeshayahu 48:13), and My right hand spread out the heavens, where some precise sefarim point טפחה with a chataf kamatz. אֲשֶׁר־טִפַּחְתִּי וְרִבִּיתִי (Eichah 2:22), those whom I reared and raised: טִפַּחְתִּי is said of the rearing of children, since so they do to an infant, patting him and straightening his limbs each time they swaddle him. The noun from it is in עֹלֲלֵי טִפֻּחִים (Eichah 2:20), infants whom they would pat while they were small, tending to their rearing, and whom they afterwards ate.

הָבִי הַמִּטְפַּחַת אֲשֶׁר־עָלַיִךְ (Rus 3:15), give me the mitpachas that is on you: it is a veil, and so וְהַמִּטְפָּחוֹת (Yeshayahu 3:22), and the veils. So too in the words of Chazal (Megillah 26b): mitpachos of sefarim that have worn out are made into shrouds for a meis mitzvah, and that is their genizah. Some explain הַמִּטְפָּחוֹת from the first sense, as houses for the hands, gloves, and the vernacular word for them is given.

פאה.sense: The edge and end of anything, which is called its פאה; and a verb, to scatter into every פאה, every corner.

more.t: לַפֵּאָה הָאֶחָת (Shemos 27:9), for the one side; עַל אַרְבַּע הַפֵּאֹת (Shemos 25:26), on the four corners; and וּמָחַץ פַּאֲתֵי מוֹאָב (Bamidbar 24:17), and he will smite the corners of Moav. The edge of anything and its end, he says, is called a פאה.

קְצוּצֵי פֵאָה (Yirmiyahu 9:25) means those cut off and scattered to a פאה, a corner. The verb from this root is אָמַרְתִּי אַפְאֵיהֶם (Devarim 32:26), I said I would scatter them, which he explains as I will scatter them into every corner.

more.h: The corner of head and beard
more.t: On לֹא תַקִּפוּ פְּאַת רֹאשְׁכֶם (Vayikra 19:27), do not round off the corner of your head, Chachamim explained it (Makkos 20b) as the end of the head, and it is המשוה צדעיו לאחורי אזניו ולפדחתו, making his temples level with the back of his ears and with his forehead. פְּאַת זְקָנֶךָ in the same pasuk, the corner of your beard, is שבולת הזקן, the tip of the beard.
פָּתְהֵן יְעָרֶה (Yeshayahu 3:17), where יְעָרֶה is He will lay bare, may be explained from this root; he gives פָּתְהֵן no rendering here, and more on it is written under the root פוּת.

קצע.sense: To peel, as plaster from a house, and the tool that peels wood smooth; מִקְצֹעַ, a corner; and קציעה, on whose identity the authorities differ.

more.t: וְאֶת־הַבַּיִת יַקְצִעַ מִבַּיִת (Vayikra 14:41), and he shall have the house peeled within, as the Targum renders it, יְקַלְפוּן, they shall peel, meaning the plaster is to be removed.

And so the tool with which the craftsman peels wood and smooths it is called: יַֽעֲשֵׂהוּ בַּמַּקְצֻעוֹת (Yeshayahu 44:13), he makes it with the peeling tools. The pasuk says מקצעות in the plural because there are two tools for this work, one called simant and one plana. So Yonasan renders it, בְּאִזְמֵילַיָא, with blades, and this tool, Radak says, is like an אזמל, a blade.

בְּמִקְצֹעַ הֶֽחָצֵר (Yechezkel 46:21), in the corner of the court; in the feminine plural לִשְׁנֵי הַמִּקְצֹעֹת (Shemos 26:24), for the two corners; and in another form לִמְקֻצְעֹת הַמִּשְׁכָּן (Shemos 26:23), for the corners of the Mishkan. Their sense, he says, is פנות, corners. The verb from it is מְהֻקְצָעוֹת (Yechezkel 46:22), which he explains as having corners.

מֹר וַֽאֲהָלוֹת קְצִיעוֹת (Tehillim 45:9), myrrh and aloes and ketziah. The Targum of קִדָּה (Shemos 30:24) is קְצִיעֲתָא, which Radak has already written is the קשט, the kosht, and so the Gaon Rav Saadiah explained. But in the compounding of the ketores they are named as two kinds, for they say (Kerisos 6a) מר וקציעה, myrrh and ketziah, and count הקשט, the kosht, apart. Mar Rav Chafetz explained that the קשט is what is called in Arabic kost, and he explained קציעה as amber.

קצה.sense: To cut off, cutting and severing; and קָצֶה, the end or side of a place, and מִקְצָת, the end of a span of days.

more.t: מְקַצֶּה רַגְלַיִם (Mishlei 26:6), cutting off feet, and לְקַצּוֹת בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל (Melachim II 10:32), to cut away at Yisrael. The infinitive of the simple form is קְצֽוֹת ־עַמִּים רַבִּים (Chavakuk 2:10), cutting off many peoples; the sense is cutting off and cutting. In the words of Chazal, לקצות עמו בתאנים (Maasros 2:6), which Radak explains as cutting a cake of figs.

Likewise the end of a place, and its side, is called קָצֶה, as the end is also called קֵץ: מִן־ הַקָּצֶה אֶל־ הַקָּצֶֽה (Shemos 36:33), from end to end, and קְצֵה גְבוּלֶֽךָ (Bamidbar 20:16), the edge of your border. The plural in the feminine: עַל־שְׁנֵי קְצוֹת הַחֽשֶׁן (Shemos 28:26), on the two ends of the choshen, and עַל אַרְבַּע קְצוֹתָֽיו (Shemos 27:4), on its four ends. Another form is וּמִקְצָת יָמִים עֲשָׂרָה (Daniel 1:15), at the end of ten days.

more.h: One who sends by a fool
more.t: מְקַצֶּה רַגְלַיִם (Mishlei 26:6), cutting off feet, and חמס שותה, drinking violence, is said of one who sends a fool: it is as though his feet were cut off and he could not walk, so that he must send the fool, who is of no use to him.

אֶת־הֶֽעָפָר אֲשֶׁר הִקְצוּ (Vayikra 14:41), the dust that they moved aside: that is, they moved it to the edge of the house to clear it away and take it outside the city; so too הִקְצוֹת אֶת־הַבַּיִת (Vayikra 14:43), the clearing of the house. Targum Yonasan renders it as a word of peeling, like יַקְצִעַ, he shall scrape.

וְאֵין קֵצֶה לְמַרְכְּבֹתָֽיו (Yeshayahu 2:7), and there is no end to his chariots, is of this root and this sense, in the pattern of הַרְבֵּה־בֶֽכֶה (Ezra 10:1), much weeping, and is like קֵץ, an end. It may instead be from the root קָצַץ, with the heh added.

נתק.sense: Removal and uprooting: a thing pulled loose, men drawn away from a city, roots torn out; and נֶתֶק, the name of a nega in a place of hair.

more.t: וְלֹא נִתַּק שְׂרוֹךְ נְעָלָיו (Yeshayahu 5:27), nor is the strap of his shoes pulled loose, נִתְּקוּ כַּפּוֹת רַגְלֵי הַכֹּהֲנִים (Yehoshua 4:18), the soles of the kohanim's feet were drawn away, and כַּאֲשֶׁר יִנָּתֵק פְּתִיל־הַנְּעֹרֶת (Shoftim 16:9), as a thread of tow is pulled apart. The heavy forms carry the same: נִתְּקוּ מוֹסֵרוֹת (Yirmiyahu 5:5), they have torn off the bonds, and הֲלוֹא אֶת־שָׁרָשֶׁיהָ יְנַתֵּק (Yechezkel 17:9), will he not tear up its roots. So too of men drawn out of a city: עַד הַתִּיקֵנוּ אוֹתָם מִן־הָעִיר (Yehoshua 8:6), until we have drawn them away from the city, and הָנְתְּקוּ מִן־הָעִיר (Shoftim 20:31), they were drawn away from the city. All of them are the sense of removal and uprooting.

From this sense, וְנָתוּק וְכָרוּת (Vayikra 22:24), torn and cut, is an animal whose testicles have been pulled by hand until the cords they hang by are severed, though they are still inside the sac and the sac itself is not torn away.
נֶתֶק הוּא (Vayikra 13:30), it is a nesek: the name of a nega, a mark of plague, in a place of hair; it has been explained as a black spot.

אַתִּיק אֶל־פְּנֵי־אַתִּיק (Yechezkel 42:3), atik facing atik, may come from this root, the dagesh in the tav standing for the nun that has fallen away; so too כִּי־יוֹכְלוּ אַתִּיקִים (Yechezkel 42:5), for atikim consumed, and וְאַתִּיקֶיהָא מִפּוֹ וּמִפּוֹ (Yechezkel 41:15), its atikim on this side and on that. He gives the word no gloss of his own; Targum Yonasan renders it in the sense of זִיוְיָתָהָא, its corners.

חטב.sense: Cutting, as of wood. Rabbi Yonah takes two of its words as high and lifted up; Radak keeps them to cutting, a bed's hewn poles and a house's hewn corner stones.

more.t: וְלֹא יַחְטְבוּ מִן־הַיְּעָרִים (Yechezkel 39:10), and they shall not cut from the forests, and מֵֽחֹטֵב עֵצֶיךָ (Devarim 29:10), from the hewer of your wood: the sense is cutting. The passive of the heavy form is מְחֻטָּבוֹת תַּבְנִית הֵיכָֽל (Tehillim 144:12), hewn after the pattern of a palace.

more.h: Rabbi Yonah: high and lifted up
more.t: Rabbi Yonah explains in another sense חֲטֻּבוֹת אֵטוּן מִצְרָֽיִם (Mishlei 7:16), chatuvos of the etun of Egypt, and כזויות מְחֻטָבוֹת, like corners mechutavos: that is, high and lifted up. The Targum of הֶֽאֱמִֽירְךָ הַיּוֹם (Devarim 26:18), He has exalted you today, is חָטְבָךְ, with these letters.

Radak holds that the word should not be taken out of the first sense. In חֲטֻּבוֹת אֵטוּן מִצְרָֽיִם it goes back to the bed: the pasuk says that the poles of her bed are hewn and set right with the adze and the compass and the like, the tools with which beds are made. So too כזויות מחטבות, like hewn corners: it is the way of the world to build the corners of a house of hewn ashlar stone even where the rest of it is built of rough stones; the corner stones are cut so well and so straight that they all look like one stone, and the pasuk likens daughters even and straight in their stature to those corners.

נאם.sense: A saying (מאמר): נְאֻם is a noun, though it may be a verb; and from it the נֶאֱמָנִים, those clear of tongue and skilled in the wisdom of speech.

more.t: וַיִּנְֽאֲמוּ נְאֻֽם (Yirmiyahu 23:31), and they say a saying; נְאֻֽם־פֶּשַׁע לָרָשָׁע (Tehillim 36:2), the saying of transgression to the wicked; חָרְבוּ מְאֹד נְאֻם י"י (Yirmiyahu 2:12), be utterly desolate, the saying of Hashem. Their sense is a saying. The word נְאֻם is a noun; it may be a verb in the construct, but in וַיִּנְֽאֲמוּ נְאֻֽם it is a noun, on the pattern of זְבוּל, a dwelling.
From it comes מֵסִיר שָׂפָה לְנֶאֱמָנִים (Iyov 12:20), He removes the speech of the נֶאֱמָנִים: they are those clear of tongue, who know the wisdom of speech.

חוה.sense: Telling, which he says is the sense of all of it, verb and noun; חַוֹּת יָאִיר, Chavos Yair, he leaves to be explained under the root חיה.

more.t: אֲחַוֶּה דֵּעִי אַף־אָנִי (Iyov 32:10), I too will tell my opinion; אֲחַוְךָ שְׁמַע־לִי (Iyov 15:17), I will tell you, hear me, where the dagesh has dropped out; and כַּתַּר־לִי זְעֵיר וַאֲחַוֶּךָּ (Iyov 36:2), wait for me a little and I will tell you. The noun, with an added alef, is וְאַחֲוָתִי בְּאָזְנֵיכֶם (Iyov 13:17), and my telling in your ears. All of it is the sense of telling.

more.h: Chavos Yair, left for the root חיה
more.t: חַוֹּת יָאִיר (Bamidbar 32:41), Chavos Yair, and אֶת־חַוֹּתֵיהֶם in the same pasuk, their chavos, he says he will explain under the root חיה.

נבע.sense: Coming out from a source, as water wells up; and speech, called so because it comes out of the mouth as water from its source.

more.t: נַחַל נֹבֵעַ (Mishlei 18:4), a welling brook. The noun is מַבּוּעַ: וְצִמָּאוֹן לְמַבּוּעֵי מָיִם (Yeshayahu 35:7), and the thirsty ground to springs of water, and וְעַל־מַבּוּעֵי מַיִם יְנַהֲלֵם (Yeshayahu 49:10), and by springs of water He shall lead them. The welling of water is its coming out from its source.

וְתִשָּׁבֶר כַּד עַל־הַמַּבּוּעַ (Koheles 12:6), and the pitcher is broken at the fountain: the כַּד, pitcher, is the gall, and the מַבּוּעַ, fountain, is the liver, on which the gall rests; that is why it says the pitcher is broken at the fountain. The liver is called מַבּוּעַ because it is the source of the blood.

Speech is called by this word because it comes out of the mouth as water from its source: יוֹם לְיוֹם יַבִּיעַ אֹמֶר (Tehillim 19:3), day to day pours out speech, אַבִּיעָה חִידוֹת (Tehillim 78:2), I will pour out riddles, and תַּבַּעְנָה שְׂפָתַי תְּהִלָּה (Tehillim 119:171), my lips shall pour out praise.

more.h: The fly in the perfumer's oil
more.t: יַבְאִישׁ יַבִּיעַ שֶׁמֶן רוֹקֵחַ (Koheles 10:1) says that the fly makes the perfumer's oil stink, and the stench does not stop, since at every moment the fly makes the stench well up and brings it out. Rabbi Yonah explained it in the sense of speech; on that reading, from the strength of its stench it is as though it spoke and proclaimed its stench abroad, in the manner of וְשֶׁמֶן יְמִינוֹ יִקְרָא (Mishlei 27:16), and the oil of his right hand proclaims. Rabbi Yitzchak ibn Giat explained it from אבעבועות, bubbles, and its root, for he wrote that it is a doubled verb in the heavy form, since oil that goes bad makes bubbles.

שֹוח.sense: Speech, which he gives as its sense: the speech of prayer, and the telling of troubles and hardships; but at times שִׂיחַ is a man's affair and his doings.

more.t: Its sense is speech, like לָשׂוּחַ בַּשָּׂדֶה (Bereishis 24:63), to speak in the field, which is the speech of prayer, and like אָרִיד בְּשִׂיחִי (Tehillim 55:3), I am restless in my speech, and those like it, which are the speech of troubles and the telling of hardships; so too אֶשְׁפֹּךְ לְפָנָיו שִׂיחִי (Tehillim 142:3), I pour out my speech before Him, and מֵרֹב שִׂיחִי (Shmuel I 1:16), out of the greatness of my speech.

בְּפִקֻּדֶיךָ אָשִׂיחָה, I will speak of Your precepts; יָשִׂיחוּ בִי ישְׁבֵי שָׁעַר (Tehillim 69:13), those who sit in the gate speak of me; עַל־דֶּרֶךְ שִֽׂיחוּ (Shoftim 5:10), on the way, speak. וַֽהֲקִיצוֹתָ הִיא תְשִׂיחֶֽךָ (Mishlei 6:22), and when you awake it shall speak with you, he explains: it will be to you like a companion speaking with you.

But אַתֶּם יְדַעְתֶּם אֶת־הָאִישׁ וְאֶת־ שִׂיחֽוֹ (Melachim II 9:11), you know the man and his siach, means his affair and his doings; so too וּמַגִּיד לְאָדָם מַה־ שֵּׂחוֹ (Amos 4:13), and tells a man what his doing is, which has a tzeirei. And כִּֽי־ שִׂיחַ וְכִי־שִׂיג לוֹ (Melachim I 18:27), for he has a siach and he has a sig, means he has an affair and a dealing with another, or the overtaking of his enemies in war.

שׁוח.sense: A pit, שׁוּחָה, and שַׁחַת, whose sense is like that of a grave. Of a land, as in עֲרָבָה וְשׁוּחָה, desert and waste, שׁוּחָה means desolation and ruin.

more.t: שׁוּחָה עֲמֻקָּה (Mishlei 22:14), a deep pit, and כִּי־כָרוּ שׁוּחָה לְנַפְשִׁי (Yirmiyahu 18:20), for they have dug a pit for my soul. Another form takes a chirik: כָּרוּ לְפָנַי שִׁיחָה (Tehillim 57:7), they dug a pit before me, and כָּרוּ־לִי זֵדִים שִׁיחוֹת (Tehillim 119:85), the insolent have dug pits for me. These too may be from the root שָׁחַח.

לַשַּׁחַת יוֹרִדוּךָ (Yechezkel 28:8), they will bring you down to the pit, וְלֹא־יָמוּת לַשַּׁחַת (Yeshayahu 51:14), he shall not die to the pit, לִבְאֵר שַׁחַת (Tehillim 55:24), to the well of the pit, and בְּשַׁחְתָּם נִתְפַּשׂ (Yechezkel 19:4), he was caught in their pit. They may be from the root יָשַׁח, as דַּעַת is from יָדַע. Their sense is like that of a grave.

כִּי שָׁחָה אֶל־מָוֶת בֵּיתָהּ (Mishlei 2:18), for her house sinks down to death, Rabbi Yonah wrote under this root. The word may be from שָׁחַח, and that would be why Rabbi Yehudah did not mention it; except that most books have it with a kamatz, and were it a doubled verb it would take a patach, as is the rule with a ches, which cannot take the doubling.

בְּאֶרֶץ עֲרָבָה וְשׁוּחָה (Yirmiyahu 2:6), in a land of desert and waste: the sense of שׁוּחָה here is desolation and ruin, and so Targum Yonasan renders it בַּאֲרַע מֵישַׁר וְחָרוֹב, in a land of plain and ruin.

בגד.sense: To betray: to transgress a fellow's covenant and deal falsely with him while he trusts you. In another sense, בֶּגֶד, a garment.

more.t: כָּל־רֵעֶיהָ בָּגְדוּ בָהּ (Eichah 1:2), all her friends have betrayed her, and וּבְאֵשֶׁת נְעוּרֶיךָ אַל־ יִבְגֹּֽד (Malachi 2:15), let none betray the wife of his youth. The nouns are בֹּגְדֵי בָֽגֶד (Yirmiyahu 12:1), those who betray a betrayal, and אַנְשֵׁי בֹּֽגְדוֹת (Tzefaniah 3:4), men of treacheries. The sense, he says, is one who transgresses his fellow's covenant and deals falsely with him while the fellow trusts in him.

מַדּוּעַ נִבְגַּד אִישׁ בְּאָחִיו (Malachi 2:10), why do we deal falsely each man with his brother. Rabbi Yaakov ben Elazar wrote that the form is a passive one. Radak holds that wrong, since verbs joined to what they govern by a letter yield no passive; and this one is joined by a mem in אכן בָּֽגְדָה אשׁה מרעה (Yirmiyahu 3:20), surely as a woman betrays her companion.

In another sense, וּבֶגֶד לִלְבֹּֽשׁ (Bereishis 28:20), a garment to wear, וְלָבַשׁ בְּגָדִים אֲחֵרִים (Vayikra 6:4), he shall put on other garments, and בְּכָל־עֵת יִהְיוּ בְגָדֶיךָ לְבָנִים (Koheles 9:8), let your garments always be white. There is a feminine plural too, כָּל־ בִּגְדֹתֶיךָ (Tehillim 45:9), all your garments. He gives this word no gloss, saying its sense is known.

לבשׁ.sense: To put on a garment and to be clothed in it; and, of another, to clothe him.

more.t: אֲשֶׁר לָֽבַשׁ ־בּוֹ הַמֶּלֶךְ (Esther 6:8), which the king has worn, יִלְבַּשׁ עַל־בְּשָׂרוֹ (Vayikra 6:3), he shall put on over his flesh, and צֶדֶק לָבַשְׁתִּי וַיִּלְבָּשֵׁנִי (Iyov 29:14), I put on righteousness and it clothed me. Of a man dressed: הָיָה לָבֻשׁ בְּגָדִים צוֹאִים (Zecharyah 3:3), he was clothed in filthy garments, and לָבֻשׁ שָׁנִֽים (Mishlei 31:21), clothed in scarlet.

more.h: Why the word works both ways
more.t: Once a man has put a garment on, he is לָבוּשׁ, clothed, from the garment, and the garment too is לָבוּשׁ, worn, upon him, so that one form serves for both. So too חוֹגֵר and חָגוּר, one who girds and one girded, go the same way; and so אֲחֻזֵי חֶרֶב (Shir HaShirim 3:8), holders of the sword, and וְאַתָּה תֶּאְזֹר מָתְנֶיךָ (Yirmiyahu 1:17), and you, gird your loins, beside אָזוּר בְּמָתְנָיו (Melachim II 1:8), girded about his loins.

וַיַּלְבֵּשׁ אֹתָם אֶת־אֶלְעָזָר בְּנוֹ (Bamidbar 20:28), he clothed Elazar his son in them, הִלְבִּישַׁנִי בִּגְדֵי־יֶשַׁע (Yeshayahu 61:10), He has clothed me in garments of salvation, and וְהַלְבֵּשׁ אֹֽתְךָ מַֽחֲלָצֽוֹת (Zecharyah 3:4), and I will clothe you in fine robes.

לְבוּשׁ, the clothing, as in וְנָתוֹן הַלְּבוּשׁ וְהַסּוּס (Esther 6:9), let the clothing and the horse be given; מַלְבּוּשׁ נָכְרִֽי (Tzefaniah 1:8), foreign dress; and תִּלְבֹּשֶׁת, as in בִּגְדֵי נָקָם תִּלְבֹּשֶׁת (Yeshayahu 59:17), garments of vengeance for clothing.

שֹמל.sense: The left, and to turn or use the left; he thinks the word likely one of four letters. What belongs to this root without doubt is שִׂמְלָה, a garment.

more.t: שְׂמֹאול בַּֽעֲשׂתוֹ וְלֹא־אָחַז (Iyov 23:9), on the left where He works, and I do not grasp Him; the alef stands in place of a vav of lengthening. The verb: מַיְמִינִים וּמַשְׂמִאלִים (Divrei HaYamim I 12:2), using the right hand and the left, and without the alef לְהֵמִין וּלְהַשְׂמִיל (Shmuel II 14:19), to turn right or left, and הָשִׂימִי הַשְׂמִילִי (Yechezkel 21:21), set yourself right, go left. The adjective is הַשְּׂמָאלִי (Divrei HaYamim II 3:17), the left-hand one, and הַשְּׂמָאלִית (Vayikra 14:16), the left hand.

The alef carries a vowel in וְכִי תַשְׂמְאִֽילוּ (Yeshayahu 30:21), and when you turn left, and in וְאַשְׂמְאִֽילָה (Bereishis 13:9), then I will go left, though it is no root letter. The word may be one of four letters, and that, he says, is right in his eyes, since no added letter carrying a vowel is found within the letters of a root except in לְדַרְיוֹשׁ הַדָּבָֽר (Ezra 10:16), to inquire into the matter; and perhaps, he says, it is a compound word.

What comes from this root without doubt, he says, is שִׂמְלָה: אֶת־ הַשִּׂמְלָה (Bereishis 9:23), the garment, שִׂמְלָתְךָ לֹא בָֽלְתָה (Devarim 8:4), your garment did not wear out, and וּכְלֵי זָהָב וּשְׂמָלֹת (Shemos 3:22), vessels of gold and garments. Their sense he leaves as known.

מדד.sense: To measure, all of it one sense of measure; the noun is מִדָּה, a measure, and אִישׁ מִדָּה is a man of great measure.

more.t: מִי־מָדַד בְּשָׁעֳלוֹ מַיִם (Yeshayahu 40:12), who measured the waters in the hollow of His hand, וּמַדֹּתֶם מִחוּץ לָעִיר (Bamidbar 35:5), you shall measure outside the city, and וַיָּמֹדּוּ בָעֹמֶר (Shemos 16:18), they measured with the omer. In the passive, אִם־יִמַּדּוּ שָׁמַיִם (Yirmiyahu 31:36 in his edition), if the heavens can be measured; and in the heavy form, וַיְמַדְּדֵם בַּחֶבֶל (Shmuel II 8:2), he measured them with the line.
וַיִּתְמֹדֵד עַל־הַיֶּלֶד (Melachim I 17:21) is נשתטח עליו, he laid himself out flat upon the child.

more.h: His father on עמד וימדד ארץ
more.t: In עָמַד וַיְמֹדֶד אֶרֶץ (Chavakuk 3:6), his father explains, it is the Aron that stood, in Gilgal, and the land was divided to them by measure. וַיַּתֵּר גּוֹיִם (Chavakuk 3:6), and He made the nations leap, is that He put them out of their land, taking וַיַּתֵּר from לְנַתֵּר בָּהֵן עַל־הָאָרֶץ (Vayikra 11:21), to leap with them upon the ground, whose Targum is לְקַפָּצָא, to leap, from מְקַפֵּץ עַל־הַגְּבָעוֹת (Shir HaShirim 2:8), leaping over the hills; and it is a verb that takes an object.

אֲרֻכָּה מֵאֶרֶץ מִדָּהּ (Iyov 11:9), its measure is longer than the earth: the heh takes a mapik though the proper form is מִדָּתָהּ, as פִּנָּהּ (Mishlei 7:8), her corner, stands for פִּנָּתָהּ, and וּבָזַז בִּזָּהּ (Yechezkel 29:19), and he shall plunder her plunder, for בִּזָּתָהּ. Rabbi Yaakov ben Elazar wrote that these are masculine nouns, one saying of them מַד and בַּז.

אִישׁ מִדָּה (Divrei HaYamim I 11:23) is explained as a man of great measure; so אַנְשֵׁי מִדּוֹת (Bamidbar 13:32), men of great measures, and אֶבְנֶה־לִּי בֵּית מִדּוֹת (Yirmiyahu 22:14), I will build myself a house of great measures. וַיְהִי אִישׁ מָדֹין (Shmuel II 21:20), read מָדוֹן, and there was a man of מָדוֹן, is explained as of this sense too, a man of great measure, since in its place in Divrei HaYamim (Divrei HaYamim I 20:6) he is אִישׁ מִדָּה; so Targum Yonasan renders it, וַהֲוָה גְבַר דְמִשְׁחָן, he was a man of measures. The resting letter in it stands for the dagesh, and it is of this root; and Radak has written it as well under the root דון.

Rabbi Yonah divided the root into two senses, as the wise Rabbi Yehudah had divided them. Radak sees no need for it: though one is the measure of a surface and the other the measure of filling, it is all the sense of measure, and one.
Rabbi Yehudah put וּמִדַּד־עָרֶב (Iyov 7:4), said of the evening, in this root and called it a past verb. Radak’s father wrote it under the root נדד, and Radak says he will write of it further there.

לְמִדַּת הַמֶּלֶךְ (Nechemiah 5:4), for the king's levy, is not of this root: its proper form is מִנְדַת, the mem being an added letter, and it is of the sense of מִנְדָּה בְלוֹ וַהֲלָךְ (Ezra 4:13). Chazal explained (Nedarim 62b) that מנדה is the king's portion, בלו head money, and הלך the arnona; and Radak's gloss on the first is that the king's portion is the gift made to a king when he passes by them.

עטה.sense: Wrapping in a covering, as a garment is put about one; and a second sense, where the root's last letter shows, turning aside.

more.t: וְעָטָה אֶת־אֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם (Yirmiyahu 43:12), he shall wrap himself in the land of Mitzrayim, כַּאֲשֶׁר־יַעְטֶה הָרֹעֶה אֶת־בִּגְדוֹ, as a shepherd wraps himself in his garment; עֹטֶה אוֹר כַּשַּׂלְמָה (Tehillim 104:2), wrapped in light as in a cloak; כְּבֶגֶד יַעְטֶה (Tehillim 109:19), he puts it about him as a garment; וְעַל־שָׂפָם יַעְטֶה (Vayikra 13:45), he shall cover over his moustache; and וְעֹֽטְךָ עָטֹֽה (Yeshayahu 22:17), and wraps you round.

מְעֻטָּה לְטָבַח (Yechezkel 21:20), wrapped for the slaughter; הֶעֱטִיתָ עָלָיו בּוּשָׁה סֶלָה (Tehillim 89:46), You have wrapped him about with shame, selah; and the noun, מַעֲטֵה תְהִלָּה (Yeshayahu 61:3), a wrapping of praise. All of these, with those above, are the sense of wrapping in a covering.

A second sense, where the root's last letter shows: שַׁלָּמָה אֶהְיֶה כְּעֹטְיָה (Shir HaShirim 1:7), for why should I be as one who turns aside, that is, as one who bends away and turns aside by the flocks of your companions. So too וַיַּעַט הָעָם (Shmuel I 14:32), the people turned aside to the spoil, and וַתַּעַט אֶל־הַשָּׁלָל (Shmuel I 15:19), you turned aside to the spoil: since their yud and tav carry a patach, they are of this root. But וַיָּעַט בָּהֶם (Shmuel I 25:14), and he lashed out at them, whose yud carries a kamatz, is of the root עיט, as he says he will explain.

קשׁר.sense: To tie and bind one thing to another, and to join; of matters joined in one agreement, to conspire; and קִשֻּׁרִים, the ornaments a woman ties on.

more.t: וּקְשַׁרְתָּם לְאוֹת (Devarim 6:8), you shall bind them for a sign, and וַתִּקְשֹׁר עַל־יָדוֹ שָׁנִי (Bereishis 38:28), she tied a scarlet thread on his hand. Of love, וְנַפְשׁוֹ קְשׁוּרָה בְנַפְשׁוֹ (Bereishis 44:30), his soul is bound up with his soul, which he explains of the greatness of his love, as though the one soul were tied to the other and joined to it; so וְנֶפֶשׁ יְהוֹנָתָן נִקְשְׁרָה בְּנֶפֶשׁ דָּוִד (Shmuel I 18:1), the soul of Yehonasan was bound up with the soul of David.

וַתִּקָּשֵׁר כָּל־הַחוֹמָה עַד־חֶצְיָהּ (Nechemiah 3:38), the whole wall was joined together to half its height, which he explains: the whole building of the wall was knit together and complete, with no breach left in it.

כַּלָּה קִשֻּׁרֶיהָ (Yirmiyahu 2:32), a bride her ornaments, and וְהַקִּשֻּׁרִים (Yeshayahu 3:20), and the tied ornaments, which he explains of the ornaments and necklaces a woman ties on her head or about her throat; so וּתְקַשְּׁרִים כַּכַּלָּה (Yeshayahu 49:18), you shall bind them on as a bride does.

Likewise of matters joined together and gathered into one agreement: כִּי קְשַׁרְתֶּם כֻּלְּכֶם עָלַי (Shmuel I 22:8), you have all conspired against me, אֲחִיתֹפֶל בַּקֹּשְׁרִים עִם־אַבְשָׁלוֹם (Shmuel II 15:31), Achitofel is among the conspirators with Avshalom, and קָשַׁר עָלֶיךָ עָמוֹס (Amos 7:10), Amos has conspired against you. The noun is לֹא־תֹאמְרוּן קֶשֶׁר (Yeshayahu 8:12), you shall not say, a conspiracy, and וַיְהִי הַקֶּשֶׁר אַמִּץ (Shmuel II 15:12), the conspiracy was strong; and וַיִּתְקַשֵּׁר יֵהוּא (Melachim II 9:14), Yehu conspired.

וְהַקְּשֻׁרִים לְיַעֲקֹב (Bereishis 30:42), and the tied ones were Yaakov's, and הַצֹּאן הַמְקֻשָּׁרוֹת (Bereishis 30:41), the tied flock, the Targum renders בַכִּירַיָּא, the early ones. They are the ones born in the days of Nisan, stronger and healthier than the rest, and they are called by a word of tying because a knot is strong.

הַתְקַשֵּׁר מַעֲדַנּוֹת כִּימָה (Iyov 38:31), can you bind the chains of כִּימָה, he has already explained at the root כִּימָה. His father wrote that כִּימָה ripens the fruit early, תקשור being from וְהַקְּשֻׁרִים לְיַעֲקֹב, which the Targum renders בַכִּירַיָּא, the early ones; and ומֽשְׁכוֹת כְּסִיל תְּפַתֵּֽחַ (Iyov 38:31), or loosen the cords of כְּסִיל, is what ripens the fruit last.

קטר.sense: To burn incense or an offering in smoke, with קְטֹרֶת, incense, and קִיטוֹר, smoke or vapour. Courts called קְטֻרוֹת he takes as tied, as the word is in Aramaic.

more.t: אֲשֶׁר קִטְּרוּ־שָׁמָּה הַכֹּהֲנִים (Melachim II 23:8), where the kohanim made their burnings, וְקַטֵּר מֵחָמֵץ תּוֹדָה (Amos 4:5), and burn a thanksgiving offering of what is leavened, וְהִקְטִירָם הַכֹּהֵן (Vayikra 3:16), and the kohen shall burn them in smoke, and כָּלִיל תָּקְטָר (Vayikra 6:15), it shall be wholly burned. The noun is in הֲלוֹא אֶת־הַקִּטֵּר אֲשֶׁר קִטַּרְתֶּם (Yirmiyahu 44:21), is it not the burning that you burned.

מְקֻטֶּרֶת מוֹר וּלְבוֹנָה (Shir HaShirim 3:6), perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, that is, her garments are smoked with spices. The nouns for the incense itself are קְטוֹרָה, as in יָשִׂימוּ קְטוֹרָה בְּאַפֶּךָ (Devarim 33:10), they shall set incense before You, and, with a tav, וְשַׁמְנִי וּקְטָרְתִּי (Yechezkel 16:18), my oil and my incense.

וּקְטָרְתִּי (Yechezkel 16:18), and my incense, carries a kamatz chatuf by the reading of Ben Asher, which is the rule, and by the reading of Ben Naftali it is וּקְטַרְתִּי with a patach; and at וּקְטָרְתִּי וְשַׁמְנִי (Yechezkel 23:41), my incense and my oil, the two differ likewise.

מֻקְטָר מֻגָּשׁ לִשְׁמִי (Malachi 1:11), incense offered to My name: מֻקְטָר is a noun, on the pattern of מָשְׁחָתָם in כִּי מָשְׁחָתָם בָּהֶם (Vayikra 22:25), for their corruption is in them. That is, in every place incense would be offered to My name, and a pure mincha, had He commanded them so. Ibn Ezra reads גָּדוֹל שְׁמִי בַּגּוֹיִם (Malachi 1:11), My name is great among the nations, as: from the rising of the sun to its setting they magnify My name, and He reckons it to them as though they were bringing a pure mincha and burning incense before Him, not as you do, who offer defiled bread and profane My name; and that is what the pasuk says after it, ואתם מחללים אתו, and you profane it. Radak's father explains that though they serve idols there, it is Hashem's name that they serve, and their intent is to Heaven. It may instead be a passive participle, and then in מֻקְטָר מֻגָּשׁ the burning is said of the spice incense, the offering is said of the korbanos, and the mincha is the one of fine flour.

קִיטֹר הָאָרֶץ (Bereishis 19:28), the smoke of the land, כְּקִיטֹר הַכִּבְשָׁן (Bereishis 19:28), like the smoke of a furnace, and שֶׁלֶג וְקִיטוֹר (Tehillim 148:8), snow and vapour, which is the vapour rising off the earth that looks like smoke. In כִּי־הָיִיתִי כְּנֹאד בְּקִיטוֹר (Tehillim 119:83), for I am become like a skin bottle in smoke, the speaker likens the skin of his flesh to a skin bottle in smoke, since it is dry.

The pan in which the ketores is put: וּבְיָדוֹ מִקְטֶרֶת לְהַקְטִיר (Divrei HaYamim II 26:19), and in his hand a pan to burn incense, and וְאִישׁ מִקְטַרְתּוֹ בְּיָדוֹ (Yechezkel 8:11), each man his pan in his hand. And the altar they burn upon is מִקְטַר קְטֹרֶת (Shemos 30:1), an altar for burning incense.

חֲצֵרוֹת קְטֻרוֹת (Yechezkel 46:22), tied courts, means קשורות, tied: the Targum of וַתִּקְשֹׁר (Bereishis 38:28), and she tied, is וּקְטָרַת, and in Aramaic again וּמְשָׁרֵא קִטְרִין (Daniel 5:12) is one who unties knots, and וְקִטְרֵי חַרְצֵהּ מִשְׁתָּרַיִן (Daniel 5:6) is the knots of his loins coming loose. The courts are joined and tied at the corners of the court, one at this corner and one at that, in the way of וַתִּקָּשֵׁר כָּל־הַחוֹמָה עַד־חֶצְיָהּ (Nechemiah 3:38), and all the wall was joined together to half its height. Targum Yonasan renders it likewise, דָרָתָא מְקַטְרָן, tied courts. In Middos (2:5) Chazal say that קטורות means only that they were not roofed.

ישׁן.sense: To sleep, with sleep and the sleeper; in another sense old, as in יָשָׁן נוֹשָׁן, very old: ישן of last year, נושן of three years.

more.t: יָשַׁנְתִּי אָז יָנוּחַֽ לִֽי (Iyov 3:13), "I would have slept, then it would be restful for me", and וְיָֽשְׁנוּ שְׁנַת־עוֹלָם וְלֹא יָקִיצוּ (Yirmiyahu 51:39), "and they shall sleep an everlasting sleep and not awake".

more.h: The noun, and שֵׁנָֽא with an alef
more.t: אַל־תֶּֽאֱהַב שֵׁנָה פֶּן־תִּוָּרֵשׁ (Mishlei 20:13), "do not love sleep lest you be dispossessed"; in כֵּן יִתֵּן לִֽידִידוֹ שֵׁנָֽא (Tehillim 127:2), "so He gives His beloved sleep", the alef stands in place of a heh. Without smichus it takes a tav: אִם־אֶתֵּן שְׁנָת לְעֵינָי (Tehillim 132:4), "if I give sleep to my eyes".
The adjective in וַיִּקַץ כְּיָשֵׁן י"י (Tehillim 78:65), and Hashem awoke as one who sleeps, and אֲנִי יְשֵׁנָה וְלִבִּי עֵר (Shir HaShirim 5:2), I am asleep but my heart is awake.
The heavy form, whose sense is known: וַתְּיַשְּׁנֵהוּ עַל־בִּרְכֶיהָ (Shoftim 16:19), and she put him to sleep on her knees.

Another sense: וַֽאֲכַלְתֶּם יָשָׁן (Vayikra 26:10), and you shall eat what is old, and חֲדָשִׁים גַּם־ יְשָׁנִים (Shir HaShirim 7:14), new ones and also old. יָשָׁן נוֹשָׁן (Vayikra 26:10) means very old: ישן is of last year, נושן of three years.

עתק.sense: Thick and strong, much and great; in another sense, to uproot and move from a place, so the copyist is called מעתיק, a mover; and in a third, to grow old.

more.t: עָתְקוּ גַּם־גָּבְרוּ חָיִל (Iyov 21:7), "they have grown thick and strong in wealth"; and it is said of matters thick and strong, וְהַדְּבָרִים עַתִּיקִים (Divrei HaYamim I 4:22), "and the matters are thick and strong".
Another form of the word: יֵצֵא עָתָק מִפִּיכֶם (Shmuel I 2:3), "let hard speech go out of your mouth", and הַדֹּבְרוֹת עַל־צַדִּיק עָתָק (Tehillim 31:19), "that speak hard words against a tzaddik".

הוֹן עָתֵק וּצְדָקָה (Mishlei 8:18), "wealth much and great, and righteousness"; and וְלִמְכַסֶּה עָתִיק (Yeshayahu 23:18), "and for a thick covering", that is, to cover with something thick and of worth.

In another sense, וְצוּר יֶעְתַּק מִמְּקֹמֽוֹ (Iyov 14:18), "and a rock is removed from its place", meaning it turns aside and is uprooted; הַמַּעְתִּיק הָרִים וְלֹא יָדָעוּ (Iyov 9:5), "who removes mountains and they know not", that is, uproots them from their place; וַיַּעְתֵּק מִשָּׁם הָהָרָה (Bereishis 12:8), "and he moved from there to the mountain", meaning he moved his tent from there; הֶעְתִּיקוּ מֵהֶם מִלִּים (Iyov 32:16 in his edition), "words were moved from them": the words were uprooted from them, so that they had no more words to answer.

אֲשֶׁר הֶעְתִּיקוּ אַנְשֵׁי חִזְקִיָּה (Mishlei 25:1), "which the men of Chizkiyahu copied": one who writes from book to book is called מעתיק, a mover, because he moves and uproots the words from one book into another; and though the words of the first book are not moved out of it, the scribe is as though he moved them.

The adjective עַתִּיקֵי מִשָּׁדָיִם (Yeshayahu 28:9) means those uprooted from the breasts, who will suckle no more, like גְּמוּלֵי מֵחָלָב, "weaned from milk", in that same pasuk. His father wrote it from the first sense, which Radak spells out: thick and fat from the breasts, from the much milk they sucked, and without understanding.

In a further sense, עָתְקָה בְּכָל־צוֹרְרָי (Tehillim 6:8), "it has grown old because of all my adversaries": it has aged because of all my adversaries who anger me, and from much weeping over that anger it has aged. Like it in Aramaic is וְעַתִּיק יוֹמִין יְתִב (Daniel 7:9), "and the Ancient of Days sat", and the Targum renders ישן, old, as עתיק; and וְהַדְּבָרִים עַתִּיקִים may be explained from this sense, "and the matters are old".

דגה.sense: To increase as fish do. דָּג, a fish, may come from this root, but other forms point to דוג, and he holds the word was used in both roots.

more.t: וְיִדְגּוּ לָרֹב בְּקֶרֶב הָאָרֶץ (Bereishis 48:16), and let them multiply abundantly in the midst of the land: its sense is let them increase as the fish do.

דָּג and דָּגִים, fish, may be from this root. The plural in smichus shows it, being pointed with a sheva: דְּגֵי הַיָּם (Bamidbar 11:22), the fish of the sea, as בָּנִים, sons, gives בְּנֵי, sons of, and שְׁנַים, two, gives שְׁנֵי, two of. So too the smichus of דָּגָה: דְגַת־יְאֹרֶיךָ (Yechezkel 29:4), the fish of your rivers, and תִּבְאַשׁ דְּגָתָם (Yeshayahu 50:2), their fish shall stink, with a sheva. Had דגה been from the roots whose middle letter is weak, it would not change in smichus, as קָמָה, standing grain, does not in בְּקָמַת רֵעֶךָ (Devarim 23:26), your fellow's standing grain.

But מְבִיאִים דָּאג (Nechemiah 13:16), bringing fish, is written with an alef as the middle root letter; there is a verb from it too, דִיגוּם (Yirmiyahu 16:16), and they shall fish them; and the fishermen, with the middle root letter showing, דַּוָּגִים (Yechezkel 47:10) and דַיָּגִים (Yirmiyahu 16:16).
