Since these are found, Radak will write them again under דוג. The truth, he says, is that the word was used in both roots, as many are.

כור.sense: The crucible in which the smith melts silver and gold; the kor, a measure, which is the chomer, thirty se'ah; and the land where one dwells.

more.t: מִכּוּר הַבַּרְזֶל (Devarim 4:20), "from the iron crucible"; כְּהִתּוּךְ כֶּסֶף בְּתוֹךְ כּוּר (Yechezkel 22:22), "as silver is melted in a crucible"; and מַצְרֵף לַכֶּסֶף וְכוּר לַזָּהָב (Mishlei 17:3), "a refining pot for silver and a crucible for gold": it is the vessel in which the smith melts the silver and the gold.
כֹּרִים עֶשְׂרִים אֶלֶף (Divrei HaYamim II 2:9), "twenty thousand kor": the kor is the chomer, and it is thirty se'ah.

מְכֹרֹתַיִךְ וּמֹלְדֹתַיִךְ (Yechezkel 16:3), "your dwellings and your birthplaces", with a cholam; and with a shuruk under the kaf, בְּאֶרֶץ מְכֻרוֹתַיִךְ (Yechezkel 21:35), "in the land of your dwellings", which is like מגורותיך, your dwelling places; and so עַל־אֶרֶץ מְכוּרָתָם (Yechezkel 29:14), "to the land of their dwelling".

תנן.sense: The tannin: on dry land a kind of snake, in the water a kind of great fish shaped like a snake; it is written too with a mem in place of the nun.

more.h: On land and in the water
more.t: וַיְהִי לְתַנִּֽין (Shemos 7:10), "and it became a tannin", and the plural אֶת־ הַתַּנִּינִם הַגְּדֹלִים (Bereishis 1:21), "the great tanninim". Those spoken of on dry land are one of the kinds of snake, and those spoken of in the water one of the kinds of great fish shaped like snakes.

more.h: A mem in place of the nun
more.t: הַתַּנִּים הַגָּדוֹל הָֽרֹבֵץ בְּתוֹךְ יְאֹרָיו (Yechezkel 29:3), "the great tannim crouching in the midst of his rivers", and כַּתַּנִּים בַּיַּמִּים (Yechezkel 32:2), "like a tannim in the seas": it is the way of the language for mem and nun to come one for the other, as מוֹף and נוֹף, Mof and Nof, and כְּמֹהֶם and כְּמֹהֶן, both meaning like them.

In Eichah 4:3 the tannim חָלְצוּ שַׁד, "have drawn out the breast", and so מְעוֹן תַּנִּים (Yirmiyahu 9:10), "a lair of tannim". The feminine plural is לְתַנּוֹת מִדְבָּֽר (Malachi 1:3), "to the tannos of the wilderness", and the Targum renders תנים as ירודין, a word Radak does not explain.

more.h: Why it draws out the breast
more.t: On חָלְצוּ שַׁד, "they have drawn out the breast", the Targum in Megillas Eichah says that these creatures have breasts up to their faces, and when they suckle their young, so that the young should not see them, they choke them and eat them. Midrash Tanchuma says that when the tannin comes to suckle, its mother sees it from afar and draws out her breasts, so that it should suckle and not see them covered and refuse.

נין.sense: נִין, whose sense he says is like בן, a son; מָנוֹן is another pattern of the word, and יִנּוֹן another form of it.

more.t: וְנִין וָנֶכֶד (Yeshayahu 14:22), and son and grandson; וּלְנִינִי וּלְנֶכְדִּי (Bereishis 21:23), and to my son and to my grandson; נִינָם יָחַד (Tehillim 74:8), their sons together: their sense is like בן, a son.

On another pattern, וְאַחֲרִיתוֹ יִהְיֶה מָנוֹן (Mishlei 29:21), and at his end he will be manon, a word he glosses no further; and a passive of it, יִנּוֹן, in לִפְנֵי שֶׁמֶשׁ (Tehillim 72:17), before the sun his name shall be carried on.
Radak notes that he has already written of נִינָם יָחַד (Tehillim 74:8) under the root ינה.

תישׁ.sense: The he-goat, a known word; in Mishlei 30:31 the או beside it stands in place of "and", or it may be a plain "or".

more.t: זַרְזִיר מָתְנַיִם אוֹ־ תָיִשׁ (Mishlei 30:31), the one girt in the loins and a he-goat: the או stands here in place of the vav that joins, "and"; or או may be in its plain sense, this one or that one, each of them doing well in stride and in walk.
וּתְיָשִׁים עֶשְׂרִים (Bereishis 32:15), and twenty he-goats: the word is known.

גדה.sense: גְּדִי, the young of the flock: he holds it names the young of sheep as well as of goats, where Ibn Ezra keeps it to goats. A second sense, גְּדוֹתָיו, a river's banks.

more.t: וַיִּשְׁלַח יְהוּדָה אֶת־גְּדִי הָעִזִּים (Bereishis 38:20), "and Yehudah sent the kid of the goats": the young is called גדי whether of goats or of sheep, since the pasuk attaches גדי to עזים, so it seems there is a גדי that is not of goats.

Rabbi Avraham Ibn Ezra explained that nothing is called גדי except of the goats, and that גדי עזים means a young one that still needs the goats, and so שְׂעִיר־עִזִּים (Bamidbar 7:16), a he-goat of the goats; and he said that in Arabic too it is called גדי.

אֶחָד נֹשֵׂא שְׁלֹשָׁה גְדָיִים (Shmuel I 10:3), "one carrying three kids", and שְׁנֵי גְּדָיֵי עִזִּים (Bereishis 27:9), "two kids of the goats"; in the feminine, וּרְעִי אֶת־גְּדִיֹּתַיִךְ (Shir HaShirim 1:8), "and pasture your kids".

more.h: Why the pasuk names a kid
more.t: לֹא־תְבַשֵּׁל גְּדִי בַּחֲלֵב אִמּוֹ (Shemos 34:26), "do not cook a kid in its mother's milk": the same law holds for the flesh of any animal, and the pasuk spoke of what is usual and what people customarily ate, since they ate kids more than lambs, as Scripture shows throughout. It spoke of the young of the animal because it is not the way to cook a grown animal's flesh in milk, milk cooking quickly and flesh not, unless it is the flesh of the young, which are quick to cook.

Goats' milk is the most plentiful, and the pasuk spoke of what is common, as וְדֵי חֲלֵב עִזִּים (Mishlei 27:26 in his edition), "and enough goats' milk". So too our Rabbis spoke of what is found most, saying a goat is for its milk (Shabbos 19b), and what my goats give in milk I sell you (Bava Metzia 64a).

So too וְאֵת בַּת הַיַּעֲנָה (Vayikra 11:16), "and the daughter of the ostrich": the same law holds for the ostrich itself, and the pasuk speaks of what is usual, since it is the world's custom to eat it only while young and tender, its flesh being very hard when grown and unfit to eat. The young female's flesh is softer than the male's, so the pasuk says בת.

more.h: One that has a mother's milk
more.t: Our Rabbis expounded (Chullin 113a) that it says בחלב אמו, in its mother's milk, of one that has a mother's milk, since fowl in milk is forbidden not by the Torah but by the words of the Soferim.

Another sense: מָלֵא עַל־כָּל־גְּדוֹתָיו (Yehoshua 3:15), "full over all its banks", and וְהָלַךְ עַל־כָּל־גְּדוֹתָיו (Yeshayahu 8:7), "and it shall go over all its banks", meaning over all its edges on this side and that. Rabbi Yaakov ben Elazar wrote that in אֲשֶׁר בְּתוֹךְ־הַנַּחַל הַגָּד (Shmuel II 24:5), which is in the midst of the stream, the גָּד, the word הַגָּד is one of the stream's banks; and Targum Yonasan rendered it, in the midst of the stream of the tribe of Gad.

רחל.sense: The ewe: רְחֵלִים, which he glosses כבשות, female sheep.

more.t: וּכְרָחֵל לִפְנֵי גֹזְזֶיהָ נֶאֱלָמָה (Yeshayahu 53:7), "and as a ewe before her shearers is dumb", and רְחֵלִים מָאתַיִם (Bereishis 32:15), "two hundred ewes": he glosses them כבשות, female sheep, and says no more.

איל.sense: Strength, and the mighty. Under the same letters: the hart and the hind, the ram, a plain, as the Targum renders אֵלוֹן, and a doorpost.

more.t: כְּגֶבֶר אֵין־אֱיָל (Tehillim 88:5), "like a man without strength": אֱיָל is strength, and so אֱיָלוּתִי לְעֶזְרָתִי חוּשָׁה (Tehillim 22:20), "my strength, hasten to my help", which stands in the feminine like עזרתי, my help. Sometimes the middle root letter is quiescent: יֶשׁ־לְאֵל יָדִי (Bereishis 31:29), "it is in the power of my hand", and כִּי יֶשׁ־לְאֵל יָדָם (Michah 2:1), "for it is in the power of their hand". Another noun, on the pattern of אוֹר, is אוֹל: וּבָרִיא אוּלָם (Tehillim 73:4), their strength is sound.

As an adjective, הָאֵל (Yeshayahu 42:5) is the mighty One, and מִי־כָמֹכָה בָּאֵלִם (Shemos 15:11) is "who is like You among the mighty". In הָבוּ לַי"י בְּנֵי אֵלִים (Tehillim 29:1), "give to Hashem, בְּנֵי אֵלִים", they are the kings, בְּנֵי not being in smichus, like בְּנֵי שִׁלֵּשִׁים (Bereishis 50:23), third-generation children; or they are the stars, with בני in smichus, so that the stars are the sons and the angels the אלים, as in בְּרָן־יַחַד כּוֹכְבֵי בֹקֶר וַיָּרִיעוּ כָּל־בְּנֵי אֱלֹהִֽים (Iyov 38:7), "when the morning stars sang together and all the sons of Elohim shouted". And וּמִצְרַיִם אָדָם וְלֹא־אֵל (Yeshayahu 31:3), "and Mitzrayim are men and not אל", means not an angel. כְּאֵלָה נֹבֶלֶת עָלֶהָ (Yeshayahu 1:30), like a terebinth whose leaf withers, and כִּי יֵבֹשׁוּ מֵאֵילִים (Yeshayahu 1:29), for they will be shamed by the terebinths, and their like, may be of this root; he will write of them again at the root אלה.

וְאֶתְּנֵהוּ בְּיַד אֵיל גּוֹיִם (Yechezkel 31:11), "and I gave him into the hand of the mighty one of the nations", is written with a yud for the easterners, and the Mesorah notes it the only one full in a non-sacred sense; it means the mighty one of the nations, Nevuchadnetzar. So וְאֶת־אֵילֵי הָאָרֶץ לָקָח (Yechezkel 17:13), "and he took the mighty of the land", written with a yud, while יְדַבְּרוּ־לוֹ אֵלֵי גִבּוֹרִים (Yechezkel 32:21), "the mighty among the warriors shall speak to him", is without a yud, and the Mesorah notes it the only one lacking.

Rabbi Yehudah wrote that the adjective is written with a yud at אֵלֵי גִבּוֹרִים. Radak suggests the copyist may have erred and left words out: perhaps Rabbi Yehudah wrote it of אֵיל גּוֹיִם, then listed אֵילֵי הָאָרֶץ and אֵלֵי גִבּוֹרִים without marking which is full and which lacking. Radak adds that such a man deserves to be judged favourably in every way we can, since he lit the eyes of all who came after him in grammar and the language of Mikra; and although some books have אילי גבורים with a yud, we rely on the Mesorah in the books, where we found it lacking.

וְקֹרָא לָהֶם אֵילֵי הַצֶּדֶק (Yeshayahu 61:3), "and they shall be called the mighty of righteousness"; or אֵלֵי there is from אלה and אלים, trees, since the pasuk says מַטַּע י"י לְהִתְפָּאֵר, "the planting of Hashem, to be glorified".

אַיָּל וּצְבִי (Devarim 14:5), "hart and gazelle", אַיָּלָה שְׁלֻחָה (Bereishis 49:21), "a hind let loose", and גַּם־אַיֶּלֶת בַּשָּׂדֶה (Yirmiyahu 14:5), "even the hind in the field". In כְּאַיָּל תַּעֲרֹג עַל־אֲפִיקֵי־מָיִם (Tehillim 42:2), "as the hart longs for brooks of water", the verb comes in the feminine because אַיָּל is a general name covering male and female, like וַיְהִי־לִי שׁוֹר וַחֲמוֹר (Bereishis 32:6), "and I have oxen and donkeys"; the feminine means the herd of harts, for they go together in many droves.

אַיֶּלֶת הַשַּׁחַר (Tehillim 22:1), the hind of the dawn, is the morning star. Some explain it from the first sense, the strength of the dawn's rising. Radak holds the right reading is that it is a mashal for Knesses Yisrael, as Shir HaShirim likens them to hinds, and the dawn likewise, מִי־זֹאת הַנִּשְׁקָפָה כְּמוֹ־שָׁחַר (Shir HaShirim 6:10), "who is she that looks forth like the dawn"; the whole mizmor is about Knesses Yisrael in their galus.

אַיִל תָּמִים מִן־הַצֹּאן (Vayikra 5:15), "an unblemished ram from the flock": a lamb older than a year is called איל. In וּמֵאָה אֶלֶף אֵילִים צָמֶר (Melachim II 3:4), "and a hundred thousand rams, wool", the construct is lacking: אֵילִים means אלי צמר, rams of wool, that is, rams in their wool that had not been shorn.

אֵיל פָּארָן (Bereishis 14:6), the plain of Paran, עִם־אֵלוֹן מֻצָּב אֲשֶׁר בִּשְׁכֶם (Shoftim 9:6), by the plain of the thing set up in Shechem, and בְּאֵלֹנֵי מַמְרֵא (Bereishis 18:1), in the plains of Mamre, are as the Targum has them, מֵשְׁרֵי, a plain. אֵלוֹן מֻצָּב means that in that plain stood something set up, a stone or the like, and the plain was called after it so that the place could be known.

הָאַיִל מְזוּזוֹת חֲמִשִׁית (Melachim I 6:31), the אַיִל, doorposts, a fifth, וְאֶל־אַיִל תִּמֹרִים (Yechezkel 40:16), and on the post palm trees, and וּמִדָּה אַחַת לָאֵילִם מִפֹּה וּמִפּוֹ (Yechezkel 40:10), "and one measure for the posts on this side and that": their sense is doorposts. וְאֵלַמָּיו (Yechezkel 40:29), and its arches: their sense is a vault.

כשֹב.sense: The כֶּשֶׂב, a lamb, is one with כבש, its letters turned about: up to a year old it is called כשב or כבש, and older than a year, אַיִל, a ram.

more.t: אִם־כֶּשֶׂב הוּא־מַקְרִיב (Vayikra 3:7), "if he brings a lamb", and וְהַכְּשָׂבִים הִפְרִיד יַעֲקֹב (Bereishis 30:40), "and Yaakov separated the lambs": it is known that כשב is like כבש reversed, and the two are one.
While it is a year old it is called כשב and כבש; older than a year it is called אַיִל, a ram.

ארר.sense: To curse; מְאֵרָה, a curse, is a lack of good, the opposite of blessing, which is an addition of good.

more.t: וַיֹּאמֶר אָרוּר כְּנָעַן (Bereishis 9:25), "and he said, cursed be Canaan", אֹרוּ אָרוֹר יֹשְׁבֶיהָ (Shoftim 5:23), "curse her inhabitants bitterly", and וְאָרוֹתִי אֶת־בִּרְכוֹתֵיכֶם (Malachi 2:2), "and I will curse your blessings".
אֲשֶׁר אֵרְרָהּ י"י (Bereishis 5:29), "which Hashem cursed", and הַמַּיִם הַמְאָרְרִים (Bamidbar 5:22), "the water that brings the curse".
Rabbi Yehudah wrote that אָרָה־לִּי (Bamidbar 22:6), "curse for me", is of the heavy form; Radak says it may be of the light one.

אֶת־הַמְּאֵרָה (Malachi 2:2), "the curse": by rule it would carry a dagesh but for the resh, on the pattern of מְחִתָּה and מְגִנָּה. It is a curse and a lack of good, the opposite of blessing, since a blessing is an addition of good and a מארה the lack of blessing.

more.h: A tefillah that anger be lessened
more.t: אָרוּר אַפָּם כִּי עָז (Bereishis 49:7), "cursed be their anger for it was fierce", is a tefillah that their anger be made less.

וַאֲשֶׁר תָּאֹר יוּאָר (Bamidbar 22:6), "and whom you curse is cursed". בַּמְּאֵרָה אַתֶּם נֵאָרִים (Malachi 3:9), "you are cursed with the curse", may be from this root too, the vowel under the nun changed because the resh could not take a dagesh; Rabbi Yehudah set it under the root of נִאֵר מִקְדָּשׁוֹ (Eichah 2:7), He has spurned His Mikdash, and Radak says he will write of it there, im yirtzeh Hashem.

קלל.sense: Contempt, being made light of; close to it in sense, lightness and speed; and cursing. Also קָלָֽל, of burnished copper, and קִלְקַל, ruin, which others read otherwise.

more.t: הֵן קַלֹּתִי מָה אֲשִׁיבֶךָּ (Iyov 40:4), "behold I am of small account, what shall I answer You", וּנְקַלֹּתִי עוֹד מִזֹּאת (Shmuel II 6:22), "and I shall be yet lighter than this", וּבֹזַי יֵקָֽלּוּ (Shmuel I 2:30), "and those who despise Me shall be despised", and וַתֵּקַל גְּבִרְתָּהּ (Bereishis 16:4), "and her mistress was light in her eyes". So too וּמַדּוּעַ הֲקִלֹּתַנִי (Shmuel II 19:44), "and why have you made light of me", and לְהָקֵל כָּל־נִכְבַּדֵּי־אָֽרֶץ (Yeshayahu 23:9), "to make light of all the honoured of the earth": all of them, and those like them, carry the sense of contempt. עַל־ נְקַלָּה (Yirmiyahu 6:14), "lightly", he explains as על אמירה נקלה, by a slight saying.

קַל ־הוּא עַל־פְּנֵי־מַיִם (Iyov 24:18), "he is swift upon the face of the waters", and קַלִּים הָיוּ רֹדְפֵינוּ (Eichah 4:19), "our pursuers were swift": near in sense to the first. יִקַּלּוּ רֹֽדְפֵיכֶֽם (Yeshayahu 30:16), "your pursuers shall be swift", has a chirik under the yud and a dagesh in the kuf, to tell it apart from וּבֹזַי יֵקָֽלּוּ.

בַּלֶּחֶם הַקְּלֹקֵֽל (Bamidbar 21:5), "with the light bread", with the first root letter doubled: our Rabbis explained (Yoma 75b; Avodah Zarah 5a) that they called the mon so because it was absorbed in the limbs.

מִקֹּל זְנוּתָהּ (Yirmiyahu 3:9), "from the lightness of her harlotry", which he files under lightness; the Mesorah notes it as the only one written defective in the sense of lightness. Our Rabbis in the Yerushalmi in Challah explain it as it sounds, "from the voice of her harlotry", and said that a woman's voice is ervah, bringing this very phrase as the reason.

אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ קִלֵּל (Vayikra 20:9), "he has cursed his father and his mother", וּמְקַלֵּל אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ (Shemos 21:17), "and one who curses his father and his mother", לֹֽא־ תְקַלֵּל חֵרֵשׁ (Vayikra 19:14), "do not curse the deaf", and וְקִלֵּל בְּמַלְכּוֹ (Yeshayahu 8:21), "and he curses his king". The passive is תְּקֻלַּל חֶלְקָתָם בָּאָרֶץ (Iyov 24:18), "their portion in the land is cursed", and the noun בְּרָכָה וּקְלָלָֽה (Devarim 11:26), "blessing and curse". כִּֽי־ מְקַלְלִים לָהֶם בָּנָיו (Shmuel I 3:13), "for his sons were cursing themselves", stands here too, and he allows that it may be from contempt instead, his sons making themselves contemptible, as וּבֹזַי יֵקָֽלּוּ.

כִּֽי־קִלְלַת אֱלֹהִים תָּלוּי (Devarim 21:23), "for the cursing of Elokim he is hanged", means he hangs for having cursed Hashem. It may also be taken from the first sense: the hanged man is a disgrace to Hashem, since whoever sees him says he hangs for having blasphemed. There are two reasons in the matter, he says, and they do not reach equally far: this one is the reason for the blasphemer and the idolater, who were the men hanged, and the other, וְלֹא תְטַמֵּא אֶת־אַדְמָתְךָ (Devarim 21:23), "and you shall not defile your land", is a reason for everyone hanged in Eretz Yisrael, since a body left unburied is tumah to the land.

So Yehoshua did with the king of Ai and the five kings, commanding that they be taken down at evening and a heap of stones made over them (Yehoshua 10:27); and so Yisrael are to do with the slain of Gog and Magog, וּקְבָרוּם בֵּית יִשְׂרָאֵל לְמַעַן טַהֵר אֶת־הָאָרֶץ, "and the house of Yisrael shall bury them in order to cleanse the land": as long as the dead lie unburied, they are tumah to the land. As for the sons of Shaul, left from Nisan until Tishrei עַד נִתַּךְ־מַיִם עֲלֵיהֶם (Shmuel II 21:10), "until water was poured upon them", our Rabbis explained (Yevamos 79a) that though it is written לֹֽא־תָלִין נִבְלָתוֹ עַל־הָעֵץ (Devarim 21:23), "his body shall not remain overnight upon the tree", better one letter of the Torah be uprooted and Heaven's name sanctified in public, since passers-by asked what these were and were told they were kings' sons who laid hands on converts, and said no nation is fit to cleave to like this one.

קִלְקַל בַּֽחִצִּים (Yechezkel 21:26) and וְכָל־הַגְּבָעוֹת הִתְקַלְקָֽלוּ (Yirmiyahu 4:24), with the first root letter doubled as well. They are of the sense of קלקול in the words of our Rabbis, which is ruin and destruction, as they said (Shabbos 13:3; 108b) that all who spoil are exempt; read so, all the hills were ruined. Rabbi Yonah explained them as movement, in the sense of lightness, and Radak’s father wrote them so as well; read so, all the hills moved. Radak says what that comes to: קִלְקַל בַּֽחִצִּים is that he commanded the arrows be shot upward, and if the arrow falls toward Bnei Ammon he will go there. So Yonasan holds, rendering it קְשַׁת בְּגִרְרַיָא, "he shot with arrows".

נְחֹשֶׁת קָלָֽל (Yechezkel 1:7) means copper polished and bright, and from this וְהוּא לֹא־פָנִים קִלְקַל (Koheles 10:10), "and he has not burnished the face", that is, the face of the iron was not honed. Menachem joined קִלְקַל בַּֽחִצִּים to this sense, reading it, "he burnished the arrows".

אלה.sense: An oath, a curse included, since a curse is made with an oath and Hashem's name. Also a lament; the fat tail; a kind of tree; אוּלַי, perhaps; אֶל, to; אֵלֶּה, these.

more.t: וְאַתְּ אָלִית וְגַם אָמַרְתְּ בְּאָזְנַי (Shoftim 17:2), and you adjured, and also said it in my ears: the verb is transitive and means השבעת, you made another swear. אָלֹה וְכַחֵשׁ (Hoshea 4:2), swearing and lying, and אָלוֹת שָׁוְא (Hoshea 10:4), swearing falsely, are the infinitive, which is intransitive. The heavy form is וְנָֽשָׁא־בוֹ אָלָה לְהַֽאֲלֹתוֹ (Melachim I 8:31), and he lays an oath on him to make him swear.

תְּהִי נָא אָלָה בֵּֽינוֹתֵינוּ (Bereishis 26:28), let there now be an oath between us; בְּשָׁמְעוֹ אֶת־דִּבְרֵי הָֽאָלָה (Devarim 29:18), when he hears the words of the oath; אֵת כָּל־ הָֽאָלוֹת הַכְּתוּבוֹת עַל־הַסֵּפֶר (Divrei HaYamim II 34:24), all the oaths written in the book; and לִשְׁאֹל בְּאָלָה נַפְשֽׁוֹ (Iyov 31:30), to ask for his life with an oath. In another form, תַּֽאֲלָֽתְךָ לָהֶֽם (Eichah 3:65), Your oath upon them, the tav added as in תַּֽאֲנָתָהּ מִי יְשִׁיבֶנָּה (Yirmiyahu 2:24), her desire, who can turn it back. All of them mean an oath, for a curse is made with an oath and with mention of Hashem's name.

Another sense: אֱלִי כִּבְתוּלָה חֲגֻֽרַת־שַׂק (Yoel 1:8), lament like a maiden girded with sackcloth, which he explains as קונני, lament; and so the Targum renders שָׂא קִינָה (Yechezkel 19:1), take up a lament, as טוּל אִלְיָא, and וַיְקֹנֵן הַמֶּלֶךְ (Shmuel II 3:33), and the king lamented, as וַאֲלָא מַלְכָּא.
הָֽאַלְיָה תְמִימָה (Vayikra 3:9), the whole fat tail: the yud is the last root letter and the heh the feminine ending, and its sense is known.

תַּחַת הָֽאֵלָה אֲשֶׁר עִם־שְׁכֶֽם (Bereishis 35:4), under the elah that is by Shechem; כְּאֵלָה נֹבֶלֶת עָלֶהָ (Yeshayahu 1:30), like an elah whose leaf withers; and with a dagesh, תַּחַת הָאַלָּה אֲשֶׁר בְּמִקְדַּשׁ י"י (Yehoshua 24:26), under the elah that is in the sanctuary of Hashem, the dagesh standing in place of the quiescent letter in אלה, though that letter is no root letter, if these words are of this root. The plural is כִּי יֵבֹשׁוּ מֵאֵילִים אֲשֶׁר חֲמַדְתֶּם (Yeshayahu 1:29), for they shall be ashamed of the elah trees you desired; in Yechezkel, וְלֹֽא־יַֽעַמְדוּ אֵֽלֵיהֶם בְּגָבְהָם, and their elah trees shall not stand up in their height; and הַנֵּֽחָמִים בָּֽאֵלִים (Yeshayahu 57:5), who inflame themselves among the elah trees. All of them are the name of a tree, and they say it is the one called in the vernacular אוֹלֻמוֹ, olmo. כִּי יֵבֹשׁוּ מֵאֵילִים and הַנֵּֽחָמִים בָּֽאֵלִים, and the like, can also be read as a general name for any tree, and so אֵילֵי הַצֶּדֶק (Yeshayahu 61:3), trees of righteousness.

The pasuk says בְּמִקְדַּשׁ י"י, in the sanctuary of Hashem, though they were at Shechem: it appears that they brought the aron of Hashem there, as it says וַיִּֽתְיַצְּבוּ לִפְנֵי הָאֱלֹהִֽים (Yehoshua 24:1), and they presented themselves before Hashem.

more.h: Yonasan and Rabbi Yonah on the tree
more.t: Yonasan renders אלה and אלים as בּוּטְמָא, butma; but וַיּוֹצֵא אֵלָיו אֶל־תַּחַת הָֽאֵלָה (Shoftim 6:19), and he brought it out to him under the elah, he rendered אִילָנָא, a tree, while the earlier וַיֵּשֶׁב תַּחַת הָֽאֵלָה (Shoftim 6:11), and he sat under the elah, he rendered בּוּטְמָא. Rabbi Yonah wrote that it is called so in Arabic, בט"ם, butm. Radak adds that they may all be from the root איל.

אוּלַי יְמֻשֵּׁנִי אָבִי (Bereishis 27:12), perhaps my father will feel me; אוּלַי נָֽטְתָה מִפָּנַי (Bamidbar 22:33), perhaps she turned aside from me; and אוּלַי יַֽעֲשֶׂה זָרִים יִבְלָעֻֽהוּ (Hoshea 8:7), perhaps it will yield, strangers will swallow it: they are said of a doubtful matter, in the sense of שמא, perhaps. עַל־אוּבַל אוּלָֽי (Daniel 8:2), by the stream Ulai, is a place name, its yud the last root letter in place of a heh.

Since the pasuk says וַתֵּט לְפָנַי, which means she turned off the road and stood before me, it says: had she turned away from me and gone on her way, גַּם־אֹֽתְכָה הָרַגְתִּי (Bamidbar 22:33), I would have killed you too. Radak does not know why the commentators explained אוּלַי there as לולי, unless; and besides, מִפָּנַי is the opposite of לְפָנַי, the mem showing what is far and the lamed what is near.

וַיֹּאמֶר י"י אֶל־אַבְרָם (Bereishis 12:1), and Hashem said to Avram, and the like, whose sense is known. It also stands for other words: for מן in לִשְׁבֹּר אֶל־יוֹסֵף (Bereishis 41:57), to buy from Yosef, though that may also be the order turned about, all the land came to Mitzrayim to Yosef to buy; for על in וַיַּךְ אֶת־הַפְּלִשְׁתִּי אֶל־מִצְחוֹ (Shmuel I 17:49), and he struck the Plishti on his forehead; for עם in קִבְרוּ אֹתִי אֶל־אֲבֹתָי (Bereishis 49:29), bury me with my fathers; for a beis in הִנֵּה־הוּא נֶחְבָּא אֶל־הַכֵּלִֽים (Shmuel I 10:22), there he is, hidden among the baggage; for את in וַיִּרְדְּפוּ אֶל־מִדְיָן (Shoftim 7:25), and they pursued Midian; and for בעבור in וַיֹּאמֶר אַבְרָהָם אֶל־שָׂרָה אִשְׁתּוֹ (Bereishis 20:2), and Avraham said concerning Sarah his wife.

Another word in this root points to many, as זה, this, points to one: הָֽאֲרָצֹת הָאֵל (Bereishis 26:3), these lands, and לָֽאֲנָשִׁים הָאֵל (Bereishis 19:8), these men. With a heh added, וְאֵלֶּה שְׁמוֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (Shemos 1:1), and these are the names of the sons of Yisrael, and אֵלֶּה הַדְּבָרִים (Devarim 1:1), these are the words. It may be that this word has a quiescent middle letter, or that it is of two letters.

קבב.sense: To curse; הַקֻּבָּה, which is like a tent and, in קֳבָתָהּ, comes without the dagesh, or else קֳבָתָהּ is of קֵבָה, the maw. Chazal read קבתה as the place of ervah.

more.t: וְקַבֹּתוֹ לִי מִשָּֽׁם (Bamidbar 23:27), "and curse him for me from there", מָה אֶקֹּב לֹא קַבֹּה אֵל (Bamidbar 23:8), "how shall I curse whom Hashem has not cursed", and וְקָבְנוֹ ־לִי מִשָּֽׁם (Bamidbar 23:13), "and curse him for me from there": their sense is cursing.
וַיָּבֹא אַחַר אִישׁ־יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶל־ הַקֻּבָּה (Bamidbar 25:8), "and he came after the man of Yisrael into the kubbah", which is like אל האהל, into the tent.

In the same pasuk it comes without the dagesh: וְאֶת־הָֽאִשָּׁה אֶל־ קֳבָתָהּ, and the woman into her kovah. Or קֳבָתָהּ may be of the sense of הַזְּרֹעַ וְהַלְּחָיַיִם וְהַקֵּבָֽה (Devarim 18:3), "the shoulder, the cheeks and the maw", as the Targum renders it, לִמְעָהָא, into her innards. Their sense is the pouch in the beast's innards where the milk of the suckling is gathered, said here by way of borrowing; or it is so in a person's innards too. Chazal explained (Sanhedrin 82b; Chullin 134b) קבתה as the place of ervah in a woman.

No root can be settled for קבה. Rabbi Yonah put it under the root קבה, on the weight of חֵמָה, wrath, and Radak has already written what is good and right at חֵמָה, that its root is יחם. From the way the Mishnah is read in the construct (Chullin 8:5), קיבת הנכרי, the maw of the gentile, with a tzeirei under the kuf, and with the possessive, a kosher animal that suckled from a tereifah, its maw is forbidden, it would seem the root is קוב. Then ואל האשה אל קבתה, and the woman into her kovah, is of another form, from the roots whose middle letter is weak, the separate form being קֹבָה, with a kamatz katan in place of the cholam when joined. Or it is from those whose last letter is weak, the separate form being קֹבֶת, on the weight of שֹׁקֶת, a trough.

מאר.sense: Causing pain: its sense, he says, is like מכאיב, one that pains, as of סִלּוֹן מַמְאִיר, a brier that pains, and צָרַעַת מַמְאֶרֶת, a painful tzaraas.

more.t: סִלּוֹן מַמְאִיר (Yechezkel 28:24), a brier that pains, whose sense is like מכאיב, one that causes pain; and so צָרַעַת מַמְאֶרֶת (Vayikra 13:51), a tzaraas that pains.

דחף.sense: Pushing, the one sense he gives all its forms: the runners went out pushed on, Haman was pushed, and the noun מַדְחֵפֹת, pushes.

more.t: הָֽרָצִים יָצְאוּ דְחוּפִים (Esther 3:15), the runners went out pushed on, and in the passive וְהָמָן נִדְחַף (Esther 6:12), and Haman was pushed.
יְצוּדֶנּוּ לְמַדְחֵפֹֽת (Tehillim 140:12), it shall hunt him down with pushes. The sense of them all is pushing.

הדף.sense: Pushing, the sense he gives for every use: a man pushed without enmity, pushing with side and shoulder, one pushed from his post, enemies pushed out.

more.h: Pushing a man, pushing with shoulder
more.t: וְאִם־בְּפֶתַע בְּלֹֽא־אֵיבָה הֲדָפוֹ (Bamidbar 35:22), if he pushed him suddenly without enmity, and יַעַן בְּצַד וּבְכָתֵף תֶּהְדֹּפוּ (Yechezkel 34:21), because you push with side and shoulder.

more.h: Pushed from a post, enemies pushed
more.t: וַֽהֲדַפְתִּיךָ מִמַּצָּבֶךָ (Yeshayahu 22:19), I will push you from your station, and לַֽהֲדֹף אֶת־כָּל־אֹֽיְבֶיךָ (Devarim 6:19), to push away all your enemies. All of them, he says, are the sense of pushing.

more.h: A vowel the precise books split on
more.t: וְהַוַּת רְשָׁעִים יֶֽהְדֹּֽף (Mishlei 10:3), the craving of the wicked He pushes away. Radak found the yud pointed with segol in some of the precise books and with patach in others.

דפק.sense: Pushing: flocks pushed on for a single day; and pushing and striking on a door, of men at the door and of the beloved knocking.

more.t: וּדְפָקוּם יוֹם אֶחָד (Bereishis 33:13), and should they push them a single day: the sense is pushing.

more.h: Beating and knocking at a door
more.t: מִֽתְדַּפְּקִים עַל־הַדָּלֶת (Shoftim 19:22), pushing and beating at the door, and קוֹל דּוֹדִי דוֹפֵק (Shir HaShirim 5:2), the sound of my beloved knocking: their sense too is pushing and striking on the door.

כבס.sense: To launder: of garments, and also of a heart washed of evil and a man washed of his sin. כוֹבֵֽס is one who launders clothes.

more.t: אֶל־מְסִלַּת שְׂדֵה כוֹבֵֽס (Yeshayahu 7:3), to the highway of the launderer's field: a noun for one who launders clothes, and Chazal use it too, אשתייר ההוא כובס (Kesubos 103b), that one launderer was left.

more.h: Why it is the launderer's field
more.t: It is the field where the launderers would spread their clothes out in the sun, and Yonasan renders it חֲקַל מַשְׁטַח קְצִירַיָא, the field where the launderers spread things out.

כִּבֵּס בַּיַּיִן לְבֻשׁוֹ (Bereishis 49:11), he washes his clothing in wine, וְכִבַּסְתֶּם בִּגְדֵיכֶם (Bamidbar 31:24), you shall wash your garments, and of a person כַּבְּסִי מֵֽרָעָה לִבֵּךְ (Yirmiyahu 4:14), wash your heart clean of evil, כַּבְּסֵנִי מֵֽעֲוֹנִי (Tehillim 51:4), wash me of my sin.

more.h: The washed garment, the washed mark
more.t: וְכֻבַּס שֵׁנִית וְטָהֵֽר (Vayikra 13:58), it shall be washed a second time and be clean, and אַֽחֲרֵי הֻכַּבֵּס אֶת־הַנֶּגַע (Vayikra 13:55), after the mark has been washed. The sense is well known.

רחץ.sense: To wash, a sense he calls known; the noun רַחְצָה, the washing, and without the heh, סִיר רַחְצִי, a washing pot.

more.t: אִם רָחַץ י"י (Yeshayahu 4:4), when Hashem has washed; וְרָחֲצוּ אַהֲרֹן וּבָנָיו (Shemos 30:19), and Aharon and his sons shall wash; וְרָחַצְתָּ אֹתָם בַּמָּיִם (Shemos 29:4), and you shall wash them in water; לִרְחֹץ עַל־הַיְאֹר (Shemos 2:5), to wash at the river; וְכַנּוֹ נְחֹשֶׁת לְרָחְצָה (Shemos 30:18), and its base of copper, for washing; רְחַץ וּטְהָר (Melachim II 5:13), wash and be clean; and רַחֲצוּ הִזַּכּוּ (Yeshayahu 1:16), wash, make yourselves clean.

וְרָחַצְתְּ וָסַכְתְּ (Rus 3:3), and wash and anoint, means wash your flesh; and יִרְחֲצוּ־מַיִם (Shemos 30:20), they shall wash with water, means they shall wash their hands and their feet in the water.
All of these, Radak says, are transitive verbs, verbs that take an object. His father explained some of them as intransitive.

Where the doer is not named, וּמִצֹּאָתוֹ לֹא רֻחָץ (Mishlei 30:12), and is not washed of its filth, and לֹא־רֻחַצְתְּ לְמִשְׁעִי (Yechezkel 16:4), you were not washed smooth. Of washing oneself, אִם־הִתְרָחַצְתִּי (Iyov 9:30), if I wash myself. The noun, שֶׁעָלוּ מִן־הָרַחְצָה (Shir HaShirim 4:2), that came up from the washing.
מוֹאָב סִיר רַחְצִי (Tehillim 60:10), Moav is my washing pot, the noun without the heh; its singular would be רַחַץ, on the pattern of נַעַר, a lad, and נַעַל, a shoe. The sense of washing is known.

שׁטף.sense: Washing with force, and sweeping away: hands rinsed in water, a chariot washed down, rivers that flood a land; a galloping horse is likened to a flooding stream.

more.t: וְיָדָיו לֹֽא־שָׁטַף בַּמָּיִם (Vayikra 15:11), he did not rinse his hands in water, וַיִּשְׁטֹף אֶת־הָרֶכֶב (Melachim I 22:38), and he washed down the chariot, and וְכָל־כְּלִי־עֵץ יִשָּׁטֵף בַּמָּֽיִם (Vayikra 15:12), every wooden vessel shall be rinsed in water.

וְיִשְׁטְפוּ אֶרֶץ וּמְלוֹאָהּ (Yirmiyahu 47:2), they flood the land and its fullness, וּנְהָרוֹת לֹא יִשְׁטְפוּהָ (Shir HaShirim 8:7), rivers shall not sweep it away, שָׁטַף וְעָבַר (Yeshayahu 8:8), it sweeps through and passes on, and the noun לְשֵׁטֶף מַיִם רַבִּים (Tehillim 32:6), at the flood of many waters. All of them, the rinsing and the flooding alike, are washing with force and sweeping away.

Likewise a horse, for the speed of its running, is likened to a flooding stream, כְּסוּס שׁוֹטֵף בַּמִּלְחָמָֽה (Yirmiyahu 8:6), like a horse flooding on in battle; and likewise trouble as it passes through the world, שׁוֹט שׁוֹטֵף כִּי יַֽעֲבֹר (Yeshayahu 28:18), when the flooding scourge passes through.

דוח.sense: To be thrust away, read as נדחו; and in another sense, washing, a word Chazal use often.

more.t: דֹּחוּ וְלֹא־יָכְלוּ קֽוּם (Tehillim 36:13), they were thrust away and could not rise, which he reads as נדחו, they were thrust away. In the view of the Chacham Rabbi Yehudah, who wrote the word among the roots whose middle letter is weak, it and נדחו are two roots of one sense.
יָדִיחַ מִקִּרְבָּהּ (Yeshayahu 4:4), He will wash away from within her, and שָׁם יָדִיחוּ אֶת־הָֽעֹלָֽה (Yechezkel 40:38), there they wash the olah.

מִלָּא כְרֵשֹׂו מֵֽעֲדָנָי (Yirmiyahu 51:34), he filled his belly with my delights, and then הֱדִיחָֽנִי, he washed me out. The sense of all three is washing. Chazal use the word often, as מדיח ומולח ומדיח (Chullin 113a), he washes and salts and washes again.

מרק.sense: Scouring, a sense he calls known: spears and a vessel scoured; the women's adornment, which scours the flesh clean; and broth, since the meat is scoured in it.

more.t: מִרְקוּ הָֽרְמָחִים (Yirmiyahu 46:4), polish the spears; נְחֹשֶׁת מָרֽוּק (Divrei HaYamim II 4:16), burnished copper; וּמֹרַק וְשֻׁטַּף בַּמָּֽיִם (Vayikra 6:21), it shall be scoured and rinsed in water, which he explains as scouring it and rinsing it thoroughly; and the noun, תַּמְרוּק בְּרָע (Mishlei 20:30), a scouring of evil. The sense of scouring, he says, is known.

more.h: Hot water and cold in Chazal
more.t: Chazal (Zevachim 96a) put the scouring in hot water and the rinsing in cold, and some of them hold the scouring and the rinsing are in cold water and the purging in hot.

From this, what women adorn themselves with is called תמרוק, because it scours the grime off the flesh and cleans it: וְנָתוֹן תַּמְרוּקֵיהֶֽן (Esther 2:3), and let their adornments be given them, and וּבְתַמְרוּקֵי הַנָּשִֽׁים (Esther 2:12), with the adornments of the women.

So too the water the meat was cooked in is called מָרָק, because the scouring of the meat is in it: וְאֶת־הַמָּרַק שְׁפוֹךְ (Shoftim 6:20), and pour out the broth, and וּמְרַק פִּגֻּלִים כְּלֵיהֶם (Yeshayahu 65:4), and broth of abominations is in their vessels.

בטח.sense: To trust and be secure, whether in Hashem, in wealth, in a mountain or in a brother; to make another trust; and the noun, confidence, in many patterns.

more.t: שֹׁקֵט וּבֹטֵחַ (Shoftim 18:7), quiet and secure, אֶבְטַח וְלֹא אֶפְחָד (Yeshayahu 12:2), I will trust and not be afraid, and the adjective כִּי בְךָ בָּטֽוּחַ (Yeshayahu 26:3), because he trusts in You.

more.h: The land of peace at Anasos
more.t: וּבְאֶרֶץ שָׁלוֹם אַתָּה בוֹטֵחַ (Yirmiyahu 12:5), and in a land of peace you trust: that is, in a land of peace where you ought to have been able to trust its people, the men of Anasos, and you are in danger with them and afraid of them, as it says of the men of Anasos who seek your life. וְאֵיךְ תַּֽעֲשֶׂה בִּגְאוֹן הַיַּרְדֵּֽן (Yirmiyahu 12:5), how then will you do in the swelling of the Yarden, means when I send you to Yerushalayim. And so it says כִּי גַם־אַחֶיךָ וּבֵית־אָבִיךָ גַּם־הֵמָּה בָּגְדוּ בָךְ, for even your brothers and your father's house, they too have betrayed you.

וְהַבֹּֽטְחִים בְּהַר שֹֽׁמְרוֹן (Amos 6:1), those secure in the mountain of Shomron, אַל־תִּבְטְחוּ לָכֶם אֶל־דִּבְרֵי הַשֶּׁקֶר (Yirmiyahu 7:4), do not trust in words of falsehood, בְּטַח אֶל־י"י בְּכָל־לִבֶּךָ (Mishlei 3:5), trust in Hashem with all your heart, הַבֹּטְחִים עַל־חֵילָם (Tehillim 49:7), those who trust in their wealth, and וְעַל־כָּל־אָח אַל־תִּבְטָחוּ (Yirmiyahu 9:3), put no trust in any brother.

וַיָּבֹאוּ עַל־הָעִיר בֶּטַח (Bereishis 34:25), they came upon the city securely, מָה הַבִּטָּחוֹן הַזֶּה (Yeshayahu 36:4), what is this confidence, מִבְטָח בּוֹגֵד (Mishlei 25:19), a traitor relied upon, מִבֵּית אֵל מִבְטֶחָֽם (Yirmiyahu 48:13), Beis El their reliance, and בְּהַשְׁקֵט וּבְבִטְחָה (Yeshayahu 30:15), in quiet and in confidence.

וְאַתָּה הִבְטַחְתָּ אֶת־הָעָם הַזֶּה (Yirmiyahu 28:15), you made this people rely, וְאַל־יַבְטַח אֶתְכֶם חִזְקִיָּהוּ (Yeshayahu 36:15), let Chizkiyahu not make you rely, and מַבְטִיחִי עַל־שְׁדֵי אִמִּֽי (Tehillim 22:10), who set me secure at my mother's breasts.
וְאֵת הָֽאֲבַטִּחִים (Bamidbar 11:5), and the melons: one can say that the alef here is an addition, or the word may be one of four letters; in the vernacular it is אל בודק"ש.

חסה.sense: To take shelter, all of it the sense of הסתופף, as in the shadow of wings; and the noun מַחְסֶה, a shelter.

more.h: Sheltering in the shadow of wings
more.t: אֶחֱסֶה בְסֵתֶר כְּנָפֶיךָ (Tehillim 61:5), I will shelter in the covert of Your wings, and בְּצֵל כְּנָפֶיךָ יֶחֱסָיוּן (Tehillim 36:8), in the shadow of Your wings they take shelter.

בֹּאוּ חֲסוּ בְצִלִּי (Shoftim 9:15), come and shelter in my shade, וּבָהּ יֶחֱסוּ עֲנִיֵּי עַמּוֹ (Yeshayahu 14:32), in her the poor of His people shelter, בְךָ חָסָיָה נַפְשִׁי (Tehillim 57:2), in You my soul shelters, and מוֹשִׁיעַ חוֹסִים (Tehillim 17:7), who saves those who take shelter.

מַחְסֶה מִזֶּרֶם צֵל מֵחֹרֶב (Yeshayahu 25:4), a shelter from the downpour and a shade from the heat, סְלָעִים מַחְסֶה לַשְׁפַנִּים (Tehillim 104:18), the crags are a shelter for the hyraxes, and וְהֶחָסוּת בְּצֵל־מִצְרַיִם לִכְלִמָּה (Yeshayahu 30:3), sheltering in Mitzrayim's shade turns to disgrace. All of them are the sense of הסתופף, taking shelter.

more.h: A masorah that reverses the pointing
more.t: אֶחֱסֶה בְסֵתֶר כְּנָפֶיךָ (Tehillim 61:5), I will shelter in the covert of Your wings, is pointed with sheva alone, and וּבְצֵל־כְּנָפֶיךָ אֶחְסֶה (Tehillim 57:2), and in the shadow of Your wings I will shelter, with sheva and segol. But another masorah he found has every מַחֲסֶה, מַחֲסִי and לַחֲסוֹת, shelter, my shelter and to shelter, soft, and every אֶחֱסֶה soft like them but one, that same וּבְצֵל־כְּנָפֶיךָ אֶחְסֶה; if so, Radak says, it is the reverse of what he wrote.

יחל.sense: To wait in hope, and to give another hope; the noun תּוֹחֶלֶת is hope.

more.t: וְיִֽחֲלוּ כַמָּטָר לִי (Iyov 29:23), they waited for me as for rain, כַּֽאֲשֶׁר יִחַלְנוּ לָֽךְ (Tehillim 33:22), as we have waited for You, and וְלֹא יְיַחֵל לִבְנֵי אָדָֽם (Michah 5:6), he does not wait upon men.

עַל אֲשֶׁר יִֽחַלְתָּֽנִי (Tehillim 119:49), because You gave me hope: the verb carries over to a third party, You put hope in me by telling me to hope in You. So too וְיִֽחֲלוּ לְקַיֵּם דָּבָֽר (Yechezkel 13:6), they give the people hope that their prophecy will stand, and it is empty and false.

וַיָּחֶל עוֹד (Bereishis 8:10), and he waited again, whose proper form he gives as וַיִּיָחֶל; or it may be from the root חיל, as he has written at that root. וַיִּיָּחֶל עוֹד שִׁבְעַת יָמִים (Bereishis 8:12), and he waited yet seven more days, is standing in hope through the first seven days and seven more besides.

more.h: His father on hope that fails
more.t: וַתֵּרֶא כִּי נֽוֹחֲלָה אָֽבְדָה תִּקְוָתָהּ (Yechezkel 19:5), and she saw that she had waited, her hope was lost: Radak reads it as her standing many days in hope, and then her hope was lost. His father read נֽוֹחֲלָה as the reverse of hope, which Radak spells out as her hope being lost; and so his father held that וַיִּיָּחֶל is not the form of נֽוֹחֲלָה but the reflexive, properly וַיִּתְיָֽחֶל, since a thing and its opposite do not come in one form of the verb, only in two. Radak answers that this would be good but for the yud, which carries a kamatz, the rule after the prefix letters in the form of נֽוֹחֲלָה, as he wrote in his grammar.

more.h: Waiting for words, and not waiting
more.t: הֵן הוֹחַלְתִּי לְֽדִבְרֵיכֶם (Iyov 32:11), I waited for your words, and לֹא־כֵן אֹחִילָה לְפָנֶיךָ (Shmuel II 18:14), which he reads as: it is no good that I draw it out before you and wait for you to go and strike him, I will go myself; and he took three rods.

מֵעַי מֵעַי אֹחִולָה (Yirmiyahu 4:19), my innards, my innards, with its verb read three ways. It may be of the sense of חִיל כַּיּֽוֹלֵדָֽה (Tehillim 48:7), trembling like a woman giving birth, so that יחל and חיל are one sense, I give trembling to my innards out of the greatness of my worry and my moaning; or it means I am in pain and I tremble from the pain of my innards and of the walls of my heart; or it may be from this root itself: I said I would give my innards hope, for they still hope for good though they are now in evil.
תּוֹחֶלֶת מְמֻשָּׁכָה (Mishlei 13:12), hope drawn out long, and הֵן־תֹּחַלְתּוֹ נִכְזָבָה (Iyov 41:1), his hope proves a lie.

חכה.sense: To wait: those who wait for Hashem, those who wait for a death that does not come, bands waiting for a man. The sense of them all, he says, is like that of hope.

more.h: Waiting for what has not come
more.t: אַשְׁרֵי כָּל־חוֹכֵי לֽוֹ (Yeshayahu 30:18), fortunate are all who wait for Him; and in the heavy form וְחִכִּיתִי לַֽי"י (Yeshayahu 8:17), and I will wait for Hashem, אַשְׁרֵי הַֽמְחַכֶּה (Daniel 12:12), fortunate is the one who waits, and הַֽמְחַכִּים לַמָּוֶת וְאֵינֶנּוּ (Iyov 3:21), who wait for death and it does not come.

חִכָּה אֶת־אִיּוֹב בִּדְבָרִים (Iyov 32:4), he waited for Iyov with words, and וּכְחַכֵּי אִישׁ גְּדוּדִים (Hoshea 6:9), and as bands wait for a man, where the yud stands in place of a heh and the word is an infinitive. The sense of them all is like that of hope.

וְלָכֵן יְחַכֶּה י"י לַֽחֲנַנְכֶם (Yeshayahu 30:18), and therefore Hashem יְחַכֶּה to be gracious to you, he reads two ways. Either He draws out the time of the favour, like one who waits but does not pass on; or יְחַכֶּה is a transitive verb, in the way of עַל אֲשֶׁר יִֽחַלְתָּֽנִי (Tehillim 119:49), on which You have made me hope, that is, He assures you that you may wait for Him to be gracious to you, for so He will do. Radak holds the second correct.

סמך.sense: To lean on a support, or to hold up; close to it, drawing near and surrounding; and in another sense, the שְׂמִיכָה, written with a sin, a thick covering.

more.t: כִּֽי־סָמַךְ מֹשֶׁה אֶת־יָדָיו עָלָיו (Devarim 34:9), for Moshe had leaned his hands upon him, וְהַֽלְוִיִּם יִסְמְכוּ אֶת־יְדֵיהֶם (Bamidbar 8:12), and the Leviim shall lean their hands, and וְסָמַךְ יָדוֹ עַל־הַקִּיר (Amos 5:19), and he rests his hand on the wall.

סָמוּךְ לִבּוֹ לֹא יִירָא (Tehillim 112:8), his heart is propped and he does not fear, and יֵצֶר סָמוּךְ תִּצֹּר שָׁלוֹם שָׁלוֹם (Yeshayahu 26:3), which he reads as a mind that leans and rests on You, which You guard, and it is at peace because it trusts in You.

עָלֶיךָ נִסְמַכְתִּי מִבֶּטֶן (Tehillim 71:6), on You I have leaned from the womb, and וַיִּסָּֽמְכוּ הָעָם עַל־דִּבְרֵי יְחִזְקִיָּהוּ (Divrei HaYamim II 32:8), the people leaned on Yechizkiyahu's words. The sense of these words, and of all like them, is leaning on a support. Chazal use the word in this first sense too (Bava Kamma 100a), חזי דעלך קא סמיכנא, see that it is on you I lean; that is, my support and my hope rest on you.

There is a sense close to this one: סָמַךְ מֶלֶךְ־בָּבֶל אֶל־יְרוּשָׁלַם (Yechezkel 24:2), the king of Bavel closed in on Yerushalayim, עָלַי סָמְכָה חֲמָתֶךָ (Tehillim 88:8), Your wrath has closed in on me, and סַמְּכוּנִי בָּֽאֲשִׁישׁוֹת (Shir HaShirim 2:5), surround me with cakes. The sense of these words is drawing near and surrounding, and Chazal use the word so a great deal, as ערב שבת סמוך לחשיכה (Shabbos 11a), on erev Shabbos close to nightfall.

more.h: Grain and wine near him always
more.t: וְדָגָן וְתִירשׁ סְמַכְתִּיו (Bereishis 27:37), and grain and wine I have brought near him, meaning that they should be near and close to him for ever; and so וְרוּחַ נְדִיבָה תִסְמְכֵֽנִי (Tehillim 51:14), let a willing spirit be near me, that it be near and close to me always.

In another sense, וַתְּכַסֵּהוּ בַּשְּׂמִיכָֽה (Shoftim 4:18), and she covered him with the שמיכה, which is written with a sin: the thick covering with tufts of wool coming out of it, which Chazal call גלופקר (Shabbos 51a), and which has its own name in the vernacular. Like it, Chazal call a thick thing סמיכתא, as in סמיכתא וקלישתא (Chullin 55b), thick and thin. He means to explain it further under the letter sin.

כסל.sense: The fool and his folly; in another sense, trust and hope; Kesil, a star; and the כְּסָלִים, the flanks beside the kidneys at the roots of the thighs.

more.t: הַכְּסִיל חֹבֵק אֶת־יָדָיו (Koheles 4:5), the fool folds his hands, וְהַכְּסִיל בַּחֹשֶׁךְ הוֹלֵךְ (Koheles 2:14), the fool walks in darkness, and as a verb וּבְאַחַת יִבְֽעֲרוּ וְיִכְסָלוּ (Yirmiyahu 10:8), in one thing they are brutish and foolish. The nouns go with it: זֶה דַרְכָּם כֵּסֶל לָמוֹ (Tehillim 49:14), this is their way, their folly, and אֵשֶׁת כְּסִילוּת הֹֽמִיָּה (Mishlei 9:13), the woman of folly is loud.

אִם־שַׂמְתִּי זָהָב כִּסְלִי (Iyov 31:24), if I made gold my trust, אֲשֶׁר־יָקוֹט כִּסְלוֹ (Iyov 8:14), whose trust is cut off, and הֲלֹא יִרְאָֽתְךָ כִּסְלָתֶךָ (Iyov 4:6), is not your fear your trust: their sense is trust and hope.

more.h: Rabbeinu Saadiah on the rich man
more.t: Rabbeinu Saadiah explained טֽוֹב־רָשׁ הוֹלֵךְ בְּתֻמּוֹ מֵֽעִקֵּשׁ שְׂפָתָיו וְהוּא כְסִֽיל (Mishlei 19:1), better a poor man who walks in his integrity than one crooked of lips who is a כסיל, from this sense of trust. Radak explains the reading: the כסיל is one who trusts in his wealth, set against the poor man, as crooked of lips is set against walking in integrity; and so, when the pasuk is repeated in the third part of the book, it says וְהוּא עָשִׁיר (Mishlei 28:6), and he is rich, in place of וְהוּא כְסִיל here.

more.h: Rabbi Yonah and Ibn Ezra on the star
more.t: עָשׁ כְּסִיל וְכִימָה (Iyov 9:9), Ash, Kesil and Kimah: Rabbi Yonah wrote that Kesil is a great star, called in Arabic Suhail, and the stars joined to it are called כְּסִילִים after it, as in כִּֽי־כֽוֹכְבֵי הַשָּׁמַיִם וּכְסִילֵיהֶם (Yeshayahu 13:10), for the stars of heaven and their Kesilim. The Chacham Rabbi Avraham Ibn Ezra explained that they are two stars, one of which is called Kesil, the red one, which kills camels if they see it. Ibn Ezra's account goes on: the sense of וכסיליהם is close in derivation to עַל־ הַכְּסָלִים, on the flanks.

וַיַּעַשׂ פִּימָה עֲלֵי ־כָֽסֶל (Iyov 15:27), and he put fat upon his flank, and אֲשֶׁר עַל־ הַכְּסָלִים (Vayikra 3:4), which is upon the flanks, where a vav is missing: וַאֲשׁר על הכסלים, and which is upon the flanks. The כסלים are beside the kidneys, below the waist, and they are the roots of the thighs; the Targum renders them גִּסְסַיָּא. Chazal (Niddah 48b) speak of the daughters of the poor carrying their brothers on their flanks.

נחשׁ.sense: To divine by omens; the snake; copper, with the fetters named for it and the metal meant where strength is spoken of; and the bottom of a thing.

more.t: נִחַשְׁתִּי (Bereishis 30:27), I have divined; מְעוֹנֵן וּמְנַחֵשׁ (Devarim 18:10), a soothsayer and a diviner; וְהָֽאֲנָשִׁים יְנַֽחֲשׁוּ (Melachim I 20:33), and the men divined. The noun is כִּי לֹא־נַחַשׁ בְּיַֽעֲקֹב (Bamidbar 23:23), for there is no divining in Yaakov, and לִקְרַאת נְחָשִׁים (Bamidbar 24:1), to meet omens.

Chazal (Sanhedrin 68b) set out the forbidden divining: one who says his bread fell from his mouth, his staff fell from his hand, his son calls after him, a raven calls to him, a deer cut across his path, a snake at his right and a fox at his left, do not begin, for it is morning, it is Rosh Chodesh, it is Motzaei Shabbos. They count there too those who divine by weasel, by birds and by stars.

הֲלוֹא יְדַעְתֶּם כִּֽי־נַחֵשׁ יְנַחֵשׁ אִישׁ אֲשֶׁר כָּמֹֽנִי (Bereishis 44:15), did you not know that a man like me surely divines? Divining by it means that he would ask diviners on his behalf. Some explain that he divines by it himself; that is, he would reckon the loss of the goblet an ill omen for himself, since the vessel he drank from was lost to him.

וְהַנָּחָשׁ הָיָה עָרוּם (Bereishis 3:1), and the snake was cunning, is known. נָחָשׁ שָׂרָף (Devarim 8:15), a burning snake, is called so because it burns with the breath of its mouth. נְחָשִׁים צִפְעֹנִים (Yirmiyahu 8:17), snakes, vipers, should properly be snakes and vipers, the vav left out as in שֶׁמֶשׁ יָרֵחַ (Chavakuk 3:11), sun, moon.

more.h: His father on the copper snake
more.t: נְחַשׁ נְחשֶׁת (Bamidbar 21:9), a snake of copper: his father wrote that the physicians say a man bitten by a snake who then sees copper dies at once, and therefore Hashem told Moshe to make a snake of copper, and everyone bitten who looked at it lived, against the nature of the world, to make the miracle greater. So too the cake of figs for Chizkiyahu (Yeshayahu 38:21), and so too the tree Hashem showed Moshe (Shemos 15:25), which the Yalkut in the name of the Mechilta says was a bitter tree.

עַל לִוְיָתָן נָחָשׁ בָּרִחַ (Yeshayahu 27:1), upon Livyasan the barring serpent, and נָחָשׁ עֲקַלָּתוֹן, the twisting serpent, and אֲצַוֶּה אֶת־ הַנָּחָשׁ וּנְשָׁכָֽם (Amos 9:3), I will command the snake and it shall bite them: this is Livyasan, called a snake because it is like one. It is called tannin as well, it and the great fish, as the snakes of the dry land are also called tanninim. The barring serpent and the twisting serpent are a mashal for the kings of the nations. Some explain נָחָשׁ בָּרִחַ as the celestial dragon, called the twisting serpent because it is as though bent, and barring because it bars across from one end to the other.

more.h: Copper, and the metal of strength
more.t: נְחֹשֶׁת קָלָֽל (Yechezkel 1:7), burnished copper, נְחֹשֶׁת מְמֹרָֽט (Melachim I 7:45), polished copper, and וַיִּשְׂאוּ אֶת־כָּל־נְחֻשְׁתָּם בָּבֶֽלָה (Yirmiyahu 52:17), they carried all their copper off to Bavel. אִם־בְּשָׂרִי נָחֽוּשׁ (Iyov 6:12), if my flesh is of steel: his father explains the word as the metal called in the vernacular אצר"ו, acero, which is steel. So too וְאֶֽת־אַרְצְכֶם כַּנְּחֻשָֽׁה (Vayikra 26:19), and your land like steel, and וּמִצְֽחֲךָ נְחוּשָֽׁה (Yeshayahu 48:4), and your forehead steel; and so is every נחשת and נחושה in Scripture that is spoken of for strength.

כֻּלָּם סָרֵי סֽוֹרְרִים הֹֽלְכֵי רָכִיל נְחשֶׁת וּבַרְזֶל (Yirmiyahu 6:28), all of them lords of the rebellious, going about with tales, copper and iron: as copper is mixed with iron so that it cuts well, which is what is called in the vernacular אצרו, steel, so they are mixed with one another in talebearing to do harm; and so Yonasan renders it, walking in guile as copper is mixed with iron. Radak reads סָרֵי as though it were שָֹרֵי, with a sin, lords of the rebellious: the servants are rebellious and evil and carry tales to their masters, like copper with iron, neither of which does the work of cutting without the other.

הִכְבִּיד נְחָשְׁתִּֽי (Eichah 3:7), he made my fetter heavy, וַיַּֽאַסְרֵהוּ בַּֽנְחֻשְׁתַּיִם (Yirmiyahu 39:7), he bound him in fetters, and ורגליך לֹֽא־ לִנְחֻשְׁתַּיִם הֻגָּשׁוּ (Shmuel II 3:34), your feet were not brought into fetters: these are the shackles, named so because they are made of copper, and the Targum renders בַּֽנְחֻשְׁתַּיִם as בְּשַׁלְשְׁלָן דִנְחָשׁ, in chains of copper. יַעַן הִשָּׁפֵךְ נְחֻשְׁתֵּךְ (Yechezkel 16:36), because your lower part was poured out, is a euphemism for nakedness, and the Targum says of it, because you uncovered your shame; so too וְחָרָה נְחֻשְׁתָּהּ (Yechezkel 24:11), and its bottom grows hot, and the Mishnah (Keilim 8:3) speaks of a jar set beneath the נחשת of an oven, that is, its underside.

וַיִּקְרָא־לוֹ נְחֻשְׁתָּֽן (Melachim II 18:4), and he called it Nechushtan: the added letters make the thing small, that is, it was of no use; and so אֲמִינוֹן (Shmuel II 13:20), Aminon, where the addition likewise belittles.

צפע.sense: The צֶפַע and the צִפְעֹנִי, a kind of snake; and in these letters cattle dung, and in that same sense offspring, sons and daughters.

more.t: כִּֽי־מִשֹּׁרֶשׁ נָחָשׁ יֵצֵא צֶפַע (Yeshayahu 14:29), for out of the snake's root a tzefa will come forth; the word is pointed with segol.
נְחָשִׁים צִפְעֹנִים (Yirmiyahu 8:17), snakes, tzifonim: its meaning is נחשים וצפעונים, snakes and tzifonim. Or צפעונים may describe the snakes, the צפעוני being the hard and fierce snake.

צְפִיעֵי הַבָּקָר (Yechezkel 4:15), the tzefi'ei of the cattle, he explains as their dung; and likewise in this sense הַצֶּֽאֱצָאִים וְהַצְּפִעוֹת (Yeshayahu 22:24), the offspring and the tzefi'os, which he explains as the sons and the daughters, as though it said הצאצאים והצאצאות, the male and the female offspring. The Targum renders them sons and sons of sons.

נוס.sense: To flee, and to make another flee; the nouns all mean flight.

more.t: "And he fled outside" (Bereishis 39:13), "and we shall flee before them" (Yehoshua 8:5), "if we indeed flee they will not set their heart upon us" (Shmuel II 18:3), "when they fled from before Israel" (Yehoshua 10:11).

more.h: Ransom and the city of refuge
more.t: "And you shall take no ransom for fleeing to his city of refuge" (Bamidbar 35:32): from one who has cause to flee no ransom is taken in place of fleeing, but he flees to his city of refuge as the law requires; and once he has fled there, no ransom is taken from him to let him come back and settle in the land before the Kohen Gadol dies. The Sifri on parshas Masei reads the pasuk of one who killed deliberately: one might think he could pay money and go into exile, and the pasuk teaches that no ransom is taken for fleeing. Rabbeinu Shlomo took לָנוּס as a describing word, as though לְנָס, one who has fled; that is, as Radak puts it, from the man who has fled to his city of refuge no ransom is taken to let him come back and settle. Radak says Rabbeinu Shlomo explained it well, and adds that לָנוּס is then a describing word on the pattern of סוּג לֵב (Mishlei 14:14), the backslider in heart.

"Nor had his moisture fled" (Devarim 34:7) is borrowed speech, that his moisture had not gone. His father in Sefer HaGaluy read it "his moisture had not dried", from the Arabic used of bread drying out, and Radak says he explained it well, for what sense is there in flight said of moisture?

"And you shall flee to the valley of my mountains" (Zecharyah 14:5) is read on the pattern of "and you shall return", "and you shall arise". Yonasan rendered it as though the valley of the mountains were stopped up, which looks as though he read it as a passive of the root meaning to stop up. Some say it is found so in a few precise books, but Radak says he has not seen it; Ibn Ezra wrote that the people of the East read it that way.

"We will flee on horses" (Yeshayahu 30:16) was taken by Rabbi Yonah in the sense of height and elevation, as in "lifted up high upon His land" (Zecharyah 9:16). Radak holds there is no need to take it from its plain sense, as Rabbi Yehudah also wrote; and though Rabbi Yonah thought to catch him out here, as he did in most places, Rabbi Yehudah was not taken in his pits. Hashem had said they would be saved in their own land "in stillness and quiet" (Yeshayahu 30:15); they refused, and said they would flee to Ashur and Mitzrayim for help, so they will flee as they said, here and there, and not be saved by that flight.

more.h: Making others flee, and the nouns
more.t: The causative is "he made his servants and his cattle flee" (Shemos 9:20), "to make it flee from before Midian" (Shoftim 6:11). The nouns all mean flight: "in flight they fled and did not turn" (Yirmiyahu 46:5), "and flight is lost to them" (Iyov 11:20), "and my flight in the day of trouble" (Yirmiyahu 16:19), "and in flight you shall not go" (Yeshayahu 52:12), "and they shall flee the flight of the sword" (Vayikra 26:36).

ברח.sense: To flee, and to make another flee. In another sense, to pass through from end to end, as the bar, הַבְּרִיחַ, passes through the boards.

more.t: "And David fled and escaped" (Shmuel I 19:18), "for he was fleeing" (Bereishis 31:20), "and Yaakov fled" (Hoshea 12:13), "and they fled into hiding" (Daniel 10:7). The causative drives another away: "they drove out the inhabitants of Gas" (Divrei HaYamim I 8:13), "one who despoils his father and drives off his mother" (Mishlei 19:26), "and I drove him from me" (Nechemyah 13:28), "an arrow will not put him to flight" (Iyov 41:20).

His father held that "Yonah rose to flee to Tarshish" (Yonah 1:3) and "for he was fleeing from before Hashem" (Yonah 1:10) are not flight proper, since flight proper is only from danger to life; he read the fleeing here as hastening the errand. Yonah hastened so that Hashem should not give him a sign and a wonder, which would cause the people of Nineveh to repent, and their repentance would bring destruction on Israel. So too Yonah said "therefore I hastened to flee to Tarshish" (Yonah 4:2).

more.h: The sign given him in the sea
more.t: His father goes on: Hashem, blessed be He, who knew his intent, gave him a sign in the sea, and none is greater: they cast him into the sea, the men of the ship were on their way to Nineveh, and when they saw him there they recognised him. The matter reached the king of Nineveh, and they believed at once, since the men of the ship testified that it was they who had thrown him in.

His father read "from before" as meaning at the command of the one who sends, as in "messengers shall go out from before Me in ships" (Yechezkel 30:9); and David said "where shall I flee from You" (Tehillim 139:7) and not "from before You". So too Radak's father read וְעַתָּה בְּרַח ־לְךָ אֶל־מְקוֹמֶךָ (Bamidbar 24:11), and now flee to your place, as hurry to go. On his father's reading, Radak says, "go out from Bavel, flee from the Kasdim" (Yeshayahu 48:20) and "and the Leviim and the singers fled each to his field" (Nechemyah 13:10) can be taken the same way, as haste.

Another sense is passing through: "to pass through in the midst of the boards" (Shemos 36:33), and in the heavy form "passing through from end to end" (Shemos 26:28). The noun is the bar: the middle bar, and the five bars. עַל לִוְיָתָן נָחָשׁ בָּרִחַ (Yeshayahu 27:1), upon Livyasan the serpent that passes through, is a description in this sense, since it passes through the sea from end to end, and it is a mashal for the powerful kings. Some read וְהֽוֹרַדְתִּי בָֽרִיחִים כֻּלָּם (Yeshayahu 43:14) from this sense too: I will bring them all down bound with an iron bar.

רוץ.sense: To run, with the race and the runner, and to make another run; a separate sense, whose meaning he gives as breaking.

more.t: "The lad ran" (Shmuel I 20:36), "if I run after him" (Melachim II 5:20), "I did not send the prophets, yet they ran" (Yirmiyahu 23:21), "runner runs to meet runner" (Yirmiyahu 51:31), "and Esav ran" (Bereishis 33:4). The nouns: "the race is not to the swift" (Koheles 9:11), כִּמְרֻצַת אֲחִימַעַץ (Shmuel II 18:27), like the running of Achimaatz, and "and their course is evil" (Yirmiyahu 23:10).

"For by You I run at a troop" (Shmuel II 22:30) he explains as running at the troop of his enemies and pursuing them. Rabbi Yonah took it from the sense of breaking, and Radak holds the first sense nearer.

"Fifty men running before him" (Melachim I 1:5). With a nun in place of a mem, הָרָצִין in קוֹל הָרָצִין הָעָם (Melachim II 11:13), the sound of the runners, the people, is like הרצים, as הַיָּמִין in לְקֵץ הַיָּמִין (Daniel 12:13), to the end of the days, is like הימים. The sound of the runners is the sound of rejoicing, for they were rejoicing and saying, long live the king.

The causative: "Kush shall make his hands run to Hashem" (Tehillim 68:32), "in a moment I will make him run from her" (Yirmiyahu 49:19), "and they rushed him from the pit" (Bereishis 41:14), "and run this to the camp for your brothers" (Shmuel I 17:17), "and they brought it quickly to all the people" (Divrei HaYamim II 35:13). The intensive: "like the lightnings they dart" (Nachum 2:5).

"He shall not grow dim nor be broken" (Yeshayahu 42:4), which he explained at the root כָּהָה, and "and the golden bowl is broken" (Koheles 12:6), both of them intransitive. "And she broke his skull" (Shoftim 9:53) has chirik under the resh. The noun is "and upon oppression and upon breaking, to do them" (Yirmiyahu 22:17). Also "and they shattered and broke" (Shoftim 10:8), "and the children broke against one another within her" (Bereishis 25:22), "and the wheel is broken at the pit" (Koheles 12:6), "when they grasped you by the hand you broke" (Yechezkel 29:7). Their sense, he says, is breaking.

"The king pulled down and broke from there" (Melachim II 23:12) is transitive, that is, he overcame them and broke them from there. Yonasan rendered it "and removed from there", and on his view it belongs with "and Esav ran" (Bereishis 33:4), except that this one is transitive and means he made them run from there. It may be that "and the wheel is broken at the pit" (Koheles 12:6) belongs to the first sense, running.

ערק.sense: To flee: הָעֹרְקִים are those fleeing, and the Targum renders fleeing with the word. Also the sinews, as עֹרְקַי, my sinews, and in Arabic the sinews are called by it.

more.t: "Those who flee to the parched land" (Iyov 30:3) are the ones fleeing. The Targum of "and he fled" (Bereishis 39:12) uses this word.

וְעֹֽרְקַי לֹא יִשְׁכָּבֽוּן, and my sinews do not rest: עֹרְקַי is גידי, my sinews. The Targum renders בַּרְזֶל עָשׁוֹת (Yechezkel 27:19), wrought iron, as בְּעַרְקִין דְבַרְזֶל, that is, sinews of iron, as is said elsewhere, וְגִיד בַּרְזֶל עָרְפֶּךָ (Yeshayahu 48:4), and your neck an iron sinew. In Arabic the sinews are called by this word.

גבע.sense: A hill, which is like a mountain but not as high; other senses are the hats set on the head for splendour, and the goblet, like a cup but made differently.

more.t: בְּגֶבַע בִּנְיָמִן (Shmuel I 13:16), in Geva of Binyamin, has a segol. With the feminine hei it is גִּבְעָה, a hill, and in construct גִּבְעַת שָׁאֽוּל (Shmuel I 15:34), the hill of Shaul, and גִּבְעַת הָֽעֲרָלֽוֹת (Yehoshua 5:3), the hill of the foreskins; in the plural הֶֽהָרִים וְהַגְּבָעוֹת (Yeshayahu 55:12), the mountains and the hills. A hill is like a mountain but is not as high as a mountain.
Another sense is וּמִגְבָּעוֹת תַּֽעֲשֶׂה לָהֶם (Shemos 28:40), and hats you shall make for them, the מגבעות being hats set on the head for splendour.

Another sense again: וַיִּמָּצֵא הַגָּבִיעַ (Bereishis 44:12), and the goblet was found; וְאֶת־ גְּבִיעִי גְּבִיעַֽ הַכֶּסֶף (Bereishis 44:2), and my goblet, the silver goblet; הָאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר נִמְצָא הַגָּבִיעַ בְּיָדוֹ (Bereishis 44:17), the man in whose hand the goblet was found; שְׁלֹשָׁה גְבִעִים מְשֻׁקָּדִים (Shemos 25:33), three goblets shaped like almonds; וּבַמְּנֹרָה אַרְבָּעָה גְבִעִים (Shemos 25:34), and in the menorah four goblets. It is like a cup but made on another pattern, and that is what it says, גְּבִעִים מְלֵאִים יַיִן וְכֹסוֹת (Yirmiyahu 35:5), goblets full of wine, and cups.

צנף.sense: To wind round about, as a turban is wound; the מִצְנֶפֶת and the צָנִיף, turban and headwrap, which he says are known.

more.t: "He will surely wind you round with a winding" (Yeshayahu 22:18) means He will overturn you and turn you round about, like the winding of a turban.

"And with a linen turban he shall be wound" (Vayikra 16:4), "remove the turban and lift off the crown" (Yechezkel 21:31), "turban and sash" (Shemos 28:4), "the pure turban" (Zecharyah 3:5), "like a robe and a turban" (Iyov 29:14), and in the feminine plural "and the headwraps and the veils" (Yeshayahu 3:23). He adds nothing further, saying only that the word is known.

כבע.sense: The helmet, the gear that shields the head.

more.t: "And a helmet of salvation on His head" (Yeshayahu 59:17), "and a helmet of copper on his head" (Shmuel I 17:5), "shield and helmet they hung upon you" (Yechezkel 27:10), "all of them with shield and helmet" (Yechezkel 38:5), "and stand forth in helmets" (Yirmiyahu 46:4). It is gear that shields the head, capilo in the vernacular.

In "and a helmet of salvation on His head" (Yeshayahu 59:17) and "and a helmet of copper on his head" (Shmuel I 17:5) the stress is on the earlier syllable; in "shield and helmet they hung upon you" (Yechezkel 27:10) and the rest it falls on the last.

אזר.sense: To gird and to brace; אֵזוֹר is a belt. Of מְאַזְּרֵי זִיקוֹת the authorities differ: kindlers of fire, bringers out of fire, or gatherers of firebrands.

more.t: "They were girded with strength" (Shmuel I 2:4), "and you, gird your loins" (Yirmiyahu 1:17), "girded with a belt at his loins" (Melachim II 1:8). In the heavy form, "I gird you though you did not know Me" (Yeshayahu 45:5), and וַתְּאַזְּרֵנִי חַיִל (Tehillim 18:40), and You girded me with strength, whose proper form is וַתַּֽאַזְּרֵנִי; his father's words on it are at the root זרה, where more of them are written. So "girded with might" (Tehillim 65:7); and of girding oneself, "Hashem is clothed, He has girded Himself with strength" (Tehillim 93:1), "gird yourselves and be shattered" (Yeshayahu 8:9). The sense of all of them is girding and bracing.
The thing one girds with is the ezor: "and He binds a belt on their loins" (Iyov 12:18), "and behold, the belt was ruined" (Yirmiyahu 13:7), "nor the belt of his loins undone" (Yeshayahu 5:27).

Another sense: מְאַזְּרֵי זִיקוֹת (Yeshayahu 50:11), whose meaning is disputed. Rabbi Yonah explained it as קודחי אש, kindlers of fire. Some explain it as bringers out of fire, those who carve in wood and in stone and by the force of their carving bring fire out of them. Radak's father explained it from the first sense, which Radak takes to mean gatherers of firebrands.

רדם.sense: To fall into a heavy sleep; the noun תַּרְדֵּמָה, he says, is the strong sleep.

more.t: נִרְדַּמְתִּי עַל־פָּנַי אָרְצָה (Daniel 8:18), I fell into a deep sleep on my face to the ground; וְהֽוּא־נִרְדַּם וַיָּעַף (Shoftim 4:21), and he had fallen fast asleep and was weary, with a patach, a past verb; נִרְדָּם וְרֶכֶב וָסֽוּס (Tehillim 76:7), chariot and horse lie fast asleep, with a kamatz, a participle; and וַיִּשְׁכַּב וַיֵּֽרָדַֽם (Yonah 1:5), and he lay down and fell fast asleep.
The noun is תַּרְדֵּמָה, as in "and Hashem Elokim cast a tardemah" (Bereishis 2:21); it is the strong sleep.

נום.sense: To slumber; slumber is not strong the way sleep is, but comes only a little at a time.

more.t: "Your shepherds slumber, king of Ashur" (Nachum 3:18); נָמוּ שְׁנָתָם (Tehillim 76:6), they slumbered their sleep, which he explains as נמו בשנתם, they slumbered in their sleep; "behold, He neither slumbers nor sleeps" (Tehillim 121:4).

"And slumber clothes a man in rags" (Mishlei 23:21); with an added tav, "nor slumber to your eyelids" (Mishlei 6:4); in the plural, "a little slumber" (Mishlei 6:10), "in slumberings upon the bed" (Iyov 33:15). Slumber is not strong like sleep but comes a little at a time, and he gives a la'az for it.

פצר.sense: To press a man: all of it is the overriding of a man's will, and compulsion.

more.t: וַיִּפְצַר־בָּם מְאֹד (Bereishis 19:3), and he pressed them greatly; וַיִּפְצַר־בּוֹ לָקַחַת וַיְמָאֵֽן (Melachim II 5:15 in his edition), and he pressed him to take it, and he refused; וַיִּפְצַר־בּוֹ חֹתְנוֹ (Shoftim 19:7), and his father-in-law pressed him; וַיִּפְצְרוּ־בוֹ עַד־בֹּשׁ (Melachim II 2:17), and they pressed him until he was ashamed; and וַיִּפְצְרוּ בָאִישׁ בְּלוֹט (Bereishis 19:9), and they pressed hard upon the man, upon Lot.
The infinitive of the heavier form is in וְאָוֶן וּתְרָפִים הַפְצַר (Shmuel I 15:23), and pressing is iniquity and terafim. All of it is the sense of overriding what a man wills, and compulsion.

דחה.sense: To push and thrust away: pushed hard, a wall pushed over, the wicked thrust down, the outcasts of Yisrael; and the nouns, a stumbling and a ruin.

more.t: "You pushed me hard" (Tehillim 118:13), "who planned to thrust aside my steps" (Tehillim 140:5), "and the angel of Hashem thrusting" (Tehillim 35:5), "a wall pushed over" (Tehillim 62:4).

The passive: "the wicked man is thrust down" (Mishlei 14:32), "they shall be thrust and fall in it" (Yirmiyahu 23:12), which has a pasach and the stress on the earlier syllable, against the usual, and "He gathers the outcasts of Yisrael" (Tehillim 147:2). He allows that the last might be from the roots that drop a nun and would then have wanted a dagesh, but holds the right view to be that it is a passive of this root.

more.h: Thrust down and unable to rise
more.t: In the passive whose doer is not named, "they were thrust down and could not rise" (Tehillim 36:13), which he says he found in the precise books with the stress on the last syllable. Rabbi Yehudah wrote it among the roots whose middle letter is silent.
The nouns are "my foot from stumbling" (Tehillim 116:8) and, on another pattern with an added mem, "and a smooth mouth works ruin" (Mishlei 26:28).

נסע.sense: To set out; to pull a thing out of its place; to make others set out, or to move a thing away; and the noun is the march.

more.t: "For he had set out from Lachish" (Yeshayahu 37:8), "and a wind went forth from Hashem" (Bamidbar 11:31), "and Avram set out" (Bereishis 12:9), "and behold, Mitzrayim setting out after them" (Shemos 14:10), "and they set out from Sukkos" (Bamidbar 33:6), "let us set out and go" (Bereishis 33:12), "and we set out from the river Ahava" (Ezra 8:31), "arise, set out" (Devarim 2:24), "and it was when the aron set out" (Bamidbar 10:35). Some hold that "let us set out and go" is an imperative with an added heh.

The transitive is "and he pulled out the pin of the loom" (Shoftim 16:14) and "and he pulled them up together with the bar" (Shoftim 16:3), though these too can be read as intransitive: the second then means he set out with them, that is with the doors, and the pin the same way. The passive: "my dwelling is pulled up and carried off" (Yeshayahu 38:12), "is not their cord pulled up" (Iyov 4:21).

The causative: "and Moshe made Israel set out" (Shemos 15:22), "and the full one you shall set aside" (Melachim II 4:4), "and they moved great stones" (Melachim I 5:31), "one who moves stones" (Koheles 10:9). "Whole stone moved" (Melachim I 6:7) means that they moved the stones whole from the mountain: they did not build with those they found flawed, but moved them from the mountain.

"And he went on his marches" (Bereishis 13:3), "their goings out by their marches" (Bamidbar 33:2), "these are the marches of Bnei Yisrael" (Bamidbar 33:1). Used as an infinitive: "and for the setting out of the camps" (Bamidbar 10:2), as if to say to set the camps moving, and "arise, go on the march before the people" (Devarim 10:11).

In "the spear, the massa and the coat of mail" (Iyov 41:18), massa is the name of a weapon of war, as the commentators explained it, and the Mesorah says the word occurs twice in two senses. Rabbi Yonah explained it from the sense of moving, like "whole stone moved" (Melachim I 6:7), meaning the spear that is moved in the hand rather than the one girded on like a sword.

חגר.sense: To gird, girding being tying and binding fast; girded for war or in sackcloth; the belt itself; and to move unsteadily, limping as the lame do.

more.t: "And you shall gird them with a sash" (Shemos 29:9). In "the remnant of wrath You shall gird" (Tehillim 76:11) it means You shall gird and bind them so that they do not act on the wrath they had against Yerushalayim, for girding is tying and binding fast.

more.h: The mizmor of the camp of Ashur
more.t: The mizmor was said in prophecy about the camp of Ashur when it camped against Yerushalayim: "God is known in Yehudah" (Tehillim 76:2), "and His covert was in Shalem" (Tehillim 76:3), which is Yerushalayim, since until Yerushalayim God was not known in those wars, for Ashur had conquered all of Eretz Yisrael; when he came to Yerushalayim and spoke haughtily against Hashem, God was known and His name great, as in "and he struck in the camp of Ashur" (Melachim II 19:35). When You take vengeance on the camp of Ashur, then "the wrath of man shall praise You" (Tehillim 76:11): the one whose wrath was against You and who raged against You will praise You against his will, and his wrath will turn to thanks. Then "the remnant of wrath You shall gird": the kings of the nations who are left, who had wrath against Yerushalayim, will have their wrath girded and bound, for they will fear You from what they hear You did in the camp of Ashur. That is what the end of the mizmor says, "He cuts off the spirit of princes, awesome to the kings of the earth" (Tehillim 76:13): when He cuts off and plucks the spirit of princes, as with "every mighty man of valour and leader and officer in the camp of the king of Ashur" (Divrei HaYamim II 32:21), then He will be awesome to the kings of the earth.

more.h: Or the wrath of Mitzrayim and Kush
more.t: Or "the wrath of man shall praise You" (Tehillim 76:11) may be said of the Mitzrim and the men of Kush who were with Ashur in the camp and who, when they saw that great blow, turned to the faith of the Jews. Of them it is said "the labour of Mitzrayim and the merchandise of Kush" (Yeshayahu 45:14), and of them "an altar to Hashem in the midst of the land of Mitzrayim" (Yeshayahu 19:19) with the whole parsha.

more.h: Girded for war, girded in sack
more.t: "Your loins girded" (Shemos 12:11), "girded with weapons of war" (Shoftim 18:11), "gird your sword on your thigh, mighty one" (Tehillim 45:4), "wail like a maiden girded in sackcloth" (Yoel 1:8), "and they shall gird on sackcloth" (Yechezkel 7:18).

The adjective is "girded with a belt on their loins" (Yechezkel 23:15), with a cholam. The noun: "she gave a girdle to the merchant" (Mishlei 31:24); with the feminine heh, "and in place of a girdle, a rope" (Yeshayahu 3:24) and "in his girdle that was on his loins" (Melachim I 2:5); the plural, "and they made themselves girdles" (Bereishis 3:7); and on another pattern "a girding of sackcloth" (Yeshayahu 3:24). The sense of all of these is a belt.

"And they shall totter out of their fetters" (Shmuel II 22:46): יתנועעו מכבליהם, they will move from the fetters they are in, that is, they will limp from the weight of their fetters. In the words of Chazal, "they sat on a plank or on a bench when these are מחגירין" (Zavim 3:3), which Radak explains as when they move, for when its legs are uneven, one shorter than another, a man sitting on it moves and sways this way and that like a lame man. Some read the word as a transposition, from the Targum of "and from the chambers, terror" (Devarim 32:25), וּמִתְוָנַיָא חַרְגַת מוֹתָא, and from the rooms the trembling of death, whose חַרְגַת carries the letters of חגר turned about; its sense is then that they shall be afraid from within their strongholds, and so Yonasan rendered it, that they shall tremble from their fortresses.

לון.sense: To lodge for the night; some hold it is said also of constant persistence. A second sense, to complain, holding a grievance, mostly takes a dagesh to keep the two apart.

more.t: "And he lodged that night" (Bereishis 32:22), "and we shall lodge in Givah" (Shoftim 19:13), where the root's nun is swallowed into the dagesh of the plural nun. As an adjective, "why do you lodge over against the wall" (Nechemyah 13:21) and "and it shall lodge in the midst of his house" (Zecharyah 5:4), where a segol stands in place of a kamatz. Further: "and Yehoshua lodged" (Yehoshua 8:9), "and he lodged there that night" (Bereishis 32:14), "and they lodged there" (Shoftim 18:4), "for we shall lodge in the street" (Bereishis 19:2), "only do not lodge in the street" (Shoftim 19:20).

more.h: Lodging as persistence, as some hold
more.t: In the holy tongue, some hold, the word for lodging comes in the sense of persistence: "strength lodges in his neck" (Iyov 41:14), "he shall lodge satisfied, not visited by evil" (Mishlei 19:23), "how long shall it lodge within you" (Yirmiyahu 4:14), and so "and it shall lodge in the midst of his house" (Zecharyah 5:4), and those like them. Their sense is not the night's lodging alone but constant persistence.

וּבְהַמְּרוֹתָם תָּלַן עֵינִֽי (Iyov 17:2), and on their provocations my eye lodges, means that he did not sleep because his companions defied his words and condemned him. Some read it from persistence on a matter, taking "my eye" as his attention: he thinks and dwells on their provocation always. On that reading, since the night's lodging is a ceasing from all business and an applying of oneself to sleep and rest, Iyov said that he was awake at night and his persistence was on their provocations.

more.h: What does not lodge with a man
more.t: "And man, with what is precious to him, does not lodge" (Tehillim 49:13) means that the precious thing a man has, his money, does not lodge with him at his death, but he leaves it behind; and so at the close of the mizmor, "man with what is precious to him, who does not understand" (Tehillim 49:21), that he does not understand while he is still alive with his money. Rabbi Yehudah HaLevi read it that there is with a man something precious that will not lodge, meaning that it will not lie down and die, and that is the soul; and a man who has not learned and does not understand is therefore like the beasts; and on this reading נַפְשׁוֹ בְּטוֹב תָּלִין, his soul shall lodge in goodness, means that when he dies his soul will rest in goodness.

more.h: Causing to lodge, and the lodging place
more.t: The transitive: "they make the naked lodge without clothing" (Iyov 24:7), and מָקוֹם לָנוּ לָלִֽין (Bereishis 24:23), a place to lodge us, where לָלִֽין is as though it were לְהָלִין, to give lodging. The reflexive: "he shall lodge in the shadow of Shakai" (Tehillim 91:1). The nouns: "to the lodging place" (Bereishis 43:21), "a wayfarers' lodge" (Yirmiyahu 9:1), and with the feminine heh and a shuruk, "like a hut in a cucumber field" (Yeshayahu 1:8), "and it shall sway like a hut" (Yeshayahu 24:20). That is the watchman's booth, which he lodges in at night, and it is called מלונה because it is not for dwelling in but only for lodging in at night.

"That you have complained against Me" (Bamidbar 14:29), "and the people complained against Moshe" (Shemos 17:3); and with a dagesh in place of the quiescent letter, "and they made the whole congregation complain against him" (Bamidbar 14:36), which is causative upon a third party, "that you complain against Him" (Shemos 16:8), "that you complain against us" (Shemos 16:7). Most of this sense comes with a dagesh, to keep it apart from the other. The noun is "I have heard the complaints" (Shemos 16:12), where the dagesh stands in place of the quiescent letter, for it should have been תְּלוּנוֹת, on the pattern of תְּבוּנוֹת, understandings, and תְּשׁוּבוֹת, answers. In yet another form, "and they complained against Moshe and against Aharon" (Bamidbar 14:2). A telunah is a grievance.

שֹושֹ.sense: To rejoice, of Hashem over His people and of a man over Hashem's word and mitzvos; מָשׂוֹשׂ, joy. Chazal read יָשִׂישׂ as making others rejoice.

more.t: כַּֽאֲשֶׁר־ שָׂשׂ י"י עֲלֵיכֶם, as Hashem rejoiced over you; שָׂשׂ אָנֹכִי עַל־אִמְרָתֶךָ (Tehillim 119:162), I rejoice over Your word; פָּגַעְתָּ אֶת־ שָׂשׂ וְעֹשֵׂה צֶדֶק (Yeshayahu 64:4), You met him who rejoices and does righteousness, which means one who rejoices in Your mitzvos; וְשַׂשְׂתִּי בְעַמִּי (Yeshayahu 65:19), and I will rejoice in My people; לָשׂוּשׂ עָלֶיךָ לְטוֹב (Devarim 30:9), to rejoice over you for good.
