יְשֻׂשׂוּם מִדְבָּר (Yeshayahu 35:1), the wilderness shall rejoice in them, means ישושו בם או עמהם, they shall rejoice in them or with them; so too בִּשְּׁלָם הַבָּשָׂר (Melachim I 19:21), he cooked them the meat, is as though it said בשל להם, he cooked for them. Some explain the mem as standing in place of a nun, so that יְשֻׂשׂוּם would be like יְשֻׂשׂוּן, they shall rejoice.

The heavy forms, יָשִׂישׂוּ וְיִשְׂמְחוּ בְּךָ (Tehillim 40:17), let them rejoice and be glad in You, שִׂישׂוּ אִתָּהּ (Yeshayahu 66:10), rejoice with her, and כֵּן יָשִׂישׂ י"י עֲלֵיכֶם, so will Hashem rejoice over you, are all intransitive. Chazal (Megillah 10b) hold the heavy form transitive, for they said of יָשִׂישׂ י"י עֲלֵיכֶם that He does not rejoice but makes others rejoice, and that the wording bears it out, since it is written יָשִֹישֹ and not יָשֹוּשֹ.

more.h: Masos, the joy of a way
more.t: The noun: מָשׂוֹשׂ לְכָל־הָאָֽרֶץ (Eichah 2:15), a joy to all the earth; and הֶן־הוּא מְשׂוֹשׂ דַּרְכּוֹ (Iyov 8:19), behold, this is the joy of his way, which means: this is the joy of one who rejoiced in his way and in his evil deeds; this is his end, for he perished quickly.

גיל.sense: Likeness: מִן־הַֽיְלָדִים אֲשֶׁר כְּגִֽילְכֶם (Daniel 1:10), than the youths who are like you, is כדמותכם, in your likeness.

more.t: So too Chazal say (Megillah 11a) אחיו של ראש ובן גילו של ראש, the brother of the head and the ben gilo of the head; that is, Radak explains, one who resembles him.

רנן.sense: Crying out aloud, whether in song and gladness, in proclaiming, in prayer, or in weeping and groaning, each according to its place.

more.t: All of it is crying out aloud: some for song and gladness, some for proclaiming, some for prayer, and some for weeping and groaning, as וְכַשְׂדִּים בָּֽאֳנִיּוֹת רִנָּתָֽם (Yeshayahu 43:14), and the Kasdim, whose cry is in the ships; each one according to its place.

פצחי רנה (Yeshayahu 54:1), break out in song; ויעבר הרנה במחנה (Melachim I 22:36), the cry passed through the camp; הקשיבה רנתי (Tehillim 17:1), hear my cry. The fuller form: באו לפניו ברננה (Tehillim 100:2), come before Him with song.

more.h: Ibn Ezra on the morning stars
more.t: ברן יחד כוכבי בקר (Iyov 38:7), when the morning stars sang together: Rabbi Avraham ibn Ezra writes that the morning stars are the seven attendants, called also stars of light, and the bnei Elokim are the upper arrays, whose motion is their song and their shout.

He explains הַרְנִינוּ לֵאלֹהִים עוּזֵּנוּ (Tehillim 81:2) as say a song to Elokim our strength, and הַרְנִינוּ גוֹיִם עַמּוֹ (Devarim 32:43) as you nations who are His people, sing, for He avenges the blood of His servants. Some take הַרְנִינוּ as proclaim, like חָכְמוֹת בַּחוּץ תָּרֹנָּה (Mishlei 1:20), wisdom proclaims outside, and so רני בלילה, proclaim in the night, and ויעבר הרנה, the proclamation passed; the sense then is that wherever the people of Hashem are, proclaim concerning them that He avenges the blood of His servants.

כְּגִבּוֹר מִתְרוֹנֵן מִיָּֽיִן (Tehillim 78:65) is like a man sunk in sleep from the wine he drank, who now wakes from it and cries out and shouts. The pasuk says like a warrior because nothing but the wine took his strength from him. So Hakadosh Baruch Hu was as one asleep or sunk in sleep from wine, seeing Israel's sins and keeping silent toward them; and when their sins grew heavy upon them and they angered Him with their evil deeds, He took vengeance on them. The pasuk says this of the destruction of the Mishkan at Shiloh.

כנף רננים (Iyov 39:13), the wing of the renanim, is the name of a bird called so, perhaps because it sings and is fine of voice, or because it sings and, as the text is printed, hides itself in its wings, which are beautiful like the peacock's.

דוץ.sense: Gladness and joy: וּלְפָנָיו תָּדוּץ דְּאָבָֽה (Iyov 41:14), and before him sorrow rejoices.

more.t: It is like the Targum of שִׂישׂוּ אִתָּהּ מָשׂוֹשׂ (Yeshayahu 66:10), rejoice with her a rejoicing, which renders it דוּצוּ עִמָהּ דַיִץ, rejoice with her a rejoicing.

חדה.sense: To rejoice: וַיִּחַדְּ יִתְרוֹ (Shemos 18:9), Yisro rejoiced; with the noun חֶדְוָה, gladness, and תְּחַדֵּהוּ, You gladden him. Their sense, he says, is joy.

more.t: וַיִּחַדְּ יִתְרוֹ (Shemos 18:9) is on the pattern of וַיִּֽחַן ־שָׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל (Shemos 19:2), and Yisrael camped there. Its regular form would be וַיַּֽחֲדֶּה, and the dagesh in the dalet is to steady the reading, because the stress falls back off the last syllable.

The noun: עֹז וְחֶדְוָה בִּמְקֹמֽוֹ (Divrei Hayamim I 16:27), strength and gladness are in His place, and כִּֽי־ חֶדְוַת י"י הִיא מָֽעֻזְּכֶֽם (Nechemiah 8:10), for the gladness of Hashem is your strength. The causative: תְּחַדֵּהוּ בְשִׂמְחָה (Tehillim 21:7), You gladden him with joy. Their sense is joy.

He allows that אַל־ יִחַדְּ בִּימֵי שָׁנָה (Iyov 3:6), let it not rejoice among the days of the year, may be of this root and this sense. בַּרְזֶל בְּבַרְזֶל יָחַד וְאִישׁ יַחַד פְּנֵֽי־רֵעֵֽהוּ (Mishlei 27:17), iron sharpens iron and a man sharpens the face of his fellow, is of this root too, but belongs to the sense he set out already at the root חדד.

חדק.sense: A thorn, one of the kinds of thorns: כִּמְשֻׂכַת חָדֶק (Mishlei 15:19), like a hedge of chedek.

more.h: The best of them a thorn
more.t: טוֹבָם כְּחֵדֶק (Michah 7:4), their best is like a chedek: the pasuk says that the good one among them is like a chedek. The chedek is a thorn, one of the kinds of thorns.

שׁאה.sense: To lie desolate, and in some forms to be astonished. A second sense is tumult, the roar of peoples or of rushing water.

more.t: עַד אֲשֶׁר אִם־שָׁאוּ עָרִים (Yeshayahu 6:11), until cities lie waste, and תִּשָּׁאֶה שְׁמָמָה (Yeshayahu 6:11), it be left a desolation. The noun is in וּשְׁאִיָּה יֻכַּת־שָׁעַר (Yeshayahu 24:12), meaning and in desolation the gate is smitten. The heavy form: לְהַשְׁאוֹת גַּלִּים נִצִּים (Yeshayahu 37:26), to lay waste into ruined heaps; in its place in Melachim it is לַהְשׁוֹת (Melachim II 19:25), and it is treated at the root נָשָא. Their sense is desolation.

Some of them are in the sense of astonishment, as וְהָאִישׁ מִשְׁתָּאֵה לָהּ (Bereishis 24:21), and the man was astonished at her, just as the language of desolation gives משתומם, one who is dumbfounded.

Another sense: וּשְׁאוֹן לְאֻמִּים כִּשְׁאוֹן מַיִם כַּבִּירִים יִשָּׁאוּן (Yeshayahu 17:12), and the roar of peoples, like the roar of mighty waters they roar, and וְיָרַד הֲדָרָהּ וַהֲמוֹנָהּ וּשְׁאוֹנָהּ (Yeshayahu 5:14), and her splendour and her multitude and her tumult go down: the sense is tumult. וְעָלִיתָ כַּשֹּׁאָה (Yechezkel 38:9), and you will come up like a roaring flood: that is, a rush of water that comes with force and has the sound of a roar.

Rabbi Yonah wrote that וְשַׁאֲנַנְךָ עָלָה בְאָזְנָי (Yeshayahu 37:29), and your uproar has come up into My ears, is of this sense, the proper form being ושאונך, your roaring, with the nun doubled to intensify the uproar. The same is found in the Mesorah: every שאנן is the language of quiet except this one and its fellow, which are the language of קוֹל שָׁאוֹן מֵעִיר (Yeshayahu 66:6), a sound of uproar from the city.

more.h: Ibn Ezra and Radak's father: quiet
more.t: Rabbi Avraham ibn Ezra explains it as it sounds, the language of quiet, joined to התרגזך אלי, your raging against Me, the pasuk being elliptical: יַעַן הִתְרַגֶּזְךָ אֵלַי, because of your raging against Me, and the raging of your ease has come up into My ears; that is, you rage against Me because of the quiet and the rest you have. Radak's father explains it the same way.

ברק.sense: Lightning; a yellow gem, named for its lightning-like gleam; great brightness, and a spear's blade, which looks like lightning; and the barkanim, a kind of thorn.

more.t: בְּרוֹק בָּרָק וּתְפִיצֵם (Tehillim 144:6), flash lightning and scatter them; הַֽתְשַׁלַּח בְּרָקִים וְיֵלֵכוּ (Iyov 38:35), will you send out lightnings and they go. It is a thing known.

אֹדֶם פִּטְדָה וּבָרֶקֶת (Shemos 28:17), odem, pitdah and bareketh, and וּבָֽרְקַת וְזָהָב (Yechezkel 28:13), and bareketh and gold: a precious stone, yellow like gold, called so because it gleams like the lightning.

לְמַעַן־הֱיֵה־לָהּ בָּרָק (Yechezkel 21:15), so that it may have lightning, that is, great brightness like the look of lightning; וּבָרָק מִמְּרֹֽרָתוֹ יַֽהֲלֹךְ (Iyov 20:25), and the blade goes out from his gall, the בָּרָק being the blade of the spear, which looks like lightning; and likewise בְּרַק חֲנִיתֶֽךָ (Chavakuk 3:11), the blade of your spear, and וּבְרַק חֲנִית (Nachum 3:3), and the blade of a spear.
Rabbi Yonah explains וּבָרָק מִמְּרֹֽרָתוֹ of the red bile, which in his reading is the gall bladder.
וְאֶת־הַבַּרְקֳנִֽים (Shoftim 8:7), and the barkanim: one of the kinds of thorns.

חרל.sense: חָרוּל, a plant that some take for an herb resembling thorns and others for the thorn whose flower is used to curdle cheese.

more.t: תחת חרול יספחו (Iyov 30:7), under the charul they huddle together; ממשק חרול (Tzefaniah 2:9), a patch of charul; כסו פניו חרלים (Mishlei 24:31), its face was covered with charulim.
Some explain it as a plant resembling thorns, ortigas in the vernacular; others as the thorn with whose flower they curdle the cheese, cardon in the vernacular.

קמשׁ.sense: One of the kinds of thorns; in the vernacular, he says, ortiga.

more.t: קִמּוֹשׂ וָחוֹחַ (Yeshayahu 34:13), kimosh and briar; וְהִנֵּה עָלָה כֻלּוֹ קִמְּשֹׁנִים (Mishlei 24:31), and behold, it had all grown over with kimshonim.

שֹוך.sense: To hedge about, as a way with thorns; משוכה, a fence, called so because fences are made of thorns; שִׂכִּים, thorns; and in another sense, a bough.

more.t: הִֽנְנִי־ שָׂךְ אֶת־דַּרְכֵּךְ בַּסִּירִים (Hoshea 2:8), here I am hedging your way with thorns; שַׂכְתָּ בַֽעֲדוֹ (Iyov 1:10), You have hedged about him.

The noun from it is יָשָׁר מִמְּסוּכָה (Michah 7:4), straighter than a hedge, although it is written with a samech; and so כָּל־אֶבֶן יְקָרָה מְסֻכָתֶךָ (Yechezkel 28:13), every precious stone was your fence, as he glosses it, is written with a samech too. כִּמְשֻׂכַת חָדֶק (Mishlei 15:19), like a hedge of thorns, is with a sin. Because they make the fences of vineyards and gardens of thorns and briers, the fence is called משוכה.
הָסֵר מְשׂוּכָּתוֹ (Yeshayahu 5:5), remove its hedge, where the quiescent letter is swallowed in a dagesh; and some dispute it and read מְשׂוּכָּתוֹ soft.

more.h: Sikim, and his father on sakin
more.t: Another form is לְשִׂכִּים בְּעֵינֵיכֶם (Bamidbar 33:55), as thorns in your eyes. His father explains וְשַׂמְתָּ שַׂכִּין בְּלֹעֶךָ (Mishlei 23:2), and you shall put שַׂכִּין in your throat, from this root, as שִׂכִּים, thorns, the patach standing in place of a chirik, as in many words, and the nun and the mem being alike, as in חיים and חיין, both life, and יָמִים and יָמִין, both days. Another form is הַֽתְמַלֵּא בְשֻׂכּוֹת עוֹרוֹ (Iyov 40:31), can you fill his hide with barbs, where the dagesh stands in place of the quiescent letter; and their sense is known.
Another sense: אִישׁ שׂוֹכֹה (Shoftim 9:49), each man his bough, and שׂוֹכַת עֵצִים (Shoftim 9:48), a bough of trees: their sense is a branch.

קרע.sense: To tear or rend, garments or a kingdom; the sense of all of them is splitting and cutting, and in some pesukim, opening.

more.t: קָרַע י"י אֶת־מַמְלְכוּת יִשְׂרָאֵל (Shmuel I 15:28), Hashem has torn the kingdom of Yisrael away, and וְקָרַע אֹתוֹ מִן־הַבֶּגֶד (Vayikra 13:56), he shall tear it out of the garment; ויקרע את בגדיו (Bereishis 37:29), he rent his garments; קרעו בגדיהם (Bamidbar 14:6), they rent their garments; קרוע כתנתו (Shmuel II 15:32), his coat rent, which comes with a kamatz in the construct like לבש הבדים (Yechezkel 9:11), clothed in linen; קרועי בגדים (Yeshayahu 36:22), with garments rent, after the manner of נֹבֶלֶת עָלֶהָ (Yeshayahu 1:30), whose leaf withers, and the like of these are treated at the root נבל; יקרעה בתער הספר (Yirmiyahu 36:23), he would cut it with the scribe's knife.

more.h: The sense of all of them
more.t: In the passive, והמזבח נקרע (Melachim I 13:5), and the altar was rent, and לא יקרע (Shemos 28:32), that it not be torn: the sense of all of them is splitting and cutting.

קרעו ולא דמו (Tehillim 35:15), they tore and did not keep still, is of this sense: as though they tore my flesh by how they kept on speaking against me. So too כי תקרעי בפוך עיניך (Yirmiyahu 4:30), that you tear your eyes with paint, as though she tears her eyes by how she keeps on painting them. Or קרעו ולא דמו may fall on the cutting of the tongue in words, or on the wide opening of the mouth in laughter; and Radak says that is the correct reading.

וקרע לו חלוני (Yirmiyahu 22:14), and he cuts out windows for himself: Yonasan renders it ופצים ליה חרכין, that is, as Radak explains, he opened openings for himself. So too לוא קרעת שמים (Yeshayahu 63:19), if only You would tear open the heavens: a sense of opening.

חתך.sense: Decreed: נֶחְתַּךְ עַל־עַמְּךָ וְעַל־עִיר קָדְשֶׁךָ (Daniel 9:24), it is decreed upon your people and upon your holy city, which he explains as נגזר, decreed.

more.t: Chazal made frequent use of this word, as in their saying (Zevachim 92b) חתיכה של בשר, a piece of meat, and במקום חתך, at the place of the cut, and many more besides these.

בתר.sense: Dividing into parts, and the part itself; his sense for it is חלק: the bird he did not divide, and the parts they passed between.

more.t: וְאֶת־הַצִּפֹּר לֹא בָתָֽר (Bereishis 15:10), and the bird he did not divide; וַיְבַתֵּר אֹתָם בַּתָּוֶךְ (Bereishis 15:10), and he divided them in the middle. The noun: עַל־הָרֵי בָֽתֶר (Shir HaShirim 2:17), upon the mountains of division, and וַיִּתֵּן אִישׁ־בִּתְרוֹ (Bereishis 15:10), and he set each one's part; and the plural, וַיַּֽעַבְרוּ בֵּין בְּתָרָֽיו (Yirmiyahu 34:18), and they passed between its parts. The sense is חלק, a part.

אטד.sense: A kind of thorn, cardon in the vernacular: גֹּרֶן הָאָטָד (Bereishis 50:10), the threshing floor of the atad.

more.t: קוץ ודרדר, thorn and thistle, Onkelos renders כובין ואטדין; the atad is one of the kinds of thorns, cardon in the vernacular.

נתח.sense: Cutting into נְתָחִים, which are limbs: וְנִתַּח אֹתוֹ לִנְתָחָיו (Vayikra 1:12), and he shall cut it into its limbs.

more.t: וַֽיְנַתְּחֶהָ לַעֲצָמֶיהָ לִשְׁנֵים עָשָׂר נְתָחִים (Shoftim 19:29), and he cut her up by her bones into twelve limbs; תְּנַתֵּחַ לִנְתָחָיו (Shemos 29:17), you shall cut it into its limbs; אֱסֹף נְתָחֶיהָ אֵלֶיהָ (Yechezkel 24:4), gather its limbs into it.
כָּל־ נֵתַח טוֹב (Yechezkel 24:4), every good limb, has the nun with a segol, and there are books that have it with a tzere.

פלח.sense: Splitting. The noun פֶּלַח is used of the lower millstone, a piece of the upper one, a piece of pressed figs, and a split piece of pomegranate.

more.t: פֹלֵחַ וּבֹקֵעַ (Tehillim 141:7), splitting and cleaving; וַיְפַלַּח אֶל־סִיר הַנָּזִיד (Melachim II 4:39), and he split them into the pot of stew; יְפַלַּח כִּלְיוֹתַי (Iyov 16:13), he splits my kidneys. Their sense is splitting.

כְּפֶלַח תַּחְתִּֽית (Iyov 41:16), like the lower millstone, is the lower of the pair, since the two millstones look as though one had been split off from its fellow; פֶּלַח רֶכֶב (Shoftim 9:53) is a piece of the upper millstone, the one called רֶכֶב (Devarim 24:6).
פֶלַח דְּבֵלָה (Shmuel I 30:12) is a piece of pressed figs, and כְּפֶלַח הָֽרִמּוֹן (Shir HaShirim 4:3), like a split piece of the pomegranate.

קטב.sense: A sense of cutting off: קֶטֶב is the sickness that comes upon a man suddenly and kills him.

more.t: וְקֶטֶב מְרִירִי (Devarim 32:24), and bitter deadly sickness, and מִקֶּטֶב יָשׁוּד צָהֳרָֽיִם (Tehillim 91:6), from the deadly sickness that ravages at noon; on another pattern, אֱהִי קָֽטָבְךָ שְׁאוֹל (Hoshea 13:14), I will be your deadly sickness, O grave.
This too carries the sense of cutting off, and what is meant by it is the illness that falls on a man of a sudden and kills him.
The Targum Yerushalmi renders לַחְטֹב עֵצִים (Devarim 19:5), to hew wood, as לְמִקְטוֹעַ קֵיסִין, to cut logs.

פרם.sense: Tearing; and since Chazal set נקרעו, torn, beside נפרמו, come apart, it appears there is a difference: tearing is in the body of the garment, coming apart at the seam.

more.t: וּבְגָדָיו לֹא יִפְרֹֽם (Vayikra 21:10), he shall not tear his garments; וּבִגְדֵיכֶם לֹֽא־ תִפְרֹמוּ וְלֹא תָמֻתוּ (Vayikra 10:6), do not tear your garments and you will not die; בְּגָדָיו יִהְיוּ פְרֻמִים (Vayikra 13:45), his garments shall be torn. The sense is tearing.

more.h: Tearing and parting at the seam
more.t: Chazal say (Sotah 1:5) ואוחז בבגדיה אם נקרעו נקרעו ואם נפרמו נפרמו, he takes hold of her garments, if they tear they tear and if they come apart they come apart. Since they said so, it appears to Radak that there is a difference between קריעה, tearing, and פרימה: קריעה is in the body of the garment, away from the seam, and פרימה is at the seam.

גדע.sense: Cutting off, which is his sense for every form of it: of an arm, of horns, of sycamores and asheiros, and of the tall of stature.

more.t: גָּדַע בָּֽחֳרִי־אַף (Eichah 2:3), he cut off in fierce anger; וְגָֽדַעְתִּי אֶת־זְרֹֽעֲךָ (Shmuel I 2:31), I will cut off your arm; וְרָמֵי הַקּוֹמָה גְּדוּעִים (Yeshayahu 10:33), the tall of stature are hewn down.

נִגְדַּעְתָּ לָאָרֶץ (Yeshayahu 14:12), you were cut down to the ground; נִגְדְּעָה קֶרֶן מוֹאָב (Yirmiyahu 48:25), the horn of Moav is cut off; שִׁקְמִים גֻּדָּעוּ (Yeshayahu 9:9), sycamores were cut down.

וַֽאֲשֵֽׁירֵהֶם תְּגַדֵּעוּן (Devarim 7:5), you shall cut down their asheiros; וְכָל־קַרְנֵי רְשָׁעִים אֲגַדֵּעַ (Tehillim 75:11), all the horns of the wicked I will cut off. His sense for every one of these forms is cutting off.

קצץ.sense: To cut and sever; and of this root and sense, קֵץ, the end of a span of time, as though it were cut there, or at times its start.

more.t: וְקַצֹּתָה אֶת־כַּפָּהּ (Devarim 25:12), you shall cut off her hand; קִצֵּץ עֲבוֹת רְשָׁעִים (Tehillim 129:4), He cut the cords of the wicked; וְקִצֵּץ פְּתִילִם (Shemos 39:3), and he cut it into threads; בְּהֹנוֹת יְדֵיהֶם וְרַגְלֵיהֶם מְקֻצָּצִים (Shoftim 1:7), the thumbs of their hands and the big toes of their feet cut off; וַיְקַצְּצוּ אֶת־יְדֵיהֶם וְאֶת־רַגְלֵיהֶם (Shmuel II 4:12), they cut off their hands and their feet. It is the sense of cutting and severing.

more.h: The end, as a place of cutting
more.t: From this root and this sense come בָּא הַקֵּץ (Yechezkel 7:6), the end has come, and קֵץ כָּל־בָּשָׂר (Bereishis 6:13), the end of all flesh: the close of a stretch of time, as though it were a place of cutting.

more.h: Or the start of a stretch
more.t: מִקֵּץ שֶׁבַע־שָׁנִים תַּעֲשֶׂה שְׁמִטָּה (Devarim 15:1), at the end of seven years you shall make a release: though it is an end for the release of monies, it is a beginning for the release of land and the sending out of servants. So too מִקֵּץ שֶׁבַע שָׁנִים תְּשַׁלְּחוּ (Yirmiyahu 34:14), at the end of seven years you shall send out, is the start of the seventh year, for both head and end are called קצה.

וְעַל כָּל־קְצוּצֵי פֵאָה (Yirmiyahu 9:25), and upon all who are clipped at the corner, is of cutting; and it may be of the sense of the end, meaning those who dwell at the end of the settled world, at its edge.

more.h: A nun in place of a doubled letter
more.t: עַד־אָנָה תְּשִׂימוּן קִנְצֵי לְמִלִּין (Iyov 18:2), how long will you set ends to words, has a nun standing in for the doubling. Some of the grammarians read כִּי לֹא־תָמְנוּ (Eichah 3:22), for we are not consumed, the same way, as though it were תממו. Or it may be that קִנְצֵי and קֵץ have the root קָנַץ, and it is for the missing nun that קֵץ takes a dagesh when joined to a suffix: קִצּוֹ, its end, קִצִּי, my end.

כעס.sense: To be angry and to anger another, with the noun for anger; all of it, he says, is wrath and fierce anger.

more.t: רָשָׁע יִרְאֶה וְכָעָס (Tehillim 112:10), the wicked man will see and be angry; וְכָעַס הַרְבֵּה וְחָלְיוֹ וָקָֽצֶף (Koheles 5:16), and he is much angered, and his sickness, and wrath; וַיִּכְעַס אָסָא אֶל־הָרֹאֶה (Divrei HaYamim II 16:10), Asa was angry with the seer.

וְכִֽעֲסַתָּה צָֽרָתָהּ (Shmuel I 1:6), her rival provoked her to anger; כִּֽעֲסוּנִי בְּהַבְלֵיהֶם (Devarim 32:21), they provoked Me with their empty things; בְּגוֹי נָבָל אַכְעִיסֵֽם (Devarim 32:21), with a vile nation I will provoke them; כֵּן תַּכְעִסֶנָּה (Shmuel I 1:7), so she would provoke her; לְהַכְעִיסוֹ בְּמַֽעֲשֵׂה יְדֵיכֶֽם (Devarim 31:29), to provoke Him with the work of your hands; וְהִכְעַסְתִּי לֵב עַמִּים רַבִּים (Yechezkel 32:9), I will anger the heart of many peoples.

גַּם־ כַּעַס (Shmuel I 1:6), anger too; כַּעַס לְאָבִיו בֵּן כְּסִיל (Mishlei 17:25), a foolish son is anger to his father; כִּי מֵרֹב שִׂיחִי וְכַעְסִי (Shmuel I 1:16), for out of the abundance of my complaint and my anger; and in the plural עַל כָּל־ הַכְּעָסִים אֲשֶׁר הִכְעִיסוֹ מְנַשֶּֽׁה (Melachim II 23:26), for all the provocations with which Menashe provoked Him.

Some of them are written with a sin: כִּי לֶאֱוִיל יַֽהֲרָג־ כָּעַשׂ (Iyov 5:2), for anger kills the fool; וַתֵּכַהּ מִכַּעַשׂ עֵינִי (Iyov 17:7), my eye is dim from anger; וְתֶרֶב כַּֽעַשְׂךָ עִמָּדִי (Iyov 10:17), You increase Your anger against me; לוּ שָׁקוֹל יִשָּׁקֵל כַּעְשִׂי (Iyov 6:2), if only my anger were weighed.

more.h: Rabbi Yonah on the sin spelling
more.t: Rabbi Yonah wrote that these two, לוּ שָׁקוֹל יִשָּׁקֵל כַּעְשִׂי (Iyov 6:2) and כִּי מֵרֹב שִׂיחִי וְכַעְסִי (Shmuel I 1:16), are a root of their own, spelled with a sin, in the sense of pain. Radak holds there is no need for this, since when a man worries and is in pain he grows angry within himself; and besides, כִּי מֵרֹב שִׂיחִי וְכַעְסִי is written with a samech in all the accurate books he has seen.

כִּי הִכְעִיסוּ לְנֶגֶד הַבּוֹנִֽים (Nechemiah 3:37), for they provoked before the builders, means to Radak that they provoked us to anger before the builders, so as to turn the builders' hearts away from building. Rabbi Yonah wrote that it is a matter of mockery and scorn, and Radak holds there is no need for that.

חמה.sense: חָם and חָמוֹת, a woman's father-in-law and mother-in-law; and חוֹמָה, a wall. Wrath, חֵמָה, he files under יָחַם, its root in his view.

more.t: הִנֵּה חָמִיךְ (Bereishis 38:13), behold your father-in-law, on the pattern of אָחִיךְ, your brother, from אָחָה; וְהִיא שָֽׁלְחָה אֶל־ חָמִיהָ (Bereishis 38:25), and she sent to her father-in-law; כַּלָּה בַּֽחֲמֹתָהּ (Michah 7:6), a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. The word standing alone, without a suffix, is not found, but it is חָם, father-in-law, and חָמוֹת, mother-in-law, as it is אָח and אָחוֹת, brother and sister.

The word is said only of a woman's in-laws, and חותן וחותנת, father-in-law and mother-in-law, only of a man's. In the Mishnah, though, Radak found it used of the man too, in האוכל אצל חמיו, האוכל אצל חמותו (Kesubos 12a), one who eats at his father-in-law's, one who eats at his mother-in-law's.

חוֹמָה הָיוּ עָלֵינוּ (Shmuel I 25:16), they were a wall to us; אֲנִי חוֹמָה (Shir HaShirim 8:10), I am a wall; עַד רֶדֶת חֹֽמֹתֶיךָ (Devarim 28:52), until your walls come down; וְקָרָאת יְשׁוּעָה חוֹמֹתַיִךְ (Yeshayahu 60:18), you shall call your walls Salvation. The sense is known.
חֵמָה אֵין לִי (Yeshayahu 27:4), I have no wrath, he will write at the root יָחַם, which in his view is its root.

חרה.sense: Anger, and being incensed. At root the matter is heat, since it is out of great heat that a man grows angry.

more.t: עַל־הָֽרֹעִים חָרָה אַפִּי (Zecharyah 10:3), my anger burned against the shepherds; וְחָרָה אַפִּי בוֹ (Devarim 31:17), my anger will burn against him; and the infinitive בַּֽחֲרוֹת אַפָּם בָּֽנוּ (Tehillim 124:3), when their anger burned against us.

more.h: A second infinitive, not a noun
more.t: הֱשִׁיבוֹתָ מֵֽחֲרוֹן אַפֶּֽךָ (Tehillim 85:4), you turned back from the burning of your anger, is a second infinitive and not a noun: were it a noun it would read מֵחָרוֹן with a kamatz under the ches, since it is not in construct, and אַפֶּֽךָ is what the verb acts on.

בְּנֵי אִמִּי נִֽחֲרוּ ־בִי (Shir HaShirim 1:6), my mother's sons were incensed against me; כֹּל הַנֶּחֱרִים בָּךְ (Yeshayahu 41:11), all who are incensed against you; אַל־ תִּתְחַר בַּמְּרֵעִים (Tehillim 37:1), do not be incensed at evildoers; אַל־ תִּתְחַר בְּמַצְלִיחַ דַּרְכּוֹ (Tehillim 37:7), do not be incensed at the man who prospers in his way.

תִּתְחַר is on the pattern of וְאַל־ תִּתְגָּר (Devarim 2:9), do not contend. It may be that its root is תחר or תחרה, with תִּתְחַר on the pattern תִּפְעַל, and Radak calls this correct because of its patach, since on the pattern of תִּתְגָּר it would carry a kamatz as that word does.

הֶֽחֱרָה הֶֽחֱזִיק (Nechemiah 3:20), he heated himself to strengthen himself in the work; וַיַּחַר עָלַי אַפּוֹ (Iyov 19:11), He kindled His anger against me. The sense of all of it is anger, and the root of the matter is heat, since it is out of great heat that a man grows angry.

כִּי חָרוֹן אֶל־כָּל־הֲמוֹנָֽהּ (Yechezkel 7:12), for burning anger is upon all her multitude; תְּשַׁלַּח חֲרֹנְךָ (Shemos 15:7), you send out your burning anger; and on another pattern מֶה חֳרִי הָאַף הַגָּדוֹל הַזֶּֽה (Devarim 29:24 in his edition), what is this great heat of anger.

זעם.sense: Loathing, wrath and anger, which is his sense for the verb and the noun זַעַם alike.

more.t: וְזָעַם עַל־בְּרִֽית־קוֹדֶשׁ (Daniel 11:30), he raged against the holy covenant; אֲשֶׁר זָעַמְתָּה זֶה שִׁבְעִים שָׁנָֽה (Zecharyah 1:12), against which You have been indignant these seventy years; יִזְעָמוּהוּ לְאֻמִּֽים (Mishlei 24:24), peoples will loathe him; וּלְכָה זֹֽעֲמָה יִשְׂרָאֵֽל (Bamidbar 23:7), and come, rage against Israel.
וְאֵיפַת רָזוֹן זְעוּמָֽה (Michah 6:10), a scant measure that is loathed; וּפָנִים נִזְעָמִים (Mishlei 25:23), a face full of rage.

זַעַם מִלֵּאתָֽנִי (Yirmiyahu 15:17), you have filled me with indignation; מִזַּעַם לְשׁוֹנָם (Hoshea 7:16), because of the rage of their tongue; שְׁפָךְ־עֲלֵיהֶם זַעְמֶךָ (Tehillim 69:25), pour out your indignation upon them.

זעף.sense: Wrath and anger: of a man's heart or face, of Hashem, and of a raging sea.

more.h: Anger in the heart and the face
more.t: וְעַל־י"י יִזְעַף לִבּֽוֹ (Mishlei 19:3), and his heart rages against Hashem; אֶת־פְּנֵיכֶם זֹֽעֲפִים (Daniel 1:10), your faces angry; וְהִנָּם זֹֽעֲפִֽים (Bereishis 40:6), and behold they were angry; and as an adjective, אֶל־בֵּיתוֹ סַר וְזָעֵף (Melachim I 21:4), to his house sullen and angry.

וּבְזַעְפּוֹ עִם־הַכֹּֽהֲנִים (Divrei HaYamim II 26:19), and in his raging with the kohanim, which he counts an infinitive. The noun is זַעַף י"י אֶשָּׂא (Michah 7:9), I will bear the wrath of Hashem, and וַיַּֽעֲמֹד הַיָּם מִזַּעְפּֽוֹ (Yonah 1:15), and the sea stood still from its rage.

קצף.sense: To be wroth, its sense a boiling in anger; from this it is said of water boiling up in a strong wind, which some explain instead as the bark of a tree.

more.t: וְעַל כָּל־הָֽעֵדָה יִקְצֹף (Vayikra 10:6), and He will be wroth with the whole congregation; הַסְתֵּר וְאֶקְצֹף (Yeshayahu 57:17), hiding, I was wroth; וְהָיָה כִֽי־יִרְעַב וְהִתְקַצַּף (Yeshayahu 8:21), and when he is hungry he will fall into a rage; וּבְחֹרֵב הִקְצַפְתֶּם (Devarim 9:8), at Chorev you stirred up wrath; מַקְצִפִים הֱיִיתֶם (Devarim 9:22), you were stirring up wrath. Its sense is a boiling in anger.

כִּֽי־יָצָא הַקֶּצֶף (Bamidbar 17:11), for the wrath has gone out; עַל־אֲבֽוֹתֵיכֶם קָֽצֶף (Zecharyah 1:2), wrath against your fathers; כִּי בְקִצְפִּי הִכִּיתִיךְ (Yeshayahu 60:10), in my wrath I struck you; מִקִּצְפּוֹ תִּרְעַשׁ הָאָרֶץ (Yirmiyahu 10:10), at his wrath the earth quakes; אַל־ בְּקֶצְפְּךָ תוֹכִיחֵנִי (Tehillim 38:2), do not rebuke me in your wrath.

From this it is said of the boiling of water in the force of the wind: כְּקֶצֶף עַל־פְּנֵי־מָֽיִם (Hoshea 10:7), like a boiling up on the face of the water. So Targum Yonasan renders it, כְּרוּתְחָא עַל אַפֵּי מַיָא, like a boiling on the face of the water.

Some explain it as the bark of a tree, and likewise וּתְאֵנָתִי לִקְצָפָה (Yoel 1:7), and my fig tree for stripping, that is, it was peeled from its great dryness, as it says there, חָשׂף חֲשָׂפָהּ, he has stripped it bare. Radak adds that וּתְאֵנָתִי לִקְצָפָה can also be taken in the first sense, that is, for a curse.

עשׁן.sense: Smoke, and to smoke. Since anger and wrath are heat, and are figured as fire, they are figured as smoke as well.

more.t: וְהַר סִינַי עָשַׁן כֻּלּוֹ (Shemos 19:18), and Mount Sinai smoked, all of it: עָשַׁן is a past verb, since half of it is kamatz and half patach; גַּע בֶּהָרִים וְֽיֶעֱשָֽׁנוּ (Tehillim 144:5), touch the mountains and they will smoke; and as a description וְאֶת־הָהָר עָשֵׁן (Shemos 20:15), and the mountain smoking, and הָֽאוּדִים הָֽעֲשֵׁנִים (Yeshayahu 7:4), the smoking firebrands.

תַנּוּר עָשָׁן (Bereishis 15:17), an oven of smoke, though it may be a description, a smoking oven; כֶּעָשָׁן נִמְלָחוּ (Yeshayahu 51:6), like smoke they vanish; וְהִבְעַרְתִּי בֶֽעָשָׁן רִכְבָּהּ (Nachum 2:14), I will burn her chariots in smoke, that is, in a great fire whose smoke is seen from afar. In construct וְהִנֵּה עָלָה עֲשַׁן הָעִיר (Yehoshua 8:20), and behold the smoke of the city went up, and on another pattern כְּעֶשֶׁן הַכִּבְשָׁן (Shemos 19:18), like the smoke of the furnace.

Since anger and fury are heat, Scripture calls them fire, כִּי־אֵשׁ קָֽדְחָה בְאַפִּי (Devarim 32:22), for a fire has kindled in My anger, and calls them smoke too: עַד־מָתַי עָשַׁנְתָּ בִּתְפִלַּת עַמֶּֽךָ (Tehillim 80:5), how long have You smoked against the prayer of Your people; יֶעְשַׁן אַפְּךָ בְּצֹאן מַרְעִיתֶֽךָ (Tehillim 74:1), will Your anger smoke against the flock of Your pasture; עָלָה עָשָׁן בְּאַפּוֹ (Shmuel II 22:9), smoke went up in His nostrils; יֶעְשַׁן אַף־י"י וְקִנְאָתוֹ (Devarim 29:19), the anger of Hashem and His jealousy will smoke.

נאץ.sense: To loathe and spurn; the heavy form comes close to provoking anger, and all the forms are near one another in sense.

more.t: וְתוֹכַחַת נָאַץ לִבִּֽי (Mishlei 5:12), my heart spurned reproof; נָֽאֲצוּ כָּל־תּֽוֹכַחְתִּֽי (Mishlei 1:30), they spurned all my reproof; וַֽעֲצַת עֶלְיוֹן נָאָֽצוּ (Tehillim 107:11), they spurned the counsel of the Most High; וַיִנְאַץ בְּזַֽעַם־אַפּוֹ (Eichah 2:6), and He spurned in the rage of His anger.

נִאֵץ י"י (Tehillim 10:3), he spurns Hashem; נִֽאֲצוּ הָֽאֲנָשִׁים הָאֵלֶּה (Bamidbar 16:30), these men spurned; וְאֵת אִמְרַת קְדֽוֹשׁ־יִשְׂרָאֵל נִאֵֽצוּ (Yeshayahu 5:24), and they spurned the word of the Holy One of Israel; וְנִאֲצוּנִי וְהֵפֵר אֶת־בְּרִיתִֽי (Devarim 31:20), and they will spurn Me and break My covenant; עַד־אָנָה יְנַֽאֲצֻנִי (Bamidbar 14:11), how long will they spurn Me; וְכָֽל־ מְנַֽאֲצַי לֹא יִרְאֽוּהָ (Bamidbar 14:23), and none who spurn Me will see it; אֶפֶס כִּֽי־ נִאֵץ נִאַצְתָּ (Shmuel II 12:14), only because you have utterly spurned, where the first נאץ is an infinitive.

וְתָמִיד כָּל־הַיּוֹם שְׁמִי מִנֹּאָֽץ (Yeshayahu 52:5), and continually all the day My name is spurned, is a reflexive whose form by rule would be מִתְנָאֵץ, or else a form compounded with the passive, as he set out in the section on grammar, in the chapter on the verbs.

יוֹם־צָרָה וְתוֹכֵחָה וּנְאָצָה (Yeshayahu 37:3), a day of trouble and rebuke and contempt; and on another pattern וַֽיַּֽעֲשׂוּ נֶאָצוֹת גְּדֹלֽוֹת (Nechemiah 9:18), and they committed great acts of contempt, and שָׁמַעְתִּי אֶת־כָּל־ נָאָצוֹתֶיךָ (Yechezkel 35:12), I have heard all your words of contempt.
The sense of all of them is loathing, מיאוס, and those of the heavy form are close to provoking anger; all of them are near one another in sense.

רעם.sense: Two senses: rage in the face; and thundering, of the sea and from heaven, with the noun, thunder, whose sense he likens to a loud shaking.

more.t: רָֽעֲמוּ פָּנִֽים (Yechezkel 27:35), faces were enraged; and in the heavy form בַּֽעֲבוּר הַרְּעִמָהּ (Shmuel I 1:6), so as to enrage her, where the dagesh in the resh is like the dagesh in מִקְּדָשׁ (Shemos 15:17), the Sanctuary. The sense of these is rage in the face.

In another sense, יִרְעַם הַיָּם וּמְלֹאוֹ (Tehillim 98:7), let the sea thunder and its fullness; and in the heavy form אֵֽל־הַכָּבוֹד הִרְעִים (Tehillim 29:3), the God of glory thundered; יַרְעֵם מִן־שָׁמַיִם (Shmuel II 22:14), He thundered from heaven; וּבְקוֹל כָּמֹהוּ תַרְעֵֽם (Iyov 40:9), and can you thunder with a voice like His.

וְרַעַם גְּבוּרֹתָו (Iyov 26:14), and the thunder of His might; רַעַם שָׂרִים וּתְרוּעָֽה (Iyov 39:25), the thunder of captains and the shouting; הֲתַלְבִּישׁ צַוָּארוֹ רַעְמָֽה (Iyov 39:19), do you clothe his neck with thunder. Their sense is like that of a loud shaking.

שׁצף.sense: A little: בְּשֶׁצֶף קֶצֶף (Yeshayahu 54:8), in a little wrath, as he reads it from its place.

more.t: בְּשֶׁצֶף קֶצֶף (Yeshayahu 54:8): by its place, he says, its sense is with a little wrath, as the pasuk before says, בְּרֶגַע קָטֹן עֲזַבְתִּיךְ (Yeshayahu 54:7), for a small moment I forsook you.

אפע.sense: אֶפְעֶה, a kind of snake, said to be the female of the saraf; and מֵאָפַע in one pasuk (Yeshayahu 41:24), which he reads as from nothing.

more.t: וּפָֽעָלְכֶם מֵאָפַע (Yeshayahu 41:24), and your work is of nothing: he glosses מֵאָפַע as מאין, from nothing.

more.h: His father: a samech turned ayin
more.t: His father explained מֵאָפַע as מֵאֶפֶס, from nothing at all, the samech exchanged for an ayin.
His brother Rabbi Moshe explained it from the sense of אֶפְעֶה, the snake; on that reading, you are nothing, and your work is the work of snakes, which harm those who cling to them.

תִּבָּקַע אֶפְעֶה (Yeshayahu 59:5), an efeh breaks out; אֶפְעֶה וְשָׂרָף מְעוֹפֵף (Yeshayahu 30:6), efeh and flying saraf; תַּֽהַרְגֵהוּ לְשׁוֹן אֶפְעֶֽה (Iyov 20:16), an efeh's tongue shall slay him. It is a kind of snake. They say it is the female of the saraf, short and thick, and its venom harsher than the male's.

פתן.sense: The evil snakes; and the מִפְתָּן, the lower threshold that is trodden on.

more.t: עַל־חֻר פָּתֶן (Yeshayahu 11:8), "over the hole of a pesen"; מְרוֹרַת פְּתָנִים בְּקִרְבּוֹ (Iyov 20:14), "the gall of pesanim within him"; רֹאשׁ־פְּתָנִים יִינָק (Iyov 20:16), "he sucks the poison of pesanim". They are the evil snakes.
פֶתֶן חֵרֵשׁ (Tehillim 58:5), "a deaf pesen", is said for the greatness of its evil: that is, there is no charm for it.

כְּרֻתוֹת אֶל־הַמִּפְתָּן (Shmuel I 5:4), "cut off at the threshold"; מִתַּחַת מִפְתַּן הַבַּיִת קָדִימָה (Yechezkel 47:1), "from under the threshold of the house eastward". It is the lower threshold that is trodden on, and so the Targum says, סְקוֹפָא, the threshold.

שׁפף.sense: One line: שְׁפִיפֹן עֲלֵי־אֹרַח (Bereishis 49:17), a shefifon on the path, with no meaning given, only the word's form.

more.t: He says of שְׁפִיפֹן only that it follows the pattern of ישימון, wasteland. What it is, his entry does not say.

זחל.sense: Fear, at Iyov 32:6, as its place requires, where Rabbi Yonah reads holding back; in another sense, creeping on the belly, with Chazal's like word for flowing liquids.

more.t: עַל־כֵּן זָחַלְתִּי וָֽאִירָא (Iyov 32:6), "therefore I was afraid and feared". By what its place requires, he glosses זָחַלְתִּי as "I was afraid".
Rabbi Yonah explained זָחַלְתִּי as "I held back", comparing the Arabic.

זֹֽחֲלֵי עָפָֽר (Devarim 32:24), "creepers of the dust"; כְּזֹֽחֲלֵי אֶרֶץ (Michah 7:17), "like creepers of the earth". They are the swarming creatures that drag and move along the ground on their bellies.

Similar to it is what Chazal said of flowing liquids, זוחלים (Mikvaos 5:5); and from this, in his view, אֶבֶן הַזֹּחֶלֶת (Melachim I 1:9), the stone Zocheles, is so called because the water would flow and run beside it, as the pasuk says, אֲשֶֽׁר־אֵצֶל עֵין רֹגֵל, which is beside Ein Rogel.

Rabbeinu Shlomo explained אֶבֶן הַזֹּחֶלֶת as a great stone the young men would test their strength on, to shift it and drag it. Yonasan rendered it אֶבֶן סְכוּתָא, a stone of looking out, one they stand on to watch into the distance.

רעד.sense: To tremble, and the noun, trembling; the sense, he says, is known.

more.t: הַמַּבִּיט לָאָרֶץ וַתִּרְעָד (Tehillim 104:32), "He looks at the earth and it trembles".
יֹֽאחֲזֵמוֹ רָעַד (Shemos 15:15), "trembling seizes them"; and with the feminine heh, רְעָדָה אֲחָזָתַם שָׁם (Tehillim 48:7), "trembling took hold of them there".
The heavy form here is intransitive: עָמַדְתִּי מַרְעִֽיד (Daniel 10:11), "I stood trembling"; מַרְעִידִים עַל־הַדָּבָר (Ezra 10:9), "trembling over the matter".

רתת.sense: Trembling: the Targum renders רָעַד, trembling, with רְתֵיתָא. At Hoshea 13:1, when Yeravam of Efrayim spoke of the calves, a great trembling was raised in Israel.

more.t: The Targum renders יֹֽאחֲזֵמוֹ רָעַד (Shemos 15:15), trembling seizes them, with אַחֲדָתְנוּן רְתֵיתָא, trembling seized them.
כְּדַבֵּר אֶפְרַיִם רְתֵת (Hoshea 13:1), when Efrayim spoke, trembling: he explains it as, when Yeravam, who was of Efrayim, spoke the matter of the calves, a great trembling was raised in Israel.

רעשׁ.sense: Movement and trembling: earth, the fish of the sea, and walls quake, nations are made to quake, and רַעַשׁ is a quaking; יִרְעַשׁ in Tehillim 72:16 is read three ways.

more.h: Earth, the fish of the sea, and walls
more.t: וְרָֽעֲשׁוּ מִפָּנַי דְּגֵי הַיָּם (Yechezkel 38:20), "the fish of the sea quake before Me"; תִּרְעַשְׁנָה חֽוֹמוֹתַיִךְ (Yechezkel 26:10), "your walls shall shake"; וַתִּרְעַשׁ הָאָרֶץ (Yirmiyahu 51:29), "and the earth quaked".
הִרְעַשְׁתִּי גוֹיִם (Yechezkel 31:16), "I made nations quake"; מַרְעִישׁ מַמְלָכֽוֹת (Yeshayahu 14:16), "who shook kingdoms".

רַעַשׁ גָּדוֹל (Yechezkel 3:12), "a great quaking"; לַחְמְךָ בְּרַעַשׁ תֹּאכֵל (Yechezkel 12:18), "you shall eat your bread in trembling". Their sense is movement and trembling, and he gives a word for it in the foreign tongue.
יִרְעַשׁ כַּלְּבָנוֹן פִּרְיוֹ (Tehillim 72:16), "his fruit shall shake like Levanon". They said it is as though יעשר reversed, that it grow rich.

Rabbi Yonah explained יִרְעַשׁ as "it will be fruitful and multiply", likening it to the Arabic word said of blessing and fruitfulness. On this reading פִּרְיוֹ, "his fruit", is his sons; that is, his sons will multiply as the trees of Levanon are many.
Rabbi Avraham Ibn Ezra explained it as it stands: this fruit, which is the grain, shall shake; the sense being that it will grow so great that it shakes the trees of Levanon.

געשׁ.sense: Tossing and movement, which he gives as the sense of all of it: the earth that tossed, rivers whose waters toss, a people tossed, men who drink and toss about.

more.t: וַתִּגְעַשׁ וַתִּרְעַשׁ הָאָרֶץ (Tehillim 18:8), "the earth tossed and quaked", and the like in the reflexive at Shmuel II 22:8.
כַּנְּהָרֹות יִתְגָּֽעֲשׁוּ מֵימָֽיו (Yirmiyahu 46:7), "his waters toss like the rivers"; וְכַנְּהָרֹות יִתְגֹּעֲשׁוּ מָיִם (Yirmiyahu 46:8), "and like the rivers the waters toss".
וְשָׁתוּ וְהִתְגֹּֽעֲשׁוּ וְהִתְהֹלָלוּ (Yirmiyahu 25:16), "they shall drink and toss about and act madly". The sense of them all is tossing and movement.
In the form whose doer is not named, יְגֹֽעֲשׁוּ עָם וְיַֽעֲבֹרוּ (Iyov 34:20), "a people are tossed and pass on".

חרד.sense: Trembling: fear with movement of the body, for when sudden fear comes a man's whole body moves; and in some pesukim, movement with no fear in it.

more.t: וְחָרַד וּפָחַד (Yeshayahu 19:16), "he shall tremble and fear"; וַיֶּֽחֱרַד יִצְחָק (Bereishis 27:33), "Yitzchak trembled". Their sense is fear together with movement of the body: when sudden fear comes upon a man, his whole body moves.

מִֽי־יָרֵא וְחָרֵד (Shoftim 7:3), "who is afraid and trembling"; לִבּוֹ חָרֵד עַל אֲרוֹן הָאֱלֹהִים (Shmuel I 4:13), "his heart trembled for the Aron of Hashem"; הַֽחֲרֵדִים אֶל־דְּבָרוֹ (Yeshayahu 66:5), "those who tremble at His word".

חֲרָדָה גְּדֹלָה (Bereishis 27:33), "a great trembling"; וַתְּהִי לְחֶרְדַּת אֱלֹהִֽים (Shmuel I 14:15), "and it became a trembling of God", which he takes to mean a great trembling, having set out the like of it at the root אפל; חֶרְדַּת אָדָם יִתֵּן מוֹקֵשׁ (Mishlei 29:25), "the fear of man lays a snare"; and the plural, חֲרָדוֹת יִלְבָּשׁוּ (Yechezkel 26:16), "they will clothe themselves in tremblings".
וְכָל־הַֽמַּֽחֲנֶה הֶֽחֱרִֽיד (Shoftim 8:12), "he made all the camp tremble"; לְהַֽחֲרִיד אֶת־כּוּשׁ בֶּטַח (Yechezkel 30:9), "to make Kush tremble", Kush that had been secure.

חָרַדְתְּ אֵלֵינוּ אֶת־כָּל־הַֽחֲרָדָה הַזֹּאת (Melachim II 4:13), you have moved for us with all this movement: that is, you bestirred yourself on our account, moved your vessels from place to place and cleared a place for us. So too וַיֶּֽחֶרְדוּ זִקְנֵי הָעִיר לִקְרָאתוֹ (Shmuel I 16:4), "the elders of the city moved to meet him", and יֶֽחֶרְדוּ כְצִפּוֹר מִמִּצְרַיִם (Hoshea 11:11), "they will move like a bird from Mitzrayim"; he glosses these ינועו, they move. So too וְכָל־הָעָם חָֽרְדוּ אַֽחֲרָֽיו (Shmuel I 13:7), "and all the people moved after him", is of movement.
The forms יֶחֶרְדוּ of the movement sense all carry a segol under the ches, but יֶֽחְרְדוּ הָֽאִיִּן (Yechezkel 26:18), "the isles tremble", has a sheva.

ארה.sense: To gather; feeding troughs for beasts; and the lion, אַרְיֵה, which joined to אֵל, force, gives אֲרִיאֵל, a name for the mizbeach and for great warriors.

more.t: וְאָרוּהָ כָּל־עֹבְרֵי דָֽרֶךְ (Tehillim 80:13), and all who pass along the way have gathered her, and אָרִיתִי מוֹרִי (Shir HaShirim 5:1), I have gathered my myrrh: the sense is לקטוה, they gathered her, and לקטתי, I gathered. Some explain נָשִׁים בָּאוֹת מְאִירוֹת אוֹתָהּ (Yeshayahu 27:11), women come and gather it, from this sense, though the word is of another root. On that reading, when the boughs break the women come and gather it, since it is not the way of women to climb the tree to gather; and he has already explained the pasuk at the root אור.

וְאֻֽרָוֹת לְכָל־בְּהֵמָה וּבְהֵמָה (Divrei HaYamim II 32:28), troughs for every kind of beast; in construct, אֻרְוֹת סוּסִים (Melachim I 5:6), troughs for horses; with a yud in place of the last root letter, אֻרְיוֹת סוּסִים (Divrei HaYamim II 9:25), troughs for horses. Their sense is feeding troughs, and the Targum of אֵבוּס בְּעָלָיו (Yeshayahu 1:3), his master's trough, is אוֹרְיָא דִמְרוֹהִי, the same in Aramaic.

אַרְיֵה שָׁאָג (Amos 3:8), a lion has roared; without the heh, וְכַֽאֲרִי יִתְנַשָּׂא (Bamidbar 23:24), and like a lion he lifts himself up; the plural אֲרָיוֹת (Melachim I 10:19) and, in masculine form, אֲרָיִים (Melachim I 10:20), both lions. Of the word itself he says only that it is known.
אֶת־אַרְגֹּב וְאֶת־הָאַרְיֵה (Melachim II 15:25) are the names of two warriors who came with Pekach and helped him strike the king, and fifty men of the Giladim came with him besides.

ארי, the lion, joined to the word אל gives אֲרִיאֵל, the name of the mizbeach, and Yerushalayim was called by it for the mizbeach in her. הוֹי אֲרִיאֵל אֲרִיאֵל קִרְיַת חָנָה דָוִד (Yeshayahu 29:1), "woe, Ariel, Ariel, the city where David encamped": as blood is thrown on the mizbeach, so the whole city will be full of blood of those killed in her markets and streets, which is וְהָיְתָה לִּי כַּֽאֲרִיאֵֽל (Yeshayahu 29:2), "she shall be to Me like an Ariel".

more.h: Why he thinks it is so called
more.t: It seems to him that the mizbeach is called so for what Chazal said (Yoma 21b), that the holy fire which came down from heaven crouched upon it like a lion. Chazal said too (Middos 4:7) that the Heichal is narrow behind and wide in front and so resembles a lion, as it says הוֹי אֲרִיאֵל אֲרִיאֵל, woe, Ariel, Ariel: as the lion is narrow behind and wide in front, so is the Heichal.

הוּא הִכָּה אֵת שְׁנֵי אֲרִיאֵל מוֹאָב (Shmuel II 23:20), "he struck the two Ariels of Moav", meaning the two great warriors of Moav; so the Targum renders תְּרֵין רַבְרְבֵי מוֹאָב, the two great ones of Moav. The great and mighty are called so because the lion is great and mighty and strong among beasts, and אֵל is a term of force and strength, as יֶשׁ־לְאֵל יָדִי (Bereishis 31:29), "it is in the power of my hand"; which is why the word is compounded of ארי and אל. With the alef turned to a heh and the yud dropped, the pasuk says of the mizbeach וְהַֽהַרְאֵל אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת (Yechezkel 43:15), and the Harel, four amos.

לבא.sense: לָבִיא, the lion; its feminine is לְבִיָּא, the lioness, and its plurals are לְבָאִם, lions, and לְלִבְאֹתָיו, for his lionesses.

more.t: כְּלָבִיא שָׁכֵן (Devarim 33:20), "he dwells like a lavi". It is the lion.
מָה אִמְּךָ לְבִיָּא (Yechezkel 19:2), "what is your mother, a lioness". Its proper form is לְבִיאָה, the yud standing in place of the alef and the alef in place of the heh.

נַפְשִׁי בְּתוֹךְ לְבָאִם (Tehillim 57:5), "my soul is among lions"; the correct form is לְבִיאִים, as נָבִיא, prophet, gives נְבִיאִים, prophets. The feminine plural is וּמְחַנֵּק לְלִבְאֹתָיו (Nachum 2:13), "and strangling for his lionesses".

לישׁ.sense: The great lion. His whole entry is two pesukim and that gloss.

more.t: לַיִשׁ אֹבֵד מִבְּלִי־טָרֶף (Iyov 4:11), "the layish perishes for lack of prey"; לָבִיא וָלַיִשׁ (Yeshayahu 30:6), "lion and layish". It is the great lion.

שׁחל.sense: The lion; and under the same letters שְׁחֵלֶת, the spice the language of the Mishnah calls צפורן, a fingernail.

more.t: עַל־שַׁחַל וָפֶתֶן תִּדְרֹךְ (Tehillim 91:13), "you shall tread on shachal and pesen"; וָאֱהִי לָהֶם כְּמוֹ־שָׁחַל (Hoshea 13:7), "I was to them like a shachal". It is the lion.

נָטָף וּשְׁחֵלֶת (Shemos 30:34), "nataf and shecheles". It is the spice called in the language of the Mishnah צפורן, a fingernail (Kerisos 6a), being smooth and glossy like a nail; and so the Targum says, וְטוּפְרָא, and nail.

שׁחץ.sense: Pride: בְּנֵי־שָׁחַץ, the sons of pride; and in Chazal, by his gloss, men of pride and coarseness of spirit. His entry under these letters says nothing of a beast.

more.t: הוּא מֶלֶךְ עַל־כָּל־בְּנֵי־שָׁחַץ (Iyov 41:26), he is king over all the sons of pride; לֹא־הִדְרִיכֻוהוּ בְנֵי־שָׁחַץ (Iyov 28:8), the sons of pride have not trodden it. The sense is ענין גאוה, pride.

more.h: Chazal use it the same way
more.t: Chazal too said (Shabbos 62b) that the people of Yerushalayim were אנשי שחץ. That they are men of pride and coarseness of spirit is his own gloss on their words.

גור.sense: To dwell, with גֵּר the one who comes to dwell; other senses are to fear, and to gather, with מְגוּרָה the granary; and גּוּר is the young of beasts while small.

more.t: גּוּר אַרְיֵה יְהוּדָה (Bereishis 49:9), "Yehudah is a lion's cub"; בְּתוֹךְ כְּפִרִים רִבְּתָה גוּרֶֽיהָ (Yechezkel 19:2), "among young lions she raised her cubs"; הֵינִיקוּ גּוּרֵיהֶן (Eichah 4:3), "they nursed their cubs"; with a cholam, כְּגוֹרֵי אֲרָיֹֽות (Yirmiyahu 51:38), "like lions' cubs"; and for the females, בְּדֵי גֹֽרוֹתָי (Nachum 2:13), "enough for his female cubs". The young of beasts while still small are called גורים.

וְגָר זְאֵב עִם־כֶּבֶשׂ (Yeshayahu 11:6), "the wolf shall dwell with the lamb"; עִם־לָבָן גַּרְתִּי (Bereishis 32:5), "I have dwelt with Lavan"; מִי־ יָגוּר בְּאָהֳלֶךָ (Tehillim 15:1), "who shall dwell in Your tent"; and אֲשֶׁר־אֲנִי מִתְגּוֹרֵר עִמָּהּ (Melachim I 17:20), "with whom I dwell", ענין דירה, dwelling. גָּרִים יֹאכֵֽלוּ (Yeshayahu 5:17) is "those who come to dwell there shall eat", and may also be read as כרים, lambs.

לַגֵּר אֲשֶׁר־בִּשְׁעָרֶיךָ (Devarim 14:21), "to the ger who is in your gates", is the foreigner living in Eretz Yisrael who took upon himself not to serve avodah zarah; so too וְנִמְכַּר לְגֵר תּוֹשָׁב (Vayikra 25:47), "and he is sold to a resident ger", and so every ger the Torah names as living in Eretz Yisrael. One who converted outright is the ger whom the Torah charges with the mitzvos, as הָֽאֶזְרָח וְהַגֵּר (Vayikra 16:29), "the native and the ger".

לֹא תָגוּרוּ מִפְּנֵי־אִישׁ (Devarim 1:17), "do not fear any man"; גּוּרוּ לָכֶם מִפְּנֵי־חֶרֶב (Iyov 19:29), "fear the sword for yourselves". The nouns are כִּי אִם־ מָגוֹר מִסָּבִֽיב (Yirmiyahu 20:10 in his edition), "but fear all around", and מְגוֹרַת רָשָׁע הִיא תְבוֹאֶנּוּ (Mishlei 10:24), "what the wicked fears shall come upon him"; they are ענין פחד, fear. מְגוּרֵי אֶל־חֶרֶב הָיוּ אֶת־עַמִּי (Yechezkel 21:17) means the fears of the sword were upon My people. לוּלֵי כַּעַס אוֹיֵב אָגוּר (Devarim 32:27), "were it not that I feared the enemy's anger", is in this sense too, though the translator took the word from אָֽגְרָה בַקָּצִיר (Mishlei 6:8), "she gathers in the harvest".

יָגוּרוּ עָלַי עַזִים (Tehillim 59:4), "the strong gather against me"; עַל־דָּגָן וְתִירוֹשׁ יִתְגּוֹרָרוּ (Hoshea 7:14), "over grain and wine they gather themselves"; ענין אסיפה וקבוץ, gathering and assembling. מִי־גָר אִתָּךְ (Yeshayahu 54:15) is who will gather with you to fight, said of Gog and Magog, of whom it says עָלַיִךְ יִפּֽוֹל, "he shall fall upon you", and elsewhere עַל־הָרֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל תִּפּוֹל (Yechezkel 39:4), "you shall fall on the mountains of Israel".

הַעוֹד הַזֶּרַע בַּמְּגוּרָה (Chaggai 2:19), "is the seed still in the granary", and with two mems נֶֽהֶרְסוּ מַמְּגֻרוֹת (Yoel 1:17), "the granaries are broken down". They are the place where the grain is gathered. His father wrote that the first mem is a servile letter, and that is why the second is doubled, with a pasach in place of a chirik, as לְמַבָּרִֽאשׁוֹנָה (Divrei HaYamim I 15:13), "because at the first".

more.h: Is there seed left in the granary
more.t: הַעוֹד הַזֶּרַע בַּמְּגוּרָה (Chaggai 2:19) is a question: have you seed left in the granary to lean on? You have only what is sown in the ground, and so you need His blessing; once they began building the Bayis they knew His blessing at once, in what was sown and in the fruit of the tree. Rabbeinu Shlomo explained that they had not yet sown that year, the seed being still in the granary and the trees not yet setting their fruit, and from now they would sow in a time of blessing, for building the Bayis brings blessing on the work of their hands.

סַעַר מִתְגּוֹרֵר (Yirmiyahu 30:23) may be read from this sense of gathering, and so Targum Yonasan renders עִלְעוּל מִתְכְּנַשׁ, a storm gathering itself; the Mesorah says of the word that it occurs twice in two senses.

שֹמח.sense: Joy: to rejoice, to gladden another, one who is glad, and שִׂמְחָה, joy; and by way of borrowing, increase.

more.t: שָׂמַח מִצְרַיִם בְּצֵאתָם (Tehillim 105:38), "Mitzrayim rejoiced when they went out"; לָכֵן שָׂמַח לִבִּי (Tehillim 16:9), "therefore my heart rejoiced"; and on another pattern, יָרוּן וְשָׂמֵֽחַ (Mishlei 29:6), "he sings and rejoices".

more.h: A command that is a threat
more.t: שְׂמַח בָּחוּר בְּיַלְדוּתֶיךָ (Koheles 11:9), "rejoice, young man, in your youth", is spoken as a threat: rejoice, young man, and you will see what befalls you at your end. So too בֹּאוּ בֵֽית־אֵל וּפִשְׁעוּ (Amos 4:4), "come to Beis El and rebel", and אִישׁ גִּלּוּלָיו לְכוּ עֲבֹדוּ (Yechezkel 20:39), "go, serve each man his idols".

וְהָיִיתָ אַךְ שָׂמֵֽחַ (Devarim 16:15), "and you shall be only joyful". In the construct it changes, שִׂמְחֵי־לֵֽב (Yeshayahu 24:7), "the glad of heart", and does not change in שְׂמֵחֵי רָעָתִי (Tehillim 35:26), "those glad at my hurt".

כִּֽי־בְשִׂמְחָה תֵצֵאוּ (Yeshayahu 55:12), "for you shall go out with joy"; וְשִׁבַּחְתִּֽי אֲנִי אֶת־הַשִּׂמְחָה (Koheles 8:15), "and I praised joy"; וּבְיוֹם שִׂמְחַתְכֶם (Bamidbar 10:10), "and on the day of your rejoicing".

אֽוֹר־צַדִּיקִים יִשְׂמָח (Mishlei 13:9), "the light of the righteous rejoices", is said by way of borrowing, and its sense is increase. In this sense Chazal (Sukkah 7a) call the larger handbreadth a laughing one, and its opposite a sad handbreadth.

שַׂמֵּחַ שִׂמֳּחָֽהוּ (Yirmiyahu 20:15), "he gladdened him greatly"; חֲכַם בְּנִי וְשַׂמַּח לִבִּי (Mishlei 27:11), "be wise, my son, and gladden my heart"; and in the other causative, הִשְׂמַחְתָּ כָּל־אוֹיְבָֽיו (Tehillim 89:43), "You gladdened all his enemies".

Rabbi Yonah took וְשִׁבַּחְתִּֽי אֲנִי אֶת־הַשִּׂמְחָה (Koheles 8:15), "and I praised joy", in another sense, that it means contentment. Radak holds there is no need for that, though it is true that one who rejoices in his portion is the one content with what he has: the pasuk says that a man should rejoice in what he has, and eat and drink and let his soul see good in his labour.
